question_text: In a 65-kg adult male recovering from shock, the maintenance fluid rate is calculated using the standard formula recommended for adults weighing more than 40 kg. Based on this rule, what should be his maintenance fluid rate?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • According to the provided guideline, adult maintenance fluid rate is calculated as: weight in kilograms + 40.
  • For a 65-kg patient, maintenance fluid would be 65 + 40=105 ml/hour. This is the safest and most accurate maintenance rate for an adult of this weight after stabilization from shock.

question_text: Which among the following is not true of gompertzian growth?
option_a: The majority of the growth of a tumour occurs before it is clinically detectable
option_b: The doubling time of a tumor increases linearly.
option_c: Tumors are most sensitive to chemotherapy drugs during phase of active growth.
explanation:
The doubling time of a tumor increases exponentially in the initial stages. This is called Gompertzian growth. As the tumor grows, growth rate slows to due to difficulties with nutrition and oxygenation.

THE IMPLICATIONS OF GOMPERTZIAN GROWTH -

  • The majority of the growth of a tumour occurs before it is clinically detectable.
  • By the time they are detected, tumours have passed the period of most rapid growth, that period when they might be most sensitive to anti-proliferative drugs.
  • There has been plenty of time, before diagnosis, for individual cells to detach, invade, implant, and form distant metastases. In many patients cancer may, at the time of presentation, be a systemic disease
  • Early tumours are genetically old, yielding many opportunities for mutations to occur, mutations that might confer spontaneous drug resistance (a probability greatly increased by the existence of cell loss).
  • The rate of regression of a tumour will depend upon its age. According to the Norton-Simon hypothesis, chemotherapy results in a rate of regression in tumour volume that is proportional to the rate of growth for an unperturbed tumour of that size.

Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 12, pg: 201

question_text: Early management of shock focuses on restoring circulating volume, maintaining perfusion and using appropriate fluids. Several principles guide initial resuscitation. One of the following statements is false. Identify the incorrect statement.
option_a: First line therapy is putting a short wide bore intravenous cannula and start infusion
option_b: Albumin should not be the start in immediate period
option_c: Ringer lactate is most physiological fluid and ideal crystalloid
option_d: It is ideal to give inotropic agents regardless of preload to heart
explanation:
Explanation:

Inotropic agents should never be started without ensuring adequate preload. In shock, the first step is to restore circulating volume with crystalloids. Starting inotropes before correcting hypovolemia can worsen ischemia, increase oxygen demand and cause arrhythmias.

Principles of fluid therapy in shock:

  • The first step is to gain rapid venous access with a short, wide-bore cannula and begin crystalloid infusion. (Option A)
  • Ringer lactate is considered the most physiological crystalloid solution due to its electrolyte composition. (Option C)
  • Colloids (like albumin) are not recommended in the immediate resuscitation period because crystalloids are faster, safer and more accessible. (Option B)
  • Inotropes are only considered after adequate fluid resuscitation if hypotension persists. (Option D)

question_text: A young adult with gastric outlet obstruction presents with vomiting. Which of the following fluids is preferred in this patient for initial resuscitation?
explanation:
Explanation:

Gastric outlet obstruction leads to persistent vomiting, resulting in loss of gastric acid (HCl) and subsequent hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis. Normal saline (0.9% NaCl) is the crystalloid of choice for initial resuscitation. Its high chloride content helps correct the hypochloremia, and the volume expansion promotes bicarbonate excretion in the urine, aiding in the correction of the metabolic alkalosis. It effectively restores intravascular volume without exacerbating electrolyte imbalances.

Explanation of other options:

Ringer lactate (Option B): Ringer's lactate contains lactate, which is metabolized to bicarbonate in the liver. This would worsen the pre-existing metabolic alkalosis.

5% dextrose in water and 20% dextrose in water (Options C and D): These are hypotonic and hypertonic solutions, respectively. They do not contain the necessary chloride to correct the underlying electrolyte deficit and can cause fluid shifts that worsen hyponatremia and volume status.

Key Takeaways:

  • The fluid deficit in gastric outlet obstruction is hypochloremic and hypokalemic.
  • Normal saline is the initial fluid of choice to correct the chloride deficit and volume depletion.

question_text: How does the graft get nutrition on day 3?
explanation:
Explanation:

On day 3, the skin graft primarily derives its nutrition through imbibition, a passive diffusion process from the recipient bed.

  • The "take" of a skin graft; meaning its survival and integration into the recipient bed occurs in three phases:
    • Imbibition (Day 0-3):
      • During the first 48-72 hours, the graft is avascular and survives by diffusion of nutrients, oxygen, and plasma from the recipient bed.
      • This process is passive and does not require vascular connections.
      • The graft appears pale and edematous during this stage.
    • Inosculation (Day 3-5): (Option B ruled out)
      • Capillaries from the graft align and connect with those from the recipient site.
      • Blood flow gradually resumes in the graft via reconnection of existing vessels.
    • Neovascularization (After Day 5-7): (Option C ruled out)
      • New blood vessels sprout from the recipient site into the graft.
      • This marks the start of long-term viability and integration.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK551561/

question_text: Which of the following statement is false regarding parenteral nutrition?
option_a: Peripheral feeding is appropriate for short term feeding up to 3 weeks.
option_b: Thrombophlebitis is more commonly seen with peripheral feeding.
option_c: For central feeding, Hickman lines are ideal.
option_d: Fluid retention is indicated by change in weight of >1 kg/day.
explanation:
Option A: Peripheral feeding is appropriate for short term feeding up to 2 weeks.

Option B: Common disadvantage which is seen after peripheral feeding is Thrombophlebitis, which irreversibly damage vein.

Option C: For central parenteral feeding Hickman lines are preferable as they Minimize possibility of line dislodgement and reduce the possibility of Sepsis.

Option D: Common metabolic complications following central feeding includes fluid overload, hyperglycaemia, abnormalities of liver function and vitamin deficiencies. Fluid overload can be avoided by daily weighing of the patient. A weight change of >1 kg/day normally indicates fluid retention.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 25, Edition: 28th, Pg: 338-340

question_text: Identify the procedure being performed in the image given below.
option_c: Intraosseous route access for giving IV fluids
explanation:
Explanation:

The image shows intraosseous cannulation used for rapid vascular access to administer fluids or medications, especially in emergency settings.

  • Intraosseous (IO) access is used when peripheral IV access is difficult or delayed, such as in trauma, shock, cardiac arrest, or pediatric emergencies.
  • The technique involves inserting a needle into the medullary cavity of a long bone (usually proximal tibia, distal femur, or humeral head), which provides access to the rich venous plexus within the bone marrow that drains into the central circulation.
  • This allows for rapid administration of fluids, drugs, and even blood products.
  • Devices like the EZ-IO® use a battery-powered driver to insert the cannula quickly and reliably.

Explanation of other options:

Intraosseous cannula for pain relief (Option A): IO access is used for fluid and drug administration, not primarily for localized pain relief.

Bone marrow aspiration (Option B): Bone marrow aspiration typically involves the iliac crest and uses a specific aspiration needle, not a powered IO device. The technique and indication differ.

Bone marrow biopsy (Option D): A biopsy involves removing a solid core of marrow tissue, often done alongside aspiration. It requires a trephine biopsy needle, not the device shown in IO access.

question_text: A 45-year-old male presents to the emergency department with severe abdominal pain radiating to the back. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated serum amylase and lipase levels. Which of the following should be avoided in the management of the given condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presentation is classical for acute pancreatitis.

  • In the initial phase, the administration of 5% dextroseshould be avoided because it rapidly elevates blood glucose.
  • This leads to stimulation of pancreatic insulin secretion and indirectly increases pancreatic activity, worsening inflammation and tissue injury.
  • The mainstay of management is aggressive fluid resuscitation with isotonic crystalloids such as Ringer's lactate, effective pain control, and close monitoring.
  • Nutritional support is important in severe cases, but if required, enteral feeding via nasogastric or nasojejunal tube is preferredover parenteral nutrition.

Acute Pancreatitis

Clinical Features:

  • Severe, constant abdominal pain, frequently radiating to the back.
  • Pain may improve by sitting forward.
  • Nausea and vomiting are almost universal.
  • Patient ranges from appearing well to severely toxic, with signs of shock.
  • Tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension.
  • Mild icterus if due to gallstone pancreatitis.
  • Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome (SIRS) may be present.
  • Grey Turner's sign (flank ecchymosis) or Cullen's sign (periumbilical ecchymosis) indicate retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
  • Abdominal distension due to ileus or ascites, with tenderness and guarding.

Diagnosis:

  • Serum amylase >3× normalis highly suggestive.
  • Serum lipaseis more sensitive and specific.
  • CECT abdomenis the gold standard for confirmation and assessing severity/complications.

Management:

  • Mild cases:IV fluids, analgesics, antiemetics, nil per oral initially.
  • Severe cases:Intensive monitoring, aggressive IV resuscitation, oxygen therapy, urine output monitoring.
  • Nutrition: enteral feeding preferred over parenteral.
  • Antibiotics: only for documented infection, not prophylaxis.
  • Gallstone pancreatitis with biliary obstruction: ERCP within 72 hours.
  • Avoid 5% dextrose initially.
  • Manage complications such as shock, ARDS, renal failure, DIC, metabolic derangements, and pancreatic collections.

Explanation of Other Options:

Nil per oral (Option A): Appropriate in the acute phase to reduce pancreatic stimulation.

Parenteral nutrition (Option C): Can be used if enteral feeding is not possible, though enteral is preferred. Not contraindicated.

Early initiation of oral feedings (Option D): In mild cases, oral intake can be restarted once symptoms improve. Not harmful.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: A patient develops a severe infection and necrosis in the scrotal region after 5 days of catheterization. Based on the clinical presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture is consistent with Fournier's gangrene, a rapidly progressive, necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia.

  • Definition:Necrotizing infection of the perineal, genital, and perianal regions, commonly polymicrobial.
  • Microbiology:
    • Aerobes:Escherichia coli, Proteus, Staphylococcus, Klebsiella, Streptococcus.
    • Anaerobes:Bacteroides, Clostridium, Peptostreptococcus.
  • Risk factors:Diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, malnutrition, immunosuppression, peripheral vascular disease, prolonged catheterization.
  • Clinical course:Five progressive phases:
    • Prodromal phase:Fever, malaise.
    • Early pain phase:Severe genital pain, edema, pruritus.
    • Progressive phase:Erythema, worsening pain.
    • Crepitation phase:Dusky skin, subcutaneous crepitus.
    • Gangrene phase:Necrosis with purulent discharge, systemic toxicity.
  • Complication:Septic shock and multi-organ failure if untreated.
  • Management:
    • Aggressive resuscitation.
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics.
    • Emergency surgical debridement.
    • Diversion procedures (urinary/fecal) to avoid contamination.
    • VAC dressings, serial wound reviews, and eventual skin grafting.

Explanation of Other Options:

Gas gangrene (Option B):

  • Caused by Clostridium perfringens.
  • Involves skeletal muscle, not confined to perineum.
  • Rapidly spreading edematous myonecrosis with systemic toxicity.

Wet gangrene (Option C):

  • Refers to tissue necrosis complicated by infection.
  • Seen in extremities with vascular compromise, not specifically localized to scrotum/perineum.

Scrotal hematoma (Option D):

  • Collection of blood in scrotal sac due to trauma, torsion, or surgery.
  • No necrosis, infection, or systemic toxicity.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: Patients who are unable to maintain adequate oral intake are at risk of malnutrition and complications. Clinical guidelines recommend initiating nutritional support once intake has been insufficient for a defined period. After how many days of inadequate intake should nutritional support be considered?
explanation:
Explanation:

Nutritional support (enteral or parenteral) should be considered when a patient has inadequate intake for 5 days or more, as metabolic stress and protein-energy deficit begin to significantly affect clinical outcomes around this timeframe.

Guidelines for initiating nutritional support:

  • 5 days of inadequate intake - initiate support to prevent malnutrition
  • Earlier initiation (within 1-3 days) is recommended in critically ill or high-risk patients
  • Enteral nutrition is preferred over parenteral whenever feasible
  • Goals: maintain lean body mass, support immune function, reduce complications

question_text: What is the most common nutritional deficiency following gastrectomy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Gastrectomy removes or reduces the gastric mucosa containing parietal cells, which produce intrinsic factor (IF). Intrinsic factor is essential for Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum. Without IF, Vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed, leading to pernicious anaemia.

Clinically, this presents with megaloblastic anaemia, glossitis, and neurological manifestations such as paresthesia, ataxia, and subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord. Lifelong Vitamin B12 supplementation is required, usually via intramuscular injections or high-dose oral formulations.

Vitamin B12 Deficiency after Gastrectomy

Definition

  • Gastrectomy (partial or total removal of the stomach) causes loss of gastric parietal cells.
  • Leads to absence of intrinsic factor (IF), which is required for Vitamin B12 absorption in the terminal ileum.

Pathophysiology

  • Intrinsic Factor (IF): Secreted by gastric parietal cells.
  • Role: Binds Vitamin B12 → absorbed in the ileum.
  • After Gastrectomy: IF production stops → Vitamin B12 cannot be absorbed → deficiency develops.

Clinical Manifestations

  • Hematological: Megaloblastic anemia (macrocytic anemia).
  • Neurological: Peripheral neuropathy, paresthesias, ataxia, cognitive changes.
  • Mucocutaneous: Glossitis, angular cheilitis, pallor, fatigue.

Diagnosis

  • Low serum Vitamin B12.
  • Elevated MCV (macrocytosis).
  • Peripheral smear: Hypersegmented neutrophils.

Management

  • Lifelong Vitamin B12 supplementation:
    • Intramuscular (IM): 1000 µg every 1-3 months.
    • High-dose oral supplementation: Alternative in compliant patients.

Explanation of other options:

Folic acid deficiency (Option A): Absorbed in the jejunum, which remains intact; not directly caused by gastrectomy.

Gastric ulcer (Option C): Risk is reduced post-gastrectomy as acid production decreases.

Constipation (Option D): Not a typical complication; dumping syndrome and diarrhoea are more common.

References: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24096753/.

question_text: Which factor is not considered for the planning of skin incision?
explanation:
When planning a skin incision, four factors should be considered:

  1. Skin tension lines (Langer's lines). These lines represent the orientation of the dermal collagen fibres and any incision placed parallel to these lines results in a better scar.
  2. Anatomical structure. Incisions should avoid bony prominences and crossing skin creases if possible, and take into consideration underlying structures, such as nerves and vessels.
  3. Cosmetic factors. Any incision should be made bearing in mind the ultimate cosmetic result, especially in exposed parts of the body, as an incision is the only part of the operation the patient sees.
  4. Adequate access for the procedure. The incision must be functionally effective for the procedure in hand because any compromise purely on cosmetic grounds may render the operation ineffective or even dangerous.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 85

question_text: In a hypotensive patient with a head injury, which of the subsequent fluids should be avoided?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In a hypotensive patient with a head injury, 5% dextrose should be avoided because it is hypotonic and can lower serum sodium, potentially worsening cerebral edema and increasing intracranial pressure (ICP).
  • The goal of fluid resuscitation is to restore circulation without exacerbating cerebral edema.
  • Isotonic crystalloids like 0.9% normal saline the preferred choice. (Option A ruled out)

Explanation of other options:

Ringer Lactate (Option C): Ringer's lactate is an isotonic solution commonly used for aggressive fluid resuscitation in cases of blood loss or burn injuries. Although its osmolarity (273 mOsm/L) is slightly below that of plasma, it remains isotonic. However, in patients with traumatic brain injury, it can expand the intracellular fluid compartment, potentially raising intracranial pressure.

3% saline (Option D): 3% NS is hypertonic and is a preferred treatment for head injuries that involve increased intracranial pressure (ICP). It helps reduce brain oedema by drawing fluid out of the brain cells into the bloodstream. They also support circulatory stability by increasing blood pressure and cardiac output.

question_text: Which among the following statement is false for enterocutaneous fistulas?
option_a: Majority of the fistulae heal spontaneously in presence of distal obstruction
option_b: Skin protection is important, as small bowel effluent is caustic
option_d: High output fistula is usually > 500 ml/day of effluent
explanation:
ENTEROCUTANEOUS FISTULA

  • An abnormal connection between the small intestine and the skin can occur as a result of fistulating CD, radiotherapy or abdominal trauma, but the condition most commonly follows a surgical complication - either a leak from an anastomosis or an inadvertent enterotomy during dissection.
  • At least 50% of small bowel enterocutaneous fistulae develop after surgery in which no small bowel has been resected, as a result of injury to the intestine following division of The frequency of this complication has been shown to increase with the number of previous laparotomies.
  • Management of patients with enterocutaneous fistulae can be very challenging, especially when the fistula output is high (usually defined as >500 mL of effluent/day).
  • The majority of fistulae can be expected to heal spontaneously, provided there is no distal obstruction or disease at the fistula site.
  • Reasons for failure of spontaneous healing also include epithelial continuity between the gut and the skin and an associated complex abscess. An early return to theatre to try and treat the problem definitively in a septic, malnourished patient is doomed to failure.
  • Infected collections are best identified at CT and can be drained Skin protection is important, as small bowel effluent is caustic.
  • Nutritional support must include fluid and electrolytes, which can be lost in high quantities from a proximal fistula, as well as carbohydrates, protein, fat and vitamins.
  • Judgements have to be made between enteral and parenteral feeding - enteral feeding has advantages but if the fistula is proximal or high output, total parenteral nutrition will be required. Defining anatomy is best done after careful discussion with the radiologist - a sequence of contrast studies (follow-through, fistulogram and enema) may well be required to define bowel length and plan a surgical strategy.
  • Surgery can be extremely technically demanding, and an anastomosis should not be fashioned in the presence of continuing intra-abdominal sepsis or when the patient is hypoalbuminaemic (<32 g/dL).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 74, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1315

question_text: Which is the best method to check the correct placement of a central venous catheter in the IJV?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most reliable method to confirm the correct placement of a central venous cartheter is by obtaining a post-procedure chest X-ray.

Chest xray allows clinicians to assess the position of the catheter tip, ensuring it is located within the superior vena cava near the cavo-atrial junction or right atrium.

Central venous catheterisation

  • Central venous catheterization is the placement of a catheter into a large central vein (internal jugular, subclavian, or femoral) to allow hemodynamic monitoring, medication administration, or vascular access for complex therapies.
  • Common Sites:
    • Internal jugular vein: Reliable anatomy, accessible, low complication rates, allows ultrasound guidance.
    • Subclavian vein: Lower rates of infection and thrombosis.
    • Femoral vein: Used when other sites are not accessible.

Indications for Central Venous Catheter Placement

  • Hemodynamic instability requiring vasopressors.
  • Hemodynamic monitoring, including central venous pressure (CVP).
  • Administration of hyperosmolar or vein-sclerosing agents.
  • Inadequate peripheral IV access in urgent or multiple infusion scenarios.
  • Extracorporeal therapies: Hemodialysis, plasmapheresis, continuous renal replacement therapy.
  • Incompatible multiple infusions, e.g., total parenteral nutrition or chemotherapy.
  • Mass transfusion protocols when peripheral access is insufficient.
  • Venous interventions: IVC filter placement, thrombolysis, transvenous pacing, IV stenting.

Complications

  • During procedure:
    • Arrhythmias (ventricular or bundle branch block) from guidewire irritation
    • Arterial puncture
    • Pulmonary puncture → pneumothorax (most common with subclavian lines, 0.5-1%)
    • Bleeding/hematoma, airway compromise
    • Tracheal injury
    • Air embolism
  • Post-procedure:
    • Catheter-related bloodstream infections
    • Central vein stenosis
    • Thrombosis
    • Delayed bleeding in coagulopathic patients

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557798/

question_text: Which among the following is not a complication of home parenteral nutrition?
explanation:
SHORT BOWEL SYNDROME

  • Although there has also been interest in the use of drugs to promote intestinal adaptation, such as growth hormone, glutamine and, most recently, glucagon-like peptide 2 agonists, the mainstay of treatment for short bowel syndrome remains home parenteral nutrition (HPN).
  • The development of this treatment in the late 1960s enabled the majority of patients with short bowel syndrome to enjoy a reasonably good quality of life, with long-term survival related principally to the underlying disease.
  • HPN is, however, expensive and demanding and patients with short bowel syndrome receiving HPN are at risk from catheter-related complications (notably catheter- related sepsis and occlusion), as well as metabolic complications (fibrotic liver disease, gallstones, metabolic bone disease and kidney stones).

The most common causes of short bowel syndrome are resection resulting from the management of CD and its complications (which accounts for almost half of cases), mesenteric vascular thrombosis, radiation enteritis and tumours. Although features of short bowel syndrome usually appear when there is less than 200 cm of small bowel, the length and nature of the remaining intestine are also important. In general, diseases that result in short bowel syndrome tend to preferentially affect the distal small intestine, and there is some evidence that the ileum, with its tighter intercellular junctions and consequently better fluid absorptive capacity, can assume the functions of a missing jejunum, but not vice versa. While the ileocaecal valve used to be considered important with regard to preservation of absorptive function, it is more likely that this is a reflection of the associated preservation of the distal ileum and right colon than the valve itself.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 74, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1316

question_text: A 20-year-old female presents with complete dysphagia after ingestion of a cleaning agent containing 90% sodium hydroxide. What is the best next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

Feeding jejunostomy provides nutritional support by bypassing the severely damaged esophagus during the acute phase of caustic injury.

  • Ingestion of strong alkalis like sodium hydroxide leads to caustic esophageal injury due to liquefative necrosis, saponification, and vascular thrombosis, resulting in extensive fibrosis and stricture formation.
  • In cases with complete dysphagia or full-thickness necrosis, early surgical nutritional support is crucial.
  • A feeding jejunostomy is the most appropriate initial step to ensure enteral nutrition while bypassing the esophagus, giving it time to heal and avoiding further complications such as perforation.
  • Corrosive esophageal injuries are graded:
    • 1st-degree burns: Only mucosal damage; oral feeds resumed after 48 hrs if painless swallowing returns.
    • 2nd/3rd-degree burns: Require fluid resuscitation, IV antibiotics, PPIs, steroids, and nutritional support via jejunostomy.
  • In severe cases with full-thickness necrosis, resection and cervical esophagostomy with jejunostomy may be necessary.
  • Long-term complications include stricture formation, managed by endoscopic dilatation (Savary-Gilliard, Eder-Puestow, or balloon dilators).
  • Surgical bypass or colonic transposition may be needed later if multiple strictures develop or the stomach is also involved.

Explanation of other options:

Esophagojejunostomy (Option A): Reserved for definitive reconstructive procedures after stabilization; not appropriate as the initial step in acute caustic injury.

Stent placement (Option B): Considered in strictures after healing; contraindicated in acute severe burns due to risk of perforation.

Gastrojejunostomy (Option D): Not indicated in esophageal injury; used when the stomach or pylorus is obstructed, commonly in corrosive acid injury affecting the antrum.

question_text: Which of the following is a complication usually associated with the procedure shown in the image below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The procedure shown in the image is central line placement. A potential complication of this procedure is pneumothorax, which occurs when air enters the pleural space, leading to the partial or complete collapse of the lung. This can happen when the central line needle or catheter is inserted into the subclavian or jugular veins.

The central venous catheter is used for fluid, medication, and nutrition administration.

  • The tip is located in the superior vena cava.
  • Order of preference: Subclavian vein > Internal jugular vein > Femoral vein
    • Inside OT: Internal jugular vein
    • Outside OT: Subclavian vein.
  • Complications
    • Catheter-related sepsis
    • Pneumothorax
    • Misplacement
    • Thrombosis

Explanation of other options:

Aspiration (Option A): Involves inhaling stomach contents or foreign material into the lungs. Although it can occur in various clinical situations, it is not typically associated with central line placement.

Torticollis (Option B): Also known as wry neck, is a condition where the neck muscles involuntarily contract, causing the neck to twist to one side. This is not a complication directly related to central line placement.

Recurrent laryngeal nerve paralysis (Option D): A complication typically associated with surgeries or procedures involving the neck or chest, such as thyroid or thoracic surgery. It is not commonly linked to central line placement.

question_text: Based on the constituents, identify the fluid given to post-operative patients:
explanation:
The given composition closely matches Ringer lactate, an isotonic fluid commonly used postoperatively to maintain electrolyte balance and prevent metabolic acidosis.

  • Ringer Lactate (also called Hartmann's Solution) is a crystalloid isotonic solution designed to mimic plasma electrolyte composition.
  • It contains:
    • Na+ - 130 mmol/L
    • Cl- - 109 mmol/L
    • K+ - 4 mmol/L
    • Ca2+ - 1.5 mmol/L
    • Lactate - 28 mmol/L
    • Osmolality ~273 mOsm/kg
  • This makes it ideal for perioperative and postoperative fluid replacement, especially since lactate acts as a buffer by being metabolized into bicarbonate, which prevents hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis, unlike normal saline.
  • Ringer lactate is rapidly cleared due to suppression of ADH, promoting diuresis, making it suitable for patients at risk of volume overload.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Haemaccel (Option B): It is a colloid solution containing gelatin and electrolytes, mainly used in shock or blood loss. It is not routinely used for postoperative maintenance fluids and doesn't match the above composition.

Isolyte P (Option C): Contains more calcium (2.7 mEq/L) and includes magnesium and bicarbonate not present in the given table. It is typically used for pediatric maintenance rather than adult post-op care.

question_text: Which of the following electrolyte imbalances is typically not associated with this condition In patients at risk of refeeding syndrome?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Hyperkalemia is not associated with refeeding syndrome.
  • In fact, potassium shifts intracellularly during refeeding, leading to hypokalemia
  • The hallmark disturbances in refeeding syndrome are low phosphate, magnesium, potassium, and calcium, not elevated potassium.
  • Hence, hyperkalemia does not occur in this condition.

Refeeding syndrome:

  • One of the most significant metabolic complications of both parenteral and enteral feeding.
  • This occurs in the first days after feeding is commenced in patients who have been severely malnourished.

The patient is considered to be at risk of developing refeeding syndrome with EITHER.

Explanation of Other Options:

Hypokalemia (Option A):

  • During refeeding, insulin secretion drives potassium into cells, lowering plasma potassium.
  • This can cause dangerous arrhythmias.

Hypocalcemia (Option C):

  • Hypocalcemia may occur due to concurrent hypomagnesemia, which impairs PTH secretion and action.

Hypophosphatemia (Option D):

  • Most characteristic finding.
  • Phosphate is consumed during ATP production in glucose metabolism, leading to severe depletion.
  • Responsible for confusion, respiratory failure, and even death.

Key Takeaway Points:

Risk Factors for Refeeding Syndrome:

  • BMI <16 kg/m² or unintentional weight loss >15% (3-6 months).
  • Little/no intake >10 days.
  • Low baseline K⁺, Mg²⁺, or phosphate.
  • Alcoholism or medications (insulin, chemo, antacids, diuretics).

Mechanism:

Starvation → low insulin → fat/protein metabolism → refeeding → ↑ insulin → intracellular shift of K⁺,

Mg² ⁺, PO₄³⁻ → plasma depletion → metabolic crisis.

Management:

  • Start feeding slowly.
  • Administer thiamine before refeeding.
  • Correct electrolytes prior to initiating nutrition.

Explanation:

A Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy (PEG) tube is a long-term enteral feeding device inserted directly into the stomach through the abdominal wall, using endoscopic guidance.

It provides nutrition, hydration, and medication directly into the gastrointestinal tract for patients unable to swallow safely or who need prolonged enteral feeding.

Advantages

  • Provides direct gastric feeding, bypassing the oropharynx.
  • Reduces aspiration risk compared to nasogastric (NG) tubes.
  • Easier maintenance and better cosmetic appearance than surgical gastrostomy.
  • Allows home enteral feeding and medication delivery.

Explanation of Other Options:

Central line (Option B):

  • Inserted into major central veins (e.g., subclavian, internal jugular, femoral).
  • Used for TPN (total parenteral nutrition), drug infusion, or central venous pressure monitoring.
  • Has multiple lumens and no gastric component.

Orogastric tube insertion (Option C):

  • Inserted via the mouth into the stomach.
  • Used for short-term enteral feeding, gastric decompression, or lavage (e.g., poisoning).
  • Easily displaced, unsuitable for long-term use.

ICD (Option D):

  • Inserted into the pleural cavity (5th intercostal space, mid-axillary line).
  • Drains air (pneumothorax), blood (hemothorax), or fluid (effusion/empyema).
  • Connected to an underwater seal drainage system, not the GI tract.

question_text: Which of the following is a complication of Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) in a sepsis patient in the ICU?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Hyperglycemia is the most common metabolic complication of TPN, especially in critically ill septic patients, due to insulin resistance and glucose overload.

  • Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) is used in patients who cannot absorb nutrients from the gastrointestinal tract.
  • In ICU settings, especially in sepsis, patients are in a hypermetabolic and insulin-resistant state.
  • TPN solutions contain high concentrations of glucose to meet energy requirements, and in septic patients, this can lead to profound hyperglycemia, which increases the risk of infections, impairs wound healing, and worsens outcomes.
  • Common Indications for TPN:
    • Short bowel syndrome
    • Severe malabsorption
    • Bowel obstruction or ileus
    • Enterocutaneous fistulae
    • High-output fistulas
  • Complications of TPN:
  • Hyperglycemia is particularly important to monitor in ICU patients as it correlates with worse clinical outcomes.

Explanation of other options:

Hyperlipidemia (Option A): Though TPN contains lipids, this is less likely an acute complication in sepsis compared to hyperglycemia. 

Hyperglyceridemia (Option C): Elevated triglycerides can occur due to lipid emulsions in TPN, but it's not as common or significant in septic ICU patients as hyperglycemia.

Hypoglycemia (Option D): Can occur if TPN is suddenly discontinued or if there's insulin overdose, but during administration in sepsis, hyperglycemia is more likely.

question_text: What is the threshold for high output fistula in enterocutaneous fistula?
explanation:
ENTEROCUTANEOUS FISTULA

  • An abnormal connection between the small intestine and the skin can occur as a result of fistulating CD, radiotherapy or abdominal trauma, but the condition most commonly follows a surgical complication - either a leak from an anastomosis or an inadvertent enterotomy during dissection.
  • At least 50% of small bowel enterocutaneous fistulae develop after surgery in which no small bowel has been resected, as a result of injury to the intestine following division of adhesions.
  • The frequency of this complication has been shown to increase with the number of previous laparotomies.
  • Management of patients with enterocutaneous fistulae can be very challenging, especially when the fistula output is high (usually defined as >500 mL of effluent/day).
  • The majority of fistulae can be expected to heal spontaneously, provided there is no distal obstruction or disease at the fistula site.
  • Reasons for failure of spontaneous healing also include epithelial continuity between the gut and the skin and an associated complex abscess. An early return to theatre to try and treat the problem definitively in a septic, malnourished patient is doomed to failure.
  • Infected collections are best identified at CT and can be drained Skin protection is important, as small bowel effluent is caustic.
  • Nutritional support must include fluid and electrolytes, which can be lost in high quantities from a proximal fistula, as well as carbohydrates, protein, fat and vitamins.
  • Judgements have to be made between enteral and parenteral feeding - enteral feeding has advantages but if the fistula is proximal or high output, total parenteral nutrition will be required.
  • Defining anatomy is best done after careful discussion with the radiologist - a sequence of contrast studies (follow-through, fistulogram and enema) may well be required to define bowel length and plan a surgical strategy.
  • Surgery can be extremely technically demanding, and an anastomosis should not be fashioned in the presence of continuing intra-abdominal sepsis or when the patient is hypoalbuminaemic (<32 g/dL).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 74, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1315

question_text: A 55-year-old asthmatic man, postoperative day 3 after laparotomy, presents with hypotension (BP 90/60 mmHg) and tachycardia (110 per minute), but warm peripheries and adequate urine output. He has passed stools 4 times. ABG shows: pH 7.35, PaO2 76 mmHg, mixed venous saturation 75 percent, and high base deficit. What is the most likely cause of this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient has warm peripheries, adequate urine output, high mixed venous oxygen saturation and high base deficit. These findings are characteristic of early septic shock, also known as the warm or hyperdynamic phase.

In this phase, peripheral vasodilation occurs due to inflammatory mediators, leading to warm extremities despite hypotension, and mixed venous oxygen saturation is increased because tissues cannot extract oxygen efficiently.

Warm septic shock features include:

  • Hypotension with vasodilation
  • Warm, flushed peripheries
  • Tachycardia
  • High mixed venous oxygen saturation (due to impaired oxygen extraction at tissues)
  • Metabolic acidosis and base deficit (due to sepsis-induced hypermetabolism and lactic acidosis)
  • Adequate or even increased urine output in early stages
    Passing stools multiple times may also suggest gut dysfunction due to sepsis.

Arrythmia can produce cardiogenic shock but in it, peripheries would; be cold and mixed venous oxygen saturation would be low (Option B)

Tension pneumothorax produce obstructive shock but again in it, Mixed venous oxygen saturation would be low, and peripheries would be low, and chances of tension pneumothorax would be low as there is no any other complication occur. (Option C)

Diarrhea would lead to hypovolemic shock but in it, peripheries would be cold and mixed venous oxygen saturation would be low. (Option D)

Key Takeaways:

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding pericardial tamponade except
option_a: Presentation is similar to tension pneumothorax
option_b: Central venous pressure is always elevated
explanation:
Explanation:

The statement "CVP is always elevated" is incorrect because CVP may not be elevated in volume depletion.

Pericardial Tamponade in Trauma

Differentiation: Must be distinguished from tension pneumothorax in a shocked patient with distended neck veins.

Cause: Most commonly due to penetrating trauma.

Pathophysiology:

  • Even ~50 mL of blood in the non-distensible pericardial sac causes cardiac compression.
  • This obstructs venous return and reduces diastolic filling of the heart, producing shock.

Clinical Suspicion:

  • Any patient with penetrating injury near the heart + shock should be assumed to have cardiac injury until proven otherwise.

Classical Features:

  • Elevated central venous pressure
  • Falling arterial pressure with tachycardia
  • Muffled heart sounds

(Note: Neck veins may be flat if major bleeding is present elsewhere.)

Diagnosis:

  • eFAST showing fluid in the pericardial sac is the fastest and most reliable tool.
  • Chest radiography may show an enlarged cardiac shadow.

Management:

  • Pericardiocentesis has no role in tamponade caused by penetrating myocardial injury (clot prevents aspiration).
  • Definitive treatment is operative:
    • Subxiphoid window or
    • Open surgery (sternotomy or left anterolateral thoracotomy).
  • Repair is performed in the operating theatre, or in the emergency department if necessary.

question_text: A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a car accident. He is unresponsive and in a coma. Neurological examination reveals that he does not respond to verbal commands or painful stimuli. A CT scan shows no significant structural brain injury. Which of the following structures is most likely impaired in this patient, leading to his coma?
explanation:
Reticular Activating System (RAS):

  • The RAS is a network of neurons located in the brainstem that plays a crucial role in maintaining consciousness and alertness.
  • Coma Mechanism: Impairment or damage to the RAS can lead to a state of coma, as it fails to stimulate the cerebral cortex sufficiently for consciousness.

Why not the other options?

  • A) Thalamus:
    • The thalamus is involved in sensory relay and has a role in consciousness. However, its function depends on input from the RAS, making it a secondary factor in this scenario.
  • B) Cerebral Cortex:
    • While the cerebral cortex is vital for higher brain functions, including awareness and cognition, the issue here primarily lies in the activation of the cortex, which is managed by the RAS.
  • D) Basal Ganglia:
    • The basal ganglia regulate movement and certain behavioural aspects but are not primarily responsible for maintaining consciousness. Their impairment would not typically result in coma.

Key Takeaways:

  • The reticular activating system (RAS) is essential for consciousness; its impairment is a common cause of coma in cases where structural brain injuries are absent.
  • Understanding the roles of different brain structures can assist in diagnosing and managing neurological conditions effectively.

question_text: When evaluating a patient in shock, a fluid challenge is often given to assess responsiveness to volume expansion. This involves administering a small but adequate bolus of fluid and observing the hemodynamic response. What is the commonly recommended bolus volume to assess fluid responsiveness?
explanation:
Explanation:

A 250 ml fluid bolus is the standard amount used to assess fluid responsiveness in shock. This volume is large enough to produce measurable hemodynamic changes, yet small enough to avoid fluid overload, especially in critically ill or borderline patients. It is used in both emergency and critical care settings.

Fluid challenge principles:

  • Quickly determine whether the patient is "fluid responsive"
  • Typically uses 250 ml crystalloid bolus
  • Response assessed by:
    • Blood pressure improvement
    • Heart rate reduction
    • Improvement in perfusion (urine output, mental status)
    • Ultrasound assessment of IVC or stroke volume variation

A positive response suggests hypovolemia, while lack of response indicates need for vasopressors or search for other causes of shock.

question_text: All of the following statements are true except:
option_a: In patient with active bleeding due to major trauma first step should be controlling Bleeding rather than starting high fluid therapy.
option_b: In patient with Bowel obstruction first step should be to resuscitate a patient
option_c: In patient with active bleeding due to major trauma first step always be fluid therapy.
option_d: Airway and breathing must be ensured in every patient presenting with shock.
explanation:
In patients who are actively bleeding (major trauma, aortic aneurysm rupture, gastrointestinal hemorrhage), it is counterproductive to institute high-volume fluid therapy without controlling the site of hemorrhage.

Increasing blood pressure merely increases bleeding from the site while fluid therapy cools the patient and dilutes available coagulation factors. Thus operative hemorrhage control should not be delayed and resuscitation should proceed in parallel with surgery.

Conversely, a patient with bowel obstruction and hypovolemic shock must be adequately resuscitated before undergoing surgery otherwise the additional surgical injury and hypovolemia induced during the procedure will exacerbate the inflammatory activation and increase the incidence and severity of end-organ insult.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 2, Edition: 28th

question_text: Which of the following are indicators of shock in an injured patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Shock

Definition

Shock is the systemic state of low tissue perfusion → inadequate oxygen & glucose → anaerobic metabolism → cell death if not corrected.

Cellular Pathophysiology

  • Reduced perfusion → switch to anaerobic metabolism → lactic acid → metabolic acidosis.
  • Failure of Na+/K+ pump → cell lysis → release of potassium and intracellular enzymes.

Microvascular Changes

  • Hypoxia + acidosis → activation of complement, leukocytes, cytokines.
  • Endothelial damage → leaky capillaries → tissue oedema → worsened hypoxia.

Systemic Responses

  • Cardiovascular: tachycardia, vasoconstriction (except in sepsis).
  • Respiratory: increased respiratory rate → compensatory respiratory alkalosis.
  • Renal: decreased perfusion → low urine output; RAAS activation → sodium & water retention.
  • Endocrine: vasopressin & cortisol release → vasoconstriction + water retention.

Classification of Shock

  • Haemorrhagic/Hypovolaemic
  • Cardiogenic
  • Obstructive
  • Distributive (sepsis, anaphylaxis, spinal cord injury)
  • Endocrine

Clinical Features of Shock

General Indicators:

  • Tachycardia
  • Cool, pale peripheries with prolonged capillary refill (not always reliable)
  • Reduced urine output
  • Altered mental status: anxiety → drowsiness → coma
  • Hypotension (late sign)
  • Weak distal pulses due to vasoconstriction and low perfusion

Stages:

  • Compensated shock: tachycardia, cool peripheries, mild anxiety, normal BP.
  • Moderate shock: tachycardia, falling BP, reduced urine output, confusion.
  • Severe shock: profound tachycardia, severe hypotension, anuria, coma.

question_text: In EXIT procedures when is the umbilical cord cut?
option_a: It is not cut at all
option_d: Cut after securing the fetal airway.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The EXIT procedure is an abbreviation for ex utero intrapartum t It is used in circumstances where airway obstruction is predicted at the time of delivery, due to the presence of a large neck mass, such as a cystic hygroma or teratoma, or congenital tracheal stenosis.
  • The success of the procedure is dependent on the maintenance of utero-placental perfusion fora sufficient duration to secure the airway. To achieve this, deep uterine relaxation is obtained during a cesarean section under general anesthesia. Uterine perfusion with warmed saline also promotes relaxation and blood flow to the placenta.
  • On average, between 20 and 30 minutes of placental perfusion can be achieved. The fetal airway is secured either by placement of an orotracheal tube or performance of a tracheostomy. Once the airway is secured, the cord is cut and a definitive procedure may be performed to relieve the obstruction in the postnatal period

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: It is not cut at all

  • This is incorrect because the umbilical cord must be cut eventually once the airway is secured and the fetus is transitioned to independent ventilation.

Choice B: Cut before securing fetal airway

  • This defeats the purpose of the EXIT procedure. Cutting the cord first would result in loss of oxygenation, risking hypoxia in a baby with an obstructed airway.

Choice C: Cut after securing maternal airway

  • This option is irrelevant in this context. The maternal airway is already managed under general anesthesia. The focus is on fetal airway

Key Takeaway

  • In EXIT procedures, the umbilical cord is cut only after the fetal airway is successfully secured to maintain oxygenation and avoid neonatal respiratory compromise.

question_text: Among the options provided, which one is not acknowledged as a potential complication resulting from a significant blood transfusion?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hypernatremia is not typically a complication of blood transfusion.

Complications of massive blood transfusion:

Hypocalcemia: (Option A ruled out)

  • Packed red blood cells (PRBCs) and other blood products are preserved with citrate, an anticoagulant.
  • Citrate binds to ionised calcium (Ca²⁺) in the recipient's blood, reducing the free calcium level -
  • Presents as muscle spasms, cardiac arrhythmias, and decreased myocardial contractility.

Metabolic Alkalosis:

  • Citrate is metabolised in the liver to bicarbonate (HCO₃-).
  • Rapid transfusion of citrate-containing blood products can overwhelm the liver's ability to metabolise citrate, leading to an increase in bicarbonate levels.
  • This results in metabolic alkalosis

Hyperkalemia:

  • Stored blood undergoes hemolysis over time, releasing potassium from red blood cells into the plasma.
  • Transfusion of large volumes of stored blood can introduce a significant potassium load, causing hyperkalemia.
  • Presents with cardiac arrhythmias, especially in patients with pre-existing kidney dysfunction.

Hypothermia: (Option C ruled out)

  • Rapid transfusion of cold-stored blood products (typically kept at 1-6°C) can lower the patient's core body temperature.

Coagulopathy:

  • Massive transfusion dilutes clotting factors and platelets, leading to dilutional coagulopathy.
  • Hypothermia and hypocalcemia exacerbate this by impairing the function of coagulation enzymes and platelets.

Hypokalemia: (Option B ruled out)

Post-transfusion, potassium that had leaked out of stored red blood cells can re-enter the cells in vivo.

This shift can lead to hypokalemia, especially if the patient has a strong cellular uptake of potassium.

Key Takeaways:

Complications from massive blood transfusion:

  • Coagulopathy
  • Hypocalcaemia
  • Hyperkalaemia
  • Hypokalaemia
  • Hypothermia

Option B - Severely hypovolemic trauma patients should be resuscitated using blood and blood products. All trauma centers should have an established massive transfusion protocol

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 27, Edition: 28th, Pg: 355-356

  • Tibia fractures- 300 to 500 mL

question_text: Distributive shock is characterized by pathological vasodilation and maldistribution of blood flow. Several clinical conditions can produce this type of shock, but one of the following does not result in distributive shock. Identify the exception.
explanation:
Explanation:

Thyrotoxicosis is type of endocrine shock. Thyrotoxicosis produces a high-output cardiac state, not distributive shock.

Distributive shock is caused by loss of vascular tone and includes:

  • Septic shock: mediated by inflammatory cytokines causing vasodilation
  • Anaphylactic shock: due to histamine and mediators causing abrupt vasodilation
  • Neurogenic shock from spinal cord injury: loss of sympathetic tone results in profound vasodilation

Characteristics of distributive shock include:

  • Warm peripheries
  • Low systemic vascular resistance
  • Relative hypovolemia

question_text: Which among the following is not the step of synthesis of thyroxine from the thyroglobulin complex?
option_a: Trapping of inorganic iodide from the blood
option_d: Coupling of mono and di iodotyrosines
explanation:
Explanation:

The statement "Deoxygenation of iodine to iodide" is incorrect. The correct step in thyroid hormone synthesis is the oxidation of iodide to iodine.

The hormones tri-iodothyronine (T3) and l-thyroxine (T4) are bound to thyroglobulin within the colloid.

Synthesis within the thyroglobulin complex is controlled by several enzymes, in distinct steps:

  • Trapping of inorganic iodide from the blood;
  • Oxidation of iodide to iodine;
  • Binding of iodine with tyrosine to form iodotyrosine;
  • Coupling of monoiodotyrosines and di-iodotyrosines to form T3 and T4.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • Trapping of inorganic iodide from the blood (Option A):
    • This is a true step (Iodide trapping) which concentrates iodide inside the thyroid cell.
  • Binding of iodine with tyrosine (Option C):
    • This is a true step known as organification, resulting in the formation of iodotyrosines.
  • Coupling of mono and di iodotyrosines (Option D):
    • This is a true step where iodotyrosines combine to form the active hormones (DIT + DIT = T4; MIT + DIT = T3).

question_text: A trauma patient receiving large volumes of packed red blood cells is at high risk of dilutional coagulopathy. To improve survival and maintain hemostasis, balanced transfusion of coagulation factors and platelets is required. What additional products should be administered along with 6 units of packed red blood cells?
explanation:
Explanation:

Massive transfusion protocols follow a balanced resuscitation approach, typically using a 1:1:1 ratio of

  • Packed red blood cells
  • Fresh frozen plasma
  • Platelets

This combination prevents dilution of clotting factors and platelets, thus reducing coagulopathy and improving outcomes. Therefore, FFP and platelets must be given along with PRBCs. In massive transfusion:

  • PRBCs restore oxygen carrying capacity
  • FFP replaces coagulation factors (especially V, VIII, IX, X, XI)
  • Platelets correct thrombocytopenia from dilution
  • Cryoprecipitate is given later if fibrinogen drops below 100 to 150 mg per dL

Balanced transfusion prevents trauma induced coagulopathy and improves survival.

question_text: Before performing an invasive procedure, a minimum platelet count is required to ensure adequate haemostasis. What is the minimum platelet count considered safe for most invasive procedures?
explanation:
Explanation:

A platelet count of 50,000/µL is the widely accepted minimum for most invasive and surgical procedures. Below this level, the risk of procedure related bleeding rises significantly.

For invasive procedures platelets should be more than 50,000/μL . While for prophylactic platelet transfusion threshold is 10,000/μL.

question_text: Vasopressor agents are medications that increase vascular tone and raise blood pressure. They are useful in specific types of shock where systemic vascular resistance is decreased. In which of the following types of shock are vasopressors considered ideal and appropriate?
explanation:
Explanation:

Vasopressor agents are ideal in conditions where vasodilation causes hypotension.

  • Septic shock involves profound vasodilation and capillary leak. Vasopressors such as norepinephrine are first line to restore vascular tone and perfusion. (Option A)
  • Neurogenic shock (seen in spinal cord injury) also causes severe vasodilation due to loss of sympathetic tone. Vasopressors help restore systemic vascular resistance. (Option B)

Thus, both septic shock and spinal cord injury-related neurogenic shock benefit from vasopressors.

In thyrotoxicosis there would be already heart is overacting and vasopressor given without correcting preload it will produce detrimental effects to myocardium. (Option D)

question_text: Which of the following is not included in the qSOFA score components?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is not a component of the qSOFA (quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score.

qSOFA (quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) Score:

  • Purpose:
    • Simplified bedside tool for rapidly identifying patients with suspected infection who are at higher risk of poor outcomes.
    • Serves as a practical alternative to the full SOFA score, which requires detailed laboratory testing.
  • Components:
    • Respiratory rate ≥ 22/min
    • Altered mental status
    • Systolic blood pressure ≤ 100 mm Hg
  • Interpretation:
    • A qSOFA score ≥ 2 in a patient with suspected infection indicates a higher risk of mortality, need for ICU care, and prolonged ICU stay.
  • Note:
    • Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is not included in qSOFA, which relies exclusively on these three bedside parameters.

question_text: Which of the following tests is NOT routinely conducted before a blood transfusion for a person, when a family member is volunteering for blood donation?
explanation:
Explanation:

Mandatory screening of all donated blood units is essential to prevent transfusion-transmitted infections (TTIs).

The standard battery of tests, as per national guidelines in India and most countries, includes Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV 1 & 2, Malaria, and Syphilis. (Option B,C and D ruled out)

Hepatitis A is not part of this routine screening because it is primarily transmitted via the fecal-oral route (contaminated food/water). Viremia is short-lived, and it is very rarely, if ever, transmitted through blood transfusion, making routine screening unnecessary.

Key Takeaways:

  • Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, HIV, Malaria, and Syphilis are mandatory pre-transfusion screens.
  • Hepatitis A is not transmitted via blood transfusion and is not routinely tested for.

question_text: Which of the following complications is not associated with massive blood transfusion?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hypercalcemia is not a feature of massive blood transfusion. On the contrary, the complication seen is usually hypocalcemia, caused by citrate in stored blood binding ionized calcium.

Complications of massive blood transfusion

  • Massive blood transfusion s defined as the administration of a large volume of blood products within a short duration.
  • Although often life-saving, it carries the risk of several adverse effects and complications.

question_text: Central Venous pressure is raised in which of the following shock
explanation:
In resuscitation of patient of shock we will be measuring :

  1. Urine output: best clinical parameters in assessment of shock (adequacy of resuscitation, tissue perfusion)
  2. CVP: best measure to calculate IV fluids and drug dosage that needs to be given. CVP is measured by keeping a CVP line via internal jugular vein with tip kept in superior vena cava. CVP is high in cardiogenic shock and septic shock, best way to measure central pressure is by measuring PCWP (pulmonary capillary wedge pressure)
  3. lactate: best laboratory value to know the adequacy of resuscitation, if s.lactate <2mmol/l indicates good resuscitation, s.lactate >5mmol/l indicates poor resuscitation

Cardiogenic shock can result in an elevated CVP, because forward failure of the cardiac pump results in backup of blood within the venous side of the system. In this case, jugular veins may appear distended even with the head held high.

question_text: An alcoholic patient who is diagnosed with chronic hepatitis has been admitted to emergency room for vomiting of blood since last 2 days due to variceal bleeding. Patient is in shock. You are the doctor and you have started the first line treatment, but the patient died. What is the underlying cause of death in this patient?
explanation:
• Varices are ubiquitous in patients with portal hypertension irrespective of the etiology and usually present with an acute, large-volume haematemesis associated with a high morbidity and significant mortality.
  • The lower esophagus is the most common site and the diagnosis should be suspected in a patient known to have cirrhosis, but confirmation of the source is required following initial resuscitation.
  • Variceal hemorrhage is a medical emergency and failure to control variceal bleeding with current medical management occurs in 10-20% of cases. The most common cause of death in these patients are HEMORRHAGIC SHOCK -> HYPOVOLEMIC SHOCK
  • Patients with massive hemorrhage should be admitted to an intensive therapy unit, venous access obtained through two large-bore peripheral cannulae and resuscitation commenced, ideally with blood.

question_text: A male patient presents with impotence and absent femoral pulse. Pain in the gluteal region is observed. At which level has pathology occurred?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The triad of impotence, gluteal claudication, and absent femoral pulses is classical for Leriche's syndrome, which occurs due to occlusion at the aortoiliac bifurcation.
  • Pathology at this level compromises blood flow to the lower limbs and pelvic organs, explaining the combination of symptoms.
  • Gluteal pain occurs due to ischemia in the buttock muscles, impotence results from impaired pelvic circulation, and absent femoral pulses reflect poor distal flow.

Leriche's Syndrome (Aortoiliac Occlusion):

  • Clinical triad: Claudication (especially buttock/thigh), impotence, absent femoral pulses.
  • Pathophysiology: Progressive atherosclerotic disease at the bifurcation of the aorta into the common iliac arteries.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical exam showing absent femoral pulses.
    • Doppler and duplex ultrasonography.
    • CT/MR angiography for localization and severity.
  • Treatment:
    • Lifestyle modification and antiplatelet therapy for mild disease.
    • Endovascular stenting or aortobifemoral bypass graft for severe occlusion.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Bilateral popliteal arteries (Option A): Occlusion here causes calf and foot ischemia with absent pedal pulses, but femoral pulses remain palpable, and impotence is not a feature.

Bilateral internal iliac arteries (Option B): This could explain impotence and buttock pain due to reduced pelvic and gluteal blood flow, but femoral pulses would still be present since flow through the external iliac and femoral arteries is intact.

Bilateral femoral arteries (Option D): This causes calf claudication and absent distal pulses, but gluteal pain and impotence are not explained, as pelvic circulation is unaffected.

Key Takeaway:

The combination of impotence, gluteal pain, and absent femoral pulses is pathognomonic for Leriche's syndrome due to aortoiliac bifurcation occlusion, making this the correct site of pathology.

Reference:

NIH Link.

question_text: A patient presented with blunt trauma to the abdomen. On evaluation, liver injury was noted, for which primary repair was done. Coagulation function was monitored intraoperatively using the method shown below. What is the method used?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The test shown measures the viscoelastic properties of clotting blood, which is characteristic of thromboelastography (TEG).
  • TEG is used intraoperatively to assess clot formation, strength, and breakdown in real time.
  • This helps guide blood product replacement (plasma, platelets, cryoprecipitate, antifibrinolytics).

Thromboelastography (TEG)

Principle

  • Evaluates the whole clotting process, from initiation to clot lysis.

Key Parameters

  • R time (Reaction time): Time for initial fibrin formation.
    • Normal: 7.5-15 min.
    • Prolonged → clotting factor deficiency → treat with FFP.
  • K time (Clot kinetics): Time to achieve clot firmness.
    • Normal: 3-6 min.
    • Prolonged → fibrinogen abnormality → treat with cryoprecipitate.
  • Alpha angle: Rate of fibrin cross-linking.
    • Normal: 45°-55°.
    • Reduced → fibrinogen dysfunction → treat with cryoprecipitate.
  • Maximum amplitude (MA): Strength of the clot.
    • Normal: 50–60 mm.
    • Low → platelet dysfunction → treat with platelets.
  • LY30: % lysis 30 min after MA.
    • Normal: 0-8%.
    • Increased → excess fibrinolysis → treat with tranexamic acid.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Plethysmography (Option B): Measures volume changes in organs/limbs (eg, pulmonary function), not coagulation.

Sonography (Option C): Ultrasound imaging, useful for trauma evaluation but not for clot monitoring.

Elastography (Option D): Assesses tissue stiffness (commonly liver fibrosis), not coagulation function

Key Takeaway

Thromboelastography (TEG) is a real-time test of clot dynamics, guiding targeted transfusion therapy by assessing clotting factors, fibrinogen, platelets, and fibrinolysis during surgery.

Reference: NIH Link

question_text: A 25-year-old male patient is brought to the casualty after a road traffic accident (RTA) with suspected pelvic fractures. On examination, he is found to be in hypovolemic shock. What is the earliest treatment for control of haemorrhage in this case?
option_c: Use bedsheets to compress the pelvis
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In the case of pelvic fractures with suspected haemorrhage and hypovolemic shock, pelvic compressionis a critical step to control bleeding and stabilise the patient.
  • Using bedsheets(or a pelvic binder) to compress the pelvis helps reduce the volume of the pelvic cavity, which in turn minimises bleeding from the fractured vessels and improves hemodynamic stability.

Management of Pelvic Fractures

  • The primary goal in managing pelvic fractures with bleeding is to stop the bleeding, as these injuries pose a significant threat to circulation.
  • Initial managementinvolvesapplying a compression binder or sheet around the true pelvis at the level of the greater trochanters to reduce pelvic volume.
    • This life-saving procedure should be performed in the emergency department immediately.
  • Venous Bleeding (85% of cases)
    • Most bleeding originates from veins (85%), which can be controlled non-operatively using pelvic compression (via binding or external fixators).
    • Another technique is extraperitoneal pelvic packing, where the space between the bony pelvis and the peritoneum is packed to compress the veins.
  • Arterial Bleeding
    • If bleeding is arterial in origin, angiographic embolisationbecomes the next choice for controlling haemorrhage.
  • Techniques such as compression, packing, fixation, and angiography may be used together, as they can complement one another.
  • If the source of bleeding is unclear or if diagnostic imaging (FAST/CT) shows significant blood in the peritoneal cavity, an exploratory laparotomy is warranted to rule out or address concurrent intra-abdominal injuries.

Explanation of other options:

Immediate internal fixation (Option A): Immediate internal fixation is not done in the emergency phase, as the patient is unstable.

Multiple blood transfusions (Option B): Multiple blood transfusions help replace lost volume but do not control the source of bleeding.

Emergency external fixation (Option D): Emergency external fixation is effective for stabilisation, but is performed after initial temporary compression measures are made to stop the ongoing blood loss.

  • Donations are leukodepleted as a precaution against variant CJD (this may also reduce the immunogenencity of the transfusion)
  • In INDIA, it is mandatory to test every unit of blood collected for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV/AIDS, syphilis and malaria

question_text: What is the type of shock for a patient with hypotension, bradycardia and warm extremities?
explanation:
Explanation:

Three categories of shock may occur in spinal trauma:

  • Hypovolaemic shock: Hypotension, tachycardia, cold clammy peripheries. This is most often due to haemorrhage. It should be treated with appropriate resuscitation.
  • Neurogenic shock: Hypotension with normal heart rate or bradycardia and warm peripheries due to unopposed vagal tone from cervical spinal cord injury at or above T1-T5. It should be treated with inotropic support, and care should be taken to avoid fluid overload.
  • Spinal shock: Temporary physiological disorganisation presenting with paralysis, decreased tone, hyporeflexia; lasts minutes to weeks; bulbocavernosus reflex returns when resolved.

Hypovolaemic shock (Option A): Presents with tachycardia and cold peripheries, not bradycardia with warm extremities.

Septic shock (Option B): Not the presentation described.

Spinal shock (Option D): Characterised by paralysis and hyporeflexia, not the triad given.

Key Takeaways:

Neurogenic shock uniquely presents with hypotension + bradycardia + warm extremities.

question_text: In a patient with liver cirrhosis, what is the primary cause of mortality when esophageal varices are present?
explanation:
Explanation:

Bleeding esophageal varices in cirrhosis cause massive intravascular volume loss, resulting in hypovolemic shock. The fall in circulating volume leads to poor tissue perfusion, hypoxia, and death if uncontrolled.

Explanation of other options:

Cardiogenic shock (Option B): Due to pump failure (LV dysfunction). Not the mechanism here.

Obstructive shock (Option C): Seen in tamponade, massive PE, or tension pneumothorax, not variceal bleed.

Distributive shock (Option D): Due to vasodilatation (e.g., sepsis, anaphylaxis). Not the primary cause here.

question_text: A 26 years old male patient with RTA complicated with pelvic fracture has been resuscitated with blood transfusion. After a few hours of transfusion, he was febrile, hypotensive, dyspneic and oliguric. CVP was normal but bleeding started from NG tube and IV sites. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Complications of blood transfusion

Complications from blood transfusion can be categorized as those arising from a single transfusion and those related to massive transfusion.

Complications from a single transfusion

Complications from a single transfusion include:

  • incompatibility haemolytic transfusion reaction;
  • febrile transfusion reaction;
  • allergic reaction;
  • infection:
  • bacterial infection (usually due to faulty storage);
  • hepatitis;
  • HIV;
  • malaria;
  • air embolism;
  • thrombophlebitis;
  • transfusion related acute lung injury (usually from FFP).

Complications from massive transfusion

Complications from massive transfusion include:

  • coagulopathy;
  • hypocalcaemia;
  • hyperkalaemia;
  • hypokalaemia;
  • hypothermia.

option_a: Admit patient and all routine blood investigations should be performing first
