question_text: Which among the following statements is not true in the management of oesophageal varices?
option_a: Endoscopic sclerotherapy increases portal venous pressure
option_b: Upper GI endoscopy must be performed only after 12 hours of admission
option_c: Band ligation is the preferred endoscopic method in control of variceal bleeding
option_d: Patient should be stated on vasoactive drugs early to control haemorrhage
explanation:
Early upper GI endoscopy, preferably within 12 hours of admission should be done to identify the source of the bleed.

Treatment of oesophageal varices -

  • Resuscitation and stabilisation of the patient with IV fluids, airway protection and oxygen.
  • Consider blood transfusion if haemoglobin falls below 7gm/dl.
  • Start the patient on vasopressins, octreotide to control bleeding. Octreotide is believed to be as effective as endoscopic therapy in controlling bleeding.
  • Early upper GI endoscopy, preferably within 12 hours of admission should be done to identify the source of the bleed.
  • Because infections are common in patients with variceal bleeding, antibiotic prophylaxis should be initiated
  • Endoscopic band ligation or sclerotherapy. Band ligation is preferred over sclerotherapy as it has fewer complications. Sclerotherapy, but not band ligation, may increase portal pressures.
  • If they fail - Consider balloon tamponade or TIPS

Reference: Sabinston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1445.

question_text: Optimal ratio for PRC: FFP: PRP for massive transfusion protocol
explanation:
Explanation:

Massive transfusion protocols in severe trauma aim to supply blood and blood products in a ratio of:

1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets

Permissive Hypotension, Massive Transfusion Protocols & Tranexamic Acid

  • Initial resuscitation goal: Maintain blood supply to vital organs (brain, heart, kidneys).
  • Permissive hypotension:
    • Target systolic BP 70-90 mmHg (if no head injury).
    • If head injury suspected, target >90 mmHg.
    • Achieved with small IV fluid boluses (e.g., 250 mL O-negative blood or normal saline if blood unavailable).
    • Aim for a palpable radial pulse.
    • Avoid excessive crystalloid/colloid, risk of haemodilution, coagulopathy, ARDS.
    • This approach is time-limited, source of haemorrhage must be identified and controlled early.
  • Massive Transfusion Protocol (MTP):
    • Severely injured hypovolaemic patients should be resuscitated with blood and blood products, not crystalloids/colloids.
    • Products must be warmed.
    • Hospitals should have an MTP that provides blood components in a ratio of:
      1 packed red cells : 1 fresh-frozen plasma : 1 platelets.
  • Tranexamic Acid (TXA):
    • Antifibrinolytic that reduces mortality from bleeding in blunt and penetrating trauma.
    • Dose: 1 g IV over 10 min, followed by 1 g over 8 h.
    • Indicated in all trauma patients suspected to have significant haemorrhage.
    • Systolic BP <110 mmHg or pulse >110/min also indicates its use.
    • Should be given as early as possible, ideally within 1 hour.
    • First dose must not be given after 3 hours from injury.

Key Takeaways:

Massive transfusion follows a 1:1:1 ratio to maintain balanced component therapy.

question_text:
Which of the following are components of qSOFA scoring?
1. Respiratory rate
2. Blood pressure
3. CNS features
4. Leukocyte count
explanation: SOFA score can be cumbersome to calculate at bedside and requires laboratory test results, a simpler version was developed. The qSOFA can be calculated at a patient bedside by identifying tachypnea, altered mental status, and hypotension. If the patient meets two of these criteria and they are at risk for sepsis, further workup for an infectious source should be conducted.

question_text: A 40-year-old smoker presents with sudden, severe, tearing chest pain radiating to his back, shortness of breath, and mild nausea. His BP is 190/110 mmHg, and heart rate is 105 bpm. What is the initial management?
explanation:
Explanation:

A smoker presenting with sudden, severe tearing chest pain radiating to the back, along with shortness of breath, nausea, blood pressure of 190/110 mmHg, and a heart rate of 105 bpm is most likely experiencing aortic dissection. Initial management should prioritise strict blood pressure control.

Aortic Dissection:

Pathophysiology:

  • Defect in the aortic wall allows blood to track into the media.
  • Splits the medial layer → forms a false lumen.

Clinical Features:

  • Sudden, severe"tearing" chest pain radiating to the back (interscapular region)
  • Renal pain, possible renal failure
  • Neurological deficits → paraplegia, syncope, weakness
  • Signs of shock or hypotension

Investigations:

  • Stable patients: CT Angiography → investigation of choice
  • Unstable patients (SBP <100 mmHg, HR >100 bpm): Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE) → preferred
  • MRI: alternative if CT findings are inconclusive
  • Chest X-ray: mediastinal widening, left pleural effusion

Management:

Initial Management (all types)

  • Control hypertension (often elevated at presentation) (Option A)
  • Adequate pain relief
  • Immediate referral to specialist centre

Definitive Management

  • Type A (involving ascending aorta; Stanford type A / DeBakey I & II):
    • Requires surgical intervention
    • Options: synthetic graft, anastomosis, or endovascular stenting
  • Type B (involving descending aorta; Stanford type B / DeBakey III):
    • Initial: medical management (antihypertensives, monitoring)
    • Complicated cases (persistent pain, organ malperfusion, or worsening symptoms): endovascular stenting preferred; surgery rarely used

Explanation of Other Options:

Urgent Surgery (Option B): While surgical intervention is often required for aortic dissection, the immediate priority is blood pressure control before proceeding to surgery. Medications such as labetalol are used to stabilise the patient by reducing shear stress on the aortic wall, thereby preventing progression or rupture. Surgery is considered once the patient is hemodynamically stable.

Wait and Watch (Option C): This approach is not suitable for aortic dissection, as it is a life-threatening emergency. Delaying treatment significantly increases the risk of rupture, severe complications, or death.

Blood Transfusion (Option D): Although transfusion may be needed in cases of substantial blood loss, it is not the first-line treatment. The main priority is to control blood pressure and stabilise the dissection before addressing secondary needs like transfusion.

Key Takeaways:

Aortic Dissection - Classification

Definition:

  • Aortic dissection occurs when a tear/flap develops in the aortic wall, allowing blood to track into the media and form a false lumen.

DeBakey Classification (Based on extent/pattern of dissection)

  • Type I: Involves both ascending and descending aorta.
  • Type II: Limited to the ascending aorta.
  • Type III: Limited to the descending aorta.

Stanford Classification (Based on involvement of ascending aorta)

  • Type A:
    • Involves the ascending aorta alone or both ascending and descending aorta.
    • Corresponds to DeBakey Type I & II.
  • Type B:
    • Involves only the descending aorta.
    • Corresponds to DeBakey Type III.

question_text: Which of the following is not correct for the device depicted below:
option_a: Based on infrared emitted from RBCs
option_d: Checks thickness of artery and vein
explanation:
Explanation:

Doppler Ultrasound Machine:

Description: A Doppler Ultrasound Machine utilizes sound waves instead of infrared emissions from red blood cells to visualize blood flow. It operates using the Doppler effect, where a continuous-wave ultrasound transmits a signal to an artery. The reflected waves from moving blood cells produce a frequency shift, which is converted into a pulsatile audio signal.

Clinical Uses:

  • Evaluation of steno-occlusive arterial disease to assess blood flow limitations. (Option C ruled out)
  • Measurement of systolic pressure in small vessels using a sphygmomanometer.
  • Identification of calcified plaques within arteries. (Option B ruled out)
  • Assessment of arterial and venous wall thickness and the overall condition of blood vessels. (Option D ruled out)

question_text: A patient was brought to the emergency in hypotension with cold and clammy skin. Blood pressure was 90/60 mmHg. What is the most likely cause of shock in this patient?
explanation:
Hemorrhagic and hypovolemic shock

Hypovolemic shock is due to a reduced circulating volume. Hypovolaemia may be due to haemorrhagic or nonhaemorrhagic causes.

Non Hemorrhagic causes include poor fluid intake (dehydration), excessive fluid loss due to vomiting, diarrhea, urinary loss (e.g. diabetes), evaporation or 'third spacing', where fluid is lost into the gastrointestinal tract and interstitial spaces, as for example in bowel obstruction or pancreatitis.

Hypovolaemia is the most common form of shock, and to some degree is a component of all other forms of shock. Absolute or relative hypovolemia must be excluded or treated in the management of the shocked state, regardless of cause.

question_text: What is the level of haemoglobin which requires blood transfusion in absence of an impending surgery?
explanation:
Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: <8g/dL

  • Blood transfusion is not routinely recommended for hemoglobin levels above 6g/dL unless there is significant symptomatology, active bleeding, or an underlying cardiovascular issue. A level of <8g/dL may be considered for transfusion in patients with comorbid conditions, but in general, <6g/dL is the threshold for transfusion in stable patients without active surgery or bleeding.

Choice C: <10g/dL

  • Transfusion at <10g/dL is generally not required in stable patients without major symptoms or ongoing bleeding. This level is usually associated with mild to moderate anemia, and transfusions are typically not indicated unless the patient has significant comorbidities or is symptomatic.

Choice D: 8-10g/dL

  • As stated earlier, transfusions are usually not necessary for hemoglobin levels between 8 and 10g/dL, unless there are other significant clinical factors like active bleeding or the patient is symptomatic.

Key Takeaway

  • A hemoglobin level of <6g/dL is the threshold at which blood transfusion is typically required in stable patients without imminent surgery.

question_text: In all types of shock, which of the following is observed?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Shock is characterised by reduced tissue perfusion, a fundamental feature across all types. This results in insufficient delivery of oxygen and nutrients to tissues, ultimately causing organ dysfunction.
  • Definition: A systemic condition marked by inadequate tissue perfusion that fails to meet the requirements for normal cellular respiration. (Option A)

Classification:

Explanation of Other Options:

Increased peripheral resistance (Option B): Seen in hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock due to vasoconstriction, but not universal - septic shock shows decreased resistance from vasodilation.

Decreased respiratory rate (Option C): May occur in severe hypovolemic or neurogenic shock, but tachypnea is far more common as compensation for low oxygen delivery.

Cold, clammy skin (Option D): Typical in hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock from vasoconstriction, but absent in septic shock, where skin is often warm and flushed.

Key Takeaways:

Physiological Hemodynamic Profiles in Shock

question_text: A female patient while washing clothes in cold water exhibits color changes of her hands from white to red. Which of the following drugs is best suited for this patient?

Raynaud's disease

  • This idiopathic condition usuallyoccurs in young women and affects the hands more than the feet. There isabnormal sensitivity in the arteriolar response to cold.
  • These vessels constrict andthe digits (usually the fingers) turn white and become incapable of fine movements. The capillaries then dilate and fill with slowly flowing deoxygenated blood, resulting in the digits becoming swollen and dusky.
  • As the attack passes off, the arterioles relax, oxygenated blood returns into the dilated capillaries and the digits become red. Thus, thecondition is recognised by the characteristic sequence of blanching, dusky cyanosis and red engorgement, often accompanied by pain. Superficial necrosis is very uncommon. This condition must be distinguished from Raynaud's syndrome, which has similar features .
  • Treatment of Raynaud's disease consists of protection from cold and avoidance of pulp and nail bed infection.Calcium antagonists, such as nifedipine, may also have a role to play and electrically heated gloves can be useful in winter. Sympathectomy has been used in the past but it is either ineffective or its effects are short-lived.

question_text: Which colloid is used in resuscitation as per the Muir & Barclay formula?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Muir & Barclay burn resuscitation protocol (widely used in some centres, especially historically in the UK) prescribes human albumin solution (4.5%) as the colloid component for the post-initial period.

The formula divides the first 36 hours into short epochs and prescribes colloid infusion (albumin) in addition to or instead of large crystalloid volumes. Modern practice varies (Parkland/crystalloid-based regimens are more common), but the Muir & Barclay regimen uses human albumin as the colloid.

question_text: Which of the following is characteristic of hypovolemic shock?
explanation:
Explanation:

In hypovolemic shock, there is significant loss of intravascular volume (e.g., due to hemorrhage, burns, vomiting, diarrhea). To maintain perfusion of vital organs, the body compensates by vasoconstriction, which increases systemic vascular resistance (SVR). This is the key hemodynamic hallmark.

Hemodynamic profile of hypovolemic shock:

  • ↓ Cardiac output (due to reduced preload and stroke volume)
  • ↑ Systemic vascular resistance (compensatory vasoconstriction)
  • ↓ Central venous pressure (due to low venous return)
  • ↓ Mean arterial pressure (if uncompensated)
  • ↓ Mixed venous oxygen saturation (due to impaired oxygen delivery) 

Physiological Hemodynamic Characteristics of Shock

Explanation of Other Options:

Decreased mixed venous saturation (Option D): In hypovolemic shock, oxygen delivery is impaired, and the blood returning to the heart has a lower oxygen saturation, which is reflected in a lower mixed venous oxygen saturation.

question_text: Which is the least commonly used graft for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG)?
explanation:
Explanation:

The intercostal artery is rarely employed as a graft in Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) because of its limited availability and potential risks. Instead, more commonly utilised grafts include the long saphenous vein, internal mammary artery, and radial artery.

Coronary Artery Bypass Graft (CABG):

  • A surgical procedure where a vascular graft is used to bypass blocked segments of coronary arteries, restoring blood supply to the myocardium.

Indications:

  • Triple vessel disease
  • Left main coronary artery stenosis
  • Chronic stable angina not responding to medical therapy
  • Angina with recurrent chest pain
  • Significant coronary artery obstruction (>70%)

Classification of Vascular Grafts:

1. Bioprosthetic Grafts:

  • Left Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA): Preferred graft for CABG. (Option B ruled out)
  • Long Saphenous Vein: Most frequently used in infra-inguinal procedures due to suitability for small and medium-sized vessels. (Option A ruled out)

2. Synthetic Grafts:

  • Dacron: Commonly utilised in supra-inguinal surgeries involving large vessels.
  • Polyurethane
  • Expanded Polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE)

Note:

  • Most preferred graft for CABG: LIMA (Left Internal Mammary Artery).
  • Most commonly used graft overall: Long Saphenous Vein - due to greater length and ease of handling.

The radial artery (Option D) serves as a frequently utilised graft in CABG procedures. It demonstrates long-term patency rates comparable to the internal mammary artery and is particularly advantageous for bypassing smaller coronary vessels. While it provides a reliable alternative to vein grafts, careful harvesting techniques and vigilant postoperative monitoring are necessary to minimise complications.

question_text: A patient presents with a tender pulsatile mass, as shown in the image below. What will be done next for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A tender pulsatile mass strongly suggests a vascular origin, most often an aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm.
  • Ultrasound Doppler is the most appropriate next step as it is non-invasive, readily available, and provides real-time information on blood flow.
  • It confirms whether the swelling is vascular and distinguishes between a true aneurysm and a pseudoaneurysm.
  • It also helps determine size, morphology, and the need for further advanced imaging such as CT angiography.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Needle aspiration (Option B): Aspiration is suited for fluid-filled collections like abscesses. Attempting it in a pulsatile swelling risks catastrophic hemorrhage if the mass is vascular.

CT angiogram with percutaneous management (Option C): This is a definitive imaging and treatment modality, but it is not the first step. Ultrasound Doppler must be performed first to establish the diagnosis before moving to CT.

Intravenous antibiotics for 7 days (Option D): Antibiotics are appropriate for cellulitis or abscesses, not for a vascular swelling like an aneurysm or pseudoaneurysm.

Key Takeaway:

A tender pulsatile swelling should first be assessed with Ultrasound Doppler to confirm vascular involvement and to differentiate a true aneurysm from a pseudoaneurysm before any invasive procedure is planned.

question_text: Which among the following is a false statement for physical structure of suture material?
option_b: Monofilament sutures have poor knotting ability
option_c: Multifilament sutures have good knotting ability
option_d: Multifilament sutures have less bacterial contamination
explanation:
Physical structure. Suture material may be monofilament or multifilament.

  • Monofilament suture material is smooth and tends to slide through tissues easily without any sawing action, but is more difficult to knot effectively.
  • Such material can be easily damaged by gripping it with needle holder or forceps and this can lead to fracture of the suture material.
  • Multifilament or braided sutures are much easier to knot, but have a surface area of several thousand times that of monofilament sutures and thus have a capillary action and interstices where bacteria may lodge and be responsible for persistent infection or sinuses.
  • In order to overcome some of these problems, certain materials are produced as a braided suture, which is coated with silicone in order to make it smooth.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 90

question_text: Which among the following component is not a dependable factor for strength of the suture material?
explanation:
Strength. The strength of a suture material depends upon its constituent material, its thickness and how it is handled in the tissues.

  • Suture material thickness is classified according to its diameter in tenths of a millimetre, although the figure assigned is also dependent upon the nature of the material, e.g. absorbable material and non-absorbable material, such as polypropylene, may differ in their designations.
  • The tensile strength of a suture can be expressed as the force required to break it when pulling the two ends apart, but is only a useful approximation as to its strength in the tissues, because what matters is the material’s in vivo strength.
  • Absorbable sutures show a decay of this strength with the passage of time and although a material may last in the tissues for the stated period in the manufacturer’s product profile, its tensile strength cannot be relied on in vivo for this entire period.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 90

question_text: Which among the following statements is false for biological behaviour of suture material?
option_c: Biological sutures causes less local irritation
option_d: Synthetic sutures have non carcinogenic property
explanation:
Biological behaviour. The biological behaviour of suture material within the tissues depends upon the constituent raw material.

  • Biological or natural sutures, such as catgut, are proteolysed, but this involves a process that is not entirely predictable and can cause local irritation, and such materials are therefore seldom used.
  • Synthetic polymers are hydrolysed and their disappearance in the tissues is more predictable.
  • However, the presence of pus, urine or faeces influences the final result and renders the outcome more unpredictable.
  • There is also some evidence that, in the gut, cancer cells may accumulate at sites where sutures persist, possibly giving rise to local recurrence.
  • For this reason, synthetic materials that have a greater predictability and elicit minimal tissue reaction may have an important non-carcinogenic property.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 91

explanation:
Explanation:

In laparoscopic surgery, the azimuth's angle refers to the angle between the optical (camera) port and a working port.

It is a key ergonomic parameter that determines instrument triangulation, ease of visualization, and surgeon comfortduring minimally invasive surgery.

  • Ensures proper triangulation between camera and instruments.
  • Minimizes instrument collision (clashing).
  • Provides optimal depth perception and hand-eye coordination.
  • Enhances precision in dissection and suturing.

Explanation of Other Options:

  • May conceptually refer to instrument crossing, which is undesirable (causes poor control).

question_text: Mayo's repair for umbilical hernia is usually performed for how much centimetre radius of defect?
explanation:
• Mayo's repair for umbilical hernia repair is done for defect size of 2 cm diameter. So, in radius it is 1 cm of defect size.
  • Very small defects less than 1 cm in size may be closed with a simple figure-of-eight suture, or repaired by a darn technique where a non-absorbable, monofilament suture is crisscrossed across the defect and anchored firmly to the fascia all around.
  • Defects up to 2 cm in diameter may be sutured primarily with minimal tension, although, the larger the defect, the more tension and the more likely it is that mesh reinforcement will be beneficial.
  • The classic repair was described by Mayo. A transverse incision is made and the hernia sac dissected, opened and its content reduced. Any non-viable tissue is removed, sometimes involving bowel resection. The peritoneum is closed. The tissue is double breasted. Non-absorbable sutures are used. There is often a large subcutaneous space. A suction drain is placed. The skin is closed but stretched or redundant skin may need to be excised (apronectomy) to achieve a better cosmetic result.
  • For defects larger than 2 cm in diameter, mesh repair is recommended.

The Mayo repair remains popular for defects up to 2 cm, but the larger the defect the more tissue tension. Current evidence advises the use of mesh even in small defects, and certainly for all defects larger than 2 cm, owing to the high likelihood of recurrence.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1073

question_text: In a post-operative intensive care unit, 5 patients developed postoperative wound infection on the same wound. The best method to prevent cross infection occurring in other patients in the same ward is to:
option_a: Give antibiotics to all other patients in the ward
option_c: Disinfect the ward with sodium hypochlorite
explanation:
Hand hygiene is a way of cleaning one's hands that substantially reduces potential pathogens (harmful microorganisms) on the hands. Hand hygiene is considered a primary measure for reducing the risk of transmitting infection among patients and health care personnel. Hand hygiene procedures include the use of alcohol-based hand rubs (containing 60%-95% alcohol) and hand washing with soap and water. For surgical procedures, perform a surgical hand scrub before putting on sterile surgeon's gloves. For routine dental examinations and nonsurgical procedures, use an alcohol-based hand rub or use water and plain or antimicrobial soap specific for health care settings. Unless hands are visibly soiled (e.g. dirt, blood, body fluids), an alcohol-based hand rub is preferred over soap and water in most clinical situations.

Hand hygiene should be performed in the following situations:

  • Before and after treating each patient (e.g., before and after gloving).
  • After touching with bare hands instruments, equipment, materials, and other objects that are likely to be contaminated by blood, saliva, or respiratory secretions.
  • Before leaving the dental treatment area.
  • When hands are visibly soiled.
  • Before regloving and after removing gloves that are torn, cut, or punctured.

Reference: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page Number-61.

explanation:
Circumcision, being the removal of the foreskin, is the oldest and most common surgical procedure and is usually performed for cultural reasons. About 40% of males worldwide are circumcised. Circumcision is performed in

Judaism, on day 8 of life (brit milah), and in Islam (khitan), at varying ages. In early infancy, circumcision can be performed under local anaesthesia using simple devices like the PlastiBell or Gomco clamp. In older boys under general anaesthesia, the foreskin is removed with a blade or scissors, followed by attention to haemostasis and skin apposition with sutures or glue. Complications include bleeding, dehiscence, infection, cicatrix, adhesion formation, meatal stenosis, the removal of too little or too much tissue, cosmetic concerns and rarely urethral injury or amputation.

question_text: What type of material is used in the mesh used in Lichtenstein hernioplasty?
explanation:
Explanation:

In Lichtenstein hernioplasty, a polypropylene mesh is placed to strengthen the abdominal wall and reduce the risk of hernia recurrence. The mesh is favoured because it is long-lasting and causes only a minimal tissue reaction, making it a reliable choice for hernia repair.

Management of Inguinal Hernia:

Surgical Methods:

  • Herniotomy:
    • Removal and closure of the hernia sac.
    • Primarily performed in children with indirect hernias and congenital hydrocele.
    • In adults, herniotomy alone has a high risk of recurrence.
  • Hernioplasty:
    • Herniotomy combined with strengthening of the inguinal floor using a mesh.
  • Herniorrhaphy:
    • Herniotomy with repair of the inguinal floor using sutures instead of mesh.

Common Techniques:

  • Bassini's Repair:
    • Internal oblique, transversus abdominis, and fascia transversalis are sutured to the inguinal ligament (triple-layer closure).
    • Higher recurrence rate compared to modern methods.
  • Shouldice Repair:
    • Four-layer reconstruction involving double breasting of fascia transversalis.
    • Lower recurrence than Bassini's repair.
  • Modified Shouldice Repair:
    • Six-layer reinforcement for additional support.

Anterior Tension-Free Mesh Repair:

  • Lichtenstein Repair:
    • A tension-free technique that reinforces the inguinal floor using a flat polypropylene mesh.
    • Considered the gold standard because it reduces recurrence and allows quicker recovery.

Open Preperitoneal Mesh Repair:

  • Stoppa Repair:
    • Involves placement of a large mesh behind the peritoneum.
    • Frequently used in recurrent inguinal hernias.

Laparoscopic Techniques:

  • Totally Extraperitoneal (TEP) Repair
  • Transabdominal Preperitoneal (TAPP) Repair

Explanation of Other Options:

Polyglactin (Option B) and Polydioxanone (Option C): Absorbable sutures, not used for mesh.

Polyacrylamide (Option D): Hydrophilic biomaterial, not used in hernia repair mesh.

question_text: What is the instrument of choice for creating pneumoperitoneum in the closed technique of laparoscopic procedures?
explanation:
Explanation:

Abdominal Access Techniques in Laparoscopic Surgery

Two primary methods are used to establish abdominal access during laparoscopic procedures:

Direct Puncture Technique (Veress Needle Technique)

  • The relaxed abdominal wall is elevated using either two towel clips or a well-placed hand.
  • A small incision is made at the umbilicus, the preferred access point due to the thinness of the abdominal wall, even in obese individuals.
  • A Veress needle, which is spring-loaded, is introduced into the abdominal cavity. Two distinct "pops" are typically felt as the needle passes through the fascia and peritoneum.
  • The abdomen is then insufflated using a pressure-limited insufflator to establish pneumoperitoneum.

Direct Peritoneal Access (Hasson Technique)

  • A small infraumbilical incision is made under direct vision to expose the abdominal fascia.
  • Two Kocher clamps are used to grasp the fascia, and curved Mayo scissors are used to incise both fascia and peritoneum.
  • A finger is inserted to check for any adherent bowel.
  • Stay sutures are placed on each side of the fascia and tied to the wings of a blunt-tipped Hasson trocar, which is inserted directly.
  • Rapid insufflation compensates for time spent on dissection.
  • This technique is particularly preferred in patients with prior abdominal surgeries, where the risk of bowel adhesions is higher.

Explanation of other options:

Hegar's dilator (Option B): Used for cervical dilation in gynecological procedures, not for laparoscopic access.

Karman's cannula (Option C): A flexible suction cannula used primarily for uterine evacuation, not for laparoscopic entry.

Hassan's cannula (Option D): Used in the open technique of laparoscopic access, not the initial blind access with a Veress needle.

Though also used in laparoscopy, it is not the instrument of choice in the closed (blind) method, which the question emphasizes.

Key Takeaways:

Veress needle is the instrument of choice for creating pneumoperitoneum in the closed technique of laparoscopic procedures.

CORROSIVE INJURY

  • Alkalis cause liquefaction, saponification of fats, dehydration and thrombosis of blood vessels which usually leads to fibrous scarring. Acids cause coagulative necrosis with eschar formation, and this coagulant may limit penetration to deeper layers of the oesophageal wall.
  • The key to management is early endoscopy by an experienced endoscopist to inspect the whole of the oesophagus and stomach.
  • Deep ulcers and the recognition of a grey or black eschar signify the most severe lesions with the greatest risk of perforation.
  • Minor injuries with only oedema of the mucosa resolve rapidly with no late sequelae. These patients can safely be fed.

  • Oesophageal replacement is usually required for very long or multiple strictures. Resection can be difficult because of periesophageal inflammation in these patients.

CORROSIVE INJURY OF THE OESOPHAGOUS

explanation:

Tumour staging

The treatment and prognosis of RCC depends on its pathological staging. The most important factors are the size of the tumour and whether it is confined within the renal capsule and Gerota's fascia. Involvement of the lymph nodes, renal sinus and vein wall are associated with a poorer prognosis than the presence of tumour thrombus in the renal vein or IVC. Currently the most commonly used system for staging RCC is the TNM classification.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1483.

question_text: Most common type of arrhythmia in postoperative CABG patient is?
explanation:
• The most common postoperative arrhythmia is sinus tachycardia, closely followed by atrial fibrillation (AF).
  • It occurs in around 30% of patients undergoing CABG and often spontaneously reverts to sinus rhythm. Treatment includes correction of potassium (>4.5 mmol/L), the use of β-blockers, amiodarone or digoxin and, if necessary, cardioversion. Bradycardia is seldom seen, but temporary pacing via epicardial pacing wires inserted intraoperatively may be required in the postoperative period.

question_text: Most common primary mediastinum tumour is?
explanation:
Thymoma, neurogenic tumours, germ cell tumours and lymphoma are the usual primary tumours of the mediastinum.

  • Thymoma. This is the most common mediastinal tumour, accounting for 25% of the total, and is derived from the thymus gland.
  • Thymomas vary in behaviour from benign to aggressively invasive, as reflected in the Masoaka classification system used to stage thymomas.
  • They are often related to mysthenia gravis (MG), a neuromusclar condition which can have a high associated incidence of thymomas, and interestingly may respond to excision of the thymus gland even when the gland has no associated thymoma present.
  • The only reliable indicator of malignancy is capsular invasion. Diagnosis and treatment are best achieved by complete thymectomy, which is usually performed as a median sternotomy.
  • However, if the thymoma is small or when the patient has MG and the thymus is being excised as a treatment, a transcervical approach with or without an additional VATS procedure can be performed.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 59, Cardiac Surgery, Pg: 992.

question_text: Which is the gold standard test for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease?
explanation:
Diagnosis

  • In most cases, the diagnosis is assumed rather than proven, and treatment is empirical.
  • Investigation is required only when the diagnosis is in doubt, when the patient does not respond to a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) or if dysphagia is present.
  • The most appropriate examination is endoscopy with biopsy. If the typical appearance of reflux oesophagitis, peptic stricture or Barrett’s oesophagus is seen, the diagnosis is clinched, but visible oesophagitis is not always present, even in patients selected as above.
  • In patients with atypical or persistent symptoms despite therapy, oesophageal manometry and 24-hour oesophageal pH recording (ideally with impedance measurement) may be justified to establish the diagnosis and guide management.
  • As a matter of routine, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are stopped 1 week before oesophageal pH recording, but acid secretion is sometimes reduced for 2 weeks or more
  • Manometry and pH recording are essential in patients being considered for antireflux surgery. Although the main purpose of the test is objectively to quantify the extent of reflux disease, it is also used to rule out a diagnosis of achalasia. Patients with achalasia can also have an abnormal pH study as a result of fermentation of food residue in a dilated oesophagus. Usually, the form of the pH trace is different from that of GORD, with slow undulations of pH rather than rapid bursts of reflux, but the complete absence of peristalsis on manometry is pathognomonic of achalasia

In patients with atypical or persistent symptoms despite PPI therapy, oesophageal manometry and ambulatory pH recording (with or without impedance measurement) are justified to establish the diagnosis and guide management. In patients considered for surgery, it is also prudent to have objective proof of significant reflux before embarking on a potentially irreversible invasive procedure.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1114

question_text: Label the diagram correctly for mechanism of intussusception
explanation:
Pathology

An intussusception is composed of three parts:

  • The entering or inner tube (intussusceptum);
  • The returning or middle tube;
  • The sheath or outer tube (intussuscipiens).

The part that advances is the apex, the mass is the intussusception and the neck is the junction of the entering layer with the mass. Intussusception may be anatomically defined according to the site and extent of invagination. In most children, the intussusception is ileocolic. In adults, colocolic intussusception is more common.

The degree of ischaemia is dependent on the tightness of the invagination, which is usually greatest as it passes through the ileocaecal valve.

On CT scanning the target sign may be evident and if present is pathognomonic.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1379

question_text: Which layer of the cyst forms the germinal membrane in hydatid cyst?
explanation:
• Three weeks after infection, a visible hydatid cyst develops, which then slowly grows in a spherical manner
  • A pericyst or fibrous capsule derived from host tissues develops around the hydatid cyst
  • The cyst wall itself has two layers, an outer gelatinous membrane (ectocyst) and an inner germinal membrane (endocyst).
  • Brood capsules are small, intracystic cellular masses in which future worm heads develop into scoleces.
  • In a definitive host, the scoleces develop into an adult tapeworm; but in the intermediate host, they can differentiate only into a new hydatid cyst.
  • Freed brood capsules and scoleces are found in the hydatid fluid and form the so- called hydatid Daughter cysts are true replicas of the mother cyst. Hydatid cysts can die with degeneration of the membranes, development of cystic vacuoles, and calcification of the wall. Calcification of a hydatid cyst, however, does not always imply that the cyst is dead.

Reference: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1460

question_text: What is the route of infection of entamoeba histolytica in a case amoebic liver abscess?

  • Ingestion of E. histolytica cysts through a fecal-oral route is the cause of amebiasis.
  • Humans are the principal host, and the main source of infection is human contact with a cyst-passing carrier.
  • Contaminated water and vegetables are also routes of human infection.
  • Once ingested, the cysts are not degraded in the stomach and pass to the intestines, where the trophozoite is released and passed on to the colon.
  • In the colon, the trophozoite can invade mucosa, resulting in disease.

question_text: Your friend is teaching you about Enhanced Recovery After Surgery (ERAS). Which of the following statements made by him is inaccurate?
option_b: Epidural anaesthesia recommended in laparoscopic surgery for pain control
option_c: Reduction of hospital stay by 2-3 weeks
option_d: Beta-blockers are given after major surgery done under general anaesthesia to improve the outcome
explanation:
Explanation of Correct Answer:

ERAS protocols are designed to reduce the stress response to surgery, optimize recovery, and shorten hospital stay.

  • A key principle of ERAS is to minimize preoperative fasting, because prolonged fasting:
    • Causes insulin resistance,
    • Leads to catabolism and protein loss,
    • Increases postoperative nausea and fatigue,
    • Worsens patient discomfort (hunger, thirst, anxiety).

Hence, prolonged fasting is not recommended.

  • It allows a light meal up to six hours before surgery and clear fluids up to two hours prior.
  • It also includes carbohydrate-rich drinks up to two hours before the procedure as it helps reduce postoperative insulin resistance, preserve muscle mass, minimize protein loss, and alleviate preoperative thirst, hunger, and anxiety.
  • ERAS is a set of evidence-based guidelines aimed at improving recovery after surgery.
  • It focuses on optimising preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative care to speed up recovery, reduce complications, and shorten hospital stays.

Explanation of Other Options:

Epidural anaesthesia recommended in laparoscopic surgery for pain control (Option B):

  • Epidural analgesia or multimodal pain control is a key component of ERAS.
  • Reduces opioid requirement, improves gut motility and mobilization.
  • Especially useful for open and laparoscopic colorectal, urologic, and gynecologic surgeries.

Reduction of hospital stay by 2-3 weeks (Option C):

  • ERAS reduces hospital stay, but typically by 2–3 days, not weeks.
  • The statement exaggerates the time frame, but the concept (shorter stay) is correct.

Beta-blockers are given after major surgery done under general anaesthesia to improve outcome (Option D):

  • Continued perioperative β-blockade reduces cardiovascular complications (e.g., MI, arrhythmia).
  • Helps maintain hemodynamic stability
  • Especially beneficial in cardiac and vascular surgery

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: All of the following are shunt complications except?

  • The slit ventricle syndrome occurs in children treated with shunts, whose ventricles and subarachnoid spaces are underdeveloped, resulting in poor brain compliance. In these patients normal fluctuations in ICP are exaggerated so that coughing and straining may cause symptoms of raised ICP.
  • Shunts are vulnerable to disconnection, infection and blockage.

question_text: All of the following are correct regarding tuberculous infection of CNS except
option_a: It represents hematogenous spread from primary pulmonary foci
option_b: TB meningitis commonly affects young children
option_c: Tuberculoma is discrete tumour like granuloma at base of the cerebral hemispheres
option_d: Tuberculous abscess is predominantly in immune competent host
explanation:
• Tuberculosis (TB) infection of the central nervous system (CNS) represents haematogenous spread from primary pulmonary foci.
  • A high index of suspicion is required, especially when population or individual risk factors are present.
  • TB can result in a diverse but overlapping spectrum of pathology, including in the head:
    • Tuberculous meningitis - this commonly affects young children; CT demonstrates intense meningeal enhancement, and hydrocephalus is a common sequela;
    • Tuberculoma - discrete tumour-like granulomas at the base of the cerebral hemispheres, presenting with mass effect;
    • Tuberculous abscess - seen predominantly in immunocompromised hosts, this represents progression of a tuberculoma with prominent central caseating necrosis;
    • Miliary tuberculosis - describes a diffuse distribution of multiple small tuberculomas through brain substance.
    • Where the meninges are involved, lymphocytes can be expected to predominate in the CSF, rather than the polymorphs seen with other bacterial meningitides.
    • The increase in protein content and reduction in glucose concentration are also less marked.
    • Ziehl-Nielsen staining for mycobacteria is frequently negative, and polymerase chain reaction testing offers relatively rapid diagnosis compared to culture for acid-fast bacilli which may take weeks.
    • A 20-30 mL CSF sample allows spinning to increase the culture yield.
    • Management is with anti-tuberculous therapy; hydrocephalus may require shunt insertion.

question_text: Which stents are recently used in TIPS procedure?

This is done to alleviate complications of portal hypertension, such as esophageal varices.

One of the major complication limiting the usage of TIPS is stent stenosis and stent thrombosis. This is due to intimal hyperplasia of the metallic stent.

Use of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)-covered stents helps in overcoming this. PTFE stents have higher patency rates over time and reduced mortality rates.

question_text: A 28-year-old primigravida presents in the third trimester with a history of polyhydramnios. Soon after delivery, the neonate develops severe respiratory distress and central cyanosis, with a scaphoid abdomen and poor air entry on the left side. Auscultation reveals bowel sounds in the left hemithorax. Which of the following congenital anomalies best explains these findings?
explanation:
Explanation:

The neonate presents with features of respiratory distress, scaphoid abdomen, mediastinal shift, and bowel sounds in the chest. The X-ray confirming bowel loops above the diaphragm is diagnostic of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH), most commonly a Bochdalek hernia.

CDH is caused by a developmental defect in the diaphragm, usually due to failure of closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal, leading to herniation of abdominal viscera into the thoracic cavity. This interferes with normal lung growth, causing pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension, which are the main causes of mortality.

  • Most common side:Left (≈84%) because the left pleuroperitoneal canal closes later and the liver protects the right side.
  • Common associations:Polyhydramnios (due to impaired fetal swallowing), low lung-to-head ratio (LHR), and abnormal fetal liver position

Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia (CDH):

Types of CDH:

  1. Bochdalek hernia- Posterolateral defect (most common, left-sided). Involves herniation of stomach, small intestine, spleen.
  2. Morgagni hernia- Anteromedial defect through the foramen of Morgagni. Less common, usually right-sided, often asymptomatic and incidental.

Clinical Features:

  • Respiratory distress immediately after birth.
  • Scaphoid (sunken) abdomen.
  • Cyanosis refractory to oxygen therapy (due to pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension).
  • Mediastinal shift on imaging.

Diagnostic Tools:

  • Prenatal:Ultrasound, MRI (showing abdominal viscera in chest, polyhydramnios, abnormal liver position).
  • Postnatal:X-ray showing bowel loops in thorax with mediastinal shift and absence of diaphragmatic outline.

Management:

  • Immediate endotracheal intubation (avoid bag-mask ventilation as it worsens bowel distension).
  • Gastric decompression with nasogastric tube.
  • Stabilization (ventilation, nitric oxide for pulmonary hypertension, ECMO in refractory cases).
  • Definitive surgery after stabilization- reduction of herniated contents and repair of diaphragmatic defect.

Explanation of Other Options:

Tetralogy of Fallot (Option B): Cyanotic congenital heart disease with features of right ventricular outflow obstruction and 'boot-shaped' heart on X-ray. No bowel sounds in chest.

Transposition of the Great Vessels (Option C): Cyanotic newborn with X-ray showing 'egg-on-a-string' cardiac silhouette due to narrow mediastinum. No scaphoid abdomen or bowel in thorax.

Tracheoesophageal Fistula (Option D): Presents with excessive salivation, choking, cyanosis on feeding, and X-ray showing coiled NG tube in the upper pouch. No mediastinal shift or bowel in chest.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: What methods can be used for infusion of cardioplegic solution for myocardial protection?
option_c: Intermittent cross clamp fibrillation and total circulatory arrest
explanation:
• The methods of myocardial protection include intracoronary infusion of a cardioplegic solution (antegrade), infusion via the coronary sinus (retrograde), intermittent cross-clamp fibrillation and total circulatory arrest.
  • Intermittent cross-clamp fibrillation is a technique in which intermittent ventricular fibrillation is induced by a small electrical charge. The heart does not eject and is relatively still but not bloodless. The aorta is cross-clamped to render the heart ischaemic. The heart can tolerate short periods (10-20 min) of ischaemia, provided the heart is reperfused when the cross-clamp is released and allowed to beat following cardioversion for short periods during the operation.
  • Total circulatory arrest becomes necessary when visibility and clarity of the operative area is crucial, as in paediatric surgery or in surgery of the ascending aorta and arch of the aorta. CPB is instituted and the core body temperature reduced to 15-18°C (profound hypothermia). The metabolic rate of all organs of the body is reduced by 50% with every 7°C drop in temperature. Using this technique, circulatory arrest can be tolerated for up to 20-30 min. Additional cerebral protection can be provided with ice packs placed around the head, pharmacological agents and cerebral perfusion techniques.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 59, Cardiac Surgery, Pg: 945 -946

question_text: A 5 years old child was brought to the hospital with a history of constipation. After taking stool softeners, the child was able to pass on only one stool in a week. There was a history of passage of meconium after 48 hours of birth. Which of the following should be done in this child?
option_a: Ask the mother to give high fiber diet
explanation:
Case suggest Hirschsprung's disease

  • Genetic defects (e.g.RET, EDNRB, EDN3) can affect the migration of neural crest-derived intestinal neurons (neurocristopathy), leading to aganglionosis and thickened nerve trunks in the distal bowel.
  • There may be a family history. Aganglionic bowel fails to relax, causing a functional obstruction. A transition zone lies between dilated, proximal, normal bowel and narrow, distal aganglionic bowel.

  • Neonatal Hirschsprung's disease presents with delayed passage of meconium, abdominal distension and bilious vomiting requiring resuscitation, gastric decompression, antibiotics and a bowel washout.
  • The diagnosis is made on a cot-side suction rectal biopsy. A contrast enema may show the narrow aganglionic segment, a cone and dilated proximal bowel .
  • Definitive surgery removes the aganglionic segment and brings ganglionic bowel to the anus; Swenson, Duhamel, Yancey-Soave and transanal 'pull-throughs' are options. Most children achieve reasonable bowel control, but some have residual constipation, incontinence or episodes of enterocolitis.

question_text: Secondary causes of severe constipation in children except?
explanation:
CONSTIPATION

  • The passage of hard or infrequent stools is common in children in the West.
  • Severe constipation may be secondary to an anal fissure, Hirschsprung’s disease, an anorectal malformation or a neuropathic bowel. A detailed history and examination of the abdomen, anus and spine will identify most causes.

question_text: Identify the pathology in the given radiograph of a newborn.
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation and radiograph are classic for imperforate anus (anorectal malformation). In a newborn, the absence of gas in the rectal pouch on a prone cross-table lateral radiograph (invertogram) is a key diagnostic finding. This indicates a distal obstruction due to the lack of a patent anal opening. The associated abdominal distension is due to the inability to pass meconium.

Anorectal malformations (ARM) result from imperfect fusion of the post-allantoic gut with the proctodaeum and occur in 1 in 4500 newborns, often associated with VACTERL anomalies (vertebral, anorectal, cardiac, tracheoesophageal, renal, limb, spinal). In males, the common type is a rectobulbar fistula, while in females it is a rectovestibular fistula.

Diagnosis involves Wangensteen's invertogram (rectal pouch level relative to Stephen's line), Murugassu's technique(meconium aspiration and dye injection), along with USG abdomen, echocardiography, and MRI spine to evaluate associated anomalies.

Treatment depends on fistula level:

  • Low fistula: Single-stage procedures such as anoplasty, anovestibuloplasty, anal dilation, or membrane incision with excellent prognosis.
  • High fistula: Requires staged repair initial colostomy, followed by posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP)(definitive pull-through), and later colostomy closure.

Complications include infection, fecal fistula, stenosis, colitis, malnutrition, and fecal incontinence.

Explanation of other options:

Meningocele (Option A): This is a neural tube defect involving herniation of meninges through a spinal defect. It is not diagnosed with an abdominal radiograph and does not cause gasless rectum or abdominal distension.

Congenital megacolon (Hirschsprung's disease) (Option C): While this causes distal obstruction and distension, gas is typically visible in the rectum and sigmoid colon proximal to the aganglionic segment. A contrast enema is diagnostic, not a plain film.

Pyloric stenosis (Option D): This causes non-bilious projectile vomiting in infants aged 2-8 weeks, not failure to pass meconium at birth. Diagnosis is made by ultrasound, not plain abdominal film.

Key Takeaways:

  • Failure to pass meconium within 24-48 hours of birth suggests anorectal malformation.
  • A prone cross-table lateral radiograph (invertogram) assesses the level of the rectal pouch.

question_text: MEN 2 A true is/are
option_b: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is a hallmark of MEN 2 B
explanation:
• Other conditions that occur within MEN2A include cutaneous lichen amyloidosis and Hirschsprung disease.
  • Cutaneous lichen amyloidosis is uncommon and typically occurs with codon 634 mutations. It is characterized by the symptom of pruritus and it is thought that repeated scratching then leads to amyloid deposition in the papillary dermis of the skin. As a result, patients develop cutaneous plaques, often located on the back.
  • Hirschsprung disease may also occur in patients with either MEN2A or FMTC.
  • MEN2A is the most common subtype of the MEN2 syndromes, comprising the majority of cases.
  • The hallmark characteristic of MEN2A is the development of MTC, with a greater than 90% penetrance.
  • In addition to MTC, pheochromocytoma develops in 50% to 60% of patients and PHPT in up to 30% with both adrenal glands and all parathyroid glands at risk.
  • The degree of penetrance of each tumor type is associated with specific codon mutations, and all patients are at risk for the development of multiple tumors within each endocrine organ, including multifocal MTC.
  • Patients with MEN2A have a normal physical appearance and body habitus, unlike those with MEN2B that are associated with a Marfanoid habitus and neurofibromas of the tongue.

Reference: Sabinston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION VIII ENDOCRINE, Chapter 41, The Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia Syndromes, Pg: 1005.

question_text: Which is the first line investigation for oesophageal cancer?
explanation:
Investigation

  • Endoscopy is the first-line investigation for most patients. It provides an unrivalled direct view of the oesophageal mucosa and any lesion allowing its site and size to be documented.
  • Cytology and/or histology specimens taken via the endoscope are crucial for accurate diagnosis. The combination of histology and cytology increases the diagnostic accuracy to more than 95%.
  • The chief limitation of conventional endoscopy is that only the mucosal surface can be studied and biopsied. Other investigations are therefore usually required to define the extent of local or distant spread.
  • The improved image resolution of modern endoscopes and novel techniques involving magnification and the use of dyes to enhance surface detail may lead to more early lesions being recognised.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1136-1137

question_text: A chronic smoker was undergoing major surgery under general anesthesia with oxygen and nitrous oxide. Suddenly he collapsed on the table and breath sounds were not heard on left side chest. What will be the cause?
explanation:
Pneumothorax is the presence of air outside the lung, within the pleural space. It must be distinguished from bullae or air cysts within the lung. Bullae can be the cause of an air leak from the lung and can therefore coexist with pneumothorax.


  • Spontaneous pneumothorax occurs when the visceral pleura ruptures without an external traumatic or iatrogenic cause.
  • Cases are divided into primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) and secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP).
  • Pneumothorax can also occur following trauma or iatrogenic injury such as insertion of a central line. Tension pneumothorax is when (independent of etiology) there is a build-up of positive pressure within the hemithorax, to the extent that the lung is completely collapsed, the diaphragm is fattened, the mediastinum is distorted and, eventually, the venous return to the heart is compromised.
  • Triad of tension pneumothorax:
    1. Raised JVP
    2. Hypotension
    3. Absent breath sounds

  • Surgical emphysema is the presence of air in the tissues. It requires a breach of an air-containing viscous in communication with soft tissues, and the generation of positive pressure to push the air along tissue planes. The most serious cause is a ruptured esophagus.
  • Mediastinal surgical emphysema can also occur with asthma or barotrauma from positive-pressure ventilation. A poorly managed chest drain, with intermittent build-up of pressure, allows air to track into the chest wall through the point where the drain breaches the parietal pleura.

    Immediate management of tension pneumothorax: needle decompression in

    1. Adults: 5th intercostal space midaxillary line
    2. Children: 2nd intercostal space mid clavicular line

    Definitive management: ICD tube insertion in 5th intercostal space midaxillary line in triangle of safety

    Indications for surgical intervention for pneumothorax

    include:

    • Second ipsilateral pneumothorax
    • First contralateral pneumothorax
    • Bilateral spontaneous pneumothorax
    • Pneumothorax fails to settle despite chest drainage
    • Spontaneous haemothorax: professions at risk (e.g. pilots, divers)
    • Pregnancy

question_text: Which among the following statements is false for sigmoid colon?
option_a: It begins at the level of iliac crest
option_c: It is approximately 38 cm in length
option_d: It is thicker and mobile than the descending colon
explanation:
• The sigmoid colon begins at or below the level of the iliac crest, where the colon becomes completely intraperitoneal again, acquiring a mesentery covered on both sides with peritoneum.
  • The sigmoid is thicker and more mobile compared to the descending colon varying in length from 15 to 50 cm (average, 38 cm).
  • The mobile portion of the sigmoid colon is attached by the sigmoid mesocolon to the posterior abdominal wall and pelvis in the pattern of an inverted V creating the intersigmoid fossa.
  • When mobilizing the sigmoid colon, this mesenteric fold is a surgical landmark for the underlying left ureter.
  • The sigmoid colon ends at the rectosigmoid junction, which is recognized as the point where the colonic taeniae confluence to form a complete longitudinal muscle layer, and the colon loses its mesentery, usually between the level of the sacral promontory and the S3 vertebra.

question_text: What is the position of deep inguinal ring clinically?
option_a: 2.5 cm above the midpoint of anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis
option_b: 2.5 cm above the midpoint of anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle
option_c: 1 cm above the midpoint of anterior superior iliac spine and pubic symphysis
option_d: 1 cm above the midpoint of anterior superior iliac spine and pubic tubercle
explanation:
• Deep ring is located 1 cm above the midpoint of inguinal ligament, that extends from ASIS to Pubic tubercle
  • As the testis descends from the abdominal cavity to the scrotum in males it first passes through a defect called the deep inguinal ring in the transversalis fascia, just deep to the abdominal muscles.
  • This ring lies midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, approximately 2-3 cm above the femoral artery pulse in the groin.
  • The inferior epigastric vessels lie just medial to the deep inguinal ring, passing from the iliac vessels to rectus abdominis.
  • Muscle fibres of the innermost two layers of the lateral abdominal wall, the transversus muscle and the internal oblique muscle, arch over the deep inguinal ring from lateral to medial before descending to become attached to the pubic tubercle.
  • These two muscles fuse and become tendinous, hence this arch is referred to as the conjoint tendon. Below this arch there is no muscle but only transversalis fascia and external oblique aponeurosis, resulting in weakness.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1065-1066

question_text: During thyroid surgery, which of the following nerve injuries is considered the most dangerous or life-threatening?
explanation:
Explanation:

The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) supplies all intrinsic muscles of the larynx except the cricothyroid.
These muscles are essential for vocal cord movement and airway protection.

Complete bilateral RLN injury results in paralysis of both vocal cords in the paramedian position → causing:

  • Severe airway obstruction
  • Inspiratory stridor
  • Respiratory distress
  • Potential fatality without prompt airway management (intubation or tracheostomy)

Hence, bilateral complete RLN palsy is the most lethal nerve injury during thyroid surgery.

  • Unilateral injury is generally less dangerous than bilateral injury because the contralateral vocal cord can compensate to a significant degree. (Options A & C ruled out)
  • The individual may experience hoarseness or aspiration of fluids through the glottis.
  • Partial injury typically does not lead to significant airway compromise. (Option B ruled out)

question_text: What is the usual age of occurrence of fibroadenoma?
explanation:
Fibroadenoma

  • These usually arise in the fully developed breast between the ages of 15 and 25 years, although occasionally they occur in much older women.
  • They arise from hyperplasia of a single lobule and usually grow up to 2-3 cm in size.
  • They are surrounded by a well-marked capsule and can thus be enucleated through a cosmetically appropriate incision.
  • Does not require excision unless associated with suspicious cytology, it becomes very large or the patient expressly desires the lump to be removed.
  • Alternatives to surgery include cryoablation, heating with high-frequency ultrasound (echotherapy) or removal with a large core vacuum biopsy system.
  • A biopsy should be obtained if the patient is over 25 or there are any atypical features on ultrasound.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28th, Pg: 922

question_text: Where does the recurrent laryngeal nerve insert the thyroid gland?
explanation:
• The nerve runs posterior to the thyroid and enters the larynx at the cricothyroid joint.
  • This entry point is at the level of Berry's ligament, a condensation of pretracheal fascia that binds the thyroid to the trachea.
  • This is the point at which the nerve is at most risk of injury during surgery.
  • In terms of surgical anatomy, the nerve can be located in the tracheoesophageal groove where it forms one side of Beahrs' triangle (the other two sides are the carotid artery and the inferior thyroid artery) or at the cricothyroid joint.
  • The nerve will normally be found as the thyroid lobe is mobilised laterally, lying under the most posterolateral portion of the gland called the tubercle of Zuckerkandl.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 851-852

explanation:

  • However, it has been reported that widespread liberal CT use is responsible for 1.5-2.0% of all cancers in the USA. Of interest, WBCT equates to 76 chest x-rays or 6 months of background radiation.

question_text: What is the margin of resection in oesophageal cancer?
explanation:
PRINCIPLES

  • The principle of oesophagectomy is to deal adequately with the local tumour in order to minimise the risk of local recurrence and achieve an adequate lymphadenectomy to reduce the risk of staging error.
  • Although studies in Japan would indicate that more extensive lymphadenectomy is associated with better survival, this may simply reflect more accurate staging.
  • A number of studies support the view that the proximal extent of resection should ideally be 10 cm above the macroscopic tumour and 5 cm distal.
  • When such a margin cannot be achieved proximally, particularly with squamous cell carcinoma, there is evidence that postoperative radiotherapy can minimise local recurrence, although this does not improve survival.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1141

question_text: Where is the BRCA 2 gene located?
explanation:
BRCA2 gene-

  • Located on chromosome 13.
  • Accounts for 30% of familial breast cancers.
  • In contrast to BRCA1, BRCA2 is associated with increased breast cancer risk in men.
  • Women with a mutation in BRCA2 also have a 20% to 30% lifetime risk for ovarian cancer.
  • Founder mutations of BRCA2 include the 617delT mutation (in Ashkenazi population), 8765delAG mutation (in French Canadian population), and 999del15 mutation (in Icelandic population).

question_text: Which among the following is not the indication of haemorrhoidectomy?
explanation:
INDICATIONS

The indications for haemorrhoidectomy include:

  • third- and fourth-degree haemorrhoids;
  • second-degree haemorrhoids that have not been cured by non-operative treatments;
  • fibrosed haemorrhoids;
  • interno-external haemorrhoids when the external haemorrhoid is well defined.
  • If there is any doubt about the diagnosis of haemorrhoids, examination under anaesthesia and, if indicated, biopsy, are necessary.
  • The other strong indication for surgery is haemorrhoidal bleeding sufficient to cause anaemia. Beyond these, the indications summarised above are more relative than absolute, because in these situations surgery aims simply to improve symptoms and, of course, is not without risk.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 80, Edition 28th, Pg: 1431

question_text: What is the average daily iodine requirement for adult human?
explanation:
• Iodine plays a primary role in thyroid hormone physiology, and it is predicated on there being an adequate supply in the body.
  • The average daily iodine requirement for adult humans is 0.1 mg, and this is entirely derived from dietary intake.
  • The thyroid is the target for the overwhelming majority of the body’s iodine stores.
  • Seafood such as fish, shrimp, and seaweed are rich in iodine stores.
  • Since 1924, the United States has iodized salt, which effectively has eliminated iodine deficiency in this country.
  • Many regions of the world remain at risk for iodine deficiency despite worldwide efforts to improve access to iodized salt; the World Health Organization estimates that 54 countries remain iodine-deficient.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 879

Selection of thyroid procedure

  • Risk of thyroid failure
  • Risk of RLN injury
  • Risk of recurrence
  • Grave's disease
  • Multinodular goitre

question_text: What is the mechanism of rays used in mammography?
explanation:
Mammography

  • Soft tissue radiographs are taken by placing the breast in direct contact with ultrasensitive film and exposing it to low-voltage, high-amperage x-rays.
  • The dose of radiation is approximately 0.1 cGy and, therefore, mammography is a very safe investigation.
  • The sensitivity of this investigation increases with age as the breast becomes less dense.
  • In total, 5% of breast cancers are missed by population- based mammographic screening programmes; even in retrospect, such carcinomas are not apparent.
  • Thus, a normal mammogram does not exclude the presence of carcinoma.
  • Digital mammography is being introduced, which allows manipulation of the images and computer-aided diagnosis.
  • Tomo-mammography is also being assessed as a more sensitive diagnostic modality.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28th, Pg: 916

question_text: What is the development of angiosarcoma in ipsilateral arm to surgery occurring secondary to long standing lymphoedema called as?
explanation:
This is a case of lymphangiosarcoma, or Stewart Treves syndrome.

  • Develops as a complication of long-standing (usually more than 10 years) lymphedema after mastectomy or radiation therapy.
  • Patients present with acute worsening of the edema and appearance of subcutaneous nodules that can ulcerate or bleed.
  • Treatment - Preoperative chemotherapy and radiation followed by surgical excision (radical amputation of arm).
  • The tumor has a very poor prognosis.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 35, Edition: 21st, Pg: 832

question_text: Most common benign cardiac tumour in children is?
explanation:
Rhabdomyoma

This is the most common benign cardiac tumour in children. It usually presents with symptoms related to valve dysfunction or arrhythmias. There are usually multicentric pedunculated masses in either or both ventricles. Rhabdomyoma is associated with tuberous sclerosis in >50% of the cases. Treatment is usually by surgical excision.

Fetal Cardiac Rhabdomyoma

question_text: Which of the following is not included in the MELD score?
explanation:
Assessment of chronic liver disease

A number of parameters are required to accurately assess the degree of liver dysfunction, enable predictions about a patient's ability to tolerate surgical or radiological procedures and assess the prognosis following transplantation.

Two prognostic models commonly used are the Child-Turcotte-Pugh (CTP) classification and the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score. The original Child classification was developed to predict mortality following shunt surgery in patients with cirrhosis, with the CTP classification modified to predict mortality after any surgery.

The MELD score was devised to predict the short-term prognosis following transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic stent shunt (TIPSS) but has been adopted to prioritize patients on liver transplant waiting lists. In the MELD model survival probability is calculated based on the patient's international normalized ratio (INR), serum bilirubin and creatinine.

question_text: Which among the following is not an indication for surgical therapy in treatment of  Crohn's disease?
explanation:
Surgical treatment.

  • Although medical management is indicated during acute exacerbations of disease, most patients with chronic Crohn disease will require surgery at some time during the course of their illness.
  • The goals are to preserve bowel length while minimizing postoperative complications and disease recurrence
  • Approximately 70% of patients will require surgical resection within 15 years after diagnosis
  • Indications for surgery include failure of medical treatment, bowel obstruction, fistula or abscess formation, steroid dependence, dysplasia or milgnancy
  • Most patients can be treated with elective surgery, especially with the improvement of medical management in the past decade. However, patients with intestinal perforation, peritonitis, excessive bleeding, or toxic megacolon require urgent surgery
  • Children with Crohn disease and resulting systemic symptoms, such as growth retardation, may benefit from resection. The extraintestinal complications of Crohn disease, although not primary indications for operation, often subside after resection of the involved bowel; exceptions are that problems may continue with ankylosing spondylitis and hepatic complications

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1267

question_text: Only definite treatment for secondary hyperparathyroidism
explanation:
• Renal transplantation remains the only definite treatment for secondary hyperparathyroidism.
  • Other therapies are a bridge to this or aim to provide symptom relief.
  • Standard management includes replacement of calcium and vitamin D and the reduction of phosphate levels by the use of phosphate binders.
  • Treatment of this disease changed radically with the introduction of calcimimetic drugs, such as cinacalcet.
  • Calcimimetics alter the set point of the CaR, thereby reducing the constant stimulation of the parathyroid glands and lowering the PTH level.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, CHAPTER 56, The parathyroid glands, Pg:885.

question_text: Which is the most common infection in a transplant patient after 3-4 months? In renal transplant recipients, which is the likely organism causing reactivation disease within 3-4 months after surgery?
explanation:
Cytomegalovirus

  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is present asymptomatically in 40-100% of adults. It usually remains latent within the host but can reactivate in immunocompromised patients.
  • Commonly affected are those with acquired immunodeficiency syndrome (AIDS) (where it is the most common indication for colectomy) and patients on immunosuppressive therapy for IBD.
  • Symptoms include profuse bloody diarrhea and colicky pain. Severe disease may lead to perforation.
  • Treatment is with ganciclovir with surgery necessary for severe disease or complications.

question_text: Treatment for primary hyperparathyroidism true is/are
option_a: All symptomatic patients should be offered surgery.
explanation:
• All symptomatic patients should be offered surgery.
  • An expert panel recently published recommendations on which asymptomatic patients should be considered for surgical intervention (Bilezikian et al., 2014).
  • When criteria have been met and where a single adenoma has been identified by radiological means, a minimally invasive parathyroidectomy may be offered.
  • Conversely, where there is discordant imaging or where imaging fails to identify any parathyroid abnormalities, then a bilateral neck exploration and three and a half-gland parathyroidectomy or a four- gland parathyroidectomy and autotransplantation should be performed.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, CHAPTER 56, The parathyroid glands, Pg:879.

question_text: Most common  brain tumour is?
explanation:
• Cerebral metastases are the most common brain tumours, and affect about one quarter of cancer sufferers, a proportion that is increasing with extended survival associated with more effective treatment of primary cancers.

question_text: Which is the most effective drug among the medical management of gastro- oesophageal reflux disease?
explanation:
Medical management

  • Most sufferers from GORD do not consult a doctor and do not need to do so. They self-medicate with over-the-counter medicines such as simple antacids, antacid– alginate preparations, H2-receptor antagonists or PPIs.
  • Consultation is more likely when symptoms are severe, prolonged and unresponsive to the above treatments.
  • Simple measures that are often neglected include advice about weight loss, smoking, excessive consumption of alcohol, tea or coffee, the avoidance of large meals late at night and a modest degree of head-up tilt of the bed. Tilting the bed has been shown to have an effect that is similar to taking an H2-receptor antagonist. The common practice of using additional pillows has no significant effect.
  • PPIs are the most effective drug treatment for GORD. Indeed, they are so effective that, once started, patients are very reluctant to stop taking them. Given an adequate dose for 8 weeks, most patients have a rapid improvement in symptoms (within a few days), and more than 90% can expect full mucosal healing at the end of this time
  • As most patients do not make major lifestyle changes and as PPIs are so effective, many remain on long-term treatment. For the minority who do not respond adequately to a standard dose, a trial at an increased dose or the addition of an H2-receptor antagonist is recommended. If unsuccessful, these patients should be formally investigated.
  • PPI therapy is also important in patients with reflux induced strictures, resulting in significant prolongation of the intervals between endoscopic dilatation. As yet, fears that chronic acid suppression might have serious long-term side effects including the risk of gastric cancer seem unwarranted.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1115

question_text: Which one of the following is most common benign tumour of lung?
explanation:
BENIGN LUNG TUMOURS

  • Benign tumours of the lung are uncommon and account for fewer than 15% of solitary lesions seen on chest radiographs.A peripheral tumour usually causes no symptoms until it is large; a central tumour may present with haemoptysis and signs of bronchial obstruction while still small.
  • A tumour is likely to be benign if it has not increased in size on chest radiographs for more than 2 years or it has some degree of calcification; however, a tissue diagnosis is usually pursued.
  • Most benign nodules are granulomas (tuberculosis or histoplasmosis).
  • The most common benign tumour is a hamartoma, a developmental abnormality containing mesothelial and endothelial elements.
  • Diagnosis (and definitive treatment) is achieved by excision of the lesion. Any of the mesodermal elements of the lung may form a mesodermal tumour (chondroma, lipoma, leiomyoma). Deposits of amyloid may have a similar radiographic appearance to a nodule (pseudotumour).

Lung Hamartoma

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 59, Cardiac Surgery, Pg: 991.

question_text: 60 year old patient brought to emergency room after patient developed sudden onset of headache. On examination patient's GCS is 11/15 and patient has focal neurological deficit. What is WFNS grade of this patient?

question_text: What frequency transducers are used in endoscopic ultrasound?
explanation:
Endosonography

  • Endoscopic ultrasonography relies on a high-frequency (5-30 MHz) transducer located at the tip of the endoscope to provide highly detailed images of the layers of the oesophageal wall and mediastinal structures close to the oesophagus.
  • Radial echoendoscopes have a rotating transducer that creates a circular image with the endoscope in the centre, and this type of scanner is widely used to create diagnostic transverse sectional images at right angles to the long axis of the oesophagus.
  • Linear echoendoscopes produce a sectoral image in the line of the endoscope and are used to biopsy submucosal oesophageal lesions, mediastinal masses such as lymph nodes or suspicious lesions that might lie outside a proposed surgical area.
  • Radial scanners without optical components are available for passage through narrow strictures over a guidewire, and catheter probes are available that can be passed down the endoscope biopsy channel.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1109-1110

question_text: Which among the following modality is helpful in detecting the presence of prevertebral fascia invasion in thyroid swelling?
explanation:
• In the setting of an invasive primary thyroid cancer, both CT and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) may have a role.
