question_text: Which is the most frequent cause of hypothyroidism in iodine replete population?
explanation:
Autoimmune Thyroiditis

  • Autoimmune thyroiditis is the most frequent cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-replete populations.
  • The most common type is chronic lymphocytic thyroiditis, otherwise known as Hashimoto thyroiditis.
  • This disorder is found predominantly in females at up to a 10:1 female-to-male incidence ratio.
  • In addition, there is a strong hereditary component, with first-degree relatives of Hashimoto's patients having a nine-fold risk of also developing the disease.
  • The etiology of Hashimoto thyroiditis is due to the presence of circulating autoantibodies to thyroid antigens, resulting in a chronic autoimmune destructive process involving the formation of immune complexes and complement in the basement membrane of follicular cells.
  • This leads to the infiltration of lymphocytes into the thyroid follicles and eventually results in fibrosis, which decreases the effective number of follicles needed to produce thyroid hormones.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 884

question_text: Which among the following is the investigation of choice in discrete thyroid swelling?
explanation:
Fine-needle aspiration cytology

  • Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is the investigation of choice in discrete thyroid swellings.
  • FNAC has excellent patient compliance, is simple and quick to perform in the out-patient department and is readily repeated. This technique, developed in Scandinavia 40 years ago, is now routine throughout the world.
  • FNAC results should be reported using standard terminology. As stated above there is a trend to use ultrasound to guide the needle to achieve more accurate sampling and reduce the rate of unsatisfactory aspirates.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 855

question_text: Which among the following is not the most commonly used thyroid autoantibodies for the diagnosis of autoimmune thyroid disease?
explanation:
• The measurement of serum thyroid autoantibodies is useful in the diagnosis of various autoimmune thyroid diseases, although their variable sensitivities and specificities require caution in test interpretation.
  • The three most commonly measured autoantibodies today are anti-TPO (TPOAb), anti-Tg (TgAb), and anti-TSH receptor (TRAb).

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 881

question_text: Which among the following is not the eye changes in grave's disease?
explanation:
• Because of its autoimmune etiology, Graves disease can have other manifestations in addition to the classic symptoms and signs of hyperthyroidism.
  • The most common is Graves orbitopathy, which occurs in up to 25% to 30% of patients.
  • In this process, autoimmune reactions at the orbital and periorbital soft tissues lead to proptosis, eyelid retraction, chemosis, periorbital edema, and diminished ocular muscle motility; if left untreated, the orbitopathy can lead to vision loss from corneal lesions or optic nerve compression.
  • Skin manifestations also can occur, including pretibial myxedema and acropachy (edema at the digits).
  • Other autoimmune conditions that have been associated with Graves disease include Hashimoto thyroiditis, lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, pernicious anaemia, and Addison disease, among others.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 887

question_text: When should be the levels of PTH measured for postoperative hypocalcemia in a patient of thyroid surgery?
explanation:
Postoperative Care and Complications

  • Postoperatively, patients are positioned in a low Fowler position with the head and shoulders elevated at least 10 to 20 degrees in order to maintain low venous pressure in the neck. Diet is advanced quickly as the patient emerges from the effects of anesthesia.
  • For patients who have undergone total thyroidectomy, serum calcium levels can be tracked periodically during the hospital stay.
  • Prophylactic oral calcium supplementation can be administered, and additional supplementation may be given for symptomatic hypocalcemia. Prophylactic calcitriol also may be started preoperatively in patients at higher risk of postoperative hypocalcemia, such as those with Graves disease.
  • Some practitioners measure preclosure intraoperative PTH or 4-hour postoperative intact
  • PTH levels to help guide the dosing of calcium/ calcitriol supplementation.
  • There are several variations of these strategies with evidence-based literature, and any one of them would be helpful in the prevention and treatment of postoperative hypocalcemia.
  • Patients who had undergone first time unilateral lobectomy do not require any biochemical evaluation or calcium supplementation.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 913

question_text: Which of the following statement is not true for Mallory Weiss tear?
option_b: Vertical split in gastric mucosa on endoscopy
option_d: Mucosal tear below the squamocolumnar junction
explanation:
MALLORY-WEISS SYNDROME

  • Forceful vomiting may produce a mucosal tear at the cardia rather than a full perforation.
  • The mechanism of injury is different. In Boerhaave's syndrome, vomiting occurs against a closed glottis and pressure builds up in the oesophagus. In Mallory-Weiss syndrome, vigorous vomiting produces a vertical split in the gastric mucosa, immediately below the squamocolumnar junction at the cardia in 90% of cases. In only 10% is the tear in the tear in the oesophagus.
  • The condition presents with haematemesis. Usually, the bleeding is not severe, but endoscopic injection therapy may be required for the occasional, severe Surgery is rarely required.
  • Severe chest pain, with odynophagia is seen in intramural rupture.

Patients present with acute onset of chest discomfort or odynophagia. If the haematoma ruptures into the oesophageal lumen haematemesis ensues. When the dissection or haematoma is confined to the oesophageal wall, treatment is conservative. Anticoagulation is corrected and the haematoma usually resolves in 7-14 days.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1129

question_text: Which among the following statements is false for Mondor's disease?
option_b: Thrombophlebeitis of the superficial veins of the breast
explanation:
Mondor's Disease -

  • There is thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of the anterior chest wall and breast.
  • Patient presents with pain and a tender firm cord in the region of the involved vein.
  • Frequently involved veins include the lateral thoracic vein and the thoracoepigastric vein.
  • This benign, self-limited (usually resolves within 4 to 6 weeks) disorder is not indicative of cancer.
  • Rarely, the presentation is bilateral, and most women have no evidence of thrombophlebitis in other anatomic sites.
  • When the diagnosis is uncertain, or when a mass is present near the tender cord, biopsy is indicated.
  • Treatment - Anti-inflammatory medications and warm compresses.
  • When symptoms persist or are refractory to therapy, excision of the involved vein segment may be considered.

Reference: Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 11th, Pg: 550

question_text: Which among the following tests is not used for detecting H. pylori infection?
explanation:
• One of the characteristics of the organism is its ability to hydrolyse urea, resulting in the production of ammonia, a strong alkali.
  • The effect of ammonia on the antral G cells is to cause the release of gastrin via the previously described negative-feedback loop.
  • This is probably responsible for the modest, but inappropriate, hypergastrinemia in patients with peptic ulcer disease, which, in turn, may result in gastric acid hypersecretion.
  • The organism’s obligate urease activity is utilised by various tests used to detect the presence of the organism, including the 13C and 14C breath tests and the CLO test (a commercially available urease test kit), which is performed on gastric biopsies.
  • The organism can also be detected histologically, using the Giemsa or the Warthin– Starry stains, and cultured using appropriate media.
  • Previous or current infection with the organism may also be detected serologically.
  • Breath tests or faecal antigen tests are recommended for the pre-treatment diagnosis of H. pylori infection in the community.
  • Less accurate, hospital-based serology tests have a place within the non-invasive test and-treat strategy.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1155

question_text: What is the most common cause of isolated splenic vein thrombosis?
explanation:
• Isolated splenic vein thrombosis (left-sided portal hypertension) is usually secondary to pancreatic inflammation or neoplasm.
  • The result is gastrosplenic venous hypertension, with superior mesenteric and portal venous pressures remaining normal.
  • The left gastroepiploic vein becomes a major collateral vessel, and gastric rather than esophageal varices develop.
  • This variant of portal hypertension is important to recognize because it is easily reversed by splenectomy alone.

Reference: Sabinston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1444.

question_text: Which among the following obstruction leads to profuse early vomiting, rapid dehydration and minimal distention?
explanation:
Features of obstruction

  • In high small bowel obstruction, vomiting occurs early, is profuse and causes rapid dehydration. Distension is minimal with little evidence of dilated small bowel loops on abdominal radiography
  • In low small bowel obstruction, pain is predominant with central distension. Vomiting is delayed. Multiple dilated small bowel loops are seen on radiography
  • In large bowel obstruction, distension is early and pronounced. Pain is less severe and vomiting and dehydration are later features. The colon proximal to the obstruction is distended on abdominal radiography. The small bowel will be dilated if the ileocaecal valve is incompetent.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1381

question_text: Which among the following antibiotics is not useful in the treatment of Crohn's disease?
explanation:
Antibiotics.

  • Certain antibiotics were found to be effective as a primary therapy for Crohn disease.
  • Promising results were initially reported for metronidazole, but later studies determined that it was no more effective than placebo for inducing remission.
  • Other antibiotics that have been used with varying success include ciprofloxacin, rifaximin, clofazimine, ethambutol, isoniazid, and rifabutin.
  • Antibiotic therapy has a clear role in the septic complications associated with Crohn disease and is beneficial in perianal disease.
  • The mechanism of action of antibiotics in Crohn disease is unclear, and side effects of these antibiotics preclude their Longterm use.
  • Therefore, antibiotics may play an adjunctive role in the treatment of Crohn disease and, in selected patients, may be useful in treating perianal disease, enterocutaneous fistulas, or active colonic disease but should not be used in maintenance therapy or to induce remission.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1266

question_text: Which age group patients are primarily affected by Crohn's disease?
explanation:
Incidence and Epidemiology

  • Crohn disease primarily attacks young adults in the second and third decades of life. However, a bimodal distribution is apparent, with a second smaller peak occurring in the sixth decade of life.
  • Crohn disease is more common in urban dwellers, and although earlier reports suggested a somewhat higher female predominance, the two genders are affected equally.
  • The risk for development of Crohn disease is about twice as high in smokers as in non-smokers.
  • Several studies indicate an increased incidence of Crohn disease in women using oral contraceptives; however, more recent studies have shown no differences.
  • Certain ethnic groups, particularly Ashkenazi Jews, have a two- to four-fold higher incidence of Crohn disease than age- and gender-matched control subjects
  • Individuals born during the spring months (e.g., April to June) are more likely to develop Crohn disease;
  • there also appears to be a north-south gradient worldwide, and populations in higher latitudes have higher incidence rates than populations in lower latitudes. There is a strong familial association, with the risk for development of Crohn disease increased about 30-fold in siblings and 14- to 15-fold for all first-degree relatives.
  • Other analyses that support a genetic role for Crohn disease have shown a concordance rate of only 4% in dizygotic twins but a 20% to 50% rate in monozygotic twins.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1259

question_text: Which among the following disease shows redcurrant jelly stools and sausage shaped lump?
explanation:
Clinical features of intussusception

  • The classical presentation of intussusception is with episodes of screaming and drawing up of the legs in a previously well male infant. The attacks last for a few minutes and recur repeatedly.
  • During attacks the child appears pale; between episodes he may be listless.
  • Vomiting may or may not occur at the outset but becomes conspicuous and bilestained with time.
  • Initially, the passage of stool may be normal, whereas, later, blood and mucus are evacuated - the 'redcurrant jelly' stool.
  • Whenever possible, examination should be undertaken between episodes of colic, without disturbing the child.
  • Classically, the abdomen is not initially distended; a lump that hardens on palpation may be discerned but this is present in only 60% of cases.
  • There may be an associated feeling of emptiness in the right iliac fossa (the sign of Dance).
  • On rectal examination, blood-stained mucus may be found on the finger.
  • Occasionally, in extensive ileocolic or colocolic intussusception, the apex may be palpable or even protrude from the anus.
  • Unrelieved, progressive dehydration and abdominal distension from small bowel obstruction will occur, followed by peritonitis secondary to gangrene. Rarely, natural cure may occur as a result of sloughing of the intussusception.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1383

question_text: Which among the following is not a presenting sign in a patient of Budd-Chiari syndrome?
explanation:
Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS) is a posthepatic cause of portal hypertension characterized by the obstruction of hepatic venous outflow. Patients may present with -

  • Acute signs and symptoms of abdominal pain
  • Ascites
  • Hepatomegaly

BCS is defined as primary when the obstructive process involves an endoluminal venous thrombosis.

BCS is considered as a secondary process when the veins are compressed or invaded by a neighbouring lesion originating outside the vein.

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter 31, Liver, Pg: 1368.

question_text: Which is the first symptom in the patient of Crohn's disease?
explanation:
• Crohn disease can occur at any age, but the typical patient is a young adult in the second or third decade of life.
  • The onset of disease is often insidious, with a slow and protracted course.
  • Characteristically, there are symptomatic periods of abdominal pain and diarrhoea interspersed with asymptomatic periods of varying lengths.
  • With time, the symptomatic periods gradually become more frequent, more severe, and longer lasting.
  • The most common symptom of Crohn disease is chronic diarrhoea, followed by intermittent and colicky abdominal pain, most commonly noted in the lower abdomen.
  • The pain, however, may be more severe and localized in the right lower quadrant and may mimic the signs and symptoms of acute appendicitis.
  • In contrast to ulcerative colitis, patients with Crohn disease typically have fewer bowel movements, and the stools rarely contain mucus, pus, or blood.
  • Systemic nonspecific symptoms include a low-grade fever present in about one third of the patients, weight loss, loss of strength, and malaise.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1261

question_text: Which among the following is not a diagnostic criteria included in the Amsterdam II criteria for lynch syndrome?
option_a: One affected patient is a second degree relative of other two
option_b: Two or more successive generations are affected
option_c: Cancer in one or more affected relatives is diagnosed before the age of 50 years
option_d: Pathological diagnosis of cancer is verified
explanation: Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1373

question_text: What is the type of inheritance in familial adenomatous polyposis?
explanation:
Familial Adenomatous Polyposis

  • FAP is an autosomal dominant inherited disease that occurs in approximately 1:10,000 live births and affects genders and races equally.
  • FAP is a syndrome caused by germline mutation in the APC tumor suppressor gene which is responsible for regulation of β-catenin and located on chromosome 5q21.
  • Depending on the location of the APC mutation, the affected individuals can have a range of disease severity.
  • Severe FAP is characterized by thousands of colorectal adenomas.
  • Classical polyposis is described as having between 100 and 1000 colorectal adenomas.
  • Patients with fewer than 100 adenomas are considered to have attenuated FAP (AFAP).
  • Germline mutations in the APC gene are found in 80% to 90% of patients with classic FAP and in 10% to 30% of patients with AFAP. About 25% of patients with FAP have a de novo mutation and thus have no family history. For individuals with the classic phenotype, the lifetime risk for CRC may exceed 90%, nearly 100% in the absence of treatment. If left untreated, patients with FAP develop CRC at an average age of 39 years (range 35–43 years).

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1368

question_text: Which of the following is not a method of overcoming the shortage of organs for transplantation?
option_b: Use of marginal donation after brain death deceased donors
option_c: Use of donation after circulatory death donors
explanation:
Increased living brain donors is not a method of overcoming the shortage of organs for transplantation.

Living donation is limited to donation of the kidney and, to a much lesser extent, liver, or lung lobe.

Methods of overcoming the shortage of organs for transplantation include:

  • Maximising donation after brain-death (DBD) donation.
  • Use of marginal DBD deceased donors.
  • Use of donation after circulatory death (DCD) donor.
  • Increased use of split-liver transplantation - can be used for two recipients.
  • Increased living donor kidney (and liver) transplantation.

Reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page Number -1596.

question_text: Identify the type of procedure done for pilonidal sinus from the given figure.
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts a gluteal flap closure technique used for pilonidal sinus, where the excised defect is closed with an off-midline flap, typical of the Karydakis procedure.

Karydakis's surgery involves excising the sinus tract and closing the defect with an asymmetric flap where the suture line is shifted off the midline to flatten the natal cleft and reduce tension.

Explanation for the other options:

  • Limberg's surgery uses a rhomboid-shaped flap.
  • Z-plasty is used to change the direction of a scar or relieve linear contractures.
  • Bascom's surgery is another flap technique, but the Karydakis technique is the classic asymmetric closure technique.

Key Takeaways:

The Karydakis flap is a popular surgical technique for pilonidal sinus closure, characterized by its off-midline closure to prevent recurrence by reducing the depth of the natal cleft.

Must know

question_text: Which of the following defines sepsis according to SEPSIS-3 criteria?
option_a: Suspected or documented infection & increase in any two of the SOFA points
option_b: Suspected or documented infection plus vasopressor therapy needed to maintain MAP>65 mmHg and serum lactate >2.0mmol/L despite adequate fluid restriction
option_c: Suspected or documented infection plus two SIRS criteria
explanation:
Sepsis is defined by SEPSIS-3 criteria as suspected or documented infection and an acute increase in >2 sepsis-related organ failure assessment (SOFA) points.

Documented or suspected infection + Need for vasopressors to maintain MAP more than or equal to 65mmHg and elevated lactate (>2 mmol/L) defines the septic shock according to SEPSIS -3 criteria.SIRS criteria were included in earlier criteria (SEPSIS I & II).

Reference: Harrison's principles of internal medicine 20th Ed chap 297, pg.2045

question_text: All of the following strategies done for Damage control resuscitation except:
explanation:
The four central strategies of DCR are:

  1. Anticipate and treat acute traumatic coagulopathy.
  2. Permissive hypotension until hemorrhage control.
  3. Limit crystalloid and colloid infusion to avoid dilutional coagulopathy.
  4. Damage control surgery to control hemorrhage and preserve physiology.

question_text: Where does the parafollicular C cells develop from?
explanation:
• The embryology of the thyroid and parathyroid glands underlies the anatomical position, anatomical variations and congenital conditions of these structures and is therefore vital for surgery.
  • The thyroglossal duct develops from the median bud of the pharynx.
  • The foramen caecum at the junction of the anterior two-thirds and posterior one-third of the tongue is the vestigial remnant of the duct.
  • This initially hollow structure migrates caudally and passes in close continuity with, and sometimes through, the developing hyoid cartilage.
  • The parathyroid glands develop from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
  • The thymus also develops from the third pouch.
  • As it descends, the thymus takes the associated parathyroid gland with it, which explains why the inferior parathyroid, which arises from the third pharyngeal pouch, normally lies inferior to the superior gland.
  • However, the inferior parathyroid may be found anywhere along this line of descent.
  • The developing thyroid lobes amalgamate with the structures that arise in the fourth pharyngeal pouch, i.e. the superior parathyroid gland and the ultimobranchial body.
  • Parafollicular cells (C cells) from the neural crest reach the thyroid via the ultimobranchial body.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 850

question_text: Which among the following is not the common causes of xerostomia?
explanation:
Xerostomia

  • Common causes of xerostomia are:
  • Normal salivary flows decrease with age in both men and women, although many patients with xerostomia are postmenopausal women who also complain of a burning tongue or mouth.
  • Xerostomia is a common symptom in many aspects of medical practice.
    1. Chronic anxiety states and depression;
    2. Dehydration;
    3. Anticholinergic drugs, especially antidepressants;
    4. Salivary gland disorders - Sjögren's syndrome. Ascending parotitis is an occasional complication of xerostomia and is managed with antibiotics and increased fluid intake;
    5. Radiotherapy to the head and neck.

question_text: All of the following are true regarding nephrolithiasis, except?

Patients with a family history of stone disease are 2.5 times more likely to develop stone disease themselves. Examples of hereditary forms of stone disease include cystinuria, type I renal tubular acidosis (RTA) and primary hyperoxaluria.

question_text: Management of the acute phase of Peyronie's disease includes which of the following?
explanation:
Explanation:

While the etiology is uncertain, there is an association with Dupuytren's contracture.

The natural history of the condition is that it typically progresses for 18-24 months before stabilising.

During this acute (or active) phase of the disease, surgery is not indicated, and a variety of medical treatments have been tried, although none with any good evidence of benefit.

When the disease has stabilised (the chronic or stable phase), the crucial issue is whether the patient is still able to have sexual intercourse.

  • If he can, no treatment is indicated.
  • If the deformity prevents penetration or makes it difficult, then corrective treatment is indicated.

Using this criterion, only around a quarter of men require treatment.

question_text: Which among the drug is as effective as endoscopic therapy in control of acute variceal bleeding?
explanation:
Somatostatin and its longer-acting analogue octreotide are as efficacious as endoscopic treatment for control of acute variceal bleeding.

Medical management of variceal bleeding -

  • It works by reducing variceal blood flow, which in turn reduces variceal pressure.
  • Medical therapy should be initiated at the onset of variceal bleeding.
  • Because infections are common in patients with variceal bleeding, antibiotic prophylaxis should be initiated. This reduces rebleeding and infection rate, and improves survival.
  • Somatostatin and its longer-acting analogue octreotide are as efficacious as endoscopic treatment for control of acute variceal bleeding.
  • The combination of octreotide and endoscopic therapy is more effective than octreotide alone in controlling bleeding and is the preferred treatment for most patients.
  • In severe cases of hemorrhage, vasopressin (ex: terlipressin) can be used to diminish splanchnic blood flow. It should be given with nitroglycerin simultaneously and then titrated to achieve blood pressure control.

Reference: Sabinston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1445.

question_text: Which among the following is not a clinical manifestation of acute postoperative compartment syndrome?
explanation:
Compartment syndrome

  • Acute postoperative compartment syndrome refers, in the context of surgery, to the consequences of increased pressure in a muscle compartment, usually in the lower limb, that can result in permanent disability or amputation.
  • This occurs as a result of underperfusion, usually during prolonged surgery, often with elevation of the leg.
  • Postoperatively, the pressure in the affected compartment rises to the point beyond which irreversible ischaemic damage to muscles and nerves occurs.
  • It manifests with pain, reduced power, swelling, numbness and tingling.
  • Early recognition is essential and prompt surgical fasciotomy is required to avoid the disastrous and permanently disabling sequelae.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 85

question_text: Secondary hyperparathyroidism false is/are
option_b: Primarily as a result of chronic kidney disease
explanation:
• Secondary hyperparathyroidism is defined as a derangement in calcium homeostasis, which leads to a compensatory increase in PTH secretion.
  • It occurs primarily as a result of chronic kidney disease and is therefore sometimes referred to as renal hyperparathyroidism. Other underlying causes include gastro-intestinal malabsorption, vitamin D deficiency, liver disease or chronic lithium usage.
  • The pathogenesis of secondary hyperparathyroidism is related to renal dysfunction. Abnormalities in the renal tubular absorption of phosphate lead to hyperphosphataemia. This acts directly on the parathyroid cells and stimulates PTH secretion.
  • More recent translational research has identified a novel phosphaturia hormone, fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF 23). This is progressively secreted from osteocytes to compensate for chronic phosphate retention that in turn leads to a reduction in 1,25- dihydroxyvitamin D, which by reducing the intestinal absorption of calcium, also acts to increase secretion of PTH.
  • Previous studies in patients with chronic renal disease have shown that there is a reduction in the expression of the vitamin D receptor and the CaR, with associated skeletal resistance to PTH.
  • These factors interact to form the complex pattern leading to progressive secondary hyperparathyroidism in the setting of chronic renal disease.
  • The pathological characteristics associated with secondary hyperparathyroidism include hyperplasia, asymmetrical glandular enlargement or nodularity.
  • This differentiation is important, as when the parathyroid gland becomes nodular it loses expression of the vitamin D and Ca receptors. It has been proposed that nodular parathyroid glands may be resistant to calcimimetics and therefore be refractory to medical management.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, CHAPTER 56, The parathyroid glands, Pg:884.

question_text: Which among the following statements is false for human leukocyte antigen?
option_a: Most common cause of graft rejection
option_b: Physiologically function as antigen recognition unit
option_d: HLA -A, B, C fall under class I
explanation:
Human leukocyte antigens are highly polymorphic (amino acid sequence differs widely between individuals).

Human leukocyte antigen (HLA) -

  • Are the most common cause of graft rejection.
  • Their physiological function is to act as antigen recognition units.
  • Are highly polymorphic (amino acid sequence differs widely between individuals).
  • HLA-A, -B, -C (class I), and -DR, -DP and -DQ (class II) are most important in organ transplantation

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 88, Kidney transplantation and the principles of transplantation, Pg: 1599.

question_text: All of the following are normal urodynamic findings, except?
option_a: The normal bladder will accept approximately 400-550 mL when filled at room temperature at a rate of
option_b: The pressure increase in the bladder should be more than 15 cmH2O
option_c: Phasic pressure increases should not be seen
option_d: The normal voiding pressure should not exceed 60 cmH2O in men
explanation:
Urodynamic study findings -

  • The normal bladder will accept approximately 400-550 mL when filled at room temperature at a rate of <50 mL/min.
  • The pressure increase in the bladder should be less than 15 cm H2O.
  • Phasic pressure increases should not be seen. When present, they may be indicative of detrusor instability.
  • The normal voiding pressure should not exceed 60 cm H2O in men and about 40 cm H2O in women, with a flow rate of between 20 mL/s and 25 mL/s.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 81 Urinary symptoms and investigations, Pg:1463-1465.

question_text: Which statement is not correct regarding medical management of RCC?
option_a: Tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting the VEGF signalling axis that are approved in the first-line therapy
option_b: Anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody, bevacizumab, is approved for use with interferon
option_c: The average duration of disease control with these drugs is 3-4 weeks in the first-line Setting
option_d: Many studies are currently investigating combinations of anti-VEGF therapy with a new generation of immunotherapy agents in the form of T cell-immune checkpoint inhibitors such as antibodies against programmed cell death protein 1 ligand 1 (PDL1)
explanation:
• The past 10 years have seen the approval of several targeted therapeutic agents for the treatment of metastatic RCC.
  • Given the highly vascular nature of RCCs, it is unsurprising that several therapies are available to exploit this feature.
  • Indeed, tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting the VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) signalling axis that are approved in the first-line and second-line settings for the treatment of metastatic RCC are sorafenib, sunitinib, pazopanib, axitinib, lenvatinib and cabozantinib.
  • In addition, the anti-VEGF monoclonal antibody, bevacizumab, is approved for use with interferon-α.
  • The motor inhibitors everolimus and temsirolimus, are approved as single agents in the second-line setting and in the first-line setting in patients with poor risk status.
  • The average duration of disease control with these drugs is 8-9 months in the first-line setting and 5-6 months in the second-line setting.
  • Most of the phase III RCTs leading to approval of these agents have excluded patients with nccRCC.
  • Many studies are currently investigating combinations of anti-VEGF therapy with a new generation of immunotherapy agents in the form of T cell-immune checkpoint inhibitors such as antibodies against programmed cell death protein 1 ligand 1 (PDL1), which include avelumab and atezolizumab, and antibodies against programmed cell death protein 1 (PD1) which include nivolumab and pembrolizumab.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1484-1485.

question_text: All of the following are indications for percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), except?
option_a: Obese patients in whom extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL) is contraindicated
option_d: Anatomic abnormalities such as PUJ Obstruction along with the stone
explanation:
Indications for percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) include -

Any obstruction -

  • Anatomic abnormalities such as PUJ obstruction, calyceal diverticula
  • Ureteric obstruction a prevents the passage of stone fragments after ESWL.

Obese patients in whom ESWL is contraindicated.

Lower calyceal stones - these are less likely to pass after ESWL.

Stone composition -

  • Struvite stones need to be completely removed because of associated infection.
  • Some stones with a very hard composition are difficult to fragment using ESWL, including calcium oxalate monohydrate and cystine stones.

Percutaneous nephrolithotomy PCNL involves removal of renal stones by creating a track between the skin and the pelvicalyceal system. Typically, this procedure is done in the prone position. Fluoroscopy or US is used for localisation. The posterolateral calyx is commonly chosen for entry. US in conjunction with pneumatic and laser lithotripsy is the most common energy source used. Complications include bleeding, infection and pleural violation in cases of supracostal puncture. Severe bleeding may require selective angioembolisation.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1477.

question_text: Hemorrhage occurring after 7 days due to sloughing of wall of vessel categorized into:
explanation:
Option A: Primary hemorrhage is hemorrhage occurring immediately due to an injury (or surgery).

Option B: Secondary hemorrhage is due to sloughing of the wall of a vessel. It usually occurs 7-14 days after injury and is precipitated by factors such as infection, pressure necrosis (such as from a drain) or malignancy.

Option D: Reactionary hemorrhage is delayed hemorrhage (within 24 hours) and is usually due to dislodgement of a clot by resuscitation, normalization of blood pressure and vasodilatation. Reactionary hemorrhage may also be due to technical failure, such as slippage of a ligature.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 2, Edition: 28th, Pg: 15

question_text: A person collapses following a road traffic accident (RTA). You initiate CPR, and soon the rescue team arrives. Which is the correct action among the given options?
option_a: Perform 5 cycles of CPR at 30:2 before applying AED
option_b: Continue CPR while the AED is being attached
option_c: Stop CPR to allow AED paddles to be applied
option_d: Hand over the patient and leave the scene
explanation:
Explanation:

CPR must be continued without interruption until the AED is ready for use. Pausing chest compressions decreases perfusion and lowers survival chances. AED application should not be delayed or prioritized over CPR.

Explanation of Other Options:

Perform 5 cycles of CPR at 30:2 before applying AED (Option A): Incorrect, as AED should be applied immediately once available, not delayed.

Stop CPR to allow AED paddles to be applied (Option C): Wrong approach, since interrupting CPR during AED preparation reduces perfusion and lowers survival.

Hand over the patient and leave the scene (Option D): Inappropriate, as leaving before confirming safe transfer to the emergency team is both unethical and unsafe.

Key Takeaways:

During cardiac arrest management, uninterrupted CPR is critical until the AED is functional and ready to deliver a shock.

question_text: Which among the following is not the symptoms of external branch of superior laryngeal nerve injury in thyroidectomy surgery?
option_c: Decreased ability to reach higher pitch
option_d: Decreased ability to project the voice
explanation:
• Injury to the EBSLN also can lead to postoperative voice abnormalities due to its innervation of the cricothyroid muscle and contribution to vocal cord muscle tone.
  • Symptoms of EBSLN injury include vocal fatigue, decreased ability to reach higher pitch, and decreased ability to project the voice.
  • Definitive diagnosis of EBSLN injury is challenging as laryngoscopy is often normal and may require electromyographic studies; as such, estimates of the rate of injury are imperfect and range from 2.5% to 28.4%.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 915

question_text: All of the following are correct regarding Ventriculoperitoneal shunt except?
option_a: A shunt valve opening pressure may be high, medium or low
option_b: Anti-siphon system incorporated to prevent excessive drainage
option_c: High pressure valves can overdrain CSF
option_d: Programmable valves offer variable opening pressure.
explanation:
High pressure valves may fail to allow adequate CSF drainage, whereas low pressure valves can overdrain CSF.

Ventriculoperitoneal shunting -

  • Ventricular catheter inserted into the frontal or occipital horn of the lateral ventricle, while a distal catheter is tunnelled subcutaneously to the abdomen.
  • Ventriculoatrial and ventriculopleural shunting is also possible.
  • A shunt valve, with an opening pressure that may be high, medium or low, is inserted at the junction of these catheters.
  • An anti-siphon system may be incorporated to prevent excessive drainage in the standing position.
  • Programmable valves offer variable opening pressures, adjusted magnetically using a device applied externally over the valve.
  • The valve system will also typically incorporate a CSF reservoir, which allows for percutaneous sampling.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 705.

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding administration of tranexamic acid to trauma patient except

  • Tranexamic acid should be given to all trauma patients suspected to have significant hemorrhage, including those with a systolic blood pressure of <90 mmHg or a pulse of over 110 per minute.

Option B- It needs to be administered within 3 hours of injury

question_text: For frost-bite rewarming, the temperature should be:
explanation:
Cold injuries

Cold injuries are principally divided into two types:

acute cold injuries from industrial accidents and frostbite.

  • Exposure to liquid petroleum gas (LPG), liquid nitrogen and other such liquids will cause epidermal and dermal destruction.
  • The tissue is more resistant to cold injury than to heat injury, and the inflammatory reaction is not as marked. The assessment of depth of injury is more difficult, so it is rare to make the decision for surgery early.
  • Frostbite injuries affect the peripheries in cold climates. The initial treatment is with rapid rewarming in a bath at 42°C. The cold injury produces delayed microvascular damage similar to that of ischaemia-reperfusion injury.
  • The level of damage is difficult to assess, and surgery usually does not play a role in its management, which is conservative, until there is absolute demarcation of the level of injury.

question_text: Inferior parathyroid gland and the thymus arise from the ____ pharyngeal pouch
explanation:
• The parathyroid glands, of which there are four, develop from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches between the fifth and twelfth week of gestation.
  • They are typically described as ‘Portland brick’ (yellow/brown) in colour and weigh approximately 30 mg.
  • Approximately 13% of the population have abnormal parathyroid tissue, with 5% having a true supernumerary gland.
  • The blood supply of both the superior and inferior parathyroid glands arises from the inferior thyroidal artery.
  • While the location of the individual glands may vary significantly, there appears to be a degree of symmetry between opposite sides that can be helpful during surgical dissection.
  • The inferior parathyroid gland and the thymus arise from the third pharyngeal pouch.
  • As a result of the longer normal embryological descent, there is correspondingly more variation in their anatomical position.
  • However, in more than 50% of cases they are located at the inferior pole of the thyroid gland, on the anterior, lateral or posterior surface.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, CHAPTER 56 The parathyroid glands, Pg:874.

question_text: Which among the following terminologies denotes the transplant of graft between different species?
explanation:
Xenograft is a graft performed between different species.

Some common terminology in organ transplantation include -

  • Allograft - An organ or tissue transplanted from one individual to another.
  • Xenograft - A graft performed between different species.
  • Orthotopic graft - A graft placed in its normal anatomical site.
  • Heterotopic graft - A graft placed in a site different from that where the organ is normally located.
  • Alloantigen - Transplant antigen.
  • Alloantibody -Transplant antibodies.
  • HLA (Human Leukocyte Antigen) - The main trigger to graft rejection.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27th Edition, Chapter 82, Transplantation, Pg: 1533.

question_text: Which among the following is not a reason for dehydration and electrolyte loss in a case of intestinal obstruction?
option_c: Losses as a result of vomiting
explanation:
Fluid: this is made up of the various digestive juices. (saliva 500 mL, bile 500 mL, pancreatic secretions 500 mL, gastric secretions 1 litre - all per 24 hours). This accumulates in the gut lumen as absorption by the obstructed gut is retarded.

Dehydration and electrolyte loss in a case of intestinal obstruction are therefore due to:

  • reduced oral intake;
  • defective intestinal absorption;
  • losses as a result of vomiting;
  • sequestration in the bowel lumen;
  • transudation of fluid into the peritoneal cavity.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1375

question_text: 'Puff of smoke' appearance on angiography seen in which condition?
explanation:
• Moya moya disease describes the progressive obliteration of one or both internal carotid arteries, thought to represent an autoimmune process.
  • The development of external carotid circulation collaterals produces the angiographic 'puff of smoke' appearance responsible for this Japanese-derived name. It presents in youth or early middle age with ischaemia or haemorrhage.
  • Untreated, the majority of patients suffer major deficit or die within 2 years.
  • Ischaemia may be addressed by a variety of bypass techniques, for example by anastomosing the superficial temporal artery (arising from the external carotid) to the middle cerebral artery.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 712

  • This is the commonest ‘birth mark’, occurring most commonly on the head and neck.

90% appear at birth, and, as a consequence of intravascular thrombosis, fibrosis and mast cell infiltration, 10% resolve each subsequent year, with 70% resolved by 7 years old.

Whites skin is affected most commonly and girls are affected three times more than boys.

question_text: In a patient with parathyroid adenoma, how do we confirm the removal of the correct gland after surgery?
option_a: 50% reduction in PTH within 10 mins of gland removal
option_b: 50% reduction in PTH within 5 mins of gland removal
option_c: 25% reduction in PTH within 10 mins of gland removal
option_d: 25% reduction in PTH within 5 mins of gland removal
explanation:
80% of individuals with PHPT have a single adenoma, and therefore undergo a focused or minimally invasive parathyroidectomy , where the localised abnormal parathyroid gland is removed

Once the gland is removed, the surgeon can ensure that there is no other hyperactive gland remaining by u performing an intraoperative PTH assay.

The basic concept is that the half-life of circulating PTH is 3-5 minutes and there should therefore be a significant drop detected in the plasma PTH following resection of a single adenoma.

If no such drop is detected, then multigland disease may be suspected and conversion to a bilateral neck exploration should be considered.

The Miami criteria were developed to determine the extent of resection. A drop in the PTH into the normal range and to less than half the maximum preoperative PTH at 10 minutes appears to accurately predict single-gland disease

question_text: Which is not a part of standard urethral disruption injury management protocol?
option_a: A suprapubic catheter should be inserted as soon as practicable using the Seldinger technique
option_b: The conventional management of such an injury is delayed surgical reconstruction
option_c: Excision of the scar tissue and end-to-end anastomosis
explanation:
• A suprapubic catheter should be inserted as soon as practicable using the Seldinger technique.
  • The distended bladder may be palpable, making suprapubic catheterisation straight-forward, but often the bruising and swelling associated with the fracture makes this difficult and ultrasound guidance is required.
  • The two ends of the urethra, having been torn apart, become separated by a haematoma.
  • With time, this haematoma resolves and is replaced by fibrosis.
  • This pelvic fracture urethral disruption injury is technically not a stricture of the urethra but is often, erroneously, described as being one.
  • The conventional management of such an injury is delayed surgical reconstruction with excision of the scar tissue and end-to-end anastomosis.
  • This surgery should be delayed until the patient has recovered from any other injuries and is usually undertaken 3-6 months later.
  • It is a highly challenging technical procedure and should be undertaken only in specialist centres.
  • Some surgeons continue to undertake early attempts to realign the urethral ends endoscopically, and while there are some successful reports, most experts feel that there is an increased risk of sepsis, true stricture, incontinence and erectile dysfunction (ED).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 83 The urinary bladder, Pg : 1509.

question_text: Patient after parotid gland surgery is experiencing sweating while eating. Which complication is most likely responsible for this condition?
option_b: Pain due to the preauricular nerve
explanation:
Explanation:

Frey Syndrome occurs due to abnormal regeneration of parasympathetic fibers following parotid surgery.

  • Normally, preganglionic parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) travel via the Jacobson nerve to the tympanic plexus, then through the lesser petrosal nerve to synapse in the otic ganglion and finally reach the parotid gland via the auriculotemporal nerve to stimulate salivation.
  • After surgery, these fibers may misroute to sweat glands in the overlying skin, causing gustatory sweating and flushing during eating.

Explanation of other options:

Pain due to the preauricular nerve (Option B): Would cause local pain or dysesthesia, not sweating.

Horner's syndrome (Option C): Characterized by ptosis, miosis, and anhidrosis, not gustatory sweating.

Facial nerve palsy (Option D): Causes motor deficits of facial muscles, not sweating.

Key Takeaways:

  • Frey Syndrome = gustatory sweating after parotid surgery
  • Caused by misdirected parasympathetic fibers to sweat glands
  • Diagnosis: Minor starch-iodine test can confirm
  • Management: Botulinum toxin injections or surgical correction

question_text: A patient develops a rapidly bulging wound site 12 hours after thyroidectomy, and surgical exploration reveals a dislodged ligature from the superior thyroid pedicle. This type of bleeding occurs within hours of surgery due to slipped ligatures or inadequate haemostasis. What type of haemorrhage does this represent?
explanation:
Explanation:

Reactionary haemorrhage occurs within 24 hours of surgery, typically in the first 6 to 12 hours. It is usually caused by:

  • Slipped ligature
  • Dislodged clot
  • Rise in blood pressure after anaesthesia wears off
  • Restlessness or coughing postoperatively

The scenario states that the bleeding occurred 12 hours postoperatively and was due to suture (ligature) dislodgement, which is classic for reactionary haemorrhage.

Types of postoperative haemorrhage:

  • Primary haemorrhage: Occurs during surgery or immediately after closure. (Option A)
  • Reactionary haemorrhage: Occurs within the first 24 hours, especially 6 to 12 hours, commonly due to technical issues such as slipped ligatures.
  • Secondary haemorrhage: Occurs 7 to 14 days after surgery, usually due to infection or sloughing of a vessel wall. (Option B)

question_text: Which among the following is not a preventive technique for frey's syndrome following parotidectomy?
explanation:
The incidence of Frey's syndrome is minimal when extracapsular dissection is performed as the parotid fascia is primarily repaired and communication between denuded parotid parenchyma and subcutis sealed off.

  • There are a number of quite invasive techniques described to prevent Frey's syndrome following parotidectomy. These include:
    • Sternomastoid muscle flap;
    • Temporalis fascial flap;
    • Insertion of artificial membranes between the skin and the parotid bed.

All these methods replace the barrier between the skin and the parotid bed to minimise inappropriate regeneration of autonomic nerve fibres.

MANAGEMENT OF ESTABLISHED FREY'S SYNDROME

Methods of managing Frey's syndrome include:

  • Antiperspirants, usually containing aluminium chloride;
  • Denervation by tympanic neurectomy;
  • The injection of botulinum toxin into the affected skin.

The last is the most effective and can be performed as an out-patient.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 54, Edition: 28th, Pg: 849

question_text: Which among the following is the distal splenorenal shunt?
explanation:
The surgical shunt currently used most often is the distal splenorenal or Warren shunt. It has two components -

  • Interruption of all collateral vessels (e.g., left gastric (coronary) vein and gastroepiploic veins) that connect the superior mesenteric vein and gastrosplenic components of the splanchnic venous circulation.

Advantages -

  • Lower rate of hepatic encephalopathy and decompensation.
  • Does not interfere with subsequent liver transplantation.

Great saphenous vein: saphenous nerve

Short saphenous vein: aural nerve

  • The long saphenous vein is the most commonly used venous conduit in CABG as it is straightforward to harvest, provides good length and is easy to handle. Historical studies showed a limited long term patency rate for long saphenous vein grafts (50-60% at 10 years).

Complications of standard varicose vein surgery

Complications (minor and major) are reported in up to 20% of patients who undergo traditional varicose vein surgery.

Wound infections, the most common complication, are reduced by prophylactic antibiotics.

Nerve injury is the most common serious complications. The incidence of saphenous nerve neuralgia is up to 7% following GSV stripping to the knee (the incidence is higher with stripping to the ankle).

The incidence of sural nerve neuropraxia and common peroneal nerve injury may be as high as 20% and 4%, respectively, following SSV surgery.

The incidence of venous thromboembolic complications is approximately 0.5% following varicose vein surgery; however, patient risk factors must be individually assessed and appropriate prophylaxis administered according to guidelines.

question_text: What is the ideal time and method of removing hair before surgery to avoid surgical site infection?
option_a: On the OT table with electric hair clippers
option_b: With a razor 24 hours before surgery
option_c: With a hair removal cream on the previous day
option_d: On the OT table with a razor
explanation:
Explanation:

The best practice to minimize the risk of surgical site infection (SSI) is to avoid hair removal unless absolutely necessary. If hair must be removed, electric clippers should be used immediately before the surgery in the operating theater. This method minimizes microscopic skin abrasions and cuts that serve as niduses for bacterial colonization, unlike razors which significantly increase this risk. (Option B and D ruled out)

Key strategies for reducing surgical site infections (SSIs):

  • Hand Hygiene: Proper handwashing and use of alcohol-based hand rubs are crucial in preventing cross-contamination.
  • Minimizing Length of Stay: Reducing hospital stays lowers the risk of hospital-acquired infections.
  • Avoiding Preoperative Shaving: If hair removal is necessary, clippers should be used instead of razors to reduce micro-abrasions that can harbor bacteria.
  • Standardized Antiseptic Skin Prep: Chlorhexidine-alcohol is often preferred over povidone-iodine due to its superior efficacy.
  • Theatre Discipline: Adherence to sterile techniques, minimal door openings, and controlled airflows help prevent contamination.
  • Avoiding Hypothermia & Ensuring Oxygenation: Hypothermia impairs immune function, and supplemental oxygen helps improve wound healing and reduces the risk of infections.

Explanation of other options:

With a hair removal cream on the previous day (Option C): While depilatory creams cause less skin injury than razors, applying them the day before surgery is suboptimal. Skin irritation can occur, and the timing allows for potential bacterial growth before the incision is made.

Key Takeaways:

  • The gold standard is no hair removal.
  • If essential, use electric clippers immediately before surgery in the OT.

question_text: A 25-year-old with a 5-year history of unilateral varicose veins on the left leg presents to the surgery OPD as shown below. Identify the correct statement regarding this condition.
option_a: The most common cause is pelvic tumours
option_c: Recommended treatment is sclerotherapy in all cases
option_d: It can lead to eczema and pigmentation
explanation:
Explanation:

Among the given options, the true statement regarding varicose veins, which arises due to venous hypertension, is that it can lead to eczema and pigmentation.

  • Varicose veins are dilated superficial veins that can be classified as uncomplicated or complicated.
  • Complications may include thrombophlebitis, bleeding, or venous ulcers. While some cases remain asymptomatic, others present with noticeable symptoms.
  • It is seen more commonly in women compared to men, and the prevalence increases with age.
  • Higher BMI and taller stature are linked with a greater risk and are also associated with long periods of standing.
  • Symptoms include aching, heaviness, throbbing, burning, or bursting sensations in affected limbs, worsening with prolonged standing and easing with elevation or compression.
  • Other common complaints are itching, ankle swelling, and vague venous discomfort
  • These symptoms may interfere with work, recreation, and caregiving, reducing quality of life.
  • Clinically, varicose veins appear as enlarged, twisted subcutaneous veins.
  • Duplex ultrasound scanning is the gold standard, replacing older methods.
  • Venous hypertension of the leg presents with multiple characteristic features, including varicose veins, telangiectasia, and oedema.
  • Other manifestations include eczema, which may start as mild erythematous dermatitis with itching but can advance to blistering and weeping.
  • Pigmentation (haemosiderosis) manifests as brown discolouration of the skin, usually permanent and often seen near varicose veins and incompetent perforators.
  • Lipodermatosclerosis (LDS) results from chronic inflammation and fibrosis of the skin and subcutaneous tissues, producing a tight, woody leg on examination and occasionally leading to Achilles tendon contractures.
  • The CEAP system (Clinical-Aetiology-Anatomy-Pathophysiology) is a widely used descriptive classification for categorising chronic venous disorders and is given below.

Explanation of other options:

The most common cause is pelvic tumours (Option A): Pelvic tumours are not the most common cause of varicose veins. Other common risk factors include female sex, multiparity, obesity, and prolonged standing.

Graded as C6 (Option B): The image does not show an active venous ulcer, and so this option can be ruled out.

Recommended treatment is sclerotherapy in all cases (Option C): Sclerotherapy is not the recommended treatment in all cases.

question_text: All of the followings are correct regarding preoperative operation except:
option_a: Preoperative skin shaving should be done in the operation theatre immediately before surgery
option_b: Hair clipping is the best method for shaving
option_c: Alcohol hand gel is more effective than hand washing with soap, and it should be given priority than hand washing with soap
option_d: Short preoperative hospital stay is ideal before surgery
explanation:
Option A: If Skin shaving is performed the night before, the rate of SSI gets doubled because minor skin injury enhances superficial bacterial colonization. So preoperative skin shaving should be done in the operation theatre immediately before surgery.

Option B: Hair clipping is the best method with lowest infection rate. Cream depilation is messy.

Option C: Hand washing is more effective than any other method. Alcohol hand gel is ineffective against clostridium difficile. Soap plus povidone iodine is ideal for hand washing.

Option D: A short preoperative hospital stay lowers the risk of acquiring MRSA, Multiple resistant coagulase negative staphylococci and other antibiotic resistant organism from the hospital environment.

question_text: All of the following are correct regarding enteral feeding except:
option_a: Sip feed typically provide 200 kcal and 2 g of nitrogen per 200 ml carton.
option_b: Ryle's tube feeding started with 20-30ml/hour initially and then gradually increased within 1 week and should be continued in night also as there is less chance of vomiting.

explanation:
Option A: Sip feeds used in those who can drink but whose appetites are impaired. They typically provide 200 Kcal and 2 g Nitrogen per 200 ml carton.

Option B: Ryle’s tube feeding started initially with 20-30 ml/hour and gradually Increased to goal rates within 48-72 hours. Feeding is discontinued for 4-5 hours overnight to allow gastric pH to return to normal. This reduces the incidence of nosocomial pneumonia and aspiration.

Option C: If feeding is maintained for more than week or so, a fine bore feeding tube is preferable and is likely to cause fewer gastric and esophageal erosions.

Option D: If enteral feeding required for 4-6 weeks or more than PEG is preferable than Nasogastric tube. This minimizes the traumatic complications related to indwelling tubes.

Through an anterior submammary incision the LIMA can be dissected down with the aid of a thoracoscope and grafted to the LAD.

question_text:
COVID 19 positive patient requiring hospitalization can be planned for surgery after
How many weeks?
explanation:
If a patients tests positive for covid-19, elective surgical procedures should be delayed until the patient is no longer infectious and has demonstrated recovery from COVID-19.

The timing of elective surgery after recovery from COVID-19 uses both symptom- and severity-based categories.

  • Four weeks for an asymptomatic patient or recovery from only mild, non-respiratory symptoms.
  • Six weeks for a symptomatic patient (e.g., cough, dyspnea) who did not require hospitalization.
  • Eight to 10 weeks for a symptomatic patient who is diabetic, immunocompromised, or hospitalized.
  • Twelve weeks for a patient who was admitted to an intensive care unit due to COVID-19 infection

Key aspects in COVID-19 surgical patient management

  • All suspected or infected patients must be managed with the maximum attention.
  • All personnel in contact with the patient must wear PPE.
  • Transfers must be protected.
  • Infected patients must be moved as little as possible through the hospital.
  • Transfer routes must be precisely planned and be as short as possible.
  • The COVID operating area should be in a dedicated and possibly separate area.
  • COVID operating room must be dedicated and as close as possible to the entrance of the theater block.
  • Disposable material should be preferred.
  • Minimal material should be used for each intervention.
  • Transport personnel should be the same from transport origin to destination.
  • Once the patient has entered, the OR doors must be closed.
  • Operators (i.e., surgeon, anesthetist, nurses, technicians) should enter the OR in a timely manner to minimize exposure to infected patients.
  • Personnel involved in the intervention should not leave the OR during the procedure.
  • High OR air exchange cycles are recommended (> 25 exchanges/h).
  • Clinical documentation must remain outside the OR
  • At the end of each intervention all disposable materials must be disposed of and all surfaces and electromedical devices accurately cleaned and disinfected.
  • PPE must be removed and disposed of outside the OR in dedicated doffing areas ensuring the virus is not transmitted to the healthcare worker.
  • OR and surrounding donning/doffing areas must be sanitized as soon as possible after each procedure.
  • After each procedure, all involved personnel, whenever possible, should shower.
  • Recovery phase after surgery must be done in OR, before transfer to the ward/ICU.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7137852/

https://www.asahq.org/in-the-spotlight/coronavirus-covid-19-information/elective-surgery

Postoperative management

Currently; the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) recommends that prophylactic antibiotics are not required for patients with prosthetic valves undergoing dental procedures. Other leading European bodies have recently supported the above recommendation as there is no strong evidence to the contrary.

  • Antithrombotic therapy
  • All patients with mechanical valves require warfarin, usually started on the first or second postoperative day. The use of anticoagulation or antiplatelet therapy with biological valves is variable and depends on the patient's underlying rhythm postoperatively and surgeons' preference.

option_b: The fibrous cortex from the entrapped underlying lung is removed

Decortication

  • If the lung fails to re-expand after drainage of the empyema, the more radical operation of decortication may be required. The fibrous cortex or peel from the entrapped underlying lung is removed so that the lung can expand to obliterate the pleural space.
  • This is usually performed through a posterolateral thoracotomy, though in selected cases it can be performed as a VATS procedure. It requires careful dissection to remove the parietal and visceral cortex, taking care not to damage the visceral pleura, so allowing the lung to re-expand fully.

question_text: Which of the following is not true about Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis?
option_b: Caused by hypertrophy of longitudinal muscles
option_c: USG is the gold standard investigation for this condition
explanation:
Explanation:

This condition arises due to hypertrophy of the circular muscle fibres of the pylorus, rather than the longitudinal muscle layer.

Clinical Presentation of Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS):

  • Typical Age of Onset: 3-6 weeks
  • Key Symptoms:
    • Projectile, non-bilious vomiting (Option A ruled out)
    • Visible gastric peristaltic waves
    • Palpable "olive-shaped" mass (hypertrophied pylorus), best felt from the left side
    • Test Feed Findings:
      • Gastric peristalsis seen moving left → right across the upper abdomen
      • In a calm, feeding infant, the pyloric "olive" can be palpated in the right upper quadrant
  • Electrolyte Disturbances:
    • Hypochloraemia
    • Hypokalaemia (due to repeated vomiting)
    • Metabolic alkalosis (Option D ruled out)

Investigations:

  • Ultrasound - Gold Standard (Option C ruled out)
    • Findings:
      • Doughnut sign: Thickened pyloric muscle
  • Diagnostic Criteria:
    • Pyloric muscle thickness ≥ 4 mm
    • Pyloric canal length > 14 mm
  • Sonographic Signs:
    • "Cervix sign" (long-axis view)
  • "Target sign" (short-axis view)
  • Barium Meal (Less Common, rarely used today):
    • Radiological Signs:
      • "String sign": Thin streak of contrast through a narrowed pylorus
  • "Railroad track sign": Two parallel thin contrast lines from partial narrowing
  • "Double track sign": Variant of railroad track due to marked muscle hypertrophy

question_text: A patient with oral cancer underwent radical surgery with PMMC flap reconstruction. What is the important indicator for adjuvant radiotherapy?
explanation:
Explanation

Extranodal extension (ENE) is a major criterion for adjuvant radiotherapy following surgery in oral cancer patients.

  • In oral cancer management, adjuvant radiotherapy is considered when certain adverse pathological features are present in the postoperative histopathology report.
  • These features are categorized as major and minor criteria.
  • Extranodal extension (ENE) where cancer has breached the capsule of a lymph node is a major indication for adjuvant radiotherapy, even if present alone.
  • The aim of adjuvant radiotherapy in such cases is to reduce the risk of local and regional recurrence and to improve overall survival.
  • The external beam radiotherapy is typically delivered postoperatively.
  • Indications for Adjuvant Radiotherapy:

Explanation of other options:

Multiple lymph node metastasis (Option B): It is considered a minor criterion. Alone, it is not sufficient to indicate adjuvant radiotherapy unless accompanied by at least one other minor criterion.

T3 tumor (Option C): Also a minor criterion. It may suggest an aggressive tumor, but adjuvant radiotherapy requires at least two minor or one major criterion.

Close margin (Option D): Defined as a surgical margin between 1–4.9 mm. It is a minor criterion and not an independent indication for adjuvant radiotherapy.

question_text: A 33-year-old man was referred to the surgery OPD from the infertility clinic. On inspection, the scrotum appeared as in the image. On palpation, a bag of worm sensation was felt. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The description of a "bag of worms" sensation on palpation is pathognomonic for a varicocele. This condition is caused by dilatation and tortuosity of the pampiniform plexus of veins within the scrotum. It is a common finding in men presenting with infertility, as it can increase scrotal temperature and impair spermatogenesis. The swelling is typically more prominent when standing and often reduces when lying down.

  • Symptoms: Swelling at scrotal root, dragging groin/scrotal pain, "bag of worms" on palpation, impulse on coughing, swelling that reduces when lying down (except in RCC).
  • Investigations: Venous Doppler (scrotum/groin), abdominal USG (to exclude renal tumor), semen analysis.
  • Treatment: Surgical correction → Palomo's operation (suprainguinal ligation of testicular vein), simple ligation or excision of veins.

Explanation of other options:

Hydrocele (Option A): A hydrocele is a fluid collection around the testis. It presents as a smooth, cystic, transilluminable swelling, not a tortuous "bag of worms."

Testicular torsion (Option C): This is a surgical emergency presenting with acute, severe testicular pain, nausea, and vomiting. The testis is exquisitely tender and often high-riding. It is not associated with a chronic "bag of worms" feeling.

Epididymo-orchitis (Option D): This is an infection causing a painful, swollen, and tender testis and epididymis, often with fever. It does not present with the classic palpation finding of a varicocele.

Key Takeaways:

  • The "bag of worms" sensation is diagnostic of a varicocele.
  • Varicoceles are a common correctable cause of male infertility.

question_text: A 25-year-old male presents with a long-standing midline neck swelling. Recently, it became painful, inflamed, and started discharging clear fluid. On examination, the swelling is noted to move with deglutition and protrusion of the tongue. Which of the following statements is correct regarding this condition?
option_a: Untreated condition may lead to squamous cell carcinoma
option_c: They are remnants of thyroid tissue
option_d: Acid-fast bacilli staining should be done to come to diagnosis
explanation:
Explanation:

The features described (midline neck swelling, moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion, watery discharge after inflammation) are classic for a thyroglossal duct cyst, which arises from persistence of the embryological thyroglossal duct, a transient connection between the developing thyroid gland and tongue.

 Thyroglossal Duct Cyst

  • Embryology: Remnants of the thyroglossal duct along the midline from foramen caecum (tongue base) to thyroid isthmus.
  • Typical site: Subhyoid (most common), but can also occur suprahyoid, intralingual, or at thyroid cartilage level.
  • Clinical features:
    • Midline neck swelling.
    • Moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion (due to tract attachment to foramen caecum).
    • May become infected and rupture, forming a thyroglossal fistula (always acquired).

Management

  • Definitive surgery: Sistrunk’s procedure – excision of cyst, tract, and central portion of the hyoid bone to reduce recurrence risk.
  • Incision & drainage: Contraindicated, as it increases fistula risk.

Malignant Potential

  • Long-standing untreated cysts have a small risk of malignant change.
  • Most common carcinoma: Papillary thyroid carcinoma (not squamous cell carcinoma).

Untreated condition may lead to squamous cell carcinoma (Option A): While rare, a thyroglossal duct cyst can undergo malignant transformation. However, the most common malignancy associated with it is papillary thyroid carcinoma, not squamous cell carcinoma.

Excision is not contraindicated for thyroglossal duct cysts (Option B): Surgical removal (via the Sistrunk procedure) is the definitive treatment. This involves excising the cyst, the tract, and a portion of the hyoid bone to reduce the risk of recurrence.

Acid-fast bacilli staining should be done to come to diagnosis (Option D): Acid-fast bacilli (AFB) staining is typically done to diagnose tuberculosis. However, there is no indication that tuberculosis is likely here, as the clinical presentation and location are more consistent with a thyroglossal duct cyst.
