question_text: A 58-year-old diabetic man presents with septic shock. He is febrile, tachycardic, and has a blood pressure of 80/50 mmHg, despite adequate fluid resuscitation with crystalloids. His urine output is low and he is drowsy. What is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

Norepinephrine is the preferred first-line vasopressor for treating hypotension in septic shock, and should be initiated after fluid resuscitation if blood pressure remains low.Sepsis is defined as a life-threatening condition caused by a dysregulated immune response to infection, resulting in organ dysfunction.It is clinically diagnosed when there is suspected or confirmed infection along with an increase of 2 or more points in the SOFA (Sequential Organ Failure Assessment) score.Septic shock is a more severe subset, characterized by:

  • The need for vasopressors to maintain a mean arterial pressure (MAP) ≥ 65 mmHg
  • A serum lactate level > 2 mmol/L, despite adequate fluid resuscitation

Initial Management Approach:

  • Antibiotic Therapy:
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics should be administered within the first hour of recognition.
    • Blood cultures must be obtained prior to antibiotic administration, if possible, but treatment should not be delayed.
  • Fluid Resuscitation:
    • Crystalloids (e.g., normal saline or lactated Ringer’s) should be administered at a dose of 30 mL/kg within the first 3 hours.
    • The goal is to restore tissue perfusion and prevent progression of organ dysfunction.
  • Vasopressors:
    • If hypotension persists despite fluids, norepinephrine is the vasopressor of choice.
    • The target MAP is 65 mmHg, and arterial line monitoring is recommended for accurate pressure measurement.

Additional Considerations in Sepsis Management:

  • Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS):
    • In sepsis-associated ARDS, mechanical ventilation with low tidal volume (6 mL/kg) and high PEEP settings is advised to minimize ventilator-induced lung injury.
  • Supportive Care Measures:
    • Venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis unless contraindicated
    • Stress ulcer prevention using proton pump inhibitors or H2 blockers
    • Tight glucose control to avoid both hyperglycemia and hypoglycemia
    • Renal replacement therapy (RRT) when indicated in patients with acute kidney injury (AKI)

Dopamine is no longer preferred in the management of septic shock because it has a higher risk of causing arrhythmias and provides less consistent effects on blood pressure compared to norepinephrine. It may be considered in rare cases with bradycardia, but it is not the best choice for this patient.

Explanations for other Options:

Administer dopamine (Option A): Dopamine is no longer preferred in the management of septic shock because it has a higher risk of causing arrhythmias and provides less consistent effects on blood pressure compared to norepinephrine. It may be considered in rare cases with bradycardia, but it is not the best choice for this patient.

Administer hydrocortisone (Option C): Hydrocortisone is used only in patients with septic shock who do not respond to both fluids and vasopressors, i.e., refractory shock. Since this patient has not yet received vasopressors, starting hydrocortisone at this point would be premature.

Administer vasopressin (Option D): Vasopressin is used as a second-line vasopressor and is usually added to norepinephrine when blood pressure is still not maintained with norepinephrine alone. It is not recommended as an initial vasopressor, so it is not the next best step in this case.

Key takeaway:

SOFA SCORE

question_text: A neonate presents with forceful, non-bilious vomiting after feeds, lethargy, and dehydration. On abdominal examination, visible gastric peristalsis is noted. A barium meal study shows findings as illustrated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The barium meal shows the classical string sign, which is suggestive of hypertrophic pyloric stenosis, further supported by the clinical presentation of non-bilious projectile vomiting, visible gastric peristalsis, dehydration, and lethargy in the neonate.

Congenital Hypertrophic Pyloric Stenosis (CHPS).

  • Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (CHPS) is caused by hypertrophy of the circular muscle of the pylorus, resulting in gastric outlet obstruction.
  • It is seen four times more commonly in boys, especially in first-born male infants.
  • Typically presents between 2-6 weeks of age with projectile, non-bilious vomiting after feeds.
  • Persistent vomiting leads to dehydration and hypokalemic hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis due to loss of gastric HCl.
  • Physical examination shows
    • Visible gastric peristalsis (left to right)
    • Palpable olive-shaped mass in the epigastrium.

Diagnosis:

  • Abdominal X-ray
    • Findings are generally non-specific, but may reveal a distended stomach with minimal gas in the distal intestines.
  • Ultrasound is the investigation of choice.
    • Pyloric muscle thickness: > 3 mm
    • Pyloric length: > 14 mm
    • Ultrasound findings in presence of functional gastric outlet obstruction is diagnostic.
  • Contrast Studies (Upper GI Series): The barium meal shows an elongated pylorus with a narrow lumen giving the classic string sign.

Treatment: Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy

  • Involves incising the thickened pyloric musculature to relieve obstruction.

Explanation of other options:

Hirschsprung's disease (Option A): Hirschsprung disease is characterized by the absence of ganglion cells in the distal intestine, which can present as delayed passing of meconium or constipation. Barium enema shows the dilated proximal segment and the transition zone. Forceful vomiting without bile and visible stomach movements are not typical of Hirschsprung's disease.

Jejunal atresia (Option C): A congenital obstruction of the jejunum, usually presenting with bilious vomiting and abdominal distension. On X-ray, it shows multiple dilated small bowel loops and the triple bubble sign. In this case, the vomiting is non-bilious, making jejunal atresia unlikely.

Duodenal atresia (Option D): Another congenital condition where there is a complete or partial obstruction of the duodenum, which results in bilious vomiting. It often presents with a double bubble sign on the X-ray.

question_text: A neonate presents with mild, intermittent upper abdominal pain. On examination, the infant has a scaphoid abdomen with decreased breath sounds bilaterally. The X-ray is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The neonate's features of intermittent upper abdominal pain, scaphoid abdomen, and decreased bilateral breath sounds, together with X-ray evidence of bowel loops within the thoracic cavity, are highly suggestive of a Bochdalek hernia, a type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).

Congenital diaphragmatic hernia

  • The most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH).
  • CDH is due to the failure of the development of the pleuroperitoneal canal.
  • There are two classical congenital sites for herniation of abdominal viscera into the thorax:
    • Foramen of Morgagni
      • An anterior diaphragmatic defect located between the sternal and costal attachments. The transverse colon is the most commonly herniated organ.
    • Foramen of Bochdalek
      • An posterolateral defect in the dome of the diaphragm, typically on the left side, allowing abdominal contents to enter the thoracic cavity.
  • Congenital diaphragmatic hernias are associated with:
    • Lung hypoplasia
    • Pulmonary hypertension
    • Cardiac defects
    • Gastroesophageal reflux.

Management

  • Postnatal Stabilization:
    • Intubation, muscle relaxation, and gentle ventilation to maintain pH and oxygenation, avoiding right-to-left shunting.
    • Permissive hypercapnia and high-frequency oscillation may be used.
    • Pulmonary hypertension can cause hypoxia, hypercapnia, and cardiac dysfunction; managed with:
      • Nitric oxide, prostaglandin E1, milrinone, and inotropes
      • Extracorporeal life support (ECLS) if severe.
  • Surgical Repair:
    • Performed once pulmonary circulation stabilizes.
    • Approach: abdominal or thoracic, open or minimally invasive.
    • Defect repair:
      • Small defects: few sutures
      • Large defects: patch (Silastic or GORE-TEX)
    • Hernial sac may be removed or plicated.

Explanation of other options:

Pneumonia (Option B): while being a common cause of respiratory distress, would not typically present with bowel loops in the thoracic cavity on X-ray. It usually shows lung consolidation, infiltrates, or pleural effusion on imaging, not abdominal organs in the chest.

Gastric volvulus (Option C) involves twisting of the stomach, which can lead to obstruction, pain, and vomiting, but it does not cause bowel loops in the thoracic cavity.

Eventration of the diaphragm (Option D): In eventration of diaphragm, there is diaphragmatic weakness or paralysis, leading to the upward displacement of abdominal contents into the chest. While it may cause respiratory distress, it does not lead to bowel loops in the chest on X-ray.

question_text: A 65-year-old male with a history of thromboembolic stroke on warfarin and aspirin presents with headache, confusion, and a fall in the toilet. NCCT head given below. What is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The CT finding of a crescent-shaped hemorrhage crossing suture lines is diagnostic of subdural hematoma (SDH).
  • The patient is on warfarin (anticoagulant), which worsens bleeding risk.
  • First priority = reverse coagulopathy:
    • Vitamin K → restores clotting factor synthesis (but acts slowly).
    • Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) → provides immediate clotting factors.
  • Second priority = neurosurgical evaluation for potential evacuation (craniotomy, craniectomy, or burr hole, depending on severity).

Management of Subdural Hematoma (especially in anticoagulated patients):

  1. Stabilize patient (ABC approach).
  2. Reverse anticoagulation:
    1. Vitamin K
    2. FFP or Prothrombin Complex Concentrate (PCC, if available).
  3. Neurosurgical intervention:
    1. Burr hole drainage (chronic SDH).
    2. Craniotomy or craniectomy (acute large SDH with mass effect).
  4. Adjuncts: Mannitol, head elevation, hyperventilation (if signs of raised ICP).

Explanation of other options:

Aspirin + Clopidogrel (Option A) would not be appropriate because they both increase bleeding risk and do not address the anticoagulation from warfarin.

IV Mannitol (Option C) is used to reduce intracranial pressure, but the priority in this case is reversing anticoagulation and consulting neurosurgery.

Observation (Option D) alone is not sufficient, especially with the anticoagulant therapy involved and the size of the SDH shown on CT, which may require surgical intervention.

question_text: During thyroid surgery, which of the following surgical steps is least likely to result in hoarseness of voice postoperatively?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ligation of the superior thyroid vessels is least likely to cause hoarseness of voice, because injury at this step affects the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (EBSLN) - which primarily supplies the cricothyroid muscleresponsible for pitch modulation, not phonation.

Hence, while pitch may be altered slightly, voice hoarseness results mainly from recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN)injury, not from superior laryngeal nerve involvement.

Sites of Risk of damage of RLN:

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN), due to its anatomical location, runs in close proximity to the inferior thyroid artery, which makes it vulnerable during dissection or ligation of the artery during thyroidectomy.
  • The strap muscles (sternohyoid, sternothyroid, omohyoid) are located in the anterior neck and are often retracted or dissected during thyroid surgery; they could possibly lead to RLN injury. (Option A ruled out)
  • Beahrs' triangle boundaries are:
    • Medially: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) ascends in the tracheoesophageal groove.
    • Laterally: The common carotid artery.
    • Superiorly: The inferior thyroid artery.
  • Exploring Beahr's triangle is a procedure that can lead to hoarseness if the RLN is injured or affected during dissection. (Option B ruled out)
  • The Zuckerkandl tubercle is a projection of normal thyroid tissue, and during thyroidectomy, these tubercles are usually removed. RLN injury can occur in this area. (Option C ruled out)

question_text: Most commonly bypassed artery during CABG surgery is?
explanation:

question_text: Inflation during laparoscopy is done with the help of which instrument?
explanation:
There are two fundamental ways to access the abdomen laparoscopically:

  1. the open technique (Hasson's or modifed Hasson's)
  2. the closed technique (Veress needle and/or visual entry trocar).

Veress needle is used for creating initial pneumoperitoneum so that the trocar can enter safely and the distance of the abdominal wall from the abdominal viscera should increase.

Veress needle consists of an outer cannula with a beveled needlepoint for cutting through tissues. Inside the cannula is an inner stylet, which is loaded with a spring that "springs forward" in response to the sudden decrease in pressure encountered upon crossing the abdominal wall and entering the peritoneal cavity. The lateral hole on this stylet enables CO2 gas to be delivered intra-abdominally.

For the patient with scars from previous abdominal surgery, the safest technique is an open approach at Palmer's point, 3 cm below the left subcostal margin in the mid-clavicular line. Adequate lighting and good assistance with retraction are essential

question_text: A 20-year-old man presents with episodic headaches, palpitations, and paroxysmal hypertension. Clinical suspicion of pheochromocytoma is raised. Which of the following is the preferred initial investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The preferred initial investigation in a suspected pheochromocytoma is a biochemical test is specifically, measurement of 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines (or plasma free metanephrines).

This is because pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumour, and biochemical confirmation must precede imaging.

  • Metanephrines are metabolites of catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine).
  • They are continuously produced, making them more reliable than episodic catecholamine levels.
  • Elevated urinary metanephrines and VMA (vanillyl mandelic acid) confirm excessive catecholamine secretion.

Explanation of Other Options:

USG-abdomen (Option A):

  • Can detect large adrenal masses, but lacks sensitivity for small or extra-adrenal lesions.
  • Poor at differentiating pheochromocytoma from other adrenal masses.
  • Used only as an initial screening tool in resource-limited settings or pediatrics.

MIBG (Option C):

  • Used after biochemical confirmation to:
    • Detect extra-adrenal or multifocal tumours
    • Evaluate metastatic disease
    • Confirm residual or recurrent lesions post-surgery
  • Not a first-line investigation.

question_text: Where is the epiphrenic diverticula most commonly situated?
explanation:
• Epiphrenic diverticula are pulsion diverticula situated in the lower oesophagus above the diaphragm.
  • They may be quite large, but cause surprisingly few symptoms.
  • They probably reflect some loss of coordination between an incoming pressure wave and appropriate relaxation of the LOS. This needs to be acknowledged in the surgical management of the patient.
  • The diverticulum, in isolation, should not be assumed to account for a patient’s illness just because it looks dramatic on a radiograph. Large diverticula may be excised, and this should be combined with a myotomy from the site of the diverticulum down to the cardia to relieve functional obstruction.

question_text: The most common congenital diaphragmatic hernia seen in neonates is:
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Left posterolateral (Bochdalek) hernia is the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) in neonates.

  • Congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH) is a birth defect where abdominal organs herniate into the thoracic cavity due to a defect in the diaphragm, leading to pulmonary hypoplasia and respiratory distress in neonates.
  • Bochdalek hernia is the most common type (90%), occurring due to failure of closure of the pleuroperitoneal canal.
  • Left side involvement is more common (84%) because the left pleuroperitoneal canal closes later than the right, and the presence of the liver on the right provides a protective effect.
  • Symptoms in neonates include:
    • Severe respiratory distress soon after birth
    • Scaphoid (sunken) abdomen
    • Mediastinal shift
    • Pulmonary hypertension
  • Types of CDH:

Explanation of other options:

Right anteromedial (Option B): Refers to Morgagni hernia, which is rare, usually asymptomatic, and less common than left-sided Bochdalek hernias.

Esophageal hiatus (Option C): Hiatal hernias typically present later in life and are usually acquired, not the most common congenital type in neonates.

Central location (Option D): Central tendon defects are very rare and not associated with typical neonatal diaphragmatic hernia presentations.

question_text: Which segment of the liver denotes caudate lobe according to couinauds classification?
explanation:
• The caudate lobe (segment I) is the dorsal portion of the liver
  • It embraces the IVC on its ventral surface and lies posterior to the left portal triad inferiorly and the left and middle hepatic veins superiorly.
  • The main bulk of the caudate lobe is to the left of the IVC, but inferiorly, it traverses between the IVC and left portal triad, where it fuses to the right liver (segments VI and VII).
  • This part of the caudate lobe is known as the right portion or the caudate process
  • The left portion of the caudate lobe lies in the lesser omental bursa and is covered anteriorly by the gastrohepatic ligament (lesser omentum) that separates it from segments II and III anteriorly.
  • The gastrohepatic ligament attaches to the ligamentum venosum (sinus venosus remnant) along the left side of the left portal triad

Reference: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1428

question_text: A 45-year-old patient with a history of kidney stones that were surgically removed 2 years ago presents with fever and flank pain. The imaging done is shown here. What would be the most appropriate next step in managing this patient?
explanation:
Explanation

  • The patient's fever and flank pain point toward infection and obstruction.
  • Imaging demonstrates a retained foreign body in the bladder (likely a residual stone fragment or surgical material from prior stone surgery).
  • Cystoscopy is the minimally invasive procedure of choice:
    • Allows direct visualization of the bladder.
    • Facilitates foreign body retrieval or stone removal without open surgery.
    • Prevents ongoing infection and obstruction.
  • Thus, cystoscopic retrieval is the safest and most effective step.

Cystoscopy

Explanation of Other Options:

Laparotomy (Option A): Incorrect. Too invasive for a bladder foreign body. Reserved for cases where minimally invasive options fail or in complex retroperitoneal pathology.

Lithotripsy (Option B): Incorrect. Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL) is used mainly for renal or ureteric stones, not for bladder foreign bodies that can be directly removed.

Leave the foreign body inside (Option C): Incorrect. Retained foreign bodies can cause recurrent infection, calculus formation, hematuria, or even bladder perforation. They must always be removed.

question_text: A patient with a history of tuberculosis presents with dysuria and sterile pyuria. The cystoscopy image provided below indicates what condition?
explanation:
Golf hole ureter is a classical cystoscopic finding in genitourinary tuberculosis, reflecting fibrotic contraction around the ureteric orifice.

  • In genitourinary tuberculosis (GUTB), especially in chronic cases, the bladder becomes fibrotic and contracted due to ongoing inflammation and healing by fibrosis.
  • This leads to changes in the appearance of the ureteric orifices seen during cystoscopy.
  • One of the hallmark findings is the "golf hole ureter", a sharply demarcated, rigid, gaping ureteric orifice caused by periureteric fibrosis.
  • This case is also supported clinically by:
    • History of TB
    • Dysuria
    • Sterile pyuria (WBCs in urine without bacterial growth)
  • Additional findings of GUTB:
    • "Thimble bladder": contracted, non-compliant bladder on imaging
    • Beaded vas deferens or scrotal sinuses in male genital involvement
    • Calcifications or irregular ureteric narrowing on IVU or CECT
    • Early calyceal changes: "moth-eaten" calyces
  • Investigations:
    • Urine for AFB (acid-fast bacilli) or PCR
    • CECT urography or IVU
    • Cystoscopy (as shown in this case)
  • Treatment:
    • Antitubercular Therapy (ATT) is the cornerstone
    • Surgery for complications like strictures or severe fibrosis

Explanation of other options:

Ureterocele (Option B): This is a congenital dilation of the distal ureter protruding into the bladder. On imaging, it shows the "cobra head sign." Cystoscopically, it appears as a ballooning mass, not a gaping rigid orifice.


Hunner lesions (Option C): These are seen in interstitial cystitis, presenting as ulcerative patches in the bladder mucosa. They are unrelated to TB and do not involve the ureteric orifices.

Urethral stricture (Option D): Refers to narrowing of the urethra, not involving the ureteric orifices or bladder mucosa. Symptoms include weak urinary stream and incomplete emptying but no golf-hole appearance.

question_text: A newborn male is noted to have an underdeveloped scrotum, with the testis found close to the peritoneum. Which of the following factors helps facilitate the descent of the testis into the scrotum?
option_d: Manual repositioning of the testis into scrotum
explanation:
Explanation:

Administration of GnRH analogues stimulates the release of gonadotropins, which in turn increase androgen production. Since testicular descent is an androgen-dependent process, GnRH analogues assist in descent by enhancing endogenous androgen levels.

Explanation of other options:

Testosterone (Option B): Although testosterone is important for testicular descent, direct testosterone therapy in neonates is less preferred. GnRH analogues are favored because they increase androgen levels without prematurely stimulating spermatogenesis or adversely affecting Sertoli cell count (important for fertility).

Cold compressions (Option C): There is no role for cold compresses in testicular descent.

Manual repositioning (Option D): This refers to orchidopexy, a surgical procedure performed by specialists. It is not a conservative measure performed by caregivers. Surgery is the definitive treatment but not the answer in this scenario.

Undescended Testis (Cryptorchidism)

Key Takeaways:

  • Testicular descent is androgen-dependent.
  • GnRH analogues are used to stimulate gonadotropin → androgen surge.
  • Orchidopexy is definitive treatment if descent does not occur by 6-12 months.

question_text: A cricket player was struck on the head by a cricket ball and initially appeared well. He later collapsed, regained consciousness, continued to play, and was subsequently found unconscious in the dressing room. Based on the CT scan findings provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the clinical scenario of initial transient loss of consciousness, a subsequent lucid interval, and CT scan revealing a biconvex, lens-shaped hematoma, the most likely diagnosis is Extraduralal (Epiduralhaemorrhage

Extradural hematoma

  • Extradural hematoma is a neurosurgical emergency resulting from rupture of an artery, vein, or venous sinus, often associated with a skull fracture.
  • The classical mechanism involves a fracture of the thin squamous temporal bonewith injury to the middle meningeal artery.

Clinical Features:

  • Transient loss of consciousness immediately after trauma.
  • Followed by a lucid interval, where the patient appears awake, may have a headache, but shows no neurological deficits.
  • As the hematoma expands, intracranial compensation is exhausted, leading to:
    • Contralateral hemiparesis
    • Reduced consciousness
    • Ipsilateral pupillary dilation

Imaging:

  • CT scan shows a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain, confined by the dura.
  • May show mass effect, compression of adjacent brain, and midline shift.

Management:

  • Urgent neurosurgical transfer is essential for all patients.
  • Immediate evacuation is indicated for patients who are deteriorating, comatose, or have large hematomas.
  • Close observation with serial imaging is appropriate for stable patients with smaller hematomas.
  • Surgical options:
    • Emergency: Burr hole surgery for rapid decompression.
    • Definitive: Craniotomy with hematoma evacuation to remove the clot and control bleeding

Explanation of other options:

Artifact (Option B): Artifacts on a CT scan refers to image distortion or interference that does not represent actual pathology. Given the clear clinical scenario of trauma and the CT finding of a hematoma, an artefact is unlikely to be the cause of the findings.

Subdural haemorrhage (Option C): Subdural hematoma ccurs when blood accumulates between the dura mater and the arachnoid membrane. They tend to be crescent-shaped on CT, unlike the biconvex lens-shaped appearance of an extradural haemorrhage.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage (Option D): Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH) involves bleeding into the subarachnoid space, located between the arachnoid membrane and pia mater. On CT imaging, SAH typically appears diffuse, with blood spread throughout the subarachnoid space.

question_text: A 25-year-old female presents with rapidly worsening swelling and severe pain in her right hand, five days after sustaining a thorn prick while gardening. On examination, the hand is diffusely swollen, the patient experiences excruciating pain on passive extension of the fingers, and marked tenderness is elicited along the palmar aspect. Despite oral antibiotics and analgesics prescribed earlier, her symptoms have worsened. Which of the following statements best describes the next step in management?
option_a: More common in the dorsal aspect of the hand
option_b: X-ray imaging will aid in the location of the foreign body in all patients
option_d: Oral analgesics are the mainstay of treatment
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical features point to a deep palmar abscess (deep hand infection), which occurs following penetrating trauma such as a thorn prick. Severe pain, swelling, and pain on passive stretching of the hand are classical signs of a closed-space infection.

The definitive management is surgical incision and drainage (I&D) to evacuate pus, relieve pressure, prevent compartment syndrome, and remove any retained foreign body. Antibiotics and analgesics are adjuncts, but surgery is the mainstay.

Deep Palmar Infection: These infections begin in the palm and may be confined to a web space initially. As the infection progresses, the entire hand becomes swollen and tender due to the accumulation of pus on either side of the septum.

  • Management:
    • The treatment involves incision and drainage (I&D) with a thorough washout of the wound.
    • It's essential to open all affected deep spaces. In some cases, incisions may be needed on both the dorsal and volar sides of the hand.
    • If the extent of the infection is unclear, imaging techniques like ultrasound or MRI can be used to delineate the spread within the deep palmar spaces.

Explanation of Other Options:

More common in the dorsal aspect of the hand (Option A): Infections or abscesses caused by foreign bodies are more common in the palmar aspect due to the tighter fascial compartments.

X-ray imaging will aid in the location of the foreign body in all patients (Option B): X-rays are not always helpful, especially for non-radio-opaque foreign bodies (wood), so other imaging like ultrasound might be more useful.

Oral analgesics (Option D) may help manage pain, but they are not sufficient for treating the underlying infection/abscess, which requires I&D.

question_text: A 65-year-old man with severe triple-vessel coronary artery disease is scheduled for a Coronary Artery Bypass Grafting (CABG) procedure. The surgeon plans to use the left internal mammary artery (LIMA) and saphenous vein grafts. The procedure will be performed on cardiopulmonary bypass. Which of the following surgical incisions will provide the best access to the heart, great vessels, and the LIMA?
explanation:
Explanation:

Median Sternotomy is the workhorse incision for the vast majority of cardiac surgical procedures, including CABG, valve replacements, and repair of congenital heart defects in adults.

A median sternotomy provides excellent, unparalleled exposure to all critical structures required for on-pump cardiac surgery:

  • The entire heart (all four chambers)
  • The ascending aorta (for arterial cannulation)
  • The right atrium (for venous cannulation)
  • The great vessels
  • Both internal mammary arteries, especially the Left Internal Mammary Artery (LIMA), which is the gold standard conduit for bypassing the Left Anterior Descending (LAD) artery.

Common Surgical Approaches to the Heart:

Explanation of Other Options:

Left anterolateral thoracotomy (Option B): This incision provides poor access to the ascending aorta and right side of the heart, making cannulation for cardiopulmonary bypass very difficult.

Right anterolateral thoracotomy (Option C): This approach is used for isolated mitral or tricuspid valve surgery but provides no access to the LIMA and poor access for a full CABG.

Subxiphoid approach (Option D): This is a very limited incision used for pericardial drainage and does not provide sufficient access for any open-heart procedure.

explanation:
• Clinical examination for DVT is unreliable. Physical signs may also be absent. Mild pitting oedema of the ankle, dilated surface veins, a stiff calf and tenderness over the course of the deep veins should be sought.
  • Leg pain occurs in about 50% of patients with DVT but is non-specific.Homans' sign - resistance ( not pain) of the calf muscles to forcible dorsiflexion - is not specific and should not be elicited.Tenderness occurs in 75% of patients but is also found in 50% of patients without objectively confirmed DVT.
  • The pain and tenderness associated with DVT does not usually correlate with the size, location or extent of the thrombus. Clinical signs and symptoms of pulmonary embolism occur in about 10% of patients with confirmed DVT.
  • A low-grade pyrexia may be present, especially in a patient who is having repeated pulmonary embolism. Patients may have signs of cyanosis, dyspnoea, raised neck veins, a fixed split second heart sound and a pleural rub if they have pulmonary emboli causing right heart strain, although these signs may be subtle or absent

question_text: A patient, on the 5th postoperative day, develops low-grade fever along with calf pain and pedal edema. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's postoperative low-grade fever, calf pain, and unilateral pedal edema are classic signs of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), a common complication after surgery due to venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability (Virchow's triad).

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT)

  • Acute DVT is the formation of a thrombus in the deep veins, most commonly in the lower extremities.
  • DVT is the major cause of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized, especially surgical, patients.

Pathophysiology (Virchow's Triad)

  • Venous stasis - due to immobilization or surgery
  • Endothelial injury - trauma or surgery
  • Hypercoagulable state - malignancy, pregnancy, obesity, age >60, tobacco use, prior DVT

These factors often coexist in surgical patients, increasing the risk of thrombosis.

Signs and symptoms

  • Common features: Calf pain, swelling, warmth, redness, and engorged veins.
  • On examination: Muscle tenderness and possibly a positive Homan's sign (calf pain on dorsiflexion).
  • Most patients may have no physical signs, and Homan's sign is neither sensitive nor specific for diagnosis.

Wells Score for Depp vein thrombosis

Diagnosis of DVT

  • Imaging: Duplex Doppler ultrasound or venography to detect thrombus and assess blood flow.
  • Risk stratification: If DVT is unlikely by Wells score, perform a D-dimer test.
    • Negative D-dimer → DVT is unlikely, but patients should be educated about PE signs and when to seek help.

Management of DVT

  • Significant DVT (above-knee involvement):
    • Initial therapy: Parenteral anticoagulation (e.g., heparin).
    • Long-term therapy: Oral anticoagulants such as warfarin or direct oral anticoagulants.
  • Large DVT with high PE risk: Consider inferior vena cava (IVC) filter to prevent pulmonary embolism.

Explanation of other options:

Cellulitis (Option A): Usually presents with redness, warmth, and tenderness, often with systemic symptoms like fever.

Varicose veins (Option B): Varicose veins are typically painless or cause pain in chronic cases; not associated with acute fever or sudden calf swelling.

Necrotising fasciitis (Option D): Rapidly progressive, severe pain, systemic toxicity, and skin changes, usually more dramatic than postoperative low-grade fever.

question_text: A patient who recently underwent surgery has been immobilised. On the 5th postoperative day, she develops leg pain. On examination, Homan's sign is positive. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Deep venous thrombosis (DVT) is a condition in which thrombus formation occurs in the deep veins, most commonly in the lower limbs. Postoperative immobilisation is a major risk factor. Homan's sign-pain in the calf on dorsiflexion of the foot-is a classical but non-specific finding. Other features include calf swelling, tenderness, erythema, and dilated superficial veins.

Explanation of other options:

Urinary sepsis (Option B): Presents with fever, dysuria, and urinary urgency. Does not cause isolated leg pain or positive Homan's sign.

Peripheral vascular disease (Option C): Characterized by intermittent claudication and diminished peripheral pulses, not acute postoperative calf pain.

Lymphangitis (Option D): Inflammation of lymphatic vessels, usually with red streaks along the limb and tender lymphadenopathy, not calf tenderness or Homan's sign.

Clinical Features of DVT

Key Takeaways:

  • Immobilisation + calf pain + positive Homan's sign → DVT.
  • Homan's sign is non-specific but still clinically relevant.
  • Early recognition is important to prevent pulmonary embolism.

explanation:
Chronic lymphocytic (autoimmune) thyroiditis (Hashimoto's disease)

  • This common condition is usually associated with raised titres of thyroid antibodies. It commonly presents as a goiter, which may be diffuse or nodular with a characteristic 'bosselated' feel or with established or subclinical thyroid failure.
  • The diagnosis often follows investigation of a discrete swelling. Features of chronic lymphocytic (focal) thyroiditis are commonly present on histological examination in association with other thyroid disease, notably toxic goiter.
  • Primary myxoedema without detectable thyroid enlargement represents the end stage of the pathological process.

question_text: Among the options provided, which pairing correctly matches the trauma patients brought to the casualty?
option_b: Penetrating injury to eustachian tube - CSF otorrhea
option_c: Penetrating injury to eye - Battle sign
explanation:
Explanation:

Gaze palsy refers to impaired movement of the eyes, often caused by injury to specific midbrain structures. Key areas involved include the third cranial nerve nucleus and the paramedian pontine reticular formation, both of which play essential roles in coordinating ocular motility.

Secondary Survey

History (AMPLE):

  • A: Allergies → Check for drug/food/other allergies.
  • M: Medications → Enquire about anticoagulants, antiplatelets, corticosteroids, immunosuppressive therapy.
  • P: Past History → Medical/surgical history including anaesthetic exposure and complications.
  • L: Last Meal/Drink → Time of last oral intake.
  • E: Events → Circumstances leading to current injury.

Systematic Examination (Head-to-Toe with Focus on Injured Limb):

  • Look → Inspect for deformity, swelling, wounds, bruises, foreign bodies.
  • Feel → Palpate for tenderness, warmth, crepitus, abnormal mobility.
  • Move → Assess active and passive range of motion.
  • Special Tests → Perform as relevant to suspected injury.
  • Investigations → Order imaging or lab tests based on findings.
  • Neurovascular Assessment → Evaluate pulses, capillary refill, sensation, and motor function.

Explanation of Other Options:

Extradural Hemorrhage (EDH) - Pinpoint Pupil (Option A):

  • EDH typically produces a dilated, fixed pupil due to compression of the oculomotor nerve (cranial nerve III).
  • Pinpoint pupils are more commonly associated with pontine haemorrhage or opioid intoxication, not EDH.

Penetrating Injury to the Eustachian Tube - CSF Otorrhea (Option B):

  • Penetrating trauma to the Eustachian tube may cause local damage but does not usually result in CSF leakage.
  • CSF otorrhea is more often linked to basilar skull fractures, especially involving the temporal bone.

Penetrating Eye Injury - Battle's Sign (Option C):

  • Battle's sign (ecchymosis over the mastoid region) is a hallmark of basilar skull fracture.
  • Penetrating injuries of the eye present with hyphema, corneal laceration, visual disturbance, but not Battle's sign.

question_text: A young patient presents with a 5-day history of fever along with hypotension, tachycardia, tachypnea, and altered mental status. Laboratory investigations reveal elevated WBC count, increased neutrophil percentage, and raised serum creatinine. The intern decides to use the quick Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (qSOFA) score to assess prognosis and predict hospitalization duration. Which of the following are components of the qSOFA score?
explanation:
Explanation:

qSOFA score includes systolic blood pressure ≤100 mmHg, respiratory rate ≥22/min, and altered mental status (GCS).

  • The qSOFA score is a bedside clinical tool used to identify patients with suspected infection at risk for poor outcomes like sepsis.
  • It includes three parameters:
    • Systolic Blood Pressure (SBP) ≤100 mmHg
    • Respiratory Rate (RR) ≥22/min
    • Altered mental status, assessed via Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
  • Meeting ≥2 of these 3 criteria indicates a higher risk of sepsis and the need for urgent evaluation and management.
  • Unlike full SOFA scoring, qSOFA does not require lab investigations, making it practical for initial bedside assessment.

Explanation of other options:

BP, RR, and CBC (Option A): CBC is not part of qSOFA; only SBP, RR, and GCS are used.

Creatinine, PR, and BP (Option B): Creatinine and pulse rate (PR) are part of full SOFA, not qSOFA.

RR, Body temperature, and PR (Option C): Body temperature and pulse rate are not qSOFA criteria.

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding trauma assessment except:
option_a: Knowledge of timelines for important diagnosis is important
option_b: Initial assessment should focus on what kills first
option_c: Screen high risk patient before clinical sign become apparent
explanation:
Explanation:

Principles of Trauma Assessment

  • Consider the Mechanism + Patient Factors: Predict Injuries
    Always evaluate injuries in the context of the trauma mechanism and individual patient characteristics.
  • Use Obvious Findings to Uncover Hidden Injuries
    Visible or dramatic injuries should prompt a systematic search for associated, less obvious internal or secondary injuries.
  • When Findings Don't 'Add Up,' Think Beyond the Expected
    A mismatch between the clinical picture and the apparent injuries should alert the clinician to reassess, reconsider alternative diagnoses, and "connect the dots."
  • Knowledge of timelines for important diagnoses is essential.
  • Initial assessment should focus on what kills first.
  • Screen high-risk patients before clinical signs become apparent, as it may be too late to intervene once signs develop.

Key Takeaways:

Trauma assessment prioritizes conditions that can lead to rapid deterioration.

question_text: Which of the following TNM stage denotes early-stage oesophageal cancer?
explanation:
GENERAL ASSESSMENT AND STAGING

  • Most potentially curative therapies include radical surgery, although definitive chemoradiotherapy is an alternative in squamous cell carcinoma.
  • Those patients suitable for potentially curative therapies should proceed to staging investigations to rule out haematogenous spread (CT scan) and then to assess locoregional stage (endoscopic ultrasonography [EUS] +/- laparoscopy). This will distinguish between early (T1/T2, N0) and advanced lesions (T3/T4, N1) and indicate whether surgery alone or multimodal therapy is most appropriate.
  • The most widely used pathological staging system is that of the World Health Organization (tumour–nodes–metastasis TNM).
  • Similar to all pathological systems, it relies on the nature and extent of the surgery performed, e.g., performing more extensive radical surgical lymphadenectomy provides a more accurate assessment of the ‘N’ stage.
  • There is evidence that many patients described as N0 in the past were probably N1, a phenomenon described as stage migration. Staging information may be gathered before the commencement of therapy, during therapy (e.g., at open operation) or following treatment (histology or postmortem examination).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1138

question_text: A 42-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with complaints of progressive fatigue, excessive thirst, and increased urination for the past few months. explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's clinical features (polyuria, polydipsia, nephrolithiasis, abdominal pain, neuropsychiatric symptoms) and biochemical findings (raised calcium and PTH) are highly suggestive of Primary Hyperparathyroidism, most commonly due to a parathyroid adenoma.

  • Angiography of renal arteries:
    This investigation is used for diagnosing vascular abnormalities such as renal artery stenosis in secondary hypertension. It has no role in diagnosing primary hyperparathyroidism and therefore is not useful in this patient's context.

Explanation of Other options:

Nuclear sestamibi scan (Option A) is used to identify parathyroid adenomas. It is a key investigation in the diagnosis of primary hyperparathyroidism, especially in localising the adenoma.

USG neck (Option B) can also help in visualising parathyroid glands and is commonly used for parathyroid adenomas.

Dual energy radiographic absorptiometry (DEXA) (Option C) is a test used to assess bone density and is often ordered to evaluate for osteoporosis, which is common in primary hyperparathyroidism due to bone resorption from elevated calcium.

question_text: A middle-aged woman presents with flank pain and dysuria. She had temporary pain relief with IV analgesics at a local clinic. Investigations suggest ureteric colic secondary to a ureteric calculus. What is the most appropriate diagnostic modality to confirm the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Non-contrast CT KUB is the gold standard investigation for suspected ureteric or renal calculi.
It provides rapid, detailed, and highly accurate imaging of the entire urinary tract - identifying both radiopaque and radiolucent stones.

Key Advantages:

  • Detects all stone types, including uric acid and cystine stones (radiolucent on X-ray)
  • High sensitivity (~98%) and specificity (~97%)
  • No contrast needed, which avoids nephrotoxicity
  • Can localize exact site, size, and density of the stone
  • Helps rule out other causes of flank pain (appendicitis, AAA, ovarian cysts, etc.)

Explanation of Other Options:

CECT (Option B):

  • Contrast can obscure small calculi in the urinary tract.
  • Reserved for complicated cases (suspected renal mass, abscess, or vascular pathology).
  • Avoided in renal colic until the stone diagnosis is confirmed.

Ureteroscopy (Option D):

  • Endoscopic procedure used to visualize and remove stones.
  • Performed after diagnosis is established via imaging.
  • Invasive, requires anesthesia.

question_text: A patient of RTA was brought to the hospital with a left flank bruise associated with hematuria. Patient was hemodynamically stable. Which of the following investigations should be done for hematuria?

Renal trauma

Ominous sign is : hematuria and flank bruise

Investigation:

Unstable patient: IOC: IVP( on table IVP is done)

IVP( intravenous pyelogram is done to all patients undergoing surgery for renal trauma to look for renal perfusion

RTA having left flank bruise associated with hematuria suggest renal trauma.

Conservative management with close surveillance is sufficient in the majority of cases of isolated renal trauma.

question_text: A patient presents with a right scrotal swelling and a right hydrocele. The left testis is normal, but there is an enlargement of the pre-aortic lymph nodes with suspected metastasis. Which of the following investigations is most appropriate to identify the underlying cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

Initial treatment of suspected testicular tumor is radical inguinal orchiectomy, which involves removal of the testicle and spermatic cord at the level of the inguinal ring. Because of the characteristic and well-described lymph drainage of the testicle, there is no role for trans-scrotal biopsy or orchiectomy. If the intrascrotal tissue planes are violated during orchiectomy, the lymphatic drainage can be altered, affecting future treatment

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Biopsy of scrotal mass

  • A biopsy of the scrotal mass is not recommended because it can cause local seeding of malignant cells, affecting lymphatic drainage and complicating the treatment.
  • The primary treatment for suspected testicular cancer is orchiectomy, not biopsy. A biopsy would violate the scrotal tissue planes, altering the lymphatic pathways and possibly spreading the tumor.

Choice B: Biopsy of lymph nodes

  • A biopsy of the lymph nodes is typically not performed initially to diagnose testicular cancer. The focus is on the testicle, as testicular cancer has characteristic lymphatic spread to the para-aortic nodes.
  • The appropriate approach is orchiectomy, and if necessary, imaging or further assessment will be done to evaluate the lymph nodes.

Choice D: Excision of right testis

  • Excision of the right testis without removal of the spermatic cord is not an adequate approach for suspected testicular cancer. This would not remove the lymphatic drainage of the testicle, and would potentially affect future treatment or staging.
  • The correct procedure is high inguinal orchidectomy, which includes removal of the testis and spermatic cord, preserving lymphatic drainage and minimizing risks.

Key Takeaway

  • The most appropriate investigation for suspected testicular cancer with lymph node enlargement is high inguinal orchidectomy, which ensures proper lymphatic drainage

question_text: A soldier arrives at a referral hospital 24 hours after experiencing a shrapnel injury to his right thigh caused by a high-speed projectile. He expresses significant discomfort at the site of the wound. Upon examination, there is evidence of crepitus. Which of the following microorganisms is the probable culprit behind his current state?
explanation:
Explanation:

A soldier with a shrapnel wound to the right thigh presenting with intense pain and crepitus (indicating the presence of gas within the tissues) is highly suggestive of gas gangrene, typically caused by Clostridium perfringens.

A rapidly progressive and potentially fatal infection characterized by extensive muscle necrosis and soft tissue destruction, frequently arising from delayed management of missile wounds or crush injuries.

Causative Organism:

  • Predominantly caused by Clostridium perfringens (Option D)

Incubation Period:

  • Usually less than 24 hours, but can range from 1 hour to 6 weeks

Sources & Predisposing Factors:

  • Soil or fecal contamination
  • Necrotic or foreign material within wounds
  • Crush injuries, road traffic accidents, amputations
  • Anaerobic conditions in the wound

Common Infection Sites:

  • Adductor region of the lower limb and buttocks
  • Subscapular area of the upper limb

Clinical Features:

  • Severe, rapidly increasing pain with marked limb swelling
  • Serosanguineous discharge
  • Skin changes from brown to blue-black with hemorrhagic bullae
  • Sweet, sticky odor and palpable crepitus (gas in tissues)

Complications:

  • Septicemia, toxemia, renal failure, hepatic failure
  • Circulatory collapse, DIC, secondary infections
  • High mortality in critically ill patients

Investigations:

  • X-ray: Gas in soft tissues
  • Gram stain & blood culture: Large Gram-positive bacilli without neutrophils
  • Biochemistry: Metabolic acidosis or evidence of renal impairment
  • Peripheral smear: Hemolysis
  • CT scan: Assessment of chest or abdominal wounds

Treatment:

  • High-dose intravenous penicillin + clindamycin, with third-generation cephalosporins
  • Polyvalent antiserum intravenously
  • Aggressive surgical debridement of necrotic tissue until healthy bleeding tissue is visible
  • Amputation for extensive involvement
  • Hyperbaric oxygen therapy as supportive care

Prevention:

  • Early, thorough debridement of crushed or devitalized wounds
  • Avoid primary closure of devitalized wounds
  • Irrigation with hydrogen peroxide and normal saline
  • Prophylactic penicillin for high-risk injuries

Explanation of Other Options:

Clostridium septicum (Option A) is responsible for spontaneous, non-traumatic gas gangrene and is frequently associated with underlying conditions such as colorectal cancer or states of immunosuppression. In contrast, Clostridium perfringens is more typically linked to gas gangrene following traumatic injuries.

Clostridioides difficile (Option B) is primarily associated with antibiotic-related diarrhea and colitis rather than gas gangrene, and it does not produce the gas formation or soft-tissue necrosis seen in traumatic cases.

Clostridium novyi (Option C) is a rarer cause of gas gangrene, more often linked to specific scenarios such as soil-contaminated or animal-related injuries, and is an unlikely pathogen in a shrapnel wound scenario.

question_text: Identify the fourth stage from the philosophy of 'damage control orthopedic' or the 'damage control surgery'

• Knowledge acquired at the molecular level related to the immune-inflammatory response to injury and the concepts of the phenomena of the first hit (the impact exerted on the homeostatic mechanisms as a result of the original trauma sustained) and the second hit (the additional physiological stress induced by surgical procedures) led to the acceptance and implementation of the so call 'damage control orthopaedics' (DCO) philosophy, which is called damage control surgery (DCS) in more generalized settings.

Explanation:

  • In any patient presenting with a thyroid swelling, the first step is to perform a Thyroid Function Test(TFT) to assess the gland's functional status.
  • This helps determine whether the patient is euthyroid, hyperthyroid, or hypothyroid, which is essential before any further diagnostic or surgical intervention.
  • When a patient presents with a large thyroid swelling, an ultrasound of the neck is usually the next step.
  • Ultrasoundprovides high-resolution imaging of the thyroid, allowing detailed evaluation of parenchymal and nodular abnormalities.
  • It gives valuable information about the size, characteristics, and composition of the swelling, differentiating cystic from solid nodules.
  • Additionally, ultrasound guides further management by identifying which nodules require fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC)for definitive diagnosis.
  • FNAC is preferred over surgical biopsy for initial diagnosis.

question_text: A 25 years old female presented with rapid weight gain, loss of appetite. Investigations show increased TSH with low T4. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
The above history and investigation is suggestive of hypothyroidism, with hashimotos thyroiditis being the most commmon cause of hypothyroidism in females

  • This common condition is usually associated with raised titres of thyroid antibodies.
  • It commonly presents as a goitre, which may be difuse or nodular with a characteristic 'bosselated' feel or with established or subclinical thyroid failure.
  • The diagnosis often follows investigation of a discrete swelling.
  • Features of chronic lymphocytic (focal) thyroiditis are commonly present on histological examination in association with other thyroid disease, notably toxic goitre.
  • Primary myxoedema without detectable thyroid enlargement represents the end stage of the pathological process

question_text: A 32-year-old male chronic smoker presents with finger pain for several months. On examination, gangrenous ulcers are seen on the fingers. Investigations show normal blood glucose and lipid profile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Buerger's disease is a non-atherosclerotic, segmental vasculitis strongly associated with smoking. It presents in young males with ulcers, claudication, rest pain, Raynaud's phenomenon, and gangrene of digits. Angiography shows corkscrew collaterals. Smoking cessation is the key management.

Explanation of other options:

Diabetic ulcers (Option B): More common in diabetics, usually on feet, with neuropathy/ischemia.

Acute paronychia (Option C): Localized infection around the nail fold, often due to trauma/nail biting.

Raynaud's phenomenon (Option D): Episodic color changes in extremities due to vasospasm, not gangrene with ulcers.

question_text: Which of the following investigations or interventions is not a part of the primary survey in trauma assessment?
explanation:
Explanation:

A Non-contrast CT (NCCT) of the head is an imaging study used to assess intracranial injuries such as contusions, hemorrhages, or fractures.
However, it is not performed during the primary survey - it is part of the secondary survey, conducted after the patient has been stabilized (i.e., airway, breathing, and circulation secured).

The primary survey focuses exclusively on rapid identification and correction of life-threatening conditions, following the ABCDE approach as per ATLS (Advanced Trauma Life Support) guidelines.

Secondary survey:

  • This includes a complete patient history and a thorough head-to-toe assessment. It is done almost immediately in stable patients and includes radiological investigations.
  • The AMPLE history mnemonic is used to gather key details (Allergies, Medications, Past medical history, Last meal, Events/Environment related to the injury).
  • Face deformities, posterior neck injuries, the torso, a per-rectal examination for GI bleed, and prostate location are all included in this step.
  • A thorough neurological examination and evaluation of superficial injuries are done.
  • The complete physical re-examination and use of follow up imaging are now included in the tertiary survey.

question_text: Primary survey of ATLS does not include:
explanation:
PRIMARY SURVEY

The primary survey aims to identify and manage the most immediately life-threatening pathologies first and follows cABCDE.

c: Exsanguinating external hemorrhage

Experience from war zones over the past 20 years has shown that exsanguinating external hemorrhage from massive arterial bleeding needs to be controlled even before the airway is managed.

A: Airway with cervical spine control

B: Breathing and ventilation

C: Circulation and hemorrhage control

D: Disability and E: Exposure

Mechanical testing of the pelvis in the emergency room ('springing the pelvis') adds no useful clinical examination and will disrupt any blood clot that has formed around a pelvic fracture. It should never be performed - a pelvic fracture should always be diagnosed radiographically.

question_text: Which of the following is the correct sequence for damage control surgery?
explanation:
Explanation:

The correct sequence in damage control surgery

  • The initial goal is to stabilise the patient and control life-threatening bleeding, followed by physiological optimisation in the ICU, and then definitive abdominal closure once the patient is stable.

Explanation of Other Options:

1, 2, 3, 4 (Option A): Resuscitation before controlling hemorrhage is incorrect; bleeding must be addressed first.

1, 2, 4, 3 (Option C): ICU resuscitation is placed too early before hemorrhage control.

2, 1, 3, 4 (Option D): Identification of the patient must come first, so this sequence is incorrect.

question_text: In a 3-year-old child, the mother notices a huge abdominal swelling with Ballot-ability. H/O Hematuria which was resolved in 2 days. O/E ballot-able abdominal swelling is the only significant finding. what all the investigations you will do?
explanation:
The c/f of a 3 yr old child with ballotable mass h/o hematuria suggests the child with Wilms tumor.

The tumour has mixed elements derived from the embryonic nephrogenic tissue, namely blastemal or undifferentiated tissue, epithelial tubules and stroma.

The typical presentation is a child aged between 1 and 4 years of either gender with a large, palpable abdominal mass that may cross the midline. It may also be associated with haematuria, hypertension, fever and weight loss. Pain is relatively uncommon. Hematuria is a bad prognostic factor of wilms tumor.

Investigation:

CECT or MRI is necessary to stage the disease.

The tumours usually infiltrate the kidneys and normal renal parenchyma is compressed at the periphery around the tumour (claw sign). A CT of the chest should be obtained as the lung is the most common site of distant metastasis.

It is important to know radiological features of neuroblastoma while comparing it with wilms tumor:

  1. Crosses midline
  2. Calcification present
  3. Drooping lily sign on IVP

PET CT should be done to find out distant metastasis.

Treatment:

Current treatment is nephrectomy with pre- or postoperative chemotherapy

2 protocol:

  • SIOP protocol: preoperative chemotherapy → shrink the tumor → staging → surgery
  • NWTSG protocol: surgery → chemotherapy

Both have good prognosis, but SIOP is preferred in

  1. Bilateral Wilma tumor
  2. Patient with single kidney developing Wilms tumor
  3. Altered renal function test

question_text: A hypertensive patient presents with a 5-day history of severe headaches. On evaluation, he demonstrates classical features of pheochromocytoma, with significantly elevated plasma metanephrines and supportive biochemical investigations. What is the best imaging modality for confirming the diagnosis and assessing the extent of disease?
explanation:
Explanation

  • MIBG scintigraphy is the most specific imaging technique for pheochromocytomas and paragangliomas.
  • It not only localizes adrenal tumors but also detects extra-adrenal sites and metastases, which are common in malignant pheochromocytoma.
  • This makes it superior to conventional cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) for functional assessment.
  • Hence, in a biochemically proven pheochromocytoma with suspicion of metastasis, MIBG is the investigation of choice.

Malignant Pheochromocytoma

Explanation of Other Options:

CECT Chest and Abdomen (Option A): Incorrect. CT is excellent for visualizing adrenal tumors and defining anatomy but lacks functional specificity. It may miss extra-adrenal or metastatic lesions that MIBG detects.

Sestamibi Scan (Option B): Incorrect. Used primarily for parathyroid adenomas and cardiac imaging. It has no role in pheochromocytoma diagnosis.

USG (Option D): Incorrect. Ultrasound may detect adrenal masses but is insensitive for small lesions and metastases, making it inadequate for staging or confirmation.

question_text: A young boy presented with scrotal enlargement. On investigations- LDH is increased, HCG and AFP are normal. Histopathology of the testis is shown after orchiectomy. What is your diagnosis?
explanation:
Seminoma

  • A seminoma typically has a cut surface that is homogeneous and pinkish cream in color. It appears to compress neighboring testicular tissue.
  • It consists of oval cells with clear cytoplasm and large, rounded nuclei with prominent acidophilic nucleoli. Sheets of cells resembling spermatocytes are separated by a fine fibrous stroma.
  • Active lymphocytic infiltration of the tumor suggests a good host response and a better prognosis.Seminoma accounts for 50% of all testicular germinal cell tumors.
  • They seldom occur in childhood, in young adults or in patients over 70 years of age. Seminomas metastasise mainly via the lymphatics and haematogenous spread is uncommon.
  • The lymphatic drainage of the testes is to the para-aortic lymph nodes near the origin of the gonadal vessels. The contralateral para-aortic lymph nodes are sometimes involved by tumor spread, but the inguinal lymph nodes are affected only if the scrotal skin is involved. Ultrasound is the first-line investigation.

question_text: Most probable diagnosis in the images given below
explanation:
Explanation:

Chest radiograph shows a widened mediastinum. Aortogram shows aortic disruption.
Erect chest radiography can suggest thoracic aortic disruption, with a widened mediastinum being the most common radiological finding.

Diagnosis is confirmed by CT scan of the mediastinum or by transesophageal echocardiography in unstable patients.

Thoracic Aortic Disruption

Mechanism & Pathology

  • A common cause of sudden death following high-impact trauma (vehicle collisions, falls from height).
  • The thoracic aorta is relatively fixed distal to the ligamentum arteriosum, just beyond the left subclavian artery.
  • Sudden deceleration → shear forces → disruption of intima and media.
  • If the adventitia remains intact, the patient may be physiologically stable despite the injury.

Clinical Suspicion

Suspect thoracic aortic injury in trauma patients with:

  • Marked systolic BP asymmetry
    • Between upper limbs, or
    • Between upper vs lower limbs
  • Widened pulse pressure
  • Chest wall contusion

Radiological Findings

  • Erect chest radiograph:
    • Most common finding → widened mediastinum.
  • Definitive diagnosis:
    • CT scan of the mediastinum.

In hypotensive patients, aortic injury is not the cause of hypotension; other injuries are responsible, as complete aortic rupture rarely allows survival to hospital.

Management

  • Initial goal: Control systolic BP < 120 mmHg.
  • Definitive options:
    • Endovascular intra-aortic stent, or
    • Operative repair (direct repair, or excision with Dacron graft).

question_text: A patient suffered from blunt trauma to the abdomen and was brought to the emergency room. He is unstable having BP 90/60 mmHg. You are the doctor, basic reusucitation is done with IV fluids, FAST is positive. He is not improving despite IV fluids. Next step in the management is?
explanation:
Blunt trauma abdomen:

After resuscitating the patient with IV fluids: next immediate step is FAST (focused abdominal sonography for trauma).

If patient's vitals are stable: CECT abdomen is done

If patient's vitals are unstable: exploratory laparotomy done

  • Some patients will be so hemodynamically unstable on arrival that they need immediate surgical control of their hemorrhage before a CT scan.
  • The most likely sources are abdominal or pelvic bleeding. An immediate chest radiograph will exclude catastrophic intrathoracic hemorrhage.
  • An immediate pelvic radiograph is essential but should not delay transfer to the operating theater. A focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) scan (if immediately available) may also be useful in this scenario to locate the major source of hemorrhage.
  • All patients undergoing immediate laparotomy in the operating theater should have a pelvic binder applied and not removed.
  • A correctly positioned pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters does not obstruct trauma laparotomy. These patients will invariably require a WBCT (whole body CT) scan after surgical control of hemorrhage has been achieved

question_text: A patient presents to the emergency room after a road traffic accident with shock and hypotension. The extended focused assessment with sonography for trauma (eFAST) is negative, the X-ray is normal, and the ECG shows no abnormalities. The patient's SpO₂ is 93%, blood pressure is 80/60 mmHg, and pulse rate is 40/min. Based on this information, what type of shock is most likely?
explanation:
Explanation:

The scenario is most consistent with neurogenic shock.

  • Bradycardia (pulse 40/min):Characteristic finding due to loss of sympathetic tone and unopposed vagal influence.
  • Hypotension with warm extremities:Caused by vasodilation of peripheral vessels below the level of spinal cord injury.
  • Normal eFAST and imaging:Excludes hemorrhagic and obstructive causes.
  • No ECG abnormality:Excludes cardiogenic origin.
  • Mechanism:
    • Loss of sympathetic outflow → vasodilation → ↓ systemic vascular resistance → hypotension.
    • Unopposed parasympathetic activity → bradycardia.
    • Pink, warm skin (distinct from cold, clammy extremities in other shock types).

Neurogenic shock:

In neurogenic shock, there is a loss of sympathetic tone, leading to vasodilation of the peripheral vasculature, resulting in decreased peripheral vascular resistance and hypotension. This is the primary mechanism underlying neurogenic shock.

Causes:

  • Neurogenic shock is a critical condition that results from the dysregulation of the autonomic nervous system following spinal cord injury, especially in the cervical and upper thoracic vertebrae above the T6 level, as a result of traumatic events. The dysregulation arises due to the lack of sympathetic tone and decreased peripheral vascular resistance.
  • The decline in sympathetic tone prompts the dilation of capacitance blood vessels in the lower extremities. This, in turn, results in decreased cardiac filling, leading to hypotension and shock.
  • Reduced sympathetic control over the heart leads to a situation where unopposed vagal cardiac influence causes
  • Patients with neurogenic shock may also exhibitpink and warm skin due to the dilation of subcutaneous blood vessels.
  • Severe brain injury.
  • Certain anaesthetics.

Pathophysiology

Clinical Manifestations:

  • Hypotension
  • Bradycardia (unlike other forms of shock)
  • Warm, dry skin below injury level
  • Priapism in males
  • Respiratory compromise (if high cervical injury)
  • Poikilothermia (inability to regulate body temperature)

Explanation of Other Options:

Septic shock (Option A):

  • Characterized by hypotension, tachycardia, fever, leukocytosis, and warm peripheries.
  • Bradycardia is not typical.
  • Not consistent with acute post-trauma presentation.

Hemorrhagic shock (Option B):

  • Caused by blood loss. Presents with hypotension, tachycardia, cold clammy extremities.
  • Negative eFAST and X-ray rule out intra-abdominal or thoracic bleeding.

Cardiogenic shock (Option C):

  • Due to pump failure (e.g., MI, arrhythmia). Presents with hypotension, tachycardia, pulmonary edema, raised JVP.
  • Normal ECG and absence of chest pain or pulmonary findings argue against this.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text:
Inferior thyroid artery supplies which structures
1. Esophagus
2. Thyroid
3. Parathyroid
4. Thymus
explanation:
• The inferior thyroid artery (ITA) is considered the principal blood supplier of the thyroid gland.
  • The ITA gives rise to the ascending cervical artery, the inferior laryngeal artery, and also gives pharyngeal, tracheal, and esophageal
  • ITA also supplies the four parathyroid glands.

Blood supply of esophagus:

Cricopharyngeal muscle (inlet of esophagus) is supplied by superior thyroid artery

  1. Cervical esophagus: predominantly by inferior thyroid artery
  2. Thoracic esophagus: aorta, both right and left bronchial artery, along with descending branch from inferior thyroid artery, intercostal artery and ascending branch from inferior phrenic artery
  3. Abdominal esophagus: left gastric artery and inferior phrenic artery

Blood supply to the thymus comes from the internal thoracic artery.

question_text: FAST stands for:
explanation:
Focused abdominal sonography for trauma and extended FAST (FAST and eFAST)

  • Focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) is a technique whereby ultrasound (sonography) imaging is used to assess the torso for the presence of free fluid in the abdominal cavity, and is extended into the thoracic cavities and pericardium (eFAST).
  • There should be no attempt to determine the nature or extent of the specific injury. eFAST is usually a rapid, reproducible, portable and non-invasive bedside test and can be performed at the same time as resuscitation.
  • eFAST is accurate at detecting >100 mL of free blood; however, it is very operator dependent and, especially if the patient is very obese or the bowel is full of gas, it may be unreliable.
  • Hollow viscus injury and solid organ injury are difficult to diagnose, even in experienced hands, as small amounts of gas or fluid are difficult to assess and eFAST has a low sensitivity (29-35%) for organ injury without hemoperitoneum.
  • eFAST is also unreliable for excluding injury in penetrating trauma. If there is doubt, the eFAST examination can be repeated.

question_text: All of the following are correct regarding empyema except?
option_a: It is end stage of pleural infection from any cause
option_b: It can be results from complication of any thoracic operation
option_c: Pathological diagnosis requires the presence of thick pus with a thick cortex of fibrin and coagulum over the lung
option_d: Fibro purulent phase is first phase
explanation:
Pleural infection and empyema

  • When empyema presents de novo it usually follows pneumonia, and three phases are described:
  • It may be associated with pus under the diaphragm.The pathological diagnosis requires the presence of thick pus with a thick cortex of fibrin and coagulum over the lung.
  • It is seen if a traumatic haemothorax becomes infected or in the course of management of pneumothorax or pleural effusions.
  • Empyema is the end stage of pleural infection from any cause. It most commonly results from infection of the underlying lung, involving pneumonia or a lung abscess, but can occur as a complication of any thoracic operation.
    1. In the exudative phase, there is protein-rich (>30 g/L) effusion. If this becomes infected with the organisms from the lung (typically Streptococcus milleri and Haemophilus influenzae in children), the scene is set for empyema. At this stage antibiotics may be all that is required. Aspiration or drainage to dryness in addition is preferred.
    2. Over subsequent days, the fluid thickens to what is known as the fibrinopurulent phase. Drainage at this stage is prudent as antibiotics on their own are unlikely to be curative.
    3. The organising phase causes the lung to be trapped by a thick peel or 'cortex' for which surgical management may be required.

Empyema

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 59, Cardiac Surgery, Pg: 982.

question_text: Which among the following is not the shape of the body of surgical needle?
explanation:
• The body of the needle is either round, triangular or flattened.
  • Round-bodied needles gradually taper to a point, while triangular needles have cutting edges along all three sides.
  • The actual point of the needle can be round with a tapered end, conventional cutting which has the cutting edge facing the inside of the needle's curvature, or reverse cutting in which the cutting edge is on the outside.
  • Round- bodied needles are designed to separate tissue fibres rather than cut through them and are commonly used in intestinal and cardiovascular surgery.
  • Cutting needles are used where tough or dense tissue needs to be sutured, such as skin and fascia.
  • Blunt-ended needles are now being advocated in certain situations, such as closure of the abdominal wall, in order to diminish the risk of needle-stick injuries in this era of blood borne infectious diseases.
  • The choice of needle shape tends to be dictated by the accessibility of the tissue to be sutured, and the more confined the operative space, the more curved the needle.
  • Hand-held straight needles may be used on skin, although today it is advocated that needle holders should be used in all cases to reduce the risk of needle-stick injuries.
  • Half circle needles are commonly utilised in the gastrointestinal tract, while J-shaped needles, quarter circle needles and compound curvature needles are used in special situations, such as the vagina, eye and oral cavity, respectively.
  • The size of the needle tends to correspond with the gauge of the suture material, although it is possible to get similar sutures with differing needle sizes.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 94

question_text: Most common retroperitoneal tumor?
explanation:
• Approximately 15% of soft tissue sarcomas arise within the retroperitoneum.
  • In this location, the most common histologic subtypes are liposarcoma and leiomyosarcoma. Most patients present with a large abdominal mass.
  • Abdominal pain is present in about 50% of the patients.
  • Other symptoms are related to organ compression from the tumor and include early satiety, nausea, vomiting, constipation, weight loss, and lower extremity edema.
  • Symptoms due to nerve compression by the tumor, such as lower extremity paresthesia and paresis, are also reported.
  • IOC - CECT abdomen
  • Liposarcoma is diagnosed by variable fat density. No need of image guided biopsy

question_text: Gold standard investigation for a patient having signs of multiple injuries
explanation:
Explanation:

Whole-Body CT (WBCT) in Severe Blunt Trauma

  • WBCT (head-to-pelvis with IV contrast) is the gold standard for evaluating the severely injured adult with blunt trauma.
  • Selective (region-specific) imaging has no role in these patients due to the high likelihood of multisystem injury and the need for comprehensive assessment.
  • WBCT is time-critical and should be performed as early as possible during resuscitation to guide timely interventions.
  • If a patient requires immediate trauma laparotomy without prior WBCT,
    • Apply a pelvic binder and do not remove it until a pelvic fracture is excluded.
    • Obtain an immediate pelvic X-ray, either in the emergency department or on arrival to the operating theatre.

Key Takeaways:

Whole-body CT is the preferred investigation when there are signs of multiple injuries or deranged physiology.

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding flail chest except
option_a: This condition usually results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures
option_b: Defined as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places
option_c: To confirm the diagnosis the chest wall can be observed for paradoxical motion of a chest wall segment
option_d: CXR is gold standard for diagnosis
explanation:
Explanation:

Flail chest usually results from blunt trauma associated with multiple rib fractures and is defined as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places. Diagnosis is clinical, not radiographic.

Flail Chest

  • Cause & Definition:
    • Usually due to blunt trauma with multiple rib fractures.
    • Defined as three or more ribs fractured in two or more places.
    • Often associated with underlying pulmonary contusion.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Clinical diagnosis in non-ventilated patients; not made by radiography.
    • Confirmed by observing paradoxical chest wall movement:
      • Inspiration: loose segment moves inwards, reduced air entry.
      • Expiration: segment moves outwards (paradoxical respiration).
    • CT scan remains the gold standard for diagnosis.
  • Pathophysiology & Clinical Effects:
    • Pain causes voluntary splinting of the chest wall.
    • Combined with mechanical impairment and lung contusion, hypoxia.
    • High risk of pneumothorax or haemothorax.
  • Management:
    • Oxygen therapy.
    • Adequate analgesia (including opiates).
    • Physiotherapy.
    • Intrapleural local analgesia may be given via a chest tube if present.
    • Mechanical ventilation is reserved for patients who develop respiratory failure despite oxygen and analgesia.
    • Surgical stabilisation (internal rib fixation) may benefit selected patients with isolated or severe chest injury and pulmonary contusion.

Key Takeaways:

Diagnosis of flail chest is clinical; CT scan is the gold standard imaging modality.

question_text: All of the following statements are incorrect regarding thoracic injury except
option_b: Chest CT has low sensitivity for diagnosis of rib fracture
option_c: Hemothorax that does not resolve after insertion for tube thoracostomy may require thoracoscopic drainage and decortication
option_d: Chest tube may be safely removed following demonstrated pleural space evacuation, on underwater seal with <50 mL output over prior 24 hours
explanation:
• Hemothorax visible on upright chest x-ray represent an approximate volume of 400–500 mL and should be evacuated with thoracostomy.
  • Residual hemothorax that does not resolve after insertion of a chest tube should be considered for video-assisted thoracosopic (VATS) drainage.

Option A: Occult pneumothoraces not accompanied by respiratory compromise can be managed with observation and a repeated chest radiograph 12 to 24 hours later to demonstrate stability.

Option B: Chest CT is often a valuable part of the evaluation and identifies chest wall trauma as well as pleural air and blood with a great degree of sensitivity. An occult pneumothorax is defined by identification on chest CT without evidence on plain radiography. Finally, CT easily recognizes significant chest wall deformities, such as flail segment, displaced ribs, and sternal fractures, and may be used to guide considerations of chest wall reconstruction.

Option D: Chest tubes may be safely removed following demonstrated pleural space evacuation, on underwater seal, with <300 mL output over prior 24 hours.
