question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding tension pneumothorax except
option_a: A tension pneumothorax develops when a 'one-way valve' air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall
option_b: The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return and compressing the opposite lung
option_c: Treatment should never be started before radiological confirmation
option_d: Rapid insertion of a large-bore cannula into the second intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line of the affected side should be done
explanation:
• A tension pneumothorax develops when a ‘one-way valve’ air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall. Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing then compressing the affected lung. The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return and compressing the opposite lung.
  • The most common causes are penetrating chest trauma, blunt chest trauma with a parenchymal lung injury and air leak that did not spontaneously close, iatrogenic lung injury (e.g. due to central venepuncture) and mechanical positive pressure ventilation.
  • The clinical presentation is dramatic. The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins (similar to pericardial tamponade). Clinical examination may reveal tracheal deviation; this is a late finding and is not necessary to clinically confirm diagnosis. There will also be hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds over the affected hemithorax.
  • Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confirmation.
  • Treatment consists of immediate decompression, initially by rapid insertion of a large-bore cannula into the second intercostal space in the mid-clavicular line of the affected side, then followed by insertion of a chest tube through the fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 29, Edition: 28th, Pg: 374

If you or your child inhales a foreign object, see your healthcare provider. If an inhaled foreign object causes choking, you'll need to perform first aid.

If a choking person can cough forcefully, let the person keep coughing.

question_text: A child was brought to the emergency with multiple injuries which included a femur fracture as well. He was confused and dyspnoeic. There was a rash all over his body. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Fat emboli syndrome (FES)

  • Fat emboli syndrome (FES) is a condition characterized by respiratory distress, altered mental status, and skin petechiae.
  • Clinical signs are evident hours to days after an injury involving long bone or pelvic fractures.
  • Marrow fat from the fracture site is believed to enter the pulmonary circulation, where it causes activation of the coagulation cascade, platelet dysfunction, release of vasoactive substances and inflammatory cytokines, and subsequent neutrophil infiltration.
  • The treatment of FES is mostly supportive, but a metaanalysis has shown that the use of corticosteroids in patients with multiple long bone fractures reduces the rate of FES by 78% without significantly increasing the risk of complications related to treatment of the fractures.
  • FES may represent a subset of ARDS. ARDS is a pulmonary failure state defined as a Pao2/Fio2 ratio lower than 200 regardless of the level of positive end-expiratory pressure, a pulmonary artery occlusion pressure of 18 mm Hg or less, or bilateral diffuse infiltrates on chest radiographs in the absence of congestive heart failure.
  • Early fixation (<24 hours) of fractures has been shown to reduce the incidence of FES and ARDS in trauma patients

Infective emboli of bacteria or an infected clot may cause mycotic aneurysms, septicaemia or infected infarcts.

Parasitic emboli, caused by the ova of Taenia echinococcus and Filaria sanguinis hominis, may occur in some countries.

Tumor cells (e.g. hypernephroma and cardiac myxoma) are rare causes of emboli.

Fat embolism may follow major bony fractures. However, it usually causes venous emboli that travel to the lungs and cause acute respiratory distress syndrome.

question_text: Which among the following statements is true for abdominal typhoid infections?
option_a: Typhoid ulcer perforation usually occurs in the first week of infection
option_b: Typhoid ulcer perforation most commonly occurs in the proximal ileum
option_c: Drug of choice for typhoid infection is chloramphenicol
option_d: Incubation period of typhoid infection is usually 3 weeks
explanation:
• Typhoid fever is caused by typhi and presents with fever and abdominal pain after an incubation period of 10–20 days.
  • Over the next week, the patient can develop distension, diarrhoea, splenomegaly and characteristic 'rose spots' on the abdomen caused by a vasculitis.
  • Typhoid is a systemic infection and diagnosis of typhoid is confirmed by culture of blood or stool.
  • Treatment is by antibiotics, usually chloramphenicol.
  • A number of surgical complications can result, including paralytic ileus, intestinal haemorrhage, free ileal perforation and cholecystitis.
  • Perforation of a typhoid ulcer characteristically occurs during the third week of the illness, although it is sometimes the first clinical sign of the disease.
  • The ulcer is parallel to the long axis of the gut and is usually situated in the distal ileum. Perforation requires surgery to wash out and close the ulcer and intestinal resection is usually avoided. In unstable patients, notably with evidence of septic shock, the bowel should be exteriorized and the perforation closed after recovery.

Typhoid fever is caused by Salmonella enterica and presents with fever and abdominal pain after an incubation period of 10-20 days. Over the next week, the patient can develop distension, diarrhoea, splenomegaly and characteristic 'rose spots' on the abdomen caused by a vasculitis. Typhoid is a systemic infection and diagnosis of typhoid is confirmed by culture of blood or stool. Treatment is by antibiotics, usually chloramphenicol. A number of surgical complications can result, including paralytic ileus, intestinal haemorrhage, free ileal perforation and cholecystitis.

question_text: A 40-year-old male with Crohn's disease presents with diffuse abdominal pain, guarding, and rigidity. Imaging shows an ileal perforation. What is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ileal perforation in Crohn's disease is a life-threatening emergency that requires prompt surgical management.

Primary repair vs. Ileostomy:

  • Primary repair is usually avoided because the inflamed and friable bowel tissue has a high risk of breakdown and recurrence.
  • Diverting ileostomy is preferred, as it diverts faecal contents, allows sepsis to settle, and provides time for healing before a later definitive procedure.
  • Without surgical intervention, the patient is at risk of septic shock, multi-organ failure, and death.

Explanation of other options:

Antibiotics and NPO (Option A): Supportive care alone is inadequate. While antibiotics may help contain infection, they do not address the perforation. Definitive surgery is mandatory to remove or bypass the perforated segment and control peritonitis.

Upper GI endoscopy (Option B): Not useful in small bowel (ileal) disease. Moreover, in the setting of perforation, endoscopy is contraindicated as it increases the risk of worsening perforation.

CT abdomen (Option D): If imaging has already confirmed perforation, repeating CT is unnecessary and only delays treatment. The next and only appropriate step is definitive surgical intervention.

question_text: Miss X, 35 yrs old presented to the emergency with upper abdominal pain radiating to the back. On X-RAY colon cut off sign is seen. Likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Clinical presentation of acute pancreatitis

  • Pain is the cardinal symptom. It characteristically develops quickly, reaching maximum intensity within minutes rather than hours and persists for hours or even days.
  • The pain is frequently severe, constant and refractory to the usual doses of analgesics. Pain is usually experienced first in the epigastrium but may be localized to either upper quadrant or felt diffusely throughout the abdomen. There is radiation to the back in about 50% of patients, and some patients may gain relief by sitting or leaning forwards.
  • The suddenness of onset may simulate a perforated peptic ulcer, while biliary colic or acute cholecystitis can be mimicked if the pain is maximal in the right upper quadrant. Radiation to the chest can simulate myocardial infarction, pneumonia or pleuritic pain. In fact, acute pancreatitis can mimic most causes of the acute abdomen and should seldom be discounted in differential diagnosis.
  • Mild icterus can be caused by biliary obstruction in gallstone pancreatitis, and an acute swinging pyrexia suggests cholangitis. Bleeding into the fascial planes can produce bluish discoloration of the flanks (Grey Turner's sign) or umbilicus (Cullen's sign). Subcutaneous fat necrosis may produce small, red, tender nodules on the skin of the legs.
  • X-RAY features of acute pancreatitis:

    KEYTAKEAWAYS:

    • Migratory pain form preiumbilical area to McBurney's point: acute appendicitis
    • Pain radiating from loin to testicles\thigh: ureteric colic
    • Pain radiating from epigastrium to left side back- acute pancreatitis
    • Pain in the right hypochondrium radiating to back: acute cholecystitis

question_text: A 32-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after sustaining severe maxillofacial trauma in a high-speed road traffic accident. He is restless, hypoxic, and gurgling blood in his mouth. The airway is compromised, and immediate intervention is required. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Cricothyroidotomyis the procedure of choice for establishing a surgical airway in 'cannot intubate, cannot ventilate' situations, especially in severe maxillofacial trauma where anatomical distortion prevents intubation and bag-mask ventilation.
  • It is performed rapidly by creating an opening through the cricothyroid membrane, allowing life-saving oxygenation and ventilation.
  • It is an emergency, temporizing procedure, often later converted to a formal tracheostomy if prolonged airway support is required.
  • ATLS protocol: In facial trauma → attempt intubation → if not possible and bag-mask fails → emergency cricothyroidotomy.

Explanation of Other Options

Tracheostomy (Option A):

  • Definitive surgical airway but time-consuming, requires neck dissection, and not suitable for immediate airway rescue.
  • Indicated for long-term airway management, not acute obstruction.

Orotracheal intubation (Option B):

  • First-line airway interventionin trauma.
  • However, in severe maxillofacial injuries, distorted anatomy, bleeding, and edema make intubation nearly impossible.

Bag-mask ventilation with jaw thrust (Option D):

  • Temporizing measure but ineffective in severe facial trauma, as airway cannot be sealed and blood obstructs ventilation.
  • Contraindicated as sole management in this case.

Key Takeaways Points:

  • Airway management in maxillofacial trauma follows ATLS guidelines:
    • Attempt intubation.
    • If unsuccessful and bag-mask fails → emergency cricothyroidotomy.
    • Later convert to tracheostomy if prolonged airway needed.
  • Cricothyroidotomy = most rapid surgical airwayin trauma.

question_text: A patient presented to emergency after blunt abdominal trauma with low Blood pressure. What should be the initial step?
option_c: Get a CT Scan done and start IV fluids later
explanation:
ABDOMINAL INJURY

Patients who have suffered abdominal trauma can generally be classified into the following categories based on their physiological condition after initial resuscitation:

  • physiologically 'normal' - investigation can be completed before treatment is planned;
  • physiologically 'non-compromised' - investigation is more limited; it is aimed at establishing whether the patient can be managed nonoperatively, whether angioembolization can be used or whether surgery is required;
  • physiologically 'compromised' - investigations need to be suspended as immediate surgical correction of the bleeding is required.

A trauma laparotomy is the final step in the pathway to delineate intra-abdominal injury. Occasionally it is difficult to determine the source of bleeding in the shocked, multiple injured patient. If doubt still exists, especially in the presence of other injuries, a laparotomy may still be the safest option.

The key is to make a decision, as indecision leads to delay in definitive control. The patient's physiology must be assessed constantly; if there is an indication that the patient is still actively bleeding, the source must be identified unless the patient is unstable and requires immediate surgery. Blood loss into the abdomen can be subtle and there may be no clear clinical signs. Blood is not an irritant and does not initially cause any abdominal pain. Distension is subjective, and a drop in the blood pressure may be a very late sign in a young ft patient. Examination in compromised patients should take place either in the emergency department or in the operating theater if the patient is deteriorating rapidly.

question_text: In FAST, which of the following sites cannot be evaluated?
explanation:
Focused abdominal sonography for trauma and extended FAST (FAST and eFAST)

  • Focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) is a technique whereby ultrasound (sonography) imaging is used to assess the torso for the presence of free fluid in the abdominal cavity, and is extended into the thoracic cavities and pericardium (eFAST).
  • There should be no attempt to determine the nature or extent of the specific injury. eFAST is usually a rapid, reproducible, portable and non-invasive bedside test and can be performed at the same time as resuscitation.
  • eFAST is accurate at detecting >100 mL of free blood; however, it is very operator dependent and, especially if the patient is very obese or the bowel is full of gas, it may be unreliable.
  • Hollow viscus injury and solid organ injury are difficult to diagnose, even in experienced hands, as small amounts of gas or fluid are difficult to assess and eFAST has a low sensitivity (29-35%) for organ injury without hemoperitoneum.
  • eFAST is also unreliable for excluding injury in penetrating trauma. If there is doubt, the eFAST examination can be repeated.

question_text: A 3-day old neonate presents with abdominal distension and bilious vomiting. Among the following, which is the most appropriate investigation to diagnose the condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a neonate with bilious vomiting and distension, the leading concern is malrotation with midgut volvulus, a life-threatening surgical emergency. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the abdomen is the most appropriate initial investigation as it is rapid, highly accurate for identifying the abnormal position of the duodenojejunal flexure (malrotation) and the "whirlpool sign" of volvulus, and can assess bowel viability. It avoids the risks of barium aspiration in a vomiting neonate.

Although an upper GI series with barium swallow, barium meal, or barium meal follow-through is the classic test for malrotation, giving a large volume of barium to a vomiting and potentially unstable neonate carries a high risk of aspiration pneumonia; hence, CECT is faster and safer. (Options A, B and C ruled out)

Key Takeaways:

  • Bilious vomiting in a neonate is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.
  • CECT is a rapid and accurate first-line imaging modality for this critical condition.

References: https://insightsimaging.springeropen.com/articles/10.1186/s13244-021-01045-y

question_text: A 27-year-old male, restrained driver, presents to the emergency department following a high-velocity motor vehicle collision. On examination, he is hemodynamically stable but demonstrates a transverse ecchymotic band across the lower abdomen consistent with the "seat belt sign." FAST scan reveals no significant intraperitoneal free fluid. Despite stable vitals, the patient continues to complain of localized abdominal pain and mild distension. Considering the mechanism of injury and clinical findings, which organ system is most likely to be injured in this scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Hollow viscus injuries(most commonly the small intestine, followed by the large intestine) are the hallmark of seat belt injuries.
  • The shearing force of rapid deceleration, combined with compression from the seat belt, predisposes the mesentery and bowel loops to lacerations, contusions, mesenteric tears, or ischemia.
  • The 'seat belt sign' has a strong predictive value for underlying bowel and mesenteric injuries even if initial imaging appears normal.
  • CT abdomen with contrast is the gold standard in stable patients and may show free air, bowel wall thickening, mesenteric hematoma, or contrast extravasation.
  • Delayed recognition can lead to perforation, peritonitis, and sepsis.

Management of seat belt-related injuries:

  • FASTis a quick and widely available method to detect intraperitoneal fluid or blood.
  • Computed tomography (CT)scanning offers significant advantages by identifying critical details such as extraluminal air or contrast leakage, which can guide the need for surgical intervention.
  • In cases where spinal injury is suspected, imaging of the entire spine should be conducted to rule out fractures, such as the Chance fracture commonly associated with seat belt injuries.
  • Treatment:Immediate laparotomy.

Seat belt syndrome describes the combination of the seat belt sign with associated internal injuries, such as abdominal organ damage or spinal fractures, particularly in the thoracolumbar region.

Explanation of Other Options

Liver (Option A):

  • The liver is the most frequently injured solid organin blunt trauma.
  • However, in seat belt syndrome, the pattern of injury is more commonly mesenteric or hollow viscusrather than solid organ.

Spleen (Option B):

  • Like the liver, the spleen is a common solid organ injured in blunt abdominal trauma.
  • But seat belt compression across the abdomenmakes mesenteric/intestinal injury more likely.

Pancreas (Option C):

  • Pancreatic trauma usually occurs due to direct epigastric blowagainst the vertebral column (e.g., handlebar injury).
  • Rare in seat belt injuries unless the force is directed specifically at the epigastrium.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: What is sweet esophagectomy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Left thoracic resection (Sweet esophagectomy). Via a single posterolateral incision on the left chest wall (usually fifth to sixth intercostal space), the oesophagus is mobilised. The diaphragm is opened and the gastroplasty prepared from this opening. The stomach is delivered to the left thoracic cavity for anastomosis

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: McKeown esophagectomy

  • The McKeown esophagectomy is a three-phase procedure that involves resection of the esophagus through a combination of cervical, thoracic, and abdominal incisions.
  • It differs from Sweet esophagectomy, which is done through a single thoracic incision, and is typically used in patients with esophageal cancer.

Choice C: Lewis-Tanner procedure

  • The Lewis-Tanner procedure involves reconstruction of the esophagus using a gastric tube in the neck after esophagectomy. It is not specifically related to Sweet esophagectomy, which uses a different approach.

Choice D: Transhiatal esophagectomy

  • The transhiatal esophagectomy is performed through abdominal and cervical incisions rather than thoracic access.
  • It involves resecting the esophagus via the abdomen and neck without opening the chest cavity, typically for esophageal cancer located in the lower esophagus.

Key Takeaway

  • Sweet esophagectomy (left thoracic resection) involves mobilizing the esophagus through a left thoracic incision, preparing the stomach for anastomosis in the thoracic cavity.

question_text: A patient presents with a headache, recurrent episodes of high blood pressure, and tachycardia. Her urine shows elevated levels of vanillylmandelic acid, and a CT scan reveals a retroperitoneal tumour in the right lumbar region. Which of the following syndromes is not typically associated with this condition?
explanation:
Pheochromocytoma is associated with MEN 2A, VHL, HPPS, and NF1, but not with NF2, which primarily involves schwannomas and meningiomas.

  • This patient has classic features of pheochromocytoma:
    • Symptoms: Headache, hypertension, tachycardia, sweating
    • Biochemical marker: Elevated urinary vanillylmandelic acid (VMA), a catecholamine metabolite
    • Imaging: Retroperitoneal tumor, possibly adrenal or extra-adrenal (paraganglioma)
  • Pheochromocytomas are rare catecholamine-secreting tumors derived from chromaffin cells, usually located in the adrenal medulla.
  • They may also arise from extra-adrenal paraganglia (called paragangliomas).

Syndromes associated with pheochromocytoma:

  • MEN 2A and 2B (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia):
    • Pheochromocytoma
    • Medullary thyroid carcinoma
    • Parathyroid hyperplasia (in MEN 2A)
  • Von Hippel-Lindau Disease (VHL):
    • Hemangioblastomas, retinal angiomas, RCC, pancreatic cysts, and pheochromocytoma
  • Hereditary:
    • Paraganglioma-Pheochromocytoma Syndromes (HPPS):
    • Caused by mutations in SDH genes (e.g., SDHB, SDHD)
    • Associated with head, neck, thoracic, or abdominal paragangliomas
  • Neurofibromatosis Type 1 (NF1) (not listed in the question):
    • Café-au-lait spots, neurofibromas, optic gliomas, and pheochromocytoma

Explanation of other options:

MEN 2A syndrome (Option A): Associated with pheochromocytoma, medullary thyroid carcinoma, and parathyroid hyperplasia.

Von Hippel-Lindau Disease (Option B): Autosomal dominant syndrome strongly linked with pheochromocytomas and other vascular tumors.

Hereditary Paraganglioma-Pheochromocytoma Syndromes (Option D): These are the classic familial syndromes associated with pheochromocytomas or extra-adrenal paragangliomas.

Neurofibromatosis Type 2 (Option C): NF2 involves bilateral vestibular schwannomas, meningiomas, and ependymomas, not typically associated with pheochromocytomas. This distinguishes it from NF1, which is associated with pheochromocytomas.

question_text: A patient presented with abdominal pain, blood in stools and a palpable mass on the abdominal examination. The following barium image was obtained from the patient. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Patients with abdominal pain with vomiting and palpable mass in the right lumbar region suggest intussusceptions.

Clinical features of intussusception

  • The classic presentation of intussusception is with episodes of screaming and drawing up of the legs in a previously well male infant.
  • The attacks last for a few minutes and recur repeatedly. During attacks the child appears pale and between episodes may be listless. Vomiting may or may not occur at the outset but becomes conspicuous and bile-stained with time.
  • Initially, the passage of stool may be normal, whereas, later, blood and mucus are evacuated - the 'redcurrant jelly' stool.
  • Classically, the abdomen is not initially distended; a lump that hardens on palpation may be discerned but this is present in only 60% of cases .
  • There may be an associated feeling of emptiness in the right iliac fossa (the sign of Dance).
  • On rectal examination, blood-stained mucus may be found on the finger. Occasionally, in extensive ileocolic or colocolic intussusception, the apex may be palpable or even protrude from the anus.

question_text: A patient presented to emergency with pain in abdomen and fever for 3 days and dehydrated face. Abdominal X-ray images are shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• Pain in abdomen and fever for 3 days and dehydrated face. Abdominal X-ray images suggest subdiaphragmatic collection. All suggest infective etiology mostly liver abscess.
  • bacteria remain the most common cause. although infection is usually polymicrobial Klebsiella, Escherichia coli and the Streptococcus milleri group are the usual organisms identifed.
  • Biliary tract pathology is the most common source (35%), followed by portal spread from the gastrointestinal tract, including diverticulitis and appendicitis (20%). Other unusual aetiologies include contiguous spread from subphrenic or intra-abdominal collections, bacteraemia secondary to trauma or infected cysts and necrotic tumours following chemotherapy.

IOC- CECT abdomen

X-ray features of liver abscess:

  • Right sided elevated diaphragm
  • Treatment of liver abscesses initially requires identification of the source, if possible, aspiration of the lesion for microbiology and culture (repeated aspirations may be required) and treatment with appropriate antibiotics.
  • Simple cysts containing debris, hydatid cysts, necrotic tumors and non-infected haematomas (after unrecognized or occasional trivial trauma) can all be mistaken for abscesses. Antibiotic treatment using a combination of two or more antibiotics is recommended.
  • Metronidazole and clindamycin provide wide anaerobic coverage and excellent penetration into the abscess cavity.
  • Third-generation cephalosporins and aminoglycosides are very effective against most Gram-negative organisms.

question_text: A 34-year-old female with a history of alcohol intake was taking NSAIDs for abdominal pain. She developed severe pain in the whole abdomen. A radiograph is given below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The history of NSAID use (a known risk factor for peptic ulcers) followed by the sudden onset of severe, generalized abdominal pain is classic for a perforated peptic ulcer.

The radiograph described show pneumoperitoneum (free air under the diaphragm), which is a definitive radiographic sign of a hollow viscus perforation. NSAIDs and alcohol are both significant risk factors for gastroduodenal ulceration and subsequent perforation.

Explanation of other options:

Rupture of ectopic pregnancy (Option A): This would cause hemorrhagic shock and lower abdominal pain, but it does not cause pneumoperitoneum.

Acute pancreatitis (Option B): While both alcohol and pain are features of pancreatitis, it does not cause free air on an X-ray.

Perforated liver abscess (Option C): A liver abscess may cause pain and sepsis, but perforation into the peritoneum is rare and would not typically present with the dramatic pneumoperitoneum seen in hollow viscus perforation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Sudden, severe generalized abdominal pain suggests perforation.
  • Pneumoperitoneum on an erect chest X-ray is diagnostic of hollow viscus perforation.

question_text: A 35-year-old male patient came to emergency department with severe pain in the chest and abdomen with history of shortness of breath since 1 day. There is upper abdominal rigidity. Patient had history of vomiting after heavy alcohol intake before the onset of symptoms. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
A young male patient vomiting after drinking causes spontaneous perforation of the lower oesophagus which causes severe pain in the chest and upper abdomen. It is also associated with shortness of breath due to mediastinitis. So most probable diagnosis is boerhaave’s syndrome.

Option a) perforated peptic perforation: there will not be severe chest pain in the initial period of perforated peptic ulcer patient

Option b) myocardial infarction: there would be pain in the chest radiating to the left arm. But vomiting might occur after the pain. But here vomiting is followed by chest and abdominal pain. And there won't be abdominal rigidity in myocardial infarction.

Option d) pancreatitis: there will not be severe chest pain and shortness of breath in the initial period or presenting complain of the patient of acute pancreatitis.

Barotrauma (spontaneous perforation, Boerhaave’s syndrome)

This occurs classically when a person vomits against a closed glottis. The pressure in the oesophagus increases rapidly, and the oesophagus bursts at its weakest point in the lower third, sending a stream of material into the mediastinum and often the pleural cavity as well.

Patients with Boerhaave's syndrome may have the classic triad of vomiting, chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema. There may or may not beassociated haematemesis. Typically, the site of perforation is the lower oesophagus towards the left pleural cavity. Gastric juice as well as ingested food is forcefully ejected into the left chest. A left pleural effusion rapidly accumulates. Physical examination reveals subcutaneous emphysema on the chest wall, sometimes extending to the cervical region as well.

Patients with cervical oesophageal or pharyngeal perforation are usually much less septic than those with intrathoracic perforations and mediastinitis. A typical example would be foreign body perforation, such as by a sharp fishbone, having lodged at the postcricoid area and perforated the oesophagus. There may be a history of foreign body ingestion and neck pain and physical examination may reveal tenderness and subcutaneous emphysema.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1127

explanation:

  • Chest haemorrhage- Hemothorax

  • Fracture of Long bones:
  • Femur

question_text: A 25-year-old male undergoes an abdominal ultrasound for vague flank pain, which reveals an empty left renal fossa. A subsequent CT urogram demonstrates the anatomical configuration shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The diagnosis is crossed renal ectopia, specifically the fused variant. The image demonstrates the key features of this anomaly:

  • Both kidneys are located on the same side of the midline.
  • The ectopic kidney has "crossed over" and is fused with the normally positioned kidney.
  • Crucially, the ureter from the crossed kidney enters the bladder on its correct, original side, meaning it must cross the midline.

This is a congenital anomaly resulting from abnormal ascent and rotation of the fetal kidney. It is often asymptomatic and discovered incidentally.

Explanation of Other Options:

Horseshoe kidney (Option A): This is the most common renal fusion anomaly, but in this condition, the kidneys are located on their respective sides of the spine and are fused at their lower poles across the midline, often anterior to the great vessels.

Pelvi-ureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction (Option C): This is a functional blockage at the junction of the renal pelvis and ureter, leading to hydronephrosis. While it can occur in an ectopic kidney, it is not the primary anatomical diagnosis depicted.

Polycystic kidney disease (Option D): This is a genetic disorder characterized by the development of numerous cysts in both kidneys, leading to massive renal enlargement. It does not involve fusion or abnormal positioning of the kidneys.

Key Takeaways: Common Renal Fusion and Ectopic Anomalies

question_text: A 30-year-old male presents with severe urgency to pass urine but is unable to do so. On examination, there is blood at the urethral meatus, and perineal swelling following a blunt trauma to the pelvis. Based on this clinical presentation, which of the following is the most likely site of injury?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient usually gives a history of a falling-astride injury, leading to blunt trauma of the perineum. Other common causes include falling from a tree, cycling, skating and industrial accidents. The bulbar urethra is crushed upwards onto the pubic bone, typically with significant bruising. The signs of a ruptured bulbar urethra are perineal bruising and haematoma, typically with a butterfly distribution. There is usually bleeding from the urethral meatus and retention of urine.

Investigations include a retrograde urethrogram (RGU). A gentle attempt at catheterisation may be made. If the catheter fails to drain urine, a suprapubic cystostomy is performed. Delayed anastomotic urethroplasty is performed after 3 months with excellent success rates

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: Posterior urethral valve

  • Posterior urethral valves are a congenital condition primarily seen in infants and children. This would not be the likely cause of blood at the urethral meatus in a 30-year-old male with a history of blunt pelvic trauma.
  • Additionally, posterior urethral valves do not typically present with perineal swelling and blood at the urethral meatus following trauma.

Choice C: Intraperitoneal bladder rupture

  • Intraperitoneal bladder rupture is typically caused by blunt trauma to the lower abdomen, leading to urinary leakage into the peritoneum.
  • The symptoms usually include lower abdominal pain, difficulty urinating, and hematuria, but blood at the urethral meatus and perineal swelling would not be characteristic signs of a bladder rupture.
  • This would more likely present with signs of peritonitis and would not cause significant perineal trauma.

Choice D: Membranous urethra

  • The membranous urethra is typically less involved in blunt trauma compared to the bulbar urethra.
  • Injuries to the membranous urethra can lead to posterior urethral injuries, but they usually involve more severe pelvic fractures and more extensive trauma than what is described here.
  • The bulbar urethra is the most common site for the type of injury described in this case.

Key Takeaway

  • The most likely site of injury in this patient with blunt pelvic trauma, blood at the urethral meatus, and perineal swelling is the bulbar urethra.

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding management of diaphragmatic injury except
option_a: Diaphragmatic injuries can bleed significantly from branches of the thoracic artery that can be exposed at the edges of the tear
option_b: Nonabsorbable synthetic materials can be used to reconstruct the diaphragm in clean surgical fields but should be avoided in the setting of contamination.
option_c: Closure is performed with a single layer of nonabsorbable suture incorporating large full-thickness bites of healthy diaphragmatic tissue.
option_d: A peripheral detachment of the diaphragm from the wall of the torso can be repaired by reinserting the injured tissue one or two interspaces superior.
explanation:
• Diaphragmatic injuries are typically repaired by debriding nonviable tissue and then closing the defect. The diaphragm exhibits enough redundancy for all, but the largest defects to be closed primarily.
  • Closure is performed with a single layer of nonabsorbable suture incorporating large full-thickness bites of healthy diaphragmatic tissue. It is important to obtain hemostasis because diaphragmatic injuries can bleed significantly from branches of the phrenic artery that can be exposed at the edges of the tear. Large areas of tissue loss are rare in traumatic rupture, but when present may require reconstruction with a prosthetic.
  • Nonabsorbable synthetic materials can be used to reconstruct the diaphragm in clean surgical fields but should be avoided in the setting of contamination. A peripheral detachment of the diaphragm from the wall of the torso can be repaired by reinserting the injured tissue one or two interspaces superior.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 21st, Pg: 411

question_text: A 55-year-old male, 7 days post-emergency laparotomy for perforated duodenal ulcer, Which of the following is considered a "sure sign" of abdominal wound dehiscence in a post-operative hypotensive patient?
option_d: Widening of the abdominal scar with palpable edges
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Serosanguinous drainage from the wound (Salmon fluid sign) is considered the "sure sign" of abdominal wound dehiscence.
  • Occurs 5-8 days postoperatively, when tensile strength of the wound is weakest.
  • Often preceded by a "popping" sensation during coughing or straining.
  • Fluid leak indicates fascial breakdown and requires urgent evaluation.
  • May progress to burst abdomen (evisceration) if untreated.

Risk Factors for Wound Dehiscence

  • Technical: Poor surgical closure, closure under tension.
  • Patient-related: Malnutrition, obesity, diabetes, renal failure, jaundice, malignancy, steroid therapy.
  • Local: Wound infection, hematoma, seroma.
  • Systemic/physiological: Increased intra-abdominal pressure (COPD, coughing, ileus), sepsis, hypotension.
  • Surgery-related: Emergency operations, contaminated cases.

Management

  • Partial/early dehiscence: Manage conservatively with dressings or VAC (if no evisceration).
  • Full-thickness/with evisceration: Requires urgent return to OT for resuturing.
  • Infected or poor-quality tissue: Leave wound open, manage with dressings ± delayed closure.

Explanation of Other Options:

Increased bowel sounds (Option A): Not specific for dehiscence; usually seen in recovery from ileus.

Persistent abdominal pain (Option B): Common after surgery, but nonspecific; pain alone does not indicate wound disruption.

Widening of scar with palpable edges (Option D): A late finding in dehiscence; the earliest sure sign is serosanguinous drainage.

question_text: A 25 year old male patient presented to the emergency with a history of road traffic accident. On examination, the patient had subcutaneous emphysema, absence of air entry on the right side & hypotension. Which of the following will be the next step of management?
option_b: Fluid resuscitation with wide bore needle
explanation:
History of road traffic accident and On examination, the patient had subcutaneous emphysema, absence of air entry on the right side & hypotension suggest massive pneumothorax or hemothorax.

So in both condition urgent ICD insertion is required

Inserting and managing a chest drain

An intercostal tube connected to an underwater seal is central to the management of chest disease; however, the management of the pleura and of chest drains can be troublesome, even in experienced hands.

The safest site for insertion of a drain is in the triangle that lies:

  • anterior to the mid-axillary line;
  • above the level of the nipple;
  • below and lateral to the pectoralis major muscle.

This will ideally find the fifth space. The technique includes the following.

  • Meticulous attention to sterility throughout.
  • Adequate local anesthesia to include the pleura.
  • Sharp dissection to cut only the skin.
  • Blunt dissection with artery forceps down through the muscle layers; these should only be the serratus anterior is in a short tunnel, which reduces the chance of entraining air.
  • A drain for pneumothorax and haemothorax should aim towards the apex of the lung. A drain for pleural effusion or empyema should be nearer the base.The drain should pass over the upper edge of the rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle that lies beneath the rib.
  • The retaining stitch should be secure but should not obliterate the drain.
  • A vertical mattress suture is inserted for later wound closure. This is vital for pneumothorax management but should be omitted if the drain is for empyema (provided there is adherence of the pleura) because that tract should lie open.
  • Connect the drain to an underwater seal device which functions as a one-way valve.
  • After completion, check that the drain has achieved its objective by taking a chest radiograph. It is preferable not to apply suction to the drain or clamp and the intercostals.
  • An oblique tract, so that the skin incision and the hole in the port is forgotten. Dangers of disconnection and siphoning the parietal pleura do not overlie each other and the drain is small or best averted in other ways apart from clamping.

question_text: All the following are true regarding tension pneumothorax except:
option_a: A common cause of tension pneumothorax is positive pressure ventilation (PPV)
option_b: Thoracic spine injury can cause pneumothorax
option_c: Breath sounds are absent on the affected side
option_d: Simple pneumothorax cannot convert into a tension pneumothorax
explanation:
Explanation:

Tension pneumothorax occurs when air enters the pleural space and cannot escape → intrapleural pressure rises; mediastinal shift and cardiovascular compromise follow. A recognized precipitant is positive-pressure ventilation (PPV) in a patient with existing alveolar/pleural injury..

Thoracic spine/penetrating chest injury can cause pneumothorax.

Absent breath sounds on the affected side are a classic sign (others include hyperresonance, distended neck veins, hypotension).

Crucially: a simple pneumothorax can progress to a tension pneumothorax (for example if a valve mechanism develops or further air entry occurs under positive pressure). So, the statement "simple pneumothorax cannot convert" is incorrect


Key takeaways:

In trauma/ventilated patients always watch for conversion of simple pneumothorax to tension. Immediate decompression (needle thoracostomy/thoracostomy) is required in unstable patients.

question_text: A 10 years old boy skids while cycling. The child was stable and abdominal examination was normal. Blood was noticed at the tip of meatus. What is the next best step?
explanation: Blood at meatus suggests urethral injury so suprapubic cystostomy is ideal.

question_text: A patient with an incident of being stabbed in the front part of the abdomen is brought to the emergency. The patient's vital signs are stable. What will be the next step in managing this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient has a penetrating abdominal injury but is hemodynamically stable, meaning there is no shock or obvious peritonitis.
  • In such cases, the next step is further evaluation with imaging or diagnostic tests (e.g., focused abdominal sonography for trauma [FAST], CT abdomen with contrast).
  • This approach helps determine whether surgical intervention is required or if conservative management can be considered.

Management of Abdominal Stab Injuries:

  • Indications for Immediate Laparotomy
    • Hemodynamic instability (shock, uncontrolled bleeding).
    • Signs of peritonitis (rigidity, guarding, rebound tenderness).
    • Evisceration or obvious major visceral injury.
  • Stable Patient Approach
    • Further investigations such as FAST or CT abdomen.
    • Serial clinical examinations to detect delayed peritonitis.
    • Laparotomy only if deterioration occurs.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Emergency laparotomy (Option A): Indicated only if unstable, peritonitis, or active bleeding is present - not appropriate in a stable patient.

Observation (Option B): While observation may be part of ongoing care, the next step is imaging/further investigation to rule out internal injury

Intravenous hydration (Option C): Supportive measure but not the primary step; definitive evaluation of the injury comes first.

Key Takeaway

In a hemodynamically stable patient with abdominal stab injury, the correct next step is further investigation with imaging (FAST or CT) before deciding on surgery.

Reference: NIH Link

question_text: A patient arrives with pain in the right upper abdomen. One week ago, the patient experienced a bout of diarrhoea. An abdominal CT scan shows a solitary liver abscess measuring approximately 25 cubic centimetres. What should be the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

A small, uncomplicated liver abscess (≤5 cm or ~25 cc) in a stable patient is initially managed with medical therapy using broad-spectrum antibiotics.

  • Liver abscesses are commonly of pyogenic or amoebic origin.
  • In this case, the history of preceding diarrhoea and solitary liver abscess suggests a likely amoebic or secondary pyogenic abscess.
  • For abscesses that are small (≤5 cm or ≤30 cc), medical management is the first line, especially if the patient is stable and there are no features of rupture, sepsis, or multiloculated abscess.
  • Medical therapy involves:
    • Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics for pyogenic abscesses (e.g., 3rd gen cephalosporins + metronidazole).
    • Metronidazole is also the drug of choice for amoebic abscesses.
  • Clinical and radiological monitoring is done.
  • Intervention (like percutaneous drainage) is only considered if:
    • There is no improvement within 48-72 hours.
    • The abscess is large (>5 cm), multiloculated, or about to rupture.
    • The patient is clinically deteriorating.

Explanation of other options:

PAIR (Option A): Puncture-Aspiration-Injection-Reaspiration is primarily used for hydatid cysts of the liver, not for pyogenic or amoebic abscesses.

Surgery (Option B): Reserved for complicated abscesses, such as those with rupture, inaccessible for percutaneous drainage, or secondary to intra-abdominal pathology (e.g., appendicitis). Not first-line for a small, uncomplicated abscess.

Percutaneous drainage (Option D): Indicated in larger abscesses (>5 cm) or when no response to medical therapy. For a 25 cc abscess, drainage is not routinely required unless there is clinical deterioration.

question_text: A 32-year-old male presents to the emergency department after sustaining a stab injury to the left side of his chest. He appears distressed with a pulse rate of 120/min, BP 90/60 mmHg, and respiratory rate 28/min. On examination, breath sounds are decreased on the left side. A chest X-ray is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of:

  • Penetrating chest trauma
  • Hypotension and tachycardia (shock signs)
  • Decreased breath sounds
  • Diffuse opacity ("white-out") on chest X-ray

is diagnostic of a Hemothorax, i.e., accumulation of blood in the pleural space causing lung collapse and impaired ventilation.

Explanation of Other Options:

Pneumothorax (Option A):

  • Results from air, not blood, entering the pleural cavity.
  • Presents with hyperresonant percussion note, absent breath sounds, and visible pleural line on CXR.
  • CXR shows a dark, radiolucent (air-filled) hemithorax, not hazy or opaque.
  • No fluid level or meniscus sign.

Tension Pneumothorax (Option C):

  • A life-threatening variant of pneumothorax where air enters but cannot escape the pleural space.
  • Clinical triad:
  • Severe respiratory distress
  • Tracheal deviation away from affected side
  • Distended neck veins and hypotension (obstructive shock)
  • CXR shows hyperlucency with mediastinal shift - unlike the hazy opacity of hemothorax.
  • Immediate needle decompression is required, followed by ICD.

Hydrothorax (Option D) :

  • Refers to serous fluid accumulation in the pleural space, commonly due to congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, or renal disease, not trauma.
  • Fluid is clear, not blood, and there are no signs of shock.
  • CXR may look similar but the context (stab wound + hypotension) makes hemothorax the correct choice.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: A 25-year-old male involved in a road traffic accident presents to the emergency department. On arrival, he is tachypneic with a respiratory rate of 25/min, hypotensive with a blood pressure of 80/45 mmHg, and exhibits hyper-resonance on the left side of the chest. Based on the chest X-ray findings, what is the most appropriate intervention?
option_a: Wide-bore needle insertion in the 2nd intercostal space
option_b: Wide-bore needle insertion in the 5th intercostal space followed by intercostal drainage in the 5th intercostal space
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation and radiographic findings are consistent with tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening emergency. Management involves immediate decompression by inserting a wide-bore needle into the 5th intercostal space within the "safe triangle," followed by placement of an intercostal chest drain in the same space to allow continuous evacuation of trapped air. This relieves intrathoracic pressure, restores venous return, and prevents cardiovascular collapse.

Explanation of other options:

Wide-bore needle insertion in the 2nd intercostal space (Option A): Needle decompression is not performed in the 2nd intercostal space in current practice; the 5th intercostal space at the mid-axillary line within the safe triangle is preferred.

Aspiration of pleural fluid (Option C): Aspiration of pleural fluid is appropriate for pleural effusion but not for pneumothorax.

No intervention required (Option D): No intervention is incorrect, as tension pneumothorax requires urgent decompression to prevent death.

Key Takeaways:

  • Tension pneumothorax is caused by a "one-way valve" mechanism where air enters the pleural cavity but cannot escape, leading to lung collapse, mediastinal shift, decreased venous return, and shock.
  • Clinical signs: hyper-resonant percussion note, absent breath sounds on the affected side, tracheal/mediastinal shift, hypotension, and distended neck veins.
  • Management: immediate decompression (needle thoracostomy in 5th ICS safe triangle) → chest tube placement.
  • Never wait for radiological confirmation in unstable patients.

question_text: A 30-year-old male presents to the ER with penetrating chest trauma. On examination, tracheal deviation is noted. What is the immediate next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical findings are diagnostic of a tension pneumothorax, a life-threatening emergency where a one-way valve mechanism traps air in the pleural cavity.

  • This causes lung collapse, mediastinal shift, reduced venous return, and compression of the contralateral lung.
  • Tracheal deviation is a late sign, and diagnosis must be made clinically without waiting for imaging.
  • The immediate treatment is needle decompression, traditionally in the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line, but current recommendations favour decompression in the safe triangle or performing a finger thoracostomy if trained.
  • This must be followed by definitive chest tube placement.

Explanation of Other Options:

e-FAST (Option A): Useful for detecting pneumothorax/haemothorax but should never delay life-saving intervention.

Chest X-ray (Option C): Not indicated in unstable patients; waiting for imaging risks death.

Intubation (Option D): Does not address the underlying problem and may worsen the pneumothorax if done before decompression.

question_text: A full-term neonate is delivered by spontaneous vaginal delivery. Soon after birth, the baby is noted to have bowel loops protruding through an abdominal wall defect located just to the right of the umbilical cord insertion. The loops are uncovered and edematous. The neonate is hemodynamically stable. What is the most appropriate management strategy?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The description is classical for gastroschisis– a congenital paraumbilical abdominal wall defect, usually right-sided, with free-floating bowel loops not covered by any membrane.
  • The treatment of choice is primary surgical closurewhen feasible. This involves reducing the bowel loops into the abdominal cavity and repairing the defect.
  • If the abdominal cavity is small or the defect is large, staged reduction using a preformed silofollowed by delayed closure is performed.
  • Early surgical management is crucial to prevent complications such as fluid/electrolyte imbalance, hypothermia, infection, and bowel necrosis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Wait and watch (Option B): Dangerous. Exposed bowel rapidly loses fluid/heat and is prone to infection, leading to acidosis, NEC, and sepsis. Not acceptable.

Slowly putting it inside (Option C): Gradual reduction is indeed part of the staged silo approach but is not an independent management strategy. Definitive repair is still required.

Surgical excision (Option D): Reserved only for non-viable segments of bowel in cases of necrosis or atresia, not the standard treatment.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: A patient presents with fever, abdominal pain, and jaundice. Imaging reveals the following findings. Which of the following statements is true regarding this condition?
option_c: Angioembolization is the treatment of choice
option_d: Echinococcus species is involved in etiology
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of a wavy internal membrane within a liver cyst strongly suggests hydatid disease caused by Echinococcus species.

  • Hydatid disease (echinococcosis) is a parasitic infection caused by Echinococcus granulosus, commonly transmitted via contact with infected dogs.
  • Humans are intermediate hosts, infected through oral ingestion of eggs from dogs.
  • The liver is the most frequently affected organ.
  • Typical features include abdominal pain, fever, and jaundice due to pressure effects or cyst rupture.
  • Imaging often reveals a characteristic serpentine or detached germinal membrane within the cyst.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Confirmed by serology (ELISA, immunoelectrophoresis) and imaging (USG, CT, MRCP).
    • Fine-needle aspiration is generally avoided due to risk of cyst rupture and anaphylaxis.
  • Treatment:
    • Options include the PAIR technique (Puncture, Aspiration, Injection, Reaspiration) combined with albendazole or praziquantel.
    • Surgery (pericystectomy, marsupialization) is reserved for large or complicated cysts.
    • Scolicidal agents like hypertonic saline or ethanol are used intraoperatively.
    • Cyst aspiration, followed by scolicidal agent application and sealing biliary communications.
    • Laparoscopic marsupialization (deroofing) for cysts.

Explanation of other options:

Surgery is mandatory (Option A): Surgery is not always necessary; medical and percutaneous options exist, especially for uncomplicated cysts.

Fine-needle aspiration cytology is diagnostic (Option B): FNA is contraindicated due to the risk of cyst rupture and anaphylactic shock.

Angioembolization is the treatment of choice (Option C): Angioembolization is not a standard treatment in hydatid disease and is typically unrelated to its management.

question_text: Which of the following statements is true about retroperitoneal hematoma occurring after trauma?
option_a: In zone 2 penetrating injuries hematoma, surgical exploration should be done always
option_b: Mattox maneuver to explore aorta involves mobilization of ascending colon to right
option_c: Penetrating trauma in pelvic region should be explored
option_d: In zone 1, injured vessels embolization is done
explanation:
Injury to the retroperitoneum is often difcult to diagnose, especially in the presence of other injury, when the signs may be masked. Diagnostic tests (such as ultrasound and DPL) may be negative. The best diagnostic modality is CT, but this requires a physiologically stable patient.

The retroperitoneum is divided into three zones for the purposes of intraoperative management in blunt trauma:

  1. Zone 1 (central): central haematomas should always be explored, once proximal and distal vascular control has been obtained.
  2. Zone 2 (lateral): lateral haematomas should only be explored if they are expanding or pulsatile or penetrating injury is present. They are usually renal in origin and can be managed non-operatively, although they may sometimes require angioembolisation.
  3. Zone 3 (pelvic): as with zone 2, these should only be explored if they are expanding or pulsatile or penetrating injury is present. Pelvic haematomas are exceptionally difcult to control and, whenever possible, should not be opened; they are best controlled with compression orextraperitoneal packing, or, if the bleeding is arterial in origin, with angioembolisation

question_text: A 25 years male after a massive RTA was brought to casualty with breathlessness and tachycardia. X ray chest image shown here is
explanation:
X Ray chest suggest right side grossly pneumothorax

Indications for surgical intervention for pneumothorax

include:

  • Second ipsilateral pneumothorax
  • First contralateral pneumothorax
  • Bilateral spontaneous pneumothorax
  • Pneumothorax fails to settle despite chest drainage
  • Spontaneous haemothorax: professions at risk (e.g. pilots, divers)
  • Pregnancy

Current recommendations focus on the use of small bore (10-14 Fr) chest drains, usually of a Seldinger type, inserted ideally under ultrasound guidance. However, knowledge of the role of the 'surgical' chest drain and how to insert it safely is still required.

question_text: A 25-year-old male is brought to the ER following an RTA. On examination, there is hyper-resonance over the left hemithorax, with RR 25/min and BP 80/45 mmHg. The chest X-ray revealed findings shown below. What is the most appropriate immediate management for this patient?
option_a: Wide bore needle insertion in the right 5th ICS
option_b: Wide bore needle insertion in the left 5th ICS followed by an intercostal drain
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The chest X-ray demonstrates complete darkening of hyperlucency with mediastinal shift, and the patient's respiratory distress and hypotension support the diagnosis of tension pneumothorax.
  • First intervention done in suspected tension pneumothorax is immediate decompression with a wide-bore needle inserted into the 5th intercostal space at the mid-axillary line to relieve trapped air.
  • This is followed by chest tube (intercostal drain) insertion at the same site for continuous drainage.

Tension Pneumothorax

  • A tension pneumothorax is a life-threatening condition that requires emergency intervention.
  • It occurs when a one-way valve mechanism allows air to enter the pleural space but prevents its escape, leading to complete collapse of the affected lung.
  • The mediastinum shifts to the opposite side, reducing venous return and compressing the contralateral lung.
  • Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confrmation.

Common causes include:

  • Penetrating chest trauma
  • Blunt chest trauma with parenchymal lung injury and persistent air leak
  • Iatrogenic lung injury (e.g., central venous catheterization)
  • Mechanical positive-pressure ventilation

Clinical Presentation of Tension Pneumothorax:

  • Tachypnea and dyspnea
  • Distended neck veins (jugular venous distension)
  • Tracheal deviation away from the affected side
  • Hyperresonance on percussion of the affected hemithorax
  • Decreased or absent breath sounds on the affected side

question_text: A 42-year-old alcoholic and a chronic smoker presented with bouts of vomiting and stabbing pain in the epigastrium. He was binge drinking shortly before the symptoms started. He is febrile and tachycardic. The given findings were seen on bedside radiological imaging. Which among the following is a likely cause of this?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture (epigastric pain, vomiting, history of smoking/alcohol) and systemic signs (fever, tachycardia) point towards an acute surgical abdomen. The key clue is the "bedside radiological imaging," which would be an erect chest X-ray or supine abdominal X-ray showing pneumoperitoneum (free air under the diaphragm or Rigler's sign). This is a classic finding for a perforated peptic ulcer, a common complication in alcoholics and smokers.

Explanation of other options:

Tension pneumothorax (Option A): This causes respiratory distress and unilateral absent breath sounds, not epigastric pain and vomiting. The X-ray would show a collapsed lung and mediastinal shift, not free air under the diaphragm.

Boerhaave syndrome (Option C): This is an esophageal rupture that also causes vomiting and can show pneumomediastinum on X-ray. However, the pain is typically severe and thoracic, not epigastric, and it is far rarer than a perforated ulcer.

Mallory Weiss tear(Option D): This causes upper GI bleeding (hematemesis) from a mucosal tear but does not cause peritonitis, fever, or free air on X-ray.

Key Takeaways:

  • Pneumoperitoneum on an X-ray is a surgical emergency.
  • Perforated peptic ulcer is a common cause in patients with risk factors like alcohol and smoking.

question_text: A patient presents with upper abdominal discomfort. A CT scan is done and is shown below. Based on Gharbi classification, what is the type of hydatid cyst?
explanation:
Explanation:

Type 2 hydatid cysts (Gharbi) show internal septations and daughter cysts, often with detached membranes, resembling a "water lily" sign.

  • Hydatid disease (echinococcosis) caused by Echinococcus granulosus leads to liver cysts.
  • The Gharbi classification, based on ultrasound and imaging findings, categorizes the cysts into five types:
    • Type 1: Purely anechoic, simple cyst-early stage, intact cyst.
    • Type 2: Cyst with internal membranes or daughter cysts-detached membranes produce the classic "water lily" sign.
    • Type 3: Multivesicular cysts with daughter cysts in a matrix-resembles honeycomb.
    • Type 4: Heterogeneous, solid-looking degenerative cyst.
    • Type 5: Calcified, inactive cyst.
  • The presence of floating membranes and daughter cysts indicates Type 2, corresponding to CE3a in WHO classification.

question_text:
A newborn presents within the first 48 hours of life with bilious vomiting and no abdominal distension. An abdominal X-ray is performed and is shown below.

What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation

  • Classical triad:
    • Neonatal onset (first 1-2 days of life)
    • Bilious vomiting (due to obstruction distal to the ampulla of Vater)
    • Minimal or absent abdominal distension
  • Imaging clue: The double-bubble sign (gas-filled stomach + proximal duodenum, no distal bowel gas) is pathognomonic for duodenal atresia.
  • Etiology: Failure of duodenal lumen recanalization during embryogenesis.

Duodenal Atresia

Etiology: Failure of normal duodenal lumen recanalization during embryonic life.

Associations:

  • Polyhydramnios (antenatal)
  • Down syndrome (Trisomy 21)
  • Annular pancreas, malrotation

Clinical features:

  • Early bilious vomiting
  • No abdominal distension
  • May develop dehydration/jaundice if untreated

Radiology:

  • X-Ray: Double-bubble sign (diagnostic hallmark).
  • Prenatal USG: Polyhydramnios, absent duodenal fluid passage

Types:

  • Type I
    • The lumen is blocked by a mucosal-submucosal membrane (duodenal web/diaphragm).
    • The muscular wall is intact.
    • The proximal bowel becomes dilated, but continuity is preserved.
    • On imaging: "double-bubble" but sometimes a small amount of distal gas may be seen if the web is perforate.
  • Variant: Type I with"windsock deformity"
    • Here the mucosal web is not fixed flat but balloons distally into the duodenal lumen due to peristalsis and pressure.
    • It resembles a "windsock" hanging down inside the lumen.
    • Functionally, it's still Type I atresia (intraluminal web/diaphragm), but it looks different radiologically/endoscopically.
  • Type II
    • The duodenum is discontinuous, with the two blind ends joined by a fibrous cord.
    • The mesentery remains intact.
  • Type III
    • Complete separation of the duodenum into two blind ends with a gap in the mesentery.
    • The most severe form.

Classification of duodenal atresia. (A) Type 1, (B) Type 1 with windsock variant, (C) Type 2, and (D) Type 3.

Management:

  • Stabilization with NG tube + IV fluids
  • Definitive surgery: Duodenoduodenostomy (preferred) or duodenojejunostomy

Key Clinical Pearl

"Bilious vomiting + double-bubble sign = Duodenal Atresia."
Always suspect in newborns, especially with Down syndrome and polyhydramnios history.

Explanation of Other Options:

Pyloric stenosis (Option B): Incorrect. Presents at 2-6 weeks of age, not within the first days. Vomiting is projectile, non-bilious. Imaging shows string sign, not double-bubble.

Esophageal atresia (Option C): Incorrect. Presents with drooling, choking, and respiratory distress. X-ray shows air in the proximal pouch ± air in the stomach (if TEF present). Not associated with double-bubble sign.

Gas in bowel (Option D): Incorrect. Gas in the bowel is a nonspecific finding. The double-bubble sign is diagnostic of duodenal atresia.

question_text: In a patient with aortic dissection, injury to which of the following structures is most likely to produce persistent hiccups?
explanation:
Explanation

  • Hiccups are involuntary spasms of the diaphragm, usually triggered by irritation of the phrenic nerve or diaphragm itself.
  • The phrenic nerve (C3-C5) descends through the mediastinum in close relation to the thoracic aorta and pericardium.
  • In aortic dissection, the expanding hematoma can compress or irritate the phrenic nerve → diaphragmatic spasm → hiccups.

Phrenic Nerve

  • The phrenic nerve as it passes through the thorax to supply the diaphragm.
  • The phrenic nerve emerges from the cervical plexus, with the right brachial plexus shown here.

    • Key Clinical Point

    "C3-C5 keeps the diaphragm alive."Any irritation of the phrenic nerve in thoracic pathology (aortic dissection, mediastinal tumors, pericarditis) can manifest as hiccups or referred shoulder pain.

    Explanation of Other Options:

    Abdominal aorta (Option B): Incorrect. Located inferiorly; no direct relationship with phrenic nerve. Injury doesn't cause hiccups.

    Thoracic aorta (Option C): Incorrect. The aorta itself does not trigger hiccups; irritation arises when the phrenic nerve adjacent to the aorta is involved.

    Spinal accessory nerve (Option D): Incorrect. Supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius. No role in diaphragmatic movement or hiccups.

  • Lateral View: The edge of the coin is seen, confirming its esophageal location.

Explanation of other options:

Foreign body in trachea (Option A): Usually seen in sagittal orientation on X-ray and presents with stridor/cough.

Foreign body in lungs (Option C): Lodges in bronchi (commonly right main); symptoms include cough, wheeze, respiratory distress.

question_text: A 35-year-old man sustained a blow to a distended bladder, leading to sudden severe hypogastric pain and syncope. Later, as the pain subsided, the abdomen became distended, and he had no desire to urinate. Which of the following statements is true regarding his condition?
option_a: This is a typical case of extraperitoneal bladder rupture
option_b: MRI is the ideal investigation to diagnose bladder rupture
option_c: Repair is done by suturing edges with single-layer 2/0 absorbable suture
option_d: Laparoscopic method is avoided as it can be done only on laparotomy
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's blow to a distended bladder caused sudden hypogastric pain with syncope, followed by abdominal distension due to urine leaking into the extraperitoneal space. These findings are characteristic of an extraperitoneal bladder rupture.

Bladder trauma

  • Bladder injuries can either be extraperitoneal or intraperitoneal.
  • Extraperitoneal bladder rupture
    • The bladder wall is disrupted but the peritoneal lining remains intact.
    • This causes urine to extravasate into the retropubic space.
  • Intraperitoneal bladder rupture
    • The peritoneum over the bladder is injured.
    • Urine extravasates into the peritoneal cavity.

Investigations

  • CT cystography reveals characteristic features like a flame-shaped appearance, pear sign, and teardrop appearance.
  • Retrograde cystography is the imaging modality of choice for diagnosing bladder ruptures, including extraperitoneal injuries. (Option B ruled out)
  • Extravasation of contrast limited to the perivesical space is a key finding that helps differentiate extraperitoneal from intraperitoneal ruptures, where contrast would outline bowel loops.

Management

question_text:
A 39-year-old male involved in a road traffic accident presents with severe chest trauma. A chest tube is inserted in the emergency room, draining ~1800 mL of blood within the first hour.
What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation

  • In massive hemothorax, the key determinant is the volume and rate of blood loss through the chest tube.
  • Drainage of >1500 mL in blunt trauma or >1000 mL in penetrating trauma is a definitive indication for emergency thoracotomy.
  • Likewise, ongoing drainage of 200-300 mL/hr despite resuscitation also mandates surgery.
  • In this case, 1800 mL in 1 hr = massive hemothorax → thoracotomy is lifesaving.

Indications for Emergency Thoracotomy

Key Clinical Pearl

Massive chest tube output = go to OR.

  • 1500 mL at once (blunt trauma) or >1000 mL (penetrating trauma) OR
  • 200-300 mL/hr ongoing → Emergency Thoracotomy

Explanation of Other Options:

Conservative for next 6 hours (Option B): Incorrect. Delaying surgery in a patient with such brisk blood loss risks hypovolemic shock and death.

Continue resuscitation (Option C): Incorrect. Resuscitation is necessary but not definitive; it cannot stop intrathoracic bleeding.

Wait & watch (Option D): Incorrect. Unsafe, as ongoing hemorrhage requires immediate surgical control.

After this if the patient is

  • Unstable: patient is taken up for laparotomy

Focused abdominal sonography for trauma and extended FAST (FAST and eFAST)

Focused abdominal sonography for trauma (FAST) is a technique whereby ultrasound (sonography) imaging is used to assess the torso for the presence of free fluid in the abdominal cavity, and is extended into the thoracic cavities and pericardium (eFAST).

There should be no attempt to determine the nature or extent of the specific injury. eFAST is usually a rapid, reproducible, portable and non-invasive bedside test and can be performed at the same time as resuscitation.

eFAST is accurate at detecting >100 mL of free blood;however, it is very operator dependent and, especially if the patient is very obese or the bowel is full of gas, it may be unreliable.

question_text: A patient presents with acute-onset, severe abdominal pain. He is hemodynamically stable. A chest X-ray is shown below. What is the next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The chest X-ray shows free air beneath the diaphragm, which indicates pneumoperitoneum.
  • Pneumoperitoneum in the context of an acute abdomen strongly suggests a perforated hollow viscus, most commonly a perforated peptic ulcer.
  • In a hemodynamically stable patient, the immediate priority is resuscitation with fluids and antibiotics, followed by exploratory laparotomy to repair the perforation.

Pneumoperitoneum

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Gastric lavage (Option A): Used in poisoning or drug overdose; not appropriate when perforation is suspected.

Chest tube insertion (Option B): Indicated in pleural conditions like pneumothorax or hemothorax, not in intra-abdominal free air.

Tracheostomy (Option C): Done for upper airway obstruction or prolonged ventilation; no airway compromise here.

Key Takeaway

Free air under the diaphragm in a patient with acute abdominal pain is diagnostic of pneumoperitoneum, and the next step is resuscitation followed by laparotomy to identify and repair the source of perforation.
