question_text: A man presented to the emergency after a road traffic accident (RTA) with chest pain and breathing difficulty. An X-ray was done. What type of breathing pattern is observed in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Paradoxical breathing is observed in flail chest, which typically results from multiple rib fractures following blunt trauma, as seen in this patient.

  • In this scenario, a road traffic accident (RTA) patient with chest pain and dyspnea following trauma and imaging suggestive of multiple adjacent rib fractures likely has a flail chest.
  • Flail chest occurs when three or more consecutive ribs are fractured in at least two places, resulting in a free-floating chest segment.
  • This segment exhibits paradoxical movement:
    • Inward movement during inspiration (while the rest of the chest expands)
    • Outward movement during expiration (while the rest of the chest contracts)
  • This abnormal motion disrupts normal ventilation mechanics, leading to:
    • Hypoventilation
    • Mediastinal flutter (which may cause cardiovascular compromise)
    • Pendular air movement (air shunts between lungs inefficiently)
  • Management of flail chest includes:
    • Analgesia to relieve pain and promote effective breathing
    • Oxygen supplementation
    • Intercostal chest drain (if pneumothorax/hemothorax present)
    • Intubation with positive pressure ventilation (IPPV) if respiratory failure occurs
    • Rib fixation in selected severe cases

Explanation of other options:

Cheyne Stokes (Option A): Characterized by cyclic crescendo-decrescendo respirations with apnea. Seen in congestive heart failure and central nervous system disorders—not associated with trauma or flail chest.

Biot (Option B): Irregular breaths with intermittent apnea, usually due to brainstem injury or raised intracranial pressure, not trauma-induced.

Kussmaul (Option C): Deep, rapid breathing seen in metabolic acidosis (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis), not typical of thoracic trauma or rib fractures.

question_text: What is the additional benefit of doing E-FAST?
option_c: Sub dural and dural trauma can be identified
explanation:
The FAST (Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma) examination looks for the presence of fluid-presumed to be blood in the appropriate clinical setting-visualizing 10 structures or spaces in 4 areas:

  • Pericardial
  • Perihepatic
  • Perisplenic
  • Pelvic

The E-FAST (Extended-FAST) additionally surveys the anterior and lateral pleural spaces (thoracic view) to evaluate for a pneumothorax or pleural effusion, assumed to be a hemothorax in trauma patients.

E-FAST has high sensitivity and specificity (especially in patients with hypotension). It can be done quickly, noninvasively, and without radiation exposure, and may be repeated. Due to these benefits, ultrasonography has essentially replaced diagnostic peritoneal lavage (DPL) in evaluation of trauma patients.

In a patient who is hemodynamically unstable, a positive E-FAST may indicate the need for immediate intervention (eg, tube thoracostomy, pericardial window, diagnostic laparotomy).

In a patient who is hemodynamically stable, the E-FAST can direct further diagnostic testing.

Although E-FAST was designed to expedite care in injured patients, the components have proven to be useful as a point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) for patients who are hypotensive but not injured to identify free fluid as a result of other causes (eg, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm).

question_text: A 65 year old male presented to emergency with abdominal pain for 6 hours. On examination, blood pressure was 90/50 mm Hg, respiratory rate of 24/minute, and oxygen saturation was 92%. Abdominal X-ray showed extraluminal air in abdomen. Which of the following must be done before shifting the patient to OT?
option_b: Initial IV access of choice is central venous catheter
option_d: Infusion of 2 to 3 liters of crystalloids
explanation:
Treatment of peptic perforation

  • The initial priorities are resuscitation and analgesia. Analgesia should not be withheld for fear of removing the signs of an intra-abdominal catastrophe. In fact, adequate analgesia makes the clinical signs more obvious. It is important, however, to titrate the analgesic dose.
  • Following resuscitation, the treatment is principally surgical. Laparotomy is performed, usually through an upper midline incision if the diagnosis of perforated peptic ulcer can be made with confidence.
  • Alternatively, laparoscopy may be used. The most important component of the operation is a thorough peritoneal toilet to remove all of the fluid and food debris.
  • If the perforation is in the duodenum, it can usually be closed by several well-placed sutures, closing the ulcer in a transverse direction as with a pyloroplasty.
  • It is important that sufficient tissue is taken in the suture to allow the edges to be approximated, and the sutures should not be tied so tight that they tear out.
  • It is common to place an omental patch over the perforation in the hope of enhancing the chances of the leak sealing. If the perforation is difficult to close primarily it is frequently possible to seal the leak with an omental patch alone, and many surgeons now employ this strategy for all perforations.

question_text: Identify the condition given in the image below.
explanation:
Explanation:

X-ray findings for tension pneumothorax include a collapsed lung on the affected side, a shift of the mediastinum and trachea away from the affected side, a depressed diaphragm, and increased air and hyperlucency (whiteness) on the affected side with absent lung markings.

Tension Pneumothorax

Definition & Mechanism

  • Caused by a one-way valve air leak from the lung or chest wall.
  • Air enters the thoracic cavity but cannot escape, causing:
    • Complete collapse of the affected lung
    • Mediastinal shift to the opposite side
    • Decreased venous return
    • Compression of the opposite lung

Common Causes

  • Penetrating chest trauma
  • Blunt trauma with persistent air leak
  • Iatrogenic lung injury (e.g., central venepuncture)
  • Mechanical positive-pressure ventilation

Clinical Features

  • Restlessness, tachypnoea, dyspnoea
  • Distended neck veins (similar to pericardial tamponade)
  • Hyper-resonance over the affected side
  • Decreased/absent breath sounds
  • Tracheal deviation (late sign-not required for diagnosis)

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. Never delay treatment for radiology.

Management

  • Immediate decompression is mandatory.
  • Historically:
    • Large-bore needle in 2nd intercostal space, mid-clavicular line.
  • Current teaching:
    • Decompress in the safe triangle:
      • Posterior: latissimus dorsi
      • Anterior: lateral border of pectoralis major
      • Inferior: line from the nipple, perpendicular to the floor, just anterior to the mid-axillary line
    • Finger thoracostomy in the same location in extremis
    • Follow with chest tube insertion.

Reference: https://radiopaedia.org/articles/tension-pneumothorax.

question_text: A 20 years old boy is brought to the emergency following a RTA with respiratory distress and hypotension. He has subcutaneous emphysema and no air entry on the right side. What is the next best step in management?
option_a: Start IV fluids after insertion of wide bore IV line
option_b: Needle decompression in the 5th intercostal space
explanation:
Tension pneumothorax

A tension pneumothorax develops when a 'one-way valve' air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall. Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing and then compressing the affected lung. The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return and compressing the opposite lung. The most common causes are penetrating chest trauma, blunt chest trauma with a parenchymal lung injury and air leak that did not spontaneously close, iatrogenic lung injury (e.g. due to central venepuncture) and mechanical positive-pressure ventilation.

The clinical presentation is dramatic. The patient is increasingly restless with tachypnoea, dyspnoea and distended neck veins (similar to pericardial tamponade). Clinical examination may reveal tracheal deviation; this is a late finding and is not necessary to clinically confirm diagnosis. There will also be hyper-resonance and decreased or absent breath sounds over the affected hemithorax.

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confirmation. Always treat it with a high index of suspicion of being present .

Treatment consists of immediate decompression. This was historically taught by rapid insertion of a large-bore cannula into the second intercostal space in the midclavicular line of the affected side, followed by insertion of a chest tube through the fifth intercostal space in the anterior axillary line. However, current teaching advocates undertaking decompression in the safe triangle- defined posteriorly by latissimus dorsi, anteriorly by the lateral border of pectoralis major and inferiorly by a line perpendicular to the nipple going to the back, just anterior to the mid-axillary line -or, in extremis, a finger thoracostomy at the same location.

question_text: A 25 year old male patient came to ER with history of trauma, his RR is 35/min and BP is 100/60 mmHg. on percussion hyper resonance is heard over entire right side of the chest. FAST was performed by the doctor which was normal. After looking at the chest X-ray what is the next step in management of this patient
option_a: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th ICS
option_b: Wide bore needle insertion followed by intercostals drain in the 5th ICS
explanation:
The above clinical scenario of history of trauma, unstable vitals, hyper resonance on percussion, points towards tension pneumothorax

  • A tension pneumothorax develops when a 'one-way valve' air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall.
  • Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any means of escape, completely collapsing and then compressing the afected lung.
  • The mediastinum is displaced to the opposite side, decreasing venous return and compressing the opposite lung.
  • Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confirmation. Always treat it with a high index of suspicion of being present

Management:

Immediate next step: needle decompression

  • In children: 2nd intercostal space mid clavicular line
  • In adults: 5th intercostal space mid axillary line

Definitive management: insertion of ICD drain in the triangle of safety

question_text: Central line was being put in the subclavian vein and the patient collapsed during insertion of the central line. On examination, breath sounds suddenly were found to be absent on the side of insertion of central line, on percussion hyper resonance sounds were heard on the same side of insertion of central line. Most likely cause in this patient?
explanation:
Tension p thorax is when (independent of aetiology) there is a build-up of positive pressure within the hemithorax, to the extent that the lung is completely collapsed, the diaphragm is fattened, the mediastinum is distorted and, eventually, the venous return to the heart is compromised.

  • Triad of tension pneumothorax:
  1. Raised JVP
  2. Hypotension
  3. Absent breath sounds

If diagnosed clinically, a tension pneumothorax need not be confrmed with a chest radiograph before needle thoracocentesis and placing a chest drain

Immediate management of tension pneumothorax: needle decompression in

  1. Adults: 5th intercostal space midaxillary line
  2. Children: 2nd intercostal space mid clavicular line

Definitive management: ICD tube insertion in 5th intercostal space midaxillary line in triangle of safety

question_text: An infant was brought to the hospital with abdominal distention. Image is given below. This disease is due to:
option_c: Failure of migration of neural crest cells
explanation:
Hirschsprung's disease

  • Genetic defects (e.g. RET, EDNRB, EDN3) can affect the migration of neural crest-derived intestinal neurons (neurocristopathy), leading to aganglionosis and thickened nerve trunks in the distal bowel.
  • There may be a family history. Aganglionic bowel fails to relax, causing a functional obstruction.
  • Aganglionosis extends from the anus to the sigmoid colon in 75%, the proximal colon in 15%, and the terminal ileum in 10% of cases.
  • A transition zone lies between dilated, proximal, normal bowel and narrow, distal aganglionic bowel. Neonatal Hirschsprung's disease presents with delayed passage of meconium, abdominal distension and bilious vomiting requiring resuscitation, gastric decompression, antibiotics and a bowel washout.
  • The diagnosis is made on a cot-side suction rectal biopsy. A contrast enema may show the narrow aganglionic segment, a cone and dilated proximal bowel.

Definitive surgery removes the aganglionic segment and brings ganglionic bowel to the anus; Swenson, Duhamel, Yancey-Soave and transanal 'pull-throughs' are options. Most children achieve reasonable bowel control, but some have residual constipation, incontinence or episodes of enterocolitis.

question_text: A 65-year-old male with a stab injury to the abdomen presents to the casualty. Examination reveals abdominal tenderness and guarding. Which of the following is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The next best step in the management of a stab injury leading to features of peritonitis is emergency laparotomy.

  • The evaluation of penetrating abdominal trauma requires a structured approach, beginning with airway and breathing assessment, followed by identification of injuries.
  • Positive FAST may indicate the need for exploration, but it cannot rule out major bleeding.
  • For stab wounds, unstable patients with peritonitis or evisceration need immediate laparotomy, while stable patients may undergo wound exploration, ultrasound, CT, or laparoscopy depending on the location. (Options A, C, and D ruled out)
  • Flank or back stab wounds often require contrasted CT, and left upper quadrant injuries may necessitate laparoscopy for diaphragmatic assessment.
  • Anterior stab wounds may be observed or discharged if no fascial penetration is present, but any suspected penetration warrants serial examinations or further imaging.
  • Diagnostic laparoscopy is accurate for detecting peritoneal violation but is user-dependent.
  • Development of peritonitis, hemodynamic instability, anaemia, or leukocytosis demands prompt laparotomy to systematically explore the abdomen and repair injuries.
  • The abdomen is opened widely for exposure, with division of the falciform ligament and use of retractors and sponges to aid hemostasis and visualisation.
  • The gastrointestinal tract, stomach, pancreas, and lesser sac are carefully inspected. Injuries are repaired, but physiologic deterioration may necessitate abbreviated damage control surgery with temporary abdominal closure.
  • When feasible, definitive closure is achieved, with subcutaneous wounds addressed based on intra-abdominal contamination.
  • The algorithm for the evaluation and management of abdominal stab wounds is illustrated below.

question_text: A car driver is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident, presenting with breathlessness. On examination, his vital signs are PR 112/min, BP 100/70 mmHg, SpO₂ 90%. There is extensive bruising over the chest. Chest X-ray is as shown. What is the appropriate management for this patient?
option_d: Internal operative fixation of the fracture's segments
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient's presentation, along with the X-ray showing multiple rib fractures, indicates a flail chest.
  • The most appropriate initial management for a patient of flail chest with respiratory failure is intermittent positive pressure ventilation (IPPV).

Flail chest

  • Occurs when three or more consecutive ribs are fractured in at least two places, creating a flail segment that moves independently.
  • Clinical features
    • Exhibits paradoxical chest movement: the fractured segment moves inwards on inspiration and outwards on expiration.
    • Hypoventilation: Reduced lung ventilation leads to low oxygen and high CO₂ levels.
    • Mediastinal Flutter: Abnormal mediastinal movement risks sudden cardiac arrest.
    • Pendular Air Movement: Inefficient air exchange between lungs.
  • Complications: Hemothorax and pneumothorax.
  • CT is the gold standard for diagnosis.

Management

Conservative measures

  • Treatment consists of oxygen administration, adequate analgesia and physiotherpay. (Option B ruled out)
  • Intercostal tube drainage if pneumothorax or hemothorax is present. (Option A ruled out)

Ventilation

  • Reserved for patients developing respiratory failure despite analgesia and oxygen.
  • Intermittent positive pressure ventilation is the preferred treatment of choice in such case.
  • Positive pressure ventilation stabilizes the flail segment, reduces paradoxical chest wall movement, and improves oxygenation.

Rib fracture stabilisation

  • Surgically stabilizes the chest wall by internally fixing rib fractures.
  • Useful in patients with isolated or severe chest injuries and associated pulmonary contusions to improve chest wall mechanics and respiratory function. (Option D ruled out)

question_text: A 40-year-old male presents with diffuse abdominal pain. On examination, there is rigidity and guarding. An abdominal X-ray shows free air under the diaphragm. The patient undergoes exploratory laparotomy, where an ileal perforation with gross enteric and purulent contamination is noted. What is the most appropriate management?
explanation:
Explanation:

In cases of ileal perforation with widespread contamination, the safest surgical strategy is faecal diversion (ileostomy). This prevents leakage from the repair site or anastomosis, reduces risk of intra-abdominal sepsis, and allows the peritoneum to heal.

  • The ileum is exteriorized as a loop ileostomy or end ileostomy depending on intraoperative findings.
  • Once the patient recovers, a second surgery may be performed later for stoma closure/re-anastomosis.

This approach prioritizes life-saving over bowel preservation, which is crucial in emergency settings with peritonitis.

Types of Stomas:


Explanation of Other Options:

Resection and anastomosis (Option A) is typically used in cases of multiple perforations, malignancy, suspected gangrene, or if there is significant tissue loss. It is not recommended in cases with severe peritoneal contamination, as the risk of infection, abscess formation, and anastomotic leak is high.

Primary repair (Option B) is typically reserved for small perforations with minimal contamination and no signs of peritonitis.

Omental patch closure (Option D): While duodenal perforations are often treated with an omentum patch without resection, ileal perforations with significant contamination generally require more aggressive management, such as an ileostomy, to prevent sepsis and further complications.

question_text: During an endoscopy, when a constriction is detected at the esophageal junction approximately 25 cm from the incisor, what is the likely cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

The esophageal constriction located approximately 25 cm from the incisors is primarily due to the aortic arch. At this point, the esophagus runs posterior to both the aorta and the left main bronchus, resulting in a physiological narrowing of the lumen.

Physiological Constrictions of the Oesophagus

The oesophagus demonstrates three natural points of narrowing, which can be measured endoscopically from the incisors:

  1. Cricopharyngeus Muscle (Upper Oesophageal Sphincter): Located proximally and acts as the first point of constriction.
  2. Crossing of the Left Main Bronchus and Aortic Arch: Around 25 cm from the incisors, where the oesophagus passes behind the arch of the aorta and left main bronchus, producing a physiological narrowing.
  3. Oesophagogastric Junction (Lower Oesophageal Sphincter): The distal sphincter located at the entry into the stomach, marking the final constriction site.

Explanation of Other Options:

The inferior vena cava (Option A) lies alongside the aorta within the abdomen and does not cross the thoracic esophagus, hence it is not responsible for the constriction near the esophageal junction.

The right bronchus (Option C) intersects the esophagus lower in the thorax, not at the 25 cm point from the incisors. At this level, the esophagus is more closely related to the left main bronchus and the arch of the aorta, which are the actual causes of narrowing.

The diaphragmatic opening (Option D) is situated at approximately 40 cm from the incisors, much lower than the 25 cm region, and therefore does not contribute to the constriction at that level.

question_text: A middle aged man complains of upper abdominal pain after a heavy meal. There is tenderness in the upper abdomen and on X-ray, widening of the mediastinum is seen with pneumo-mediastinum. What is the diagnosis?

question_text: A 40-year-old man presents with diffuse abdominal pain and a history of peptic ulcer disease. On examination, there is abdominal rigidity. What is the next best step in management for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The abdominal X-ray demonstrates air under the diaphragm, which is a classic sign of
  • Pneumoperitoneum is a sign of perforated viscus, most commonly due to a perforated peptic ulcer which is a surgical emergency.
  • Physical examination findings of rigidity and past history of peptic ulcer disease also support this diagnosis.
  • Hence, the most appropriate next step in management is urgent surgical exploration to repair the perforation and address any potential complications, such as peritonitis.

Upper GI endoscopy (Option B): Upper GI endoscopy is useful for identifying ulcers in the non-perforated stage.

CT abdomen (Option D): CT abdomen can provide valuable information in many cases of abdominal pain, including suspected perforation, but it is not the next best step when there are signs of peritonitis, such as rigidity during physical examination.

question_text: A female who was taking NSAID's for long period of time for her arthritis presented to the emergency with severe pain abdomen. Abdominal radiograph done is given below, likely diagnosis is?
explanation:
• The classical presentation of perforated duodenal ulcer is instantly recognisable . The patient, who may have a history of peptic ulceration, develops sudden-onset severe generalized abdominal pain due to the irritant effect of gastric acid on the peritoneum.
  • Although the contents of an acid-producing stomach are relatively low in bacterial load, bacterial peritonitis supervenes over a few hours, usually accompanied by a deterioration in the patient's condition. Initially, the patient may be shocked with tachycardia, but a pyrexia is not usually observed until some hours after the event.
  • The abdomen exhibits a board-like rigidity, and the patient is disinclined to move because of the pain. The abdomen does not move with respiration. Patients with this form of presentation need an operation, without which the patient will deteriorate with septic peritonitis.

An erect chest radiograph will reveal free gas under the diaphragm in more than 50% of cases with perforated peptic ulcer, but CT imaging is now most commonly used and is more accurate.

  • Rigler sign

question_text: What is the preferred method of intubation for a patient with severe maxillofacial trauma and extensive soft-tissue swelling?
explanation:
Explanation:

In patients presenting with severe maxillofacial trauma accompanied by significant soft-tissue swelling, the preferred airway management technique is tracheostomy.

Emergency Airway Management: Indications for Tracheostomy:

Purpose: Tracheostomy is performed urgently when there is acute airway obstruction and standard laryngeal intubation is not feasible.

Indications:

  • Acute upper airway obstruction
  • Inhaled foreign body
  • Large pharyngolaryngeal tumor
  • Severe pharyngolaryngeal infections in children
  • Anticipated airway compromise
  • Preoperative or postoperative airway protection for major surgeries involving the oral cavity, pharynx, larynx, or neck
  • Protection of the lower airway in patients at risk of aspiration
  • Management of head injuries
  • Severe maxillofacial trauma
  • Comatose state
  • Bulbar poliomyelitis
  • Tetanus
  • Requirement for prolonged mechanical ventilation (within the first 10 days)

Explanation of Other Options:

Laryngeal Mask Airway (LMA) (Option B):

  • Can maintain an airway in some cases.
  • Not recommended for patients with significant maxillofacial trauma or extensive soft-tissue swelling.
  • May fail to secure the airway if facial injuries or swelling interfere with placement.

Orotracheal Intubation (Option C):

  • Standard method for airway management in many trauma situations.
  • Challenging or sometimes impossible in patients with severe facial injuries due to obstruction from swelling or fractures.
  • Tracheostomy is generally a safer and more effective alternative in these cases.

Mask Ventilation (Option D):

  • Usually used for initial airway management or emergency resuscitation.
  • Not suitable for long-term airway maintenance in patients with severe facial trauma.
  • May not provide sufficient ventilation if the airway is compromised and is inadequate for prolonged airway protection.

question_text: Which of the following statement about breast tissue is false?

option_d: Myoepitheliocytes facilitates the passage of the milk along the ducts
explanation:

The fibrous stroma forms septa (suspensory ligaments of Cooper) which anchor the skin and gland to the pectoral fascia. It forms the major part of the gland but is absent beneath the areola and nipple.

question_text: In lymphatic drainage of the breast, the major portion (about 75%) enters eventually into which group of nodes?
explanation:
About 75% of the lymph draining the breast goes to the axillary lymph nodes, via the pectoral lymph nodes. All of this lymph from the pectoral lymph nodes must drain to the central lymph nodes as well. This is why it is so important to examine all these groups of axillary lymph nodes when performing a breast exam. Most of the rest of the lymph drainage from the breast goes to the parasternal nodes, although a small amount goes to the opposite breast and a small amount drains to the abdominal wall.

question_text: What is the probable diagnosis shown in the given picture?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The given image shows phyllodes tumor.
  • Phyllodes tumour, previously called cystosarcoma phyllodes, is a benign breast tumour usually seen in women over 30 years, though it can occur in younger women.
  • It often presents as a large, bosselated, mobile mass, sometimes causing ulceration of the overlying skin due to pressure necrosis.
  • Phyllodes tumours are true mixed neoplasms containing both epithelial and mesenchymal elements, resembling fibroadenomas.
  • Metastases from malignant phyllodes tumors occur via hematogenous spread.
  • Common sites of metastasis include lung, bone, abdominal viscera, and mediastinum.
  • Excisional biopsy followed by careful pathologic review is the best method of diagnosing phyllodes tumor.
  • Mastitis (option A): Usually presents with pain, redness, and systemic symptoms; often associated with lactation.
  • Fibroadenosis (option B): Represents benign fibrocystic changes; usually diffuse nodularity and cyclical breast pain.
  • Eczema of the breast (option D): Skin changes such as redness, scaling, or itching, often involving the nipple or areola.

Key Takeaways:

  • Phyllodes tumour should be suspected in any rapidly enlarging breast mass.
  • Histopathology is essential for diagnosis and grading.
  • Surgical excision with adequate margins reduces recurrence risk.

question_text: A lactating woman comes in the hospital 3 days history of painful, red, fluctuating, 2cm mass in the breast. USG shows fluid collection. What will you do in the management of this patient?

  • Breastfeeding from both the breasts should be encouraged 2-hourly, followed by emptying the breast. A breast support garment , cold compression on the breast and analgesia aid in symptomatic relief.

Contrary to the practice of incision and drainage, in a breast abscess ultrasound-guided drainage gives an excellent cosmetic result, does not hamper breastfeeding and can be done as a day-care procedure with a high rate of success.

question_text: Which group of lymph nodes of the breast are included in the external mammary group?
explanation:
Six axillary lymph node groups recognized by surgeons:

  • Axillary Vein Group (Lateral Group):
    • Location: Medial or posterior to the axillary vein.
    • Number: Four to six lymph nodes.
    • Function: Receives most lymph drainage from the upper extremity.
  • External Mammary Group (Anterior or Pectoral Group):
    • Location: Along the lower border of the pectoralis minor muscle, contiguous with lateral thoracic vessels.
    • Number: Five to six lymph nodes.
    • Function: Receives most lymph drainage from the lateral aspect of the breast.
  • Scapular Group (Posterior or Subscapular):
    • Location: Along the posterior wall of the axilla, at the lateral border of the scapula, contiguous with subscapular vessels.
    • Number: Five to seven lymph nodes.
    • Function: Receives lymph drainage primarily from the lower posterior neck, posterior trunk, and posterior shoulder.
  • Central Group:
    • Location: Embedded in the fat of the axilla, immediately posterior to the pectoralis minor muscle.
    • Number: Three or four sets of lymph nodes.
    • Function: Receives lymph drainage from the axillary vein, external mammary, and scapular groups of lymph nodes, and directly from the breast.
  • Subclavicular Group (Apical):
    • Location: Posterior and superior to the upper border of the pectoralis minor muscle.
    • Number: Six to twelve sets of lymph nodes.
    • Function: Receives lymph drainage from all other groups of axillary lymph nodes.
  • Interpectoral Group:
    • Description: Lymph nodes in this group pass directly into the central and subclavicular groups.

These axillary lymph node groups play a crucial role in draining lymphatic fluid from different regions of the breast and upper extremity, contributing to the overall lymphatic system's function in the chest and arm area.

Reference: Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 11th, Pg: 546

question_text: Which among the following doesn't have profound trophic effect in the normal development and function of the breast?
explanation:
Breast Development and Function

  • Breast development and function are initiated by a variety of hormonal stimuli, including estrogen, progesterone, prolactin, oxytocin, thyroid hormone, cortisol, and growth hormone.
  • Estrogen, progesterone, and prolactin especially have profound trophic effects that are essential to normal breast development and function.
  • Estrogen initiates ductal development, whereas progesterone is responsible for differentiation of epithelium and for lobular development.
  • Prolactin is the primary hormonal stimulus for lactogenesis in late pregnancy and the postpartum period.
  • It upregulates hormone receptors and stimulates epithelial development.
  • The gonadotropins luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) regulate the release of estrogen and progesterone from the ovaries.
  • In turn, the release of LH and FSH from the basophilic cells of the anterior pituitary is regulated by the secretion of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) from the hypothalamus.
  • Positive and negative feedback effects of circulating estrogen and progesterone regulate the secretion of LH, FSH, and GnRH.
  • These hormones are responsible for the development, function, and maintenance of breast tissues.
  • In the female neonate, circulating estrogen and progesterone levels decrease after birth and remain low throughout childhood because of the sensitivity of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to negative feedback from these hormones.
  • With the onset of puberty, there is a decrease in the sensitivity of the hypothalamic-pituitary axis to negative feedback and an increase in its sensitivity to positive feedback from estrogen.
  • These physiologic events initiate an increase in GnRH, FSH, and LH secretion and ultimately an increase in estrogen and progesterone secretion by the ovaries, leading to establishment of the menstrual cycle.
  • At the beginning of the menstrual cycle, there is an increase in the size and density of the breasts, which is followed by engorgement of the breast tissues and epithelial proliferation.
  • With the onset of menstruation, the breast engorgement subsides and epithelial proliferation decreases.

Reference: Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 11th, Pg: 547

question_text: Active substance used in PET scan
explanation:
Explanation:

  • PET (Positron Emission Tomography) uses positron-emitting radionuclides.
  • The most commonly used tracer is 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG).
  • FDG is a glucose analogue taken up by metabolically active cells, making PET ideal for cancer detection, cardiac imaging, and brain studies.
  • The fluorine-18 isotope emits positrons, which interact with electrons to produce gamma rays, detected by the PET scanner.

Explanation of Other Options:

I-131 (Option B): Used in thyroid imaging and therapy (radioiodine scan), not for PET.

Technetium-99m (Option C): Widely used in SPECT scans, not PET.

Deoxyglucose (non-radioactive) (Option D): The glucose analogue itself and PET requires the radioactive 18F label to be detected.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • PET requires positron-emitting radionuclides.
  • 18F-FDG is the most common tracer.
  • PET is functional imaging, showing metabolic activity, unlike CT or MRI which show anatomy.

References: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5124833/

  • Cytology is obtained using a 21G or 23G needle and 10-mL syringe with multiple passes through the lump with negative pressure in the syringe.
  • The aspirate is then smeared on to a slide, which is air dried or fixed.
  • Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) is the least invasive technique of obtaining a cellular diagnosis and is rapid and very accurate if both operator and cytologist are experienced.
  • However, false negatives do occur, mainly through sampling error, and invasive cancer cannot be distinguished from in situ disease.
  • A histological specimen taken by core biopsy allows a definitive preoperative diagnosis, differentiates between DCIS and invasive disease and also allows the tumour to be stained for receptor status.
  • This is important before commencing neoadjuvant therapy.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28th, Pg: 918

question_text: A 40 yr male a known case of varicose veins, on examination eczema and lipodermatosclerosis was found. It comes under ____ of CEAP classification system
explanation:
Classification system

The descriptive CEAP (Clinical-aEtiology-Anatomy-Pathophysiology) classification for chronic venous disorders is widely utilized.

For clinical classification:

  • C0: no signs of venous disease.
  • C1: telangiectasia or reticular veins.
  • C2: varicose veins.
  • C3: oedema.
  • C4a: pigmentation or eczema;
  • C4b: lipodermatosclerosis or atrophie blanche;
  • C4c: Corona phlebectatica
  • C5: healed venous ulcer;
  • C6: active venous ulcer.

Clinical class can be further characterized as symptomatic (s), asymptomatic (a) or recurrent following previous successful treatment or healing (r), e.g. C2a, C2s, C6r.

For aetiological classification:

  • Ec: congenital;
  • Ep: primary;
  • Es: secondary (post-thrombotic);
  • En: no venous cause identified.

For anatomical classification:

  • As: superficial veins;
  • Ap: perforator veins;
  • Ad: deep veins;
  • An: no venous location identified.

For pathophysiological classification:

  • Pr: reflux;
  • Po: obstruction;
  • Pr,o: reflux and obstruction;
  • Pn: no venous pathophysiology identifiable.

question_text: Which among the following arteries doesn't supply blood to the breast?
explanation:
Arterial Blood Supply:

  1. Internal Thoracic Artery: It's a branch of the subclavian artery, and it supplies the mammary gland through its perforating branches.
  2. Axillary Artery: Several branches of the axillary artery provide blood supply to the breast. These include the lateral thoracic artery, superior thoracic artery, and acromiothoracic (thoracoacromial) artery.
  3. Posterior Intercostal Arteries: Lateral branches of the posterior intercostal arteries also contribute to the blood supply of the mammary gland. These arteries distribute blood to the breast primarily from its anterior surface.

Venous Drainage:

  1. Superficial Veins: These veins gather and drain blood from the mammary gland toward the base of the nipple. They form an anastomotic venous circle at this point.
    • From there, the superficial veins connect to the internal thoracic vein.
    • They may also connect to the superficial veins in the lower part of the neck.
  2. Deep Veins: The deep veins of the breast drain into major venous pathways.
    • They typically drain into the axillary vein.
    • Some deep veins may connect to the posterior intercostal veins.

This vascular arrangement ensures the mammary gland receives an adequate blood supply, primarily from the front (anterior surface) of the breast. The posterior surface is relatively less vascular.

Reference: Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 11th, Pg: 545

question_text: Which among the following is not included in the pathological change in aberrations of normal development and involution of the breast?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Nipple eversion is part of normal breast development and is not a pathological change.
  • This can be considered in three phases: lobule development at 15-25 years, cyclical changes at 15-50 years and involution at 35-55 years of age. It is believed that lobular proliferation leads to the formation of fbroadenoma and involution leads to cyst formation. Aberration in the above phases may lead to a number of benign conditions.
  • Pathological changes in ANDI include:
    • Cyst formation (option A):Stroma involution can kink or narrow ductules, leading to secretory accumulation in lobules. Microcysts may coalesce into macro cysts
    • Fibrosis (option B): Fat and elastic tissues are replaced by dense fibrous trabeculae; chronic inflammatory cells may infiltrate interstitial tissue.
    • Hyperplasia: Defined as more than two layers of cells in ducts or acini; may occur with or without atypia. Atypical ductal hyperplasia (ADH) or atypical lobular hyperplasia may be precursors to malignancy. DCIS is diagnosed if ADH involves >2 ducts or lesions >2 mm.
    • Papillomatosis (option D): Extensive epithelial hyperplasia within ducts can result in papillomatous overgrowth

Key Takeaways:

  • Nipple eversion is normal and not considered a pathological finding.
  • ANDI includes cyst formation, fibrosis, hyperplasia, and papillomatosis.

question_text: Which among the following is used in premenopausal women for receptor positive breast tumour?
explanation:
Women with hormone receptor-positive (ER+ or PR+) breast tumours can be treated with-;

  • Tamoxifen in premenopausal women. It is a selective estrogen receptor modulator with antagonistic activity at breast and agonistic activity at the uterus and bone.
  • Aromatase inhibitors(AIs) like anastrozole, letrozole and exemestane in postmenopausal women. AIs inhibit aromatase enzyme which converts androstenedione into estrone.

question_text: Which among the following are the two views used in the mammography of the breast?
explanation:
• Breast imaging techniques are used to detect small, nonpalpable breast abnormalities, evaluate clinical findings, and guide diagnostic procedures.
  • The primary imaging modality for screening asymptomatic women is mammography.
  • During mammography, the breast is compressed between plates to reduce the thickness of the tissue through which the radiation must pass, separate adjacent structures, and improve resolution.
  • On screening mammography, two views of each breast are obtained, mediolateral oblique and craniocaudal and ready at a later time usually in batches.
  • For further evaluation of abnormalities identified on a screening mammogram or of clinical findings or symptoms, diagnostic mammography is indicated, which is read at the time of performance so additional views may be performed.
  • Magnification views are obtained to evaluate calcifications, and compression views are used to provide additional detail for mass lesions.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 35, Edition: 21st, Pg: 817

question_text: A 32-year female patient on tamoxifen after a breast cancer surgery. For around 5 years she was on tamoxifen. When will she stop tamoxifen if she wants to conceive?
explanation:
TAMOXIFEN is a SERM (selective Estrogen receptor modulator) given for women with ER+ breast cancer for minimum of 5 years, but latest atlas trial advise for 10 years use

During pregnancy, tamoxifen and its metabolites interact with rapidly growing and developing embryonic or fetal tissues.

The relatively high frequency of severe congenital abnormalities indicates that reliable birth control during tamoxifen treatment is mandatory.

After tamoxifen use, a washout period of 1-2 months is advisable based on the known half-life of tamoxifen.

In case of an inadvertent pregnancy, risks and options should be discussed.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC3233288

question_text: Which among the following structure doesn't relate to the posterior surface of the breast?
explanation:
Functional Anatomy

  • The breast is composed of 15 to 20 lobes, which are each composed of several lobules.
  • Fibrous bands of connective tissue travel through the breast (Cooper’s suspensory ligaments), insert perpendicularly into the dermis, and provide structural support.
  • The mature female breast extends from the level of the second or third rib to the inframammary fold at the sixth or seventh rib.
  • It extends transversely from the lateral border of the sternum to the anterior axillary line.
  • The deep or posterior surface of the breast rests on the fascia of the pectoralis major, serratus anterior, and external oblique abdominal muscles, and the upper extent of the rectus sheath.
  • The retromammary bursa may be identified on the posterior aspect of the breast between the investing fascia of the breast and the fascia of the pectoralis major muscles.
  • The axillary tail of Spence extends laterally across the anterior axillary fold. The upper outer quadrant of the breast contains a greater volume of tissue than do the other quadrants. The breast has a protuberant conical form.
  • The base of the cone is roughly circular, measuring 10 to 12 cm in diameter.
  • Considerable variations in the size, contour, and density of the breast are evident among individuals.
  • The nulliparous breast has a hemispheric configuration with distinct flattening above the nipple.
  • With the hormonal stimulation that accompanies pregnancy and lactation, the breast becomes larger and increases in volume and density, whereas with senescence, it assumes a flattened, flaccid, and more pendulous configuration with decreased volume.

Reference: Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 11th, Pg: 544

question_text:
Smoking increases the risk of which of the following diseases?
i. Duct ectasia
ii. Fibroadenoma
iii. Mondor disease
iv. Breast carcinoma
explanation:
Explanation :

  • Smoking is not directly associated with an increased risk of fibroadenomas, which are benign breast tumours often occurring in younger women.
  • Smoking increases the risk of duct ectasia, Mondor disease, and breast carcinoma, but not fibroadenoma.

Duct ectasia

  • Refers to the dilation or enlargement of the milk ducts in the breast, often leading to inflammation and possible discharge.
  • It is often seen in older women, particularly during menopause.
  • Smoking is considered a risk factor for this condition as it contributes to vascular changes and may affect the ducts.

Mondor's disease

  • A rare condition that involves thrombophlebitis (inflammation of veins caused by blood clots) of the superficial veins in the breast or chest area.
  • Smoking has been linked to vascular changes, which may increase the likelihood of developing Mondor's disease.

Breast cancer

  • Smoking is a well-established risk factor for breast cancer, especially in postmenopausal women.

question_text: Which among the following findings is seen in duct ectasia of breast?
explanation:
Duct ectasia/periductal mastitis-

  • This is a dilatation of the breast ducts, which is often associated with periductal inflammation.
  • The disease is more common in smokers.
  • Nipple discharge (of any colour), a subareolar mass, abscess, mammary duct fistula and/or nipple retraction are the most common symptoms.

Pathogenesis -

  • Initially, there is a dilatation in one or more of the larger lactiferous ducts, which fill with a stagnant black or green secretion. This may discharge.
  • These fluids then set up an irritant reaction in surrounding tissue, leading to periductal mastitis or even abscess and fistula formation.
  • In some cases, a chronic indurated mass forms beneath the areola, which mimics a carcinoma.
  • Fibrosis eventually develops, which may cause slit-like nipple retraction.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28th, Pg: 929

question_text: A female patient presented to the outpatient department with a breast mass, as shown, with HER2 positivity and liver metastasis. What is the appropriate management?
explanation:
Explanation:

HER2-positive metastatic breast cancer is best managed with targeted therapy (Trastuzumab), systemic chemotherapy, and palliative surgery for symptom relief.

  • This patient has Stage IV HER2-positive breast cancer with distant metastasis (liver).
  • The standard of care involves systemic therapy with Trastuzumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting HER2 receptors, combined with chemotherapy agents such as taxanes or capecitabine.
  • In selected cases where the primary tumor is symptomatic (e.g., ulceration, bleeding), palliative mastectomy is done to improve quality of life.
  • HER2-positive tumors respond well to targeted biologic therapy, which forms the cornerstone of management in metastatic settings.
  • Surgery is not curative but may be considered to control local disease.

Stage Grouping

Stage 0: Tis N0 M0

Stage IA: T1/T1mi N0 M0

Stage IB: T0 N1mi M0; T1/T1mi N1mi M0

Stage IIA: T0 N1 M0; T1 N1 M0; T2 N0 M0

Stage IIB: T2 N1 M0; T3 N0 M0

Stage IIIA: T0 N2 M0; T1 N2 M0; T2 N2 M0; T3 N1 M0

Stage IIIB: T3 N2 M0

Stage IIIC: T4 N0 M0; T4 N1 M0; T4 N2 M0; Any T N3 M0

Stage IV: Any T Any N M1

Explanation of other options:

Tamoxifen + Radiation Therapy + Bone-targeted therapy (Option B): Tamoxifen is indicated in hormone receptor-positive cancers, not HER2-positive tumors. Radiation helps local control but not systemic metastasis.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by surgery (Option C): This is used in locally advanced breast cancer (Stage III), not in Stage IV disease with distant metastasis.

Surgical Resection of Metastases + Radiotherapy (Option D): This is not standard for widespread metastasis. Surgery for metastasis is rarely curative and usually not performed unless solitary and resectable

question_text:
Which of the following is correct about Peutz-Jeghers syndrome?
1. Congenital hypertrophy of retinal pigment epithelium is most common extra-intestinal manifestation
2. Arborizing pattern
3. STK11 mutation
4. Autosomal recessive
5. Multiple GI polyps seen
explanation:
• This is an autosomal dominant condition characterised by melanosis of the mouth and lips, with multiple hamartomatous (benign tumour-like malformations resulting from faulty development in an organ) polyps in the small bowel and colon.
  • Mutation of the STK11 gene on chromosome 19 has been found in a proportion of patients.
  • Despite the increased risk of malignancy in general, malignant change in the polyps themselves is uncommon. Resection may be indicated, however, for heavy and persistent or recurrent bleeding or intussusception.
  • Polyps may be removed by enterotomy or, at laparotomy, snared via a colonoscope introduced via an enterotomy.
  • The histological hall mark is the presence of smooth muscle fibres in an arborizing pattern.

question_text: A patient with a history of left upper quadrant breast cancer underwent Cobalt-60 radiotherapy. She is now presenting with respiratory distress / difficulty, and chest x-ray shows haziness in the left lung. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: Recurrence of Breast Cancer

  • Pulmonary metastasis from breast cancer typically presents as multiple nodular opacities, pleural effusion, or lymphangitic spread, not isolated hazy opacities.
  • It also wouldn't acutely cause respiratory distress unless very advanced.

Choice C: Pulmonary Embolism

  • PE presents with sudden-onset dyspnea, chest pain, and possible hemoptysis.
  • Chest X-ray may be normal or show wedge-shaped infarct (Hampton's hump), oligemia (Westermark sign), but not usually haziness confined to a radiation field.

Choice D: Infective Pneumonia

  • Would present with fever, productive cough, localized crepitations, and chest x-ray findings consistent with lobar or bronchopneumonia, often not restricted to the radiation portal.
  • Radiation pneumonitis often lacks signs of systemic infection (like high-grade fever or leukocytosis).

Key Takeaway

  • Radiation pneumonitis is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with left-sided breast cancer, treated with Cobalt-60 radiotherapy, who now presents with respiratory symptoms and unilateral lung haziness in the irradiated area.

question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding the anatomy of the breast?
option_a: The superior medial quadrant has more tissue
option_c: The axillary tail of Spence crosses the anterior axillary fold
option_d: The nipple is located at the level of the fourth intercostal space in most women
explanation:
Explanation:

The axillary tail of Spence is an extension of breast tissue that projects from the upper outer quadrant of the breast into the axilla, passing over the anterior axillary fold. This tail contains a significant portion of glandular tissue and is clinically important during breast examinations.


Breast and Mammary Glands:

Breast: The breast contains mammary glands located within the superficial fascia. It extends vertically from the 2nd to the 6th rib along the midclavicular line and horizontally from the lateral border of the sternum to the midaxillary line at the level of the 4th rib.

Suspensory Ligaments of Cooper: These ligaments anchor the breast tissue (parenchyma) to the overlying skin and the underlying pectoral fascia. In cases of malignancy, tumor invasion along these ligaments can cause skin dimpling.

Nipple: The nipple's position varies among adult women, influenced by breast size and shape. In nulliparous women, it is typically located at the level of the 4th intercostal space (Option D ruled out). The nipple is pierced by 15-20 lactiferous ducts through which milk is secreted.

Areola: This is the pigmented ring of skin surrounding the nipple.

Mammary Gland: The mammary gland is a modified sweat gland. The axillary tail of Spence is a tail-like extension of breast tissue that projects from the upper outer quadrant into the axilla.

Retromammary Space: This space contains loose connective tissue situated between the base of the breast gland and the deep fascia covering the mammary bed.

The breast is composed of 15-20 lobes of glandular tissue, separated by fibrous septa radiating outward from the nipple (Option B ruled out). Each lobe drains through a lactiferous duct, which widens to form a lactiferous sinus near the nipple.

Explanation of other options:

The superior medial quadrant has more tissue (Option A): The superior lateral quadrant of the breast contains more glandular tissue than the superior medial quadrant. This increased tissue volume is due to the axillary tail of Spence, which carries a substantial portion of the glandular elements into the axilla.

Reference:

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519575/

question_text: A 28-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast. Which of the following is the most likely cause of acute mastitis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Acute mastitis most commonly arises due to a fissure or crack in the nipple, which provides a portal of entry for infection into the breast tissue.

Mastitis:

Explanation of Other Options:

Breast engorgement (Option A):

  • Leads to fullness and discomfort in the breasts but does not progress to mastitis unless associated with blocked ducts or nipple injury.
  • Unlike mastitis, it does not present with fever, warmth, or redness.

Hormonal influence (Option B):

  • Hormonal changes during pregnancy or menstruation can cause breast tenderness and swelling.
  • These changes do not directly result in mastitis.
  • They may contribute to engorgement but are not a cause of infection or inflammatory response.

Absence of lactation (Option C):

  • May cause breast discomfort or engorgement, but not typically mastitis.
  • Mastitis most often arises in breastfeeding women due to milk stasis, duct blockage, or nipple trauma that allows bacterial invasion.
  • In non-lactating women, mastitis is uncommon and usually related to other underlying infections.

question_text: Which of these is not a contraindication to breast-conserving therapy (BCT)?
explanation:
Explanation:

Breast-conserving therapy (lumpectomy + whole-breast radiation) is appropriate when the tumour can be completely excised with acceptable cosmesis. It is aimed at removing the tumour along with a 1-cm margin of normal breast tissue.

Classic contraindications include:

  • Prior chest/breast irradiation (would preclude re-irradiation).
  • Diffuse/multicentric tumours not amenable to single excision.
  • Persistently positive margins that cannot be re-excised.
  • Severe connective tissue diseases (e.g., scleroderma) - because radiotherapy causes exaggerated soft-tissue injury.

Conversely, a tumour limited to one quadrant is an indication for BCT (not a contraindication). The tumour being confined to one quadrant generally allows adequate resection with good cosmesis.

Explanation of other options:

Prior chest radiation (Option A): contraindication (cannot safely give required adjuvant breast irradiation).

Positive margins after resection (Option B): if margins cannot be cleared with re-excision, BCT is contraindicated.

Scleroderma (Option C): relative/absolute contraindication due to radiosensitivity and risk of severe radiation-induced injury.

Key takeaways:

BCT = lumpectomy + radiotherapy; suitability depends on tumour location/size, prior radiation status, connective tissue disease, and ability to achieve clear margins.

question_text: All of the following statements are correct for lymphatics of the breast except:
option_a: A plexus of lymph vessels deep to the areola is called subareolar plexus of Sappey.
option_b: The lymph from the lateral quadrant of the breast drains into the anterior axillary lymph nodes.
option_c: About 25 percent of the lymph from the breast is drained into axillary lymph nodes.
option_d: Superficial lymphatics drain the skin of the breast except the nipple and areola.
explanation:
Explanation:

Approximately 75 percent of lymph from the breast drains into the axillary lymph nodes, not 25 percent.

The majority of breast lymphatics drain toward the axilla, which is clinically important due to the lymphatic spread of breast carcinoma.

Lymph nodes involved in drainage:

  • Axillary nodes (anterior/pectoral, posterior, central, lateral, apical)
  • Internal mammary (parasternal) nodes
  • Supraclavicular nodes
  • Posterior intercostal nodes
  • Cephalic (deltopectoral) nodes

Lymphatic pathways:

  • Superficial lymphatics: Drain the skin of the breast, except the nipple and areola (Option D)
  • Deep lymphatics: Drain the breast parenchyma, and the nipple and areola
  • Subareolar plexus of Sappey: Network deep to the areola that collects lymph from the nipple-areola complex (Option A)

Lymph distribution:

  • 75 percent → Axillary nodes
  • 20 percent → Internal mammary nodes
  • 5 percent → Posterior intercostal nodes

Quadrant-wise drainage:

  • Lateral quadrants → Anterior (pectoral) axillary nodes (Option B)
  • Medial quadrants → Internal mammary nodes
  • Lower lateral quadrants → Posterior intercostal nodes

question_text: Which among the following carcinoma is caused by ionising radiation?
explanation:
Ionising radiation is known to cause -

  • Leukemia
  • Breast cancer
  • Lymphoma
  • Thyroid cancer

The mechanism of action of radiotherapy is that ionising radiation causes single- and double-stranded DNA breaks. Cells most sensitive to radiotherapy are in mitosis or late G2 in the cell cycle. Damage may be caused by the direct effect of the ionising radiation on the DNA. However, the predominant therapeutic effect is indirect, and is achieved by ionising radiation causing the creation of oxygen free radicals, which then damage the DNA. The fact that the indirect damage is predominant explains why hypoxic cells are relatively resistant to radiotherapy.

Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 12, pg: 201

question_text: A 46-year-old woman presents with a noticeable change in the size and appearance of her left nipple. On examination, the doctor finds a painless, hard lump in the breast that is fixed to the underlying tissues and immobile. Additional findings include nipple retraction, peau d'orange appearance of the skin, and enlarged axillary lymph nodes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of a painless hard mass, fixation to deeper structures, nipple retraction, skin dimpling (peau d'orange), and axillary lymphadenopathy is characteristic of breast carcinoma.

These features indicate infiltration of surrounding ligaments, ducts, and lymphatic channels.

Carcinoma of breast:

  • Most common malignancy in females.
  • Typically arises from the epithelial lining of the lactiferous ducts (invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common type).

Common clinical features:

  • Painless hard lump: due to malignant proliferation.
  • Fixation of the breast mass: caused by tumor infiltration into suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments, making the breast immobile.
  • Skin retraction: infiltration and tethering of Cooper's ligaments.
  • Nipple retraction: fibrosis and shortening of lactiferous ducts.
  • Peau d'orange appearance: obstruction of superficial lymphatics, causing edema while hair follicles remain anchored, giving an orange-skin appearance.
  • Enlarged axillary lymph nodes: common pathway of lymphatic spread.

Fibroadenoma (Option A): Benign mobile breast lump; smooth, non-fixed, and typically painless. Does not cause nipple retraction or peau d'orange.

Breast abscess (Option B): Painful, warm, red swelling often with fever; usually associated with lactation.

Galactocoele (Option C): Milk-filled cyst seen during or after lactation; soft, cystic, and non-adherent.

question_text: Which among the following images in the given options shows microcalcification of the breast?
explanation:
FIG. 35.7 Mammography, ultrasound, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) findings in breast disease.

  1. Stellate mass in the breast. The combination of density with spiculated borders and distortion of surrounding breast architecture suggests a malignancy.
  2. Clustered microcalcifications. Fine, pleomorphic, and linear calcifications that cluster together suggest the diagnosis of ductal carcinoma in situ.
  3. Ultrasound image of breast cancer. The mass is solid, contains internal echoes, and displays an irregular border. Most malignant lesions are taller than they are wide.
  4. Ultrasound image of a simple cyst. On ultrasound, the cyst is round with smooth borders, there is a paucity of internal sound echoes, and there is increased through-transmission of sound with enhanced posterior echoes.
  5. Breast MRI showing gadolinium enhancement of a breast cancer. Rapid and intense gadolinium enhancement reflects increased tumor vascularity. Lesion contour and size may also be assessed by MRI.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 35, Edition: 21st, Pg: 820

question_text: On post-operative day 2 of mastectomy for left breast cancer, routine X-ray of the patient was performed. The patient is not complaining of any respiratory distress and is comfortable in hospital bed. On auscultation, bilateral equal air entry is heard. What is the next step in the management?
option_a: Wait and watch, give supplemental oxygen if required
option_c: Do a thoracostomy with wide bore tube and under water seal
option_d: Perform elective intubation and positive pressure ventilation
explanation:
Explanation:

The chest X-ray demonstrates a pneumothorax, but since the patient is asymptomatic, no immediate intervention is required.

Pneumothorax management

Conservative Management

  • Indications: Small, asymptomatic pneumothorax, including post-needle biopsy pneumothorax.
  • Approach
    • Observation and monitoring with serial chest X-rays.
    • Oxygen therapy may be given if needed to hasten resorption.
    • No immediate intervention (e.g., chest tube) is required unless the patient becomes symptomatic or the pneumothorax enlarges.

Chest tube insertion

  • Indications: Symptomatic or large spontaneous pneumothorax.
  • Placement of a small-bore catheter or chest tube allows drainage of air, leading to resolution of the pneumothorax and cessation of the air leak. (Option C ruled out)
  • Chest drain insertion site: Triangle of safety
    • Anterior to the mid-axillary line
    • Above the nipple level
    • Below and lateral to the pectoralis major muscle
  • This typically corresponds to the 5th intercostal space, providing safe access for pneumothorax drainage while minimizing risk to underlying structures.

Surgical management

Indications

  • Second ipsilateral pneumothorax - recurrence on the same side.
  • First contralateral pneumothorax - first occurrence on the opposite side.
  • Bilateral spontaneous pneumothorax - both lungs affected simultaneously.
  • Persistent pneumothorax - fails to resolve despite adequate chest drainage.
  • Spontaneous haemothorax - particularly in high-risk professions (e.g., pilots, divers).
  • Pregnancy - due to increased risk to mother and fetus.

Procedure

  • Thoracoscopy (VATS) to identify and resect apical blebs with endoscopic staplers.
  • Mechanical abrasion of the parietal pleura.
  • Chemical pleurodesis (e.g., talc) may be used in malignant cases or older patients.

Explanation of other options:

Perform needle thoracotomy urgently (Option B): Needle thoracostomy is an emergency procedure for tension pneumothorax. It is indicated only when there is severe respiratory distress, hypotension, tracheal deviation, or absent breath sounds.

Perform elective intubation and positive pressure ventilation (Option D): Intubation and mechanical ventilation are indicated only in severe respiratory compromise or respiratory failure. Moreover, positive pressure ventilation can worsen a pneumothorax, so it’s contraindicated here.

question_text: A 30-year-old female presents with a painless, rapidly growing lump in her left breast that she noticed over the past few months. On examination, the lump is well-defined, mobile, and firm in consistency. A breast ultrasound reveals a solid mass, and a core needle biopsy is performed. Histopathological examination shows a leaf-like pattern with an overgrowth of the stromal component and ductal structures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Mammographic evidence of calcifications and morphologic evidence of necrosis do not distinguish between benign, borderline, and malignant phyllodes tumors. Consequently, it is difficult to differentiate benign phyllodes tumors from the malignant variant and from fibroadenomas. Phyllodes tumors are usually sharply demarcated from the surrounding breast tissue, which is compressed and distorted. Connective tissue composes the bulk of these tumors, which have mixed gelatinous, solid, and cystic areas. Cystic areas represent sites of infarction and necrosis. These gross alterations give the gross cut tumor surface its classical leaf-like (phyllodes) appearance. The stroma of a phyllodes tumor generally has greater cellular activity than that of a fibroadenoma. After microdissection to harvest clusters of stromal cells from fibroadenomas and from phyllodes tumors.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: Galactocele

  • A galactocele is a cystic lesion filled with milk and typically occurs in women who are lactating or have recently stopped breastfeeding. It is not a solid mass with a leaf-like pattern. Galactoceles are usually painless but do not present with the same histopathological findings seen in phyllodes tumors.

Choice C: Fibroadenoma

  • Fibroadenomas are the most common benign breast tumors and generally have a well-defined, firm However, they do not exhibit the leaf-like pattern or significant stromal overgrowth seen in phyllodes tumors. Fibroadenomas usually have a simpler structure with less stromal cellular activity compared to phyllodes tumors.

Choice D: Paget's disease

  • Paget's disease typically presents as eczema-like changes of the nipple and is associated with underlying breast carcinoma, particularly invasive ductal carcinoma. It does not present as a rapidly growing, painless lump with a leaf-like pattern on histology.

Key Takeaway

  • The leaf-like pattern with stromal overgrowth and ductal structures on histopathology is highly suggestive of a phyllodes tumor, which is the most likely diagnosis in this case.

question_text: 30 years old lady presenting with mobile breast lump like a moving mouse feel. Diagnosis?
explanation:
Fibroadenoma

  • A fibroadenoma is the most common cause of a breast lump in women aged 15-25 years.
  • It arises from hyperplasia of a lobule and usually grows to 2-3 cm in size.
  • It is surrounded by a well-defined capsule. A clinically typical fibroadenoma, confirmed on ultrasonography, may be observed without a biopsy.
  • A biopsy should be obtained if the patient is over 25 or if there are atypical features on ultrasonography. Regression with anti estrogen drugs has been observed with tamoxifen and ormeloxifene.
  • Giant fibroadenomas occasionally occur during puberty. They are over 5 cm in diameter, often rapidly growing and can be enucleated through a submammary incision.
  • Indications for surgical excision are: age over 30 years; suspicious features on imaging, such as microlobulation; atypia on histology; size >5 cm; family history of breast cancer; and the patient's preference.
  • Excision of fibroadenoma in the elderly should include a rim of normal tissue as it may contain malignancy or a phyllodes tumor.

question_text: A 30-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast and a fever. On examination, the left breast appears as shown in the image below. There is mild axillary lymphadenopathy on the affected side and the contralateral breast is normal. Repeated aspirations under antibiotic cover were unsuccessful. A USG done showed fluid collection. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient has a breast abscess complicating lactational mastitis. Key indicators are:

  • Lactating female (common risk group)
  • Pain, fever, erythema, tenderness, lymphadenopathy
  • Ultrasound-confirmed fluid collection
    The failure of repeated needle aspirations and antibiotics indicates that the abscess is loculated or has thick pus that requires formal surgical drainage. Incision and drainage (I&D) is the definitive next step to evacuate the pus, break up loculations, and allow healing.

Breast abscess Types:

  • Lactational abscess - occurs in breastfeeding women (3-20% incidence).
  • Non-lactational abscess - occurs outside lactation, often with periductal mastitis, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, or TB.

Causes & Risk Factors:

  • Lactational: Entry via cracked/retracted nipple or blocked ducts; most common pathogen Staphylococcus aureus(including MRSA in hospital settings).
  • Non-lactational: Associated with smoking, diabetes, or chronic mastitis.

Clinical Features:

  • Fever, leukocytosis, erythema, painful tender breast swelling, malaise, difficulty feeding, enlarged/tender axillary nodes.

Diagnosis:

  • Ultrasonography → differentiates cellulitis vs abscess, detects liquefaction, loculation, and guides drainage.

Treatment:

  • Lactational abscess:
    • Antibiotics: anti-staphylococcal (cloxacillin, flucloxacillin, erythromycin).
    • Continue breastfeeding/pumping.
    • Supportive: cold compresses, breast support, analgesia.
    • Drainage: US-guided aspiration preferred over incision.
    • Culture-guided therapy + follow-up with US.
  • Non-lactational abscess:
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics.
    • Needle aspiration for drainage.
    • Major duct excision if recurrent or complicated (e.g., fistula, sepsis).

Explanation of other options:

Broad spectrum antibiotics only (Option B): Antibiotics are adjunctive therapy but are insufficient once a well-formed abscess has developed, as they cannot penetrate the pus-filled cavity effectively.

Breast conservation surgery (Option C): This term refers to lumpectomy for breast cancer treatment. It is not a procedure for managing an infectious abscess.

Punch biopsy (Option D): A biopsy is a diagnostic tool for tissue sampling to rule out malignancy. It is not a treatment for a known infective abscess and could potentially spread the infection.

Key Takeaways:

  • Needle aspiration is first-line for breast abscesses.
  • Incision and drainage is indicated for failed aspiration, large abscesses (>5cm), or recurrent cases.

question_text: Which among the following is not the clinical finding of the fibrocystic disease of the breast?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Nipple discharge is not a typical clinical finding of fibrocystic disease.
  • Fibrocystic changes represent a spectrum of benign breast alterations seen most commonly in women in their 4th-5th decades, usually resolving after menopause. They result from an exaggerated hormonal response of breast epithelium and stroma to circulating and local growth factors.
  • Clinically, patients present with premenstrual cyclic mastalgia characterized by breast pain, tenderness, and nodularity, although breast pain alone is rarely associated with breast cancer.
  • These cysts are fluid-filled cavities that may be single, multiple, or recurrent and are readily detected on ultrasonography. Most simple cysts require no intervention unless symptomatic; aspiration relieves discomfort and, if the cyst collapses completely and the aspirate is not bloody, further cytologic evaluation is unnecessary.
  • Recurrent cysts or those with solid components require core-needle biopsy, and vacuum-assisted excision may be indicated for persistent, symptomatic cysts. Surgical excision is rarely needed and is reserved for cases with atypia, incomplete removal, or recurrent large cysts.
  • Histologically, fibrocystic changes may include microcysts, macrocysts, adenosis, stromal fibrosis, apocrine metaplasia, epithelial hyperplasia, and sclerosis.
  • Treatment of significant mastalgia may involve hormonal agents such as danazol, tamoxifen, or GnRH analogs, although these drugs carry notable side effects, while milder symptoms can be managed conservatively with NSAIDs, supportive bras, and reassurance.

Key Takeaways:

  • Fibrocystic disease presents with pain, tenderness, nodularity.
  • Nipple discharge is not a consistent feature.
  • Hormonal influences drive symptoms, which usually resolve after menopause.

question_text: A 30-year-old lactating woman presents with fever, breast pain, erythema, tenderness, fluctuation, and axillary lymphadenopathy. Repeated aspirations under antibiotics failed, and USG shows fluid collection. What is the next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

Established lactational breast abscess requires incision and drainage after failure of aspiration. Antibiotics (anti-staphylococcal) are given concurrently. USG helps locate the collection.

Breast Abscess

Definition:

A breast abscess is a localized pus-filled cavity within the breast tissue, resulting from infection and inflammation.

Types:

  • Lactational abscess: Occurs during breastfeeding, typically due to infection through cracked or retracted nipples or blocked ducts.
  • Non-lactational abscess: Occurs in non-lactating women, often associated with periductal mastitis, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, or tuberculosis.

Causes and Risk Factors:

  • Lactational abscess: Seen in 3-20% of lactating mothers, commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus, including methicillin-resistant strains in hospital settings.
  • Non-lactational abscess: Seen in nulliparous or post-lactational women. Risk factors include smoking and diabetes.

Clinical Features:

  • Local signs: Pain, tenderness, erythema, swelling, warmth, fluctuation.
  • Systemic signs: Fever, malaise, leukocytosis.
  • May present with difficulty feeding and tender axillary lymphadenopathy.

Diagnosis:

  • Ultrasonography (USG): Confirms abscess by detecting cellulitis, liquefaction necrosis, size, and loculation.

Treatment:

  • Lactational abscess:
    • Antibiotics: Anti-staphylococcal agents (cloxacillin, flucloxacillin, erythromycin).
    • Continue breastfeeding or milk expression to empty the breast.
    • Supportive care: Breast support garment, cold compresses, analgesics.
    • Drainage: Ultrasound-guided aspiration is preferred over surgical incision.
    • Follow-up with clinical and ultrasound monitoring, modify antibiotics as per culture.
  • Non-lactational abscess:
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics for subareolar infections.
    • Needle aspiration for drainage.
    • Surgical excision of major ducts in recurrent or complicated cases (e.g., sepsis or fistula formation).

Explanation of other options:

Broad-spectrum antibiotics only (Option B): Not sufficient once abscess is formed.

Breast conservation surgery (Option C): For malignancy, not needed in infection.

Punch biopsy (Option D): Reserved for suspected malignancy, not in lactational abscess.

question_text: Which of the following benign breast conditions has the LEAST associated risk of developing invasive ductal carcinoma?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on consensus pathological classification (e.g., from the American College of Pathologists), benign breast conditions carry varying risks for subsequent breast cancer:

  • No Increased Risk: Conditions like squamous metaplasia, adenosis, cysts, and fibroadenoma.
  • Slightly Increased Risk (1.5-2x): Florid epithelial hyperplasia and papilloma with a fibrovascular core. (Option A and B ruled out)
  • Moderately Increased Risk (~5x): Atypical hyperplasia (a high-risk lesion). (Option C ruled out)
    Therefore, squamous metaplasia is a benign change with no documented increased risk of breast cancer development.

Key Takeaways:

  • Not all benign breast disease carries the same cancer risk.
  • Atypical hyperplasia confers the highest risk among the options given.
