question_text: A 40-year-old female diagnosed with breast cancer was advised for an estrogen receptor (ER) screening test. To which class does the ER marker belong?
explanation:
Explanation:

The estrogen receptor (ER) is classified as a prognostic marker in breast cancer because it provides information about the likely clinical outcome and the biological behaviour of the tumour - independent of the specific therapy used.

  • Prognostic markers reflect the natural course and aggressiveness of a tumour, helping to estimate recurrence risk and survival.
  • ER-positive tumours are generally low-grade, grow slowly, and have a better prognosis than ER-negative tumours.
  • They are more likely to respond to hormone therapy (e.g., tamoxifen, aromatase inhibitors).

Prognostic markers help estimate the overall prognosis and risk of recurrence, whereas predictive markers indicate how cancer will respond to specific treatments and guide the selection of appropriate systemic therapy for individual patients. (Option D ruled out)


Explanation of Other Options:

Diagnostic marker (Option A):

  • ER is not used to diagnose breast cancer.
  • Diagnosis is established by biopsy and histopathological examination.
  • ER testing is done after diagnosis to determine tumour biology and prognosis.

Surrogate molecular marker (Option C):

  • Surrogate molecular markers are IHC-based markers used to approximate gene-expression subtypes (e.g., Luminal A/B, HER2-enriched, triple negative).
  • ER, PR, HER2, and Ki-67 together form a surrogate molecular profile - but ER alone functions primarily as a prognostic

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: Which of the following is not used for diagnosis of breast carcinoma?
explanation:
TRIPLE ASSSESSMENT OF BREAST

The positive predictive value and diagnostic accuracy of this combination approach 100%.

The clinical assessment should involve a thorough history and clinical breast examination that includes inspection and palpation.

Moreover Positron emission tomography (PET) scans are used as a staging investigation in patients with T3, T4, N2, N3 breast cancer and in patients with T1, T2, N0, N1 and not in diagnosis of breast cancer.

question_text: Which of these is not included in stage T4b breast cancer?
explanation:
Explanation:

TNM definitions: T4b = tumour of any size with ulceration and/or ipsilateral macroscopic satellite nodules and/or edema (including peau d'orange) of the skin that does not meet criteria for inflammatory carcinoma.

T4d = inflammatory carcinoma - defined clinically as diffuse erythema and edema involving ≥1/3 of the breast (rapid onset, pathologic confirmation required).

Therefore a skin erythema/excoriation occupying >1/3rd suggests inflammatory carcinoma (T4d), not routine T4b. Ulceration, satellite nodules and peau d'orange are T4b features. (Options A, B, D are ruled out)

Key takeaways:

T4b = skin involvement (ulceration, nodules, localized peau d'orange).

T4d = inflammatory carcinoma (diffuse erythema/edema ≥1/3 breast).

References: AJCC/NCI staging summaries

question_text: A woman after 2 weeks of delivery comes in with fever and complains of difficulty in breastfeeding. On examination, diffuse lump under areola is felt, the mass is associated with redness, tenderness and mild warmth. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The incidence of acute mastitis in lactating mothers varies from 3% to 20%. Most cases are caused by S. aureus and, if hospital acquired, may be due to methicillin-resistant S. aureus. Mastitis may be bacterial or non-bacterial. Bacteria may enter the nipple through a cracked or retracted nipple. In many cases the lactiferous ducts get blocked by epithelial debris, leading to stasis, which is followed by infection. Once within the ampulla of the duct, staphylococci causes clotting of the milk and then multiplies within the clot. Abscess formation is most commonly seen at two stages during lactation: in the first month after the first childbirth owing to inexperience or inappropriate and inadequate breastfeeding; and at weaning owing to engorgement and trauma to the nipple by the baby's teeth. Initially there is generalised cellulitis, which if left untreated progresses to suppuration and abscess formation. An abscess presents as a fluctuant lump (in a deep-seated abscess fluctuation may be absent) with pain, signs of inflammation, fever, malaise and difficulty in feeding. It may also be associated with enlarged tender axillary nodes. Ultrasonography reveals cellulitis (seen as an area of increased echogenicity) and liquefaction necrosis (pus is seen as a hypoechoic collection with floating debris that changes with posture). During the cellulitic stage, the patient should be treated with anti-staphylococcal antibiotics such as cloxacillin, flucloxacillin or erythromycin. Breastfeeding from both the breasts should be encouraged 2-hourly, followed by emptying the breast. A breast support garment, cold compression on the breast and analgesia aid in symptomatic relief. Any pus seen on ultrasonography should be aspirated and sent for culture and sensitivity. In a breast abscess ultrasound-guided drainage gives an excellent cosmetic result, does not hamper breastfeeding and can be done as a day-care procedure. In abscesses >3 cm in diameter or those containing more than 30 mL of pus (assessed on ultrasonography), a vacuum suction catheter is inserted under ultrasound guidance to drain the pus. The patient should be reviewed on alternate days by clinical examination and ultrasonography. Any residual collection should be aspirated. The antibiotics are modified according to the microbiological culture report. In patients with a suction drain, the catheter is irrigated with cold normal saline (cold to reduce pain) on each visit until complete resolution. Antibiotics should be continued for 14 days.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Galactocele

  • A galactocele is a milk-filled cyst that may cause a painless lump in the breast. It does not typically present with redness, tenderness, or fever. The presentation described here is more consistent with mastitis, which involves infection and inflammation.

Choice C: Mondor disease

  • Mondor disease is a rare condition involving thrombophlebitis of the superficial veins of the breast, which presents with a cord-like mass rather than a diffuse lump. It does not cause significant tenderness, fever, or difficulty breastfeeding, and it is less likely to cause the acute inflammatory changes seen in this case.

Choice D: Fibrocystic disease

  • Fibrocystic disease refers to benign changes in the breast, characterized by lumps, tenderness, and pain, but it is usually non-inflammatory. It does not present with fever, redness, or warmth, and is not associated with difficulty breastfeeding in the acute setting described.

Key Takeaway

  • The patient's symptoms of fever, redness, tenderness, and difficulty breastfeeding are most consistent with lactational mastitis, which requires antibiotic treatment and possibly drainage if an abscess develops.

question_text: A female patient presents to the outpatient department 10 days postpartum with complaints of a fluctuant breast mass with tenderness, high-grade fever, and cracked nipples. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A breast abscess is a localized pus-filled cavity within the breast tissue, commonly occurring in lactating women.

  • Pathogenesis: Most cases are secondary to acute mastitis progressing to abscess formation, with entry via cracked nipples.
  • Causative organism: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA in hospital settings).
  • Clinical features: Fluctuant tender mass, high fever, localized erythema, systemic toxicity, and difficulty breastfeeding.
  • Diagnosis: Confirmed by ultrasound, which detects liquefaction necrosis and guides drainage.
  • Treatment:
    • Antibiotics (anti-staphylococcal agents such as cloxacillin, flucloxacillin, or erythromycin).
    • Continued milk evacuation (breastfeeding/pumping).
    • Drainage - ultrasound-guided aspiration preferred; incision and drainage reserved for recurrent/large abscesses.

Explanation of Other Options:

Breast engorgement (Option A): Presents with bilateral breast fullness, pain, and engorgement in the early postpartum period but lacks a fluctuant mass or systemic toxicity.

Acute mastitis (Option C): Causes localized breast pain, erythema, and fever, but typically presents beforeabscess formation and without a fluctuant swelling.

Fibroadenoma (Option D): A benign mobile breast lump, usually painless, not associated with fever, fluctuation, or postpartum status.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Breast abscess = fluctuant, tender, febrile mass in lactating women → requires drainage + antibiotics.
  • Acute mastitis = precursor stage without fluctuation.
  • Engorgement = diffuse, bilateral, no fever.
  • Fibroadenoma = firm, mobile, painless, no systemic features.

question_text: Postpartum lactating female presents with redness and swelling in the breast. Identify the pathology in the given image:
explanation:
• Lactational infections are thought to arise from entry of bacteria through the nipple into the duct system and are characterized by fever, leukocytosis, erythema, and tenderness.
  • Infections of the breast are most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus and may manifest as cellulitis with breast parenchymal inflammation and swelling, termed mastitis, or as abscesses.
  • Treatment requires antibiotics and frequent emptying of the breast. True abscesses require drainage. Initial attempts at drainage should include needle aspiration;
  • surgical incision and drainage should be reserved for abscesses that do not resolve after aspiration and treatment with antibiotics.
  • In such cases, abscesses are generally multiloculated. Ultrasound evaluation can assist in characterizing a breast abscess and help to guide needle aspiration.

question_text: Which among the following is not the clinical finding of the staphylococcal breast abscess?
explanation:
Staphylococcal abscess -

  • Present with point tenderness, erythema, and hyperthermia.

Treatment -

Initial approach is with analgesics, antibiotics and repeated aspiration of the abscess.

Incision and drainage is done if

  • Abscess is not resolving with repeated aspiration and antibiotic therapy
  • Thinning or necrosis of the overlying skin

Staphylococcus aureus (localised, involves deeper breast tissue) and Streptococcus species (diffuse superficial involvement) are the organisms most frequently recovered from nipple discharge from an infected breast.

Reference: Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 11th, Pg: 550

question_text: A patient is diagnosed with an 8 cm chylolymphatic cyst. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
option_b: Resection of cyst and adjacent bowel
explanation:
Explanation:

The treatment of choice for a chylolymphatic cyst is enucleation because the cyst has no shared wall or vascular supply with the adjacent bowel.

  • This allows the cyst to be safely removed without resecting the intestine.
  • Chylolymphatic cysts are the most common mesenteric cysts, usually arising in the ileal mesentery from congenitally misplaced lymphatic tissue with no efferent lymphatic communication.
  • They are typically unilocular, thin-walled, and filled with lymph or chyle.

Explanation of Other Options:

Resection of cyst and adjacent bowel (Option B): Required for enterogenous cysts, which share a common wall or blood supply with bowel, not for chylolymphatic cysts.

Observation with serial imaging (Option C): Not appropriate as these cysts can enlarge, cause symptoms, or lead to complications (torsion, infection, rupture).

Percutaneous aspiration (Option D): Ineffective due to recurrence and risk of infection; not a definitive treatment.

question_text: Patient presents with a soft non tender fluctuant swelling on the upper back. The lesion has a black punctum on top of it, and the patient reports foul smelling discharge with cheesy material draining from the lesion. What is the most appropriate management for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

These cysts are lined with true stratified squamous epithelium, derived from hair follicle infundibulum or traumatic inclusion. Commonly known as sebaceous cysts, they can occur anywhere. They are fixed to the skin and usually have a central punctum. Treatment depends on the clinical state of the cyst. When inflamed or infected, they should be incised and drained initially; they should be removed later once the inflammation and induration has subsided. It is important to excise the cyst in its entirety as failure to do so usually results in recurrence

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Wide local excision

  • Wide excision is not required as this is a benign lesion. It would cause unnecessary tissue loss and scarring.

Choice B: Incision and drainage only

  • I&D is appropriate only if the cyst is acutely inflamed or infected. In this case, the cyst is not inflamed (non-tender), so I&D alone is insufficient and inappropriate.

Choice C: Antibiotic therapy

  • Antibiotics are not indicated unless there is significant infection or cellulitis. In the absence of active infection, they provide no benefit.

Key Takeaway

  • Definitive treatment of a sebaceous cyst is complete surgical excision, especially when the lesion is not inflamed.

question_text: which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for the given condition?
explanation:
• Dermoid cysts are benign congenital choristomas of the orbit that originate from fetal bone suture lines during development, most commonly the frontozygomatic suture, although they may also occur more medially.
  • Dermoid cysts account for about half of childhood orbital neoplasms and consist of keratinised epithelium and adnexal structures such as sweat glands and hair follicles.
  • They often cause a bony depression and they may have a dumbbell extension into the orbit, which is of particular importance should they need to be excised. Dermoid cysts can also erode the orbital plate of the frontal bone to become attached to dura; for this reason it is important to image the area by computed tomography (CT) before excision.
  • Treatment of choice is surgical excision

question_text: Which among the following anti-TNF therapy agent is used in pregnant women for the treatment of Crohn's disease?
explanation:
Anti-TNF therapy.

  • The introduction of anti-TNF therapy for Crohn disease was considered a breakthrough in medical management.
  • The first anti-TNF agent introduced was infliximab, a chimeric monoclonal antibody to TNF-α.
  • Infliximab is efficacious and safe as a monotherapy in the treatment of moderate to severe Crohn disease and effective both an induction and maintenance agent.
  • Multiple studies demonstrated that treatment with infliximab results in perineal fistula closure in approximately two thirds of patients.
  • Other FDA-approved TNF antagonists include adalimumab (humanized IgG1 monoclonal antibody), which is an effective maintenance agent that can be self- administered, and certolizumab (humanized antibody fragment), which is ideal in pregnant and nursing women as it is linked to a polyethylene glycol moiety and does not cross the placenta and is not excreted in breast milk.
  • Safety profiles for these three anti-TNF medications are There is an increased risk for tuberculosis reactivation, invasive fungal and other opportunistic infections, demyelinating central nervous system lesions, activation of latent multiple sclerosis, exacerbation of congestive heart failure, and concerns for increased risk of melanoma.
  • Patients who develop a flare while on anti-TNF agents require measurement of serum drug concentrations and antidrug antibodies (antibodies binding to competitive and non-competitive sites to inhibit drug function).
  • Measured levels would indicate the need to increase dosage (if low drug concentration and low antibodies), switch to another anti-TNF agent (high antidrug antibodies), or switch to another drug class (normal drug concentration).
  • Due to the potential for immunogenicity of monoclonal antibodies, the combination of an anti-TNF agent and an immunosuppressive provides optimal drug levels and low antidrug antibodies

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1266

question_text: Which is ideal procedure for oesophageal varices in patients who fail to respond to endoscopic therapy?
explanation:
Explanation:

TIPS (Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic stent) is now the treatment of choice in variceal haemorrhage that has not responded to drug treatment and endoscopic therapy.

The major advantage of TIPS is that it is a nonoperative approach. Thus, it is ideal when only short-term portal decompression is required. TIPS is also effective for the treatment of medically intractable ascites.

Complications:

  • Post shunt encephalopathy
  • Perforation of liver capsule - main early complication of TIPS which can cause fatal intraperitoneal haemorrhage
  • Shunt stenosis secondary to neointimal hyperplasia.
  • Shunt thrombosis

Explanation for the other options:

  • Variceal banding is an endoscopic therapy, which the patient has already failed.
  • Sclerotherapy is an endoscopic therapy, which the patient has already failed.
  • Balloon tamponade is only a temporary, bridge therapy.

Key Takeaways:

Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPS) is the primary non-surgical procedure used for refractory variceal bleeding (failure of combined medical and endoscopic therapy) as it effectively decompresses the portal system.

Level:

Must know

question_text: An elderly chronic smoker male is diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the lower lip with no lymph node involvement. What is the treatment of choice?
option_c: Wide local excision with negative borders
option_d: Wide local excision with frozen section
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Wide local excision with histologically negative margins is the standard treatment for localized, node-negative squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the lip.
  • Surgical excision allows definitive histopathological assessment (tumor depth, differentiation, perineural/vascular invasion) and removal of the lesion with an oncologic margin to minimize recurrence.
  • Margin guidance commonly used in practice (as per the source provided): small lesions (<2 cm) aim for ~4 mm margins; larger lesions (>2 cm) require wider margins (approximately 1 cm) to achieve clearance.
  • Functional and cosmetic reconstruction considerations follow excision; surgery offers the best long-term local control when resection with negative margins is achievable.

Explanation of Other Options:

Radiotherapy (Option A): Used as an alternative in patients unfit for surgery or when surgical excision would result in severe cosmetic/functional compromise. However, surgery remains superior in localized, node-negative SCC of the lip.

Combined chemoradiotherapy (Option B): Indicated in advanced, unresectable, or metastatic SCC cases; not appropriate for small, operable lesions without nodal disease.

Wide local excision with frozen section (Option D): Frozen section margin analysis is an intraoperative adjunct in difficult or recurrent cases, but routine use is not mandatory for early, well-circumscribed SCC. Standard wide excision with permanent histology is usually sufficient.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Treatment of choice for localized, node-negative lower-lip SCC = wide local excision with negative margins.
  • Radiotherapy/chemoradiotherapy are alternatives for inoperable cases or advanced disease.
  • Frozen section margin assessment is an adjunct for selected cases (recurrent, ill-defined, cosmetically critical sites), not mandatory for every early, well-circumscribed lesion.
  • Ensure reconstruction planning to optimize function and cosmesis after excision.

question_text: Which of the following is the next step in the management of an elderly patient who has undergone complete excision of glioblastoma?
explanation:
Explanation:

The standard of care for glioblastoma (GBM) after maximal safe surgical resection is adjuvant radiotherapy (Option B ruled out). Even with a radiologically "complete" excision, microscopic disease invariably remains due to the infiltrative nature of GBM. Radiotherapy is crucial to target these residual cells and delay recurrence.

The Stupp protocol (concurrent temozolomide chemotherapy with radiotherapy) is the benchmark, but for elderly patients or those with poor performance status, radiotherapy alone is often the chosen adjuvant treatment to balance efficacy with tolerability and reduced toxicity.

Explanation of other options:

Chemotherapy with Bevacizumab (Option A): Chemotherapy is an essential component of the treatment for glioblastoma, particularly in conjunction with radiotherapy, but Bevacizumab is an anti-angiogenic agent used for recurrent or progressive GBM, not as first-line adjuvant therapy after initial resection.

Chemoradiation (Option C): While chemoradiation (e.g., the Stupp protocol) is standard for younger, fit patients, radiotherapy alone is a common and evidence-based choice for elderly patients to minimize additive toxicity.

Key Takeaways:

  • Adjuvant radiotherapy is mandatory after resection of glioblastoma.
  • For elderly patients, radiotherapy alone is a common and appropriate treatment strategy.

question_text: How is empyema thoracis treated?
explanation:
Explanation:

The standard treatment for empyema thoracis is intercostal chest drainage (ICD) along with intravenous antibiotics. Drainage removes pus mechanically, while antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole, or piperacillin-tazobactam) control the infection. In resistant or loculated collections, intrapleural fibrinolytics (streptokinase/urokinase) may be required.

Explanation of other options:

Antibiotics alone (Option A): Inadequate, because pus within the pleural cavity cannot be cleared effectively without drainage. Antibiotics cannot penetrate the thick, fibrinous collections.

Intercostal drainage (Option C): Drainage without concurrent antibiotics fails to control the underlying infection and may lead to recurrence or sepsis.

Wait and watch (Option D): Empyema requires urgent intervention. Delayed treatment may lead to fibrothorax, lung entrapment, or systemic sepsis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Empyema = ICD + IV antibiotics (mainstay of management).
  • If loculated → fibrinolytics may be added.
  • Delay in treatment can cause fibrothorax and chronic lung impairment.

References: Thoracis empyema.

question_text: A patient was in admitted for pelvic fracture under treatment. He suddenly developed breathlessness and died on 3rd POD. What's the reason probably?
explanation:
Patient operated for pelvic fractures are immobilised for long period of time, which causes venous stasis leading to deep vein thrombosis

  • Leg pain occurs in about 50% of patients with DVT but is non-specific.Homans' sign - resistance ( not pain) of the calf muscles to forcible dorsiflexion - is not specific and should not be elicited.Tenderness occurs in 75% of patients but is also found in 50% of patients without objectively confirmed DVT.
  • The pain and tenderness associated with DVT does not usually correlate with the size, location or extent of the thrombus. Clinical signs and symptoms of pulmonary embolism occur in about 10% of patients with confirmed DVT.

question_text: Identify the procedure in the given diagram for a patient with variceal bleeding?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (Banding), where an oesophageal varix is suctioned into a cap and a rubber band is deployed at its base to stop blood flow.

Endoscopic therapy for variceal haemorrhage includes endoscopic ligation and endoscopic sclerotherapy.

The advantages of endoscopic ligation over sclerotherapy include:

  • Lesser rebleeding and mortality rates
  • Fewer sessions needed to complete treatment

The combination of variceal ligation and pharmacotherapy with nonselective beta blockade is more effective than variceal ligation alone.

Explanation for the other options:

  • Sclerotherapy involves injection, not banding.
  • Balloon tamponade uses an external tube (Sengstaken-Blakemore).
  • Intralesional glue therapy is typically used for gastric varices.

Endoscopic Variceal Ligation (EVL/Banding) is generally the preferred endoscopic treatment for oesophageal varices, using elastic bands to strangulate the varix.

question_text: Which among the following is the most common parotid gland tumour?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign tumour of the parotid gland, comprising about 60–70% of all parotid tumours.
  • Typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, well-defined, mobile mass.
  • Most commonly arises in the parotid gland (>80%), but can also occur in the submandibular gland and hard palate.
  • Risk of malignant transformation exists (carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma), especially if long-standing or with sudden onset of facial nerve palsy.
  • Histology: Mixture of epithelial, myoepithelial, and stromal elements.
  • Treatment: Surgical excision with a cuff of normal tissue; enucleation is avoided due to high recurrence risk from capsular breach.

Pleomorphic Adenoma:

  • Clinical Presentation:
    • Painless, well-defined, solitary, mobile masses.
    • Commonly located in the parotid glands (>80% of cases).
    • It can also occur in the submandibular gland and hard palate.
    • Sudden growth of facial nerve palsy may suggest malignant transformation (rare).
  • Imaging:
    • USG: Well-lobulated, hypoechoic lesions with possible calcifications.
    • CT: Provides detailed anatomical imaging along with the extent of the tumour.
    • MRI: Helps differentiate between benign and malignant tumours
  • Fine-Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC):
    • Differentiates between inflammatory conditions and tumour- high sensitivity and specificity
  • Histopathology:
    • Gross Examination:
      • Tumours are well-circumscribed, nodular, and firm, with a white to tan cut surface.
      • May show cartilaginous areas; large tumours may exhibit degeneration or cystic changes.
    • Microscopy:
      • A mixture of epithelial, myoepithelial, and stromal components.
      • Possible malignant changes: Ductal atypia, diffuse fibrosis, or necrosis

Treatment:

  • Surgical Excision of the tumour along with a cuff of normal tissue.
  • Enucleation is not recommended due to the risk of capsular breach, tumour spillage, and recurrence.

Explanation of Other Options:

Warthin's Tumor (Option B):

  • Second most common benign parotid tumour.
  • Typically occurs in older males and has strong association with smoking.
  • Usually bilateral or multifocal.
  • Also known as adenolymphoma.

Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma (Option C):

  • A malignant salivary gland tumour, most common in minor salivary glands (e.g., palate).
  • Notorious for perineural invasion, leading to pain and nerve deficits.
  • Tends to have late recurrences and distant metastases.

Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma (Option D):

  • The most common malignant salivary gland tumour overall.
  • Also the most common malignant tumour in children and young adults.
  • Variable behaviour depending on histologic grade (low-grade behaves indolently, high-grade is aggressive).

Key Takeaway Points:

• Lactational infections are thought to arise from entry of bacteria through the nipple into the duct system and are characterized by fever, leukocytosis, erythema, and tenderness.
  • Infections of the breast are most often caused by Staphylococcus aureus and may manifest as cellulitis with breast parenchymal inflammation and swelling, termed mastitis, or as abscesses.
  • Treatment requires antibiotics and frequent emptying of the breast. True abscesses require drainage.
  • Initial attempts at drainage should include needle aspiration; surgical incision and drainage should be reserved for abscesses that do not resolve after aspiration and treatment with antibiotics.
  • In such cases, abscesses are generally multiloculated. Ultrasound evaluation can assist in characterizing a breast abscess and help to guide needle aspiration.

question_text: A male patient complains of loss of appetite and dysphagia, with a weight loss of approximately 6 kg over the last three months. He had a previous diagnosis of esophageal cancer and underwent treatment. What might be the cause of his current symptoms?
explanation:
Explanation:

Given the patient's prior history of treated esophageal cancer, the combination of loss of appetite, difficulty swallowing, and notable weight loss raises a strong suspicion for recurrence of esophageal cancer.

Esophageal Cancer:

Fibrosis (Option B): Post-treatment esophageal fibrosis may cause swallowing difficulties; however, it rarely accounts for the combination of recurrent dysphagia and marked weight loss, making cancer recurrence a more likely explanation.

Achalasia Cardia (Option C): This motility disorder leads to progressive dysphagia, but its onset is gradual. Given the patient's history of esophageal cancer and rapid weight loss, achalasia is less probable.

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) (Option D): GERD can induce dysphagia and discomfort, but it is unlikely to cause significant weight loss or mimic the clinical presentation of recurrent cancer, making recurrence the more probable cause.

question_text: A 42-year-old woman presents with fever, vomiting, and right hypochondriac pain radiating to the neck. She has had similar episodes before. On examination, Murphy's sign is positive. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Murphy's sign: On deep inspiration, placing fingers over the gallbladder region causes sudden inspiratory arrest due to pain. This is highly suggestive of acute cholecystitis caused by gallstones leading to gallbladder inflammation.

  • Tokyo guidelines 2018 for diagnosis:
    • Local signs: Murphy's sign, RUQ tenderness/mass.
    • Systemic signs: Fever, ↑CRP, ↑WBC.
    • Imaging: Gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, USG Murphy's sign.
  • Investigations: USG (initial), HIDA scan (gold standard if doubt).

Explanation of Other Options:

Carcinoma gallbladder (Option B): Chronic painless lump, not Murphy's positive.

Peptic ulcer (Option C): Epigastric pain, no Murphy's sign.

Appendicitis (Option D): RLQ tenderness, not RUQ pain.

Key Takeaways:

  • Positive Murphy's = acute cholecystitis hallmark.
  • USG = first-line investigation.
  • Early laparoscopic cholecystectomy is the treatment.

question_text: 65 years old male presented with a mass in the left lumbar region which was ballotable. He was having abdominal discomfort and on investigations he was found to have a 7*5*3 cm which was confined within the kidney and diagnosed as Renal cell carcinoma. What would be the treatment in this patient?
explanation:
• Nephron-sparing surgery
    • with the recent increase in incidental detection of small renal masses (tumours <4cm), more nephron-sparing surgery is being performed.
    • Partial nephrectomy should be the treatment of choice in tumours less than 4cm, in well-selected tumours between 4 and 7cm, in bilateral tumours, in tumours in solitary kidneys and in patients with pre-existing renal dysfunction.
    • Radical nephrectomy is limited to tumors >7cm
    • Minimally invasive techniques by laparoscopy or robots have reduced postoperative morbidity.
    • Because of the limitation of ischaemia time, minimally invasive techniques should be reserved for tumours with non-complex anatomy, as predicted by nephrometry scores.
    • Alternative techniques such as surveillance, cryoablation or radiofrequency ablation of small renal tumours may be offered in patients with high surgical risk (e.g. elderly patients, patients with multiple comorbidities).

question_text: A 42-year-old woman presents with progressive, non-pitting swelling of her right upper limb, 12 years after undergoing a modified radical mastectomy with axillary clearance and radiotherapy. She now notes violaceous nodules over the edematous skin which have gradually increased in number. There is no associated pain, fever, or recent breast lump. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lymphangiosarcoma, also known as Stewart-Treves syndrome, is a rare but aggressive malignancy of lymphatic endothelial origin. It is strongly associated with chronic lymphedema following mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection and radiotherapy.

  • Onset:Typically develops after an average of 10 years post-mastectomy (range 5-15 years).
  • Clinical features:Presents with violaceous or bluish cutaneous nodules and plaques in the lymphedematous arm. The lesions progressively enlarge, may ulcerate, and can metastasize early.
  • Pathogenesis:Chronic lymph stasis results in tissue hypoxia, impaired immune clearance, and persistent endothelial proliferation, which eventually undergo malignant transformation.
  • Prognosis:Poor; survival averages 2-3 years despite radical surgical management.

Explanation of Other Options:

Post-radiation sarcoma (Option A): Usually arises in irradiated chest wall or ribs; presents as a firm mass rather than bluish nodules on a lymphedematous limb.

Chronic Venous Insufficiency (Option C): Manifests with varicosities, pigmentation, lipodermatosclerosis, and venous ulcers, typically in the lower limb. Not associated with post-mastectomy lymphedema.

Recurrent Breast Cancer (Option D): Presents with chest wall lump, nodules along scar, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Diffuse bluish nodules on an edematous arm are not typical

question_text: A 32-year-old patient presents with a midline cervical swelling situated in the thyroid region. The swelling is noted to move on swallowing and on protrusion of the tongue. Recently, the lesion ruptured spontaneously and began discharging pus. What is the most appropriate definitive treatment modality?
explanation:
Explanation:

The described features are pathognomonic for a Thyroglossal Duct Cyst, a congenital anomaly that arises from persistence of the embryological thyroglossal duct.

  • The key diagnostic clue is that the swelling moves with deglutition (swallowing) and tongue protrusion due to its attachment to the hyoid bone and tongue base.
  • Spontaneous rupture or prior incision and drainage leads to a thyroglossal fistula, which is always an acquired complication.
  • The Sistrunk procedure is the gold standard.
    • This involves complete excision of the cyst, the entire tract, and the central portion of the hyoid bone up to the base of the tongue.
    • This prevents recurrence and complications.
  • Long-standing thyroglossal cysts carry a small risk of malignant transformation, most commonly to papillary thyroid carcinoma.
  • Simple incision and drainage (Option B ruled out) or antibiotics (Option C ruled out) alone do not provide cure and predispose to recurrence.

question_text: A 30-year-old female who is receiving cyclosporine A following renal transplantation develops multiple and bilateral breast lumps that regress after cessation of the treatment. Biopsy image is given below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given biopsy slide demonstrates ductal proliferation in both intracanalicular and pericanalicular patterns, embedded within a fibromyxoid stroma, which is diagnostic of Fibroadenoma. This lesion is strongly influenced by hormonal activity, explaining its association with Cyclosporine A therapy, which exerts estrogen-like effects.

Fibroadenoma:

  • Epidemiology: Most common benign breast tumor in women aged 15-35 years.
  • Clinical characteristics:
    • Firm, well-circumscribed, non-tender, spherical mass (1-10 cm).
    • Highly mobile and slippery → classically termed "breast mouse."
    • Usually solitary, but multiple lesions can occur.
  • Hormonal influence:
    • Sensitive to estrogen.
    • Increases in size during pregnancy, lactation, or estrogen therapy.
    • Typically regresses after menopause.

Histopathology (HPE):

  • Encapsulated lesion with proliferating fibrous stroma, which may compress and distort ducts.
  • Intracanalicular pattern: ducts compressed and elongated by stroma.
  • Pericanalicular pattern: ducts remain round, surrounded by proliferating stroma.
  • Characteristic features:
    • Staghorn clusters → ductal cells arranged in horn-like patterns.
    • Bare nuclei → nuclei visible without cytoplasm on cytology smears.

Radiology:

  • Mammogram: may show "popcorn calcification" in older fibroadenomas.
  • Ageing effect: Epithelium atrophies with age, and the stroma becomes more hyalinised.
  • Molecular alteration: Alterations in MED12 gene
  • Drug associated with bilateral fibroadenomas: Cyclosporine

Explanation of Other Options:

Fat necrosis (Option A) typically presents with firm, tender breast lumps following trauma or surgery and shows fatty tissue changes on biopsy, not ductal proliferation.

Phyllodes tumour (Option B) can have similar histological features with ductal proliferation but is typically more cellular and can have a leaf-like architecture. It also tends to grow rapidly and is more common in older women.

Carcinoma breast (Option D) would be expected to present with more aggressive histological features, such as invasion of surrounding tissue and atypical cells, rather than benign ductal proliferation.

Debridement

Taken from the French, meaning to 'unleash or cut open', debridement plays a crucial part in the management of trauma. Wounds sustained in disasters are often heavily contaminated, containing foreign bodies and non-viable tissues. Debridement reduces the chances of anaerobic and necrotising infections and can prevent systemic sepsis. The following principles of debridement apply to all contaminated wounds.

Assessing the viability of degloved tissue can be difcult and may therefore require more than one surgical exploration and debridement before defnitive reconstruction. The definitive treatment is debridement and rotational advancement flap

Non-viable skin may show fixed staining and thrombosis of subcutaneous veins. Most surgeons serially excise the degloved skin until punctate dermal bleeding is seen from viable tissue. Intravenous fluorescein may also help delineate non-viable tissue, but it requires specialist equipment and there is a small risk of anaphylaxis. More recently, the use of indocyanine green fluorescence has been reported

question_text: According to triage, which of the following categories of patients comes under green?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In a mass-casualty triage system, patients are divided into categories by urgency of care.
  • The green category includes ambulatory patients-those who can walk, have non-life-threatening injuries, and can tolerate a delay in treatment without significant risk of deterioration.
  • They are often called "walking wounded."

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Moderate priority (Option B): Refers to the yellow category, where patients are injured but stable enough to wait for a few hours before intervention.

High priority (Option C): Refers to the red category, which requires immediate life-saving intervention.

Dead patients (Option D): Classified as black, representing expectant/unsalvageable cases. They are not treated in triage systems where resources are limited.

Key Takeaway:

In triage, ambulatory and stable patients fall under the green category, as they can tolerate treatment delays while resources are directed toward red and yellow categories.

question_text: What is the preferred management of the condition in the image below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image is indicative of an angular dermoid cyst. The treatment of choice is surgical excision, which ensures complete removal of the cyst and prevents recurrence.

Dermoid cyst

  • Dermoid cysts are benign congenital choristomas of the orbit.
  • They arise from fetal bone suture lines, most commonly at the frontozygomatic suture, though they can also occur more medially.
  • Account for approximately half of all childhood orbital tumors.
  • These cysts are composed of keratinized epithelium along with adnexal structures such as hair follicles and sweat glands.

Clinical features

  • Often asymptomatic
  • May cause bony depressions and can extend into the orbit in a dumbbell shape, which is important to recognize prior to surgical excision.
  • Dermoid cysts can erode the orbital plate of the frontal bone and attach to the dura, making preoperative imaging with computed tomography (CT) essential.

Management

  • Surgical Excision: Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice, especially if the cyst is causing cosmetic concerns or other symptoms.
  • Careful dissection is required to ensure the cyst is fully removed and avoid recurrence.
  • If left untreated, angular dermoids sometimes undergo resorption or indentation of the underlying base.

Explanation of other options:

Radiotherapy (Option B): Radiotherapy is typically used for malignant tumours or conditions such as cancer and is not indicated for benign lesions like dermoid cysts.

Antibiotics (Option C): Antibiotics are used for managing bacterial infections; only needed if the cyst becomes infected.

Intralesional steroids (Option D): Intralesional steroids are used for conditions like keloids or hypertrophic scars and are not effective in treating dermoid cysts.

question_text: A patient with renal cell carcinoma has a 10 cm tumour in the lower pole of the kidney, with no lymph node involvement. What is the best treatment?
explanation:
Explanation:

For large tumours (>7 cm, T2 stage) without nodal or distant spread, radical nephrectomy (removal of kidney with Gerota's fascia and ureter up to the pelvic brim) is the treatment of choice. Partial nephrectomy is only for <7 cm tumours. RCC is resistant to radiotherapy and chemotherapy.

Explanation of other options:

Partial nephrectomy (Option B): Reserved for T1 tumours <7 cm, solitary kidney, or bilateral disease.

Radiotherapy (Option C): RCC is radioresistant; used only for palliation in metastasis.

Chemotherapy (Option D): RCC is chemo-resistant; systemic therapy uses targeted and immunotherapy for advanced disease.

In the context of Breast Conservation Surgery (BCS), radiotherapy (RT) is not optional but a necessary component of treatment.

question_text: A patient arrives at the emergency department after a car accident. They are experiencing difficulty breathing and have dilated neck veins. A chest x-ray reveals a significant amount of air on the left side. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
option_a: Wide bore needle insertion in the 5th intercostal space
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation acute respiratory distress, dilated neck veins, and unilateral air on x-ray after a trauma (road traffic accident) is classic for a tension pneumothorax. This is a life-threatening condition where air trapped in the pleural space increases pressure, collapsing the lung and impairing cardiac venous return. The immediate life-saving treatment is needle decompression to release the trapped air. The standard site for this procedure is the 2nd intercostal space in the midclavicular line.

However, the 5th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line (the site for subsequent chest tube insertion-Definitive treatment) is also a recognized and acceptable alternative site for needle decompression, especially in the field or specific protocols.

Explanation of other options:

Endotracheal intubation (Option B): While the patient may need respiratory support, intubation does not address the root cause of the problem, which is the pressurized air in the pleural space. Positive pressure ventilation could even worsen the condition.

Tracheostomy (Option C): This is a surgical airway procedure for upper airway obstruction, which is not present here.

Pericardiocentesis (Option D): This procedure removes fluid from the pericardial sac to treat cardiac tamponade. While tamponade can also cause dilated neck veins and shock (Beck's triad), the x-ray finding of air confirms a pulmonary issue, not a cardiac one.

Key Takeaways:

  • Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis requiring immediate treatment without waiting for radiological confirmation.
  • Needle decompression is the first-line emergency treatment.
  • The classic site is the 2nd intercostal space, midclavicular line.

question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents to OPD with a history of a lump in the left breast. Clinical examination revelaed a lump in the left breast of size 9x10 cm, with no axillary lymphadenopathy. The histopathology of the biopsy from the lump is shown below. What is your likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The histopathology of the breast lump shows hypercellular stroma with stromal overgrowth, forming the characteristic leaflike architecture, which is indicative of a phyllodes tumor.

Phyllodes tumour

  • Phyllodes tumours, also called cystosarcoma phyllodes, are stromal tumours developing from the breast's connective tissue.
  • Common among middle-aged women (40 - 50 years).
  • Most phyllodes tumours are benign (noncancerous), but a small number (about 10% to 15%) can be borderline or malignant (cancerous).
  • They present as a lump in the breast, which may be firm, smooth, and well-defined.
  • It may also grow quickly from a few centimetres to massive lesions involving the entire breast.
  • The overlying skin over the tumour may sometimes ulcerate owing to pressure necrosis.
  • Phyllodes tumour is differentiated from fibroadenoma based on its overgrowth of stroma, increased mitotic activity and cellularity, and nuclear pleomorphism.

Treatment of Phyllodes Tumor:

  • Wide local excision with at least a 2 cm margin, including overlying skin and underlying pectoralis major if involved.
  • Large or recurrent tumors: Mastectomy may be required.
  • Adjuvant therapy: Postoperative radiotherapy can be considered in selected cases to reduce recurrence risk.

Explanation of other options:

Giant fibroadenoma (Option B): Fibroadenoma is the most common cause of breasr limp in women between 15-25 years. It typically presents as a firm, mobile, painless, well-circumscribed lump. Histologically, it also shows stromal and epithelial proliferation.

Inflammatory carcinoma (Option C): Presents with redness, swelling, warmth, and skin changes such as peau d'orange. It is typically aggressive, often associated with axillary lymphadenopathy and breast pain.

Ductal carcinoma (Option D): Typically presents with irregular breast masses, skin changes, and often axillary lymphadenopathy. Histologically, it shows variable architectural patterns - comedo, cribriform, micropapillary and papillary pattern with malignant epithelial proliferation within ducts.

question_text: A 30-year-old female presents with a painless, palpable mass in her left breast. On examination, the 3x3 cm mass is highly mobile and has a rubbery consistency. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In the given clinical scenario the presentation is highly characteristic of a fibroadenoma.
  • It is the most common benign breast tumor in young women (15-35 years).
  • Etiology: Increased estrogen sensitivity in focal breast tissue.
  • Pathology: Encapsulated spherical lesion of fibrous and glandular tissue, arising from interlobular stroma.
  • Types:
    • Pericanalicular (hard): Connective tissue inside elastic lamina.
    • Intracanalicular (soft): Connective tissue outside elastic lamina.
  • Clinical Features:
  • Classic triad: Painless, highly mobile ("breast mouse"), rubbery/firm consistency.
  • Solitary, slowly growing lump.
  • Distinguishing point: Unlike malignant lumps, which are hard, fixed, and irregular.
  • Diagnosis:
    • IOC - FNAC: "Antler horn" epithelial pattern.
    • Mammography: "Popcorn" calcification in older lesions.
  • Treatment:
    • No treatment if diagnosis is certain.
    • Excision biopsy if lesion is suspicious, enlarging, or for cosmetic reasons.

Explanation of other options:

Breast abscess (Option A): This is an infectious collection that presents as a painful, tender, warm, and erythematous mass, often with systemic fever.

Phyllodes tumor (Option B): It can mimic a fibroadenoma but is often larger (>5 cm), grows rapidly, and may feel more firm or bulky.

Invasive ductal carcinoma (Option D): The most common breast cancer, but it typically presents in older women as a hard, irregular, fixed mass, often with skin dimpling or nipple retraction.

Key Takeaways:

  • A painless, mobile, rubbery breast mass in a young woman is a fibroadenoma until proven otherwise.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed with ultrasound and/or fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC).

question_text: A lactating woman presents with pain in one breast. On examination, the breast is tender and engorged, and the infant refuses to feed from the affected side. What is the preferred treatment approach?
explanation:
Explanation:

A lactating woman with painful, tender, engorged breast and infant refusal to feed suggests lactational mastitis with breast abscess, most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.

Lactational (Puerperal) Mastitis

  • Occurs in 3-20% of lactating women.
  • Most cases are caused by Staphylococcus aureus; hospital-acquired infections may involve MRSA.
  • Infection usually enters through cracked or retracted nipples.
  • Duct blockage by epithelial debris leads to milk stasis, which predisposes to infection.
  • Staphylococci multiply within the milk clot inside the duct (ampulla).

Clinical Features

  • Starts as cellulitis (pain, redness, swelling, fever, malaise).

Explanation:

  • Figure B shows Paget's disease of the nipple.
  • Paget's disease of the breast is a distinct form of ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) that originates in the nipple.
  • Clinically, it presents with progressive erosion and destruction of the nipple, gradually spreading to involve the areola. In some cases, it can become invasive and metastasize to the axillary lymph nodes.
  • A full triple assessment is required to rule out any underlying breast malignancy.
  • When Paget's disease occurs without an associated underlying cancer, treatment involves a central core excision that removes the nipple-areolar complex and a cone of major ducts down to the pectoralis major muscle, followed by radiotherapy.
  • If an underlying malignancy is present, the recommended treatment is mastectomy along with evaluation of axillary lymph node status.
  • Nipple discharge (option A) - in the given figure nipple discharge shown. Most nipple discharges are physiological and occur as part of ANDI (aberrations of normal development and involution). They may arise from single or multiple ducts and can be unilateral or bilateral. However, a single duct discharge that is serous, sanguineous, and spontaneous is considered pathological and requires triple assessment.
  • Skin dimpling (option C) - Traction on Cooper ligaments (by a tumor) distorts the surface of the breast and produces a dimple best seen during abduction of the arms upward.
  • Peau d'orange (skin of the orange)(option D) - This is seen in carcinoma breast when there is infiltration of the dermal lymphatics by malignant cells.

  • Paget's disease presents with eczematous destruction of the nipple-areolar complex

question_text: What is the preferred management of an angular dermoid cyst?
option_c: Wide local excision with a 2 cm margin
explanation:
Explanation:

Angular dermoid cysts are benign congenital lesions at the frontozygomatic suture, often near the lateral canthus. They are treated with complete surgical excision, which ensures no recurrence.

Angular Dermoid

Definition:

Angular dermoid is a type of dermoid cyst that presents as a smooth, soft, non-tender swelling typically located at the fronto-zygomatic suture.

Etiology / Pathogenesis:

  • Arises due to sequestration of ectodermal tissue during embryonic development.
  • The cyst contains dermal elements such as hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and sweat glands.

Common Sites:

  • Most often occurs near the lateral canthus (outer corner of the eye).
  • May also develop along cranial suture lines, particularly the fronto-zygomatic region.

Clinical Features:

  • Usually asymptomatic.
  • Appears as a smooth, soft, non-tender swelling.
  • Symptoms may arise if cyst becomes large (cosmetic deformity, pressure effects on adjacent structures) or if it gets infected.

Diagnosis:

  • Clinical examination is often sufficient for superficial lesions.
  • Imaging (Ultrasound/CT scan): Used to assess depth, orbital involvement, or extension.
  • CT scan is especially important to rule out dural attachment in deep lesions.

Treatment:

  • Complete surgical excision is the treatment of choice.
  • Indicated for cosmetic reasons, symptomatic lesions, or suspected complications.
  • Careful dissection is essential to ensure total removal and avoid recurrence.
  • If untreated, cyst may rarely cause resorption or indentation of underlying bone.

Prognosis:

  • Excellent if completely excised.
  • Recurrence uncommon with proper removal.

Explanation of other options:

Wait and watch (Option B): Not recommended, as cysts can enlarge or get infected.

Wide local excision with 2 cm margin (Option C): Unnecessary; these are benign cysts, not malignancies.

Laser ablation (Option D): Inappropriate, as it does not ensure complete removal.

question_text: what should be the treatment in a patient who presented in the emergency with respiratory distress. He was having dilated large veins. Large amount of air was seen on the left side along with mediastinal shift as shown?
option_a: Wide bore needle insertion in intercostal space
explanation:
Pneumothorax

  • Pneumothorax is the presence of air outside the lung, within the pleural space. It must be distinguished from bullae or air cysts within the lung. Bullae can be the cause of an air leak from the lung and can therefore coexist with pneumothorax.
  • Spontaneous pneumothorax occurs when the visceral pleura ruptures without an external traumatic or iatrogenic cause. Cases are divided into primary spontaneous pneumothorax (PSP) and secondary spontaneous pneumothorax (SSP).
  • Pneumothorax can also occur following trauma or iatrogenic injury such as insertion of a central line.
  • Tension pneumothorax is when (independent of etiology) there is a build-up of positive pressure within the hemithorax, to the extent that the lung is completely collapsed, the diaphragm is fattened, the mediastinum is distorted and, eventually, the venous return to the heart is compromised.

Immediate management of tension pneumothorax: wide bore needle decompression in

  1. Adults: 5th intercostal space midaxillary line
  2. Children: 2nd intercostal space mid clavicular line

Definitive management: ICD tube insertion in 5th intercostal space midaxillary line in triangle of safety

question_text: Which of the following is the recommended treatment for the condition shown in the image, here size of stone is 2 mm?
explanation:
Explanation:

A 2 mm ureteric stone is typically managed with conservative measures, as the majority of such small stones pass spontaneously with adequate fluid intake and symptomatic management. However, if the stone fails to pass, causes obstruction, persistent pain, or other complications, ureteroscopy may be indicated to remove or fragment the stone.

Conservative Management of Renal Stones

Indications for Conservative Approach:

  • Stone size ≤ 5 mm
  • Non-dilated ureter
  • Stone located in the lower third of the ureter
  • Evidence of progressive downward movement on follow-up scans

Conservative Measures:

  • Adequate fluid intake to promote diuresis and facilitate stone passage
  • Medical Expulsive Therapy (MET):
    • Alpha-blockers (e.g., Tamsulosin)
    • Calcium channel blockers (e.g., Nifedipine)
    • Mechanism: Relax ureteric smooth muscle to aid spontaneous stone passage
    • Typically used for stones ≤ 10 mm

Indications for Intervention:

  • Failure of stone to pass spontaneously
  • Persistent or worsening symptoms (pain, obstruction, infection)

Interventional Options:

Follow-up:

  • Regular imaging to monitor stone size, location, and movement

Wait and Watch (Option D):

  • Suitable for ureteric stones <5 mm that are asymptomatic and not causing complications.
  • Ureteroscopy is preferred if the stone is symptomatic, causing pain, obstruction, or other issues.
  • Even a small 2 mm stone may result in discomfort or obstruction.
  • Ureteroscopy allows rapid removal or fragmentation, providing a proactive and effective treatment compared to conservative observation.

question_text: A 55-year-old male presents with a verrucous carcinoma involving the glans penis. On examination, inguinal lymph nodes are not palpable. What is the most appropriate management for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Partial penectomy is the treatment of choice for localized penile cancer limited to the glans.

  • In cases of localized verrucous carcinoma confined to the glans without lymph node involvement, partial penectomy is the standard approach.
  • It provides adequate oncological control while preserving penile function.
  • A surgical margin of 2 cm is typically recommended for distal lesions.
  • Total penectomy is reserved for more proximal or extensive tumors, while topical therapies like 5-fluorouracil are used for carcinoma in situ or superficial lesions.

question_text: A 35-year-old man presents with scrotal enlargement. Laboratory findings reveal elevated LDH, while hCG and alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) levels are within normal limits. Histopathological examination shows characteristic findings. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Seminoma is the most common pure testicular germ cell tumor, typically occurring in men aged 25-45 years. Patients usually present with a painless, firm testicular swelling. Biochemical markers show elevated LDH, while AFP is normal and hCG is usually normal or only mildly elevated.
Histologically, seminomas display sheets of large oval cells with clear cytoplasm, large nuclei, and prominent nucleoli.

Explanation of other options:

Leydig cell tumor (Option A): A benign stromal tumor usually presenting in adults aged 30-60 years. Does not characteristically elevate hCG or AFP. Can cause endocrine manifestations like gynecomastia due to hormone secretion.

Embryonal carcinoma (Option B): An aggressive germ cell tumor often presenting in younger men. It is typically associated with elevations in both AFP and hCG, unlike seminoma. Histology is more heterogeneous.

Teratoma (Option D): Often occurs in young men and may present with a painless testicular mass. Tumor markers are usually normal (AFP and hCG not elevated). Ultrasound shows a heterogeneous mass with cystic and solid areas, not the homogenous appearance seen in seminoma.

Seminoma

Key Takeaways:

  • Seminoma = LDH ↑, AFP normal, hCG normal/mild ↑.
  • Seminoma histology → large clear cells with prominent nucleoli.
  • Orchidectomy is definitive treatment.

question_text: Which gene is responsible for the occurrence of the medullary carcinoma of the thyroid?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Medullary carcinoma may occur in combination with adrenal phaeochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism (usually due to hyperplasia) in the syndrome known as multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN-2A).
  • It is an autosomal dominant condition caused by germline mutations in RET, which encodes a transmembrane tyrosine kinase receptor (TKR) that activates pathways involved in proliferation, survival, migration and angiogenesis.
  • Gain-of-function RET mutations lead to activation of the TKR and cancer initiation through deregulated proliferation and increased cell survival.

question_text: Which among the following arteries do not supply the thyroid gland?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The thyroid is a highly vascular gland with an abundant and redundant blood supply.
  • The arterial supply to the thyroid gland generally derives from two bilateral pairs of arteries.
    • The superior thyroid arteries originate from the external carotid arteries and divide as they enter the superior poles of the thyroid lobes.
    • The inferior thyroid arteries are branches from the thyrocervical trunks of the subclavian arteries. Because they branch fairly proximally from the thyrocervical trunk, their course runs cephalad and posterior to the carotid sheath before making a turn and entering the mid thyroid lobes.
    • In about 2% of people, a third artery called the thyroid ima artery arises directly from the aorta or innominate artery. This artery follows a midline path and enters the thyroid isthmus or the inferior poles of the thyroid lobes.
  • The occurrence of the Middle thyroid artery is not found in the human body.

question_text: In which of the following conditions is serum calcitonin the most sensitive biomarker for detection and surveillance?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Calcitonin is a 32-amino acid protein secreted by the parafollicular C cells.
  • Normally, serum calcitonin levels are highest in infancy, decline rapidly in early childhood, then remain relatively stable through adulthood (although absolute levels can fluctuate minute to minute).
  • Calcitonin does not appear to play a significant role in calcium homeostasis despite its known mechanisms of action at the level of the bone, gut, and kidney.
  • Serum calcitonin is the most sensitive biomarker for the detection and surveillance of medullary thyroid cancer (MTC), which is a malignancy of the parafollicular C cells.
  • This test is performed in patients with or family members at risk for MTC or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2).
  • There is controversy around the utility of measuring serum calcitonin as a routine screening test in the evaluation of a thyroid nodule.
  • Calcitonin is currently measured using a variety of methods, including radioimmunoassays, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays, and immunochemiluminometric assays, with differing sensitivities, specificities, and reference ranges.

question_text:
A 34-year-old man presents with hypercalcemia (serum calcium: 12.8 mg/dL) and elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels.
Ultrasound of the neck shows a 1.5 × 1.5 cm lesion in the right inferior thyroid lobe.Which of the following is the most appropriate management for this patient?
option_a: MIBI followed by focussed parathyroidectomy to be done
option_b: Normal DEXA scan rules out the need for surgery
option_c: Only observation, no need for surgery
option_d: Creatinine clearance > 80 ml/min mandates the surgery
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient has primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) - characterized by elevated serum calcium and high PTH.
The most common cause (>85%) is a single parathyroid adenoma.

Localization:
A Technetium-99m sestamibi (MIBI) scan is performed to localize the hyperfunctioning gland.
If the lesion is confirmed as a single adenoma, a focused (minimally invasive) parathyroidectomy is the treatment of choice.
Even if the patient is asymptomatic, parathyroidectomy is indicated if: (Option C)

  • Serum calcium >1 mg/dL above normal range
  • Age <50 years
  • Reduced bone density (osteopenia/osteoporosis)
  • Nephrolithiasis or nephrocalcinosis
  • Impaired renal function (CrCl <60 mL/min)

This patient is young with significant hypercalcemia → surgery indicated.

Explanation of Other Options:

Normal DEXA scan rules out the need for surgery (Option B):

  • DEXA assesses bone density but normal results do not exclude systemic complications of PHPT.
  • Surgery is indicated even with normal DEXA if serum calcium is significantly elevated or patient <50 years.
  • Remember: biochemical criteria, not just DEXA, guide management.

Creatinine clearance > 80 ml/min mandates the surgery (Option D):

  • Actually, impaired renal function (CrCl <60 ml/min) is an indication for surgery, not a contraindication.
  • Normal renal function (CrCl >80) alone does not necessitate surgery.

Key Takeaway Points:

Indications of surgery in an asymptomatic case are:

  • Serum calcium 25 mmol/L (1.0 mg/dL) above the upper limit of normal
  • Bone mineral density (BMD) by DEXA; T score - 2.5 at lumbar spine, total hip, femoral neck, or distal one-third of radius
  • Vertebral fracture
  • Creatinine clearance <60 mL/min
  • 24-hour urinary calcium >10 mmol/dL (>400 mg/day) or increased risk of stone formation by risk analysis
  • Age <50 years
  • When medical therapy is not possible

question_text: A patient comes with thyroiditis- has High TSH value and TPO value- Diagnosis is?
explanation:
Chronic lymphocytic (autoimmune) thyroiditis (Hashimoto's disease)

  • This common condition is usually associated with raised titres of thyroid antibodies.
  • It is the most common cause of hypothyroidism world wide
  • It commonly presents as a goiter, which may be diffuse or nodular with a characteristic 'bosselated' feel or with established or subclinical thyroid failure.
  • The diagnosis often follows investigation of a discrete swelling. Features of chronic lymphocytic (focal) thyroiditis are commonly present on histological examination in association with other thyroid disease, notably toxic goiter.
  • Serum levels of antibodies against thyroid peroxidase (TPO) and thyroglobulin are useful in determining the cause of thyroid dysfunction and swellings.
  • Autoimmune thyroiditis may be associated with thyroid toxicity, failure or euthyroid goiter. Levels above 25 units/mL for TPO antibody and titres of greater than 1:100 for antithyroglobulin are considered significant,although a proportion of patients with histological evidence of lymphocytic (autoimmune) thyroiditis are seronegative.
  • People with hashimotos thyroiditis are at risk of papillary thyroid carcinoma and lymphoma.
  • The presence of antithyroglobulin antibodies interferes with assays of serum thyroglobulin, with implications for follow-up of thyroid cancers.
  • TSH receptor antibodies (TSH-RAb or TRAB) are often present in Graves' disease. They are largely produced within the thyroid itself.

KEYTAKEAWAYS:

Anti-TPO antibody- hashimotos thyroiditis

Anti- TSH receptor antibody (enhancing antibody) - GRAVES DISEASE

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding neuroendocrine tumours of lung except?
option_a: It includes small cell cancer and large cell undifferentiated lung cancer
option_b: They are slow growing and highly vascular
option_d: Segmental or wedge resection may be sufficient for small peripheral tumour
explanation:
Neuroendocrine tumours of the lung are a group of lung cancers that include small cell cancer and large cell undifferentiated lung cancer, but also include other less aggressive tumour types including typical carcinoid and atypical carcinoid tumours.

  • These occur in the major (central) bronchi and 20% are found peripherally. They are characteristically slow growing and highly vascular. Most behave in a benign way; however, approximately 15% metastasis. The patient often presents with a history of recurrent pneumonia or haemoptysis, but carcinoid syndrome is rare unless there are extensive pulmonary or hepatic metastases. Surgical excision is preferred because the prognosis following complete resection is excellent (>90% 10-year survival).
  • Segmental or wedge resection may be sufficient for a small peripheral tumour, while lobectomy or pneumonectomy may be necessary for central tumours. Where possible, a lung-sparing bronchoplastic or sleeve resection should be considered.
  • This allows resection of proximal endobronchial lesions in an effort to preserve more distal, uninvolved lung parenchyma.

Lung neuroendocrine tumors according to subtype. A: typical carcinoid tumor, B: atypical carcinoid tumor, C: large-cell neuroendocrine carcinoma, and D: small-cell lung carcinoma.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 59, Cardiac Surgery, Pg: 985.

question_text: Which among the following condition is not associated with hyperthyroidism in thyroid storm?
explanation:
Thyroid Storm Thyroid storm is a condition of hyperthyroidism accompanied by fever, central nervous system agitation or depression, and cardiovascular and GI dysfunction, including hepatic failure.

  • The condition may be precipitated by abrupt cessation of antithyroid medications, infection, thyroid or nonthyroid surgery, and trauma in patients with untreated thyrotoxicosis.
  • Occasionally, thyroid storm may result from amiodarone administration or exposure to iodinated contrast agents or following RAI therapy.
  • This condition was previously associated with high mortality rates but can be appropriately managed in an intensive care unit setting. β-Blockers are given to reduce peripheral T4 to T3 conversion and decrease the hyperthyroid symptoms.
  • Oxygen supplementation and hemodynamic support should be instituted. Nonaspirin compounds can be used to treat pyrexia, and Lugol's iodine or sodium ipodate (intravenously) should be administered to decrease iodine uptake and thyroid hormone secretion.
  • PTU therapy blocks the formation of new thyroid hormone and reduces peripheral conversion of T4 to T3.
  • Corticosteroids often are helpful to prevent adrenal exhaustion and block hepatic thyroid hormone conversion.

Reference: Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 38, Edition: 11th, Pg: 1638

question_text: Which among the following pharyngeal pouches develop the parathyroid gland?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The parathyroid glands develop from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
  • The inferior parathyroid glands arise from the third pouch, along with the thymus. As the thymus descends, it pulls the inferior parathyroid glands with it, explaining their lower anatomical position.
  • The superior parathyroid glands arise from the fourth pouch.
  • This embryological origin is important for understanding anatomical variations and surgical implications.

Explanation of Other Options

  • Option A - 1st pharyngeal pouch: Gives rise to structures like the middle ear cavity and auditory tube, not the parathyroid glands.
  • Option B - 2nd pharyngeal pouch: Contributes to palatine tonsils, not involved in parathyroid development.
  • Option D - 5th pharyngeal pouch: Often considered rudimentary or part of the fourth pouch; not responsible for parathyroid gland formation.

question_text: In a 35-years old pregnant female with hyperthyroidism, which antithyroid drug should be given in the first trimester?
explanation:
Antithyroid drugs

  • Those in common use are carbimazole and propylthiouracil: these are ANTI-TPO drugs.
  • Antithyroid drugs are used to restore the patient to a euthyroid state and to maintain this for a prolonged period in the hope that a permanent remission will occur, i.e. that production of TSH-RAb will diminish or cease. Propylthiouracil has no teratogenicity effect. Antithyroid drugs cannot cure a toxic nodule.
  • The overactive thyroid tissue is autonomous and recurrence of the hyperthyroidism is certain when the drug is discontinued.

Anti-thyroids in pregnancy:

1st trimester: propylthiouracil is used (carbimazole not used because it's teratogenic and may cause aplasia cutis)

2nd trimester onwards: carbimazole (propylthiouracil not used throughout pregnancy due to risk of hepatitis)

question_text: Adrenal incidentaloma true is/are
option_a: Lesions <6 cm in diameter have an approximate risk of malignancy of about 25%
option_b: Benign adrenal adenomas tend to be homogeneous, well encapsulated
option_c: T2-weighted imaging, adenomas demonstrate high signal intensity when compared to the liver
explanation:
Determination of the malignant potential of an incidentaloma is more difficult. The risk of malignancy in an adrenal lesion is related to its size.

  • Lesions >6 cm in diameter have an approximate risk of malignancy of about 25%. However, this size cutoff is not absolute because adrenal carcinomas also have been reported in lesions <6cm
  • Carcinomas account for 2% of lesions <4cm and 6% lesions 4.1 to 6 cm in size .This has led to increased use of the imaging characteristics of incidentalomas to predict malignancy.
  • Benign adrenal adenomas tend to be homogeneous, well encapsulated, and have smooth and regular margins. They also tend to be hypoattenuating lesions (<10 Honse field units) on CT Scanning .
  • In contrast, adrenal cancers tend to be hyperattenuating (>18 Hounsfield units) and inhomogeneous, have irregular borders, and may show evidence of local invasion or adjacent lymphadenopathy.
  • On MRI T2-weighted imaging, adenomas demonstrate low signal intensity when compared to the liver (adrenal mass-to-liver ratio <1.4), whereas carcinomas and metastases have moderate intensity (mass-to-liver ratio 1.2:2.8). Pheochromocytomas are extremely bright, with mass-to-liver ratios >3.

Adrenal incidentaloma

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 10th edition, Chapter, Thyroid, Parathyroid, and Adrenal, Pg: 1588.

question_text: Which among the following radioactive substance is not used in the thyroid scintigraphy technique?
explanation:
• Thyroid scintigraphy is performed using either technetium-99m pertechnetate or a radiolabelled iodine nuclide (typically 123I or 131I).
  • Depending on the specific study, the tracer can be administered intravenously, orally, or via inhalation, and images are obtained anywhere from 30 minutes (for intravenous [IV] injection) to 24 hours (for oral administration) afterward.
  • The thyroid normally displays symmetric uptake bilaterally. Nodular disease can be classified into whether there is increased focal uptake (the so-called "hot" nodule) or not (the "cold" nodule).
  • Classically, "hot" nodules in the setting of hyperthyroidism are thought to be benign toxic nodules with extremely low risk of malignancy, whereas "cold" nodules carry a 15% risk of malignancy.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 882

question_text: What is the preferred treatment for a benign tumour of the superficial parathyroid gland?
explanation:
Explanation:

Management of Benign Parathyroid Tumour (Adenoma)

The treatment of choice for a benign parathyroid tumour is surgical excision (parathyroidectomy). This is necessary because parathyroid adenomas commonly cause primary hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemia, which can lead to significant systemic complications. Surgery offers a definitive and curative option.

 Indications for Parathyroidectomy

  • Severe/symptomatic disease
  • Young patients
  • Marked osteoporosis or reduced bone density
  • Serum calcium >11 mg/dL
  • Recurrent renal stones
  • Neuromuscular manifestations
  • 24-hour urinary calcium >400 mg

 Indications for Surgery in Asymptomatic Patients

  • Serum calcium ≥0.25 mmol/L (≈1 mg/dL) above upper limit of normal
  • Bone mineral density (DEXA): T-score ≤ -2.5 at lumbar spine, hip, femoral neck, or distal radius
  • Vertebral fracture on imaging
  • Creatinine clearance <60 mL/min
  • 24-hr urinary calcium >10 mmol/day (>400 mg/day) or stone risk on metabolic evaluation
  • Age <50 years
  • Failure of medical management

Intraoperative & Diagnostic Protocols

  • Miami Protocol: Intraoperative PTH estimation. A >50% drop from baseline after excision confirms adequate removal.
  • Casanova Test: Used when all 4 parathyroid glands are excised with autotransplantation. PTH levels are compared in neck vein vs. brachial vein.
    • Positive test → brachial PTH >20 times higher than neck sample (indicates recurrence at graft site).

Contraindications for Surgery

  • Absolute: Familial hypocalciuric hypercalcemia (FHH)
    • Features: high serum calcium & PTH, but low urinary calcium excretion and low calcium/creatinine clearance ratio.
    • Parathyroidectomy does not correct hypercalcemia in FHH.
  • Relative:
    • Contralateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
    • Vocal cord dysfunction

question_text: What is the size of the lesion in papillary microcarcinoma of thyroid?
explanation:
• Recently, increasing interest has focused on ‘papillary micro carcinoma’.
  • This term is used to describe PTC that is <10 mm in size.
  • These lesions are common (detected in about 10% of benign thyroid resections) and not associated with adverse outcomes, including recurrence or non-survival.
  • As such, management and follow-up of patients with these lesions of doubtful clinical significance is controversial.
  • In Korea, for example, national screening has led to a significant increase in these cases.
  • In Japan groups are opting for an observational approach without surgery.
  • These studies have shown that at least two-thirds never progress.
  • In the USA some groups are attempting non-surgical management with ablation techniques using ethanol or radiofrequency.
