question_text: A man came with complaints of recurrent discharge and pain due to lesions around the anus for 3 years. A diagnosis of fistula-in-ano is made. What is the gold standard investigation for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

MRI is considered the gold standard diagnostic test for Fistula-in-Ano.

Fistula-in-Ano

A persistent, abnormal tract connecting the anorectal canal (internal opening) with an external opening on the perineal skin, buttock, or occasionally the vagina in women.

Causes:

  • Idiopathic/Cryptoglandular: Most frequent cause, commonly linked to previous anorectal sepsis.
  • Associated Conditions:
    • Crohn's disease
    • Tuberculosis
    • Lymphogranuloma venereum
    • Actinomycosis
    • Rectal duplication
    • Foreign bodies
    • Rare: Malignancy (may arise in a long-standing fistula)

Clinical Features:

  • Intermittent purulent discharge: Sometimes mixed with blood; discomfort builds until pus drains, giving temporary relief.
  • History of previous anorectal abscess.
  • Passage of flatus/faeces through external opening: Suggestive of rectal origin.

Investigations:

  • MRI (Gold standard): Best for mapping the fistula tract and assessing sphincter/pelvic floor structures.
  • Endoanal Ultrasound: High-frequency imaging to detect tract, sphincters, and adjacent tissues.
  • Fistulography: X-ray with contrast to outline the tract (historically first-line but less used now). (Option A ruled out)
  • Examination under Anaesthesia (EUA): Direct evaluation of the fistula path and complications.
  • Fistula Probe: Instrument passed through tract to delineate course.
  • Anoscopy: Endoscopic inspection of the anal canal to assess internal openings.

Management:

  • Fistulotomy:
    • Opens the tract to heal by secondary intention.
    • Suitable for intersphincteric/trans-sphincteric fistula involving <30% of external sphincter.
    • Avoided in anterior fistulas in women.
  • Fistulectomy:
    • Complete excision of tract, often with diathermy.
    • Provides clear anatomical definition of fistula and extensions.
  • Setons:
    • Thread/elastic material inserted into tract.
    • Loose seton: For drainage.
    • Cutting seton: Gradually divides tissue while preventing abscess.
  • Advancement Flaps:
    • Internal opening closed using anorectal mucosal flap.
    • Used when sphincter integrity needs to be preserved.
    • Effective for selected fistula patterns.

Explanation of Other Options:

USG (Ultrasonography) (Option B) is helpful for identifying superficial fistulas but has limitations in detecting deep or complex tracts, as it does not provide detailed views of surrounding structures like MRI.

CECT (Contrast-Enhanced CT) (Option C) is less suitable for fistula-in-ano because its soft tissue resolution is inferior to MRI. MRI remains superior for detailed mapping and accurate evaluation of fistula anatomy.

Key Takeaways:

Classifications of Fistula-in-Ano:

  • Based on Level of Internal Opening
    • Low-level fistulas: Open into the anal canal below the internal ring.
    • High-level fistulas: Open into the anal canal at or above the internal ring.
  • Based on Complexity
    • Simple fistula: No secondary extensions.
    • Complex fistula: Presence of extensions or multiple tracts.

Parks Classification

question_text: What is the diagnosis of a patient who had a history of bronchospasm and was found to have a tumor in their ileum along with elevated levels of 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid in their urine?
explanation:
Explanation:

This is a classic presentation of a carcinoid tumor with carcinoid syndrome. These neuroendocrine tumors, often located in the ileum, secrete serotonin and other vasoactive substances. The serotonin metabolite 5-HIAA (5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid) is elevated in the urine and is a key diagnostic marker. The secreted serotonin can cause bronchospasm (as well as flushing and diarrhea), especially when liver metastases are present, allowing the vasoactive substances to bypass hepatic metabolism and enter the systemic circulation.

Investigations for Neuroendocrine Tumors:

  • Initial test: 24-hr urinary 5-HIAA
  • Localization/Staging: Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (SRS) (except insulinoma)
  • Most accurate: DOPA-PET
  • Commonly used: Triple-phase CECT (low sensitivity ~50%)

Explanation of other options:

Neuroblastoma (Option B): This is a tumor of childhood that arises from the adrenal medulla or sympathetic chain and secretes catecholamines, not serotonin. It does not cause carcinoid syndrome.

Leiomyoma (Option C): This is a benign smooth muscle tumor of the GI tract that is hormonally inactive and does not cause elevated 5-HIAA or bronchospasm.

Chromaffinoma (Pheochromocytoma) (Option D): This adrenal tumor secretes catecholamines, causing hypertension, headaches, and sweating, but not bronchospasm or elevated urinary 5-HIAA.

Key Takeaways:

  • The triad of ileal tumor, bronchospasm, and elevated urinary 5-HIAA is diagnostic of carcinoid syndrome.
  • Carcinoid syndrome typically occurs after the tumor has metastasized to the liver.

Benign tumours

question_text: Which among the following pouches develop the parathyroid gland?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The parathyroid glands develop from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
  • The thymus also develops from the third pouch.
  • As it descends, the thymus takes the associated parathyroid gland with it, which explains why the inferior parathyroid, which arises from the third pharyngeal pouch, normally lies inferior to the superior gland.
  • However, the inferior parathyroid may be found anywhere along this line of descent.
  • The developing thyroid lobes amalgamate with the structures that arise in the fourth pharyngeal pouch, i.e. the superior parathyroid gland and the ultimobranchial body.

question_text: A patient presents with profuse bleeding, cold limbs, and low central venous pressure (CVP). Which type of shock is most likely in this scenario?
explanation:
Explanation:

In a patient with profuse bleeding, cold extremities, and low central venous pressure (CVP), the observed type of shock is hypovolemic shock.

Hypovolemic shock

  • Results from significant loss of blood or fluid volume, leading to insufficient circulation and oxygen delivery to tissues.
  • Hypovolemic shock is the most common form of shock.
  • The decreased cardiac output leads to
    • Inadequate tissue perfusion, lactic acidosis, metabolic acidosis along with
    • Compe nsatory mechanism activation & increased sympathetic tone cause an increase in PR & TPR.

Explanation of other options:

Cardiogenic shock (Option A): Cardiogenic shock occurs when the heart fails to pump blood effectively to the tissues. Common causes include myocardial infarction, cardiac arrhythmias, valvular heart disease, blunt cardiac injury, and cardiomyopathies.

Obstructive shock (Option C): Obstructive shock occurs due to a mechanical obstruction that reduces cardiac preload. Common causes include cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, massive pulmonary embolism, and air embolism.

Endocrine shock (Option D): Endocrine shock can manifest with features of hypovolemic, cardiogenic, or distributive shock. Common causes include adrenal insufficiency, hypothyroidism, and hyperthyroidism.

question_text: A 23-year-old male patient presents with a swelling in the midline of his neck that shifts when he swallows or sticks out his tongue. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A thyroglossal cyst presents as a midline neck swelling that moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion due to its embryological attachment.

  • A thyroglossal cyst arises from the persistence of the thyroglossal duct, an embryological remnant that connects the foramen cecum to the thyroid gland.
  • It typically presents as a midline neck mass that characteristically moves with deglutition and tongue protrusion-due to its anatomical relation with the hyoid bone.
  • The most common site is just below the hyoid (subhyoid region), though it may occur anywhere along the duct's course.
  • The definitive treatment is the Sistrunk procedure, which includes removal of the cyst, the tract, and the central portion of the hyoid bone to prevent recurrence.
  • Incision and drainage are contraindicated, as they may lead to thyroglossal fistula formation, which is always acquired and never congenital.

Explanation of other options:

Brachial cyst (Option A): Typically located laterally along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, not in the midline.

Plunging ranula (Option C): A mucous retention cyst from the sublingual gland, located in the floor of the mouth and lateral in position; does not move with swallowing or tongue movement.

Dermoid cyst (Option D): A congenital midline lesion, but it generally does not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion, distinguishing it from a thyroglossal cyst.

Papillary thyroid carcinoma

PTC is the most common thyroid malignancy. Interestingly, up to 30% of patients who die of non-thyroid disease have deposits of PTC in autopsy studies, suggesting that many patients live with this disease undetected. Nonetheless, when PTC is diagnosed most patients will be offered treatment. The disease is known for its propensity for lymph node metastases.

These are more common in younger patients, in whom they do not affect the otherwise excellent survival. This finding is in contrast to most malignancies, where the finding of metastatic disease confers a poor outcome. One contentious finding in patients with PTC is a high rate of occult micrometastases (as high as 40% of N0 patients in the central neck). Despite the presence of metastases, few patients progress to have clinically meaningful disease and the role of elective nodal surgery is in question. Distant metastases are uncommon in PTC.

Recently, increasing interest has focused on 'papillary microcarcinoma'. This term is used to describe a PTC that is <10 mm in size. These lesions are common (detected in about 10% of benign thyroid resections) and not associated with adverse outcomes, including recurrence or non-survival. As such, management and follow-up of patients with these lesions of doubtful clinical significance is controversial.

question_text: A 40-year-old female patient known case of papillary carcinoma thyroid was advised radioiodine ablation after total thyroidectomy. All of the following statements about preparation of patient for radioiodine ablation are true except?

explanation:
Explanation:

The following are necessary to be done beforeradioiodine ablation or scan.

  1. Patient is weaned off form iodine containing drugs like cough suppressant and iodine contrast based imaging. (Option B)
  2. Food stuff such as sea foods and iodinated salts should be avoided for 3 to 4 weeks.
  3. It is mandatory tostop tablet thyroxineso that serum thyroid level is elevated to more than 30 micro IU /ml. (Option C)
  4. Amount of residual thyroid is calculated usingthyroid uptake probeat 4, 6 and 24 hours after 20 micro curie 131 I application. (Option D)
  5. Normal dosage of 131I used to ablation residual thyroid tissue is in the range of30 to 70 mCi. ( Option A )

Selection of patient for radio iodine ablation:

  1. Patient with I 131 concentrating in distant metastasis.
  2. Patient with multicentric, multifocal, and microscopic differentiated thyroid malignancy.
  3. All patients with follicular, papillary and mixed carcinoma of more than 1.5 cm in size with or without capsular invasion.
  4. Patient with residual thyroid disease in which revision surgery is not possible.

  2. Patient withmedullary carcinomabecause they are based on parafollicular C cells which can't concentrate radioiodine. Hence, they are treated with 131 I labelled meta iodo benzyl guanidine (MIBG).

Normal dosage of 131I used to ablation residual thyroid tissue is in the range of30 to 70 mCi.

question_text: A 50-year-old woman after thyroidectomy comes to you for a 2<sup>nd</sup> opinion for further treatment of papillary thyroid cancer. What would you recommend for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Following thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid carcinoma, performing a radioiodine (I-131) scan is recommended to detect any remaining thyroid tissue or potential metastases.
  • Papillary thyroid cancer generally exhibits radioactive iodine (RAI) avidity, allowing it to take up and concentrate the radioactive iodine, which makes this scan a reliable method for evaluation.

Roles of Radioactive Iodine Therapy:

  • Remnant Ablation: Eliminates any residual normal thyroid tissue following total or subtotal thyroidectomy.
  • Adjuvant Therapy: Provides additional post-surgical treatment to lower the risk of recurrence.
  • Treatment of Known Disease: Targets and destroys residual cancer cells or recurrent structural/biochemical disease.

Radioactive Iodine Ablation (RAI):

  • Isotope Used: Iodine-131 (Half-Life: 8 days)
  • Emissions:
    • Beta Rays (90%): Deliver therapeutic effect to thyroid tissue while minimizing damage to surrounding tissues.
    • Gamma Rays (10%): Used for imaging and contribute to potential side effects.
  • Indications: Primarily for differentiated thyroid cancers such as Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC) and Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (FTC).
  • Side Effects (Dose-Dependent): Can include inflammation of salivary glands (sialadenitis), blockage of the nasolacrimal duct, transient swelling, infertility, and rare secondary cancers like leukemia.

Indications and Contraindications for Radioactive Iodine (RAI) Therapy

Indications:

  • Differentiated Thyroid Cancers:
    • Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC)
    • Follicular Thyroid Carcinoma (FTC)
    • Hurthle Cell Carcinoma
  • Tumors larger than 2 cm
  • Presence of one or more high-risk factors
  • Evident extrathyroidal invasion
  • Patients aged over 45 years
  • Involvement of lymph nodes or presence of distant metastases

Contraindications:

  • Poorly Differentiated Thyroid Cancers:
    • Medullary Thyroid Carcinoma
    • Anaplastic Thyroid Carcinoma
  • Absolute Contraindications: Pregnancy and breastfeeding
  • Relative Contraindications: Active vomiting or diarrhea

Radiotherapy (Option A): Not the preferred follow-up after thyroidectomy for papillary thyroid cancer (PTC). Radioactive Iodine (RAI) therapy is favored since it specifically targets residual thyroid tissue. Radiotherapy is usually reserved for advanced disease or metastatic cases and is less effective than RAI for eliminating remaining thyroid cells.

Chemotherapy (Option B): PTC generally does not respond to chemotherapy, making it unsuitable for standard treatment. RAI remains the primary therapy, while chemotherapy is reserved for aggressive thyroid cancers like anaplastic carcinoma.

Wait-and-Watch Approach (Option D): In low-risk PTC cases, where the tumor is small, localized, and completely resected, observation may be considered. However, following thyroidectomy, a radioiodine scan (RAI) is typically performed to detect any residual thyroid tissue or metastasis, even in low-risk scenarios.

  • This can be done using a core or open technique.

question_text: What is the mean age of presentation for papillary thyroid carcinoma?
explanation:
Papillary Carcinoma

  • Papillary carcinoma accounts for 80% of all thyroid malignancies in iodine-sufficient areas and is the predominant thyroid cancer in children and individuals exposed to external radiation.
  • Papillary carcinoma occurs more often in women, with a 2:1 female-to-male ratio, and the mean age at presentation is 30 to 40 years.
  • Most patients are euthyroid and present with a slow-growing painless mass in the neck. Dysphagia, dyspnea, and dysphonia usually are associated with locally advanced invasive disease.
  • Lymph node metastases are common, especially in children and young adults, and may be the presenting complaint.
  • “Lateral aberrant thyroid” almost always denotes a cervical lymph node that has been invaded by metastatic cancer.
  • Suspicion of thyroid cancer often originates through physical examination of patients and a review of their history.
  • Diagnosis is established by FNAB of the thyroid mass or lymph node.
  • Once thyroid cancer is diagnosed on FNAB, a complete neck ultrasound is strongly recommended to evaluate the contralateral lobe and for lymph node metastases in the central and lateral neck compartments.
  • Distant metastases are uncommon at initial presentation, but may ultimately develop in up to 20% of patients. The most common sites are lungs, followed by bone, liver, and brain.

Reference: Schwartz Principles of surgery, chapter: 38, Edition: 11th, Pg: 1647

question_text: Which among the following is the undifferentiated primary thyroid malignancy?
explanation:
• The vast majority of primary malignancies are carcinomas derived from the follicular cells. Such tumors were thought of as differentiated (papillary, follicular and Hürthle cell) and undifferentiated (anaplastic).
  • However, now an intermediate class of ‘poorly differentiated carcinoma’ is recognised, which is likely to represent a state of dedifferentiated, between classic differentiated and undifferentiated diseases.
  • The parafollicular C cells can undergo malignant transformation into medullary carcinoma, and thyroid lymphoma is another primary thyroid malignancy.
  • In addition, the thyroid can be involved by direct spread from surrounding structures (larynx and oesophagus) or metastases (most commonly from renal cell carcinoma).
  • Lymph node and blood-borne metastases of thyroid cancer occur primarily to bone and lung and may be the mode of presentation.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 866-867

question_text: How much grams of tissue is left in subtotal thyroidectomy?
explanation:
• The extent of thyroid resection was a topic of much discussion historically, but in modern practice, the vast majority of thyroid resections fall under two categories: total thyroidectomy, in which all or nearly all of the visible thyroid gland is excised, and thyroid lobectomy (also referred to as hemi thyroidectomy), in which all of the visible thyroid on one side is excised along with the isthmus and, if present, the pyramidal lobe.
  • Near-total thyroidectomy, in which less than 1 g of remnant thyroid tissue is left at the ligament of Berry, is also commonly performed.
  • Subtotal thyroidectomy, in which 3 to 5 g of thyroid tissue is left, is less commonly performed today. Bailey Says - 8 gm tissues is left on both sides.
  • The rationale for these lesser-extent lobar resections has been to protect the RLN and blood supply to the parathyroids, as well as to preserve thyroid function without the need for thyroid hormone replacement.
  • Lastly, isthmusectomy is resection of only the thyroid isthmus and pyramidal lobe.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 910

question_text: Hyperparathyroidism-jaw tumour syndrome false is/are
option_b: Activating mutations in the HRPT2 gene
option_c: Pathognomonic ossifying jaw fibromas of the maxilla or mandible
option_d: Younger population is most commonly involved
explanation:
• HPT-JT is a rare cause of PHPT.
  • It arises due to inactivating mutations in the HRPT2 gene on chromosome 1 q21- 32, encoding parafibromin.
  • It classically presents with early-onset PHPT (mean age of 32 years), the aetiology of which can be either single- or multiple-gland disease but is predominantly cystic in nature.
  • It presents with severe hypercalcemia and is associated with an increased risk of an underlying parathyroid carcinoma.
  • Approximately 40% of patients will have the pathognomonic ossifying jaw fibromas of the maxilla or mandible.
  • Other associated abnormalities include renal pathology (hamartomas, polycystic kidney disease and adult Wilms' tumors) and female patients may have uterine malignancies.
  • Surgical intervention involves removal of all enlarged parathyroid glands.

Hyperparathyroidism jaw tumor

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, CHAPTER 56, The parathyroid glands, Pg:882.

question_text: A 45-year-old female with a history of thyroid disorder underwent a total thyroidectomy and has been started on Iodine-131 (I-131) therapy. What is the most likely adverse effect associated with I-131 treatment in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Iodine-131 (I-131) therapy is commonly used for the treatment of thyroid disorders, especially in cases of hyperthyroidism or thyroid cancer.

  • Adverse Effects of I-131 Therapy:
    • The most common long-term adverse effect of I-131 therapy is hypothyroidism.
    • This is a result of radiation-induced destruction of thyroid tissue. In many cases, the treatment causes the thyroid to become underactive (hypothyroid), either immediately or over time.
  • Mechanism and Timeline of Hypothyroidism:
    • I-131 is absorbed by thyroid tissue, where it emits radiation that destroys the gland.
    • In most cases, hypothyroidism develops gradually, with about 5% of patients developing hypothyroidism each year following I-131 therapy.
    • After one year of treatment, around 50% of patients will become hypothyroid, and the rest may remain hyperthyroid or become euthyroid.
    • The higher the dose of I-131, the earlier the onset and higher the incidence of hypothyroidism.

Patient Selection & Contraindications:

  • Indications for I-131 Therapy:
    • Older patients with small to moderate-sized goiters.
    • Patients with relapsed hyperthyroidism after medical or surgical treatments.
    • Patients in whom surgery or antithyroid drugs are contraindicated.
  • Contraindications:
    • Absolute contraindication: Pregnant women or those planning pregnancy within 6 months, and breastfeeding women.
    • Relative contraindications: Younger patients (especially children), those with thyroid nodules, and those with ophthalmopathy (e.g., Grave's disease).

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: Thyroid storm

  • Thyroid storm is a rare and severe exacerbation of hyperthyroidism, often triggered by factors such as surgery or infection, but it is not a common adverse effect of I-131 therapy.
  • In fact, I-131 is used to treat hyperthyroidism, and its main effect is to reduce thyroid function, making thyroid storm less likely post-treatment.

Choice C: Osteoporosis

  • Osteoporosis is not a direct adverse effect of I-131 therapy. While hyperthyroidism can lead to bone density loss over time, hypothyroidism due to I-131 treatment is more likely to be associated with weight gain, fatigue, and other symptoms of low thyroid hormone rather than osteoporosis.

Choice D: Hyperthyroidism

  • Hyperthyroidism is the condition I-131 therapy aims to treat, and it is not an adverse effect of the treatment.
  • In fact, I-131 therapy is often used when patients have hyperthyroidism or have relapsed after thyroid surgery, aiming to reduce thyroid function.

Key Takeaway

  • The most likely adverse effect of I-131 therapy in a patient who has undergone total thyroidectomy is hypothyroidism, which may develop months or years after treatment.

question_text: Which among the following is not the criteria for total thyroidectomy in a patient of differential thyroid carcinoma?
explanation:
Total thyroidectomy remains the preferred evidence-based approach for DTCs associated with higher risk factors, such as:

  • Tumor size of at least 4 cm.
  • Presence of gross extrathyroidal extension.
  • Evidence of metastatic disease.
  • Radiation-induced DTC.
  • Familial non medullary thyroid cancer.
  • Multifocal bilateral DTC.

In summary, the management of differentiated thyroid carcinomas has evolved to consider a more tailored approach, with total thyroidectomy reserved for higher-risk cases. Smaller tumors, between 1 and 4 cm, without specific high-risk features may be managed with thyroid lobectomy or near-total thyroidectomy based on the patient's clinical profile.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 903

question_text: A 40-year-old patient, previously treated for Hodgkin's lymphoma with neck radiation, presents with a right-sided thyroid nodule. FNAC confirms papillary thyroid carcinoma with no evidence of lymph node involvement. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_a: Hemi-thyroidectomy with modified radical neck dissection
option_c: Total thyroidectomy with modified radical neck dissection
explanation:
Explanation of Correct Answer:

This patient has papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) in the setting of prior radiation exposure which is a well-known risk factor for multifocal and bilateral disease.

In such patients, the recommended management is a total thyroidectomy, even in the absence of nodal involvement.

  • Radiation exposure predisposes to multicentric foci of malignancy within both lobes.
  • Hemi-thyroidectomy would risk residual disease in the contralateral lobe.
  • Total thyroidectomy allows:
    • Complete tumour removal
    • Better disease control
    • Easier follow-up with thyroglobulin monitoring and radioiodine ablation (RAI)
  • The next step in the management of papillary thyroid carcinoma, especially in a patient with a history of radiation exposure, is Total thyroidectomy.
  • If lymph node enlargement or metastasis is present, then total thyroidectomy, along with the removal of an enlarged group of lymph nodes with or without ipsilateral modified radical neck dissection (MRND), is done. (Option C ruled out)
  • Hemithyroidectomy involves the removal of one lobe of the thyroid gland and isthmus; it would not be sufficient in this scenario due to the higher risk of multifocal disease and recurrence. (Options A & D ruled out)
  • A total thyroidectomy ensures that there is no residual thyroid tissue, making these post-surgical follow-up strategies more reliable.

Key Takeaway Points:

Exceptions for Hemithyroidectomy:

  • Multifocal bilateral differentiated thyroid cancers
  • Radiation-induced differentiated thyroid cancers
  • Extra-thyroid extension
  • Familial non-medullary thyroid cancer.

Differentiated thyroid cancers (follicular and papillary carcinoma)

question_text: Which among the following criteria is associated with suggestive of locally advanced thyroid cancer?
explanation:
Clinical features of thyroid cancers

  • The annual incidence is about 0.6 per million of the population and the sex ratio is three females to one male.
  • However, the incidence of papillary thyroid cancer is increasing rapidly across the world.
  • This is mostly due to increased rates of imaging detecting previously occult disease. For that reason, although the incidence is increasing, the mortality rates remain static at over 80% 5-year survival for all groups.
  • In particular, anaplastic carcinoma predicts poor outcome with differentiated carcinomas generally having excellent outcomes.
  • The most common presenting symptom is a thyroid swelling.
  • Enlarged cervical lymph nodes may be the presentation of papillary carcinoma (PTC). RLN paralysis is very suggestive of locally advanced disease.
  • Anaplastic growths are usually hard, irregular and infiltrating.
  • A differentiated carcinoma may be suspiciously firm and irregular, but is often indistinguishable from a benign swelling.
  • Small papillary tumours may be impalpable, even when lymphatic metastases are present.
  • Pain, often referred to the ear, is suggestive of nerve involvement from infiltrating tumours.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 867-868

question_text: A 40-year-old had the following structure resected. Which of the following complications can be seen 4 days later?
option_a: Deviation of the angle of the mouth
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows a specimen post-total thyroidectomy, and among the given options, the complication that can be seen after 4 days is carpopedal spasm secondary to hypocalcemia.

  • Thyroidectomy is performed for hyperthyroidism not manageable with nonsurgical therapy, goitres (with or without compressive symptoms), thyroid nodules, and thyroid cancer.
  • Resections are classified into:

Postoperative Care:

  • Patients are positioned to reduce venous pressure, and calcium levels are monitored, particularly after total thyroidectomy.
  • Prophylactic calcium or calcitriol may be used, especially in high-risk patients (Graves' disease, reoperations).
  • Most patients are discharged within 24 hours, and thyroid hormone replacement is required after total thyroidectomy.

Complications of thyroidectomy:

Explanation of other options:

Deviation of angle of mouth (Option A): Occurs due to facial nerve injury, which is seen commonly in surgeries of the parotid, ear and temporal bone tumours.

Neck hematoma (Option C): Neck hematoma is a dangerous complication of thyroidectomy, but it is usually seen in the first 6 hours.

Migratory thrombophlebitis (Option D): It is associated with pancreatic cancer and is known as Trousseau's sign.

question_text: A woman noticed neck swelling 2 months back. Clinical examination reveals a solitary nodule on the right side. What is the most appropriate initial investigation in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Thyroid function tests (TSH, T3, T4) are the most appropriate initial investigation for a newly discovered thyroid nodule to assess thyroid hormonal status.

  • In the evaluation of a solitary thyroid nodule, the first step is to assess thyroid function through serum TSH, T3, and T4 levels.
  • This helps determine whether the nodule is functioning autonomously (suggesting a toxic nodule or hyperfunctioning adenoma) or is non-functioning (which has a higher risk of malignancy).
  • Approach to Thyroid Nodule:
    • Initial test: Serum TSH ± T3/T4.
    • If TSH is suppressed: Do a thyroid scintigraphy (radioisotope scan) to check for a hot nodule (typically benign).
    • If TSH is normal or high: Proceed to ultrasound and FNAC (Fine-needle aspiration cytology) based on sonographic features.
    • Algorithm:
  • This logical stepwise approach helps avoid unnecessary imaging and radiation in the early stages.

Explanation of other options:

Radioisotope I123 assay (Option B): Though useful for assessing nodule functionality (hot vs. cold), it is not the first-line investigation. It is done only after TSH testing, especially if TSH is low.

PET scan (Option C): Used to assess metabolic activity and identify metastases in known malignancies. It is not part of initial evaluation and is reserved for staging or identifying recurrence.

Radioisotope I131 assay (Option D): Primarily used for therapy in hyperthyroidism or thyroid cancer ablation, not for diagnostic evaluation of a thyroid nodule.

question_text: A 45-year-old female patient undergoes a routine thyroid examination, during which a palpable thyroid nodule is discovered. Fine-needle aspiration cytology confirms the presence of papillary thyroid cancer. All of the following statements are true regarding papillary thyroid cancer Except:
option_a: It often presents with cervical lymphadenopathy
option_b: It is the most common type of thyroid cancer
explanation:
Explanation:

Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC):

Cell of Origin:

  • Arises from thyroid follicular cells
  • Not derived from parafollicular C-cells (which produce calcitonin and give rise to medullary thyroid carcinoma)

Epidemiology:

  • Most common type of thyroid cancer (Option B ruled out)

Hormonal Dependence:

  • TSH-dependent: Elevated thyroid-stimulating hormone can promote tumor growth (Option D ruled out)

Clinical Presentation:

  • Solitary anterior neck nodule
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy (Option A ruled out)

Histopathological Features:

  • Papillary projections of the tumor cells
  • Optically clear nuclei (Orphan Annie eye nuclei)
  • Nuclear pseudo-inclusion bodies
  • Psammoma bodies (Dystrophic calcification)

He also complained more recently of pain on swallowing. An OGD and biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma of the oesophagus. All of the following can be risk factors except?

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 80, Pg: 627

question_text: What is less the 3cm of columnar epithelium in Barrett's oesophagus denoted as?
explanation:
Barrett’s oesophagus (columnar lined lower oesophagus)

Until recently, Barrett’s oesophagus was not diagnosed until there was at least 3 cm of columnar epithelium in the distal oesophagus.

The relative risk of cancer rises with increasing length of abnormal mucosa in Barrett’s oesophagus

The following terms are widely used:

  • classic Barrett’s (≥3 cm columnar epithelium);
  • short-segment Barrett’s (<3 cm of columnar epithelium);
  • cardia metaplasia (intestinal metaplasia at the oesophagogastric junction without any macroscopic change at endoscopy).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1119

question_text: Zenker's diverticulum protrudes through the dehiscence of Killian in which direction?
explanation:
• Zenker's diverticulum (pharyngeal pouch) is not really an oesophageal diverticulum as it protrudes posteriorly above the cricopharyngeal sphincter through the natural weak point (the dehiscence of Killian) between the oblique and horizontal (cricopharyngeus) fibres of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor.
  • The exact mechanism that leads to its formation is unknown, but it involves loss of the coordination between pharyngeal contraction and opening of the upper sphincter.
  • When the diverticulum is small, symptoms largely reflect this incoordination with predominantly pharyngeal dysphagia.
  • As the pouch enlarges, it tends to fill with food on eating, and the fundus descends into the mediastinum. This leads to halitosis and oesophageal dysphagia.
  • Treatment can be undertaken endoscopically with a linear cutting stapler to divide the septum between the diverticulum and the upper oesophagus, producing a diverticulo- oesophagostomy, or can be done by open surgery involving pouch excision, pouch suspension (diverticulopexy) and/or myotomy of cricopharyngeus. All techniques have good results.

ZENKER'S DIVERTICULUM

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1126

question_text: A patient is diagnosed with varicose veins, and the condition is classified as C4a according to the CEAP classification. What is the most appropriate treatment for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The descriptive CEAP (Clinical-aEtiology-Anatomy-Pathophysiology) classification for chronic venous disorders is widely utilised.

For clinical classification:

  • C0: no signs of venous disease;
  • C1: telangiectasia or reticular veins;
  • C2: varicose veins;
  • C3: oedema;
  • C4a: pigmentation or eczema;
  • C4b: LDS or atrophie blanche;
  • C4c Corona phlebectatica
  • C5: healed venous ulcer;
  • C6: active venous ulcer.

Clinical class can be further characterised as symptomatic (s), asymptomatic (a) or recurrent following previous successful treatment or healing (r), e.g. C2a, C2s, C6r.

For aetiological classification:

  • Ec: congenital;
  • Ep: primary;
  • Es: secondary (post-thrombotic);
  • En: no venous cause identified.
  • For anatomical classification:
  • As: superficial veins;
  • Ap: perforator veins;
  • Ad: deep veins;
  • An: no venous location identified.
  • For pathophysiological classification:
  • Pr: reflux;
  • Po: obstruction;
  • Pr,o: reflux and obstruction;
  • Pn: no venous pathophysiology identifiable

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Compression

  • While compression stockings are helpful for managing symptoms of venous disease, such as swelling and discomfort, they do not address the underlying reflux or varicose veins directly. Compression is more of an adjunctive measure and not a primary treatment for C4a varicose veins.

Choice C: Non endothermal non tumescent ablation

  • Techniques like mechanical ablation or sclerotherapy (non-endothermal, non-tumescent) are used in certain cases but are typically not the first choice for significant venous reflux with complications like pigmentation or eczema. They are less effective in treating large or deep veins compared to endothermal ablation.

Choice D: Open surgery

  • Open surgery (ligation and stripping) is now largely obsolete in the treatment of varicose veins, particularly when compared to minimally invasive techniques like endothermal ablation. It requires general anaesthesia and involves more invasive procedures, longer recovery times, and more potential complications. It is reserved for specific cases where other techniques are not suitable.

Key Takeaway

  • Endothermal ablation (laser or radiofrequency) is the preferred treatment for C4a varicose veins, offering a minimally invasive, effective, and safe option with rapid recovery.

question_text: A 44 year old Asian man presents with epigastric pains of burning nature. The pain was worst at night. He was prescribed combinations of antacids for a year and but this did not relieve his symptoms entirely. He had an endoscopy which did not show any significant abnormalities 3 months ago. Which is the best test for further investigation for this patient?
explanation:
This patient presents with features of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). In some cases of GERD, endoscopic signs may be absent due to-

  • A partially treated disease

In such instances, 24 hour oesophageal pH study can demonstrate excessive esophageal exposure to refluxed gastric fluid, the physiologic abnormality of GERD.

Urease breath test is done to identify Helicobacter pylori.

Gastric biopsy is done in cases of suspected gastric carcinoma.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2424

question_text: A 38 year old man presents with epigastric pains which are burning in nature and worse at night. He undergoes endoscopy and the investigation confirms a diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD). Which of the following is most likely to relieve his symptoms?
explanation:

question_text: A 58-year-old male presents with dysphagia, retrosternal discomfort and weight loss. Studies reveal achalasia. Which of the following is most definitive way to provide symptomatic relief?
explanation:
The only durable therapies for achalasia are pneumatic dilation and LES myotomy (Heller myotomy). The patient shows excellent symptom improvement. Reflux is the most common side effect and a concomitant anti-relfux procedure (Nissen's fundoplication) may be performed.

Both calcium channel blockers (nifedipine) and nitrates relax the lower oesophageal sphincter. However the effect on symptoms is variable, short-lived and usually suboptimal. Use is frequently limited by adverse effects.

Consequently medical therapy is typically limited to those patients too frail or unwilling to undergo definitive treatment or other therapies.

Latest treatment is POEM.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 23,Pg: 2427-2428

question_text:
A 42 year old man who usually drinks only 2 units of alcohol a day went on an 
alcohol binge with his friends. On that day, he vomited 10 times and was brought to hospital feeling very unwell. He has not previously had any symptoms of dyspepsia or abdominal pains. During physical assessment, he vomits a large bowlful of blood.
What is the likely cause of his haemetemesis?
explanation:
This is a case of Mallory Weiss tear.

  • Longitudinal tear in the mucosa at the gastroesophageal junction.
  • Caused by forceful or prolonged vomiting or coughing.
  • They may also be caused by epileptic convulsions.
  • Usually seen in alcoholics, bulimia nervosa patients.
  • The tear may be followed by vomiting bright red blood or by passing blood in the stool.
  • Active bleed can be treated by endoscopy (band ligation or coaptive coagulation).

A transmural rupture at gastroesophageal junction is called Boerhaave's syndrome.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2433

question_text: Which among the following cytokines is not a contributing factor in intestinal inflammatory disease?
explanation:
Immunologic factors.

  • Humoral and cell-mediated immune reactions directed againstintestinal cells in Crohn disease suggest an autoimmune phenomenon.
  • Attention has focused on the role of cytokines, such as interleukin (IL)-1, IL-2, IL- 8, and TNF-α, as contributing factors in the intestinal inflammatory response.
  • The role of the immune response remains controversial in Crohn disease and may represent an effect of the disease process rather than an actual cause.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1259

question_text: A patient presents with a history of dysphagia, which is more pronounced for liquids than solids. Which of the following radiological signs is likely present?
explanation:
Explanation:

The classic triad of presenting symptoms of achalasia consists of dysphagia, regurgitation, and weight loss. Heartburn, postprandial choking, and nocturnal coughing are commonly seen. The dysphagia that patients experience often begins with liquids and progresses to solids. Barium contrast study typically shows a hold-up of contrast in the distal oesophagus, abnormal contractions in the esophageal body and a tapering stricture in the distal oesophagus, described as a 'bird's beak' or 'rat's tail'. Progressive dilatation leads to a 'sigmoidal shaped oesophagus

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Irregular filling defect

  • Suggests esophageal carcinoma or ulcerating lesions, not typical for achalasia.
  • Dysphagia in carcinoma is usually progressive and starts with solids, not liquids.

Choice C: Smooth filling defect

  • May suggest benign tumors like leiomyomas or esophageal webs, but not associated with classic achalasia.

Choice D: Corkscrew esophagus

  • Seen in diffuse esophageal spasm (DES), a different motility disorder.
  • Characterized by intermittent dysphagia for both solids and liquids with chest pain.

Key Takeaway

  • A "rat tail" sign on barium swallow is highly suggestive of achalasia, especially when dysphagia is more pronounced for liquids than solids.

question_text: A patient presents with a combination of symptoms, including retrosternal chest pain that radiates towards the jaw, and dysphagia. A barium swallow study was performed, and the resultant image is provided. Which of the following is the most probable medical condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Diffuse esophageal spasm is an esophageal motility disorder. On barium swallow, it produces a "corkscrew esophagus" appearance. Patients present with chest pain and dysphagia, especially on consuming spicy food. Sacculations and pseudodiverticula may also be noted.

Explanation of other options:

Infectious esophagitis (Option A): Radiographs show linear, plaque-like lesions rather than corkscrew morphology.

Barrett's esophagus (Option C): Does not show any distinctive radiological finding on barium study.

Esophageal stricture (Option D): Barium swallow demonstrates a narrowed segment with a "shouldering" appearance, not a corkscrew.

Key Takeaways:

Diffuse esophageal spasm shows a corkscrew pattern on barium swallow and is associated with chest pain and dysphagia.

question_text: Peritonitis
explanation: Answer-A. Neutrophils > 250mm3 More than 250 neutrophills/cumm of ascitis fluid suggest an acute inflammatory process, the most common of which is spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. An ascites lactate level of more than 25 mg/di was found to be 100% sensitive and specific in predicting active spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

question_text: A middle-aged man presenting to surgical opd with history of haematemesis after vigorous vomiting. There is no history of chest pain or odynophagia. Patient is not on any anticoagulant therapy. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
MALLORY-WEISS SYNDROME

  • Forceful vomiting may produce a mucosal tear at the cardia rather than a full perforation
  • The mechanism of injury is different. In Boerhaave's syndrome, vomiting occurs against a closed glottis and pressure builds up in the oesophagus. In Mallory-Weiss syndrome, vigorous vomiting produces a vertical split in the gastric mucosa, immediately below the squamocolumnar junction at the cardia in 90% of cases. In only 10% is the tear in the oesophagus.
  • The condition presents with haematemesis. Usually, the bleeding is not severe, but endoscopic injection therapy may be required for the occasional, severe Surgery is rarely required.
  • There are two other injuries to the oesophagus that lie within the spectrum of the mucosal tear of Mallory-Weiss and the full-thickness tear of Boerhaave
  1. Intramural rupture produces a dissection within the oesophageal wall that causes severe chest pain, often with odynophagia. It is best diagnosed by contrast radiology.
  2. Intramural haematoma is seen most often in elderly patients on anticoagulants or patients with coagulation disorders, and usually follows an episode of Large haematomas causing dysphagia can occur, extending from the cardia up to the carina. The diagnosis is readily made on endoscopy.
  • Both intramural rupture and intramural haematoma can be managed conservatively. Symptoms usually resolve in 7-14 days, and oral intake can be reinstituted as soon as symptoms allow.

Patients present with acute onset of chest discomfort or odynophagia. If the haematoma ruptures into the oesophageal lumen haematemesis ensues. When the dissection or haematoma is confined to the oesophageal wall, treatment is conservative. Anticoagulation is corrected and the haematoma usually resolves in 7-14 days.

question_text: A non smoker patient with a history of cardiac disease suddenly develops chest pain and breathlessness, X-ray is performed and given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Initial Clinical Presentation:

  • Dyspnea
  • Tachypnea
  • Hypoxemia
  • Mild hypocapnia
  • CXR: Diffuse bilateral infiltrates (due to increased interstitial fluid)

Pathological Features:

  • Vascular congestion
  • Alveolar collapse
  • Pulmonary edema
  • Inflammatory cell infiltration

Underlying Mechanism:

  • Increased pulmonary capillary permeability → fluid and protein leak into interstitium and alveoli
  • Leukocytes are key mediators:
    • Activated by triggers (e.g., sepsis via complement pathway)
    • Release mediators:
      • Oxygen free radicals
      • Arachidonic acid metabolites
      • Proteases

Progression (If underlying disease not controlled):

  • Vascular thrombosis
  • Interstitial fibrosis
  • Hyaline membrane formation in alveoli

Clinical Consequences:

  • Hypoxemia
  • Pulmonary hypertension
  • CO₂ retention
  • Secondary infections
  • Right heart failure
  • Hypoxia and death

Diagnostic Criteria (Noncardiac Pulmonary Edema):

  • PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio < 200 mmHg
  • Pulmonary edema present without cardiac failure
  • Pulmonary capillary wedge pressure < 18 mmHg

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: Hydrothorax

  • Refers to serous fluid accumulation in the pleural cavity, often due to congestive heart failure or hypoalbuminemia.
  • It would present as a pleural effusion, which typically causes blunting of the costophrenic angles on chest X-ray-not diffuse bilateral infiltrates.

Choice C: Pleural effusion

  • Shows up on imaging as homogeneous opacification with a meniscus sign and obliteration of the costophrenic angle.
  • It typically causes dullness to percussion and reduced breath sounds, not fine crepitations or rales which are more common in pulmonary edema.

Choice D: Pulmonary fibrosis

  • A chronic condition presenting with gradual onset of exertional dyspnea and dry cough.
  • Chest X-ray shows reticulonodular shadowing, especially in the basal zones, and honeycombing in advanced cases-not acute bilateral infiltrates.

Key Takeaway

  • In a non-smoker with cardiac history presenting acutely with dyspnea and chest pain, and chest X-ray showing bilateral infiltrates, pulmonary edema is the most likely diagnosis.

question_text: Clinical question: A 35-year-old male presents to the ER with complaints of epigastric pain for 1 day. On examination, his heart rate is 120/min, and blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg. There is tenderness, guarding, and rigidity on palpation. Based on the clinical presentation and the X-ray findings, what is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of acute abdominal pain, peritonitis (rigidity, guarding, tenderness), hemodynamic instability, mentioned in the clinical vignette and X-ray evidence of free intraperitoneal air is diagnostic of a hollow viscus perforation.

Hollow viscus perforation

A rupture of a hollow abdominal organ (e.g., stomach, small bowel, colon, duodenum) leading to spillage of contents into the peritoneal cavity, causing peritonitis and sepsis.

Clinical features:

  • Sudden, severe abdominal pain (sharp/stabbing).
  • Signs of peritonitis: generalized tenderness, guarding, rigidity (board-like abdomen).
  • Tachycardia due to pain/sepsis.
  • Hypotension due to septic shock or third-space fluid loss.
  • Nausea, vomiting, and fever may occur.

Common causes:

  • Peptic ulcer perforation (most frequent, usually duodenal).
  • Trauma (blunt or penetrating).
  • Diverticulitis with rupture.
  • Crohn's disease or other inflammatory bowel disorders.
  • Perforated appendicitis.
  • Ingested foreign body perforation.

Investigations:

  • X-ray: Free air under the diaphragm = pathognomonic.
  • May also show air-fluid levels if obstruction coexists.
  • CECT scan: Most sensitive for small pneumoperitoneum.

Management:

  • Immediate resuscitation: IV fluids, oxygen, correction of shock.
  • Broad-spectrum antibiotics to cover gram-negative and anaerobes.
  • Definitive treatment: Exploratory laparotomy with repair/resection depending on etiology.

Explanation of Other Options:

Acute cholecystitis (Option A): RUQ pain with fever and Murphy's sign and does not cause free air under the diaphragm.

Sigmoid volvulus (Option C): Presents with abdominal distension and constipation and X-ray shows "coffee bean sign," not free gas.

Small bowel obstruction (Option D): Shows dilated loops with ladder-like valvulae conniventes; free air is not typical unless perforation complicates obstruction.

question_text: Which is the most recent minimal invasive procedure performed for achalasia disease?
explanation:
Treatment

  • Alone among motility disorders, achalasia responds well to treatment. The two main methods are forceful dilatation of the cardia and laparoscopic cardio myotomy (conventionally performed together with a partial fundoplication), although in recent years there has been growing interest in the use of peroral endoscopic myotomy (POEM).
  • Comparative studies between pneumatic dilatation and surgical myotomy suggest equivalence in terms of safety, effectiveness and cost when considered over a number of years.

PNEUMATIC DILATATION

  • This involves stretching the cardia with a balloon to disrupt the muscle and render it less competent.
  • Balloons of 30–40 mm in diameter are available and are inserted over a guidewire. Perforation is the major complication.
  • Forceful dilatation is curative in 75-85% of cases. The results are best in patients aged over 45 years.

HELLER'S MYOTOMY

  • This involves cutting the muscle of the lower oesophagus and cardia.
  • The major complication is gastro- oesophageal reflux, and most surgeons therefore add a partial anterior fundoplication (Heller-Dor operation).
  • The procedure is ideally suited to a minimal access laparoscopic approach, and most surgeons use intraoperative endoscopy to judge the extent of the myotomy and to ensure that the narrow segment is abolished.
  • It is successful in more than 90% of cases and may be used after failed dilatation.

ENDOSCOPIC MYOTOMY

  • This was introduced in Japan in 2009.
  • It involves the creation of a submucosal tunnel in the mid-oesophagus that can be developed distally, allowing a long myotomy to be performed.
  • The oesophageal mucosal defect is clipped shut at the end.

BOTULINUM TOXIN

  • This is done by endoscopic injection into the LOS.
  • It acts by interfering with cholinergic excitatory neural activity at the LOS.
  • The effect is not permanent, and the injection usually has to be repeated after a few months. For this reason, its use is restricted to elderly patients with other comorbidities.

DRUGS

  • Drugs such as calcium channel antagonists have been used but are ineffective for long-term use. However, sublingual nifedipine may be useful for transient relief of symptoms if definitive treatment is postponed.

PRE-ORAL ENDOSCOPIC MYOTOMY

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1122

question_text: All of the following are true for the anatomy of the esophagus except:
option_b: Esophagus starts from the cricopharyngeus muscle
option_d: Lower esophageal sphincter is 40 cms from the incisors teeth
explanation:
Surgical anatomy

  • The oesophagus is a muscular tube, approximately 25 cm long, mainly occupying the posterior mediastinum and extending from the upper oesophageal sphincter (the cricopharyngeus muscle) in the neck to the junction with the cardia of the stomach.
  • The musculature of the upper oesophagus, including the upper sphincter, is striated. This is followed by a transitional zone of both striated and smooth muscle with the proportion of the latter progressively increasing so that, in the lower half of the oesophagus, there is only smooth muscle.
  • It is lined throughout with squamous epithelium.
  • The parasympathetic nerve supply is mediated by branches of the vagus nerve that has synaptic connections to the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus. Meissner's submucosal plexus is sparse in the oesophagus.

In the neck, it descends behind the trachea and anteriorly to the vertebral column following its curvature into the thorax. At the lower part of the thoracic cavity, it transverses the diaphragmatic hiatus, clasped by the crura of the diaphragm and into the stomach. There are slight curvatures of the oesophagus; in the neck, it leans slightly more towards the left side, while in the mid-chest it curves slightly towards the right and in the lower part of the thorax edges to the left again. Thus, in the neck exposure of the cervical oesophagus is generally easier from the left side. The recurrent laryngeal nerves lie in the tracheo-oesophageal grooves. On the right side, the recurrent laryngeal nerve at the lower neck is often at a small distance from the tracheooesophageal groove, while on the left side the nerve is opposed closely to the oesophagus and trachea. This is an important anatomical detail when exposing the oesophagus and when cervical lymphadenectomy is performed.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1106

option_c: I - c, II - d, III - a, IV - b
option_d: I - d, II - a, III - b, IV - c
explanation:
Symptoms of oesophageal disease

  • Difficulty in swallowing described as food or fluid sticking (oesophageal dysphagia): must rule out malignancy
  • Pain on swallowing (odynophagia): suggests inflammation and ulceration
  • Regurgitation or reflux (heartburn): common in gastrooesophageal reflux disease

Chest pain: difficult to distinguish from cardiac pain

According to the Rome IV classification, functional oesophageal disorders include a variety of oesophageal symptoms (heartburn, chest pain, dysphagia, globus) that are not explained by mechanical obstruction (stricture, tumour, EOO), major motor disorders (achalasia, OGJOO, absent contractility, distal oesophageal spasm, jackhammer oesophagus) or GORD. The mechanisms responsible are unclear but are likely to be more related to visceral hypersensitivity and hypervigilance. The diagnosis is generally by exclusion. Physiological and psychological factors should be considered.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1106-1107

question_text: Which scoring system is used for creating a numerical value for cut-off of pathological gastroesophageal reflux?
explanation:
• Ransom and apache-II scoring system are used for pancreatitis
  • Alvarado scoring system is used for appendicitis

Twenty-four-hour pH and combined pH impedance recording

  • Prolonged measurement of pH is now accepted as the most accurate method for the diagnosis of gastro-oesophageal
  • A small pH probe is passed into the distal oesophagus and positioned 5 cm above the upper margin of the LOS, as defined by manometry. The probe is connected to a miniature digital recorder that is worn on a belt and allows most normal activities. Patients mark symptomatic events such as heartburn. A 24-hour recording period is usual, and the pH record is analysed by an automated computer
  • An oesophageal pH <4 at the level of the pH electrode is conventionally considered the cut-off value and, in most oesophageal laboratories, the total time when pH is <4 in a 24-hour period does not exceed 4% in a healthy adult. Patterns of reflux and the correlation between symptoms and oesophageal pH <4 can be calculated. Most laboratories use a scoring system (Johnson–DeMeester) to create a numerical value, above which reflux is considered
  • Radiotelemetry pH probes are also available that can be fixed to the oesophageal wall endoscopically without the need for a transnasal

question_text: Which among the following is better modality for the screening of gastric cancer?
explanation:
• Gastric cancer screening has been implemented in some regions with high incidence, such as Japan, Korea, and Chile.
  • The two primary modalities for screening are upper endoscopy and barium radiography, with upper endoscopy having better sensitivity.
  • While there is evidence suggesting that screening in high-incidence populations improves oncologic outcomes, this has not been evaluated in a randomized trial.
  • The optimal screening modality and interval have not been universally established and varies by region. Selective screening of patients with specific risk factors can be considered, including gastric polyps/adenomas, pernicious anemia, and certain genetic disorders.
  • Of note, this should not include patients with hereditary diffuse gastric cancer as these tumors often arise beneath an intact mucosa and would be missed by routine screening.

question_text: Which among the following gene is not associated with inflammatory bowel disease?
explanation:
Genetic factors.

  • Genetic factors play an important role in the pathogenesis of Crohn disease because the single strongest risk factor for development of disease is having a first-degree relative with Crohn disease.
  • The genes with the strongest and most frequently replicated associations with Crohn disease are NOD2, MHC, and MST1 3p21.
  • Putative inflammatory bowel disease loci have been identified on chromosomes 16q, 5q, 19p, 7q, and 3p.
  • The most important gene in Crohn disease development is NOD2. The NOD2 gene is associated with a decreased expression of antimicrobial peptides by Paneth Heterozygosity of one NOD2 variant confers a 2- to 4-fold increase in risk of Crohn disease, while homozygosity confers a 17- to 40-fold increase in risk. In addition, NOD2 has been identified as a genetic predictor of ileal disease, ileal stenosis, fistula, and Crohn-related surgery.
  • Another gene, CARD15, leads to impaired activation of the transcription factor nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) and also specifically codes for a protein expressed in monocytes, macrophages, dendritic cells, epithelial cells, and Paneth cells.
  • CARD15 is also helpful in distinguishing Crohn disease from ulcerative colitis as it is more strongly associated with Crohn disease, especially in patients of northern European descent.
  • The FHIT gene located on 3p14.2 has been identified as a tumor suppressor gene and is suggested to play a role in the pathogenesis of Crohn disease as well as in the development and progression of Crohn disease-related cancers.
  • A complex cellular and molecular crosstalk occurs between the genes NOD2/CARD15 and the autophagy gene ATG16L1, which is associated with a synergistic increase in earlier onset and disease severity.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1259

question_text: Which of the following statements is false for corrosive injury of the oesophagus?
option_a: Acids are ingested in large amount than alkalis
option_b: Alkalis cause liquefaction, saponification of fats, dehydration and thrombosis of blood vessels which usually leads to fibrous scarring.
option_c: Acids cause coagulative necrosis with eschar formation, and this coagulant may limit penetration to deeper layers of the oesophageal wall.
option_d: Alkalis cause more gastric damage than acids
explanation:
CORROSIVE INJURY

  • Corrosives such as sodium hydroxide (lye, caustic soda) or sulphuric acid may be taken in an attempted suicide.
  • Accidental ingestion occurs in children and when corrosives are stored in bottles labelled as beverages.
  • All can cause severe damage to the mouth, pharynx, larynx, oesophagus and stomach. The type of agent, its concentration and the volume ingested largely determine the extent of damage.
  • In general, alkalis are relatively odourless and tasteless, making them more likely to be ingested in large volume.
  • Alkalis cause liquefaction, saponification of fats, dehydration and thrombosis of blood vessels which usually leads to fibrous scarring.
  • Acids cause coagulative necrosis with eschar formation, and this coagulant may limit penetration to deeper layers of the oesophageal wall.
  • Acids also cause more gastric damage than alkalis because of the induction of intense pylorospasm with pooling in the antrum.

CORROSIVE INJURY OF THE OESOPHAGOUS

This is a longitudinal tear at the GOJ, which is induced by repetitive and strenuous vomiting. Doubtless, many such lesions occur and do not cause bleeding. question_text: A patient with a history of heavy alcohol consumption presents with repeated vomiting and hematemesis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
