question_text: A 45-year-old alcoholic with a history of binge drinking presents with an episode of vomiting bright red blood. His vitals are stable. An endoscopy was performed; what is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The history of binge drinking followed by forceful vomiting and hematemesis is classic for a Mallory-Weiss tear. This is a longitudinal mucosal laceration at the gastroesophageal junction caused by a sudden rise in intra-abdominal pressure during vomiting. It typically presents with bright red hematemesis after retching. The patient's stable vitals are consistent with this diagnosis, as bleeding is often self-limiting.

Treatment:

Endoscopic Methods:

  • Multipolar electrocoagulation
  • Epinephrine injection
  • Endoscopic band ligation
  • Endoscopic hemoclipping

For Persistent/Recurrent Bleeding:

  • Angiographic transarterial embolization
  • Surgical intervention (rare):
    • Approach through the anterior gastrotomy
    • Oversew bleeding site with deep 2-0 silk ligatures

Severe/Ongoing Bleeding:

  • Endoscopic therapy (injection or electrocoagulation)
  • Angiographic embolization with absorbable material (e.g., gelatin sponge)
  • High gastrotomy and suturing of the mucosal tear if other methods fail

Explanation of other options:

Tension pneumothorax (Option A): This is a respiratory emergency with absent breath sounds and tracheal deviation, not associated with vomiting blood.

Boerhaave syndrome (Option B): This is a full-thickness esophageal rupture also caused by vomiting. It presents with severe chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema, and shock (Mackler's triad), not just hematemesis with stable vitals.

Gastric ulcer perforation (Option D): Perforation causes sudden, severe abdominal pain peritonitis, not isolated hematemesis.

Key Takeaways:

  • Mallory-Weiss tear: Hematemesis after forceful vomiting/retching.
  • Boerhaave syndrome: Full-thickness rupture with pain, sepsis, and shock.

question_text: A barium swallow radiographic image of a woman with dysphagia is given below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Achalasia is a motility disorder of the esophagus caused by the progressive degeneration of ganglion cells in the myenteric plexus. This results in failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax and loss of peristalsis in the distal esophagus.

  • Barium swallow finding: Classically shows a bird-beak appearance with proximal esophageal dilatation.
  • Manometry (gold standard): Elevated LES resting pressure, incomplete LES relaxation, and absent peristalsis.
  • Clinical features: Dysphagia (liquids and solids), regurgitation, halitosis, chest pain, and weight loss.
  • Endoscopy: Excludes malignancy or structural obstruction.

Explanation of Other Options:

Distal Esophageal Spasm (Option B): This condition presents with characteristic "corkscrew" appearance on barium swallow, due to irregular, simultaneous contractions in the distal esophagus.

Jackhammer Esophagus (Option C): This condition involves excessive peristalsis with very strong contractions, resulting in a tight, hypercontractile esophagus. It can cause dysphagia but has a different radiographic appearance.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: The provided barium swallow indicates:
explanation:
Explanation:

Achalasia cardia is characterized by a dilated esophagus with a narrowed distal end, producing a "bird beak sign" on barium swallow. Patients often have greater difficulty swallowing liquids than solids.

Explanation of other options:

Diffuse esophageal spasm (Option B): Shows a corkscrew pattern, not a bird beak.

Nutcracker esophagus (Option C): Radiologically similar to diffuse spasm with corkscrew appearance, not bird beak.

Hypertensive lower esophageal sphincter (Option D): Does not produce the bird beak appearance seen in achalasia.

Key Takeaways:

Achalasia cardia shows bird beak narrowing on barium swallow and is associated with dysphagia, more severe for liquids than solids.

question_text: Barium swallow demonstrates
explanation:
• Distal esophageal spasm is a condition in which there are incoordinate, premature and rapidly propagated contractions of the esophagus, causing dysphagia and/or chest pain.
  • The condition may be dramatic, with marked hypertrophy of the circular muscle and a corkscrew esophagus on the barium esophagogram .
  • These abnormal contractions are more common in the distal two-thirds of the esophageal body.
  • Hypercontractile (jackhammer) esophagus is characterized by high-amplitude contractions and should be differentiated from contractility disorder secondary to outflow obstruction. Patients may present with dysphagia or pain. There is no well-proven treatment strategy for hypercontractile motility disorders.
  • Patients should avoid any identifiable triggering factors (e.g. dietary or GORD related). Similar to achalasia, medical therapy such as calcium channel blockers, nitrates, 5′-phosphodiesterase inhibitors and pain modulators have been used with limited efficacy. Botulinum toxin injection in the esophageal body may be useful.

Long-segment surgical myotomy has been attempted with good results. POEM with extended myotomy is also advocated as a minimally invasive approach to treat these disorders.

question_text: A middle-aged man presents with progressive difficulty in swallowing both solids and liquids for the past 8 months. The barium swallow findings are as shown below. Upper GI endoscopy and esophageal manometry are performed. Which of the following statements regarding this condition is incorrect?
option_a: Loss of lower oesophageal sphincter pressure causing reflux
option_b: <75% relaxation of the lower oesophageal sphincter
option_c: It is a primary motility disorder
explanation:
Explanation:

Barium swallow imaging demonstrates the classic bird-beak appearance, which, together with the clinical presentation, is suggestive of achalasia cardia. Achalasia cardia is associated with increased pressure rather than a loss of pressure of the LES.

Achalasia cardia

  • A primary motility disorder characterised by the progressive degeneration of ganglion cells in the esophageal wall. (Option C ruled out)
  • Leads to a loss of peristalsis in the lower oesophagus and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) to relax during swallowing. (Option D ruled out)
  • Clinical features
    • Dysphagia: May initially affect liquids more than solids.
    • Regurgitation
    • Halitosis
    • Chest Pain
    • Weight Loss

Investigations

Oesophageal Manometry: Gold Standard

  • Definitive diagnostic test for achalasia.
  • Measures the pressure and pattern of muscle contractions in the esophagus. Characteristic findings include:
    • Elevated resting LES pressure (typically > 45 mmHg).
    • Incomplete LES relaxation. (< 75%) (Option B ruled out)
    • Absence of peristalsis in the esophageal body.
    • Periodic contractions with normal amplitude or high amplitude contractions (type I and II achalasia).

Barium swallow

  • Shows dilated esophagus with a narrowing at the LES giving the bird beak appearance or the rat tail appearance.

Endoscopy

  • Normal mucosa but may show dilated esophagus with possible food debris.
  • It is important to rule out other causes of dysphagia, such as tumours.

question_text: A 47-year-old patient presents with progressive dysphagia for both solids and liquids, regurgitation of undigested food, and unintentional weight loss over the last several months. A barium swallow test is performed. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The classic "rat tail" or "bird beak" appearance on barium swallow is pathognomonic of achalasia cardia, a primary esophageal motility disorder.

It is caused by degeneration of ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, leading to:

  • Loss of peristalsis in the lower esophagus, and
  • Failure of relaxation of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) during swallowing.

This results in functional obstruction at the gastroesophageal junction, causing gradual dilatation of the proximal esophagus and symptoms of dysphagia, regurgitation, and chest pain.

Explanation of Other Options:

Esophageal carcinoma (Option B):

  • Presents with progressive dysphagia, but typically solids first, then liquids.
  • Barium swallow: Irregular, constricted, "apple-core" or "shouldering" defect (not smooth tapering).
  • May cause mucosal irregularity, not the uniform narrowing seen in achalasia.
  • Often accompanied by weight loss and cachexia.

Zenker's diverticulum (Option C):

  • A pulsion diverticulum arising from the posterior hypopharyngeal wall (Killian's dehiscence).
  • Presents with regurgitation of undigested food, gurgling neck swelling, and halitosis.
  • Barium swallow: Shows a pouch-like outpouching posterior to the esophagus, not a tapering distal narrowing.
  • Typically occurs in elderly men.

Diffuse esophageal spasm (Option D):

  • Characterized by uncoordinated, simultaneous contractions of the esophageal body.
  • LES relaxation remains normal.
  • Barium swallow: Shows a "corkscrew" or "rosary bead" appearance - multiple irregular indentations rather than smooth tapering.
  • Symptoms include intermittent dysphagia and chest pain mimicking angina.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: A 54-year-old male with a history of repeated vomiting, binge alcohol intake, and heavy meals presents to the emergency department with sudden, severe left-sided chest pain radiating to the left shoulder. Chest X-ray shows pneumoperitoneum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is esophageal perforation, specifically Boerhaave's syndrome (spontaneous rupture of the esophagus following forceful vomiting).

  • The classic triad includes: severe chest pain, vomiting, and subcutaneous emphysema.
  • Risk factors include alcohol binge and heavy meals (increase intraluminal pressure).
  • The presence of pneumoperitoneum on imaging suggests leakage of air from the gastrointestinal tract, supporting esophageal rupture.

Boerhaave's syndrome is characterized by spontaneous esophageal perforation due to forceful vomiting. Key features include severe chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema.

Explanation of Other Options:

Mediastinal air leak (Option A): Can occur due to trauma or spontaneous rupture of alveoli (Macklin effect), but the classic history of vomiting and chest pain favors Boerhaave's syndrome.

Pneumoperitoneum (Option C): Represents free intraperitoneal air, usually from perforated peptic ulcer or hollow viscus perforation. However, isolated pneumoperitoneum does not explain the severe chest pain radiating to the shoulder.

Peptic ulcer (Option D): Typically presents with epigastric pain, may cause perforation and peritonitis, but not sudden chest pain after vomiting as seen here.

question_text: A 25 year female patient presents with progressive dysphagia to solids and liquids. Barium swallow was done. What are the investigation needed to confirm your diagnosis?
explanation:
Clinical features such as dysphagia(to both solid and liquid), regurgitation and heartburn are suggestive of achalasia cardia, milder form of which can be often confused with GERD.

The barium swallow shows typical "bird beak sign" Or "rat tail appearance".

Endoscopy typically shows frothy saliva pooling in the oesophagus and the presence of food residue.

Endoscopy must also be performed in all suspected cases of Achalasia to rule out narrowing due to pseudoachalasia (GEJ tumors, stricture, neuropathy)

Definitive diagnosis relies on HRM(high resolution manometry).

question_text: The likely diagnosis for a newborn infant presenting with signs of intestinal obstruction, as indicated by the x-ray image and CT abdomen showing an annular pancreas, is:
explanation:
Explanation:

The given x-ray shows a classic finding of double bubble sign seen in duodenal atresia.

Duodenal atresia

  • Results from the failure of recanalisation of the intestinal lumen during embryogenesis and development.
  • Associated conditions
    • Congenital anomalies like heart disease, malrotation, annular pancreas
    • Chromosomal abnormalities like trisomy 21
  • Clinical Presentation
    • Bilious vomiting without abdominal distention.
    • Symptoms typically present within the first few days of life.
  • Diagnosis is confirmed by the double bubble sign on the abdominal X-ray and prenatal ultrasonography.
  • Treatment
    • Initial: Nasogastric decompression and IV fluids
    • Definitive: Surgical repair (Duodenoduodenostomy)
    • Postoperative care: Gastrostomy tube, nutritional support

Explanation of other options:

Jejunoileal atresia (Option A): Jejunal atresia is characterised by multiple dilated loops of the small bowel and a triple bubble sign on X-ray, not the double bubble sign. It can cause bilious vomiting, and polyhydramnios association is less common compared to duodenal atresia.

Esophageal atresia (Option B): Oesophageal atresia involves a discontinuity or abnormality of the oesophagus, often presenting with excessive drooling, coughing, difficulty feeding, and respiratory distress. Imaging shows a gas-filled or gasless abdomen and a coiled tube in the upper oesophagus.

Colonic atresia (Option D): Refers to a blockage or absence of a portion of the colon, which is less common than other forms of atresia. It would not present with the classic double bubble sign in duodenal atresia or annular pancreas.

question_text: A 32-year-old patient who is a chronic tobacco chewer presents with a whitish lesion on the gingivobuccal sulcus for 7 months. What is the next best step in the management of this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient presents with a whitish lesion on the gingivobuccal sulcus persisting for 7 months, alongside a history of tobacco chewing. This clinical picture is indicative of Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSMF). Local excision with biopsy is essential to establish the diagnosis and to exclude the presence of malignancy or dysplastic changes.

Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSMF):

Definition: A chronic, progressive condition of the oral mucosa characterized by fibrous bands, leading to stiffness and recognized as a precancerous disorder.

Key Etiology:

  • Hypersensitivity to tobacco, betel nut, areca nut, and chilli.
  • Vitamin deficiencies and nutritional insufficiencies.
  • Localized collagen disorders, causing altered collagen metabolism.
  • Results in juxtaepithelial inflammatory fibrosis, mucosal atrophy, and potential dysplasia.

Clinical Features:

  • More common in Asian populations.
  • Males and females are equally affected.
  • Symptoms: mouth soreness (especially during meals), burning sensation, vesicular eruptions, trismus, and difficulty protruding the tongue.
  • Fibrosis, scarring, and ankylosing glossitis are prominent signs.

Management:

  • Cessation of causative factors: tobacco, areca nut, chilli.
  • Oral hygiene maintenance.
  • Local corticosteroid injections: dexamethasone, hydrocortisone.
  • Submucosal HCG injections.
  • Vitamin and iron supplementation.
  • Surgical excision with grafting for severe cases.
  • Stem cell therapy as an emerging treatment.

Explanation of Other Options:

Avoid smoking + Wait and watch (Option B) ignores the seriousness of the lesion and its potential for malignant transformation. Delaying biopsy and treatment may allow progression and worsen outcomes.

Steroidal Injection (Option C) can help reduce inflammation in Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSMF) but is not the first step. A biopsy is essential initially to confirm the diagnosis and rule out malignancy before starting steroid therapy.

Sclerotherapy (Option D) is intended for vascular abnormalities, not OSMF, and is not appropriate as initial treatment. A biopsy must be performed first to accurately assess and manage the lesion.

question_text: Which one of the following is symptom of lung cancer?
explanation:
Clinical features

Clinical features of lung carcinoma depend on:

  • the site of the lesion;
  • the invasion of neighbouring structures;
  • the extent of metastases.
  • Common symptoms include a persistent cough, weight loss, dyspnoea and non-specific chest pain.
  • Haemoptysis occurs in fewer than 50% of patients presenting for the first time.
  • Cough, or a changed cough, is a common presentation but non-specific in this population.
  • Severe localised pain suggests chest wall invasion with the infiltration of an intercostal nerve. Invasion of the apical area may involve the brachial plexus, leading to Pancoast's syndrome.
  • Dyspnoea may come from loss of functioning lung tissue,lymphatic invasion or the development of a large pleural effusion.
  • Pleural fluid is an ominous feature and the presence of blood in a pleural effusion suggests that the pleura has been directly invaded.
  • Clubbing and hypertrophic pulmonary osteoarthropathy accompany some lung cancers and may resolve with excision of the primary lesion.
  • Invasion of the mediastinum may result in hoarseness (because of recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement), dysphagia (because of the involvement of, or extrinsic pressure on, the oesophagus) and superior vena caval obstruction.
  • Small cell carcinoma is associated with the development of myopathies including the Eaton-Lambert syndrome, which is similar to myasthenia gravis.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 59, Cardiac Surgery, Pg: 985.

question_text: Which of the following is not the surgical method of oesophagectomy performed for oesophageal cancer?
explanation:
SURGERY

  • Histological tumour type, location and the extent of the proposed lymphadenectomy all influence the surgical approach. This is largely an issue of surgical preference, although it should be recognised that a left thoracoabdominal approach is limited proximally by the aortic arch and should be avoided when the primary tumour is at or above this level.
  • Similarly, transhiatal oesophagectomy is unsuitable for most patients with squamous cell carcinoma because a complete mediastinal lymphadenectomy is not easily achieved by this approach.
  • The most widely practised approach in the west is the two-phase Ivor Lewis (sometimes called Lewis-Tanner) operation with an initial laparotomy and construction of a gastric tube, followed by a right thoracotomy to excise the tumour and create an oesophagogastric anastomosis. The closer this is placed to the apex of the thoracic cavity, the fewer problems there are with reflux disease.
  • Three-phase oesophagectomy (McKeown) may be more appropriate for more proximal tumours in order to achieve better longitudinal clearance, although the additional distance gained is less than many surgeons believe. A third cervical incision also permits lymphadenectomy in this region.

TWO-PHASE OESOPHAGECTOMY (ABDOMEN AND RIGHT CHEST, IVOR LEWIS)

  • Mobilisation of the stomach must be done with care because it is essential to have a tension-free, well-vascularised stomach for transposition.
  • The left gastric, short gastric and left gastroepiploic arteries are all divided. The viability of the transposed stomach mainly depends on the right gastroepiploic and, to a lesser extent, the right gastric vessels.
  • It should be noted that venous drainage is as important as arterial supply, and it is essential to perform an accurate anatomical dissection that preserves the right gastroepiploic vein as well as the artery. The stomach is divided to remove the cardia and the upper part of the lesser curve, including the whole of the left gastric artery and its associated lymph nodes.

TRANSHIATAL OESOPHAGECTOMY (WITHOUT THORACOTOMY)

  • This approach was popularised for cancer by Orringer, adapting a technique developed in Brazil by Pinotti for the removal of chagasic megaoesophagus.
  • The stomach is mobilised through a midline abdominal incision or by laparoscopy, and the cervical oesophagus is mobilised through an incision in the neck.
  • The diaphragm is then opened from the abdomen, and the posterior mediastinum is entered. The lower oesophagus and the tumour are mobilised under direct vision, and the upper oesophagus is mobilised by blunt dissection. This approach can provide an adequate removal of the tumour and lymph nodes in the lower mediastinum, but it is not possible to remove the nodes in the middle or upper mediastinum.
  • It may be a useful procedure for lesions of the lower oesophagus, but is hazardous for a middle third lesion that may be adherent to the bronchus or to the azygos vein.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1141

question_text: A patient underwent bronchoscopy, during the procedure a perforation occurred at 25 cm. Which structure is most likely to be damaged?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The arch of the aorta indents the esophagus at the level of T4 vertebra.
  • From the central incisor, this point is approximately 25 cm.
  • This site represents one of the physiological constrictions of the esophagus (important for endoscopy, foreign body impaction, and carcinoma spread).

Explanation of Other Options:

Cricopharynx (Option A): Located at the level of C6 vertebra, ~15 cm from the incisors. First and narrowest esophageal constriction.

Left principal bronchus (Option C): Causes esophageal constriction at ~28 cm from incisors (T5 vertebral level).

Diaphragm (Option D): Esophagus passes through diaphragm at T10 vertebral level, ~40 cm from incisors.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: Which of the following is the best investigation to establish a diagnosis of GERD?
explanation:
Explanation:

24-hour ambulatory pH monitoring is considered the gold standard for objectively diagnosing GERD. It directly measures the frequency and duration of acid reflux episodes (pH <4) in the esophagus over a full day, providing quantitative data that correlates with symptoms. This is especially useful for patients with typical symptoms but a normal endoscopy.

Explanation of other options:

Upper GI endoscopy (Option B): Endoscopy is excellent for visualizing complications of GERD (esophagitis, Barrett's esophagus, strictures) but is often normal in patients with non-erosive reflux disease (NERD), making it less sensitive for establishing the initial diagnosis.

CECT & MRI (Options C and D): Cross-sectional imaging like CT and MRI have no role in the routine diagnosis of GERD, as they cannot detect acid reflux.

Key Takeaways:

  • 24-hour pH monitoring is the gold standard for diagnosing GERD.
  • Endoscopy is used to assess for complications, not primarily for diagnosis.

question_text: What is the diagnosis based on the given barium swallow image?

Which of the following is/are extra-oesophageal manifestations of GERD?
1.Asthma
2.Laryngitis
3.Pulmonary Fibrosis
4.Chronic cough
explanation:
Explanation:

All the listed conditions can be considered extra-esophageal manifestations of GERD.

GERD is not confined to the oesophagus; the refluxate (acid and pepsin) can travel proximally to affect the upper aerodigestive tract, resulting in ENT, respiratory, and even dental complications.

Mechanism:

Micro-aspiration or direct acid injury to the laryngeal and respiratory mucosa leads to inflammation and hyperresponsiveness, explaining the respiratory symptoms.

question_text: Which among the following is not the symptom for gastric carcinoma?
explanation:
• The symptoms of gastric cancer are generally vague and nonspecific, contributing to its frequently advanced stage at the time of diagnosis.
  • Symptoms include epigastric pain, early satiety, and weight loss.
  • These symptoms are frequently mistaken for more common benign causes of dyspepsia including PUD and gastritis.
  • The epigastric pain associated with gastric cancer tends to be constant and non radiating and is generally not relieved by eating.
  • More advanced lesions may manifest with either gastric outlet obstruction or/strong> dysphagia depending on the location of the tumor. Some degree of GI bleeding is common, with 40% of patients having some form of anemia.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 49, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1222

question_text: All of the following are localized variety of Basal cell carcinoma except?
explanation:
BCC can be divided into

  • localised (nodular; nodulocystic; cystic; pigmented and naevoid) and
  • generalised (superficial: multifocal and superficial spreading; or infiltrative: morphoeic, ice pick and cicatrizing).

Nodular and nodulocystic variants account for 90% of BCC.

Typical naevi can be sporadic or familial (familial atypical multiple mole-melanoma [FAMMM] syndrome). Possession of more than five lesions confers a relative risk of melanoma six times greater than usual; within FAMMM syndrome, they confer a 100% risk of malignant melanoma and patients with FAMMM syndrome should be screened for melanoma 6-monthly, lifelong.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 45 Pathophysiology of the skin and subcutaneous tissues, Pg: 651-652

question_text: Which is the most common site of occurrence of gastric cancer?
explanation:
Site

  • The proximal stomach is now the most common site for gastric cancer in resource-rich western countries.
  • Because so many malignancies occur at the oesophageal-gastric junction, and because the lower oesophagus is also a very common site of adenocarcinoma, it is artificial to separate the stomach from the oesophagus. Therefore, it is best to consider the whole of the upper gastrointestinal tract from the cricopharyngeus to the pylorus. It can be seen that just under 60% of all of the malignancies occurring in the oesophagus and stomach occur in proximity to the oesophagogastric junction.
  • Adenocarcinoma at this site has doubled in incidence in the UK over the last 30 years. This high prevalence of proximal gastric cancer is not seen in Japan, where distal cancer still predominates, as it does in most of the rest of the world.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1170

question_text: What are the laboratory findings seen in medullary carcinoma of thyroid?
option_a: Low calcitonin and high carcinoembryonic antigen
option_b: Low calcitonin and low carcinoembryonic antigen
option_d: High calcitonin and high carcinoembryonic antigen
explanation:
• These are tumours of the parafollicular (C cells) derived from the neural crest. rather than the cells of the thyroid follicle as are other primary thyroid carcinomas.
  • The cells are not unlike those of a carcinoid tumour and on histological analysis a characteristic amyloid stroma is seen.
  • High levels of serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen are produced by many medullary tumours, which should be tested for in suspected cases.
  • Calcitonin levels fall after resection and rise again with recurrence, making it a valuable tumour marker in the follow-up of patients with this disease.
  • Diarrhoea is a feature in 30% of cases and this may be due to 5-hydroxytryptamine or prostaglandins produced by the tumour cells.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 870-871

question_text: Which of the following is reduced in achalasia?
option_a: NO and VIP in lower esophagus
explanation:
Achalasia

Pathology and etiology

  • The term achalasia originated from the Greek word 'khalasis', meaning 'failure to relax'.
  • The etiology remains uncertain but is postulated to be due to loss of the inhibitory ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus, possibly related to a virus-induced autoimmune effect.
  • Histology of muscle specimens generally shows a reduction in the number of ganglion cells with a variable degree of chronic inflammation.
  • During a normal swallow, the food bolus will trigger primary peristalsis in the esophagus by sequential activation of excitatory lower motor neurons. At the same time, relaxation of the LOS allows esophageal emptying.
  • The mismatch in excitatory and inhibitory activity results in the failure of LOS relaxation and absent peristalsis. With time, the esophagus dilated and contractions disappeared, so that the esophagus empties mainly by the hydrostatic pressure of its contents. This is nearly always incomplete, leaving residual food and fluid.
  • The air-fluid level in the stomach evidenced on radiography taken in the erect position in normal individuals is frequently absent, as no bolus with its accompanying air passes through the LOS.
  • The esophagus becomes progressively more tortuous and dilated (megaesophagus); persistent retention of oesophagitis due to fermentation of food residues may predispose to the increased incidence of carcinoma of the esophagus.

question_text: Identify the procedure commonly performed in patients with recurrent gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD):
explanation:
Explanation:

360-degree Nissen fundoplication is the most commonly performed surgical procedure for recurrent GERD unresponsive to medical therapy.

  • GERD is caused by dysfunction of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES), allowing stomach contents to reflux into the esophagus.
  • While lifestyle changes and medications like PPIs and H2 blockers are first-line therapies, surgical intervention is indicated in refractory cases or when complications arise.
  • Nissen fundoplication involves a 360-degree wrap of the gastric fundus around the lower esophagus, strengthening the LES and preventing reflux.
  • It remains the gold standard surgery for GERD, especially when symptoms persist despite optimal medical therapy.
  • Key components of anti-reflux surgery:
    • Restore intra-abdominal esophagus
    • Crural (diaphragmatic) repair
    • Fundoplication - reinforcement of the LES
  • Fundoplication types:
    • Nissen (360°) - complete wrap, more effective long-term control of reflux
    • Toupet (270° posterior) and Dor (anterior) - partial wraps used in patients with poor esophageal motility

Explanation of other options:

Partial gastrectomy (Option B): Not a treatment for GERD; typically used for gastric malignancies or refractory peptic ulcer disease.

Esophageal banding (Option C): A treatment for esophageal varices in portal hypertension, not used for reflux disease.

270-degree Nissen fundoplication (Option D): A misleading term, this refers to Toupet fundoplication, which is a partial posterior wrap. It’s used in selected cases, especially with esophageal dysmotility, but has higher long-term recurrence rates than full Nissen.

question_text: A 70-year-old man reports progressively worsening difficulty in swallowing both solids and liquids. Esophageal manometry reveals loss of coordinated peristaltic contractions in the lower esophagus and a markedly elevated resting tone of the lower esophageal sphincter (LES). What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation

  • The simultaneous involvement of both solids and liquids at an early stage strongly suggests a motility disorder rather than a structural narrowing.
  • Manometry, the gold standard test, confirms the diagnosis by showing:
    • Raised basal LES pressure (often >45 mmHg).
    • Failure of LES relaxation after swallowing.
  • These features are diagnostic of achalasia cardia.

Achalasia Cardia

Quick Diagnostic Mnemonic- Dysphagia Patterns

  • "Solids first → then liquids" = Mechanical obstruction (e.g., carcinoma, stricture).
  • "Solids + liquids together" = Motility disorder (e.g., achalasia, scleroderma).

Explanation of Other Options:

Stomach cancer (Option A): Dysphagia is not an early feature; obstruction develops late from bulky tumors at the cardia or pylorus. Associated symptoms include vomiting, anemia, and early satiety. Manometry does not show aperistalsis with high LES tone.

Cancer esophagus (Option B): Classically produces progressive dysphagia beginning with solids and later involving liquids due to a luminal narrowing. Manometry indicates obstruction but not a hypertonic LES with absent peristalsis.

GERD (Option C): Gastroesophageal reflux disease typically causes heartburn and regurgitation. Manometry shows low LES pressure or transient relaxations, not increased tone with aperistalsis.

question_text: The endoscopic image shows the following finding: What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Prominent, tortuous veins along the esophageal wall seen on endoscopy are characteristic of esophageal varices.

  • Esophageal varices are dilated submucosal veins in the lower third of the esophagus that develop as a complication of portal hypertension, most commonly due to liver cirrhosis.
  • The increased pressure in the portal venous system causes collateral blood flow through the esophageal veins, leading to their dilation.
  • On endoscopy, they appear as bluish, tortuous, bulging vessels within the esophageal lumen.
  • These varices are clinically important due to their potential for massive upper gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Management includes non-selective beta-blockers for prophylaxis, endoscopic variceal ligation (EVL) for active bleeding, and in severe cases, procedures like TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt).

Explanation of other options:

Barrett's esophagus (Option A): This presents as a salmon-pink mucosa replacing the pale squamous epithelium in the distal esophagus due to chronic GERD. It lacks prominent vascular structures.

Gastric erosion (Option C): These appear in the stomach as superficial mucosal breaks or red inflamed areas, not in the esophagus and not as dilated veins.

Chronic GERD (Option D): May show erosive esophagitis, strictures, or Barrett’s changes, but does not result in variceal veins in the esophagus.

question_text: A patient presents with dysphagia, retrosternal pain, and regurgitation with coughing after meals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Esophageal diverticula are outpouchings of the esophageal wall that trap food and secretions. They cause dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, halitosis, cough, and aspiration, especially at night.

Types, Features, and Management

Explanation of other options:

Brown-Patterson-Kelly syndrome (Option A): Triad of iron deficiency anaemia, dysphagia, and esophageal webs; not associated with regurgitation.

Achalasia (Option B): Failure of LES relaxation; dysphagia for solids and liquids with "bird's beak" appearance on barium swallow.

Reflux esophagitis (Option D): Causes heartburn and regurgitation due to GERD; dysphagia is late and usually due to stricture formation.

question_text: A patient who recently underwent Nissen fundoplication is currently asymptomatic with stable vital signs during evening rounds. What should be the next step in management?
option_a: Nasogastric tube to prevent gas bloat syndrome
option_b: Insert chest tube to prevent pneumothorax
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Since the patient is asymptomatic with stable vital signs after Nissen fundoplication, the next step is careful monitoring of vitals and clinical status.
  • Nissen fundoplication is a surgical procedure used to treat gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

Explanation of other options:

Nasogastric tube to prevent gas bloat syndrome (Option A): While gas bloat syndrome can be a complication post-fundoplication procedure, it would not necessitate routine nasogastric tube insertion unless symptoms of bloating or distension arise.

Insert chest tube to prevent pneumothorax (Option B), Imaging to rule out perforation (Option D): There is no indication for a chest tube or imaging to rule out perforation, as the patient is asymptomatic with stable vitals and shows no signs of pneumothorax or perforation.

question_text: During ward rounds, you evaluate a patient diagnosed with esophageal carcinoma.Which of the following is the most characteristic presenting symptom pattern in this condition?
option_a: Dysphagia of liquids followed by solids
option_b: Dysphagia of solids followed by liquids
explanation:
Explanation:

The classic presenting feature of esophageal carcinoma is progressive dysphagia, which starts with solids and gradually progresses to liquids.

This sequence reflects the mechanical obstruction caused by a growing intraluminal tumour that narrows the esophageal lumen.

  • Initially, only solid food (which requires more luminal space) is difficult to swallow.
  • As the tumour enlarges, even liquids cannot pass easily, leading to complete dysphagia.

Associated symptoms include odynophagia, weight loss, anorexia, regurgitation, and aspiration in advanced disease.

Explanation of Other Options:

Dysphagia of liquids followed by solids (Option A):

  • Seen in achalasia cardia, where there is loss of peristalsis and failure of LES relaxation.
  • The dysphagia is non-progressive and equal for solids and liquids early on.
  • Barium swallow: "bird-beak" appearance.

Chest pain (Option C):

  • Occurs later, due to tumour invasion into the mediastinum, pleura, or trachea.
  • May present as retrosternal discomfort or pain radiating to the back.
  • Not the earliest or most common symptom.

Neck mass (Option D):

  • Represents lymphatic metastasis (e.g., left supraclavicular / Virchow's node).
  • Rarely an initial sign unless upper esophageal carcinoma.

question_text: Which part of the stomach contains chief cells?
explanation:
Chief cells

  • These lie principally proximally in the gastric crypts and produce pepsinogen.
  • Two forms of pepsinogen are described: pepsinogen I and pepsinogen II. Both are produced by the chief cell, but pepsinogen I is produced only in the stomach.
  • The ratio between pepsinogens I and II in the serum decreases with gastric atrophy.
  • Pepsinogen is activated in the stomach to produce the digestive protease, pepsin.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1150

question_text:
A 46 year woman is admitted due to a single episode of haematemesis after taking a tablet of 
ibuprofen 6 hours previously. On examination, she had a blood pressure of 120/75 mmHg (lying) and 95/60 mmHg (standing). Her haemoglobin concentration is 7.5 g/dL. What is the likely cause of the haemetemesis?
explanation:
The likely answer is gastric erosions because the bleeding occurred after only one dose of Ibuprofen. There is no previous history of dyspepsia or upper GI bleeding.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) such as aspirin, ibuprofen, and naproxen cause gastric erosions via -

  • Can be direct irritants of gastric mucosa
  • Prostaglandins have a protective role in maintaining mucosal integrity. NSAIDs inhibit prostaglandin production.

Because of gravity, the irritants lie on the greater curvature of the stomach, and therefore, gastritis and ulcers are seen distally on or near the greater curvature of the stomach.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 48, Pg: 312

question_text: A patient presents with haematemesis. A esophagogastroduodenoscopy detects a bleed in the lesser curvature of the stomach. Which of the following arteries is most likely to be the cause of the bleeding?
explanation:
The lesser curvature of stomach is supplied by -

  • Left gastric artery - direct branch of celiac trunk
  • Right gastric artery - branch of common hepatic artery

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine , 21st Ed, Ch:  322, Pg:2403

question_text: A 52 year old lady complains of epigastric burning pains due to stress. She finally undergoes an UGI endoscopy which shows gastro-oesophageal reflux. Which medication is the most effective for her condition?
explanation:
The main pharmacological therapy for GERD is inhibition of gastric acid suppression.

Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole, lansoprazole and pantoprazole are more effective than H2 receptor blockers such as ranitidine, cimetidine or nizatidine. Healing in oesophagitis is better with a PPI.

Bismuth is a mucosal protective agent used in the treatment of peptic ulcer disease.

Magnesium hydroxide is an antacid. It is not as effective as PPI for GERD.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st ed, Ch: 323, Pg: 2429-2431

question_text: In some individuals, peptic ulcers do not develop despite the presence of Helicobacter pylori. This is most likely due to:
option_a: NSAIDs causing ulceration independent of H. pylori
option_b: Variation in host and bacterial virulence factors
option_c: Colonization limited to the antrum in asymptomatic individuals
option_d: All strains of H. pylori being non-ulcerogenic in certain hosts
explanation:
Explanation:

The development of peptic ulcer disease in a person infected with Helicobacter pylori is not inevitable; it reflects a complex interaction between the bacterium's properties, the host's response, and environmental cofactors.

Some H. pylori strains carry virulence determinants (for example, the cag pathogenicity island including cagA, cytotoxin-associated vacA genotypes, adhesins such as babA) that provoke a stronger inflammatory response, more mucosal damage and a higher risk of ulcers. At the same time, host factors - including genetic polymorphisms in cytokine genes (e.g., IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-10), patterns of gastric acid secretion, and the effectiveness of mucosal defence (mucus, bicarbonate, prostaglandins) - alter how much damage a given bacterial insult produces.

Thus, an infected person with a less virulent strain and/or a host genetic profile that limits inflammation or preserves mucosal defence may remain asymptomatic and ulcer-free, whereas another with a virulent strain and a pro-inflammatory host genotype may develop ulcers.

Explanation for other Options:

NSAIDs causing ulceration independent of H. pylori (Option A): This is true as a separate statement: NSAIDs can produce ulcers by inhibiting cyclooxygenase and lowering mucosal prostaglandins, so they can cause ulcers regardless of H. pylori status. However, this statement does not explain why some H. pylori-infected people do not develop ulcers; it only describes an alternate cause of ulcers.

Colonization limited to the antrum in asymptomatic individuals (Option C): Antral infection can actually increase acid secretion and ulcer risk, so location alone is not protective.

All strains of H. pylori being non-ulcerogenic in certain hosts (Option D): Many strains carry virulence genes; it is the interaction between host factors and bacterial virulence, not a universal lack of pathogenicity, that explains differing outcomes.

question_text: A 35 years old male with gastric outlet obstruction presented to emergency with multiple episodes of vomiting. Which of the following fluids is preferred for this patient?
explanation:
Treatment of gastric outlet obstruction:

Treating the patient involves correcting the metabolic abnormalities and dealing with the mechanical obstruction. The patient should be rehydrated with intravenous isotonic saline with potassium supplementation. Replacing the sodium chloride and water allows the kidney to correct the acid-base abnormality. The metabolic abnormalities may be less if the obstruction is due to malignancy, as the acid-base disturbance is less pronounced.

question_text: Patient is having retching pain, vomiting and retrosternal burning. Most likely cause?
explanation:
Esophageal inflammation secondary to repeated exposure of the esophageal mucosa to the acidic gastric secretions in gastroesophageal reflux disease leads to an inflammatory response that can result in chronic blood loss. Ulceration may accompany this, but the superficial mucosal ulcerations generally do not bleed acutely and are more commonly manifested as anemia or guaiac-positive stools.

Symptoms of reflux esophagitis include dysphagia, food sticking, early satiety, regurgitation, chest pain, and vomiting

question_text:
A 35 year old male patient of peptic ulcer disease came with pain abdomen of 2 days duration and obstipation for 2 days, X-ray erect abdomen was done, what is the next line of management of this patient

1. USG abdomen
2. IV fluids
3. Exploratory laparotomy
4. Keep the patient in observation
explanation:
Perforation of duodenal ulcer is the most common cause of this pneumoperitoneum

Treatment of peptic ulcer perforation

  • The initial priorities are resuscitation and analgesia. Analgesia should not be withheld for fear of removing the signs of an intra-abdominal catastrophe. In fact, adequate analgesia makes the clinical signs more obvious. It is important, however, to titrate the analgesic dose.
  • Following resuscitation, the treatment is principally surgical. Laparotomy is performed, usually through an upper midline incision if the diagnosis of perforated peptic ulcer can be made with confidence.
  • Alternatively, laparoscopy may be used. The most important component of the operation is a thorough peritoneal toilet to remove all of the fluid and food debris.
  • <1cm perforation: closed primarily and buttress with vascularised omentum
  • 1-3 cm perforation: Graham's omental patch closure
  • >3cm: pyloric exclusion with Roux En Y limb jejunal serosal patch (if the omental is unhealthy) + gastrojejunostomy performed

question_text: On pentagastrin stimulation test-in which of the following condition acid is not increased
explanation:
Normal response by assessment of free and total acidity:

PENTAGASTRIN STIMULATION TEST

  • Fasting gastric juice is aspirated by ryle's tube → 'residual juice'
  • Gastric juice collected for next 1 hr is collected → 'basal secretion'
  • Gastric secretion is stimulated by giving 'pentagatrin'
  • Dose: 6mg/kg body weight
  • Gastric secretion is collected every 15min for next 1 hr

question_text: What is the name of the syndrome caused by the impaction of gall stones in the pylorus or duodenum causing gastric outlet obstruction?
explanation:
Gallstone Ileus.

  • Gallstone ileus can occur when a large gallstone erodes through the wall of the gallbladder directly into the intestine via a choledochoenteric fistula.
  • These stones can then pass through the intestinal tract until they reach an area of fixed obstruction.
  • Proximal stones can become impacted in the pylorus or proximal duodenum causing gastric outlet obstruction (Bouveret syndrome).
  • Those that travel distally may become lodged at surgical anastomoses or the ileocecal valve, where they can become impacted and cause small bowel obstruction.
  • These patients present with symptoms of obstipation, nausea, and abdominal pain.
  • Plain films may show an obstructive bowel gas pattern but may fail to identify aradiolucent stone. Ultrasound evaluation may be limited by extensive bowel gas. CT is highly sensitive and specific for gallstone ileus and will help to determine the location of the obstruction.
  • Management of gallstone ileus focuses on relieving the intestinal obstruction and removing the stone.
  • In cases of very proximal obstructions in the stomach or duodenum, endoscopic retrieval can be effective. For more distal stones, surgical enterolithotomy can be accomplished either laparoscopically or open.
  • This procedure entails the removal of the stone through an enterotomy that is then either repaired or resected depending on its size. Stones that have successfully traversed the ileocecal valve are likely to pass without further intervention. The role of pursuing cholecystectomy and/or choledochoenteric fistula closure at the time of enterolithotomy or addressing it at a later time remains a topic of debate, but it should be considered to reduce the risk of recurrence.

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter 32, Gallbladder and the Extrahepatic Biliary System, pg no: 1409

question_text: What is the investigation of choice for peptic ulcer?
explanation:
Explanation:

Gastroduodenoscopy is the investigation of choice for peptic ulcers as it allows direct visualization, biopsy, and assessment of complications.

Gastroduodenoscopy

  • This is the investigation of choice in the management of suspected peptic ulceration and in the hands of a well-trained operator is highly sensitive and specific.
  • In the stomach, any abnormal lesion should be multiply biopsied, and in the case of a suspected benign gastric ulcer numerous biopsies must be taken in order to exclude, as far as possible, the presence of a malignancy.
  • Commonly, biopsies of the antrum will be taken to see whether there is histological evidence of gastritis and a CLO test performed to determine the presence of pylori.
  • A 'U' manoeuvre should be performed to exclude ulcers around the gastro-oesophageal junction.
  • This is important as the increasing incidence of cancer at the gastro-oesophageal junction requires that all mucosal abnormalities in this region should undergo multiple biopsies.
  • Similarly, if a stoma is present, for instance after gastroenterostomy or Billroth II gastrectomy, it is important to enter both afferent and efferent loops.
  • Almost all stomal ulcers will be very close to the junction between the jejunal and gastric mucosa. Attention should be given to the pylorus to note whether there is any pre-pyloric or pyloric channel ulceration, and also whether it is deformed, which is often the case with chronic duodenal ulceration.
  • In the duodenum, care must be taken to view all of the first part. It is not infrequent for an ulcer to be just beyond the pylorus and easily overlooked.

Explanation for the other options:

  • A. CT scan is not sensitive enough for small mucosal ulcers.
  • B. MRI is not sensitive enough for small mucosal ulcers.
  • D. Barium meal (contrast radiography) has been largely replaced by endoscopy due to the inability to biopsy or perform therapeutic intervention.

Key Takeaways:

Gastroduodenoscopy (EGD/endoscopy) is the investigation of choice for peptic ulcers as it allows for direct visualization, precise diagnosis, biopsy (to exclude malignancy), and H. pylori testing (CLO test).

Level:

Must know
