question_text: Which is the common site for peptic ulcer?
explanation:
• Common sites for peptic ulcers are the first part of the duodenum and the lesser curve of the stomach, but they also occur on the stoma following gastric surgery, the oesophagus and even in a Meckel's diverticulum, which contains ectopic gastric epithelium.
  • In general, the ulcer occurs at a junction between different types of epithelia, the ulcer occurring in the epithelium least resistant to acid damage.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1157

question_text: Which artery is eroded by the posterior part of the kissing ulcer?
explanation:
Pathology

  • Most occur in the first part of the duodenum. A chronic ulcer penetrates the mucosa and into the muscle coat, leading to fibrosis.
  • The fibrosis causes deformities such as pyloric stenosis.
  • When an ulcer heals, a scar can be observed in the mucosa.
  • Sometimes there may be more than one duodenal ulcer. The situation in which there is both a posterior and an anterior duodenal ulcer is referred to as ‘kissing ulcers’.
  • Anteriorly placed ulcers tend to perforate and, in contrast, posterior duodenal ulcers tend to bleed, sometimes by eroding into the gastroduodenal artery.
  • Occasionally, the ulceration may be so extensive that the entire duodenal cap is ulcerated and devoid of mucosa. With respect to the giant duodenal ulcer, malignancy in this region is so uncommon that under normal circumstances surgeons can be confident that they are dealing with benign disease, even though from external palpation it may not appear so. In the stomach the situation is different.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1157

question_text: Which among the following condition shows hourglass contraction of stomach?
explanation:
Pathology

  • This is essentially similar to that of a duodenal ulcer, except that gastric ulcers tend to be larger.
  • Fibrosis, when it occurs, may result in the now rarely seen hourglass contraction of the stomach.
  • Large chronic ulcers may erode posteriorly into the pancreas and, on other occasions, into major vessels such as the splenic artery. Less commonly, they may erode into other organs such as the transverse colon.
  • Chronic gastric ulcers are much more common on the lesser curve (especially at the incisura angularis; than on the greater curve and, even when high on the lesser curve, they tend to be at the boundary between the acid-secreting and the non-acid secreting epithelia.
  • With atrophy of parietal cell mass, non-acid-secreting epithelium migrates up the lesser curvature.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1158

question_text: Which cells of the stomach are denervated in highly selective vagotomy?
explanation:
Highly selective vagotomy

  • In 1968 Johnston and Amdrup independently devised the operation of highly selective vagotomy in which only the parietal cell mass of the stomach was denervated.
  • This proved to be the most satisfactory operation for duodenal ulceration, with a low incidence of side effects and acceptable recurrence rates when performed to a high technical standard.
  • This operation became the gold standard for operations on duodenal ulceration in the 1970s.
  • The operative mortality was lower than any other definitive operation for duodenal ulceration, in all probability because the gastrointestinal tract was not opened during this procedure.
  • The unpleasant effects of peptic ulcer surgery were largely avoided, although loss of receptive relaxation of the stomach did occur, leading to epigastric fullness and sometimes mild dumping.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1161

question_text: Which layer is denoted as the fourth layer of the stomach in endoscopic ultrasound technique?
explanation:
• EUS is recommended by NCCN guidelines as part of the staging workup for gastric cancer if there is no evidence of metastatic disease.
  • EUS provides the most accurate evaluation of the depth of tumor invasion, assessment of perigastric lymph node involvement, and can sometimes identify involvement of surrounding organs or the presence of ascites.
  • EUS is performed using a flexible endoscope with a 7.5- to 12-MHz ultrasound transducer. The stomach is filled with water to provide an acoustic window, and the stomach wall is visualized as five alternating hypoechoic and hyperechoic layers.
  • The mucosa and submucosa represent the first three layers (T1).
  • The fourth layer is the muscularis propria, invasion of which signifies a T2 tumor.
  • Expansion of the tumor beyond the muscularis propria causing an irregular border correlates with expansion into the subserosa, or a T3 tumor.
  • The serosa is the fifth layer, and loss of this bright line correlates with penetration through it, indicating a T4a tumor.
  • Direct invasion of surrounding structures, including named vessels, indicates a T4b tumor.
  • Nodes are evaluated based on their size and ultrasound appearance and can additionally be sampled using fine-needle aspiration (FNA) under EUS guidance.
  • FNA can also be performed if ascites is present to evaluate for peritoneal spread.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 49, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1224

question_text:
An elderly man underwent Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery for obesity. He now presents to his physician with complaints of dizziness, fatigue, and tremors 2 hours after the ingestion of a carbohydrate-rich meal. His symptoms occur mainly due to:
1. Hypoglycemia
2. Small volume of food intake
3. High osmotic load of food
4. Increased release of insulin
5. Increased release of glucagon
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's symptoms are classic for late dumping syndrome, a common complication of gastric surgery like Roux-en-Y bypass. The pathophysiology involves:

  1. Rapid gastric emptying of a carbohydrate-rich meal into the small intestine.
  2. Quick absorption of glucose leads to a sharp spike in blood sugar (hyperglycemia).
  3. This hyperglycemia triggers an exaggerated release of insulin (Statement 4).
  4. The excessive insulin response then causes a subsequent sharp drop in blood glucose, leading to reactive hypoglycemia (Statement 1), which manifests as dizziness, fatigue, and tremors.

Prevention and Management of Dumping Syndrome

  • Dietary modification (first-line):
    • Small, frequent meals
    • Low-carbohydrate, high-protein, high-fat diet
    • High-fiber intake
    • Separate liquids from solid meals
  • Medical therapy (if dietary measures fail):
    • Tincture of opium or loperamide for diarrhea
    • Meclizine for nausea
    • Anticholinergics to reduce spasms and delay gastric emptying
    • Octreotide (somatostatin analogue): slows gastric emptying, prolongs intestinal transit
  • Surgical options (for refractory cases):
    • Pyloric reconstruction
    • Conversion of loop gastrojejunostomy to Roux-en-Y (post-distal gastrectomy)
    • Conversion of Billroth-II to Billroth-I
    • Interposition of an anti-peristaltic jejunal segment

Key Takeaways:

  • Late dumping syndrome is characterized by reactive hypoglycemia 1-3 hours after a meal due to hyperinsulinemia.
  • It is distinct from early dumping, which occurs 30 minutes post-meal due to fluid shifts from a high osmotic load.

question_text: A patient presents with haematemesis. An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy detects a bleed in the greater curvature of the stomach. Which of the following arteries is most likely to be the source of the bleeding?
explanation:
The greater curvature of the stomach is supplied by -

  • Left gastroepiploic and short gastric arteries -branches of splenic artery. Short gastric arteries also supply fundus of stomach.
  • Right gastroepiploic artery -branch of the common hepatic artery

The stomach s exclusively supplied by the branches of the celiac trunk.

The right gastric artery supplies the pylorus and the lesser curvature of the stomach.

The right hepatic artery supplies the right lobe of the liver and part of the caudate lobe.

Cystic artery supplies the gallbladder.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st Ed, Ch: 322, Pg:2403

question_text: What is the most common site of abdominal tuberculosis?
explanation:
The most common site of the gastrointestinal TB is ileocecal location (ileocecal TB), followed by jejunum and colon. The esophagus, stomach and duodenum are rarely involved.

Reference: www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4209546

question_text: Which cells in the stomach produces gastrin?
explanation:
Endocrine cells

  • The stomach has numerous endocrine cells, which are critical to its function.
  • In the gastric antrum, the mucosa contains G cells, which produce gastrin.
  • Throughout the body of the stomach, enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells are abundant and produce histamine, a key factor in driving gastric acid secretion.
  • In addition, there are large numbers of somatostatin-producing D cells throughout the stomach, and somatostatin has a negative regulatory role.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1150

question_text: Not seen in a case of gastrinoma
option_b: Fulminating ulcer diathesis in the stomach, duodenum
option_d: Non-beta islet cell tumours of the pancreas
explanation:
Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES)/gastrinoma is a condition that includes: (1) fulminating ulcer or atypical sites; (2) recurrent ulceration despite 'adequate' therapy; and (3) non-beta islet cell tumours of the pancreas (gastrinoma).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, CHAPTER 57, The adrenal glands and other abdominal endocrine disorders, Pg:907.

question_text: Which among the following is the possible complication of pancreatic pseudocyst due to enlargement of the cyst?
explanation:
Explanation:

A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of fluid (pancreatic juice and necrotic debris) encapsulated by a wall of granulation tissue.

Complications due to enlargement are typically mechanical.

  • Bowel obstruction (gastric outlet or duodenal obstruction) can occur when a large pseudocyst presses directly on the adjacent stomach or duodenum.
  • Systemic sepsis and peritonitis are complications due to infection or rupture, not simple enlargement.
  • Hemoperitoneum (bleeding into the peritoneal cavity) is a rare but severe complication, usually due to erosion into a splenic or peripancreatic vessel (pseudoaneurysm), not enlargement alone.

Key Takeaways:

The mechanical complication of an enlarging pancreatic pseudocyst is compression of adjacent hollow viscera, leading to gastric outlet or small bowel obstruction.

Level:

Must know

question_text: Where are the Brunner's glands located in the gastrointestinal tract?
explanation:
Duodenum

  • The duodenum is lined by a mucus-secreting columnar epithelium.
  • In addition, Brunner’s glands lie beneath the mucosa and are similar to the pyloric glands in the pyloric part of the stomach.
  • Endocrine cells in the duodenum produce cholecystokinin and secretin.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1150

question_text: A 1.5-month-old male infant is brought to the outpatient department with complaints of vomiting after feeding and failure to thrive. On examination, a firm, olive-shaped mass is palpable in the upper abdomen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Clinical Presentation:

  • Age of onset: 2-6 weeks.
  • Vomiting: Non-bilious, projectile; increases in frequency and forcefulness daily.
  • Differentiation from other causes:
    • Unlike infective causes (e.g., meningitis, UTI): baby remains hungry after vomiting.
    • Unlike gastro-oesophageal reflux (GOR):
      • GOR starts shortly after birth.
      • GOR symptoms wax and wane.

Epidemiology:

  • Incidence: 1 in 300 infants (UK).
  • Male: Female ratio = 4:1.
  • Often associated with maternal family history.

Physical Findings:

  • Early presentation: Often unremarkable.
  • Late presentation: Weight loss and dehydration, possibly requiring resuscitation.
  • Test feed findings:
    • Gastric peristalsis visible from left to right across abdomen.
    • In relaxed, feeding baby: palpable 'olive-shaped' mass (pyloric tumour) in right upper quadrant.

Diagnosis:

  • Abdominal ultrasound: Shows thickened and elongated pylorus.
  • Test feed: Useful if ultrasound not immediately available.

Preoperative Management:

  • Discontinue feeds.
  • Insert 8-10 Fr nasogastric tube to empty stomach.
  • Vomiting leads to hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
  • Correction typically takes 24-48 hours.
  • Use 9% saline + 0.15% KCl in 5% glucose at 6-7.5 mL/kg/h for:
    • Maintenance fluid.
    • Electrolyte correction.
  • As chloride is replaced, kidneys help correct the pH.

Surgical Treatment - Ramstedt's Pyloromyotomy:

  • Performed via:
    • Laparoscopy, or
    • Supraumbilical/right upper quadrant incision.
  • A serosal incision is made; the pyloric mass is spread open.
  • Must extend from duodenal fornix to gastric antrum, including onto the stomach to prevent recurrence.

Postoperative Care:

  • IV fluids continued until feeding resumes (typically within 24 hours).
  • Early postoperative vomiting is usually self-limited.
    • Persistent vomiting more likely due to GERD than incomplete myotomy.
  • GERD management:
    • Often resolves with maturity.
    • May require thickened feeds and antireflux medications.
    • Failure to thrive or respiratory issues warrant investigation.
    • Laparoscopic fundoplication may be indicated in severe cases.

Explanation of other options:

Subacute Intestinal Obstruction (Option A):

  • Subacute intestinal obstruction presents with symptoms of bowel obstruction, such as bilious vomiting, abdominal distention, and possibly constipation. The presence of an olive mass and non-bilious vomiting points more specifically to pyloric stenosis, not subacute obstruction.
  • Additionally, subacute obstructions usually involve issues further down in the GI tract, not just the pylorus.

GERD (Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease) (Option C):

  • GERD in infants presents with spitting up, irritability, and sometimes poor feeding, but it typically does not cause forceful, projectile vomiting or the presence of a palpable mass.
  • The vomiting in GERD is usually less severe than that seen in pyloric stenosis, and it tends to improve over time, whereas pyloric stenosis worsens without intervention.

Esophageal Atresia (Option D):

  • Esophageal atresia presents much earlier, often in the first few hours to days of life with inability to pass a feeding tube or signs of respiratory distress and aspiration. It does not present with a palpable "olive mass" or the classic projectile vomiting of pyloric stenosis.
  • This condition is usually diagnosed shortly after birth, unlike pyloric stenosis, which presents a bit later in infancy.

Key Takeaways:

Pyloric stenosis is characterized by non-bilious projectile vomiting, a palpable olive-like mass in the right upper abdomen, and failure to thrive, making it the most likely diagnosis in this case.

question_text: A patient with a long history of GERD is found to have a mass in the duodenum. Which of the following hormone levels should be checked?
explanation:
Explanation:

A duodenal mass in the context of long-standing severe GERD and recurrent ulcers raises suspicion of Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES) caused by a gastrin-secreting tumour (gastrinoma).

  • The cornerstone of diagnosis is fasting serum gastrin (FSG) levels.
  • A >10-fold increase in FSG with gastric pH <2 confirms the diagnosis.
  • If levels are borderline, a secretin stimulation test is performed.
  • Most gastrinomas are located within the "gastrinoma triangle" (duodenum, pancreas, peri-biliary region).

Explanation of Other Options:

Insulin (Option A): Checked in insulinoma, which causes fasting hypoglycemia with Whipple's triad, not GERD/ulcer disease.

Glucagon (Option B): Elevated in glucagonoma, which presents with necrolytic migratory erythema, diabetes, and weight loss.

VIP (Option D): Elevated in VIPoma, which causes WDHA syndrome (watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria), not peptic ulcer disease.

Key Takeaways:

  • GERD + duodenal mass + refractory ulcers → suspect gastrinoma.
  • Fasting serum gastrin is the diagnostic test of choice.
  • Always rule out MEN 1 association in confirmed cases.

question_text: A 51-year-old male laborer presents with a haematemesis. Which of the following features confers the greatest risk of a poor outcome?
option_b: A history of ischaemic heart disease (IHD)
option_d: A pulse of 90 beats per minute
explanation:
Among the options given, history of ischemic heart disease confers the greatest risk of a poorer outcome.

There are a number of available scoring systems which stratify subjects with GI bleed into high and low risk groups.

The Rockall scoring system is based on:

  • Age (the higher the age the worse the prognosis)
  • Comorbidities (like IHD)
  • Presence of shock
  • Endoscopic abnormalities.

The Canadian Consensus Conference Statement utilizes a similar system, incorporating endoscopic factors including:

  • Active bleeding
  • Major stigmata of recent haemorrhage
  • Ulcers greater than 2 cm in diameter
  • The location of ulcers in proximity to large arteries.

The Blatchford score is based on clinical parameters alone:

  • Elevated blood urea nitrogen
  • Reduced haemoglobin
  • A drop in systolic blood pressure
  • Raised pulse rate
  • The presence of melaena or syncope
  • Evidence of hepatic or cardiac disease.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st Ed, Ch: 48, Pg: 313

question_text: A 60 year old man is investigated for weight loss and dyspepsia. Endoscopic examination reveals an ulcerated lesion in stomach. Biopsy shows the presence of a low grade mucosa associated lymphoma and Helicobacter pylori. CT of chest & abdomen shows no metastases. What is the best treatment option for this patient?
explanation:
Helicobacter pylori colonization of the Upper GIT is associated with the following outcomes:

  1. Peptic Ulcer disease. It is more commonly associated with duodenal ulcer than gastric ulcer.
  2. Non cardio gastric adenocarcinoma
  3. Low grade gastric B cell MALT lymphoma

H Pylori provides protection against Reflux esophagitis and its sequelae like Barret esophagus and esophageal adenocarcinoma.

The diagnosis here is a gastric MALT (Mucosa Associated Lymphoid Tissue) tumour.

  • These are usually marginal zone B cell lymphomas associated an excellent prognosis.
  • MALT lymphoma is the third most common type of non-Hodgkin lymphoma.
  • MALT lymphomas are most commonly found in the gastrointestinal tract (stomach is the commonest). But they can be found in any extranodal site.

Low grade gastric MALT tumours are associated with Helicobacter Pylori infection and respond in over 80% of cases to helicobacter eradication.

A proportion of patients will not respond to eradication therapy alone and will go on to more conventional anti-lymphoma therapies such as cyclophosphamide, chlorambucil, nucleoside analogues or radiotherapy.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 163, Pg: 1280-1283

question_text: Which among the following factors is not associated with poor outcome in case of perforated peptic ulcer?
explanation:
• There are patients who have small leaks from a perforated peptic ulcer and relatively mild peritoneal contamination, who may be managed with intravenous fluids, nasogastric suction and antibiotics. These patients are in the minority.
  • A number of factors have been associated with poor outcome after perforated peptic ulcer, including:
  • Delay in diagnosis (>24 hours);
  • Medical comorbidities;
  • Shock;
  • Increasing age (>75).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1164-1165

question_text: Which anastomosis is performed in bilroth-II surgery?
explanation:
Billroth II gastrectomy

  • In Billroth II gastrectomy, or its close relation Pólya gastrectomy, the antrum and distal body of the stomach are mobilised by opening the greater and lesser omentum and dividing the gastroepiploic arteries, right gastric artery and the left gastric artery arcade at the limit of the resection.
  • The duodenum is closed off either by suture or using staples, sometimes with difficulty in patients with a very deformed duodenum.
  • Following resection, the distal end of the stomach is narrowed by the closure of the lesser curve aspect of the remnant.
  • The greater curve aspect is then anastomosed, usually in a retrocolic fashion, to the jejunum, leaving as short an afferent loop as feasible.
  • A common cause of morbidity in this procedure is leakage from the duodenal stump, which is particularly associated with kinking of the afferent loop.
  • Leakage from the gastrojejunal anastomosis is unusual unless it is under tension or the stomach has been devascularised during the mobilisation.
  • Recurrence of the ulcer at the stoma is uncommon but can occur, especially as this procedure is traditionally not combined with the vagotomy.
  • In the majority of expert centres, a Roux-en-Y reconstruction rather than the Billroth II procedure is performed because postoperative function is better.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1160

question_text: Which among the following is not the metabolic change in gastric outlet obstruction?
explanation:
Metabolic effects

  • These are most interesting, as the metabolic consequences of benign pyloric stenosis are unique.
  • The vomiting of hydrochloric acid results in hypochloraemic alkalosis.
  • Initially the sodium and potassium may be relatively normal.
  • However, as dehydration progresses, more profound metabolic abnormalities arise, partly related to renal dysfunction.
  • Initially, the urine has a low chloride and high bicarbonate content, reflecting the primary metabolic abnormality. This bicarbonate is excreted along with sodium, and so with time the patient becomes progressively hyponatraemic and more profoundly dehydrated.
  • Because of the dehydration, a phase of sodium retention follows and potassium and hydrogen are excreted in preference. This results in the urine becoming paradoxically acidic and hypokalaemia ensues.
  • Alkalosis leads to a lowering in the circulating ionised calcium, and tetany can occur.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1169

question_text: A 60 years old male patient presented to the hospital with gastric outlet obstruction. On evaluation, there was antral gastric carcinoma extending to the head of pancreas with multiple metastasis to the right lobe of liver. What is the most appropriate management?
option_a: Right lobe hepatectomy with radical gastrectomy
explanation:
Above history of gastric antral carcinoma extending to the head of pancreas with multiple mets to right lobe of liver is a high grade(stage 4) cancer making it surgically inoperable so palliative management is done

Palliative surgery

  • In patients with significant symptoms of either obstruction or bleeding, palliative resection is appropriate.
  • A palliative gastrectomy need not be radical as it is sufficient to remove the tumor and reconstruct the gastrointestinal tract.
  • Sometimesit is impossible to resect an obstructing tumor in the distal stomach and other palliative procedures need to be considered.
  • A high gastroenterostomy is a poor operation that very frequently does not allow the stomach to empty adequately and may produce the additional problem of bile reflux.
  • A Roux loop with a wide anastomosis between the stomach and jejunum may be a better option, although even this may not allow the stomach to empty well.
  • For inoperable tumors situated in the cardia, palliative intubation or stenting can be used.

question_text: A middle-aged chronic alcoholic male, previously diagnosed with a hollow viscus perforation, is taken up for emergency laparotomy. Intraoperatively, a 2 cm perforation is identified in the duodenal wall (as shown in the figure). Which of the following is the most appropriate surgical management?
explanation:
Explanation:

In the setting of a duodenal ulcer perforation, the preferred surgical management is omentoplasty (Modified Graham's patch / omental pedicle repair).

  • A vascularized pedicle of the omentum is mobilized and sutured over the perforation.
  • This provides a biologic seal, enhances healing, and reduces the risk of persistent leakage or sepsis.
  • It is simple, safe, and effective for most anterior duodenal perforations, even in unstable patients.

Duodenal ulcer perforation:

  • In the setting of a duodenal ulcer perforation, the preferred surgical management is omentoplasty (Modified Graham's patch / omental pedicle repair).
    • A vascularized pedicle of the omentum is mobilized and sutured over the perforation.
    • This provides a biologic seal, enhances healing, and reduces the risk of persistent leakage or sepsis.
  • It is simple, safe, and effective for most anterior duodenal perforations, even in unstable patients.
  • The vascularized pedicle of the greater omentum is patched over the defect.

Bleeding duodenal ulcer:

  • Usually posterior duodenal ulcer → erodes into the gastroduodenal artery.
  • Presents with hematemesis, melena, or both.
  • Often associated with NSAID use.

Management of bleeding ulcer:

  • Endoscopic therapy (first-line):
    • Adrenaline injection
    • Mechanical clips
    • Thermal or plasma coagulation
    • Fibrin glue application
  • If refractory: Angiographic embolization.
  • Surgery: Duodenotomy with vessel ligation ± truncal vagotomy + pyloroplasty.

Explanation of Other Options:

Primary Closure of the Defect (Option A):

  • Involves simple suturing of the perforation edges without reinforcement.
  • Indicated only for very small perforations (<1 cm) with healthy margins.
  • For a 2 cm perforation, risk of suture line breakdown and peritoneal contamination is high if no reinforcement is used.
  • Hence, not appropriate in this case.

Billroth I (Gastroduodenostomy) (Option C):

  • A definitive ulcer surgery involving distal gastrectomy with end-to-end gastroduodenal anastomosis.
  • Indications:
    • Chronic gastric outlet obstruction
    • Non-healing gastric ulcer
    • Suspected malignant gastric ulcer
  • Not suitable in acute perforated duodenal ulcer because:
    • Patient often unstable
    • Tissue inflamed and friable → poor anastomotic healing
    • Longer operative time increases morbidity.

Billroth II (Gastrojejunostomy) (Option D):

  • Another form of definitive ulcer surgery, distal gastrectomy with gastrojejunostomy.
  • Historically used in refractory duodenal ulcer disease (especially for intractable bleeding, obstruction, or chronic recurrent ulcers).
  • Rarely used now due to complications like dumping syndrome, bile reflux gastritis, afferent loop syndrome.
  • Similar to Billroth I, it is not appropriate for acute perforation due to unstable physiology and poor tissue condition

question_text: A 45-year-old patient presents after undergoing a Billroth II gastrectomy operation and complains of symptoms suggestive of dumping syndrome, including vomiting and diarrhoea occurring approximately 20 minutes after meals. What should be the initial management for this patient's condition?
option_d: Reverse Billroth II to Billroth I
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Dumping Syndrome after Billroth II Gastrectomy:
    • Definition:
      • Dumping Syndrome is a set of gastrointestinal and vasomotor symptoms that occur due to the rapid passage of hyperosmolar stomach contents into the proximal small intestine, commonly following Billroth II gastrectomy.
    • Initial Management
      • Consume small, frequent meals to slow gastric emptying and alleviate symptoms.
  • Etiology
    • Accelerated gastric emptying leading to hyperosmolar contents entering the small intestine.
  • Clinical Features
    • Gastrointestinal symptoms: Abdominal pain, early satiety, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, bloating.
    • Vasomotor/systemic symptoms: Sweating (diaphoresis), rapid heartbeat (tachycardia), palpitations, headache, and episodes of fainting (syncope).
  • Epidemiology
    • More frequently observed after Billroth II type gastric surgeries.

Types of Dumping Syndrome

Prevention of Dumping Syndrome

  • Dietary Measures:
    • Consume small, frequent meals throughout the day (Option B)
    • Follow a diet low in carbohydrates but rich in proteins and fats (Option A ruled out)
    • Include high-fiber foods to slow gastric emptying (Option C ruled out)
    • Take liquids separately from solids during meals
  • Medical Management (if dietary changes are insufficient):
    • Antidiarrheal agents: Tincture of opium or loperamide for diarrhea control
    • Antiemetics: Meclizine to alleviate nausea
    • Antispasmodics: Anticholinergic medications to reduce spasms and delay gastric emptying
    • Octreotide (Somatostatin analogue): Slows gastric emptying and modulates intestinal motility to prolong food transit
  • Surgical Management (if medical therapy fails):
    • Pyloric reconstruction to improve gastric emptying
    • Roux-en-Y conversion: In patients with prior distal gastrectomy, converting loop gastrojejunostomy to Roux-en-Y
    • Anti-peristaltic jejunal interposition: To regulate food transit and reduce dumping
    • Conversion from Billroth-II to Billroth-I (Option D ruled out)

question_text: A 57 year old man is suspected of having a duodenal ulcer recurrence despite being on omeprazole. Which of the following is the most sensitive test in detecting ongoing infection with Helicobacter pylori?
option_b: The urease test on a gastric biopsy
explanation:
• The urea breath test is expensive but has up to 98% sensitivity. It requires stringent test conditions like fasting and may not be convenient as serology. It can be used for detecting response to treatment.
  • Serology is simple and convenient and is not affected by the use of PPI or antibiotic use. So in this patient who is already on PPI this may be the most convenient investigation.
  • The gastric biopsy culture has high specificity but sensitivity of 90%.
  • Histology of gastric biopsy (not listed above) has both high sensitivity and specificity.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, ch: 163, Pg: 1281

question_text: What is the treatment of a patient diagnosed with H.pylori?
option_a: A combination of a proton pump inhibitor and an antibiotic
explanation:
Explanation:

The treatment regimen for a patient with H.pylori is a combination of a proton pump inhibitor and antibiotics.

  • Although pylori is sensitive to many antibiotics in vitro, monotherapy is generally ineffective due to insufficient antibiotic delivery to its colonization site.
  • The failure of single-drug therapy led to the development of multidrug regimens.
  • At present, standard treatment consists of a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) combined with two or three antimicrobial agents for 10-14 days.

Common Treatment Regimens for H.pylori

question_text: Ligation of common hepatic artery will impair blood supply in:
option_a: Right gastric and right gastroepiploic artery
option_b: Right gastric and left gastric artery
option_c: Right gastroepiploic artery and short gastric vessels
option_d: Right gastric and short gastric vessels
explanation:
• The stomach has an arterial supply on both the lesser and greater curves . On the lesser curve, the left gastric artery, a branch of the coeliac axis, forms an anastomotic arcade with the right gastric artery, which arises from the common hepatic artery.
  • Branches of the left gastric artery pass up towards the cardia. The gastroduodenal artery, also a branch of the hepatic artery, passes behind the first part of the duodenum, which is highly relevant with respect to a bleeding duodenal ulcer. Here it divides into the superior pancreaticoduodenal artery and the right gastroepiploic artery.
  • The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery supplies the duodenum and pancreatic head and forms an anastomosis with the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery, a branch of the superior mesenteric artery.
  • The right gastroepiploic artery runs along the greater curvature of the stomach, eventually forming an anastomosis with the left gastroepiploic artery, a branch of the splenic artery.
  • This vascular arcade, important during construction of a gastric conduit in oesophageal resection is often variably incomplete.
  • The fundus of the stomach is supplied by the vasa brevia (or short gastric arteries), which arise from near the termination of the splenic artery.

question_text: A patient presents with sudden onset of hematemesis. She has a history of arthritis for which she takes aspirin, consumes alcohol occasionally, and also reports sporadic abdominal pain. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Peptic ulcer is the most likely diagnosis due to the presence of risk factors like aspirin use, alcohol intake, and abdominal pain.

  • Peptic ulcers, occurring in the stomach or duodenum, are a common cause of upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding and typically present with hematemesis.
  • In this case, the patient's history of aspirin use (a known ulcerogenic NSAID), occasional alcohol consumption (which irritates the gastric mucosa), and episodic abdominal pain all support the diagnosis of a peptic ulcer.
  • These factors compromise the gastric mucosal barrier and increase the risk of ulcer formation and bleeding.
  • Most common artery involved in bleeding ulcers:
    • Duodenal ulcer - Gastroduodenal artery
    • Gastric ulcer - Left gastric artery

Reference:

Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf

question_text: A 35-year-old man with a history of alcohol binge drinking presents with hematemesis after repeated vomiting. He is stable, pale, and has normal liver function tests. Endoscopy is scheduled. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Mallory-Weiss tear = longitudinal mucosal lacerations at the gastroesophageal junction due to forceful retching/vomiting.

  • Strongly associated with alcohol abuse.
  • Presents with hematemesis, often self-limiting.
  • Endoscopy: Confirms tear.
  • Risk factors: Alcohol binge, severe retching, coughing.
  • Treatment: Supportive; endoscopic therapy (banding, clipping, epinephrine injection) for persistent bleeding.
  • Course: Usually heals spontaneously within 72 hours.

Explanation of other options:

Esophageal varices (Option A): Related to portal hypertension, abnormal LFTs expected.

Gastric ulcer (Option B): Related to H. pylori/NSAIDs, not sudden vomiting.

Alcoholic gastritis (Option D): May cause bleeding but less likely than Mallory-Weiss with this presentation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Mallory-Weiss = tear at GE junction after vomiting.
  • Common in alcoholics with hematemesis.
  • Endoscopy is both diagnostic and therapeutic.

question_text: Which of the following procedures has the highest risk of causing the recurrence of duodenal ulcers?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Highly Selective Vagotomy (also termed Parietal Cell Vagotomy or Proximal Gastric Vagotomy) carries the greatest likelihood of duodenal ulcer recurrence.
  • This operation preserves vagal supply to the gastric antrum and pylorus while selectively interrupting only the vagal fibres serving the acid-secreting regions of the stomach (corpus and fundus).
  • Because the drainage pathways remain intact, additional drainage procedures are not routinely required.

question_text: With respect to gastric carcinoma, which of the following statements is true?
option_a: Aspirin use is a risk factor for gastric carcinoma
option_b: Early diagnosis of gastric carcinoma results in a five year survival rate of 20%
option_c: Endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning for local tumour staging
option_d: Helicobacter pylori infection is not associated with gastric carcinoma
explanation:
Incidence of distal stomach tumors is actually decreasing while the incidence of tumors in the proximal stomach is increasing.

Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use is associated with decreased risk of certain gastric tumors.

  1. pylori infection has been associated in a number of studies with increased risk of gastric carcinoma.

Screening for gastric carcinoma in Japan detects up to 40% of gastric carcinomas at an early stage and in skilled hands five year survival can be upwards of 90%.

Computed tomography (CT) with gastric dilatation is a useful complementary investigation in the staging of gastric carcinoma, but endoscopic ultrasonography is superior to conventional CT scanning as it is able to assess depth of infiltration and lymphatic dissemination of tumor.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 80, Pg: 629-632

question_text: A visible mass in epigastrium with CD117 positive, but cytokeratin and S-100 negative. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Gastrointestinal stromal tumours (GISTs) may arise in any part of the gastrointestinal tract but 50% will be found in the stomach. Previously named leiomyoma and leiomyosarcoma, the term GIST is now used, recognising the distinct phenotype. They are tumours of mesenchymal origin and are observed equally commonly in males and females. The tumours are universally associated with a mutation in the tyrosine kinase c-kit oncogene.

Most GISTs occur due to gain of function mutation in receptor tyrosine kinase KIT or PDGFR-alpha.

Most useful marker is CD-117.

Carney triad - GIST + paraganglioma + pulmonary chondroma.

question_text: A 4-year-old child presents with a rectal polyp and painless rectal bleeding. Histopathological examination reveals enlarged and inflamed glands filled with mucin. The child is diagnosed with a juvenile rectal polyp. Which of the following best describes the polyp in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

Juvenile rectal polyps are hamartomatous growths most commonly seen in children under 5 years of age.

  • Juvenile rectal polyps are benign, hamartomatous growths, typically presenting in young children under the age of 5.
  • The hallmark clinical feature is painless rectal bleeding, often discovered incidentally or during evaluation for per rectal bleeding.
  • Histologically, these polyps exhibit dilated, mucus-filled glands lined by inflamed epithelium and surrounded by a lamina propria rich in inflammatory cells.
  • Though usually solitary, multiple polyps may be seen in juvenile polyposis syndrome, a condition that can be associated with mutations in genes like SMAD2, SMAD4, and BMPR1A.
  • These syndromic cases may also show extra-intestinal features such as digital clubbing and vascular malformations.
  • While juvenile polyps are benign, syndromic forms can carry a slightly increased risk of malignancy over time, especially if multiple or dysplastic polyps are present.

Explanation of other options:

Adenoma (Option A): Adenomas are benign neoplastic polyps that arise from glandular epithelium and are considered pre-malignant. While common in adults, they are rare in children and not the histological pattern seen in juvenile polyps.

Choristoma (Option B): Choristomas are ectopic normal tissue in abnormal locations, like pancreatic tissue in the stomach. They are not associated with juvenile polyps, which are overgrowths of normal colonic tissue.

Carcinoma (Option D): Carcinomas are malignant tumors derived from epithelial cells. They are exceptionally rare in children, especially under age 5, and do not match the benign histological findings of a juvenile polyp.

question_text: A 14-year-old girl presented with pain over right upper abdomen and rash over abdomen. With help of antihistamines rash disappears, but pain persists even after pain killers. CT abdomen was done which shows the following findings. All of the statements are correct regarding it except:
option_a: This is type I cyst which is composed three layers- inner endocyst, intermediate ectocyst and outer pericyst.
option_b: In case of cyst rupture anaphylactic shock can develop.
option_c: Casoni test is type IV hypersensitivity test which is used to confirm hydatid disease.
option_d: PAIR is the ideal method of management for this case
explanation:
Option A: This is case of hydatid cyst. CT scan shows type I Hydatid cyst. Three layers of hydatid cyst are inner endocyst that contain germinal membrane, intermediate ectocyst and outer pericyst. Pericyst is derived from compressed host organ tissue.

Option B: Due to highly antigenicity of hydatid fluid, if cyst ruptures patients develop severe anaphylactic shock.

Option C: Casoni test which was used mostly in past is type I hypersensitivity reaction.

Option D: PAIR (Puncture, Aspiration, Injection and Re-aspiration) would be ideal as there is no septation and it is less invasive.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 6, Edition: 28th

question_text: Indications for circumcision are all, except?
option_b: An inability to retract the foreskin for intercourse
explanation:
• In infants and young boys, circumcision is most usually performed at the request of the parents for social or religious reasons.
  • Medical indications for circumcision in boys include true phimosis, BXO (rare under the age of 5 years), recurrent attacks of balanoposthitis and recurrent urinary tract infections with an abnormal upper urinary tract.

question_text: The immediate postoperative period is associated with predictable hormonal and metabolic shifts. Several electrolyte and metabolic abnormalities commonly occur, while some do not. Which one of the following is not typically seen in the immediate postoperative period?
explanation:
Explanation:

In the immediate postoperative period, patients often develop hyperkalaemia or normal potassium levels due to tissue breakdown, acidosis and decreased renal excretion. Hypokalaemia is not typically seen.

Normal metabolic changes in the immediate postoperative period include:

  • Negative nitrogen balance due to catabolic stress hormones (Option A)
  • Glucose intolerance due to increased cortisol, catecholamines and insulin resistance (Option C)
  • Hyponatremia due to ADH surge and water retention (Option D)
  • Potassium tends to be normal or high, not low, because of increased catabolism, acidemia and reduced renal clearance

question_text: Which among the following artery doesn't supply the thyroid gland?
explanation:
• Blood and Lymphatic Supply: The thyroid gland has a rich blood supply and a complex network of vessels. It receives arterial blood from several sources.
  • Superior Thyroid Arteries: The superior thyroid arteries arise from the external carotid arteries. These arteries split into branches as they enter the upper poles of the thyroid lobes.
  • Inferior Thyroid Arteries: The inferior thyroid arteries originate from the thyrocervical trunks of the subclavian arteries. They branch fairly close to the thyrocervical trunk, and their course takes them upward and posteriorly, running behind the carotid sheath. They then turn and enter the mid-portion of the thyroid lobes.
  • Thyroid Ima Artery: In about 2% of individuals, a third artery known as the thyroid ima artery can be present. This artery has an unusual origin, arising directly from either the aorta or innominate artery. It follows a midline path and enters either the thyroid isthmus or the lower poles of the thyroid lobes.
  • The occurence of Middle thyroid artery is not found in human body.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 876

question_text: Which among the following is not the boundary of posterior triangle of the neck according to the classification of cervical lymph nodes of neck?
explanation:
Level I is subdivided:

  • Level IA is bounded by the anterior belly of the digastric muscle, hyoid bone, midline, and mandible.
  • Level IB is bounded by the anterior and posterior bellies of the digastric muscle and the inferior border of the mandible.

Level IB contains the submandibular gland.

Level II is bounded superiorly by the skull base, anteriorly by the stylohyoid muscle, inferiorly by a horizontal plane extending posteriorly from the hyoid bone, and posteriorly by the posterior edge of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. Level II is further subdivided:

  • Level IIA is anterior to the spinal accessory nerve.
  • Level IIB, or the so-called submuscular triangle, is posterior to the nerve.
  • Level III begins at the inferior edge of level II and is bounded by the laryngeal strap muscles anteriorly, by the posterior border of the sternocleidomastoid muscle posteriorly, and by a horizontal plane extending posteriorly from the inferior border of the cricoid cartilage.
  • Level IV begins at the inferior border of level III and is bounded anteriorly by the strap muscles, posteriorly by the posterior edge of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, and inferiorly by the clavicle.
  • Level V is posterior to the posterior edge of the sternocleidomastoid muscle, anterior to the trapezius muscle, superior to the clavicle, and inferior to the base of the skull.
  • Level VI is bounded by the hyoid bone superiorly, the common carotid arteries laterally, and the sternum inferiorly. Although
  • level VI is large in area, the few lymph nodes that it contains are mostly in the paratracheal regions near the thyroid gland.
  • Level VII (superior mediastinum) lies between the common carotid arteries and is superior to the aortic arch and inferior to the upper border of the sternum.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 34, Edition: 21st, Pg: 775

question_text: A 45-year-old male patient with BMI > 50 kg/m2 is suffering from hypertension. What should be the risk score for bariatric surgery according to the Obesity Surgery-Mortality Risk Score?
explanation:
Using risk scores such as the Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS) and Obesity Surgery-Mortality Risk Score (OS-MRS) can help the team discuss with patients the likely prognosis without surgery, and the risk of complications. The OS-MRS scores one point for each of:

  1. Age ≥45,
  2. BMI ≥50,
  3. Male gender (due to central obesity),
  4. Hypertension (due to central obesity),
  5. Increased deep vein thrombosis (DVT)/pulmonary embolism (PE) risk.

The more points that are present, the greater is the risk.

Swedish registry data indicates that obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) is a risk factor for anastomotic leak. Therefore, OSA should be actively investigated, as treatment with continuous positive airway pressure might reduce risk. Uncontrolled diabetes must also be considered a risk factor, as it is for all other operations.

Reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Page Number 1183-1184.

  • Very obese sick patients with, for instance, sleep apnoea with complications need careful multidisciplinary team (MDT) work-up in bariatric surgery.
  • Using risk scores such as the Edmonton Obesity Staging System (EOSS) and Obesity Surgery-Mortality Risk Score (OS-MRS) can help the team discuss with patients the likely prognosis without surgery, and the risk of complications.
  • The OS-MRS scores one point for each of: age ≥45, BMI ≥50, male gender (due to central obesity), hypertension (due to central obesity), increased deep vein thrombosis (DVT)/pulmonary embolus (PE) risk. The more points that are present the greater is the risk.
  • Swedish registry data indicate that obstructive sleep apnoea (OSA) is a risk factor for anastomotic leak. Therefore, OSA should be actively investigated, as treatment with continuous positive airway pressure might reduce risk.
  • Uncontrolled diabetes must also be considered a risk factor, as it is for all other operations.
  • It is routine to put patients on a ‘liver shrinkage diet’ for at least 2 weeks before surgery, especially when there is central obesity, as this is associated with large livers that can make surgery impossible.
  • If a patient cannot lose weight or comply with the liver diet it implies there may be important psychological blocks that need addressing.
  • Male patients especially, with central obesity, a very dense/hard abdomen, OSA/diabetes and a BMI >50 may need more, supervised, mandatory weight loss to make surgery safe.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 68, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1184

question_text: Which among the following statements is false for action of thyroid hormones?
option_a: Metabolic effects are due to bound T3 and T4
option_b: T3 is more important physiological hormone
explanation:
• The metabolic effects of the thyroid hormones are due to unbound free T4 and T3 (0.03% and 0.3% of the total circulating hormones, respectively).
  • T3 is the more important physiological hormone and is also produced in the periphery by conversion from T4.
  • T3 is quick acting (within a few hours), whereas T4 acts more slowly (4-14 days).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 55, Edition: 28th, Pg: 852

question_text: An 18 months old male child was brought to the hospital with multiple episodes of non-bilious vomiting and poor feeding. The child was passing dry pellets like stools. Which of the following findings will be seen?
explanation:
INFANTILE HYPERTROPHIC PYLORIC STENOSIS

  • Pyloric stenosis presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting starting between 2 and 6 weeks of age.
  • The diagnosis is made on a test feed or on abdominal ultrasound showing a thickened and lengthened pylorus.In a test feed, gastric peristalsis is seen passing from left to right across the abdomen, and in a relaxed (feeding) baby, the pyloric 'tumor' is palpable as an 'olive' in the right upper quadrant.
  • Feeds are discontinued, and the stomach is emptied with an 8-10Fr nasogastric tube.
  • Loss of gastric acid causes a hypochloremic, hypokalaemic alkalosis and renal compensation results in paradoxical aciduria.
  • correction may take 24-48 hours; 0.9% saline with 0.15% KCl in 5% glucose given at 6-7.5 mL/kg/h provides maintenance and corrects defects in most babies.
  • Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy is performed laparoscopically or through a supraumbilical or right upper quadrant incision.
  • Postoperatively, intravenous fluids are continued until feeds are re-established within 24 hours. Early postoperative vomiting usually swiftly resolves, with GOR being more likely than an incomplete myotomy if it persists.

question_text: Which is the most commonly used radioisotope in positron emission tomography (PET) scan?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most widely used radioisotope in PET scanning is Fluorine-18 (¹⁸F). It is incorporated into fluorodeoxyglucose (¹⁸F-FDG), a glucose analogue that accumulates in tissues with high metabolic activity (e.g., cancers, brain, myocardium). The half-life of ¹⁸F is ~110 minutes, making it ideal for clinical imaging due to sufficient availability and imaging resolution.

Explanation of other options:

¹³C (Option A): A stable isotope, not a positron emitter. Used in metabolic studies and breath tests (e.g., H. pylori urea breath test), not PET scans.

¹⁴C (Option B): A beta emitter used for radiolabeling in research and in carbon dating, but not applicable in PET imaging.

All of the above (Option D): Incorrect, since only ¹⁸F is widely used in PET scanning.

Key Takeaways:

  • ¹⁸F-FDG PET is the standard in oncology, neurology, and cardiology imaging.
  • Half-life ~110 minutes → optimal for clinical applications.
  • Other isotopes like ¹³C and ¹⁴C are not used for PET.

References: Johns Hopkins Medicine - Positron Emission Tomography (PET) overview

(https://www.hopkinsmedicine.org/health/treatment-tests-and-therapies/positron-emission-tomography-pet)

question_text: Which of the following statement is not true for metabolic surgery?
option_a: Type 2 diabetes is a part of metabolic syndrome
option_c: GLP-1 is an incretin which stimulates alpha cells of pancreas
explanation:
METABOLIC SURGERY

  • 'Metabolic' or 'diabetes' surgery is increasingly being used in conjunction with, or instead of, 'bariatric surgery' due to the highly effective way surgery improves the metabolic syndrome, with weight loss being a welcomed additional effect.
  • Type 2 diabetes is part of the 'metabolic syndrome' that includes high blood pressure, dyslipidaemia and polycystic ovary syndrome.
  • Remarkably, after several types of bariatric surgery diabetes control appears to improve before significant weight loss occurs.
  • Some of the effects on glucose metabolism can be attributed to the caloric restriction, but changes in gut hormone levels, particularly glucagon-like-peptide 1(GLP-1), have provoked much interest. GLP-1 is an incretin, which stimulates the beta cells in the pancreas to restore the normal first phase insulin response after eating. Bile acids are also involved.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 68, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1183

question_text: Which of the following is the most common deficiency observed after gastric bypass/bariatric surgery?
explanation:
Explanation:

Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency following Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB). This occurs due to two main reasons:

  1. Bypass of the Duodenum: The primary site of iron absorption is bypassed.
  2. Reduced Gastric Acid: The new gastric pouch produces little acid, and iron requires an acidic environment for conversion into its absorbable ferrous (Fe2+) form.
    This often leads to iron-deficiency anemia, presenting as fatigue and pallor.

Copper and zinc deficiencies may occur but are less common than iron deficiency, while calcium deficiency is frequent due to reduced intake and vitamin D malabsorption, yet iron deficiency remains the most common. (Options B,C and D ruled out)

Key Takeaways:

  • Iron deficiency is the most prevalent micronutrient deficiency after gastric bypass.
  • Lifelong supplementation and monitoring are required after bariatric surgery.

question_text: Which deficiency occurs after this surgery?
explanation:
The given image is of a ROUX EN Y BYPASS bariatric surgery done for weight loss.

Nutritional Complications

Iron

  • Iron deficiency is the most common nutritional deficiency in an RYGB patient, with a 30% to 50% prevalence.
  • Iron absorption is promoted when exposed to gastric acid and duodenal proteolytic enzymes resulting in molecular transformations. It can be absorbed at any level in the intestinal tract but is the most efficient in the duodenum.
  • Deficiency in RYGB patients is due to the bypass of the mechanism mentioned above of absorption or slow chronic bleeding from marginal ulceration. Patients may present with fatigue and generalized weakness.

Calcium and Vitamin D

  • There is a high prevalence of vitamin-D deficiency and resulting secondary hyperparathyroidism in obese patients preoperatively.
  • Obesity, however, results in a higher preoperative bone mineral mass. Calcium is preferentially absorbed in the duodenum and proximal jejunum, while vitamin D is primarily absorbed in the distal small bowel.
  • After bypassing these segments, there is malabsorption of calcium with a resulting deficiency leading to a further increase in PTH.
  • The long-term actions of PTH will release calcium from the bone causing osteopenia and eventually osteoporosis. Treatment and prevention are with oral supplementation.

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK519489/

question_text: All of the following metabolic responses are seen in response to starvation except:
option_a: After 12 hours of fast liver glycogen converted into glucose.
option_b: After 24 hours of fasting, gluconeogenesis started from non-carbohydrate precursors.
option_c: After 1week of fasting, Central nervous system adapts to using ketone bodies as their primary Fuel.
option_d: Even though muscle contain glycogen it cannot be utilized directly.
explanation:
Option A: After 12 hours of fast plasma insulin level falls and glucagon level rise which Facilitates conversion of liver glycogen into glucose.

Option B: After more than 24 hours of fasting, Gluconeogenesis started from Amino acids particularly glutamine and alanine.

Option C: After 48-72 hours not a week, central nervous system may adapt to using ketone bodies as their primary fuel source.

Option D: Glycogen also exist in muscle but cannot be utilized directly. Muscle Glycogen is converted to lactate which is then exported to liver where It is converted to glucose.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 25, Edition: 28th, Pg: 329

question_text: All of the following are correct regarding bronchoscopy except?
option_a: Flexible bronchoscopy can be performed under local anesthesia
option_b: Rigid bronchoscopy is ideal for therapeutic maneuver
option_c: Rigid bronchoscopy can be done only in awake patients
option_d: Biopsies are relatively small and suction is limited with flexible bronchoscopy
explanation:
BRONCHOSCOPY

  • Flexible bronchoscopy may be performed with the patient awake and the oropharynx anaesthetised with topical lignocaine. The bronchoscope is passed into the nose or mouth and through the vocal folds under direct vision. As the scope is flexible, its tip can be directed into the segmental bronchi with ease. Tissue and sputum samples may be obtained for diagnostic purposes. There is a greater range of movement with this instrument, but the biopsies are relatively small and suction limited.
  • Rigid bronchoscopy requires general anaesthesia in most instances. It is ideal for therapeutic manoeuvres, such as removal of foreign bodies, aspiration of blood and thick secretions, and intraluminal surgery (laser resection or stent placement). The surgeon and the anaesthetist share control of the airway. Continuous ECG and pulse oximetry monitoring are now essential. The technique involves the operator standing behind the patient and lifting the maxilla by the upper teeth, using the middle finger and forefinger of the left hand. The bronchoscope rests on the left thumb as it is introduced over the tongue in the midline. Care must be taken not to trap the lips or tongue between the teeth and the bronchoscope, and the fulcrum should be the left thumb and not the teeth. The bronchoscope is passed under direct vision into the oropharynx, behind the epiglottis, until the vocal folds are seen. Turning the instrument through 90° will help to negotiate the vocal folds; only then should the neck be extended.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 59, Cardiac Surgery, Pg: 984.

question_text: Which among the following is not the landmark commonly used for location of the facial nerve trunk?
option_b: Upper border of the anterior belly of digastric muscle
explanation:
LOCATION OF THE FACIAL NERVE TRUNK

  • The main methods of facial nerve trunk localisation can be divided into antegrade and retrograde.
  • The former utilises anatomical landmarks to identify the nerve trunk after its exit from the stylomastoid foramen, which is then traced distally. Landmarks commonly used are:
    1. The inferior portion of the cartilaginous canal. This is termed Conley's pointer (tragal pointer) and indicates the position of the facial nerve, which lies 1 cm deep and inferior to its tip
    2. The upper border of the posterior belly of the digastric muscle. Identification of this muscle not only helps to mobilise the parotid gland, but also exposes an area immediately superior, in which the facial nerve is usually located
    3. The squamotympanic fissure
    4. The styloid process (the nerve is superficial to it)
    5. The mastoid process can be drilled and the nerve identified more proximally.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 54, Edition: 28th, Pg: 846

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding escharotomy except
option_a: Upper limb - Mid-axial, anterior to the elbow medially to avoid the ulnar nerve
option_b: Hand - Midline in the digits. Release muscle compartments if tight
option_c: Lower limb - Mid-axial. Posterior to the ankle laterally to avoid the saphenous vein
option_d: Chest - Down the chest lateral to the nipples, across the chest below the clavicle and across the chest at the level of the xiphisternum
explanation:
• Key features of escharotomy placement.
    • Upper limb - Mid-axial, anterior to the elbow medially to avoid the ulnar nerve
    • Hand - Midline in the digits. Release muscle compartments if tight. Best done in theatre and with an experienced surgeon
    • Lower limb - Mid-axial. Posterior to the ankle medially to avoid the saphenous vein
    • Chest - Down the chest lateral to the nipples, across the chest below the clavicle and across the chest at the level of the xiphisternum
    • General rules extend the wound beyond the deep burn.
    • Diathermy any significant bleeding vessels.

Apply haemostatic dressing and elevate the limb postoperatively

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 46, Edition: 28th, Pg: 673

question_text: Which among the following structures is not removed in the patey's mastectomy?
explanation:
In Patey's mastectomy, the breast and associated structures are dissected en bloc and the excised mass is composed of -

  • Whole breast tissue
  • Skin over the breast tissue
  • Nipple areola complex
  • Fat, fascia and lymph nodes of the axilla.

The pectoralis minor muscle is either divided or retracted to gain access to the upper two-thirds of the axilla.

The axillary vein and nerves to the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi should be preserved.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28th, Pg: 935

question_text: A child with recurrent vomiting undergoes an x-ray, as shown below. What is the most likely associated electrolyte imbalance in this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The described features are consistent with congenital hypertrophic pyloric stenosis (HPS). Persistent vomiting in HPS leads to:

  • Loss of gastric HCl → metabolic alkalosis
  • Renal compensation → excretion of potassium
  • Overall result → hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis

Key clinical features of HPS:

  • Projectile, non-bilious vomiting (appears between 3rd–6th week of life)
  • Visible gastric peristalsis (VGP)
  • Palpable "olive-shaped" mass in the epigastrium/left hypochondrium
  • Dehydration, constipation, weight loss
  • Investigations:
    • Ultrasound abdomen → diagnostic; "doughnut/target sign," pyloric muscle thickness ≥ 4 mm, canal length ≥ 14 mm
    • X-ray (single bubble sign) → dilated stomach with absent distal gas due to obstruction
  • Management:
    • Correct dehydration + electrolytes first
    • Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy (open/laparoscopic) is the definitive treatment

Explanation of Other Options:

Hyperkalemia (Option B): Opposite of the expected metabolic derangements in HPS; not seen here.

Hyponatremia (Option C): Vomiting can cause sodium depletion, but the hallmark abnormality is hypokalemia + metabolic alkalosis.

Hypernatremia (Option D): Not typically associated with HPS; dehydration more commonly leads to hypochloremic, hypokalemic alkalosis.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Hypertrophic pyloric stenosis → projectile vomiting in infants.
  • Classic metabolic profile: Hypochloremic, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis.
  • Must always correct fluid & electrolytes before surgery.

question_text:
Which of the following symptoms are seen in the child with the following X-ray?

1. Bilious vomiting
2. Palpable mass
3. Hypochloremia and hypokalemia
4. Metabolic alkalosis
explanation:
The X-ray given shows single bubble appearance

INFANTILE HYPERTROPHIC PYLORIC STENOSIS

  • Pyloric stenosis presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting starting between 2 and 6 weeks of age. Its presentation differs from infective causes of vomiting (e.g. meningitis, urinary tract infections [UTIs]) because of postprandial hunger.
  • Once vomiting starts, it's frequency and forcefulness increase daily,
  • The diagnosis is made on a test feed or on abdominal ultrasound showing a thickened and lengthened pylorus. In a test feed, gastric peristalsis is seen passing from left to right across the abdomen, and in a relaxed (feeding) baby, the pyloric 'tumor' is palpable as an 'olive' in the right upper quadrant.
  • Feeds are discontinued, and the stomach is emptied with an 8-10Fr nasogastric tube. Loss of gastric acid causes a hypochloremic, hypokalaemic alkalosis with paradoxical
  • correction may take 24-48 hours; 0.9% NaCl with 0.15% KCl in 5% glucose given at 6-7.5 mL/kg/h provides maintenance and corrects defects in most babies. As the chloride deficit is replaced, the kidneys correct the pH.
  • Ramstedt's pyloromyotomy is performed laparoscopically or through a supraumbilical or right upper quadrant incision. A pyloric serosal incision is made, and the 'tumor' spreads, leaving an intact submucosa from the duodenal fornix to gastric antrum. The incision must extend onto the stomach; short incisions cause an early recurrence.
  • Postoperatively, intravenous fluids are continued until feeds are re-established within 24 hours. Early postoperative vomiting usually swiftly resolves, with GOR being more likely than an incomplete myotomy if it persists.

question_text: Most common graft used as conduit for CABG?
explanation:
The long saphenous vein is the most commonly used venous conduit as it is straightforward to harvest, provides good length and is easy to handle. Alternative vein conduits include the short saphenous vein or upper limb veins such as the cephalic vein; however, these grafts are associated with poorer long-term patency rates.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 59, Cardiac Surgery, Pg: 950.

question_text: Which among the following artery gives the branch to the inferior thyroid artery?
explanation:
• Blood and Lymphatic Supply: The thyroid gland has a rich blood supply and a complex network of vessels. It receives arterial blood from several sources.
  • Superior Thyroid Arteries: The superior thyroid arteries arise from the external carotid arteries. These arteries split into branches as they enter the upper poles of the thyroid lobes.
  • Inferior Thyroid Arteries: The inferior thyroid arteries originate from the thyrocervical trunks of the subclavian arteries. They branch fairly close to the thyrocervical trunk, and their course takes them upward and posteriorly, running behind the carotid sheath. They then turn and enter the mid-portion of the thyroid lobes.
  • Thyroid Ima Artery: In about 2% of individuals, a third artery known as the thyroid ima artery can be present. This artery has an unusual origin, arising directly from either the aorta or innominate artery. It follows a midline path and enters either the thyroid isthmus or the lower poles of the thyroid lobes.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 876

question_text: What is the relation of the rotter's lymph nodes in relation to the pectoralis minor muscle?
explanation:
• Axillary nodes are typically described as three anatomic levels defined by their relationship to the pectoralis minor muscle.
  • Level I nodes are located lateral to the lateral border of the pectoralis minor muscle.
  • Level II nodes are located posterior to the pectoralis minor muscle as well as anterior to the pectoralis minor and posterior to the pectoralis major (Rotter or interpectoral nodes).
  • Level III nodes are located medial to the pectoralis minor muscle and include the subclavicular nodes.
  • The apex of the axilla is defined by the costoclavicular ligament (Halsted ligament), at which point the axillary vein passes into the thorax and becomes the subclavian vein.
  • However, functionally, the lymph nodes of the axilla are made up of lymphatics from the upper extremity, the back, and the breast.
  • Boneti and colleagues1 described the anatomic drainage of the lymphatics from the arm within the axilla, including the traditional position just below the vein, above the vein or going directly into the subclavian, a sling pattern that comes well below the axilla, a medial or lateral apron pattern, and a twine pattern.
  • Four percent of the time, the nodes from the breast merge with those draining the upper extremity within Level I.
  • The functional anatomy of these lymph nodes is important in preventing lymphedema during lymphadenectomy for breast cancer.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 35, Edition: 21st, Pg: 809

explanation:
