question_text: A 25 years old female who had pain in the right iliac fossa with vomiting was managed conservatively. He was stable for 2 days after which He had worsening of the symptoms for which Extra peritoneal drainage was done by USG guidance. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
• Acute appendicitis is one of the most frequent acute surgical pathologies. The inflammation in acute appendicitis may sometimes be fixed by the patient's own defense mechanisms, by the formation of an inflammatory mass (an appendiceal phlegmon) or a circumscribed abscess (an appendiceal abscess), often presenting as a palpable mass days following the onset of symptoms. This complication occurs in 2 to 7% of all cases of appendicitis.
  • Management of appendiceal mass and abscess is either operative or conservative. More evidence is needed to identify which method is superior.
  • Immediate appendectomy may be technically demanding because of the distorted anatomy and difficulties in closing the appendiceal stump due to the inflamed tissues. According to the aforementioned, the operation could be finished with colonic resections (ileocecectomy or right hemicolectomy).
  • OSCHNER SHERREN REGIMEN : Conservative management with interval appendectomy has traditionally remained the gold standard management. The need for interval appendectomy after a successful nonsurgical treatment has recently been questioned as the risk of recurrence is relatively small. After successful nonsurgical treatment of an appendiceal mass, the true diagnosis is uncertain in some cases and underlying diagnosis of cancer or Crohn's disease (CD) may be delayed.

 https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4587501/

question_text: Which artery gives the branch to appendicular artery?
option_a: Lower division of right colic artery
option_b: Upper division of right colic artery
explanation:
Explanation:

The appendicular artery arises from the lower division of the ileocolic artery, which supplies the appendix, cecum, and terminal ileum.

  • The mesentery of the appendix or mesoappendix arises from the lower surface of the mesentery or the terminal ileum and is itself subject to great variation. Sometimes, as much as the distal one-third of the appendix is bereft of mesoappendix.
  • Especially in childhood, the mesoappendix is so transparent that the contained blood vessels can be seen. In many adults, it becomes laden with fat, which obscures these vessels. The appendicular artery, a branch of the lower division of the ileocolic artery, passes behind the terminal ileum to enter the mesoappendix a short distance from the base of the appendix.
  • It then comes to lie in the free border of the mesoappendix. An accessory appendicular artery may be present but, in most people, the appendicular artery is an 'end-artery', thrombosis of which results in necrosis of the appendix (synonym: gangrenous appendicitis). Four, six or more lymphatic channels traverse the mesoappendix to empty into the ileocaecal lymph nodes.

Explanation for the other options:

  • A.Right colic artery supplies the ascending colon.
  • B.Right colic artery supplies the ascending colon.
  • D.Upper division of the ileocolic artery contributes to the marginal artery.

Key Takeaways:

The Appendicular artery is a branch of the lower division of the Ileocolic artery. It is an important end-artery, meaning its occlusion causes gangrene of the appendix (gangrenous appendicitis).

Level:

Must know

question_text: A patient has fever and right lower quadrant pain for 5 days. Examination shows a tender mass in the right iliac fossa, with leukocytosis. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture is consistent with an appendicular mass (appendicitis complication).

Based on the clinical presentation, the most probable diagnosis is appendicitis.

Appendicitis is defined as the inflammation of the appendix, which is a small, blind-ended pouch located in the right lower abdomen (right iliac fossa).

The classic clinical features that strongly support this diagnosis include:

  • The presence of fever.
  • Abdominal pain localized to the right lower quadrant (right iliac fossa).
  • An elevated white blood cell count (leukocytosis).
  • The finding of a painful lump (mass) in the right iliac fossa further increases the likelihood of appendicitis, often indicating a peri-appendiceal phlegmon or abscess formation.
  • Appendicitis stages: Catarrhal → Suppurative → Gangrenous → Perforated → Appendicular mass/abscess.
  • Management: Initial conservative (Ochsner-Sherren regimen), interval appendectomy later.

Explanation of Other Options:

Hydronephrosis (Option B): Causes flank pain, not RLQ tenderness.

Tuberculosis (Option C): Chronic course with weight loss, low-grade fever, no leukocytosis.

Carcinoma colon (Option D): Elderly, insidious onset, firm non-tender mass.

Key Takeaways:

  • Tender RIF mass + fever + leukocytosis = appendicular mass.
  • Always differentiate from ileocecal TB and cecal carcinoma.

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding acute appendicitis in children except?
option_a: Classical presentation is anorexia and vomiting with central abdominal pain that settles in RIF
option_b: Persistent guarding in RIF differentiates from NSAP
option_c: Surgery should be avoided in children
option_d: Right lower lobe pneumonia pain also referred as pain of acute appendicitis
explanation:
• Classically there is anorexia and a few vomits with central abdominal pain which settles in the right iliac fossa. In early acute appendicitis there is a fever of 37.3–38.4°C and localized tenderness. Finding persistent guarding in the right iliac fossa on repeated examination is the key to making the diagnosis and distinguishing it from NSAP, which usually resolves over 24–48 hours. NSAP does not have persistent guarding.
  • Acute appendicitis was principally always a clinical diagnosis but more recently early ultrasound is proving useful. Investigations may help but cannot replace regular expert clinical review. The pitfalls include wrongly making the diagnosis of gastroenteritis when there are loose stools or attributing pain on micturition and pyuria to a urinary tract infection (UTI).
  • Both of these can occur when there is pelvic appendicitis or a pelvic collection.
  • Referred pain from a right lower lobe pneumonia should be considered and it is important to remember that if antibiotics have been given the signs may be reduced and presentation can be delayed.
  • The diagnosis can be difficult in those under 5 years of age. Many under-fives present with a perforated appendix, not because the diagnosis is made late but rather because the omentum is less well developed and inflammation is not well contained.
  • The treatment starts with resuscitation with intravenous fluids, analgesia and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Appendicectomy can be performed laparoscopically or through a muscle splitting right iliac fossa incision. An appendix mass in a child who is not obstructed may respond to non-operative management with antibiotics, and an interval appendicectomy can be considered 6 weeks later.

Reference: Bailey and love's short practice of surgery, 27th edition, Page -130

question_text: Lady in the first trimester of pregnancy, presents to ER, with acute abdominal pain. She is diagnosed with acute appendicitis. Next step in the management will be?
option_b: Give antibiotics and wait till 2nd trimester
explanation:
• Appendicitis is slightly more common in the second trimester and, when compared with the non-pregnant population, presentation during pregnancy is more likely to be complicated.
  • Obstetric teaching has been that the caecum and appendix are progressively pushed to the right upper quadrant of the abdomen as pregnancy develops during the second and third trimesters. However, pain in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen remains the cardinal feature of appendicitis in pregnancy.
  • Investigation of choice for appendicitis in pregnancy- MRI
  • There is insufficient evidence to support a non-operative approach and the pregnant patient with acute appendicitis should proceed to surgery.
  • If the fetus is at a viable gestational age (23 weeks or more), appropriate obstetric and neonatal support should ideally be available.
  • A laparoscopic approach is now considered to be safe in any trimester and, if used, should be initiated via the open Hasson technique.

question_text: Which of the following statements is false for carcinoid tumour of appendix?
option_a: Carcinoid tumour arises from kulchitsky cells
option_b: Carcinoid tumour most commonly occurs in appendix
option_c: Most common site is middle part of appendix
option_d: It rarely give rise to metastasis
explanation:
Carcinoid tumour (synonym: argentaffinoma):

  • Carcinoid tumours arise in argentaffin tissue (Kulchitsky cells of the crypts of Lieberkühn) and are most common in the vermiform appendix.
  • Carcinoid tumour is found once in every 300-400 appendices subjected to histological examination.
  • In many instances, the appendix had been removed because of symptoms of subacute or recurrent appendicitis.
  • The tumour can occur in any part of the appendix, but it is frequently found in the distal third.
  • The neoplasm feels moderately hard and, on sectioning the appendix, it can be seen as a yellow tumour between the intact mucosa and the peritoneum.
  • Microscopically, the tumour cells are small, arranged in small nests within the muscle and have a characteristic pattern using immune histochemical stain for chromogranin B.
  • Unlike carcinoid tumours arising in other parts of the intestinal tract, carcinoid tumour of the appendix rarely gives rise to metastases.

Treatment:

  • Appendicectomy has been shown to be sufficient treatment unless the caecal wall is involved, the tumour is 2 cm or more in size or involved lymph nodes are found, when right hemicolectomy is indicated.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter 72, Edition 27th, Pg: 1315

question_text: What is the name of the sign when deep palpation of the left iliac fossa causes pain in the right iliac fossa?
explanation:
• Deep palpation of the left iliac fossa may cause pain in the right iliac fossa, Rovsing's sign, which is helpful in supporting a clinical diagnosis of appendicitis.
  • Occasionally, an inflamed appendix lies on the psoas muscle, and the patient, often a young adult, will lie with the right hip flexed for pain relief (the psoas sign).
  • Spasm of the obturator internus is sometimes demonstrable when the hip is flexed and internally rotated. If an inflamed appendix is in contact with the obturator internus, this manoeuvre will cause pain in the hypogastrium (the obturator test; Zachary Cope).
  • Cutaneous hyperaesthesia may be demonstrable in the right iliac fossa, but is rarely of diagnostic value.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 76, Edition 28th, Pg: 1339

question_text: What will be the position of the appendix in silent appendicitis?
explanation:
Retrocaecal

  • Rigidity is often absent, and even application of deep pressure may fail to elicit tenderness (silent appendix), the reason being that the caecum, distended with gas, prevents the pressure exerted by the hand from reaching the inflamed structure in case of retrocaecal appendix.
  • However, deep tenderness is often present in the loin, and rigidity of the quadratus lumborum may be in evidence.
  • Psoas spasm, due to the inflamed appendix being in contact with that muscle, may be sufficient to cause flexion of the hip joint.
  • Hyperextension of the hip joint may induce abdominal pain when the degree of psoas spasm is insufficient to cause flexion of the hip.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 76, Edition 28th, Pg: 1339

question_text: What is the predictive score for clinical acute appendicitis according to Alvarado  scoring system?
explanation:
Investigation

The diagnosis of acute appendicitis is essentially clinical; however, a decision to operate based on clinical suspicion alone can lead to the removal of a normal appendix in 15-30% of cases.

  • A number of clinical and laboratory- based scoring systems have been devised to assist diagnosis.
  • The most widely used is the Alvarado score.
  • A score of 7 or more is strongly predictive of acute appendicitis.
  • In patients with an equivocal score (5-6), abdominal ultrasound or contrast-enhanced CT examination further reduces the rate of negative appendicectomy.
  • Abdominal ultrasound examination is more useful in children and thin adults, particularly if gynaecological pathology is suspected, with a diagnostic accuracy in excess of 90%.
  • Modern CT is both sensitive and specific (approximately 95%) in the diagnosis of acute appendicitis and worldwide there has been a steady increase in its use for this purpose.
  • CT has been shown to reduce the rate of negative appendicectomy without an associated increased perforation rate (due to delay in diagnosis) and may be cost effective due to shorter hospital stay.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 76, Edition 28th, Pg: 1342

question_text: Which statement best describes McBurney's point in appendicitis?
option_a: Located in the left lower quadrant
option_b: Site of maximal tenderness in acute appendicitis
option_c: Used to assess rebound tenderness in appendicitis
option_d: Located at the umbilicus in appendicitis
explanation:
Explanation:

McBurney's point is situated at the junction of the lateral one-third and medial two-thirds of a line drawn from the right anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS) to the umbilicus. It corresponds anatomically to the base of the appendix. In acute appendicitis, this is the classical site of maximum localized tenderness, making it a reliable clinical sign.

Explanation of other options:

Left lower quadrant (Option A): Incorrect, since McBurney's point lies in the right lower quadrant (RIF), not the left.

Used to assess rebound tenderness (Option C): Wrong, rebound tenderness is elicited at a site away from the pathology (often left iliac fossa - Rovsing's sign), not at McBurney's point.

Located at the umbilicus (Option D): Incorrect, while appendicitis pain may initially be periumbilical due to visceral innervation, the point itself lies between the right ASIS and umbilicus, not directly at the umbilicus.

question_text: After appendectomy, exploration was done for the bleeding. Ligation of which artery is beneficial?
explanation: The appendicular artery, a branch of the lower division of the ileocolic artery, passes behind the terminal ileum to enter the mesoappendix a short distance from the base of the appendix.

question_text: A 23-year-old male had acute appendicitis 3 days ago and presented to the surgery department with abdominal pain and tenderness. Which of the following incisions would be appropriate for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario describes a case of suspected acute appendicitis. The standard and most appropriate incision for an appendicectomy is McBurney's incision (Option 3).

This is a muscle-splitting incision made in the right iliac fossa, centered on McBurney's point (located two-thirds of the way from the umbilicus to the anterior superior iliac spine). It provides direct access to the appendix with minimal tissue damage and a lower risk of postoperative hernia compared to midline incisions.

Explanation of other options:

1 (Kocher's incision) (Option A): A Kocher's incision is a subcostal incision used primarily for open cholecystectomy and access to the gallbladder and biliary tree.

2 (Midline incision) (Option B): A midline laparotomy is used for exploratory surgery or procedures requiring access to multiple abdominal organs but is not the first choice for a straightforward appendicectomy due to increased morbidity.

5 (Lanz incision) (Option D): While a Lanz incision (a transverse incision in the right iliac fossa) is also used for appendicectomy and has cosmetic advantages, the image label points to Option 3 as the correct McBurney's incision.

Key Takeaways:

  • McBurney's incision is the classic muscle-splitting approach for appendicectomy.
  • It is made over McBurney's point in the right iliac fossa.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding appendiceal carcinoid tumors is incorrect?
option_a: Size appears to be the best predictor of malignant behaviour and metastatic potential
option_b: Arise from Kulchitsky cells of the crypts of Leiberkuhn
option_c: Most common location is the base of the appendix
option_d: Most common tumor of the appendix
explanation:
Explanation:

The most common location of carcinoid tumours in the appendix is the tip of the appendix, not the base.

Carcinoid tumor of the appendix (Argentaffinoma)

  • Neuroendocrine tumours that originate from the enterochromaffin cells (Kulchitsky cells) of the crypts of Lieberkuhn. (Option B ruled out)
  • Most common tumours of the appendix. (Option D ruled out)
  • Most common site: Tip of appendix (70%)
  • These tumors are mostly discovered incidentally during appendicectomy for acute appendicitis.
  • Larger tumours may cause abdominal pain, flushing, and diarrhoea due to hormones secreted like serotonin and other vasoactive substances.
  • In appendiceal carcinoid (neuroendocrine) tumors, tumor size is the most reliable predictor of malignancy and risk of metastasis. (Option A ruled out)
    • Tumors <1 cm: Very low risk of metastasis
    • Tumors >2 cm: Significantly higher risk of lymph node involvement and distant metastases
  • The diagnosis of neuroendocrine tumours (NETs) relies on immunohistochemical staining for synaptophysin and chromogranin A.
  • NETs are graded 1-3 based on proliferative activity, assessed by the Ki-67 index and mitotic rate.

Management

  • <1 cm, low-grade, minimal invasion:
    • Appendectomy alone is curative
    • No further treatment or follow-up required
  • 1-2 cm, fully resected:
    • Rare metastases may occur
    • Single CT or MRI recommended to rule out metastasis
    • Further surgery usually not required unless high-risk features
  • >2 cm, incomplete resection, high-grade (2-3), T4, or vascular invasion:
    • Right hemicolectomy recommended due to increased lymph node involvement
    • Follow-up needed if nodal disease or high-grade tumor is present

question_text: A 20-year-old female has fever, nausea and rebound tenderness with migration of pain to the right iliac fossa (RIF). Lab investigation shows raised TLC of 15,000. What is the Alvarado score?
explanation:
Explanation:

Alvarado score components (MANTRELS mnemonic):

  • Migration of pain → 1 (present)
  • Anorexia → 1 (not mentioned → assume 0)
  • Nausea/vomiting → 1 (present)
  • Tenderness in RIF → 2 (explicitly not stated as "tenderness" in stem - the stem mentions rebound tenderness with migration to RIF; since rebound is explicitly stated but localized tenderness is not separately stated, the conservative exam interpretation used here is to score rebound = 1 but not assume the 2-point RLQ tenderness)
  • Rebound tenderness → 1 (present)
  • Elevated temperature → 1 (fever reported)
  • Leukocytosis (>10,000) → 2 (TLC 15,000)
  • Left shift → not mentioned → 0

Summing the clearly provided items without assuming an extra RLQ tenderness = 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 = 6.

Key takeaways:

Alvarado score ranges 0-10; ≥7 suggests probable appendicitis; 5-6 equivocal; ≤4 low probability.

question_text: Which among the following is not the common site for carcinoid tumour?
explanation:
Carcinoid tumours

  • These neuroendocrine tumours occur throughout the gastrointestinal tract, most commonly in the appendix, ileum and rectum in decreasing order of frequency.
  • Appendicular carcinoid tumours are commonly noted as an incidental finding at appendicectomy, and are said to occur in approximately 2% of appendices removed surgically.
  • The tumour arises from Kulchitsky cells at the base of intestinal crypts (of Lieberkuhn).
  • They may produce dense fibrosis in the surrounding tissues, resulting in distortion and scarring of the bowel and associated mesentery, giving them a characteristic radiological appearance.
  • Carcinoid tumours can produce a number of vasoactive peptides, most commonly 5- hydroxytryptamine (serotonin), but also histamine, prostaglandins and kallikrein.
  • When they metastasise to the liver, the 'carcinoid syndrome' can become evident, because the vasoactive substances escape the filtering actions of the liver.
  • The clinical syndrome itself consists of reddish-blue cyanosis, flushing attacks, diarrhoea, borborygmi, asthmatic attacks and, eventually, pulmonary and tricuspid stenosis.
  • Classically, the flushing attacks are induced by alcohol.
  • Surgical resection is usually sufficient for patients with primary disease, but the incidence of recurrence is significant. The extent of disease can be assessed preoperatively using octreotide scanning, which may detect otherwise clinically unapparent primary and secondary tumours.
  • Plasma markers of tumour bulk, such as chromogranin A concentrations, may be useful markers of disease recurrence, as well as of prognostic value.
  • Hepatic resection can be carried out in patients with metastatic disease.
  • The treatment has been transformed by the use of octreotide (a somatostatin analogue), which reduces both flushing and diarrhoea, and octreotide cover is usually used in patients with a carcinoid syndrome who have surgery to prevent a carcinoid crisis resulting from liberation of vasoactive substances following handling of the tumour.
  • Carcinoid tumours are not usually sensitive to chemo or radiotherapy.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 74, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1310

question_text:
Most common ectopic tissue found in meckel's diverticulum is/are type?
1.Gastric
2. Colonic
3. Pancreatic
4.Adrenal
explanation:
• Meckel's diverticulum is a persistent remnant of the vitellointestinal duct and is present in about 2% of the population.
  • It is found on the antimesenteric side of the ileum approximately 60 cm from the ileocaecal valve and is classically 5 cm long (2% prevalence; 2 feet [60 cm] from ileocaecal valve; 2 inches [5 cm] long).
  • A Meckel's diverticulum is a congenital diverticulum. It contains all three coats of the bowel wall and has its own blood supply. It may be vulnerable to obstruction and infammation in the same way as the appendix;
  • indeed, when a normal appendix is found at surgery for suspected appendicitis, a Meckel's diverticulum should be looked for by examining the small bowel, particularly if free fuid or pus is found.
  • In approximately 20% of cases, the mucosa of a Meckel's diverticulum contains heterotopic epithelium of gastric, colonic or pancreatic type. The presence of heterotopic mucosa may predispose to the development of complications.

The vast majority of Meckel's diverticula are asymptomatic and a Meckel's diverticulum is notoriously difcult to visualise with contrast radiology.

question_text: Which of the following symptom is not included in murphy's triad?
explanation:
Explanation:

Murphy's triad include

  1. Abdominal pain
  2. Vomiting
  3. Fever
  • The classical features of acute appendicitis begin with poorly localised colicky abdominal pain.
  • This is due to mid-gut visceral discomfort in response to appendiceal inflammation and obstruction.
  • The pain is frequently first noticed in the periumbilical region and is similar to, but less intense than, the colic of small bowel obstruction. Central abdominal pain is associated with anorexia, nausea and usually one or two episodes of vomiting that follow the onset of pain (Murphy).
  • Anorexia is a useful and constant clinical feature, particularly in children. The patient often gives a history of similar discomfort that settled spontaneously. A family history is also useful as up to one-third of children with appendicitis have a first-degree relative with a similar history.
  • With progressive inflammation of the appendix, the parietal peritoneum in the right iliac fossa becomes irritated, producing more intense, constant and localised somatic pain that begins to predominate.
  • Patients often report this as an abdominal pain that has shifted and changed in character. Typically, coughing or sudden movement exacerbates the right iliac fossa pain.
  • During the first 6 hours, there is rarely any alteration in temperature or pulse rate. After that time, slight pyrexia (37.2-37.7∘C) with a corresponding increase in the pulse rate to 80 or 90 is usual.
  • In children, a temperature greater than 38.5∘C suggests other causes (e.g. mesenteric adenitis [see below]).
  • Typically, two clinical syndromes of acute appendicitis can be discerned, acute catarrhal (non-obstructive) appendicitis and acute obstructive appendicitis, the latter characterised by a more acute course.
  • The onset of symptoms is abrupt and there may be generalised abdominal pain from the start. The temperature may be normal and vomiting is common, so the clinical picture may mimic acute intestinal obstruction.

Explanation for the other options:

  • Vomiting is a component.
  • Pain (abdominal) is a component.
  • Fever is a component.

Key Takeaways:

Murphy's Triad (for acute appendicitis) consists of Pain, Vomiting, and Fever. Muscle Guarding/Rigidity is a sign of localized peritonitis, which usually develops later.

Level:

Must know

question_text: Which among the following is a doubled ended retractor with a blade on one end?
explanation:
Czerny retractor. This is a double-ended retractor used to retract wound edges for intermediate-type procedures.

  • One end has a blade with a lip which helps to retract without the edge slipping.
  • The other end has two prongs and helps to retract the ends of an incision.
  • When using it, a slight upward tilt gives a better exposure.
  • It is used where a Langenbeck retractor can also be used, but the lip here is broader making it more versatile. Vincenz Czerny (1842-1915) was Professor of Surgery at Freiberg and Heidelberg in Germany.
  • He was a disciple of Theodor Billroth.
  • He was the originator of the concept of multidisciplinary management in cancer.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, Appendix: 1, Edition: 27th, Pg: 1561

question_text: Identify the given instrument
explanation:
Kocher dissector. This is used during a thyroidectomy to dissect the upper pole of the thyroid.

  • The instrument is blunt and therefore the surgeon is highly unlikely to inadvertently damage the superior thyroid artery or the external laryngeal nerve.
  • It is used to dissect the superior pedicle, the superior thyroid artery.
  • Once it has been isolated, the dissector is pushed under the pedicle.
  • A tie is then put through the eye of the dissector which at this stage doubles up as an aneurysm needle.
  • The pedicle is thus tied three times as close to the gland as possible.
  • With the dissector under the tied pedicle, a fine knife is now used to cut leaving two ties in the patient.
  • The presence of the dissector under the pedicle prevents any damage to the underlying structures.
  • Emil Theodor Kocher (1841–1917), Professor of Surgery at Berne, Switzerland, was awarded the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine in 1909 for his work on the thyroid.
  • The first surgeon to be a Nobel Laureate.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, Appendix: 1, Edition: 27th, Pg: 1562

question_text: Which among the following statement is false for hyperplastic type of abdominal tuberculosis?
option_a: Occurs due to ingestion of mycobacterium bovis
option_b: Occurs most commonly in the ileocaecal junction
option_d: Presents with abdominal pain and intermittent diarrhoea
explanation:
Hyperplastic tuberculosi

  • This is caused by the ingestion of Mycobacterium tuberculosis by patients with a high resistance to the organism.
  • The infection usually occurs in the ileocaecal region, although solitary and multiple lesions in the lower ileum are also sometimes seen.
  • The infection establishes itself in lymphoid follicles, and the resulting chronic inflammation causes thickening of the intestinal wall and narrowing of the lumen.
  • There is early involvement of the regional lymph nodes, which may caseate.
  • Unlike in CD, abscess and fistula formation are rare.
  • Patients usually present with attacks of abdominal pain and intermittent diarrhoea.
  • There is incomplete ileal obstruction, leading to stasis and bacterial overgrowth. This in turn causes steatorrhoea, anaemia and loss of weight.
  • Patients may present with a mass in the right iliac fossa and vague ill
  • The differential diagnosis is that of an appendix mass, lymphoma, carcinoma of the caecum, CD, tuberculosis or actinomycosis.
  • A barium follow-through or small bowel enema will show a long narrow filling defect in the terminal ileum (which may result in a differential diagnosis of CD). CT will also demonstrate the narrowed segment with proximal distension and the associated lymphadenopathy.
  • When the diagnosis is clear and the patient has not yet developed obstructive symptoms, treatment with chemotherapy is advised and may be curative. Where obstruction is present, or the possibility of CD or lymphoma require clarification, ileocaecal resection is often required.

This is caused by the ingestion of Mycobacterium tuberculosis by patients with a high resistance to the organism. The infection usually occurs in the ileocecal region, although solitary and multiple lesions in the distal ileum are also sometimes seen. The infection establishes itself in lymphoid follicles, and the resulting chronic inflammation causes thickening of the intestinal wall and narrowing of the lumen.

question_text: Which among the following is not included in the pathogenesis of intussusception in infancy?
option_d: Loss of passively acquired maternal immunity
explanation:
Acute intussusception

  • This occurs when one portion of the gut invaginates into an immediately adjacent segment; almost invariably, it is the proximal into the distal.
  • The condition is encountered most commonly in children, with a peak incidence between 5 and 10 months of age.
  • About 90% of cases are idiopathic but an associated upper respiratory tract infection or gastroenteritis may precede the condition.
  • It is believed that hyperplasia of Peyer’s patches in the terminal ileum may be the initiating event.
  • Weaning, loss of passively acquired maternal immunity and common viral pathogens have all been implicated in the pathogenesis of intussusception in infancy.
  • Children with intussusception associated with a pathological lead point such as Meckel's diverticulum, polyp, duplication, Henoch-Schönlein purpura or appendix are usually older than those with idiopathic disease.
  • After the age of 2 years, a pathological lead point is found in at least one-third of affected children.
  • Adult cases are invariably associated with a lead point, which is usually a polyp (e.g. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome), a submucosal lipoma or other tumour.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1378

question_text: Which among the following is not the clinical presentation of meckel's diverticulum?
explanation:
Meckel's diverticulum

Meckel's diverticulum may present clinically in the following ways:

  • Haemorrhage: If gastric mucosa is present, peptic ulceration can occur and present as painless dark rectal bleeding or melaena. If the stomach, duodenum and colon are excluded as a source of bleeding by endoscopy, radioisotope scanning with technetium-99m may demonstrate a Meckel's diverticulum.
  • Diverticulitis: Meckel's diverticulitis presents like appendicitis, although if perforation occurs the presentation may resemble a perforated duodenal ulcer.
  • Intussusception: A Meckel's diverticulum can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.
  • Chronic ulceration: Pain is felt around the umbilicus, as the site of the diverticulum is midgut in origin.
  • Intestinal obstruction: A band between the apex of the diverticulum and the umbilicus (also part of the vitellointestinal duct) may cause obstruction directly, or by predisposing to the development of a volvulus around it.
  • Perforation: When found in the course of abdominal surgery, a Meckel's diverticulum can safely be left alone, provided it has a wide mouth and is not thickened. When there is doubt, it can be resected. The finding of a Meckel's diverticulum in an inguinal or femoral hernia has been described as 'Littre's hernia'.

Meckel's diverticulectomy

  • A broad-based Meckel's diverticulum should not be Amputated at its base and invaginated (as for an appendix), as there is the risk of stricture and of leaving heterotopic epithelium behind.
  • It is safer simply to excise the diverticulum, either by resecting it and suturing the defect at its base, or with a linear stapler-cutter.
  • If the base of the diverticulum is indurated, it is on balance more logical to perform a limited small bowel resection of the involved segment followed by an anastomosis.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 74, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1312

question_text: A 30-year-old man undergoing evaluation for abdominal pain has a CECT abdomen that reveals the finding shown below. What is the likely condition as indicated by the arrow in the image?
explanation:
Explanation:

Given CT abdomen shows fusion of the lower poles of both kidneys across the midline, suggesting a diagnosis of horse-shoe kidney.

Horseshoe kidney

  • A congenital anomaly where the two kidneys are fused at their lower poles, forming a "U" or horseshoe shape.
  • During fetal development, the kidneys fuse at their lower poles, forming a U-shaped structure leading to this condition.
  • The fusion results in the inferior mesenteric artery preventing the ascent of the isthmus of the kidney to its normal position in the abdomen, leading to an abnormal location lower in the abdomen.

Clinical features

  • Mostly
  • Pain: due to obstruction or renal stones.
  • Recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs).
  • Hydronephrosis.
  • Hematuria
  • Rovsing's syndrome: Hyperextension of the spine- nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain.

Investigations

  • CT Angiography: Investigation of choice for diagnosing a horseshoe kidney, as it allows for detailed visualisation of the renal anatomy, the abnormal vascular supply, and associated complications.
  • Contrast-Enhanced CT (CECT): Used when CT Angio is not available
  • Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP):
    • Medial Orientation of Calyces: Referred to as the Hand Joining Sign.
    • High Insertion of Ureters with Anterior Transposition: This creates a Flower Vase appearance of the ureters.

Fig: IVP findings in horse-shoe kidney: A) Flower vase appearance; B) Hand-joining sign

Treatment

  • Asymptomatic Patients: Typically do not require treatment but should be monitored periodically.
  • Symptomatic Patients:
    • UPJ Obstruction: Surgical intervention such as pyeloplasty
    • Kidney Stones: Management may include conservative measures like increased fluid intake, medical therapy, or surgical removal.
    • UTIs: Treated with antibiotics, and preventive measures may be considered if infections are recurrent.
    • Isthmus Management: The isthmus of the horseshoe kidney should not be divided surgically as it contains functional renal tissue.
    • Pregnancy Considerations: A horseshoe kidney can lead to dystocia (difficult labour) due to the kidney's abnormal position.

Explanation of other options:

Appendicitis (Option A): Presents with right lower quadrant abdominal pain, and in CT, it typically shows a dilated, inflamed appendix.

Wilms tumour (Option C): Wilms tumor is a pediatric renal malignancy, most commonly presenting as a well-defined, lobulated renal mass. It typically arises as a solitary mass in one kidney.

Abdominal aortic aneurysm (Option D): An abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is identified on imaging as a focal dilation of the abdominal aorta, typically located in the midline of the abdomen. Clinically, it may present with abdominal or back pain. However, it does not resemble a kidney-shaped mass and would not show the characteristic "horseshoe" configuration seen in renal fusion anomalies such as a horseshoe kidney.

question_text: Which of the following is not a poor prognostic factor for pseudomyxoma peritonei?
explanation:
Pseudomyxoma peritonei

  • PMP is a rare condition typified by progressive peritoneal tumour deposits, mucinous ascites, omental cake and ovarian involvement in females.
  • The vast majority of cases arise as a result of perforation of a mucinous appendiceal tumour.
  • Patients typically present with progressive and massive abdominal distension, anorexia and symptoms of bowel dysfunction.
  • The condition is invariably fatal without intervention.

TREATMENT - ESTABLISHED PMP

  • The standard accepted treatment for established PMP is cytoreductive surgery (CRS) combined with heated intraperitoneal chemotherapy HIPEC (Sugarbaker).
  • This approach combines multiple peritonectomy procedures with multivisceral resections as required to achieve a complete surgical clearance of the tumour (complete cytoreduction), which is augmented by HIPEC to eradicate presumed residual microscopic disease.
  • The combined operation can take in excess of 10 hours and may require total abdominopelvic peritonectomy, greater and lesser omentectomy, bilateral salpingoophorectomy, hysterectomy, cholecystectomy, splenectomy, partial gastrectomy, colectomy and anterior resection of the rectum.
  • Following a complete cytoreduction 5- and 10-year survival rates of 87% and 70%, respectively, can be achieved.
  • Poorer outcomes are seen in males, patients with elevated tumour markers and following resection of tumour showing high-grade or invasive features.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 76, Edition 28th, Pg: 1351

question_text: A 27-year-old male presents to the emergency room with complaints of pain in the right iliac fossa and melena. On examination, there is tenderness in the right iliac fossa along with nausea and vomiting. Following surgical intervention, the finding shown in the image was observed. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Meckel's Diverticulum

A Meckel's diverticulum is a persistent remnant of the vitellointestinal duct and is present in approximately 2% of the population. It is located on the antimesenteric border of the ileum, typically about 60 cm (2 feet) from the ileocecal valve, and measures around 5 cm (2 inches) in length - hence the rule of twos:

  • 2% prevalence
  • 2 feet from ileocecal valve
  • 2 inches in length

Anatomical Characteristics:

  • It is a true congenital diverticulum, containing all three layers of the bowel wall.
  • It has its own blood supply.
  • It may become obstructed or inflamed, similar to the appendix.

If a normal appendix is found during surgery for suspected appendicitis, especially in the presence of free fluid or pus, a Meckel's diverticulum should be sought by examining the small bowel.

Heterotopic Epithelium:

  • About 20% of cases contain heterotopic mucosa (gastric, colonic, or pancreatic).
  • This may predispose to ulceration and complications.

Clinical Presentations of Meckel's Diverticulum:

  • Hemorrhage
    • Common if gastric mucosa is present.
    • Presents as painless dark rectal bleeding or melena.
    • If upper GI sources are ruled out via endoscopy, a Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan may detect the diverticulum.
  • Diverticulitis
    • Mimics appendicitis.
    • If perforated, may resemble a perforated duodenal ulcer.
  • Intussusception
    • May act as a lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.
  • Chronic Ulceration
    • Causes umbilical pain, consistent with its midgut origin.
  • Intestinal Obstruction
    • Caused by a fibrous band between the diverticulum and umbilicus (remnant of vitellointestinal duct).
    • May lead to volvulus or direct obstruction.
  • Perforation
    • Can occur due to inflammation or ulceration.

Surgical Considerations:

  • Asymptomatic Meckel's diverticulum found during surgery may be left alone if:
    • It has a wide mouth
    • It is not thickened
  • If suspicious:
    • Simple diverticulectomy is performed, with closure of the bowel wall.
    • If the base is indurated or narrow, a segmental small bowel resection with anastomosis is preferred.
    • A linear stapler-cutter may be used for resection.

A Meckel's diverticulum found in a hernia sac (inguinal or femoral) is termed a Littre's hernia.

  • Do not amputate a broad-based diverticulum and invaginate as for an appendix - this may lead to stricture or retention of ectopic mucosa.

Explanation of other options:

Mucocele appendix (Option B):

  • Refers to mucus accumulation in the appendix leading to distension.
  • Usually presents as a palpable mass in the right iliac fossa or is found incidentally.
  • Does not present with melena or typical Meckel's features.

Carcinoid appendix (Option C):

  • Most common tumor of the appendix, typically asymptomatic or found incidentally.
  • May cause appendicitis-like pain but melena is not typical.
  • Found near the tip of the appendix; not associated with a diverticular structure.

Appendiceal serous tumor (Option D):

  • Rare epithelial tumor of the appendix, not typically associated with melena or congenital features.
  • More often presents with non-specific abdominal symptoms or is discovered incidentally.

Key Takeaways:

Meckel's diverticulum is the most likely diagnosis in a young male with right iliac fossa pain, melena, and appendix-like clinical features with a normal appendix on surgery.

question_text: A 48-year-old woman presents with progressive abdominal distension, vague abdominal discomfort, and early satiety. Ultrasound reveals massive mucinous ascites, omental caking, and bilateral ovarian masses. Diagnostic paracentesis confirms mucin-rich ascitic fluid. Histopathology of an appendiceal lesion demonstrates a mucin-producing epithelial neoplasm. Which appendicular carcinoma is most commonly implicated in the pathogenesis of pseudomyxoma peritonei ?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The majority of pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP)cases originate from rupture or dissemination of a mucinous cystadenoma of the appendix.
  • These tumors produce abundant extracellular mucin, which progressively accumulates in the peritoneal cavity, leading to characteristic mucinous ascites, peritoneal implants, and ovarian involvement.

Although mucinous adenocarcinoma of the appendix and, rarely, ovarian tumors may also cause PMP, the most frequent association is with appendiceal mucinous cystadenoma.

Pseudomyxoma Peritonei:

  • Definition:A rare, progressive condition marked by accumulation of gelatinous mucinous material in the peritoneal cavity.
  • Etiology:Most often rupture of mucinous appendiceal tumors, occasionally ovarian mucinous tumors.
  • Pathology:Mucinous ascites, 'jelly belly,' peritoneal implants, omental caking, and bowel/ovarian involvement.
  • Symptoms:Abdominal distension, weight loss, anorexia, bowel dysfunction, hernia recurrence (in males).

Classification (Histological subtypes):

  1. Acellular mucin-deposits without epithelial cells, best prognosis.
  2. Low-grade mucinous carcinoma peritonei (LG-MCP):Minimal atypia.
  3. High-grade mucinous carcinoma peritonei (HG-MCP):Significant cytological atypia.
  4. HG-MCP with signet ring cells:Worst prognosis.

Treatment:

  • Gold Standard:Cytoreductive surgery (CRS) + Hyperthermic Intraperitoneal Chemotherapy (HIPEC).
  • Principle:Remove visible tumor deposits + deliver heated chemotherapy (mitomycin, oxaliplatin, etc.) intraperitoneally to eradicate residual disease.
  • Outcome:5-year survival ~87%, 10-year survival ~70% after complete cytoreduction.
  • Chemotherapy:Systemic chemotherapy reserved for unresectable or recurrent high-grade disease.

Explanation of Other Options:

Adenocarcinoma (Option B): Can occasionally cause PMP but less common than mucinous cystadenoma. Prognosis is worse if PMP arises from adenocarcinoma.

Carcinoid tumor (Option C): Common appendiceal tumor but does not secrete mucin; typically causes obstruction or metastasis, not PMP.

Serous cystadenoma (Option D): Benign ovarian tumor, not associated with mucin production or PMP.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: Which of the following is used for prostate cancer?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Gleason score is the specific histopathological grading system used for prostate adenocarcinoma. It is based on the architectural pattern of the tumor glands under a microscope. The two most prevalent patterns are graded from 3 (well-differentiated) to 5 (poorly differentiated), and their sum gives the Gleason score (ranging from 6 to 10). This score is a critical determinant of prognosis and treatment strategy for prostate cancer.


Explanation of other options:

Bethesda score (Option B): The Bethesda System is used for reporting thyroid cytology (FNA results), not prostate cancer.

Alvarado score (Option C): The Alvarado score is a clinical tool used to aid in the diagnosis of acute appendicitis.

Nottingham score (Option D): The Nottingham (Bloom-Richardson) score is used to grade breast cancer, not prostate cancer.

Key Takeaways:

  • The Gleason score is the cornerstone for grading prostate cancer aggressiveness.
  • A higher Gleason score indicates a more aggressive tumor with a worse prognosis.

question_text:
A 20-year-old male presents with a 5-day history of abdominal pain, fever, and vomiting. On examination, there is a tender mass in the right iliac fossa. Blood investigations reveal leukocytosis.
What is the most appropriate management plan for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A palpable lump in the right iliac fossa several days after onset of appendicitis represents an appendicular mass (inflamed appendix, cecum, and adjacent bowel matted together by omentum).
  • Attempting immediate surgery is hazardous due to distorted anatomy and high complication risk.
  • Therefore, conservative management with the Ochsner-Sherren regimen is the preferred approach.
  • Once inflammation subsides, an interval appendectomy may be planned at 6-8 weeks, particularly in recurrent cases.

Ochsner-Sherren Regimen

Clinical Pearl

"Appendicular mass in a stable patient is managed conservatively with the Ochsner-Sherren regimen, not immediate appendectomy."

Explanation of Other Options:

Alvarado scoring (Option B): Used to assess probability of acute appendicitis, not for treatment.

Laparoscopic appendectomy (Option C): Contraindicated in appendicular mass stage; surgery is difficult and risky until inflammation resolves.

Cholecystectomy (Option D): Unrelated; this is a gallbladder procedure, not applicable here.

explanation:
Deaver retractor. This retractor is specifically designed for holding the liver up out of the way during a cholecystectomy.

question_text: Which is the site of maximum pain in Acute appendicitis?
explanation:
• The diagnosis of appendicitis rests more on thorough clinical examination of the abdomen than on any aspect of the history or laboratory investigation.
  • The cardinal features are those of an unwell patient with low-grade pyrexia, localized abdominal tenderness, muscle guarding and rebound tenderness. Inspection of the abdomen may show limitation of respiratory movement in the lower abdomen.
  • The patient is then asked to point to where the pain began and where it moved (pointing sign). Gentle superficial palpation of the abdomen, beginning in the left iliac fossa and moving anticlockwise to the right iliac fossa, will detect muscle guarding over the point of maximum tenderness, classically McBurney's point. Asking the patient to cough or gentle percussion over the site of maximum tenderness will elicit rebound tenderness.

question_text: Which is the most common position of appendix?
explanation:
• During childhood, continued growth of the caecum commonly rotates the appendix into a retrocaecal but intraperitoneal position. In approximately one-quarter of cases, rotation of the appendix does not occur, resulting in a pelvic, subcaecal or paracaecal position.
  • Occasionally, the tip of the appendix becomes extraperitoneal, lying behind the caecum or ascending colon. Rarely, the caecum does not migrate during development to its normal position in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen. In these circumstances, the appendix can be found near the gall bladder or, in the case of intestinal malrotation, in the left iliac fossa, causing diagnostic difficulty if appendicitis develops.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 76, Edition 28th, Pg: 1335

question_text: Which of the following incision is not used for conventional appendicectomy?
explanation:
CONVENTIONAL APPENDICECTOMY

  • When the preoperative diagnosis is considered reasonably certain, the incision that is widely used for appendicectomy is the so-called gridiron incision (gridiron: a frame of crossbeams to support a ship during repairs). The gridiron incision (described first by McArthur) is made at right angles to a line joining the anterior superior iliac spine to the umbilicus, its centre being along the line at McBurney's point.
  • If better access is required, it is possible to convert the gridiron to a Rutherford Morison incision by cutting the internal oblique and transversus muscles in the line of the incision.
  • In recent years, a transverse skin crease (Lanz) incision has become more popular, as the exposure is better and extension, when needed, is easier. The incision, appropriate in length to the size and obesity of the patient, is made approximately 2 cm below the umbilicus centred on the midclavicular- mid-inguinal line. When necessary, the incision may be extended medially, with retraction or suitable division of the rectus abdominis muscle.
  • When the diagnosis is in doubt, particularly in the presence of intestinal obstruction, a lower midline abdominal incision is to be preferred over a right lower paramedian incision. The latter, although widely practised in the past, is difficult to extend, more difficult to close and provides poorer access to the pelvis and peritoneal cavity.
  • Rutherford Morison's incision is useful if the appendix is para- or retrocaecal and fixed. It is essentially an oblique muscle- cutting incision with its lower end over McBurney's point and extending obliquely upwards and laterally as necessary. All layers are divided in the line of the incision.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 76, Edition 28th, Pg: 1344

question_text: A male child experiences acute scrotal pain while playing. He is brought to the emergency department, where a Doppler ultrasound is performed followed by immediate surgical exploration, which showed the following findings. What is the most probable diagnosis?
option_b: Torsion of testicular appendages with gangrene
explanation:
Explanation:

Sudden onset scrotal pain with necrotic testicular findings on surgical exploration confirms testicular torsion with gangrene.

  • Testicular torsion is a urological emergency where the spermatic cord twists, cutting off blood supply to the testis.
  • It is most common in children and adolescents and presents with sudden, severe unilateral scrotal pain often during activity or sleep.
  • If not treated within 6-12 hours, it can lead to ischemia and eventually gangrene of the testis.
  • On surgical exploration, a gangrenous testis appears black or dark purple due to complete vascular compromise.
  • Early recognition and prompt surgical detorsion and fixation (orchidopexy) are key to salvaging the testis.
  • If gangrene has already occurred, orchiectomy is required.
  • Doppler ultrasound usually reveals absent or significantly reduced blood flow to the affected testis.
  • Predisposing factors include:
    • Bell-clapper deformity (high investment of tunica vaginalis)
    • Horizontal lie of testis
    • Inversion or high mobility of the testis
  • Clinical signs:
    • Sudden onset pain
    • High-riding testis (Deming's sign)
    • Transverse lie of contralateral testis (Angell's sign)
    • Nausea and vomiting

Explanation of other options:

Torsion of testicular appendages with gangrene (Option B): Localized pain due to infarction of appendix testis or appendix epididymis, but testicular blood supply remains intact; necrosis of the testicle itself is not seen.

Strangulated inguinal hernia (Option C): Causes scrotal swelling and pain due to trapped bowel loops, not testicular necrosis. Intraoperative findings would show ischemic bowel, not a gangrenous testis.

Testicular hematoma (Option D): Occurs post-trauma with intact testicular blood flow. Doppler may show hypoechoic collection but not absent perfusion or necrotic testis unless severely complicated.

question_text: What is the type of polyp seen in juvenile polyposis syndrome?
explanation:
Explanation:

Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome (JPS) is an autosomal dominant condition characterized by the presence of multiple hamartomatous polyps, primarily in the colon. These polyps carry a risk of malignant transformation, although less than adenomatous polyps.

Key Takeaways:

Juvenile Polyposis Syndrome is defined by Hamartomatous polyps, which are benign malformations of normal tissue, distinct from neoplastic (adenomatous) polyps.

question_text: Which among the following stage of colorectal tumorigenesis is caused by DNA hypomethylation?
explanation:
Colorectal tumorigenesis proceeds through a series of genetic alterations involving oncogenes (ras) and tumor suppressor genes (particularly those on chromosomes 5q, 12p, 17p, and 18q).

  • In patients with familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), a mutation on chromosome 5q (APC gene) is inherited. This alteration may be responsible for the hyperproliferative epithelium present in these patients.
  • The three stages of adenomas in general represent tumors of increasing size, dysplasia, and villous content.
  • Hypomethylation is present in very small adenomas in patients with or without polyposis, and this alteration may lead to aneuploidy, resulting in the loss of suppressor gene alleles.
  • Allelic deletions of chromosome 17p and 18q usually occur at a later stage of tumorigenesis than do deletions of chromosome 5q or ras gene mutations.
  • The accumulation of these changes, rather than their order with respect to one another, seems most important.
  • Tumors continue to progress once carcinomas have formed, and the accumulated loss of suppressor genes on additional chromosomes correlates with the ability of the carcinomas to metastasize and cause death.

Reference: sabiston 21st edition page 671

explanation:
• The goal of curative surgical treatment of CRC is the resection of the primary tumor with adequate free margins, en bloc with loco regional lymphadenectomy.
  • Regional lymph nodes are located in the mesocolon along the main vascular pedicles.
  • Therefore, an oncologically adequate resection implies the removal of the portion of colon where the primary cancer is located with its vascular pedicles, which must be ligated and divided at their origin.
  • The aim of lymphadenectomy is to ensure an adequate pathologic staging and to remove any possible residual lymph node metastasis.
  • No less than 12 lymph nodes are required for an oncologically adequate resection and for proper staging, but, in most cases, more than 20 nodes are retrieved from the specimen.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1374

question_text: What is the most common cause of death of middle aged women in western countries?
explanation:
Breast cancer is the most common cause of death in middle-aged women in western countries.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28th, Pg: 931

question_text: What is the TNM stage of the colorectal cancer for a patient with tumour invading the muscularis propria with two reginal lymph nodes positive and no distant metastasis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the AJCC/UICC TNM staging system for Colorectal Cancer (8th Edition):

  • T stage (Tumour): Tumour invading the muscularis propria → T2
  • N stage (Nodes): Two regional lymph nodes positive → N1 (1 to 3 regional lymph nodes positive)
  • N sub-stage: N1 is subdivided: N1a (1 positive node), N1b (2-3 positive nodes). Two positive nodes → N1b
  • M stage (Metastasis): No distant metastasis → M0

Combined Stage: T2N1bM0

Key Takeaways:

Accurate TNM staging requires knowing the anatomical definitions: T2 = invasion of muscularis propria. N1b = 2-3 regional lymph nodes positive. M0 = no distant metastasis.

Level:

Must know

question_text: Which among the following gene mutation is not associated with the occurrence of colorectal cancer?
explanation:
Chromosomal Instability Pathway

  • Much of our initial understanding of the genetic basis of CRC comes from the work of Vogelstein and colleagues, who evaluated nearly 200 samples of colorectal neoplasia ranging from polyps to invasive cancers. By checking for alterations in specific genes, they were able to propose a step-wise model of CRC carcinogenesis, involving the activation of an oncogene (a gene that can induce cancer formation) and loss of several genes that act as tumor suppressors.
  • Currently, it is thought that the majority of sporadic CRC arise in this fashion over the course of approximately 10 years from a precursor dysplastic adenoma.
  • The molecular events involved include early APC (adenomatous polyposis coli) gene mutations, subsequent activating mutations in the oncogene KRAS, as well as mutations resulting in inactivation of the tumor suppressor gene TP53.
  • Chromosomal instability refers to changes (gains or losses) in the numbers of chromosomes (aneuploidy) as well as sub chromosomal genomic amplifications and loss of heterozygosity seen with this pathway of carcinogenesis. It is currently thought that this pathway accounts for approximately 60% of patients with CRC.
  • The second major pathway accounting for approximately 35% of patients is the CpG island methylator phenotype cancer, and then the mutator phenotype associated with Lynch syndrome, accounting for 5%.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1363

question_text: A 70 years elderly male presents,On rectal examination a mass was found suspicious of cancer. He had normal bowel habits and he actually visited your hospital for a regular Master health check up. What will you advise him next?
explanation:
Endoscopy

  • For symptomatic patients with rectal bleeding, direct referral from primary care for a flexible sigmoidoscopy is increasingly used.
  • The patient is prepared with an enema and sedation is not usually necessary. The bowel can be assessed as far as the splenic flexure, allowing detection of up to 70% of cancers and almost all that cause fresh rectal bleeding.
  • Finding left-sided colonic polyps or cancer mandates subsequent completion of colonoscopy.

Colonoscopy is the investigation of choice if colorectal cancer is suspected . It has the advantage of not only securing histological diagnosis of a primary cancer but also detecting synchronous polyps or carcinomas, which occur in 3-5% of cases. There is a small risk of perforation (1:1000).

question_text: A 60-year-old man, a smoker, presented to the OPD with complaints of fatigue. He is known to be anemic and his sister had a history of endometrial cancer. The physician is considering appropriate colorectal cancer screening methods for this patient. Which screening method should be recommended for colorectal malignancy in this patient?
option_c: Check for occult blood in stool
explanation:
Explanation:

Colorectal Cancer Screening

  • Recommended test: Colonoscopy every 10 years.
  • Target group: Individuals at average risk, with greater importance in those who have additional risk factors.
  • Advantages:
    • Direct inspection of the colon.
    • Ability to remove precancerous polyps during the same procedure.
    • Considered the most reliable method for both early detection and prevention of colorectal cancer.

question_text: Which among the following biomarkers is specific for colorectal carcinoma?
explanation:
Recently certain subtypes have been recognised to have malignant potential. Sessile serrated lesions and hyperplastic polyps ≥10 mm in diameter are associated with KRAS/BRAF mutation that may lead to methylation of tumour-suppressing genes, dysplasia and malignancy along what is termed the 'serrated pathway'.

Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 12, pg: 215

question_text: Which of the following colonoscopy findings carries the highest malignant potential?
explanation:
Explanation:

Multiple flat polyps (~100) suggest familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), a precancerous condition with nearly 100% progression to colorectal carcinoma if untreated.

  • FAP: Autosomal dominant APC gene mutation.
  • Clinical: >100 adenomatous polyps, rectal bleeding, diarrhea, abdominal pain.
  • Extra-colonic features: CHRPE, desmoid tumors, upper GI polyps, epidermoid cysts.
  • Management: Prophylactic colectomy.

Explanation of other options:

Single pedunculated polyp (Option B): Usually benign, low malignancy risk.

Multiple pedunculated polyps (Option C): Risk depends on histology, not as high as FAP.

Solitary flat polyp (Option D): Higher risk than pedunculated, but not as dangerous as FAP.

Key Takeaways:

  • 100 adenomatous polyps = FAP.
  • 100% risk of carcinoma if untreated.
  • Early surgical prophylaxis essential.

question_text: Which among the following gene mutation is not associated with colorectal carcinoma?
explanation:
• The most common abnormality found in colorectal cancer is mutation in the Wnt signalling pathway, which increases cell signalling The mutations can be inherited or acquired.
  • The most commonly mutated gene is the APC gene, which results in accumulation of the β-catenin protein. β-catenin activates the transcription of various proto- oncogenes that are responsible for normal cell renewal and differentiation, but when overexpressed can cause cancer.
  • Many other mutations, other than in the Wnt signalling pathway, are found in colorectal cancer, and include mutations in the TP53 gene that controls normal cell division and death, and mutations in genes responsible for programmed cell death, such as the gene encoding transforming growth factor (TGF)-β and DCC (deleted in colorectal cancer).
  • Other genetic abnormalities include overexpression of oncogenes, including genes encoding the proteins KRAS (Kirsten rat sarcoma homologue), RAF (rapidly accelerated fibrosarcoma) and PI3K (phosphoinositide 3-kinase), which lead to increased cell proliferation, and inactivation of tumour suppressor genes, such as PTEN (phosphatase and tensin homologue), which normally inactivates the PI3K signalling pathway.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter 73, Edition 27th, Pg: 1329

question_text: A 62 year old man with history of colorectal polyps presents with low grade fever, weight loss and night sweats. ECHO showed vegetations on the aortic valve. Which is the most likely organism to be grown in blood culture?
explanation:
Streptococcus bovis bacteremia and endocarditis have been strongly associated with colorectal neoplasia. Patient identified to have S. bovis endocarditis should be evaluated for the presence of colorectal polyps or cancer.

Penicillin G is the treatment of choice for S. bovis endocarditis typically given for 4 weeks.

Staphylococcus aureus is the most commonly isolated organism from endocarditis occurring in IV drug abusers, which preferentially affects the tricuspid valve.

Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine 21st edition Page 1023-25

question_text: Which among the following shows the carcinoma invading the stalk according to the Haggitt's classification of malignant polyp of colon?
explanation:
Malignant Polyps

  • Malignant polyps are those in which histologic examination following removal of a polyp reveals a focus of carcinoma that has invaded through the muscularis mucosa.
  • The question that arises is whether complete endoscopic removal of these polyps is sufficient.
  • Carcinomas that do not pass the muscularis mucosa are considered “carcinoma in situ” and do not carry metastatic risk.
  • However, those that invade the muscularis mucosa harbour a significant risk of local recurrence and lymph node metastasis. One of the important risk factors is the depth of penetration. This can be defined by the Haggitt classification:

Level 0: Carcinoma limited to the mucosa, carcinoma in situ.

Level 1: Carcinoma invading into the submucosa, limited to the head of the polyp.

Level 2: Carcinoma invading to the level of the neck (junction of the head and stalk).

Level 3: Carcinoma invading any part of the stalk.

Level 4: Carcinoma invading into the submucosa of the colon wall, below the level of the stalk, but above the muscularis propria.

  • Sessile polyps in which invasion of the muscularis mucosa is seen are by definition Haggitt level 4.
  • For these, the Kikuchi classification can be used, in which Sm1 describes invasion into the upper third of the submucosa; Sm2, into the middle third; and Sm3, penetration into the lower third.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1367

question_text: What is the likely diagnosis for an elderly male presenting with persistent lower back pain, a ballotable lumbar mass that becomes more prominent during inspiration, associated with generalized weakness, and laboratory findings showing red blood cells in urine but no pus cells?
explanation:
Explanation:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) is a malignant tumor originating from the renal tubular epithelium. It often manifests with lumbar pain, a ballotable flank mass, fatigue, and hematuria without pus cells. The classic triad includes hematuria, flank pain, and abdominal mass. The presence of RBCs in urine without pyuria, along with a mass more palpable on inspiration, strongly suggests RCC.

Explanation of other options:

Polycystic kidney disease (Option A): A hereditary condition with multiple renal cysts causing abdominal/flank pain, hypertension, and enlarged kidneys. Though hematuria may occur, a ballotable mass increasing with inspiration is not typical.

Hydronephrosis (Option B): Results from urinary tract obstruction leading to kidney swelling. May present with lumbar pain and palpable mass. However, urine findings in hydronephrosis usually do not show isolated RBCs without pus cells, making this less likely.

Chronic pyelonephritis (Option D): Caused by recurrent urinary tract infections, presenting with flank pain, fever, frequency, and pyuria. The absence of pus cells rules this out.

Key Takeaways:

  • RCC classic triad: Hematuria + Flank mass + Pain.
  • Hematuria without pyuria → strongly suggests malignancy rather than infection.
  • RCC is the most common primary renal malignancy in adults.

question_text: A 46-year-old male has a tumor in the left lobe of the liver, and a left-sided hemihepatectomy is planned. Which of the following liver segments will be resected in this procedure?
option_d: Segments I, II, III, IV, V
explanation:
Explanation:

Left-sided hemihepatectomy involves resection of segments II, III, and IV, which constitute the anatomical left lobe of the liver.

  • Parenchymal transection techniques such as crushing clamp, CUSA, harmonic scalpel, or RFA are used to safely divide the liver tissue while preserving vasculature.
  • Anatomical resection is preferred for hepatocellular carcinoma to ensure clear margins, whereas parenchyma-sparing approaches may be used for colorectal liver metastasis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Segments I, II, III, IV (Option A): Includes the caudate lobe (I), which is not routinely resected in standard left hemihepatectomy.

Segments V, VI, VII, VIII (Option C): These segments belong to the right lobe, resected in a right hemihepatectomy.

Segments I, II, III, IV, V (Option D): Overextends beyond the left lobe; segment V is part of the right lobe.

question_text: A 32-year-old female diagnosed with a tumor in the proximal transverse colon. What are the vessels ligated while doing extended right hemicolectomy?
option_a: Ileocolic, right colic, right branch of middle colic
option_c: Ileocolic, right colic artery, middle colic artery
explanation: Carcinomas of the trans verse colon and splenic flexure are most commonly treated by an extended right hemicolectomy. The mobilisation is as for a right hemicolectomy but dissection continues to include the tumour, this may include taking down the splenic fexure and excising the whole transverse mesocolon. Some surgeons prefer to perform a left hemicolectomy for a splenic flexure cancer.

question_text: A 65-year-old chronic smoker presents with an ulcerative lesion over the lower lip persisting for 1 year. On examination, a firm ipsilateral submental lymph node measuring 5- 5 cm is palpable. Biopsy of the lip lesion confirms squamous cell carcinoma. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
option_d: Resection of primary lesion with lip reconstruction and MRND
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient has squamous cell carcinoma of the lip with clinically palpable ipsilateral nodal involvement. Definitive management requires surgical excision of the primary lesion with adequate margins along with lip reconstruction for functional and cosmetic restoration. Since nodal disease is present, a modified radical neck dissection (MRND) is indicated to remove involved cervical lymph nodes.

Explanation of Other Options

Radiotherapy (Option A):

  • Radiotherapy can be used as definitive treatment in small, early-stage lesions (T1, N0) or in patients unfit for surgery.
  • In this case, with a large node and long-standing ulcer, radiotherapy alone would be insufficient and would not provide optimal local control.

Combined Chemoradiotherapy (Option B):

  • Used in unresectable tumors or in patients who cannot tolerate surgery.
  • It is also considered postoperatively in high-risk patients with positive margins, extracapsular spread, or multiple nodal involvement.
  • Since the patient is operable and surgery is the gold standard, this is not the preferred first-line option.

Resection with Primary Closure Alone (Option C):

  • Suitable only for small, early-stage tumors (<2 cm, N0 disease) where simple wedge excision followed by primary closure provides adequate margins and good cosmetic outcome.
  • In this case, due to large lymph node involvement (N+ disease), primary closure alone is inadequate.
