question_text: Gross specimen of colon from a 14-year-old boy is shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis in the above condition is FAP (familial adenomatous polyposis).

FAP results from an autosomal dominant APC gene mutation (5q21).

  • Findings: Hundreds of adenomatous polyps throughout colon, appearing in adolescence.
  • Clinical features: Rectal bleeding, diarrhea, abdominal pain.
  • Extra-colonic: CHRPE, desmoid tumors, epidermoid cysts (Gardner's syndrome).
  • Management: Prophylactic colectomy to prevent inevitable colorectal cancer.

Explanation of other options:

Crohn's disease (Option A) While it can cause rectal bleeding, it doesn't typically present with numerous polyps throughout the colon.

Lynch syndrome/Hereditary nonpolyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) (Option C) This condition increases cancer risk but doesn't usually cause numerous polyps. The average age of onset is later than FAP.

Juvenile polyposis syndrome (Option D) This can cause multiple polyps, but they are typically hamartomatous rather than adenomatous, fewer in number than FAP.

question_text: A male patient is diagnosed with carcinoma colon Which of the following is the correct sequence of gene mutations?
explanation:
Tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes associated with colorectal cancer

Oncogenes are genes whose expression is intimately associated with normal cell transformation to cancer cells. Tumor suppressor genes: are genes that code the synthesis of proteins with a role to maintain the function of a normal cell.

Oncogenes with a proven role in colorectal cancer are Ras, EGFR (Erb-B1), Erb - B2, TGFalfa, TGF-beta 1.

Suppressor genes are APC, p 53, p27, MSI, LOH 18q, deletion 5 q allele, DNA Hypermethylation.

question_text: A 62-year-old man is diagnosed with colorectal cancer. Histopathology reveals that the tumor has invaded the muscularis propria but there is no involvement of lymph nodes or distant metastasis. According to the Dukes staging system, what is the most appropriate stage?
explanation:
Explanation:

In this scenario, a tumour invading muscularis propria but does not penetrate it and with no involvement of lymph nodes or distant metastasis, Points to Dukes stage B1 (Stage IIa).

Explanation of other options:

Stage 0 (Option A): carcinoma in situ (no muscular invasion).

Dukes A (Option B): limited to mucosa/submucosa.

Dukes B2 (Option D): through muscularis into serosa / perirectal tissues.

question_text: Which among the following syndrome is caused by the mutation in the STK 11 gene?
explanation:
Peutz- Jeghers syndrome-

  • Caused by a mutation in STK11 gene on chromosome 19.
  • Autosomal dominant inheritance

Clinical features -

  • Hyperpigmentation of buccal mucosa and lips.
  • Hamartomatous polyps throughout the GI tract.
  • Increased risk of cancers (colorectal, stomach, breast).

Reference: Bailey and Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter: 12, pg: 202

question_text: Identify the pathology shown in the image
explanation:
• FAP is defined clinically by the presence of more than 100 colorectal adenomas but is also characterised by duodenal adenomas and multiple extraintestinal manifestations.
  • Over 80% of cases come from those with a positive family history. The remainder arise as a result of new mutations in the adenomatous polyposis coli (APC) gene on the long arm of chromosome 5.
  • FAP is inherited as an autosomal dominant condition and is consequently equally likely in men and women. The lifetime risk of colorectal cancer is up to 100% in those with an APC gene mutation.
  • FAP can also be associated with benign mesodermal tumours such as desmoid tumours and osteomas. Epidermoid cysts can also occur (Gardner's syndrome); desmoid tumours in the abdomen spread locally to involve the intestinal mesentery and, although non-metastasising, they may become unresectable.
  • Up to 50% of people with FAP have congenital hypertrophy of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), which can be used to screen affected families if genetic testing is unavailable

question_text:
Which among the following retractor is a self retaining retractors used in sigmoid colon and rectum surgeries?
A)
B)
C)
D)
explanation:
Goligher retractor. This is a self-retaining retractor used in operations on the sigmoid colon and rectum, such as anterior resection and upper end of abdominoperineal resection.

  • Once the abdomen has been opened and laparotomy performed, the patient is placed head down and all the small bowel is packed to the upper end of the abdomen.
  • The retractor is then inserted with the side blades to separate the edges of the abdominal wall.
  • The central blade is then inserted to keep the small bowel well tucked away from the operation site.
  • All three blades come in different widths to fit in with the patient's build. John Cedric
  • Goligher (1912-1998), Ulsterman by birth, Professor of Surgery at Leeds, his contributions to colorectal surgery in the world have been legendary.
  • His operating theatres at Leeds General Infirmary 'have been the Mecca for surgeons from all over the world'.
  • His book, Surgery of the Anus, Rectum and Colon, was regarded as the ultimate authority on the subject and had five editions.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, Appendix: 1, Edition: 27th, Pg: 1561

question_text: What is the diagnosis based on the given image of a newborn?
explanation:
XRAY HERE SHOWS IMPERFORATED ANUS.

  • Most infants with an imperforate anus will need surgery to fix the problem. A common repair is a posterior sagittal anorectoplasty (PSARP). It's done when the surgeon knows the location of the organs in the abdomen and where the rectum ends.

    Plain lateral invertogram is used to investigate the extent of defect in the anal or rectal atresia. The anus is marked with radiopaque marker and the baby is inverted. A lateral radiograph is taken: gas within the rectum will rise to the highest point indicating the extent of the atresia.

question_text: What is the length of the large bowel?
explanation:
• The large bowel including the colon and rectum is a tube of variable diameter, approximately 150 cm in length.
  • The terminal ileum empties into the cecum through a thickened, nipple-shaped invagination, the ileocecal valve.
  • The cecum is a capacious sac-like segment of the proximal colon, with an average diameter of 7.5 cm and length of 10 cm.
  • Although it is distensible, acute dilation of the cecum to a diameter of more than 12 cm, which can be measured by a plain abdominal radiograph, can result in ischemic necrosis and perforation of the bowel wall.
  • Surgical intervention may be required when this degree of cecal distention is caused by obstruction or pseudo-obstruction

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1321

question_text: A patient suffering from inflammatory bowel disease presented with peritonitis following ileal perforation. Exploratory laparotomy was done. Which of the following should be preferred?
option_a: Ileostomy followed by definitive surgery later
option_c: Resection of diseased segment with anastomosis with normal segment
explanation:
Emergency

  • In the emergency situation (or for a patient who is malnourished or on high-dose steroids), the safest procedure is subtotal colectomy and end-ileostomy.
  • The rectosigmoid remnant may be left long and can either be brought out as a formal mucous fistula or closed just beneath the skin as a subcutaneous mucous fistula ; alternatively, it can be closed of with staples across the upper rectum at the pelvic brim and rectal decompression achieved via a transanal catheter. This operation has the advantage that the patient avoids the risks of pelvic dissection while unwell and that colonic histology can be assessed to distinguish between UC and CD.
  • Restorative surgery can be contemplated at a later date when the patient is no longer on steroids and has fully recovered. The mesentery should be divided where convenient and there is no evidence for or against preservation of the omentum in the laparoscopic era, when resection or preservation is a matter of surgical convenience.
  • Most surgeons would recommend close dissection for UC and a greater degree of mesocolic resection for CD given the potential role for the mesentery postulated in CD.
  • Dissection of the left colon is continued to divide the sigmoid at a level that will comfortably reach the skin as a mucous fistula unless this part of the bowel is severely diseased, in which case resection at the sacral promontory is the preferred approach.
  • Urgent subtotal colectomy for acute severe colitis can be performed laparoscopically, provided the surgeon and theater team have adequate experience, with care to avoid perforation when handling friable bowel with laparoscopic instruments.

question_text: Which among the following is not the clinical presentation of familial adenomatous polyposis?
explanation:
• Clinically, FAP is characterized by early development of a wide range of colorectal adenomatous polyps after the second decade of life and many extracolonic manifestations.
  • Patients with FAP may be asymptomatic or may present with bleeding, diarrhoea, abdominal pain, or mucous discharge per rectum. Other symptoms such as anaemia, obstruction, or weight loss usually occur as polyps grow larger in size or number and may foreshadow the presence of cancer.
  • A variety of benign and malignant extracolonic manifestations have been described in FAP.
  • These include gastroduodenal adenomas and carcinoma, desmoids, osteomas, epidermoid cysts, papillary thyroid carcinoma, small bowel polyps and carcinoma, congenital hyperplasia of the retinal pigment epithelium (CHRPE), and dental anomalies.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1368

question_text: What is the investigation of choice for evaluation and staging of the rectal cancer?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pre-treatment magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is the Evaluation of choice in rectal cancer, helping to guide both surgical and oncological management.

Explanation for the other options:

  • CT scan is primarily used for abdominal and chest staging (metastasis), but is poor for local wall invasion.
  • Trans-rectal USG is excellent for early-stage local staging (T1/T2), but MRI is superior for assessing the circumferential resection margin (CRM) and predicting therapeutic response, making it the overall test of choice for staging.
  • Colonoscopy is necessary for diagnosis and visualization, but not for staging depth of invasion and relationship to the mesorectal fascia.

Key Takeaways:

MRI is the investigation of choice for local staging of rectal cancer as it accurately assesses the depth of T stage invasion and involvement of the circumferential resection margin (CRM), which is critical for planning neoadjuvant therapy.

Level:

Must know

question_text: Which of the following is the most common complication following ligation of the first vessel during abdominoperineal resection (APR) for rectal carcinoma?
option_a: Parasympathetic - bladder dysfunction and retrograde ejaculation
option_c: Sympathetic - retrograde ejaculation and bladder dysfunction
option_d: Sympathetic - impotence and loss of cutaneous sensation in the perineal region
explanation:
Explanation:

High ligation of the inferior mesenteric artery during APR may injure sympathetic nerves, causing bladder dysfunction and retrograde ejaculation.

  • In abdominoperineal resection (APR), the first vessel ligated is typically the inferior mesenteric artery (IMA).
  • High ligation of the IMA risks damage to the superior hypogastric plexus, which carries sympathetic fibers.
  • Injury to these nerves leads to loss of sympathetic control over bladder neck closure and ejaculation, resulting in retrograde ejaculation and bladder dysfunction.
  • APR (Miles procedure) is done when rectal tumors involve the sphincter complex.
  • It involves two phases:
    • Abdominal phase: Ligation of IMA, mobilization of descending colon, dissection of rectum to levator ani.
    • Perineal phase: Excision of anus, sphincters, and rectum en bloc with perineal closure. A permanent colostomy is formed.
  • APR has higher recurrence rates compared to low anterior resection due to frequent positive circumferential margins.
  • Complications include:
    • Sympathetic nerve injury (most commonly affecting ejaculation and bladder function)
    • Anastomotic leaks, bleeding, strictures, necrosis of colon
    • Sexual dysfunction and recurrence risks (up to 33%)

Explanation of other options:

Parasympathetic - bladder dysfunction and retrograde ejaculation (Option A): Parasympathetic injury causes erectile dysfunction, not retrograde ejaculation.

Sympathetic - bladder dysfunction and impotence (Option B): Sympathetic injury causes bladder dysfunction and retrograde ejaculation, not impotence.

Sympathetic - impotence and loss of cutaneous sensation in the perineal region (Option D): Impotence is more linked to parasympathetic injury; sensory loss implies pudendal nerve damage, not sympathetic.

question_text: What is the length of adult rectum?
explanation:
Anatomy of the rectum

  • The rectum measures approximately 15 cm in length
  • It is divided into lower, middle and upper thirds
  • The blood supply consists of superior, middle and inferior rectal vessels
  • The lymphatic drainage follows the blood supply. The principal route of drainage is upwards along the superior rectal vessels to the para-aortic nodes, although the lower rectum can drain to lymphatics along the lateral pelvic side walls

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 79, Edition 28th, Pg: 1393

explanation: Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 79, Edition 28th, Pg: 1393

question_text: Which structure separates coccyx and lower two sacral vertebrae from the rectum posteriorly?
explanation:
• The lower third of the rectum is separated by distinct fascial layers from the prostate/vagina anteriorly (Denonvilliers fascia), and from the coccyx and lower two sacral vertebrae posteriorly (Waldeyer's fascia).
  • These fascial layers are surgically important as they act as barriers to malignant invasion and form the anatomical envelope for total mesorectal excision (TME) to achieve complete oncological clearance of rectal cancer.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 79, Edition 28th, Pg: 1393

question_text: Which among the following diseases uses the rule of goodsall's for clinical assessment?
explanation:
Clinical assessment of fistula-in-ano

  • A full medical (including obstetric, gastrointestinal, anal surgical and continence) history and proctosigmoidoscopy are necessary to gain information about sphincter strength and to exclude associated conditions.
  • The key points to determine are the site of the internal opening; the site of the external opening(s); the course of the primary track; the presence of secondary extensions; and the presence of other conditions complicating the fistula.
  • Palpable induration between external opening and anal margin suggests a relatively superficial track, whereas supralevator induration suggests a primary track above the levators or high in the roof of the ischiorectal fossa, or a high secondary extension.
  • Intersphincteric fistulae usually have an external opening close to the anal verge.
  • Goodsall’s rule, used to indicate the likely position of the internal opening according to the position of the external opening(s), is helpful but not infallible.
  • The site of the internal opening may be felt as a point of induration or seen as an enlarged papilla.
  • Probing in an awake patient is painful, unhelpful and can be dangerous.
  • Full examination under anaesthesia should be repeated before surgical intervention.
  • Dilute hydrogen peroxide, instilled via the external opening, is a very useful way of demonstrating the site of the internal opening; gentle use of probes and a finger in the anorectum usually delineates primary and secondary tracks and their relations to the sphincters.
  • Any concerns about fistula topography at clinical examination or examination under anaesthesia (more common after previous unsuccessful surgery) should prompt further investigations before surgical intervention.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 80, Edition 28th, Pg: 1437

question_text: A patient presents with severe pain, swelling, and redness around the anal region. Based on the image and clinical features, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the symptoms described and the given clinical image, is a perianal abscess.

Perianal abscess

  • An infection of one of the small glands near the anus, known as anal glands or crypts.
  • These glands can become blocked or infected, leading to pus accumulation, resulting in an abscess.
  • It is a type of anorectal abscess that occurs in the perianal region.
  • It can also develop as a complication of Crohn's disease.
  • Treatment of perianal abscess:
    • Surgical Drainage: It is the primary treatment, often performed under anaesthesia. The abscesses are drained via perineal skin using a cruciate incision, avoiding excessive excision of healthy tissue.
    • Antibiotics: Indicated in cases with extensive cellulitis, diabetes, or immunosuppression.

Explanation of other options:

Hemorrhoids (Option A): Haemorrhoids are swollen blood vessels in the rectum or anus. While they can cause pain, discomfort, and sometime bleeding, haemorrhoids do not result in pus accumulation or an infected abscess.

Pelvirectal abscess (Option B): A pelvirectal abscess develops when the intersphincteric abscess extends cranially past the levator muscles. The infection progresses semicircularly and primarily posteriorly, resulting in the creation of a horseshoe abscess or fistula.

Pilonidal sinus (Option D): Pilonidal sinus is found in the natal cleft, the groove at the top of the buttocks, consisting of one or more skin openings connected to a subcutaneous track lined with granulation tissue, often containing hair. However, this condition is not located around the anus.

question_text: What is the length of rigid sigmoidoscope?
explanation:
Sigmoidoscope length should be 60cm. Rigid sigmoidoscope is 25 cm is correct

  • In the past, the sigmoidoscope was a rigid stainless steel instrument of variable diameter and normally 25 cm in length, but this has been replaced by disposable plastic instruments.

question_text: Which among the following is not the clinical picture in a case of Ogilvie syndrome?
explanation:
• Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction is also termed Ogilvie syndrome
  • The typical patient is elderly with multiple comorbidities who is hospitalized for an acute medical event or has undergone surgery (abdominal or nonabdominal).
  • The presenting symptoms of the condition commonly include abdominal distension, pain, nausea, and vomiting.
  • Obstipation is common, but some patients will have diarrhoea due to hypersecretion of water. Lack of intestinal contractility is often associated with decreased or absent bowel sounds, but high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds may also be encountered.
  • Systemic toxicity and peritoneal signs are uncommon and should raise suspicion of ischemia and perforation.
  • Initial evaluation should include a complete blood count, serum electrolytes, renal function assessment, and diagnostic imaging.
  • Plain abdominal radiographs typically demonstrate a distended colon, with the largest diameter usually encountered in the cecum and right colon, which can reach 10 to 12 cm in diameter.
  • Dilation and gas continuing all the way down to the distal rectum support the suspicion of pseudo-obstruction in contrast to a mechanical obstruction in which a paucity of gas is commonly encountered distal to the obstruction.
  • A water-soluble contrast enema can reliably distinguish between a mechanical obstruction and pseudo-obstruction.
  • Currently, however, abdominal CT is typically utilized as the standard confirmatory test with the ability to commonly distinguish the type of obstruction as well as to assess for signs of ischemia and impending perforation.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1343

question_text: During a routine check-up, a male patient is found to have a rectal mass on digital rectal examination (DRE). His bowel habits are normal. What is the next best investigation to confirm the diagnosis and evaluate further?
explanation:
Explanation:

A colonoscopy with biopsy is essential to confirm rectal carcinoma and to assess for synchronous lesions elsewhere in the colon. Biopsy provides histological confirmation and influences staging and management decisions.

Explanation of other options:

CT scan of the abdomen (Option A): Helps in staging but not the initial confirmatory step.

Rigid sigmoidoscopy and biopsy (Option B): Limited to distal rectum and sigmoid; cannot assess entire colon.

Barium enema (Option D): Largely replaced by colonoscopy, which is superior for diagnosis and biopsy.

Key Takeaways:

  • Colonoscopy + biopsy = diagnostic and rules out synchronous cancers.
  • CT/MRI = staging investigations, not primary diagnostic.

question_text: What is the other name for cherry tumour?
explanation:
Explanation:

Juvenile polyp

  • This is a bright red, glistening pedunculated sphere ('cherry tumour')' which is found in infants and children.
  • Occasionally, it persists into adult life.
  • It can cause bleeding, or pain if it prolapses during It often separates itself, but can be removed easily with forceps or a snare.
  • A solitary juvenile polyp has virtually no tendency to malignant change, but should be treated if it is causing symptoms.
  • It has a unique histological structure with large mucus-filled spaces covered by a smooth surface of thin rectal cuboidal epithelium. The rare autosomal dominant inherited syndrome juvenile polyposis does carry an increased risk of It is characterised by multiple polyps and a positive family history.

Explanation for the other options:

  • Inflammatory pseudopolyp is a feature of Ulcerative Colitis.
  • Hyperplastic polyp is a small, sessile, non-neoplastic epithelial polyp.
  • Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is characterized by hundreds of adenomatous polyps.

Key Takeaways:

A Juvenile Polyp is clinically referred to as a "cherry tumour" due to its appearance as a bright red, pedunculated hamartomatous lesion, commonly found in the rectum of children.

Good to know

question_text: Which among the following is not a type of small bowel malignancy?
explanation:
• Small bowel malignancy is rare and classically presents late, most often diagnosed after surgery for small bowel obstruction.
  • Four types will be considered, which account for over 99% of small bowel malignancies: adenocarcinoma, carcinoid tumours, lymphomas and mesenchymal tumours (gastrointestinal stromal tumours [GIST]).

    The buttocks are gently parted to allow inspection of the anus and perineum: the presence of any skin lesions and whether they are confined to the perineum or evident elsewhere on general examination, e.g. psoriasis, lichen planus, or on genital examination, e.g. warts, candidiasis, lichen sclerosus, the vesicles of herpes simplex virus (HSV); evidence of anal leakage; whether the anus is closed or patulous; and the position of the anus and perineum at rest and on bearing down (the latter may reveal prolapse of haemorrhoids or even the rectum). Pain on parting thebuttocks, perhaps together with the presence of a sentinel tag, may indicate the presence of an underlying fissure, but may also prompt the need for endoluminal examination under anaesthesia to exclude more suspicious pathology, for example squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the anal canal.

question_text: What is the surgical resection margin in adenocarcinoma of small bowel?
explanation:
Adenocarcinoma

  • Small bowel adenocarcinoma is more often found in the jejunum than the ileum and although the aetiology is unknown, it is more common in patients with CD, coeliac disease, familial adenomatous polyposis, hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer and Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
  • The tumours present with anaemia, overt gastrointestinal bleeding, intussusception or obstruction.
  • Prognosis is poor, particularly in patients with CD, in whom these tumours often present late, because the symptoms are commonly mistaken for those of CD and treated conservatively.
  • When suspected, the advised surgical treatment is a resection of 5 cm of non- involved bowel either side of the lesion and the affected mesentery. A right hemicolectomy is likely to be required for tumours of the distal ileum.

Adenocarcinoma within the anal canal is usually an extension of a distal rectal cancer. Rarely, adenocarcinoma may arise from anal glandular epithelium or develop within a longstanding ;(usually complex) anal fistula, hence the need to biopsy non-healing fistula-in-ano. The treatment is as for low rectal cancers (i.e. abdominoperineal excision of the rectum with or without neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy, Chapter 79). Malignant melanoma of the anus is very rare and usually presents as a bluish-black soft mass that may mimic a thrombosed external pile, although it may be amelanotic. The prognosis, irrespective of treatment, is extremely poor. Perianal Paget's disease is exceedingly rare.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 74, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1310

question_text: A 53-year-old patient presents with a complaint of per rectal bleeding. The surgeon suspects a possible colorectal pathology and wants to determine the most appropriate investigation for this patient. Which of the following options would be the best choice?
explanation:
Explanation: ;

  • Colonoscopyis the most appropriate investigation for a patient presenting with per rectal bleeding.
  • It allows direct visualisation of the colon and rectum.
  • Helps in diagnosing conditions such as colorectal cancer, diverticular disease, or inflammatory bowel disease, which could be causing the bleeding.

Explanation of other options:

CEA levels (Option B): While CEA levels can be useful for monitoring treatment response or detecting recurrence in patients with known colorectal cancer, they are not the primary diagnostic tool for the initial evaluation of per rectal bleeding.

CA-19-9 levels (Option C): CA-19-9 is a tumour marker primarily associated with pancreatic and hepatobiliary malignancies, not colorectal pathology.

CECT (Option D): CECT may be used as an adjunct in specific cases or to assess extra-colonic findings, but it is not the first-line investigation for per rectal bleeding.

question_text: Which chromosome locates the gene for Peutz jeghers syndrome?
explanation:
Explanation:

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is caused by a mutation in the STK11 (LKB1) tumour-suppressor gene, which is located on chromosome 19p.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome

PJS is an autosomal-dominant hereditary cancer syndrome that carries a 39% lifetime risk of CRC characterized by benign hamartomatous, primarily GI, polyps, mucocutaneous pigmentation (dark blue or brown macules in the vermillion border of the lips, buccal mucosa, hands, and feet), and a high predisposition to many intestinal and extraintestinal cancers.

  • Nearly 90% of PJS patients will develop hamartomatous polyps, most commonly in the small bowel, followed by the colon, stomach, and rectum in decreasing frequency.
  • PJS patients have a 90% lifetime risk of cancer, including colorectal (most common), gastric, pancreatic, lung, breast, uterine, cervical, testicular, and ovarian.
  • PJS is caused by a mutation of the STK11/LKB1 gene located on chromosome 19p.
  • Approximately half of PJS cases are inherited from a parent; the remainder occur in patients with no family history and appear to result from a spontaneous mutation.

Key Takeaways:

Peutz-Jeghers Syndrome (PJS) is caused by a mutation in the STK11/LKB1 gene located on chromosome 19p.

Level:

Must know

question_text: Which among the following statements is false for pathophysiology of the diverticular disease?
option_a: Diverticula usually occurs on the antimesenteric border
option_b: Diverticula occurs in the region where vasa recta penetrates the muscular layer
option_c: Sigmoid and descending colon are commonly affected
explanation:
• Hypertrophy of the muscular layers of the colon wall, combined with a narrowed lumen and disordered colonic motility, causes localized high-pressure zones in which the mucosa herniates through areas of relative weakness.
  • Diverticula are classically formed on the mesenteric side of the colonic wall in regions where vasa recta traverse through the muscular layer to provide blood to the mucosa.
  • The sigmoid and descending colon are typically affected, whereas the rectum, having an extra layer of muscle, is generally not affected.
  • This has implications for surgery and is why the distal anastomosis margin in operations for diverticulitis should always be within the rectum.
  • Diverticulosis increases with age and is relatively rare in young adults. Colonic diverticula are noted in approximately 40% of individuals between the ages of 50 and 60 years and in over 60% of individuals over the age of 80 years.
  • The mechanism for developing diverticulitis is thought to be a result of obstruction of the orifice of a diverticulum, with stasis leading to bacterial overgrowth, inflammation, and increased pressure within the diverticulum, causing ischemia and microperforation.
  • Interestingly, only a small proportion of patients with diverticulosis develop diverticulitis.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 52, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1337

question_text: Which among the following is not the perineal approach surgery for full thickness rectal prolapse?
explanation:
PERINEAL APPROACH : These procedures have been used most frequently:

  • Thiersch operation.
    • In this procedure, a steel wire, or silastic or nylon tape, is placed around the anal canal.
    • It has become largely obsolete owing to problems with chronic perineal sepsis, anal stenosis and obstructed defaecation.
  • Delorme's operation.
    • In this procedure, the rectal mucosa is stripped circumferentially from the rectum over the length of prolapse.
    • The underlying muscle is plicated with a series of sutures, so that the rectal muscle is concertinaed towards the anal canal.
    • The excess rectal mucosa is excised and a mucosal anastomosis performed. The resulting effect is to reduce the prolapse as a plicated ring of muscle above the anal canal.
    • This operation may be preferred in patients with short segment full rectal prolapse, but recurrence rates are high, in the region of 30% over 5 years.
  • Altemeier's procedure.
    • In this procedure, the rectum is prolapsed through the anal canal and a full-thickness resection performed, incorporating any associated colonic prolapse.
    • Restoration of colorectal continuity can be performed by either a hand-sewn or stapled anastomosis.
    • This is the procedure of choice in patients presenting with incarcerated and strangulated prolapse. It is a good alternative perineal procedure to the Delorme's operation, particularly following recurrence.

Treatment

  • Surgery is required for full-thickness rectal prolapse, and the operation can be performed via a perineal or abdominal approach.
  • Abdominal operations can be by an open or laparoscopic approach. Abdominal rectopexy, either laparoscopic or open, has a lower rate of recurrence (<10%), but when the patient is elderly and very frail a perineal operation is usually safer, and if necessary, can be performed under regional anaesthetic blockade.
  • As an abdominal procedure risks damage to the pelvic autonomic nerves, resulting in possible sexual dysfunction, a perineal approach may be preferred in young men.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 79, Edition 28th, Pg: 1399

question_text: Which of the following is not a perineal approach for rectal prolapse surgery
explanation:
In rectal prolapse surgery the approaches are as follows:

Perineal approach

  • Thiersch's operation. In this procedure, a steel wire, or silastic or nylon tape, is placed around the anal canal. It has become largely obsolete owing to problems with chronic perineal sepsis, anal stenosis and obstructed defecation, but may be used to augment perineal repair in cases of severe pelvic floor
  • Delorme's operation. In this procedure, the rectal mucosa is stripped circumferentially from the rectum over the length of the prolapse. This operation may be preferred in patients with short segment full rectal prolapse, but recurrence rates are high, in the region of 30% over 5 years.
  • Altemeier's procedure. In this procedure, the rectum is prolapsed through the anal canal and a full thickness resection performed, incorporating any associated colonic prolapse. It is often complicated by poor bowel control with faecal soiling secondary to loss of the rectal reservoir. Recurrence rates range from 0% to 20%.

Abdominal approach

The principle of all abdominal operations for rectal prolapse is to fx the rectum in its normal anatomical position. E.g. Well's procedure, Ripstein procedure, fryman goldberg (resection of sigmoid)

The advantages of a perineal approach include minimal postoperative pain, early mobility and low levels of morbidity

question_text: Which among the following is not the primary position of the internal haemorrhoids?
explanation:
HAEMORRHOIDS

  • Internal haemorrhoids (Greek: haima = blood, rhoos = flowing; synonym: piles, Latin: pila = a ball) are symptomatic anal cushions and characteristically lie in the 3, 7 and 11 o’clock positions (with the patient in the lithotomy position).
  • In addition, haemorrhoids may be observed between the main pile masses, in which case they are internal haemorrhoids at the secondary position.
  • External haemorrhoids relate to venous channels of the inferior haemorrhoidal plexus deep in the skin surrounding the anal verge and are not true haemorrhoids; they are usually only recognised as a result of a complication, which is most typically a painful solitary acute thrombosis.
  • External haemorrhoids associated with internal haemorrhoids (‘interoexternal piles’) result from progression of the latter to involve both haemorrhoidal plexuses, and are best thought of as being external extensions of internal haemorrhoids. Secondary internal haemorrhoids arise as a result of a specific condition, although the mechanisms involved may be the same as those involved in the formation of primary internal haemorrhoids. The most important cause, albeit relatively uncommon, is carcinoma of the anorectum but there may be other causes, which may be categorised as follows:
    • local, e.g. anorectal deformity, hypotonic anal sphincter;
    • abdominal, e.g. ascites;
    • pelvic, e.g. gravid uterus, uterine neoplasm (fibroid, carcinoma of the uterus or cervix), ovarian neoplasm, bladder carcinoma;
    • neurological, e.g. paraplegia, multiple sclerosis.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 80, Edition 28th, Pg: 1380

question_text: Name this position of the patient in operation theatre?
explanation:
Reverse trendelenburg position: the head end of the table is tilted up, thereby placing the head higher than the feet, it is applied in head and neck surgeries including thyroid operation, as the head end is up the veins will collapse and there is less bleeding at surgery.

Trendelenburg position: the head end of the table is tilted down on an incline with the patient's knees slightly flexed, it is applied in varicose vein operation to collapse the lower limb veins while doing surgery by head down leg up position

Lithotomy and Lloyd-Davies position:

This is commonly employed for gynaecological, perineal and urological procedures. The patient is positioned supine with the legs flexed at the hip and knee and placed in stirrups. In the lithotomy position the hips are flexed to 90°; however, the degree of hip and knee flexion can be controlled depending upon the type of procedure performed. The Lloyd-Davies position is a modification of the lithotomy position with hips minimally flexed to around 15° with a 30° head-down tilt.

The jackknife position provides visibility of the anorectal area, so it is commonly used during proctologic procedures, including anorectal and colorectal surgeries (e.g., abdominoperineal resection, when parts of the colon, rectum, and anal sphincter are removed

question_text: What is the TNM staging in a case of rectal cancer where a tumour invades the muscularis propria with metastasis in 2 regional lymph nodes with no distant metastasis?
explanation:
T represents the extent of local spread:

  • TX: primary tumour cannot be assessed;
  • T0: no evidence of primary tumour;
  • Tis: carcinoma in situ – intraepithelial or invasion of lamina propria;
  • T1: tumour invades submucosa;
  • T2: tumour invades muscularis propria;
  • T3: tumour invades through the muscularis propria into pericolorectal tissues;
  • T4a: tumour penetrates to the surface of the visceral peritoneum;
  • T4b: tumour directly invades or is adherent to other organs or structures.

N describes nodal involvement:

  • NX: regional lymph nodes cannot be assessed;
  • N0: no regional lymph node metastasis;
  • N1: metastasis in 1–3 regional lymph nodes:
  • N1a: metastasis in 1 regional lymph node
  • N1b: metastasis in 2–3 regional lymph nodes
  • N1c: tumour deposit(s) in the subserosa, mesentery or non-peritonealised pericolic or perirectal tissues without regional nodal metastasis;
  • N2: metastasis in 4 or more regional lymph nodes:
  • N2a: metastasis in 4–6 regional lymph nodes
  • N2b: metastasis in 7 or more regional lymph nodes.

M indicates the presence of distant metastases:

  • M0: no distant metastasis;
  • M1: distant metastasis:
  • M1a: metastasis confined to one organ or site (for example liver, lung, ovary, non- regional node)
  • M1b: metastases in more than one organ/site or the peritoneum.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 79, Edition 28th, Pg: 1407

question_text: What is the likely diagnosis for a 40-year-old patient presenting with passage of mucus and blood in stool, with sigmoidoscopy showing predominant rectal involvement and biopsy revealing crypt abscesses?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ulcerative colitis is a chronic inflammatory disease limited to the colon and rectum, with diffuse mucosal inflammation and crypt abscess formation. The rectum is always involved, explaining the mucus and blood in stool.

Explanation of other options:

Irritable bowel syndrome (Option B): Functional disorder with abdominal discomfort and altered bowel habits; no blood in stool or crypt abscesses.

Crohn's disease (Option C): Features skip lesions, transmural inflammation, and non-caseating granulomas; rectal sparing is common.

Pseudomembranous colitis (Option D): Occurs post-antibiotics with watery diarrhoea; colonoscopy shows yellow pseudomembranes, not crypt abscesses.

question_text: A 38-year-old male presents to the surgery outpatient department with a history of intermittent pus discharge, occasionally tinged with blood, from an external opening in the perianal region. He has undergone multiple drainage procedures without lasting relief. Examination of the perianal area showed finding shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis for this patient who presents with intermittent pus discharge, occasionally tinged with blood, from an external opening in the perianal region despite multiple prior drainage procedures is Fistula-in-Ano.

Fistula-in-Ano (Anal fistula)

  • A chronic abnormal communication between the anorectal lumen and an external opening on the skin of the perineum, buttock, or, rarely, the vagina in women.
  • Majority of anal fistula are idiopathic or cryptoglandular.
  • Fistula may be found in association with Crohn's disease, TB, lymphogranuloma venereum, maliganncy etc.
  • Patients typically present with intermittent purulent discharge, sometimes tinged with blood, accompanied by discomfort that gradually increases until temporary relief is achieved when the pus drains.

Parks classification of fistula-in-ano

Goodsall's rule

  • Goodsall's Rule is used to predict the likely location of the internal opening based on the position of the external opening(s).
  • Fistulas with an external opening anterior to the anus generally follow a radial course directly into the anal canal.
  • Fistulas with an external opening posterior to the anus typically follow a curvilinear path toward a posterior midline internal opening.

Diagnosis

  • MRI is the gold standard for fistula imaging.
  • STIR: Short tauinversion recovery sequencing helpos highlight presence of pus and granulation tissue without contrast medium.
  • Fistulography and CT are indicated if extra-sphincteric fistula is uspected.

Management

Explanation of other options:

Pilonidal sinus (Option A): Pilonidal sinus is found in the natal cleft, the groove at the top of the buttocks, consisting of one or more skin openings connected to a subcutaneous track lined with granulation tissue, often containing hair. It occurs higher up near the coccyx, not in the perianal region.

Perianal abscess (Option B): An anal gland infection, affecting the small glands or crypts near the anus, can become blocked or infected, leading to pus formation and abscess. In this patient, the history of multiple drainage procedures and persistent discharge indicates a chronic condition, making a fistula-in-ano more likely than an acute abscess.

Haemorrhoids (Option C): Haemorrhoids are swollen blood vessels in the rectum or anus. While they can cause pain, discomfort, and sometimes bleeding, pus discharge is not characteristic of haemorrhoids.

question_text: Which of the following is not a perineal approach for rectal prolapse?
explanation:
Explanation :

Frykman and Goldberg's procedure is not a perineal approach for rectal prolapse. Instead, it is an abdominal approach used for rectal prolapse repair. This procedure involves a transabdominal posterior rectopexy and resection of the redundant left colon.

Operative management of Rectal Prolapse:

Rectopexy is fixing the rectum to the sacrum by sutures or mesh after complete mobilisation of the rectum.

question_text: In clinical practice, the Truelove and Witts classification is used for assessing the severity of which condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Truelove and Witts classification is a clinical and biochemical severity grading system used to assess the severity of ulcerative colitis (UC) - a chronic inflammatory bowel disease affecting the colon and rectum.

Developed by Truelove and Witts (1955), this classification helps clinicians:

  • Distinguish mild, moderate, severe, and fulminant UC,
  • Guide management decisions,
  • Determine the need for hospitalization or surgical intervention.

Explanation of Other Options:

ARDS (Option B):

Severity assessed by PaO₂/FiO₂ ratio (Berlin criteria), not Truelove and Witts.

  • Example:
    • Mild: PaO₂/FiO₂ 200-300
    • Moderate: 100-200
    • Severe: <100

Acute encephalitis (Option C):

Severity determined by GCS, neuroimaging, and EEG, not Truelove and Witts.

  • Common etiologies: HSV, Japanese Encephalitis.
  • Managed with antivirals and supportive therapy.

Acute pancreatitis (Option D):

Severity grading done by Ranson's criteria, Glasgow-Imrie score, or Revised Atlanta classification - not Truelove and Witts.

  • Parameters: Age, WBC, glucose, LDH, AST (Ranson).
  • Determines risk of necrosis and need for ICU care.

question_text: Which of the following is not a layer of the esophagus?
explanation:
Explanation

  • The esophagus, unlike most of the gastrointestinal tract, lacks a serosal covering.
  • Instead, its outermost layer is tunica adventitia, which provides structural support and connects it to surrounding mediastinal structures.

The four layers of the esophagus are:

  1. Mucosa → epithelium (non-keratinized stratified squamous), lamina propria, muscularis mucosae.
  2. Submucosa → contains glands, blood vessels, and Meissner's nerve plexus.
  3. Muscularis propria → inner circular + outer longitudinal muscle layers, with myenteric plexus.
  4. Adventitia → outer fibrous connective tissue.

Thus, serosa is absent in the esophagus.

Key Anatomy Features of the Esophagus

Upper Esophageal Sphincter (UES)

  • Location: At esophageal inlet, in the neck.
  • Composition: Inferior pharyngeal constrictor (thyropharyngeus + cricopharyngeus).
  • Weak spot: Killian's triangle → site of Zenker's diverticulum.

Lower Esophageal Sphincter (LES)

  • Location: Terminal 4 cm of esophagus.
  • Nature: Physiological sphincter (no anatomical thickening).
  • Function: Prevents reflux of gastric/duodenal contents.

Clinical Pearl

"All GIT organs have serosa except the esophagus, duodenum (2nd-4th parts), ascending & descending colon, and rectum - which are retroperitoneal and covered by adventitia."

Explanation of Other Options:

Mucosa (Option A): Present; innermost lining with non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.

Submucosa (Option B): Present; contains esophageal glands and Meissner's plexus.

Muscularis (Option D): Present; crucial for peristalsis (inner circular + outer longitudinal muscle).

question_text: What is the most probable diagnosis from the given x-ray findings?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The abdominal X-ray indicates the presence of a rectal foreign body.
  • Rectal foreign body refers to an object that has been accidentally or intentionally inserted into the rectum and is typically visible on imaging.
  • These injuries are serious and often require surgical intervention. In some cases, a temporary colostomy may be necessary to aid recovery.
  • There is a risk of necrotizing fasciitis, making the use of broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Additionally, bladder or urethral injury can sometimes accompany these cases.

Explanation of other options:

Ureterocoele (Option A): A ureterocele is a congenital dilation of the distal ureter at the ureterovesical junction. It is typically identified on IVU by the characteristic "cobra head" appearance, which is diagnostic of the condition.

question_text: A patient presents to the outpatient department (OPD) with recurrent diarrhoea, abdominal pain, and foul-smelling stools. A colonoscopy reveals yellowish-white raised plaques over the colonic mucosa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pseudomembranous colitis presents with characteristic yellowish-white pseudomembranes on colonoscopy, typically following antibiotic use.

  • Pseudomembranous colitis is an acute colonic inflammatory condition most often caused by Clostridium difficile infection, usually following antibiotic use (especially cephalosporins, clindamycin, fluoroquinolones).
  • Pathophysiology: C. difficile produces toxins (Toxin A and B) that damage the colonic mucosa, leading to inflammation, necrosis, and the formation of pseudomembranes.
  • Colonoscopy Findings:
    • Presence of raised yellow-white plaques (pseudomembranes) on an erythematous mucosal background.
    • These plaques are made of fibrin, inflammatory cells, and necrotic debris.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Profuse watery or foul-smelling diarrhea
    • Abdominal cramps, fever
    • Recurrent or persistent symptoms after antibiotic use
  • Diagnosis:
    • Stool toxin assays (ELISA for toxin A/B)
    • Colonoscopy (in severe or recurrent cases)
  • Treatment:
    • Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin (first-line)
    • Metronidazole (alternative in mild cases)
    • Fecal microbiota transplantation (for recurrent cases)

Explanation of other options:

Familial adenomatous polyposis (Option B): Characterized by numerous adenomatous polyps in the colon, often without diarrhea or plaques. Colonoscopy reveals multiple small polyps, not pseudomembranes.

Ulcerative colitis (Option C): Presents with bloody diarrhea and continuous mucosal inflammation on colonoscopy, usually starting at the rectum. Pseudomembranes are not seen.

Acute gastritis (Option D): Affects the stomach, not colon. Presents with epigastric pain, nausea, not diarrhea. Diagnosed by upper GI endoscopy, not colonoscopy.

question_text: A 45-year-old man complained of recurrent discharge and pain due to lesions around the anus for 3 years. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The history of chronic perianal discharge and pain lasting for years strongly points toward a fistula in ano.
  • It is defined as a chronic abnormal communication between the anorectal lumen and an external opening on the perineum, buttock, or even (rarely) vagina in women.
  • Patients often report recurrent episodes of purulent or bloody discharge that relieve discomfort temporarily, and many have a history of previous anorectal abscesses.

Fistula in Ano:

  • Causes:
    • Idiopathic/cryptoglandular infection (most common).
    • Secondary to Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, actinomycosis, LGV, malignancy.
  • Clinical features:
    • Persistent or intermittent purulent discharge.
    • Pain relieved after discharge.
    • Recurrent perianal abscess.
    • Occasionally, passage of flatus or feces through the external opening.
  • Complications:
    • Chronic infection.
    • Secondary abscess formation.
    • Rare malignant transformation in longstanding cases.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Pilonidal sinus (Option A): Found in the natal cleft above the anus, caused by hair penetration into skin. Presents with midline pits and abscesses, not with a direct connection to the rectum.

Carbuncle (Option B): A cluster of boils (staphylococcal infection of hair follicles) leading to a painful swollen lump with multiple pus-discharging points, usually on the nape, back, or thighs, not chronic perianal lesions.

Boil (Option C): A single perifollicular abscess presenting as a tender nodule with a pus point. While it can occur near the anus, it is acute and self-limited, not chronic and recurrent like a fistula.

Key Takeaway:

A fistula in ano is characterized by chronic recurrent perianal discharge and pain due to an abnormal communication between the anorectal canal and perianal skin. Differentiating it from pilonidal sinus, boils, and carbuncles depends on location, chronicity, and presence of internal communication with the rectum.

question_text: A patient presented with a breast lump. On biopsy, it came out to be breast cancer with ER positivity. Tamoxifen was given to the patient. Tamoxifen increases the risk of:
explanation:
The most common side effects of tamoxifen are:

Hot flashes, vaginal discharge, nausea, mood swings, fatigue, depression, hair thinning, constipation, loss of libido, dry skin.

Tamoxifen also may cause serious side effects, including:

Endometrial cancer: Tamoxifen may cause changes to the lining of your uterus, which can lead to endometrial cancer.

Blood clots: Tamoxifen is known to increase the risk of blood clots. Tell your doctor right away if you have: sudden chest pain, shortness of breath, coughing that brings up blood pain, tenderness, or swelling in one or both of your legs. Stroke: Tamoxifen also can increase the risk of having a stroke.

Cataracts: Tamoxifen can increase the risk of needing cataract surgery, clouded, blurry, or dimmed vision trouble seeing at night sensitivity to light and glare a need for brighter light for reading and other activities seeing halos around lights

Liver problems: yellowing of the skin or the whites of the eyes dark or brown urine feeling very tired loss of appetite pain on the upper right side of the abdomen bleeding or bruising more easily than normal

Reference: https://www.breastcancer.org/treatment/hormonal-therapy/tamoxifen#section-tamoxifen-side-effects

question_text: A 26-year-old woman, 20 weeks pregnant, presents with multiple cauliflower-like growths around the anal margin associated with occasional pruritus and discomfort. She reports no systemic symptoms. Which of the following treatment modalities is considered safest and most appropriate in this clinical setting?
explanation:
Explanation:

The lesions are consistent with condyloma acuminata (genital warts) caused by low-risk HPV (types 6 and 11). During pregnancy, podophyllin and imiquimod are contraindicated because of potential teratogenicity. Similarly, systemic antivirals like acyclovir are not effective against HPV.

Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen is therefore the treatment of choice for anal/genital warts in pregnancy. It is safe, bloodless, relatively painless, and allows precise depth control while avoiding systemic drug exposure.

Condylomata Acuminata (Genital Warts):

  • Etiology:Sexually transmitted disease caused predominantly by HPV types 6 and 11.
  • Epidemiology:One of the most common STDs; not all HPV infections become clinically apparent.
  • Sites:Vulva, vagina, cervix in women; perianal region common in both sexes.
  • Characteristics:Soft, moist, verrucous or pedunculated lesions; distinct from common cutaneous warts.

Treatment Options:

  • Topical agents:Podophyllin, imiquimod (contraindicated in pregnancy).
  • Chemical cauterization:Trichloroacetic acid (can be used but less effective for extensive warts).
  • Cryotherapy:Preferred in pregnancy; precise, safe, and repeatable.
  • Other methods:Electrosurgery, CO₂ laser ablation, surgical excision for large/bulky lesions.
  • Circumcision:Considered in men with extensive sub-preputial disease.

Explanation of Other Options:

Trichloroacetic acid (Option A): Safe in pregnancy but less effective for bulky or extensive perianal lesions. Not first-line when multiple large warts are present.

Excision (Option B): Useful for giant condyloma or resistant lesions but associated with bleeding and scarring. Not preferred as first-line during pregnancy.

Oral acyclovir (Option D): Effective against HSV, not HPV; hence no role in condyloma management.

Key Takeaway Points:

Parks'Classification of Fistula-in-Ano categorizes fistulae based on their relationship to the external and internal anal sphincters. The four types are:

  1. Intersphincteric (Passes through the internal sphincter)
  2. Trans-sphincteric (Passes through both internal and external sphincters)
  3. Supra-sphincteric (Passes above both sphincters)
  4. Extra-sphincteric (Passes outside both sphincters, through the levator ani, often labeled Extra-levator in diagrams)

question_text: In the management of fissure in ano, which of the following is not routinely performed?
explanation:
Explanation:

Proctoscopy is not routinely performed in acute fissure in ano because it can worsen pain and spasm; the diagnosis is usually clinical, while sitz baths, topical calcium channel blockers, and a high-fiber diet are standard conservative measures.

Fissure-in-ano

  • An anal fissure (fissure-in-ano) is a longitudinal ulcer in the anoderm of the distal anal canal which extends from the anal verge proximally towards, but not beyond, the dentate line.
  • Posterior midline fissures are most common due to shearing forces during defecation, combined with less elastic anoderm and higher density of longitudinal muscle fibers in this region.
  • Anterior fissures occur more often in women, commonly after vaginal delivery.
  • Patients often have internal anal sphincter hypertonia, which:
    • Increases trauma from hard stools
    • Reduces blood supply causing relative tissue ischemia
  • The initial tear triggers a vicious cycle:
    • Pain → sphincter spasm → worsening stool passage → further ischemia → chronic fissure formation.

Clinical features

  • Pain on defecation
  • Bright red bleeding and mucus discharge
  • Chronic fissures are characterised by a hypertrophied anal papilla internally and a sentinel tag externally, both consequent on repeated healing and breakdown.

Management

Conservative measures

  • Adding fiber to the diet, using stool softeners, and maintaining adequate hydration are simple and effective measures to improve stool consistency. (Option D ruled out)
  • Warm sitz baths and topical local anaesthetic agents help relieve pain. (Option A ruled out)
  • If simple measures fail, chemical sphincterotomy using agents that induce smooth muscle relaxation of the internal sphincter can be used. Commonly used agents:
    • Glyceryl trinitrate (GTN) 0.2%: applied 2-3 times/day; nitric oxide donor; cure rate ~50%; may cause headaches.
    • Diltiazem 2%: applied twice daily; calcium channel blocker; similar efficacy to GTN, fewer side effects. (Option B ruled out)
    • Botulinum toxin (10–100 units): injected into internal sphincter; blocks acetylcholine and reduces anal pressure; temporary incontinence in ~10%

Surgical options

  • Lateral internal sphincterotomy: The internal sphincter is divided laterally, away from the fissure, usually on the right or left side.
  • Fissurectomy: The fissure is surgically excised, including the fibrotic edges, the base curetted, and the sentinel tag or anal papilla removed.
  • Anal advancement flap: A flap is used to cover the fissure, especially in patients at higher risk of incontinence after sphincterotomy, such as postpartum women or those with normal/low resting anal pressures.

question_text: A patient with grade 4 haemorrhoids underwent surgery. Identify the instrument from the image used during the procedure?
explanation:
Explanation:

A hemorrhoid resection kit typically includes the essential surgical instruments required for performing procedures such as Milligan-Morgan hemorrhoidectomy, Ferguson hemorrhoidectomy, or stapled hemorrhoidopexy

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: CO2 laser

  • A CO2 laser is sometimes used in hemorrhoidectomy or for treating certain types of hemorrhoids. However, it is not the primary instrument for a hemorrhoid resection in most cases, particularly in grade 4 hemorrhoids where resection and excision are the typical approaches. The CO2 laser would be more appropriate in laser hemorrhoidoplasty, a less common treatment.

Choice B: Hemorrhoids band kit

  • Rubber band ligation (often done with a hemorrhoids band kit) is usually effective for grade 1-3 hemorrhoids. It involves placing rubber bands around the hemorrhoid to cut off its blood supply, causing it to fall off. However, it is not suitable for grade 4 hemorrhoids, which require more invasive surgical techniques like resection.

Choice C: Stapler kit

  • A stapler kit is used for stapled hemorrhoidopexy, which is a procedure for grade 3 and grade 4 hemorrhoids, but it is not the same as a resection kit. The stapler kit is used for transanal hemorrhoidal dearterialization and stapled hemorrhoidectomy, but it is typically a less invasive option compared to a full resection procedure.

Key Takeaway

  • The hemorrhoids resection kit is most commonly used in the surgical removal of hemorrhoidal tissue, especially in cases of grade 4 hemorrhoids.

question_text: A jeep driver presented with pain in the gluteal region along with swelling. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pilonidal sinus is a chronic inflammatory condition in the natal cleft, especially in people with prolonged sitting habits (e.g., drivers), presenting with pain and swelling near the gluteal area.

  • Pilonidal sinus occurs in the sacrococcygeal region, typically in young, hirsute males who spend long periods sitting (like jeep or truck drivers).
  • The condition involves ingrowth of hair into the skin, causing a sinus tract or abscess formation.
  • Key Features:
    • Location: Midline over the sacrum or coccyx, in the natal cleft
    • Symptoms: Pain, swelling, discharge (sometimes foul-smelling), and intermittent abscesses
    • Risk Factors: Prolonged sitting, poor hygiene, obesity, coarse body hair
    • Diagnosis: Clinical based on symptoms and local findings
  • Treatment:
    • Acute abscess: Incision and drainage
    • Chronic/recurrent: Surgical excision (midline or off-midline closures like Bascom or Karydakis procedure)
    • Pilonidal sinus excision and repair by rhomboid flap

Explanation of other options:

Fistula in ano (Option B): Involves a tract between the anal canal and perianal skin, presenting with discharge near the anus, not in the upper gluteal region.

Fissure in ano (Option C): A painful tear in the anal mucosa, causes sharp pain during defecation and fresh bleeding, but not gluteal swelling.

Gluteal abscess (Option D): While this can present similarly with gluteal swelling and pain, it usually arises from infection or trauma and lacks the typical midline sinus tract or chronic features of a pilonidal sinus.

question_text: All of the following are factors responsible for causing Haemorrhoids, except?
option_a: Absence of valves in the superior rectal and portal veins
option_b: Poor support from the surrounding loose connective tissue
option_c: Compression of veins at sites where they pierce the muscular coat of the rectum
option_d: Rupture of one of the anal valves
explanation:
Explanation:

Haemorrhoids are saccular dilatations of the rectal venous plexus that can bleed profusely during defecation.

The primary haemorrhoids occur in 3,7, and 11 o'clock positions of the anal wall.

They are formed by enlargement of three main radicles of the superior rectal vein, which lie in the anal columns, which occupy the left lateral, right posterior and right anterior positions.

The various factors responsible for causing haemorrhoids are:

  • Poor support to the veins from the surrounding loose connective tissue (Option B).
  • Absence of valves in the superior rectal and portal veins (Option A).
  • Compression of veins at sites where they pierce the muscular coat of the rectum (Option C).
  • Direct transmission of increased portal pressure at portosystemic communications.

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis for an adult male patient with a history of intermittent purulent discharge with a slight blood tinge from an external opening located in the perianal region?
explanation:
Explanation:

A fistula in ano is a common cause of intermittent purulent discharge with a slight blood tinge from an external opening near the perianal region. It often results from a previous perianal abscess that has developed into a chronic fistulous tract.

Fistula-in-Ano

A chronic abnormal communication between the anorectal lumen (internal opening) and an external opening on the skin of the perineum, buttock, or, rarely, the vagina in women.

Classifications:

  • Low-level fistulas open into the anal canal below the internal ring.
  • High-level fistulas open into the anal canal at or above the internal ring.
  • Simple fistula without extensions
  • Complex fistula with extensions.

Parks classification

Explanation of Other Options:

Hemorrhoids (Option A):

  • Present with painless rectal bleeding during defecation, not intermittent purulent discharge.

Pilonidal sinus (Option B):

  • Occurs in the sacrococcygeal region, above the anus, associated with hair-containing sinus tracts.
  • Not typically located directly adjacent to the anal verge.

Perianal abscess (Option C):

  • Acute painful swelling with redness, fever, and tenderness.
  • Once drained, it does not persist as intermittent discharging sinus unless it progresses into a fistula.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common type of anorectal fistula?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Intersphincteric Fistula is the most frequently occurring form of anorectal fistula.
  • Anorectal Fistula (Fistula-in-Ano): A chronic abnormal tract connecting the anal canal (internal opening) to an external opening on the skin of the perineum, buttocks, or occasionally, in females, the vagina.

Classification of Anorectal Fistulas

Based on Level:

  • Low-level fistulas: Open into the anal canal below the internal sphincter ring.
  • High-level fistulas: Open into the anal canal at or above the internal sphincter ring.

Based on Complexity:

  • Simple fistula: No extensions or branches.
  • Complex fistula: With extensions or multiple tracts.

Parks Classification:

  • Type 1: Intersphincteric - Most common type, accounting for approximately 70% of cases. (Option A)
  • Type 2: Transsphincteric - Represents around 25% of cases. (Option B ruled out)
  • Type 3: Suprasphincteric - Accounts for about 4% of cases. (Option C ruled out)
  • Type 4: Extrasphincteric - Rare, about 1% of cases. (Option D ruled out)

Note: Intersphincteric fistulas are the most frequently observed form of fistula-in-ano, presenting as a persistent abnormal tract connecting the anal canal internally to an external opening on the perineal skin or, occasionally, to the vagina in females.

question_text: An elderly male presents with purulent discharge from a perianal opening. On lithotomy position, the opening is at 11 o'clock, 2 cm from the anal margin. According to Goodsall's rule, what is the likely position of the internal opening?
option_a: 12 o'clock and at the external anal sphincter
option_b: 11 o'clock and at the internal anal sphincter
option_c: 9 o'clock and at the anal verge
option_d: 6 o'clock and crypt of the dentate line
explanation:
Explanation:

According to Goodsall's rule, an anterior external opening follows a direct path to the internal opening, hence at 11 o'clock at the internal sphincter. Posterior openings typically curve to the midline (6 o'clock).

Goodsall's Rule in Anal Fistula

Rule Description

  • Anterior External Opening (within anterior half of anus):
    • The fistulous tract usually follows a straight/direct path to the internal opening inside the anus.
  • Posterior External Opening (within posterior half of anus):
    • The tract typically takes a curved path, often forming a horseshoe fistula, and opens internally at the posterior midline.

Exception to Goodsall's Rule

  • Anterior external opening >3 cm from anal verge:
    • Instead of following a direct tract, the fistula usually curves to the posterior midline to open internally.

Explanation of other options:

12 o'clock and external sphincter (Option A): External sphincter is not the origin site.

9 o'clock and anal verge (Option C): Does not follow Goodsall's rule for anterior opening.

6 o'clock and dentate line (Option D): Typical for posterior external openings, not anterior.

question_text: The internal opening in the fistula-in-ano usually begins from:
explanation:
A fistula-in-ano, or anal fistula, is a chronic abnormal communication extending from the anorectal lumen (the internal opening) to an external opening on the skin of the perineum or buttock (or rarely, in women, to the vagina).

The majority are idiopathic or cryptoglandular and are lined by granulation tissue.

Anal fistula may be found in association with Crohn's disease, tuberculosis, lymphogranuloma venereum, actinomycosis, rectal duplication, foreign body and malignancy (which may also very rarely arise within a longstanding fistula).

Presentation

Patients usually complain of intermittent purulent discharge (which may be bloody) and discomfort, which increases until temporary relief occurs when the pus discharges. There is often a history of anorectal sepsis. The passage of flatus or feces through the external opening is suggestive of a rectal rather than an anal internal opening.


Goodsals's rule:

Fistulas with an external opening anterior to the anus typically track in a radial fashion directly into the anal canal, except for those located at a distance greater than 3 cm from the anal verge; this usually indicates an anterior extension of a horseshoe fistula originating posteriorly. Fistulas with an external opening posterior to the anus often track in a curvilinear fashion to a posterior midline internal opening.

question_text: The fistula marked in the image given below is of which type according to the Park classification?
explanation:
Explanation:

The arrow in the image points to a transsphincteric fistula according to the Park classification.

  • Fistula-in-ano is caused by a persistent tract between the anal canal (internal opening) and the perianal skin (external opening), often following drainage of a perianal abscess.
  • Patients experience recurrent pain, swelling, and relief after drainage. Examination usually reveals one or more external openings, sometimes with granulation tissue.
  • Multiple openings or a watering can perineum may suggest perianal Crohn's disease.
  • MRI can be used when the tract's course is unclear, helping to map openings and anatomy.
  • Fistulas are classified into four types based on the Park classification and are shown in the image below. (Options B, C, and D ruled out)
    • Intersphincteric
    • Tanssphincteric,
    • Suprasphincteric
    • Extrasphincteric types
  • Treatment goals are to eradicate infection, remove epithelialized tracts, avoid faecal incontinence, and prevent recurrence. 
  • During surgery, identifying the fistula’s course is crucial. Goodsall’s rule can help predict the path.
  • External openings anterior to the anus usually track straight into the canal, unless they are >3 cm away, which often indicates a horseshoe extension.
  • Posterior external openings usually follow a curved tract to the posterior midline internal opening.
  • Anoscopy can detect erythematous crypts or internal openings. Probing or injecting substances like hydrogen peroxide, methylene blue, or milk into the tract can help visualise its path.
  • The anal mucosa must also be assessed to rule out causes like Crohn's disease, atypical ulcers, or malignancy.
  • Short and simple fistulas may be treated by fistulotomy (lay-open technique), which heals well and rarely causes incontinence.
  • Complex fistulas involving more sphincter muscle may first be managed with setons (silastic loops or rubber bands) to drain infection and maintain tract patency.
  • The ideal treatment closes the internal opening and eliminates all tracts without dividing the sphincter muscle.

question_text: A 10-month-old male infant presents with an empty scrotum. Ultrasonography shows the right testis in the inguinal canal and the left testis in the perineum. What is the most appropriate diagnosis?
option_c: Right-sided undescended testis and left-sided ectopic testis
option_d: Right-sided ectopic testis and left-sided undescended testis
explanation:
Explanation:

An undescended testis lies along the normal path of descent (inguinal canal, abdomen). In this case, the right testis in the inguinal canal is undescended.

An ectopic testis lies outside the usual path of descent due to abnormal gubernacular development. The left testis in the perineum is ectopic.
Therefore, the diagnosis is right-sided undescended testis with left-sided ectopic testis.

  • Ectopic testis: Located outside normal descent tract (perineum, thigh, femoral canal, suprapubic region).
  • Complications: Infertility, increased risk of malignancy.
  • Management: Orchidopexy (surgical fixation into scrotum).

Explanation of other options:

Bilateral undescended testis (Option A): Incorrect because the left testis is in the perineum (ectopic), not along the descent path.

Bilateral ectopic testis (Option B): Wrong, as the right testis is within the inguinal canal, consistent with undescended testis.

Right ectopic and left undescended (Option D): Incorrect; the findings are reversed.
