question_text: A newborn presents with severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, and a scaphoid abdomen, with lung auscultation revealing bowel sounds in the chest. A posterolateral defect in the diaphragm is seen. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient has Bochdalek Hernia which is the most common type of congenital diaphragmatic hernia (CDH). It occurs due to a defect in the posterolateral portion of the diaphragm, caused by a failure of the pleuroperitoneal membrane to close during fetal development.

Explanation of Other Options:

Morgagni hernia (Option B)

Morgagni hernia is a retrosternal or parasternal type of diaphragmatic hernia, due to a defect in the anteromedial portion of the diaphragm, located near the sternum. It is less common than Bochdalek hernia.

Hiatal hernia (Option C)

Hiatal hernia involves the herniation of the stomach through the esophageal hiatus into the thorax and is usually an acquired condition seen in adults, not a congenital diaphragmatic defect.

Inguinal hernia (Option D)

Inguinal hernia occurs in the groin region due to weakness in the abdominal wall and is unrelated to the diaphragm.

Key takeaway:

Posterolateral congenital diaphragmatic hernias are typically Bochdalek hernias, the most common type causing respiratory distress in neonates, while Morgagni hernias are anterior and hiatal hernias involve the esophageal hiatus.

question_text: A 35-year-old female came to the surgical OPD with swelling in the lower abdomen for 5 months. Swelling increases in size on coughing. Patient had been operated on for abdominal hysterectomy 4 years ago. She is also a known case of rheumatoid arthritis for the last 10 years, and is on medications. What would be the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• The patient has been complaining of lower abdominal swelling for 5 months, which increases on coughing. So, impulse on coughing is positive, which is the key feature of a hernia. Patient had an operative history ;4 years back which is associated with the patient's medical history of rheumatoid arthritis. So, the patient may be on an immunosuppressant or steroid medications, which can be the causative factor for incisional hernia.
  • Incisional hernias arise through a defect in the musculofascial layers of the abdominal wall in the region of a postoperative scar. Thus, they may appear anywhere on the abdominal surface.
  • Factors predisposing to their development are patient factors (obesity, general poor healing due to malnutrition, immunosuppressionor steroid therapy, chronic cough, cancer), wound factors (poor quality tissues, wound infection) and surgical factors (inappropriate suture material, incorrect suture placement).
  • Incisional hernia-
    • Incidence 10-50% after surgery.
    • Causation due to patient, wound and surgeon factors.
    • Wide variation in size.
    • Often multiple defects within the same scar.
    • Obstruction is common but strangulation is rare.
    • Open and laparoscopic repairs possible.

Option A: Ovarian cyst can present with lower abdominal swelling but does not present with impulse on coughing. So, it cannot be the answer.

Option C: Abdominal lipoma also cannot present with impulse on coughing, so operative and medical history are insignificant for abdominal lipoma. So, it cannot be the answer.

Option D: Umbilical hernia can present with impulse on coughing, but past medical and operative history are insignificant for umbilical hernia. Umbilical hernia usually occurs in the childhood and presents with the umbilical region swelling and not lower abdominal swelling.

Reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery, 28th Edition, Chapter 64, Page Number-1077.

question_text: Lateral border of the Hasselbach's triangle is formed by?
option_c: Lateral border of rectus abdominis muscle
explanation:
• The second type of inguinal hernia, referred to as direct or medial, is acquired. It is a result of stretching and weakening of the abdominal wall just medial to the inferior epigastric (IE) vessels.
  • Looked at from within the abdominal cavity, there is a triangle referred to as Hasselbach's triangle, the three sides of which are the IE vessels laterally, the lateral edge of rectus abdominis medially and the pubic bone below (the iliopubic tract).
  • This area is weak because the abdominal wall here consists of only transversalis fascia covered by the external oblique aponeurosis.
  • A direct, medial hernia is more likely in elderly patients. It is broadly based and therefore unlikely to strangulate.
  • The medially placed bladder can be pulled into a direct hernia.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1066

question_text: What is the histological change in Barrett's oesophagus?
option_a: Dysplasia from squamous epithelium to columnar epithelium
option_b: Metaplasia from squamous epithelium to columnar epithelium
option_c: Dysplasia from columnar epithelium to squamous epithelium
option_d: Metaplasia from columnar epithelium to squamous epithelium
explanation:
Barrett's oesophagus (columnar lined lower oesophagus)

  • Barrett's oesophagus is a metaplastic change in the lining mucosa of the oesophagus in response to chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux.
  • Many of these patients do not have particularly severe symptoms, although they do have the most abnormal pH profiles.
  • This adaptive response involves a mosaic of cell types, probably beginning as a simple columnar epithelium which becomes ‘specialised’ with time.
  • The hallmark of ‘specialised’ Barrett’s epithelium is the presence of mucus-secreting goblet cells (intestinal metaplasia).
  • In Barrett’s oesophagus, the junction between squamous oesophageal mucosa and gastric mucosa moves proximally.
  • It may be difficult to distinguish a Barrett’s oesophagus from a tubular, sliding hiatus hernia during endoscopy.
  • Strictures can occur in Barrett’s oesophagus and nearly always appear at the new squamocolumnar junction. 

The relative risk of cancer rises with increasing length of abnormal mucosa. The following terms are widely used:

  • classic Barrett’s (≥3 cm columnar epithelium);
  • short-segment Barrett's (<3 cm of columnar epithelium);
  • cardia metaplasia (intestinal metaplasia at the oesophagogastric junction without any macroscopic change at endoscopy).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1119

question_text: A 30-year-old male patient presented to the surgical opd with soft midline swelling in the upper abdomen for 6 months. Cough impulse is present over the swelling and there is no operative past history. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• A middle-aged male patient with soft midline swelling with cough impulse present is most probably epigastric hernia.
  • These hernias arise through the midline raphe (linea alba) anywhere between the xiphoid process and the umbilicus, usually midway. When close to the umbilicus they are called supraumbilical hernias. Epigastric hernias begin with a transverse split in the midline raphe so, in contrast to umbilical hernias, the defect is elliptical. It has been hypothesised that the defect occurs at the site where small blood vessels pierce the linea alba or, more likely, that it arises at weaknesses due to abnormal decussation of aponeurotic fibres related to heavy physical activity.

Clinical features

  • The patients are often fit, healthy men aged between 25 and 40 years. These hernias can be very painful even when the swelling is the size of a pea, due to the fatty contents becoming nipped sufficiently to produce partial strangulation.

Treatment

  • Very small epigastric hernias have been known to disappear spontaneously, probably due to infarction of the fat. Small to- moderate-sized hernias without a peritoneal sac are not inherently dangerous and surgery should be offered only if the hernia is sufficiently symptomatic.

Surgery

  • may be done by open or laparoscopic surgery.

Option a) incisional hernia: it cannot be incisional hernia because there is no past history of any surgical procedure done.

Option b) lipoma: it cannot be lipoma because cough impulse is present, which is not relevant to lipoma

Option d) umbilical hernia: it cannot be umbilical hernia because the swelling is in the upper abdomen and not at the umbilical region.

EPIGASTRIC HERNIA

question_text: Label the diagram correctly for the position of the mesh placement in hernia surgery
explanation:
• Onlay - placement of the mesh over the anterior rectus sheath
  • Sublay - placement of the mesh below the rectus muscle and over the posterior rectus sheath
  • Pre-peritoneal - placement of the mesh below the posterior rectus sheath and above the peritoneum
  • Intraperitoneal - placement of the mesh intraabdominally below the peritoneum

The strength of a mesh repair depends on host-tissue in-growth. Meshes should be placed on a firm, well vascularised tissue bed with generous overlap of the defect.

  • The mesh can be placed:
  • just outside the muscle in the subcutaneous space (onlay);
  • within the defect (inlay) - only applies to mesh plugs in small defects;
  • between fascial layers in the abdominal wall (intraparietal or sublay);
  • immediately extraperitoneally, against muscle or fascia (also sublay);
  • intraperitoneally.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1064

question_text: All of the following are basic principles for surgical repair of hernia except:
option_a: Reduction of the hernia content into the abdominal cavity with removal of any non-viable tissue and bowel repair if necessary
option_c: Reapproximation of the walls of the neck of the hernia if possible
option_d: Permanent reinforcement of the abdominal wall defect with sutures or mesh
explanation:
All surgical repairs follow the same basic principles:

  1. reduction of the hernia content into the abdominal cavity with removal of any non-viable tissue and bowel repair if necessary;
  2. excision and closure of a peritoneal sac if present or replacing it deep to the muscles;
  3. reapproximation of the walls of the neck of the hernia if possible;
  4. permanent reinforcement of the abdominal wall defect with sutures or mesh.
  • Reduction of hernia content is essential for a successful repair. It is rare for a surgeon to fail to reduce the hernia but extensive dissection can lead to bowel injury, sometimes requiring bowel resection with subsequent risks of infection and bowel anastomotic complications.
  • Excision and closure of the peritoneal sac are ideal but not essential. During laparoscopic repair of incisional hernia, surgeons will often leave the sac in situ after reducing the hernia contents, and simply fix a mesh over the neck to prevent recurrence.
  • Closure of the abdominal wall defect is ideal but may not be possible when the defect is large or tissues are rigid. Over the past 20-30 years, surgeons have realised that simple closure of a hernia defect by sutures alone leads to a high recurrence rate.
  • Additional reinforcement of the defect with a nonabsorbable mesh is now widely practised in most hernia repairs and evidence has shown that recurrence rates have improved.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1062

question_text: Which of the following is not a part of femoral hernia repair?
explanation:
• There is no alternative to surgery for femoral hernia and it is wise to treat such cases with some urgency. There are three open approaches and appropriate cases can be managed laparoscopically.

LOW APPROACH (LOCKWOOD)

This is the simplest operation for a femoral hernia but suitable only when there is no risk of bowel resection. It can easily be performed under local anaesthesia.

THE INGUINAL APPROACH (LOTHEISSEN)

In this, the initial incision is identical to that of Bassini's or Lichtenstein's operation into the inguinal canal.

HIGH APPROACH (McEVEDY)

This more complex operation is ideal in the emergency situation where the risk of bowel strangulation is high. It requires regional or general anaesthesia.

LAPAROSCOPIC APPROACH

Both the TEP and TAPP approaches can be used for a femoral hernia and a standard mesh inserted. This is ideal for reducible femoral hernias presenting electively, but not for emergency cases or irreducible hernia.

question_text: Which among the following is not the clinical feature of strangulation?
explanation:
Clinical features of strangulation

  • Constant pain, severe pain
  • Tenderness with rigidity and peritonism
  • Shock

In addition to the features above, it should be noted that:

  • The presence of shock suggests underlying ischaemia, especially if the shock is resistant to simple fluid resuscitation.
  • In impending or established strangulation, pain is never completely absent.
  • The presence and character of any local tenderness are of great significance and, however mild, tenderness requires frequent reassessment.
  • Generalised tenderness and the presence of rigidity indicate the need for early laparotomy.
  • In cases of intestinal obstruction in which pain persists despite conservative management, even in the absence of the above signs, strangulation should be presumed.
  • When strangulation occurs in an external hernia, the lump is tense, tender and irreducible and there is no expansile cough impulse. Skin changes with erythema or purplish discolouration are associated with underlying ischaemia.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1382

question_text: A full-term neonate is born with an abdominal wall defect, revealing herniated small bowel that is not covered by a sac. The exposed bowel appears oedematous. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in managing this neonate?
option_a: Wait for spontaneous closure of defect
option_b: Immediate repair in the operating theatre
option_c: Cover with sterile gauze/plastic wrap and shift to NICU
option_d: Order imaging tests for associated anomalies
explanation:
Explanation:

This defect mentioned here is gastroschisis, a full thickness paraumbilical abdominal wall defect (usually right of the cord) with exposed bowel without a covering sac.

  • Immediate priorities are to prevent fluid loss, heat loss, and infection, while avoiding mesenteric torsion.
  • The correct first step is to wrap the exposed bowel in sterile gauze or transparent plastic (cling film), insert a nasogastric tube, begin fluid resuscitation, and transfer the neonate to the NICU.
  • Definitive repair (primary closure or staged silo reduction) is performed after stabilization.

Explanation of Other Options:

Wait for spontaneous closure (Option A): Incorrect, as gastroschisis does not close spontaneously and requires surgical repair.

Immediate repair in OT (Option B): Not the first step; neonate must be stabilized before any surgical procedure.

Imaging tests for anomalies (Option D): More relevant for omphalocele, which has a sac and higher incidence of associated anomalies. Gastroschisis rarely has major anomalies, so immediate management takes precedence.

question_text: Which investigation is useful for intra-abdominal and hepatic metastasis?
explanation:
LAPAROSCOPY

  • This is a useful technique for the diagnosis of intra-abdominal and hepatic metastases.
  • It has the advantage of enabling tissue samples or peritoneal cytology to be obtained and is the only modality reliably able to detect peritoneal tumour seedlings.
  • This is particularly important for tumours arising from the intra-abdominal portion of the oesophagus, cardia and where there is a potential communication between a full-thickness tumour and the peritoneal cavity, for instance where there is a hiatus hernia.

Laparoscopy Laparoscopic staging is useful in adenocarcinomas, especially those of the OGJ, but not for squamous cell cancer. Laparoscopy should be reserved for patients in whom confirmation of metastatic disease that is not otherwise obtainable is essential in deciding on treatment.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1139

question_text: Which are the two fix points around which the stomach rotates in the volvulus of stomach?
explanation:
Volvulus of the stomach

  • Rotation of the stomach usually occurs around the axis and between its two fixed points, i.e. the cardia and the pylorus.
  • In theory, rotation can occur in the horizontal (organoaxial) or vertical (mesenteroaxial) direction but, commonly, it is the former which occurs.
  • This condition is usually associated with a large diaphragmatic defect around the oesophagus (paraesophageal herniation).

question_text: All of the following are open incisional hernia repair techniques except:
explanation:
• Desarda's repair is the open hernia repair used in inguinal hernia surgery not for incisional hernia.

Treatment of incisional hernia

  • Asymptomatic incisional hernias may not require treatment at all. The wearing of an abdominal binder or belt may prevent the hernia from increasing in size.

Principles of surgery

  • For most incisional hernias, surgery is relatively straightforward and both open and laparoscopic options are available.
  • The repair should cover the whole length of the previous incision.
  • Approximation of the musculofascial layers should be done with minimal tension and prosthetic mesh should be used to reduce the risk of recurrence.

OPEN REPAIR

  • Simple suture techniques without the use of prosthetic mesh for reinforcement, even with layered closure such as in Mayo, 'keel' or da Silva repairs, are not recommended today because of the high risk of recurrence. However, they may be the only option in the presence of gross contamination such as peritonitis. The previous incision is opened along its full length to reveal any clinically unsuspected defects.
  • Mesh can be placed in one of several planes as for umbilical hernia repair. The simplest approach is an onlay mesh but increasingly the retromuscular sublay repair is preferred by expert surgeons.
  • Very large incisional hernias often require careful thought before treatment begins. Ramirez's component separation technique, which incorporates relaxing incisions in the external oblique aponeurosis and/or the posterior sheath, is very useful. It may then be reinforced with a mesh.
  • Patients with poor quality or redundant skin may benefit from a wedge excision of skin and fat (lipectomy) to improve the abdominal contour postoperatively.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1078

question_text: Deep inguinal ring is the defect in which layer?
explanation:
• As the testis descends from the abdominal cavity to the scrotum in males it first passes through a defect called the deep inguinal ring in the transversalis fascia, just deep to the abdominal muscles.
  • This ring lies midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, approximately 2-3 cm above the femoral artery pulse in the groin.
  • The inferior epigastric vessels lie just medial to the deep inguinal ring, passing from the iliac vessels to rectus abdominis.
  • Muscle fibres of the innermost two layers of the lateral abdominal wall, the transversus muscle and the internal oblique muscle, arch over the deep inguinal ring from lateral to medial before descending to become attached to the pubic tubercle.
  • These two muscles fuse and become tendinous, hence this arch is referred to as the conjoint tendon. Below this arch there is no muscle but only transversalis fascia and external oblique aponeurosis, resulting in weakness.

Inguinal hernia, often referred to as a 'rupture' by patients, is the most common hernia in men and is around 10 times more common in menthan in women. There are two basic types that are fundamentally different in anatomy, causation and complications. However, they are anatomically very close to each other, the surgical repair techniques are very similar and ultimate reinforcement of the weakened anatomy is identical, so they are often referred to together as inguinal hernia.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1065

Seroma

question_text: The treatment of choice for inguinal hernia in infants is:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The treatment of choice for inguinal hernia in infants is herniotomy, which entails ligation and removal of the hernial sac.
  • This procedure is preferred because it:
    • Effectively corrects the defect
    • Prevent complications like incarceration or strangulation
    • Does not require the more complex abdominal wall repairs used in older children or adults.

Explanation of other options:

Herniorrhaphy (Option B): Involves suturing the abdominal wall defect, typically used in older children and adults. It is not preferred in infants due to the small size and delicacy of their tissues.

TRUSS (Option C): A supportive device for hernias that does not correct the anatomical defect. It is not a definitive treatment and is not recommended for infants.

Hernioplasty (Option D): Hernioplasty involves mesh repair of the hernia and is generally reserved for adults or complex/recurrent hernias. In nfants and young children, herniotomy remains the preferred treatment, with hernioplasty reserved only for special, complicated cases.

option_c: Supraumbilical hernia caused by defect in linea alba above the umbilical ring
option_d: Epigastric hernia are repaired if symptomatic
explanation:
• In the embryo, the umbilical ring is a relatively large defect in the ventral abdominal wall transmitting several structures that connect the fetus to the placenta.An umbilical hernia is common and caused by incomplete closure of the umbilical ring; incarceration is very rare.
  • Most umbilical hernias resolve by 4 years of age. question_text: During an endoscopy, a man is found to have the squamocolumnar junction located more proximally than normal. Which of the following conditions is most likely responsible for this finding?
explanation:
Explanation:

The proximal displacement of the squamocolumnar junction (Z-line) is pathognomonic of a sliding hiatal hernia (Type I).

In this condition, the gastroesophageal junction itself migrates above the diaphragm, along with part of the stomach.

This anatomical change predisposes to reflux of gastric contents into the esophagus, explaining why sliding hernia is strongly associated with GERD symptoms.

Hiatal hernia is broadly classified into four types:

  • Type I (Sliding hernia):Most common; GE junction migrates above the diaphragm.
  • Type II (Paraesophageal/rolling hernia):Fundus of the stomach herniates, but GE junction remains in normal position.
  • Type III (Mixed hernia):Features of both sliding and rolling hernia.
  • Type IV:Herniation of stomach plus other viscera (colon, small bowel, spleen).

Explanation of Other Options:

Achalasia cardia (Option A): Characterized by impaired relaxation of LES, leading to dilated esophagus with 'bird-beak' appearance on barium swallow. GE junction location is unchanged.

Rolling/paraesophageal hernia (Option C): Fundus herniates adjacent to esophagus; GE junction remains fixed. Z-line is not displaced. Can cause strangulation but not reflux.

GERD (Option D): A functional disease due to LES incompetence. While GERD often coexists with sliding hernia, GERD alone does not cause an anatomical shift of the Z-line.

Hiatal Hernia:

Clinical Features:

  • Sliding hernia: reflux symptoms- heartburn, regurgitation, chest pain.
  • Rolling hernia: obstructive or compressive symptoms- postprandial fullness, dysphagia, risk of volvulus/strangulation.

Diagnosis:

  • Barium swallow:Best initial test -sliding hernia shows upward displacement of GE junction.
  • Endoscopy:Defines Z-line position and evaluates for esophagitis/Barrett's esophagus.
  • Manometry:Assess LES tone and esophageal motility.

Treatment:

  • Medical:PPIs, H2 blockers, lifestyle modification.
  • Surgical:Nissen fundoplication ± hiatal repair (indicated for refractory GERD or complicated hernias).

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: Which among the following is not an example of potential site for internal hernia?
explanation:
Internal hernia

Internal herniation occurs when a portion of the small intestine becomes entrapped in one of the retroperitoneal fossae or in a congenital mesenteric defect.

The following are potential sites of internal herniation (all are rare):

  • The foramen of Winslow;
  • A defect in the mesentery;
  • A defect in the transverse mesocolon;
  • Defects in the broad ligament;
  • Congenital or acquired diaphragmatic hernia;
  • Duodenal retroperitoneal fossae - left paraduodenal and right duodenojejunal;
  • Caecal/appendiceal retroperitoneal fossae - superior, inferior and retrocaecal;
  • Intersigmoid fossa. Internal herniation in the absence of adhesions is rare and a preoperative diagnosis is unusual. The standard treatment of an obstructed hernia is to release the constricting agent by division. This should not be undertaken in cases of herniation involving the foramen of Winslow, mesenteric defects and the paraduodenal/duodenojejunal fossae as major blood vessels run in the edge of the constriction ring. The distended loop in such circumstances must first be decompressed (minimising contamination) and then reduced.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1376

explanation:
Inguinal hernia and femoral hernia are part of groin hernias and not ventral hernia

    • Umbilical-paraumbilical
    • Epigastric

question_text: Which hormonal component is responsible for the closure of processus vaginalis?
explanation:
• An inguinal hernia (indirect) also occurs through the developmental failure of the processus vaginalis to close. As the testis descends, it pulls a tube of peritoneum along with it. This tube should naturally fibrose and become obliterated but often it fails to fibrose and allows a hernia to form.
  • Recent studies have shown that calcitonin gene-related peptide and hepatocyte growth factor influence the closure of the processus, raising the possibility of a hormonal cause of hernia development.

question_text: For a hernia to occur weakness can be in any of the following layers except:
explanation:

  • An abdominal wall hernia has two essential components, a defect in the wall and content, i.e., tissue that has been forced outwards through the defect.
    • Muscle: weakness in the muscle layer can lead to incisional hernia
    • Bony component: weakness in the bony component can lead to femoral hernia
    • Fascia: weakness in the fascia can lead to epigastric hernia
    • The weakness in the wall is usually the narrowest part of the hernia which expands into the subcutaneous fat outside the muscle.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th

question_text: In a case of hernia, the risk of strangulation is maximum in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
• In case of hernia, the defect varies in size and may be very small or indeed very large. The nature of the defect is important to understanding the risk of hernia complications.
  • A small defect with rigid walls traps the content and prevents it from freely moving in and out of the defect, increasing the risk of complications.
  • When tissue is trapped inside a hernia it is in a confined space. The narrow neck acts as a constriction ring impeding venous return and increasing pressure within the hernia. Resulting tension leads to pain and tenderness. If the hernia contains bowel, then it may become 'obstructed', partially or totally. If the pressure rises sufficiently, arterial blood is not able to enter the hernia and the contents become ischaemic and may infarct. The hernia is then said to have 'strangulated'.
  • The wall of the bowel perforates, releasing infected, toxic bowel content into the tissues and ultimately back into the peritoneal cavity.
  • The risk of strangulation is highest in hernias that have a small neck of rigid tissue, leading first to irreducibility and on to strangulation. The term 'incarcerated' is not clearly defined and used to imply a hernia that is irreducible and developing towards strangulation.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1060

question_text: Which of the following statement is not true for umbilical hernia in children?
option_a: Whites are more commonly affected than blacks
option_c: Surgical intervention is usually done after 2 years of age
option_d: Incidence of umbilical hernia in infants is 10%
explanation:
Umbilical hernia in children

  • This common condition occurs in up to 10% of infants, with a higher incidence in premature babies.
  • The hernia appears within a few weeks of birth and is often symptomless, but increases in size on crying and assumes a classic conical shape.
  • Sexes are equally affected but the incidence in black infants is up to eight times higher than in white.
  • Obstruction and/ or strangulation is extremely uncommon below the age of 3 years.

TREATMENT

  • Conservative treatment is indicated under the age of 2 years when the hernia is symptomless. Parental reassurance is all that is necessary. Of hernias 95% will resolve spontaneously.
  • If the hernia persists beyond the age of 2 years it is unlikely to resolve and surgical repair is indicated.

SURGERY

  • A small curved incision is made immediately below the umbilicus. The neck of the sac is defined, opened and any contents are returned to the peritoneal cavity. The sac is closed and redundant sac excised. The defect in the linea alba is closed with interrupted sutures.

This common condition occurs in up to 10% of infants, with a higher incidence in premature babies. The hernia appears within a few weeks of birth and is often symptomless, but increases in size on crying and assumes a classic conical shape. Sexes are equally affected but the incidence in black infants is up to eight times higher than in white. Obstruction and/or strangulation is extremely uncommon below the age of 3 years.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1073

question_text: Spigelian fascia is the aponeurosis of which muscle?
explanation:
Spigelian hernia

  • These hernias affect men and women equally and can occur at any age, but are most common in elderly people.
  • They arise through a defect in the spigelian fascia, which is the aponeurosis of transversus abdominis. Often these hernias advance through the internal oblique as well and spread out deep to the external oblique aponeurosis.
  • The spigelian fascia extends between the transversus muscle and the lateral border of the rectus sheath from the costal margin to the groin, where it blends into the conjoint tendon.
  • Most Spigelian hernias appear below the level of the umbilicus near the edge of the rectus sheath, but they can be found anywhere along the spigelian line.

Clinical features

  • Young patients usually present with intermittent pain, due to pinching of the fat, similar to an epigastric hernia.
  • A lump may or may not be palpable because the fatty hernia is small and the overlying external oblique is intact. Older patients may have symptoms of intermittent obstruction.

Treatment

  • Surgery is recommended because the narrow and fibrous neck predisposes to strangulation. Surgery can be open or laparoscopic.
  • Laparoscopy is useful if no sac is palpable, repair can be performed using either the intraperitoneal onlay of mesh (IPOM) or TAPP technique.

SPIGELIAN HERNIA

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1075

question_text: All of the following help in reducing the risk of incisional hernia formation except:
option_a: Weight loss for obesity and improving nutritional status for malnutrition
option_b: Sutures should be taken 1 cm deep and 1 cm apart
option_c: Suture length to wound length should be 2:1
option_d: Drain should be brought out through separate incision
explanation:
Reducing the risk of incisional hernia

  • The incidence of incisional hernia may be reduced by improving the patient's general condition preoperatively where possible, e.g., weight loss for obesity or improving nutritional state for malnutrition.
  • Closing the fascial layers with non-absorbable, or very slowly absorbable, sutures of adequate gauge is important.
  • Traditional teaching was that sutures should be 1 cm deep and 1 cm apart. Recent work has shown that lower incisional hernia rates and reduced infection rates are gained when smaller and closer bites are used with a 2/0 suture rather than traditional heavier materials.
  • There is no evidence that interrupted sutures are better or worse than continuous. However, if continuous suturing is used, the tissue bites must not be too near the fascial edge or pulled too tight because they may cut out.
  • It has also been confirmed that the optimal ratio of suture length to wound length is 4:1 (Jenkins' rule). If less length than this is used, the suture bites are too far apart or too tight and the converse applies if more length than this is used.
  • Drains should be brought out through separate incisions and not through the wound itself because this leads to hernia formation.
  • Recent reports have suggested that placement of a prophylactic mesh in patients at high risk of hernia formation will substantially reduce that risk.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1078

explanation:

question_text: A 45-year-old male presents with pain over the right thigh following bilateral laparoscopic inguinal hernia repair done two weeks ago. He describes the pain as burning and tingling in nature, localized to the lateral aspect of the thigh. On examination, there is no motor weakness. What is the most likely nerve involved?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Laparoscopic hernia repairs commonly risk injury to the lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh, causing meralgia paresthetica.

  • The lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (LCNT) is a purely sensory nerve that arises from the lumbar plexus (L2-L3) and passes under the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine (ASIS).
  • In laparoscopic hernia surgeries, particularly when mesh fixation or electrocautery is used near the triangle of pain, this nerve can be injured or entrapped, leading to meralgia paresthetica-a condition characterised by burning pain, tingling, and numbness along the lateral aspect of the thigh.
  • This region is specifically vulnerable because the LCNT lies lateral to the gonadal vessels and is one of the nerves contained in the triangle of pain, a key anatomical landmark in laparoscopic surgery.
  • Overzealous dissection or improper tack placement in this triangle can result in chronic postoperative neuralgia.
  • Key Surgical Anatomy:
    • Triangle of Pain (in laparoscopic view):
      • Medial boundary: Gonadal vessels
      • Lateral boundary: Fold of peritoneum
      • Superior boundary: Iliopubic tract
  • Contents (medial to lateral):
    • Femoral branch of genitofemoral nerve
    • Anterior cutaneous nerve of the thigh
    • Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh
  • Common nerves injured in hernia surgeries:
    • Open repair: Ilioinguinal > Iliohypogastric > Genital branch of genitofemoral nerve
    • Laparoscopic repair: Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh > Genitofemoral nerve

Explanation of other options:

Ilioinguinal nerve (Option A): Injury here is more common in open hernia repairs, not laparoscopic ones. It causes sensory loss over the upper medial thigh, root of penis, and scrotum-not lateral thigh pain.

Iliohypogastric nerve (Option B): Also more likely injured in open surgery. Provides sensation to the suprapubic area; does not explain isolated lateral thigh symptoms.

Femoral nerve (Option C): A mixed motor-sensory nerve; its injury leads to quadriceps weakness and sensory loss over the anterior thigh and medial leg, not isolated lateral thigh paresthesia.

question_text: A 30 years old female presented with a mass in the inguinal region, which produced a gurgling sound on reduction and the mass completely disappeared on pressing it through the deep inguinal ring. What is your diagnosis?
explanation:
• defect in the transversalis fascia called the deep inguinal ring, just deep to the abdominal muscles.
  • This ring lies midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, approximately 2-3 cm above and marginally lateral to the femoral artery pulse in the groin.
  • The inferior epigastric vessels lie just medial to the deep inguinal ring, passing from the iliac vessels to rectus abdominis. Muscle fibers from the innermost two layers of the lateral abdominal wall, the transversus muscle and the internal oblique muscle, arch over the deep inguinal ring from lateral to medial before descending to become attached to the pubic tubercle.
  • These two muscles fuse and become tendinous, forming the conjoint tendon. Below this arch there is no muscle but only transversalis fascia and external oblique aponeurosis, resulting in an area of weakness .
  • Inguinal hernias are classified as direct or indirect. The sac of an indirect inguinal hernia passes from the internal inguinal ring obliquely toward the external inguinal ring and ultimately into the scrotum.
  • In contrast, the sac of a direct inguinal hernia protrudes outward and forward and is medial to the internal inguinal ring and inferior epigastric vessels.
  • As indirect hernias enlarge, it sometimes can be difficult to distinguish between indirect and direct inguinal hernias.

question_text: A patient presents with a history of umbilical swelling, initially asymptomatic for many years, and now complains of pain over the swelling. It was reducible initially, but now it is non-reducible. What is the appropriate management?
explanation:
Explanation:

An irreducible, painful umbilical hernia with unhealthy skin suggests incarceration or strangulation, requiring urgent surgical management with umbilical excision.

  • In adult patients, umbilical hernias that were previously reducible but become irreducible and painful indicate a high risk of incarceration or strangulation.
  • This necessitates prompt surgical intervention to prevent ischemia, necrosis, or perforation of entrapped bowel contents.
  • In such scenarios, umbilical excision is indicated to remove the non-viable tissues, address unhealthy overlying skin, and repair the defect.
  • Unlike elective hernioplasties, acute presentations with complications such as strangulation cannot wait for conservative approaches.

Explanation of other options:

Conservative management with antibiotics (Option B): Antibiotics may be used if infection is suspected but do not treat the mechanical obstruction or risk of strangulated hernia. This is inappropriate for an irreducible and painful hernia.

Mesh hernioplasty (Option C): Though mesh is commonly used in elective repairs, it is contraindicated in strangulated or infected fields. Definitive repair in this context requires initial excision and possibly delayed mesh use.

Incision and drainage (Option D): This is done for abscesses, not hernias. It would not relieve the mechanical complication or address the hernia sac content.

question_text: Hernia mesh usually shrinks by how much percentage?
explanation:
• Synthetic meshes are very strong and early meshes were much stronger than a human abdominal wall, so they are considered as 'over-engineered'. All meshes provoke a fibrous reaction.
  • Denser or heavyweight meshes provoke a greater reaction, leading to collagen contraction and stiffening.
  • The term 'mesh shrinkage' is often used to describe a progressive decrease in size of a mesh over time. It is due to natural contraction of fibrous tissue embedded in the mesh, reducing the area of mesh itself. This can lead to tissue tension and pain, a common complication of mesh repair. It can also lead to hernia recurrence if the mesh no longer covers the defect.
  • Meshes can shrink by up to 50% and, in occasional cases, even more.
  • Meshes with thinner strands and larger spaces between them, 'lightweight, large-pore meshes', are preferred because they have better tissue integration, less shrinkage, more flexibility and improved comfort.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1063

question_text: In which type of hernia in the internal organ forms a portion of the wall of the hernia sac?
explanation:
Explanation:

A sliding hernia occurs when a part of an internal organ, such as the colon or bladder, forms part of the wall of the hernia sac.

Sliding hernia (Hernia-En-Glissade):

  • It occurs when a portion of the peritoneum that normally lines the abdominal cavity slides through the hernia defect, bringing a partially retroperitoneal organ.
  • More common in males, particularly the elderly (Option A ruled out) and frequently occurs on the left side, where the sigmoid colon is the most common content, not the appendix. (Option D ruled out)
  • The posterior wall of the hernia sac is formed by the viscera (commonly bowel), not the anterior wall. (Option B ruled out)
  • Clinical presentation:
    • Patients typically present with a reducible swelling in the groin or lower abdomen that worsens on standing due to gravity.
    • Gastrointestinal symptoms like constipation and incomplete bowel emptying are common, indicating bowel involvement.
  • Managed surgically by repairing or closing the defect, but associated with a higher risk of bowel injury due to the involvement of the viscera in the hernia sac.

Explanation of Other Options:

Lumbar hernia (Option A) refers to hernias occurring in the lumbar region of the abdominal wall but does not involve an internal organ forming part of the wall of the sac.

Spigelian hernia (Option C) occurs through the Spigelian fascia, which is located on the lateral edge of the rectus abdominis muscle and does not involve an internal organ as part of the hernia sac wall.

Richter hernia (Option D) is a type of hernia in which only a portion of the bowel wall (usually the antimesenteric border) is incarcerated, but it does not form the wall of the hernia sac.

question_text: A 34-year-old male presents with a painless swelling in the right inguinal region. The swelling extends into the scrotum, shows a cough impulse, and reduces completely through the deep inguinal ring with a gurgling sound. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

An indirect inguinal hernia originates lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, passes through the deep inguinal ring, and may extend into the scrotum. Reducibility with a gurgling sound confirms bowel content in the sac.

Explanation of other options:

Femoral hernia (Option A): Occurs below the inguinal ligament, more common in females, and does not extend into the scrotum.

Direct inguinal hernia (Option B): Occurs medial to inferior epigastric vessels within Hesselbach's triangle, rarely extends into the scrotum.

Umbilical hernia (Option D): Located at the umbilicus, unrelated to inguinal canal anatomy.

question_text: All of the following statements are true for the lumbar hernias except:
option_a: Most commonly occurs through the superior lumbar triangle
option_b: Lumbar hernias can be congenital or acquired
option_c: Less commonly occurs through the grynfeltt triangle
option_d: Lumbar hernias can be approached by open or laparoscopic surgeries
explanation:
Lumbar hernia

  • Lumbar hernias can be congenital or acquired after an operation on the flank and occurs in the lumbar region of the posterior abdominal wall.
  • Most primary lumbar hernias occur through the inferior lumbar triangle (Petit triangle) bounded below by the crest of the ilium, laterally by the external oblique muscle and medially by latissimus dorsi.
  • Less commonly, the sac comes through the superior lumbar triangle (grynfeltt triangle), which is bounded by the twelfth rib above, medially by sacrospinalis and laterally by the posterior border of the internal oblique muscle.
  • Primary lumbar hernias are rare, but may be mimicked by incisional hernias arising through flank incisions for renal operations, or through incisions for bone grafts harvested from the iliac crest.
  • The natural history is for these hernias to increase in size and surgery is recommended.
  • Lumbar hernias can be approached by open or laparoscopic surgery. The defects can be difficult to close with sutures and mesh is recommended.

The only natural weaknesses caused by inadequate muscular strength are the lumbar triangles (see Lumbar hernia) and the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1076

question_text: All of the following is true for Gilmore's hernia except:
option_b: Presents with severe pain in the groin
option_c: Usually occurs in patients playing football and rugby
explanation:
Sportsmen’s groin, also called sports hernia and Gilmore groin, is one of the most frequent sports injuries in athletes and may place an athletic career at risk. It presents with acute or chronic groin pain exacerbated with physical activity. So far, there is little consensus regarding pathogenesis, diagnostic criteria, or treatment. There have been various attempts to explain the cause of the groin pain. The assumption is that a circumscribed weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal, which leads to a localized bulge, induces a compression of the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve, considered responsible for the symptoms.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1070

question_text: Which of the following statement is not true for femoral hernia?
option_a: There is a risk of developing a femoral hernia after a sutured inguinal hernia repair
option_b: Size of femoral canal is more in males
option_c: Femoral hernia is more common in elderly females
option_d: Femoral hernia is less common than inguinal hernia
explanation:
• The iliac artery and vein pass below the inguinal ligament to become the femoral vessels in the leg. The vein lies medially and the artery just lateral to the artery with the femoral nerve lateral to the artery. They are enclosed in a fibrous sheath. Just medial to the vein is a small space containing fat and some lymphatic tissue (node of Cloquet). It is this space which is exploited by a femoral hernia.
  • The walls of a femoral hernia are the femoral vein laterally, the inguinal ligament anteriorly, the pelvic bone covered by the iliopectineal ligament (Astley Cooper's) posteriorly and the lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's) medially. This is a strong curved ligament with a sharp unyielding edge which impedes reduction of a femoral hernia.
  • The female pelvis has a different shape to the male, increasing the size of the femoral canal and the risk of hernia. In old age, the femoral defect increases and femoral hernia is commonly seen in low-weight, elderly women. There is a substantial risk of developing a femoral hernia after a sutured inguinal hernia repair (Denmark Hernia Registry).
  • Less common than inguinal hernia
  • It is more common in women than in men
  • Easily missed on examination
  • Of cases 50% present as an emergency with very high risk of strangulation

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1072

question_text: Which of the following statement is true for obturator hernia?
option_a: Obturator hernia common in young age
option_b: Women are more commonly affected than men
option_c: In strangulated obturator hernia pain is referred to the back
option_d: Hernia is apparent on flexed, adducted and internal rotated limb
explanation:
Obturator hernia

  • Obturator hernia, which passes through the obturator canal, occurs six times more frequently in women than in men. Most patients are aged >60 years.
  • The swelling is liable to be overlooked because it is covered by pectineus. It seldom causes a definite swelling in Scarpa's triangle, but, if the limb is flexed, abducted and rotated outwards, the hernia sometimes becomes apparent. The leg is usually kept in a semiflexed position and movement increases the pain.
  • In more than 50% of cases of strangulated obturator hernia, pain is referred along the obturator nerve by its geniculate branch to the knee. On vaginal or rectal examination, the hernia can sometimes be felt as a tender swelling in the region of the obturator foramen. These hernias have often undergone strangulation, frequently of the Richter type, by the time of presentation.

OBTURATOR HERNIA

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1079

explanation:

  • Obturator hernia, which passes through the obturator canal, occurs six times more frequently in women than in men. Most patients are aged >60 years.

It seldom causes a definite swelling in Scarpa's triangle, but, if the limb is flexed, abducted and rotated outwards, the hernia sometimes becomes apparent. On vaginal or rectal examination, the hernia can sometimes be felt as a tender swelling in the region of the obturator foramen. question_text: A patient presents with swelling in the groin region and is diagnosed with a direct inguinal hernia. Weakness in which of the following structures is most likely responsible for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Weakness of the conjoint tendon weakens the medial posterior wall of the inguinal canal, predisposing to a direct inguinal hernia.

  • The conjoint tendon is formed by the fusion of the internal oblique and transversus abdominis muscles and reinforces the medial portion of the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.
  • A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through Hesselbach's triangle, an area bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels, lateral border of rectus abdominis, and inguinal ligament.
  • Weakness of the conjoint tendon allows abdominal contents to herniate directly through the abdominal wall in this triangle, resulting in a direct inguinal hernia.

Explanation of other options:

Pectineal ligament (Option A): This forms part of the floor of the inguinal canal but is not directly involved in the pathogenesis of direct inguinal hernias.

Reflected part of inguinal ligament (Option C): While it contributes to the anterior wall of the canal, it is not primarily responsible for hernia formation.

Lacunar ligament (Option D): Though it supports the canal medially, it is not involved in the weakness that causes direct inguinal hernias.

question_text: During indirect inguinal hernia surgery,which nerve is most commonly injured nerve ?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The ilioinguinal nerve is the most commonly injured nerve during open inguinal hernia surgery.
  • This injury can result in chronic groin pain or sensory disturbances in the medial thigh, base of the penis, scrotum (in males), or mons pubis and labia majora (in females).
  • The nerve runs close to the inguinal canal and is therefore at risk during dissection and mesh fixation.

Pattern of nerve injury in hernia repairs:

  • Open repair: Ilioinguinal > Iliohypogastric > Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve.
  • Laparoscopic repair: Lateral cutaneous nerve of thigh > Genitofemoral nerve.

Explanation of Other Options:

Femoral nerve (Option A): Runs beneath the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral vessels. Rarely injured in inguinal hernia surgery.

Genitofemoral nerve (Option B): Its genital branch may be injured, especially in laparoscopic repairs, but not the most common in open surgery.

Obturator nerve (Option C): Located deep in the pelvis, unlikely to be injured in inguinal hernia repair.

Key Takeaway Points:

Important Surgical Landmarks & Complications:

  • Triangle of Doom: Contains iliac vessels → risk of major vascular injury.
  • Triangle of Pain: Contains nerves (femoral branch of genitofemoral, lateral femoral cutaneous) → risk of postoperative neuralgia.
  • Complications of Inguinal Hernia Surgery:
  • Immediate: Hematoma, bleeding, urinary retention.
  • Early: Pain, seroma, wound infection, testicular infarction.
  • Late: Chronic pain (nerve injury/irritation), hernia recurrence.

question_text: Non-clinical question: Identify the image:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The findings are diagnostic of omphalocele- a congenital midline abdominal wall defect covered by a sac composed of outer amnion and inner peritoneum.
  • The umbilical cord inserts at the apex, which differentiates it from other abdominal wall defects.
  • Defects larger than 4 cmwith sac covering are termed omphaloceles, while defects <4 cm are sometimes labeled umbilical cord hernias.
  • Approximately 50% of infantswith omphalocele have associated anomalies, which strongly influence prognosis.

Associated Anomalies in Omphalocele:

  • Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome(macroglossia, gigantism, visceromegaly, abdominal wall defect).
  • Chromosomal abnormalities:Trisomy 13, 15, 18, 21.
  • Midline developmental anomalies:bladder exstrophy, cloacal defects.
  • Pentalogy of Cantrell:omphalocele + anterior diaphragmatic hernia + sternal cleft + ectopia cordis + intracardiac defect (often VSD).

Initial Management:

  • Preserve intact sac-prevents fluid loss, infection, hypothermia.
  • Cover sac with sterile saline gauze + cling wrap to minimize evaporative loss.
  • Evaluate for associated anomalies (cardiac, renal, chromosomal).
  • Prevent hypothermia and stabilize with IV fluids and NG decompression.

Surgical Management:

  • Primary closure→ feasible for small/medium defects.
  • Staged repairfor large defects:
    • Prosthetic patch (Gore-Tex),
    • Porcine submucosa biomaterial (Surgisis),
    • Skin flaps,
    • Preformed silo for gradual reduction.
  • Giant omphaloceles→ may be managed with topical escharotics (e.g., povidone-iodine, silver nitrate) to promote epithelialization before delayed closure.

Prognosis: Depends largely on lung maturity and severity of associated anomalies rather than size of the defect.

Explanation of Other Options:

Urachal cyst (Option B): Remnant of the urachus forming a midline cystic swelling, not a wall defect; does not contain bowel.

Umbilical hernia (Option C): Protrusion of abdominal contents through a weak umbilical ring; no sac covering, usually smaller, and resolves spontaneously in infants.

Umbilical adenoma (Option D): Benign lesion of umbilicus; no relation to congenital abdominal wall defects.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis for a patient who has a scrotal mass on the left side that is hard in texture, has irregular margins, does not reduce on lying down or with manipulation, shows no cough impulse, and is associated with enlargement of para-aortic lymph nodes?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Scrotal mass on the left side → indicate a testicular pathology.
  • Hard texture with uneven edges → Indicative of a solid tumor, likely testicular cancer (e.g., seminoma or non-seminomatous germ cell tumor).
  • Does not decrease in size when lying down or manipulated → Rules out conditions like hydrocele or hernia.
  • No cough impulse → Further rules out an inguinal hernia.
  • Enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes → Strongly indicates metastatic spread from a testicular malignancy, as testicular tumors typically metastasize to retroperitoneal (para-aortic) lymph nodes.

Explanation of other options:

Hydrocele (Option A): Presents as a cystic, soft swelling that transilluminates and decreases on lying down; no lymph node involvement.

Direct inguinal hernia (Option B): Reducible, with a positive cough impulse, and originates in Hesselbach's triangle; does not cause para-aortic node enlargement.

Indirect inguinal hernia (Option C): Extends through the deep inguinal ring into the scrotum, reducible, with cough impulse; not associated with lymph node metastasis.

References: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK563159/?utm_source.

question_text: Which of the following statement is not true?
option_a: Absorbable mesh is made from polyglycolic acid fibre
option_b: Absorbable meshes are used in temporary abdominal closure
option_c: Absorbable mesh is made from polypropylene material
option_d: Absorbable mesh has no role in hernia repair
explanation:
• There are also synthetic absorbable meshes, such as those made from polyglycolic acid fibre. They are used in temporary abdominal wall closure and to buttress sutured repairs. They have no current role in hernia repair because they absorb and induce minimal collagen deposition.
  • Polypropylene meshes are synthetic, non-absorbable.

Absorbable meshes Synthetic absorbable meshes such as those made from polyglycolic acid, collagen or polyhydroxybutyrate may be used in temporary abdominal wall closure and for short-term buttressing suture lines but are not recommended in hernia repair as they are absorbed too quickly and induce only minimal collagen deposition. In recent years a number of synthetic, slowly absorbable meshes have been developed. These are designed to be gradually degraded by the body and replaced with strong native collagenous fibrosis in order to create a lasting repair. The long-term outcomes of repairs using these meshes are as yet unknown.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1064

question_text: A young male presented with slight dragging sensation in the scrotum. On examination a bag of worm feel was noted in the left side of scrotum. However, testes was normal. Diagnosis?
explanation:
A varicocele is an abnormal dilatation and enlargement of the scrotal venous plexus draining the testis.

Clinical features

  • While most varicoceles are asymptomatic, those that are symptomatic tend to present in adolescence or early adulthood, when there may be a dragging discomfort that is worse on standing at the end of the day.
  • When examined in the erect position, the scrotum on the affected side often hangs lower than normal. on palpation, with the patient standing, the varicose plexusfeels like a bag of worms. There may be a cough impulse.
  • If the patient lies down the veins empty by gravity and this provides an opportunity to ensure that the underlying testis is normal to palpation.
  • In longstanding cases the affected testis is smaller and softer than the opposite side owing to atrophy.
  • Ultrasound can be helpful in the diagnosis of small varicoceles, and in the less common right/bilateral varicoceles (and older men with an apparently recent onset of varicocele), ultrasound of the kidneys is important in excluding a renal tumor.

The following classification of varicocele is useful in clinical practice:

  • subclinical: not palpable or visible at rest or during a Valsalva maneuver, but can be shown by special tests (Doppler ultrasound studies);
  • grade 1: palpable during Valsalva maneuver, but not otherwise;
  • grade 2: palpable at rest, but not visible;
  • grade 3: visible and palpable at rest.

question_text: What diagnosis would you suggest for a 10-month-old male baby who presented with an empty scrotum, wherein ultrasonography showed the right testis located in the right inguinal canal and the left testis located in the perineum?
option_c: Right-side undescended testis and left-sided ectopic testis
option_d: Right side ectopic testis and left side undescended testis
explanation:
Explanation:

The diagnosis hinges on the definitions of the two conditions:

  • Undescended Testis (Cryptorchidism): A testis that is arrested along its normal path of descent. The right testis in the inguinal canal is a classic location for an undescended testis.
  • Ectopic Testis: A testis that has deviated from its normal path of descent and is located in an abnormal position. The left testis in the perineum is a known ectopic site.
  • Undescended testis (cryptorchidism) is the failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum, occurring most commonly in the inguinal/palpable location (80%) and less often in the abdominal/non-palpable location (20%).
  • Causes:
    • Developmental/genetic (e.g., Klinefelter syndrome, testosterone imbalance)
    • Prematurity, maternal factors (e.g., diabetes, drugs)
    • Mechanical obstruction (inguinal canal/scrotum, associated hernia)
  • Complications (SATHI):
    • S: Sterility (impaired spermatogenesis due to high temperature)
    • A: Atrophy (testicular shrinkage/non-function)
    • T: Trauma, Tumor (↑ torsion risk, seminoma most common tumor)
    • H: Hernia (patent processus vaginalis in >90% cases)
    • I: Inflammation (increased susceptibility)

Leydig cells preserved → normal secondary sexual characters; Sertoli cells impaired → defective spermatogenesis.

  • Diagnosis:
    • Palpable: Inguinal exploration
    • Non-palpable: Diagnostic laparoscopy (gold standard)
  • Imaging: USG/MRI to aid localization
  • Treatment:
    • Orchidopexy (6-12 months age, latest by 18 months)
      • Techniques: Ombrédanne, Keetley-Torek, Stephen-Fowler, Ladd & Gross

Therefore, the baby has a combination: a right undescended testis and a left ectopic testis.

Explanation of other options:

Bilateral undescended testis (Option A): The left testis is not in a normal path of descent (the perineum is not a normal stopping point).

Bilateral ectopic testis (Option B): The right testis is in a normal path (inguinal canal), just arrested; it is not ectopic.

Right side ectopic testis and left side undescended testis (Option D): This reverses the diagnoses. The inguinal canal is a normal path, so it's undescended, not ectopic. The perineum is an abnormal path, so it's ectopic, not undescended.

Key Takeaways:

  • Undescended testis: Arrested along the normal descent path (abdomen, inguinal canal).
  • Ectopic testis: Migrated to an abnormal location (perineum, femoral canal, superficial inguinal pouch).

question_text: A 1-month-old male infant presents with bilateral empty scrotal sacs. On examination, bilateral inguinal masses are palpable. What is the next step in management?
option_b: Surgical exploration within the next 2 weeks
option_d: Wait and watch for spontaneous descent within the next 6 months
explanation:
Explanation:

Cryptorchidism is common in neonates, and spontaneous descent often occurs within the first 6 months of life. Hence, the appropriate management is observation until 6 months before considering orchidopexy.

Undescended Testis (Cryptorchidism)

Definition:

Cryptorchidism refers to the failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum from their intra-abdominal location during fetal development.

Locations:

  • Inguinal / Palpable undescended testis - ~80% cases.
  • Abdominal / Non-palpable undescended testis - ~20% cases.

Causes and Associated Conditions:

  • Developmental and genetic factors:g., Klinefelter syndrome, hormonal imbalances affecting testosterone.
  • Prematurity and maternal factors: Premature birth, maternal diabetes, or exposure to certain medications.
  • Mechanical/physical factors: Obstructions in the inguinal canal or scrotum, associated inguinal hernia.

Complications (SATHI mnemonic):

  • S - Sterility: High intra-abdominal temperature impairs spermatogenesis → infertility if untreated.
  • A - Atrophy: Heat exposure causes progressive testicular shrinkage and non-function.
  • T - Trauma, Tumor, Torsion: ↑ risk of trauma, torsion, and testicular tumors (especially seminoma, highest risk in intra-abdominal testes).
  • H - Hernia: >90% associated with patent processus vaginalis → inguinal hernia.
  • I - Inflammation: More prone to inflammatory changes.

Note: Leydig cells remain functional → secondary sexual characteristics preserved; Sertoli cells are affected → impaired spermatogenesis.

Diagnosis:

  • Palpable undescended testis: Confirmed by inguinal exploration.
  • Non-palpable undescended testis: Diagnostic laparoscopy is the gold standard.
  • Imaging: Ultrasound or MRI may help localize non-palpable testes.

Treatment:

  • Surgical repositioning (Orchidopexy): Standard treatment, ideally performed between 6-12 months of age.
  • Early surgery improves fertility potential and decreases malignancy risk.

Types of Orchidopexy:

  • Ombridanne's procedure
  • Keetley-Torek procedure
  • Stephen-Fowler procedure
  • Ladd & Gross procedure

Prognosis:

  • Excellent if corrected early.
  • Delay in surgery → higher risk of infertility and malignancy.

Explanation of other options:

  • Perform karyotyping (Option A): Indicated only if there are features of ambiguous genitalia or disorder of sexual development (DSD).
  • Surgical exploration within 2 weeks (Option B): Too early; observation is advised first.
  • Perform orchidopexy now (Option C): Orchidopexy is done between 6-12 months if descent does not occur, not at 1 month.

question_text: Which among the following is not a component of cushing's triad?
explanation:
• Uncontrolled increases in ICP result in cerebral herniation.
  • Typically, herniation of the uncus of the temporal lobe over the tentorium results in pupil abnormalities, usually occurring first on the side of any expanding haematoma.
  • Cerebellar tonsillar herniation through the foramen magnum compresses medullary vasomotor and respiratory centres, classically producing Cushing's triad; hypertension, bradycardia and irregular respiration.
  • The patient is then said to be 'coning', and brainstem death will result without immediate intervention.

question_text: A new born baby with scaphoid abdomen and breathlessness. Which of the following is not done?
option_d: High flow oxygen via nasal cannula
explanation:
• A child with a scaphoid abdomen and breathlessness leads to diagnosis of Congenital Diaphragmatic Hernia. In this case bag and mask ventilation is contraindicated.
  • congenital d matic hernias are associated with lung hypoplasia, pulmonary hypertension, cardiac defects and gastroesophageal refux
  • CDH was considered a surgical emergency. It was approached using aggressive hyperventilatory strategies with the goal of obtaining pulmonary vasodilation through hyperoxia and respiratory alkalosis. This strategy often used high peak inspiratory pressures, ventilatory frequency, and oxygen concentration.
  • After birth, intubation, muscle relaxation and gentle ventilation aim to maintain pH, and oxygen saturation so avoiding right-to-left shunting.
  • Cardiac dysfunction, assessed by echocardiography, may respond to nitric oxide, prostaglandin E1, milrinone and inotropes, but severe dysfunction requires extracorporeal life support (ECLS).
  • Repair is offered if the pulmonary circulation stabilises. Unlike in traumatic diaphragmatic hernias, urgently reducing the bowel does not improve gas exchange in a congenital diaphragmatic hernia.
  • The defect can be approached from the abdomen or the chest, either open or minimally invasively. The defect may be small, needing only a few sutures, or larger, needing a conical Silastic or GOR-TEX patch. A hernial sac may be present, which may be removed or plicated.
  • Bag-and-mask ventilation should be avoided because it may fill the displaced intrathoracic viscera with air and worsen respiratory compromise.

question_text: A 39-year-old female presented in the OPD with bloody discharge from the nipple. On examination, it was found to be from a single lactiferous duct. What is the treatment for bloody nipple discharge with single duct involvement?
explanation:
Explanation:

Microdochectomy:

Definition: Surgical excision of the affected lactiferous duct or a small segment of a duct, typically performed to manage bloody nipple discharge from a single duct.

Procedure:

  • A fine probe or stiff nylon suture is carefully inserted into the affected duct.
  • The probe is secured to the nipple skin with a silk suture to maintain its position during surgery.
  • A triangular skin flap is created by excising tissue approximately 1 mm around the probe using fine scissors.
  • The duct, along with the probe and associated skin flap, is removed for about 5 cm until the underlying papilloma is reached.
  • The surgical site is closed without placing a drain.
  • A compression bandage is applied to support healing.

Indications / Uses:

  • Persistent nipple discharge.
  • Detectable abnormality in a specific duct, such as duct ectasia.
  • Ductal papilloma.

Explanation of Other Options:

Hadfield's Procedure (Option B): An older surgical technique formerly used for mammary duct ectasia, which involves complete removal of the entire breast ductal system. It is overly aggressive for cases with bloody nipple discharge originating from a single duct, as it targets extensive ductal involvement rather than a localized issue.

Microdiscectomy (Option C): A surgical procedure designed to remove herniated spinal discs. It is unrelated to breast tissue and does not address nipple discharge, making it irrelevant in this clinical scenario.

Intravenous Antibiotics with Incision (Option D): This approach is reserved for infection-related breast conditions such as abscesses. It is not appropriate for treating bloody nipple discharge from a single duct, which typically requires a targeted surgical intervention like microdochectomy.

question_text:
A 71-year-old man developed acute monoarthritis of his right ankle on the second postoperative day following an elective inguinal hernia repair. He was on a diuretic for hypertension.
On examination his temperature was 38°C.
What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
The most likely diagnosis is gout, given the history of recent surgery and diuretic use.

Pyrophoshate arthropathy is less common, associated with deposition of calcium pyrophospate crystals chiefly in the knees, second and third metacarpophalangeal joints. There may be a history of haemochromatosis or osteoarthritis.

Rheumatoid arthritis most commonly manifests as a chronic polyarthritis and synovitis.

Septicaemia following an elective hernia repair would be uncommon as would traumatic synovitis. Examination of joint aspirate is always important however, to exclude septic arthritis as missing this diagnosis is associated with significant morbidity and mortality.

Risk factors and triggers of gout:




Reference: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 21st ed, Ch: 372, Pg: 2683-2685

question_text: An 11-month-old boy recently treated for a urinary tract infection presents with an empty right scrotum and a palpable mass in the right inguinal canal. The USG revealed the right testicle under the subcutaneous fat near the right inguinal canal, as shown in the image below. What is the next best step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient likely has cryptorchidism. Since the testis is located in a suboptimal site such as the inguinal canal on ultrasound, surgical exploration is the next best step in management.

Cryptorchidism

  • Cryptorchidism, or incomplete testicular descent, occurs when one or both testes fail to complete their normal path into the scrotum. It can be:
    • Palpable: Accounts for the majority of cases; commonly found in the inguinal canal.
    • Non-palpable: May include an intra-abdominal, absent, or vanishing testis.

Diagnosis

  • Palpable testis: Can be diagnosed clinically and confirmed with inguinal exploration.
  • Non-palpable testis: Requires diagnostic laparoscopy to locate the testis. (Option B ruled out)

Management

  • Surgical repositioning by orchidopexy is the treatment of choice, ideally performed between 6-12 months to reduce the risk of infertility, testicular malignancy, torsion, and hernia. (Option C ruled out)
  • Palpable testes are directly repositioned into the scrotum.
  • Non-palpable testes may require staged procedures (e.g., the Stephen-Fowler technique) if intra-abdominal.

question_text: A 14-year-old boy presents with sudden scrotal pain. Examination reveals a swollen, red scrotum, with the right testis retracted, absent cremasteric reflex, and negative Prehn's sign. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Testicular torsion is the most likely diagnosis, and it should be ruled out first in any adolescent presenting with acute scrotal pain. It occurs when the spermatic cord twists, leading to obstruction of blood flow and venous return. Key diagnostic findings in the clinical presentation pointing to torsion are: sudden, severe pain; a high-riding or retracted testis due to spermatic cord shortening; and the crucial signs of an absent cremasteric reflex (the muscle does not contract when the inner thigh is stimulated) and a negative Prehn's sign (lifting the scrotum worsens or does not alleviate the pain).

  • Presentation: Sudden severe scrotal pain, swelling, erythema, high-riding testis, absent cremasteric reflex.
  • Prehn's sign: Lifting the scrotum worsens pain (negative).
  • Emergency: Must be surgically corrected within 12-24 hours to prevent infarction.
  • Risk factors: Bell-clapper deformity, abnormal tunica vaginalis attachment.
  • Investigations: Doppler US (reduced/absent blood flow).
  • Management: Immediate scrotal exploration and orchidopexy (fixation of both testes).
  • Acute, painful scrotum in adolescent → testicular torsion until proven otherwise.
  • Negative Prehn's sign & absent cremasteric reflex are key clues.
  • Orchidopexy saves testis if done within 6-12 hours.

Explanation of other options:

Hydrocele (Option A): Painless fluid collection, no acute pain or absent reflex.

Strangulated inguinal hernia (Option B): Can cause ischemia but typically presents with obstructive GI symptoms.

Epididymo-orchitis (Option D): Inflammatory swelling, usually gradual onset, painful but with positive Prehn's sign.
