question_text: During laparoscopic surgery, which of the following structures is most prone to injury during trocar insertion?
explanation:
Explanation:

Principles of Secondary Trocar Placement in Laparoscopic Surgery:

  • Insertion Under Direct Vision:
    • Always insert secondary trocars under direct vision.
    • Use a two-handed or controlled single-handed technique to prevent sudden plunging and avoid injury to bowel, bladder, or vessels.
  • Perpendicular Insertion:
    • Insert trocars perpendicular to the abdominal wall.
    • Oblique insertion increases torque and fatigue, and causes more abdominal wall trauma-especially in obese patients.
  • Avoiding Epigastric Vessels:
    • The rectus sheath spans about a hand's breadth from the midline.
    • Place lateral trocars in the midclavicular line to avoid epigastric vessels.
  • Trocar Size and Closure:
    • Prefer smaller diameter trocars to reduce postoperative pain, port-site hernias, and improve cosmetic outcomes.
    • Close fascial layers for all port sites >5 mm to prevent hernia formation.
  • Removal Under Vision:
    • Remove all secondary trocars under direct vision to detect and manage port-site bleeding.

Explanation of other options:

Abdominal Aorta (Option B): Although a serious complication, it is less common. Injury to the aorta typically occurs during primary trocar or Veress needle insertion, especially with blind entry techniques. It is not the most commonly injured during trocar placement.

Both A and B (Option C): Misleading. While both can be injured, only the epigastric vessels are most prone, making this option less accurate.

Circumflex Iliac Artery (Option D): This artery is less commonly injured because it lies lower and more laterally and is not typically in the trajectory of most trocar placements.

Key Takeaways:

The superior and inferior epigastric arteries are the most commonly injured vessels during laparoscopic trocar insertion, especially when placed through the rectus sheath.

question_text: Treatment of choice for subdural empyema
option_a: Craniotomy or craniectomy and drainage of collection
explanation:
Subdural empyema refers to an infective collection in the subdural space. This may develop as a result of sinusitis, mastoiditis or meningitis, and can complicate trauma or surgery.

In empyema, pus will generally collect in the parafalcine region and over the convexity, triggering inflammation and thrombosis in the cortical veins, which helps to explain the high mortality rate.

Craniotomy or craniectomy allows drainage of the collection and relieves raised ICP and is the treatment of choice.

Burrhole drainage, and occasionally IV antibiotics without surgical intervention, may also be considered.

Lumbar puncture should not be performed given the risk of herniation.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 708

question_text: Which type of mesh have better tissue integration, less shrinkage, more flexibility and improved comfort?
explanation:
• Synthetic meshes are very strong and early meshes were much stronger than a human abdominal wall, so they are considered as 'over-engineered'. All meshes provoke a fibrous reaction.
  • Denser or heavyweight meshes provoke a greater reaction, leading to collagen contraction and stiffening. The term 'mesh shrinkage' is often used to describe a progressive decrease in size of a mesh over time. It is due to natural contraction of fibrous tissue embedded in the mesh, reducing the area of mesh itself. This can lead to tissue tension and pain, a common complication of mesh repair. It can also lead to hernia recurrence if the mesh no longer covers the defect.
  • Meshes can shrink by up to 50% and, in occasional cases, even more. Meshes with thinner strands and larger spaces between them, 'lightweight, large-pore meshes', are preferred because they have better tissue integration, less shrinkage, more flexibility and improved comfort.
  • The terms 'light', 'medium' and 'heavy' are not precisely defined but meshes <40 g/m2 are generally referred to as light and meshes >80 g/m2 as heavy.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1063

question_text: Which among the following statements is false for strangulation in a case intestinal obstruction?
option_a: Distension of the obstructed segment of bowel results in high pressure within the bowel wall
option_b: Venous return is compromised after the arterial supply
option_c: Morbidity and mortality associated with strangulation are largely dependent on the duration of the ischaemia and its extent
option_d: As the viability of the bowel is compromised, translocation and systemic exposure to anaerobic organisms and endotoxin occurs
explanation:
• It is important to appreciate that the consequences of intestinal obstruction are not immediately life-threatening unless there is superimposed strangulation.
  • When strangulation occurs, the blood supply is compromised and the bowel becomes ischaemic.
  • Ischaemia from direct pressure on the bowel wall from a constricting band such as a hernial orifice is easy to understand.
  • Distension of the obstructed segment of bowel results in high pressure within the bowel wall. This can happen when only part of the bowel wall is obstructed as seen in Richter’s hernias.
  • Venous return is compromised before the arterial supply. The resultant increase in capillary pressure leads to impaired local perfusion and once the arterial supply is impaired, haemorrhagic infarction occurs.
  • As the viability of the bowel is compromised, translocation and systemic exposure to anaerobic organisms and endotoxin occurs.
  • The morbidity and mortality associated with strangulation are largely dependent on the duration of the ischaemia and its extent.
  • When bowel involvement is extensive circulatory failure is common.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1376

question_text: A 55 years old patient underwent hysterectomy 2 years back, now presented with colicky abdominal pain and bilious vomiting. On examination, the abdomen was tender with exaggerated bowel sounds. On investigations, multiple air fluid levels were seen in the abdomen. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Presented with colicky abdominal pain and bilious vomiting. On examination, the abdomen was tender with exaggerated bowel sounds. On investigations, multiple air fluid levels were seen in the abdomen suggesting intestinal obstruction. And having a history of hysterectomy 2 years back so mostly due to adhesion.

Common causes of small bowel obstruction:

  1. Adhesions (40%)
  2. Malignancy (15%)
  3. Inflammatory bowel disease (15%)
  4. Hernia's (12%)
  5. Others

Adhesions

adhesions and bands are the most common cause of intestinal obstruction.The lifetime risk of requiring an admission to hospital for adhesional small bowel obstruction subsequent to abdominal surgery is approximately 4% and the risk of requiring a laparotomy around 2%. Adhesions start to form within hours of abdominal surgery. In the early postoperative period, the onset of such a mechanical obstruction may be difficult to differentiate from paralytic ileus.

X-RAY findings of SBO: >5 AIR FLUID LEVELS - in stepladder pattern characteristic of adhesive small bowel obstruction

Management:

  • Patient is kept nill per oral (NPO) for 24-48 hrs)
  • IV fluids
  • Ryle's tube aspiration (RTA)

If not relieved gold standard treatment: LAPAROSCOPIC ADHESIOLYSIS

question_text: What structure is marked "X" in the image provided below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The structure marked "X" is the testicular vein, which courses along the posterior abdominal wall toward the deep inguinal ring.

  • The testicular vein is part of the spermatic cord and drains blood from the testis via the pampiniform plexus.
  • It ascends in the retroperitoneum, with the right testicular vein draining into the IVC, and the left testicular vein draining into the left renal vein.
  • In surgical anatomy, this structure is identified near the deep inguinal ring, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and anterior to the psoas major.
  • It is especially important in inguinal hernia repair, orchidectomy, and varicocele surgery.

Basic Surgical Anatomy of the Testis:

Location and Structure

Paired oval-shaped organs in the scrotum.

Suspended by the spermatic cord (contains blood vessels, nerves, vas deferens).

Layers:

  • Tunica Vaginalis: Double-layered serous membrane from the peritoneum.
  • Tunica Albuginea: Dense, fibrous capsule beneath the tunica vaginalis.

question_text: What is the diagnosis based on the given image?
explanation:
• Gastroschisis is a paraumbilical abdominal wall defect associated with protrusion of the bowel through the defect.
  • A membrane does not cover the bowel exposed in utero and, as a result, may be matted, dilated, and covered with a fibrinous inflammatory rind.
  • Diagnosis is often made on the 20-week ultrasound with free-floating bowel loops in the uterine cavity.
  • Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) is elevated in pregnancies with gastroschisis.
  • The exposed infant bowel is protected following birth, an orogastric tube is placed, as are peripheral IVs.
  • The airway is stabilized. Gastroschisis closure can be performed operatively or through slow bowel reductions utilizing a spring-loaded silo to contain the bowel.

question_text: A patient presented with diffuse abdominal pain where on examination there was tenderness all over the abdomen with cardboard like abdominal rigidity. X-ray abdomen is shown below, what is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical picture -diffuse abdominal pain, generalized tenderness, and cardboard-like rigidity- is classic for peritonitis due to hollow viscus perforation.

The erect chest X-ray is the first-line imaging investigation in suspected perforation.

  • It can detect as little as 10-20 mL of free air under the diaphragm.
  • The patient should ideally be upright for ~10 minutes before imaging to allow air to rise and accumulate beneath the right hemidiaphragm.

Presence of free subdiaphragmatic air confirms perforation of a hollow organ, such as stomach, duodenum, or bowel.

This is a surgical emergency requiring prompt resuscitation and operative intervention.

Explanation of other options:

Acute pancreatitis (Option A):

  • Acute pancreatitis typically presents with epigastric pain, which may radiate to the back, rather than diffuse abdominal pain.
  • Although abdominal tenderness may occur, cardboard-like rigidity is not a typical finding.
  • X-ray findings in pancreatitis are generally nonspecific and don't show free air under the diaphragm, which would indicate perforation.

Hiatal hernia (Option B):

  • A hiatal hernia typically presents with gastroesophageal reflux symptoms, such as heartburn, regurgitation, or dysphagia, rather than diffuse abdominal pain and abdominal rigidity.
  • An X-ray in a patient with a hiatal hernia may show an abnormal position of the stomach, but it would not show free air indicative of perforation.

Peptic ulcer (Option D):

  • While a peptic ulcer can lead to perforation, the patient would generally have more localized pain initially, particularly in the epigastric region, rather than diffuse abdominal pain.
  • Additionally, the rigidity seen in perforation peritonitis is more pronounced, and an X-ray showing free air is the key distinguishing feature in perforated peptic ulcer.

Key Takeaways:

Perforation peritonitis is the likely diagnosis in this case, especially with the combination of diffuse abdominal pain, cardboard-like abdominal rigidity, and free air under the diaphragm on an erect chest X-ray, indicating a perforated hollow organ.

question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a six-month history of swelling in the right groin. On examination, a reducible hernia is noted, with no signs of strangulation or obstruction. What is the next appropriate step in management?
option_b: Reduce the swelling and later observe
option_c: Reduce the swelling and do elective surgery
explanation:
Explanation:

  • For a reducible herniawith no signs of strangulation, the correct course of action is to reduce the swelling and proceed with elective surgery.
  • A hernia in the groin can be inguinal or femoral hernia.
  • In females femoral hernia is more common.
  • Hernia occurs when abdominal contents, typically a portion of the intestine or fatty tissue, protrude through the femoral canal in the lower abdominal wall.
  • Femoral hernias are at a higher risk of incarceration and strangulation compared to inguinal hernias.
  • Hence, elective surgery is advised to repair the hernia and prevent complications.

Hernia: Management and Investigations

Investigations

  • Ultrasound is useful for irreducible hernias when the differential includes a mass, fluid collection, enlarged lymph node, or saphena varix, and for identifying uncertain hernia contents.
  • CT scan aids in diagnosing ventral and incisional hernias, determining the size and number of muscle defects, identifying hernia contents, and planning abdominal wall reconstruction. (Option D ruled out)
  • MRI is helpful in sportsman's (Gilmore's) groin, where pain is the main symptom, allowing differentiation between occult hernias and orthopedic injuries.
  • Laparoscopy serves a diagnostic role in incisional hernias by assessing the feasibility of laparoscopic repair and, during TAPP, detecting occult contralateral hernias.

Management

Conservative management

  • Elderly, high-risk surgical patients with asymptomatic inguinal hernia watchful waiting is safe.
  • Small asymptomatic umbilical/epigastric hernias
    • Often contain fat, rarely strangulate.
  • Large incisional hernias with wide neck
    • Low strangulation risk, surgery may be more harmful than helpful.

Surgical management

Indications

  • All femoral hernias
    • Always repaired because of high strangulation risk.
  • Symptomatic hernias (pain, increasing size, difficult to reduce).
  • Irreducible hernias (higher complication risk).
  • Young adults (future risk is high).

Approach in acute presentation

  • If a patient presents with acute pain and the hernia is irreducible,urgent surgery required.
  • Sometimes reduction is possible with taxis-gentle reduction under analgesia/sedation.
  • Even if reduced, recurrence risk is high, thus surgery should be done at the earliest safe opportunity. (Option C ruled out)

Surgical approaches to hernia

  • Hernia repair involves the reduction of contents with excision of non-viable tissueand bowel repair if needed.
  • Closure of defect is ideal but not always possible (e.g., femoral canal, spermatic cord).
  • Large or rigid defects may require plastic surgical techniques.
  • Reinforcement with mesh is standard; closure alone has high recurrence.
  • Non-absorbable mesh reduces recurrence but does not eliminate it.
  • Mesh repair is the cornerstone of modern hernia surgery.

Explanation of other options:

Exploratory laparotomy (Option A): An invasive procedure that is usually performed when there is concern about internal injury, peritonitis, or significant abdominal pathology. In this case, since the hernia is reducible and there are no signs of strangulation, a laparotomy is not needed.

question_text: Which of the following structures is not a boundary of Hesselbach's triangle?
explanation:
Explanation:

The vas deferens is not a part of Hesselbach's triangle. It runs within the spermatic cord through the inguinal canal and posterior to the inguinal ligament, but it does not contribute to the anatomical boundaries of the triangle.

Hesselbach's Triangle

  • Definition: A weak anatomical zone in the inguinal region, important because direct inguinal hernias protrude through this area.
  • Coverings: Transversalis fascia and external oblique aponeurosis (no muscle support, hence weakness).
  • Clinical Importance: Direct inguinal hernias pass medial to inferior epigastric vessels through this triangle.

Boundaries of Hesselbach's Triangle:

  • Lateral border: Inferior epigastric artery & vein
  • Medial border: Lateral margin of rectus abdominis muscle
  • Inferior border: Inguinal ligament (Poupart's ligament)

Explanation of Other Options:

Inferior epigastric artery (Option A): Forms the lateral border.

Rectus abdominis (Option C): Forms the medial border.

Inguinal ligament (Option D): Forms the inferior border.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: As per European Hernia Society Classification-Incisional hernia at level of umbilicus is given the term
Lucid interval is seen in?
explanation:
Extradural haematoma

  • Extradural haematoma is a neurosurgical emergency. It results from rupture of an artery, vein or venous sinus, in association with a skull fracture.
  • The classical injury is a fracture to the thin squamous temporal bone (PTERION), with associated damage to the middle meningeal artery.
  • Transient loss of consciousness is typical, and the patient may then present in the subsequent lucid interval with headache but without any neurological deficit.
  • As the haematoma expands, compensation is exhausted with rapid deterioration. There is contralateral hemiparesis, a reduced conscious level and ipsilateral pupillary dilatation, the cardinal signs of brain compression and herniation.
  • Although this 'talk and die'pattern of deterioration occurs in only one-third of cases, it is critically important to recognise the potential for rapid avoidable secondary brain injury in patients who present neurologically intact.

On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain, constrained by the adherence of the dura to the skull.

question_text: A patient presented with non reducible swelling below and lateral to the pubic tubercle. X-ray of the patient is shown below. What is your diagnosis?
explanation:
• The above X-ray shows multiple air fluid levels indicating obstruction
  • The hernia appears below and lateral to the pubic tubercle and lies in the upper leg rather than in the lower abdomen.
  • Inadequate exposure of this area during routine examination leads to failure to detect the hernia. The hernia often rapidly becomes irreducible and loses any cough impulse owing to the tightness of the neck.
  • It may only be 1-2 cm in size and can easily be mistaken for a lymph node. As it increases in size, it is reflected superiorly and becomes difficult to distinguish from a medial direct hernia, which arises only a few centimetres above the femoral canal

question_text: Identify the type of hernia shown in the following image.
explanation:
Explanation:

An umbilical hernia occurs when the umbilical ring fails to close completely, allowing abdominal contents to protrude.

  • In neonates, the defect often appears within weeks of birth and may increase in size with crying, giving a conical appearance.
  • Most resolve spontaneously by age 2, with surgery indicated only if persistence or complications occur.
  • In adults, factors such as pregnancy, obesity, and liver disease with ascites predispose to reopening of the umbilical defect.
  • These hernias often contain omentum or bowel and carry a higher risk of obstruction and strangulation compared to paediatric cases.
  • Surgery is generally recommended if bowel is involved.
  • Both open and laparoscopic techniques are available, with mesh reinforcement advised for defects >2 cm.

Explanation of Other Options:

Paraumbilical hernia (Option B): These occur immediately adjacent to the umbilicus, most often above, but under current guidelines are also classified as umbilical hernias.

Spigelian hernia (Option C): Rare hernias occurring along the semilunar line, usually at the lateral border of rectus abdominis, not at the umbilicus.

Inguinal hernia (Option D): Protrusion occurs through the inguinal canal, not around the umbilical ring, making it clinically and anatomically distinct.

question_text: A 12-week-old infant presents with a defect in the umbilical region as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis for this 12-week-old infant with a defect in the umbilical area is Umbilical Hernia.

  • It is a protrusion of abdominal contents, usually at or intestine through a weakness in the abdominal wall at the umbilical ring. This condition is more common in infants and obese adults.
  • In infants, it is a benign condition, often noticed shortly after birth, and the hernia usually appears as a soft swelling in the umbilical area that may disappear when the infant is lying down or when pressure is applied.
  • It mostly resolves spontaneously in infants before 2 years, without needing any intervention.
  • If they have not resolved by 2 years of age, surgical repair is considered.

Explanation of other options:

Omphalocele (Option A): This condition occurs when the abdominal wall fails to close completely, allowing internal organs to protrude through the umbilical area. Unlike a simple hernia, the organs are covered by a protective membrane composed of peritoneum, Wharton's jelly, and amnion. These defects are typically larger than standard umbilical hernias. However, the features described in this case are more consistent with an umbilical hernia.

Gastroschisis (Option B): Gastrochisis is the evisceration of bowel contents through a defect in the anterior abdominal wall just lateral to the umbilicus. It is characterised by a defect beside the umbilicus.

Paraumbilical hernia (Option D): A paraumbilical hernia is a protrusion of abdominal contents through a defect in the abdominal wall, typically occurring slightly above or below the umbilicus rather than at the umbilical ring. In this case, the swelling is directly at the umbilicus, which is more indicative of an umbilical hernia rather than a paraumbilical hernia.

question_text: A 70-year-old man, one month after undergoing gastrointestinal surgery, presents with a palpable bulge at the previous surgical incision site. On examination, a 12 cm reducible swelling is noted along the scar line, consistent with an incisional hernia. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
option_b: Prescribe an abdominal belt for daily use
option_c: Advise observation and reassessment in six months
explanation:
Explanation:

The standard of care for an incisional hernia is mesh repair, most commonly via a laparoscopic approach.

Laparoscopic intraperitoneal onlay mesh placement significantly lowers recurrence rates compared with primary closure alone.

For a large hernia (12 cm), tension-free repair with mesh is mandatory.

Incisional hernia (post-operative ventral hernia) arises due to failure of fascial healing, compounded by factors such as wound infection, obesity, diabetes, and poor nutritional status. Conservative approaches (e.g., abdominal belts, observation) do not address the defect and risk progression or complications such as incarceration and strangulation.

Explanation of Other Options:

Abdominal belt (Option B): May provide temporary support but does not repair the fascial defect. Only a palliative measure, not definitive treatment.

Observation and reassessment (Option C): Unsafe. Even reducible hernias risk incarceration, obstruction, or strangulation. Deferral of repair is not justified in a fit patient.

Laparoscopic closure without mesh (Option D): Associated with very high recurrence rates. Mesh placement is essential for durable repair.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: Clinical question: A 60-year-old male patient presents with a left groin swelling for a few years, which increases in size on standing and decreases when lying down. On examination, the swelling shows a positive cough impulse. What is the appropriate management?
option_d: Reduction of contents, repair defects and reinforcement with mesh
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's presentation with a groin swelling that increases in size on standing, decreases when lying down, and shows a positive cough impulse is indicative of an inguinal hernia. Thus, the most appropriate management for this patient is reduction of contents, repair of the defect, and reinforcement with mesh.

Stoppa Repair: (Option D)

  • Uses a mesh to reinforce the area behind the peritoneum
  • Done in Recurrent inguinal hernia

Management of Inguinal Hernia:

Surgical Approaches:

  • Herniotomy: (Option B ruled out)
    • It involves excising and closing the hernia sac
    • Primarily used in children with lateral hernias and congenital hydrocele.
    • In adults, herniotomy alone is insufficient due to high recurrence rates.
  • Hernioplasty: Includes herniotomy plus inguinal floor reconstruction with mesh.
  • Herniorrhaphy: (Option C ruled out)
    • Includes herniotomy plus reconstruction of the inguinal floor with sutures
    • Techniques:

Anterior Tension-Free Repair:

  • Lichtenstein Repair: Utilizes a mesh to reinforce the inguinal floor, which is considered the gold standard due to lower recurrence rates and faster recovery.

Laparoscopic Hernia Repair:

  • Totally Extraperitoneal (TEP) Repair
  • Transabdominal Preperitoneal (TAPP) Repair

Explanation of other options:

Incision and drainage (Option A) are typically used in cases of abscess or infection, which isn't the case here since the swelling is consistent with a hernia, not an infection.

question_text: A young boxer receives a blow near the eye during a boxing match. He presents to the ER with a hematoma around eye, CT scan is shown below. Identify the radiological sign shown below?
explanation:
Explanation:

Orbital floor fractures may lead to restricted upward gaze owing to trapping of orbital fat and fibrous septae resulting in diplopia on looking upwards.

Occasionally, the inferior rectus or inferior oblique muscles may also be trapped. Inferior rectus muscle entrapment in children may present as the oculocardiac reflex: a triad of bradycardia, nausea and syncope. This needs to be treated as an emergency because irreversible damage related to muscle necrosis can occur within hours.

In these cases, on imaging, the orbital floor may appear undisplaced or minimally displaced, which means that a trapdoor defect has opened and then closed again, entrapping the muscle

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Trapdoor sign

  • The trapdoor sign refers to a phenomenon seen primarily in pediatric cases where the orbital floor fractures but the bone remains displaced in a way that can entrap the inferior rectus muscle. This is more common in younger children because of their more flexible bone
  • It is not the correct answer in this case, as the description of a tear-drop sign better fits the context of a young boxer with an orbital floor fracture.

Choice C: Butterfly sign

  • The butterfly sign typically refers to a radiological finding related to intracranial hemorrhage where blood spreads in a butterfly-shaped pattern over both hemispheres of the brain.
  • It does not relate to orbital fractures or the tear-drop sign in this case.

Choice D: Panda sign

  • The panda sign is seen in orbital cellulitis and is characterized by bilateral periorbital swelling that may resemble the black patches around the eyes of a panda.
  • This sign is unrelated to the orbital floor fracture and tear-drop sign seen in this case.

Key Takeaway

  • The tear-drop sign on a CT scan is a classic finding in orbital floor fractures, indicating herniation of orbital contents such as fat or muscle into the maxillary sinus, often resulting from trauma.

question_text: A 55-year-old male presents with complaints of dysphagia, halitosis, and regurgitation. Radiological imaging shows a blind pouch at the level of the pharynx. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Esophageal Diverticulum:

  • The presence of dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), halitosis (bad breath), and regurgitation, along with a blind-ending pouch at the pharyngeal level, is highly suggestive of a pulsion diverticulum.
  • Pulsion diverticula are a subtype of esophageal diverticulum, typically caused by increased intraluminal pressure leading to herniation of the mucosa and submucosa through the muscular layer.

Explanation of Other Options:

Achalasia Cardia (Option B): This disorder is characterized by the lower esophageal sphincter (LES) failing to relax, leading to difficulty swallowing and regurgitation. Diagnosis is established using esophageal manometry and a barium swallow, which typically shows a "bird's beak" appearance at the LES. Although aspiration pneumonia can occur, Achalasia does not cause a blind pouch at the pharyngeal level.

Esophageal Cancer (CA Esophagus) (Option C): Esophageal cancer may present with dysphagia, weight loss, and sometimes regurgitation. Systemic signs such as cachexia are common. However, it does not result in the formation of a pharyngeal blind pouch, and the radiologic findings differ from those seen in a diverticulum.

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) (Option D): GERD can lead to dysphagia, halitosis, and regurgitation, and chronic aspiration is possible. Despite this, GERD does not produce a structural blind pouch at the pharyngeal level. The condition usually manifests with heartburn, acid regurgitation, and potential esophageal mucosal injury, rather than a diverticular formation.

question_text: Which of the following is least likely to cause hernia?
option_c: Weakness due to ageing and pregnancy
explanation:
Muscle damage by blunt trauma or tearing of the abdominal muscles requires exceptional force and is rare.

  • Causes of hernia
    • Basic design weakness
    • Weakness due to structures entering and leaving the abdomen
    • Developmental failures
    • Genetic weakness of collagen
    • Sharp and blunt trauma
    • Weakness due to ageing and pregnancy
    • Primary neurological and muscle diseases
    • Excessive intra-abdominal pressure
  • Despite the complex design of the abdominal wall, the only natural weaknesses caused by inadequate muscular strength are the lumbar triangles and the posterior wall of the inguinal canal.
  • An inguinal hernia (indirect) also occurs through the developmental failure of the processus vaginalis to close.
  • Failure of normal development may lead to weakness of the abdominal wall. Examples are diaphragmatic, umbilical and epigastric hernias.
  • Herniation at the umbilicus has both components, i.e., weakness due to structures passing through the abdominal wall in fetal life and developmental failure of closure.
  • Weakness of abdominal muscles may be the result of sharp trauma. Most commonly, this results from abdominal surgery but also occurs after stabbing. A surgical scar, even with perfect wound healing, has only 70% of the initial muscle strength. This loss of strength can result in herniation in at least 10% of surgical incisions. Smaller laparoscopic port-site incisions have a hernia rate of 1%.
  • Muscle damage by blunt trauma or tearing of the abdominal muscles requires exceptional force and is rare.
  • Primary muscle pathology and neurological conditions can lead to muscle weakness and occasionally present to the surgeon as a 'hernia'.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1059

question_text: What is the investigation of choice for haemorrhagic meckel's diverticulum?
explanation:
Explanation:

Technetium-99m scan (Meckel's scan) is the investigation of choice because it detects ectopic gastric mucosa, which is the usual source of bleeding in haemorrhagic Meckel's diverticulum.

Meckel's diverticulum

  • The presence of heterotopic mucosa may predispose to the development of
  • The vast majority of Meckel's diverticulae are asymptomatic and Meckel's diverticulum is notoriously difficult to see with contrast Meckel's diverticulum may, however, present clinically in the following ways:
  1. Haemorrhage,
  • If the stomach, duodenum and colon are excluded as a source of bleeding by endoscopy, radioisotope scanning with technetium-99m may demonstrate a Meckel's diverticulum.
  • If gastric mucosa is present, peptic ulceration can occur and present as painless dark rectal bleeding or melaena.

1.Diverticultis

  • Meckel's diverticulitis presents like appendicitis, although if perforation occurs the presentation may resemble a perforated duodenal ulcer.

1.Intussusception

  • A Meckel's diverticulum can be the lead point for ileoileal or ileocolic intussusception.
  1. Chronic ulceration.
  • Pain is felt around the umbilicus, as the site of the diverticulum is midgut in origin.
  1. Intestinal obstruction.
  • A band between the apex of the diverticulum and the umbilicus (also part of the vitellointestinal duct) may cause obstruction directly, or by predisposing to the development of a volvulus around it.

1.Perforation

  • When found in the course of abdominal surgery, a Meckel's diverticulum can safely be left alone, provided it has a wide mouth and is not thickened. When there is doubt, it can be resected. The finding of a Meckel's diverticulum in an inguinal or femoral hernia has been described as 'Littre's hernia'.

Explanation for the other options:

  • A.CECT abdomen is often used for complications like diverticulitis or obstruction, but is less sensitive for identifying the specific ectopic mucosa causing the bleeding.
  • B.MRI abdomen is not the first choice for this.
  • D.Ultrasound abdomen is not sensitive for the diverticulum itself.

Key Takeaways:

Haemorrhagic Meckel's diverticulum is caused by ectopic gastric mucosa leading to ulceration. The Technetium-99m pertechnetate scan is the investigation of choice because the radiotracer is selectively taken up by the ectopic gastric parietal cells.

Level:

Must know

question_text: Match the following for the type of hernia by its complexity:
option_a: I - a, II - b, III - c, IV - d
option_b: I - b, II - c, III - d, IV - a
option_c: I - c, II - d, III - a, IV - b
option_d: I - d, II - a, III - b, IV - c
explanation:
Types of hernia by complexity

  • Occult - not detectable clinically; may cause severe pain
  • Reducible - a swelling that appears and disappears
  • Irreducible - a swelling that cannot be replaced in the abdomen, high risk of complications
  • Strangulated - painful swelling with vascular compromise, requires urgent surgery
  • Infarcted - when contents of the hernia have become gangrenous, high mortality

question_text: According to the European hernia society classification, a primary indirect inguinal hernia of 3cm defect size would be classified as?
explanation:
The European Hernia Society has recently suggested a simplified system of:

  • primary or recurrent (P or R);
  • lateral, medial or femoral (L, M or F); lateral denotes for indirect hernia and medial denotes for direct hernia
  • defect size in fingerbreadths assumed to be 1.5 cm.

A primary, indirect, inguinal hernia with a 3-cm defect size would be PL2.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1067

question_text: Which of the following does not form the walls of the femoral hernia?
option_a: Lateral wall formed by femoral artery
option_b: Anterior wall formed by inguinal ligament
option_c: Posterior wall formed by Ashley cooper's ligament
option_d: Medial wall formed by lacunar ligament
explanation:
• The iliac artery and vein pass below the inguinal ligament to become the femoral vessels in the leg.
  • The vein lies medially and the artery just lateral to the artery with the femoral nerve lateral to the artery. They are enclosed in a fibrous sheath. Just medial to the vein is a small space containing fat and some lymphatic tissue (node of Cloquet). It is this space which is exploited by a femoral hernia.
  • The walls of a femoral hernia are the femoral vein laterally, the inguinal ligament anteriorly, the pelvic bone covered by the iliopectineal ligament (Astley Cooper's) posteriorly and the lacunar ligament (Gimbernat's) medially. This is a strong curved ligament with a sharp unyielding edge which impedes reduction of a femoral hernia.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1072

question_text: A 70-year-old male patient came to surgical opd presenting with reducible swelling just above the umbilicus for 5 months. Patient is suffering from copd and liver cirrhosis. On examination cough impulse is present over the swelling and one finger defect is palpable. On ultrasound scan the defect size is 1.5 cm diameter. which surgical procedure should be advisable in this patient?
explanation:
Mayo repair done for defects <2cm

According to the history given above, patient is suffering from paraumbilical hernia. As the defect size is less than 2cm diameter, mayo's repair is best advisable considering the medical history of the patient. Mayo's repair is also known as double breasting technique.

Option a) hernioplasty surgery - in hernioplasty surgery, hernia mesh is placed. But as the defect size is less than 2 cm diameter hernioplasty surgery is not required.

Option c) laparoscopic IPOM surgery - considering the medical condition of the patient and age of the patient, as patient is suffering from COPD and liver cirrhosis, the risk of general anaesthesia increases. And mayo's repair can be performed under spinal anaesthesia in favourable conditions.

Option d) simple primary closure of the defect - considering the age of the patient and medical condition of COPD, simple primary closure of the defect can lead to recurrence because of possibility of weakness of the abdominal muscle tone and chronic cough.

Umbilical hernia in adults

  • Conditions that cause stretching and thinning of the midline raphe (linea alba), such as pregnancy, obesity and liver disease with cirrhosis, predispose to reopening of the umbilical defect.
  • In adults, the defect in the median raphe is immediately adjacent to (most often above) the true umbilicus. The term 'paraumbilical hernia' is commonly used. The defect is rounded with a well-defined fibrous margin.

CLINICAL FEATURES

  • The bulge is typically slightly to one side of the umbilical depression, creating a crescent-shaped appearance to the umbilicus.
  • Women are affected more than men. Most patients complain of pain due to tissue tension or symptoms of intermittent bowel obstruction. In large hernias, the overlying skin may become thinned, stretched and develop dermatitis.

TREATMENT

  • As a result of the high risk of strangulation, surgery should be advised in cases where the hernia contains bowel.
  • Surgery may be performed open or laparoscopically.

OPEN UMBILICAL HERNIA REPAIR

  • Very small defects less than 1 cm in size may be closed with a simple figure-of-eight suture, or repaired by a darn technique where a non-absorbable, monofilament suture is crisscrossed across the defect and anchored firmly to the fascia all around.
  • Defects up to 2 cm in diameter may be sutured primarily with minimal tension, although, the larger the defect, the more tension and the more likely it is that mesh reinforcement will be beneficial. The classic repair was described by Mayo. For defects larger than 2 cm in diameter, mesh repair is recommended.

MAYO'S TECHNIQUE

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1080-1081

question_text: A surgeon examines a case of hernia and can retract the hernial sac but not its contents. Based on this examination, which type of hernia is most likely?
explanation:
Explanation:

Reduction en masse refers to the unintentional displacement or reduction of both the hernia sac and its contents into a deeper anatomical space, such as the preperitoneal or retroperitoneal space, which can occur during the attempted reduction of the hernia.

Explanation of other options:

Incarcerated hernia (Option A): In an incarcerated hernia, the lumen of the part of the colon within the hernial sac becomes obstructed by faeces. The faecal content, or scybalous material, can typically be indented with a finger, similar to putty. In this condition, the sac and its contents are firmly adhered to each other. The hernia is always irreducible and often obstructed, though it may not necessarily be strangulated.

Sliding hernia (Option C): Sliding hernia (Hernia-En-Glissade) occurs when a portion of the peritoneum that normally lines the abdominal cavity slides through the hernia defect, bringing a partially retroperitoneal organ. Patients typically present with a reducible swelling in the groin or lower abdomen that worsens on standing due to gravity

Maydl's Hernia (Option D): It involves two or more bowel loops that become incarcerated or strangulated within the hernia sac. The obstructed loop is present intraperitoneally and easily missed during surgery.

question_text: A patient presented with herniation of intestinal loop which passes along the spermatic cord and reaches till the cremaster muscle. What is the type of hernia?
explanation:
• defect in the transversalis fascia called the deep inguinal ring, just deep to the abdominal muscles.
  • This ring lies midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic tubercle, approximately 2-3 cm above and marginally lateral to the femoral artery pulse in the groin.
  • The inferior epigastric vessels lie just medial to the deep inguinal ring, passing from the iliac vessels to rectus abdominis. Muscle fibers from the innermost two layers of the lateral abdominal wall, the transversus muscle and the internal oblique muscle, arch over the deep inguinal ring from lateral to medial before descending to become attached to the pubic tubercle.
  • These two muscles fuse and become tendinous, forming the conjoint tendon. Below this arch there is no muscle but only transversalis fascia and external oblique aponeurosis, resulting in an area of weakness .
  • Inguinal hernias are classified as direct or indirect. The sac of an indirect inguinal hernia passes from the internal inguinal ring obliquely toward the external inguinal ring and ultimately into the scrotum.
  • In contrast, the sac of a direct inguinal hernia protrudes outward and forward and is medial to the internal inguinal ring and inferior epigastric vessels.
  • As indirect hernias enlarge, it sometimes can be difficult to distinguish between indirect and direct inguinal hernias.

question_text: A 27-year-old male patient presents with complaints of on-and-off discharge from the umbilicus. His CT scan image is as follows. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The CT scan shows a large urachal cyst.

The intra-abdominal portion of the allantois is termed the urachus and connects the urinary bladder with the umbilicus. At the end of gestation, it is converted into the median umbilical ligament.

Persistence of part or all of the urachus may result in the formation of:

  • Vesicocutaneous fistula: with the appearance of urine at the umbilicus.
  • Extraperitoneal urachal cyst:presenting as a lower abdominal mass.

question_text: Identify the structures of the inguinal canal in the given diagram
option_a: A - external oblique aponeurosis, B - subcutaneous fat, C - fascia transversalis, D - spermatic cord
option_b: A - subcutaneous fat, B - external oblique aponeurosis, C - iliac vein, D - spermatic cord
option_c: A - subcutaneous fat, B - external oblique aponeurosis, C - spermatic cord, D - fascia transversalis
option_d: A - subcutaneous fat, B - iliac vein, C - external oblique aponeurosis, D - spermatic cord
explanation:
A, subcutaneous fat; B, external oblique aponeurosis; C, iliac vein; D, spermatic cord; F, nerves in inguinal canal; G, transversalis fascia.

The surgeon enters the inguinal canal by opening its anterior wall, the external oblique aponeurosis. The spermatic cord is dissected free and the presence of a lateral or a medial hernia is confirmed. The sac of a lateral hernia is separated from the cord, opened and any contents reduced. The sac is then sutured closed at its neck and excess sac removed. If there is a medial hernia then the sac is inverted and the transversalis fascia is suture plicated. Sutures are now placed between the conjoint tendon above and the inguinal ligament below, extending from the pubic tubercle to the deep inguinal ring. The posterior wall of the inguinal canal is thus strengthened.

question_text: What is the most likely diagnosis in a female presenting with a reducible mass in the inguinal region, which can be pushed back through the deep inguinal ring and is associated with a gurgling sound?
explanation:
Explanation:

An indirect inguinal hernia occurs when abdominal contents protrude through the deep inguinal ring into the inguinal canal. It typically presents as a palpable bulge in the groin, which is reducible and often associated with a gurgling sound. These hernias are more common in men but can also occur in women. They may be congenital or develop later in life.

Comparison Between Direct and Indirect Inguinal Hernias

Explanation of other options:

Direct inguinal hernia (Option A): This hernia protrudes directly through a weak spot in the abdominal wall within Hesselbach's triangle, without passing through the deep ring. More common in elderly men and usually not associated with gurgling.

Femoral hernia (Option C): Herniation occurs through the femoral canal, usually seen in women. It presents as a swelling below the inguinal ligament, distinct from inguinal hernias. The narrow femoral canal prevents the gurgling characteristic.

Pantaloon hernia (Option D): A combined type, consisting of both direct and indirect hernias occurring simultaneously. Presents with dual swellings on both sides of the inferior epigastric vessels.

Key Takeaways:

  • Indirect hernia: Lateral to inferior epigastric vessels, can descend into scrotum.
  • Direct hernia: Medial to inferior epigastric vessels, remains confined to groin.
  • Femoral hernia → below inguinal ligament.
  • Pantaloon hernia = combined direct + indirect.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common hernia in females?
explanation:
Explanation:

The indirect inguinal hernia is the most common type of hernia in both males and females, although hernias overall occur less frequently in females due to their narrower inguinal canal and stronger connective tissue support.

In this type of hernia, abdominal contents herniate through the deep inguinal ring, traverse the inguinal canal, and may even extend into the labia majora (analogous to scrotal extension in males).

Mechanism:

  • Indirect hernias are congenital in origin, caused by the persistence of the processus vaginalis, allowing abdominal contents to pass through the internal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.
  • They follow the pathway of the spermatic cord (in males) or round ligament (in females).

Explanation of Other Options:

Direct Inguinal hernia (Option A):

  • Occurs due to acquired weakness in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal (Hesselbach's triangle).
  • Common in elderly males due to loss of abdominal wall tone or increased intra-abdominal pressure (e.g. chronic cough, constipation).
  • Rare in females because of stronger transversalis fascia and smaller canal size.

Femoral hernia (Option C) :

  • Second most common hernia in females and most common hernia requiring emergency surgery in women due to its high risk of incarceration and strangulation.
  • Protrudes below the inguinal ligament, through the femoral canal (medial to femoral vein).
  • Risk factors: multiple pregnancies, increased intra-abdominal pressure, weight loss (loss of preperitoneal fat).

Obturator hernia (Option D):

  • Very rare, occurring through the obturator foramen.
  • Seen mostly in elderly, emaciated women ("little old lady hernia").
  • Presents with Howship-Romberg sign - pain radiating down the medial thigh due to compression of the obturator nerve.
  • Though more common in women, it is far less frequent than inguinal or femoral hernias.

question_text: A 25-year-old patient presents to the surgical OPD with a painless left inguinal reducible mass. On examination cough impulse is positive. After further investigations, the patient is diagnosed with an inguinal hernia. What is the surgical management of this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Hernioplasty is the preferred surgical procedure for treating adult inguinal hernias. This technique uses a synthetic mesh to strengthen the abdominal wall, effectively repairing the hernia and minimizing the risk of recurrence.

Management of Inguinal Hernia: Surgical Approaches:

Herniotomy:

  • Involves excision and closure of the hernia sac.
  • Primarily indicated in children with lateral hernias or congenital hydrocele.
  • Not recommended as a standalone procedure in adults due to high recurrence rates. (Option A ruled out)

Hernioplasty:

  • Combines herniotomy with inguinal floor reconstruction using mesh.
  • Preferred method in adults. (Option B)
  • Indications:
    • Direct hernia
    • Recurrent or re-recurrent hernia
    • Incisional hernia
    • Older patients
    • Hernias with weak abdominal wall muscles
    • Sliding hernia

Herniorrhaphy:

  • Involves herniotomy plus inguinal floor reconstruction using sutures.

Techniques:

Bassini's Repair:

  • Sutures the internal oblique, transversus abdominis, and transversalis fascia to the inguinal ligament.
  • Triple-layer repair.
  • Associated with higher recurrence rates.

Shouldice Repair:

  • Four-layer repair (double-breasting of transversalis fascia).
  • Lower recurrence compared to Bassini.

Modified Shouldice:

  • Six-layer repair with additional reinforcement layers.

Anterior Tension-Free Repair:

  • Lichtenstein Repair:
    • Uses polypropylene mesh to reinforce the inguinal floor.
    • Gold standard due to lower recurrence and faster recovery.
    • Tension-free, simple, and effective. (Option A)

question_text: A 54 years old male presented with right groin swelling, located above inguinal ligament, medial to inferior epigastric artery. Cough impulse was present. What is the type of hernia and its management?
explanation:
Hernia is medial to inferior epigastric arteries through hesslebach's triangle suggesting direct hernia and nowadays Lichtenstein repair is a management option for open hernia surgery.

Open flat mesh repair

Synthetic mesh has been used since the 1950s to reinforce hernia repair, and in the 1980s Lichtenstein described a tension-free, simple, fat, polypropylene mesh repair for inguinal hernia.

The initial part of the operation is identical to Bassini's. Once the hernia sac has been removed and any medial defect closed, a piece of mesh measuring 8 * 15 cm is placed over the posterior wall, behind the spermatic cord, and is slit to wrap around the spermatic cord at the deep inguinal ring.

Loose sutures hold the mesh to the inguinal ligament and conjoint tendon. Two major advantages are claimed: lower hernia recurrence rates and accelerated postoperative recovery.

question_text: A 6-year-old boy came with a history of recurrent urinary tract infections. Imaging was done and is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The child has recurrent UTIs, which is a hallmark of vesicoureteric reflux (VUR).
  • The investigation provided is a micturating cystourethrogram (MCU), the gold standard test for VUR.
  • The MCU demonstrates retrograde flow of contrast dye from the bladder into the ureters and kidneys during voiding, confirming the diagnosis.

Vesicoureteric Reflux

Causes

  • Congenital: Often linked with anomalies such as posterior urethral valves.
  • Acquired: May occur following trauma or surgical intervention involving the urinary tract.

Clinical Features

  • Recurrent urinary tract infections and episodes of pyelonephritis.
  • Palpable renal mass may be felt in longstanding disease.
  • Renal impairment in severe bilateral cases.

Complications

  • Progressive renal scarring if untreated.
  • Risk of chronic kidney disease in advanced cases.

Investigations

  • Micturating cystourethrogram (IOC): Demonstrates reflux of urine/contrast.
  • Intravenous urography: Outlines urinary tract anatomy.
  • Urine microscopy and culture/sensitivity.
  • Renal function tests (blood urea, serum creatinine).

Treatment

  • Grades I-III: Antibiotic prophylaxis, as spontaneous resolution is common.
  • Grades IV-V: Require medical therapy plus surgery.
  • Surgical options: Ureteric reimplantation (eg, Lich-Gregoir technique), ureterovesicoplasty, or endoscopic injection (STING procedure).
  • Severe, irreversible renal damage may necessitate nephrectomy or transplantation.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Urinary bladder diverticulum (Option B): Represents an outpouching of the bladder wall, congenital or acquired; not associated with retrograde flow of urine into the ureters.

Urinary bladder hernia (Option C): Rare herniation of bladder into abdominal wall defect; unrelated to reflux or UTIs from retrograde flow.

Vesicocolic fistula (Option D): Abnormal communication between bladder and colon, typically from diverticulitis or carcinoma, presenting with fecaluria and pneumaturia; MCU would show contrast tracking into colon, not ureters.

Key Takeaway

Vesicoureteric reflux is strongly suspected in children with recurrent UTIs, and the micturating cystourethrogram is the investigation of choice to demonstrate retrograde urine flow.

question_text: Synthetic Hernia mesh fixes with the tissue by which mechanism?
option_b: Fibrous tissue in growth between the strands
option_c: Mesh gets plugged with the tissue
option_d: Neovascular ingrowth and new collagen deposition
explanation:
• Net meshes are woven or knitted. Flat sheets are not porous but can be perforated with multiple holes.
  • Net meshes allow fibrous tissue in growth between the strands and becoming adherent and integrated into host tissues within a few months.
  • 'Sheet' meshes do not allow host tissue in growth but become encapsulated by fibrous tissue. They always require strong, non-absorbable fixation to prevent mesh migration.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 64, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1063

question_text: Biological Hernia mesh fixes with the tissue by which mechanism?
option_b: Fibrous tissue in growth between the strands
option_c: Mesh gets plugged with the tissue
option_d: Neovascular ingrowth and new collagen deposition
explanation:
• There are 'biological meshes' that are sheets of sterilised, decellularised, non-immunogenic connective tissue. They derive from human or animal dermis, bovine pericardium or porcine intestinal submucosa.
  • They provide a 'scaffold' to encourage neovascular in-growth and new collagen deposition. Host enzymes eventually break down the biological implant, which is replaced and remodelled with 'normal' host fibrous tissue.
  • The rates of enzymatic degradation and collagen deposition vary between products and also depend on the local environment of the mesh. In the presence of infection, some biological meshes rapidly break down and weaken before remodelling can occur. Others remain strong, their labyrinthine microstructure allowing vascular in-growth to aid infection resistance.

Hernia mesh and hernia repair

question_text: A young sheep farmer presents to the outpatient department with right upper abdominal pain. On examination, there is tender hepatomegaly. Blood tests revealed eosinophilia and elevated liver enzymes. An abdominal ultrasound performed revealed findings as shown. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The waterlily sign on ultrasound indicates a cyst with a detached floating membrane, characteristic of stage CE 3 hydatid cyst. Combined with the clinical features in a sheep farmer, the findings are most consistent with hydatid disease.

Hydatid cyst

  • Hydatid cyst is caused by Echinococcus granulosus, most commonly affects the liver (60–70%), followed by the lungs.
  • It can rarely involve the brain, spleen, kidneys, bones, or peritoneum.

Clinical features

  • Asymptomatic Phase: Common due to slow cyst growth.
  • Symptomatic Phase:
    • Liver Involvement: Mostly right lobe; abdominal pain, hepatomegaly, obstructive jaundice, portal hypertension.
    • Lung Involvement: Cough, chest pain, dyspnea, hemoptysis, pneumothorax.

Investigations

  • Computed tomography (CT)
    • Best imaging technique.
    • Shows smooth space-occupying lesion with several septa.
  • Ultrasonography
    • Most used due to its availability, affordability, and accuracy.
    • A simple hydatid cyst is well-circumscribed, may show budding on the cyst membrane, and can contain free-floating hyperechogenic hydatid sand.
    • The rosette appearance indicates the presence of daughter cysts.
    • Calcification of the cyst wall is highly suggestive of hydatid disease and aids in diagnosis.
  • Raised eosinophil count and serological tests like ELISA and immunoelectrophoresis support diagnosis.

Management

  • Hydatid cysts are ideally managed in a tertiary center by a multidisciplinary team including a hepatobiliary surgeon, physician, and interventional radiologist.
  • Asymptomatic or inactive cysts can be left alone with ultrasound monitoring.
  • Active cysts should first be treated with a full course of albendazole.
  • Various procedures, such as PAIR, pericystectomy with omentoplasty, and hepatic segmentectomy, can be performed, with the choice tailored to the patient and organ involved.

Explanation of other options:

Amoebic liver abscess (Option A): Amoebic liver abscess can cause right upper abdominal pain and hepatomegaly, but it usually occurs in individuals with a history of travel to endemic areas and presents as a liver abscess rather than a cyst.

Pyogenic liver abscess (Option C): Pyogenic liver abscess is usually the result of bacterial infections and typically presents with fever, chills, and localized pain; it does not usually cause marked eosinophilia, as seen in this case.

Hepatocellular carcinoma (Option D): Hepatocellular carcinoma can cause hepatomegaly and may show a solid liver mass on imaging, but it does not present with eosinophilia or cystic ultrasound features seen in parasitic infections.

question_text: Which of the following statement is false for the epidemiology of amoebic liver abscess?
option_a: Commonly seen in 20-40 years of age group
option_b: Females are predominantly infected than males
option_c: Menstruating females have a low incidence rates
option_d: More commonly associated with immunocompromised states
explanation:
Epidemiologic studies specifically addressing E. histolytica infections have estimated that as many as 55% of those in endemic regions are infected, although less than 50% are symptomatic.

In contrast to pyogenic hepatic abscesses, patients with amoebic liver abscesses tend to be Hispanic men, 20 to 40 years of age, with a history of travel to (or origination from) an endemic area.

Poverty and cramped living conditions are associated with higher rates of infection.

A male preponderance of more than 10:1 has been reported in almost all studies.

For unclear reasons, menstruating women have a low incidence of invasive amebiasis, and pregnancy appears to abrogate this resistance.

Heavy alcohol consumption is commonly reported and may render the liver more susceptible to amoebic infection.

Patients with impaired host immunity also appear to be at higher risk of infection and have higher mortality rates.

Patients with amoebic liver abscess without a history of travel to an endemic area often have associated immunosuppression, such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection, malnutrition, chronic infection, or chronic steroid use.

Reference: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1457

question_text: Which among the following is the most commonly affected region of the liver in pyogenic liver abscess?
explanation:
• Most hepatic abscesses involve the right hemiliver, accounting for about 75% of cases.

  • The left liver is involved in approximately 20% of the cases; the caudate lobe is rarely involved (5%).
  • Bilobar involvement with multiple abscesses is uncommon.
  • Approximately 50% of hepatic abscesses are solitary.
  • Hepatic abscesses can vary in size from less than 1 mm to 3 or 4 cm in diameter and can be multiloculated or a single cavity.

question_text: Which is the relative contraindication of percutaneous drainage of pyogenic liver abscess?
explanation:
• Percutaneous drainage for pyogenic hepatic abscesses was first reported in 1953 but did not gain widespread acceptance until the 1980s with the development of highquality imaging and expertise in interventional radiologic techniques.
  • During the last 25 years, percutaneous catheter drainage has become the treatment of choice for most patients. Success rates range from 66% to 90%.
  • The obvious advantages are the simplicity of treatment (usually at the time of radiologic diagnosis) and avoidance of general anaesthesia and a laparotomy.
  • Relative contraindications to percutaneous catheter drainage include the presence of ascites, coagulopathy, and proximity to vital structures.
  • Percutaneous drainage of multiple abscesses is usually met with a higher failure rate, but reports have demonstrated a high enough success rate that percutaneous approaches should be made first, reserving surgery for failures.
  • There has never been a randomized prospective comparison between percutaneous and surgical therapy for hepatic abscess. However, case series have suggested that for most cases, there are similar success and mortality rates.
  • Modern series attempting to compare these two techniques retrospectively must be read with caution because most patients treated surgically have failed to respond to other less invasive techniques.
  • In general, surgery should be reserved for patients who require surgical treatment of the primary pathologic process (e.g., appendicitis) or for those who have failed to respond to percutaneous techniques.
  • Laparoscopic drainage procedures have been reported with some success, and this can be considered a reasonable option to pursue in select cases.

Reference: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1456

question_text: Which of the following conditions is depicted in the given CT image?
explanation:
Explanation:

Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH)

  • Inheritance:
    • Autosomal recessive disorder.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Defective cortisol synthesis results in hormone deficiency, prompting increased ACTH production and adrenal gland hyperplasia.
    • Most commonly due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency, which reduces cortisol and aldosterone synthesis.
  • Investigations:
    • Elevated 17-OH-progesterone
    • CT scan may reveal homogeneous adrenal hyperplasia.
  • Newborn Screening:
    • Measurement of 17-OH-progesterone in heel-prick blood samples during the first week of life allows early detection.

Explanation of Other Options:

Cirrhosis (Option A): Represents the advanced stage of liver scarring resulting from chronic liver diseases such as hepatitis or prolonged alcohol use. Imaging often reveals liver enlargement, nodular texture, and signs of portal hypertension.

Hepatocellular Carcinoma (HCC) (Option B): The most common primary liver cancer. On CT scans, it typically appears as a hypervascular lesion with arterial phase enhancement and delayed phase washout.

Hepatitis (Option D): Causes liver inflammation and may show hepatomegaly on imaging. However, definitive diagnosis requires clinical evaluation and laboratory tests, as imaging findings alone are not conclusive.

question_text: A child with a past history of intubation presented to the OPD with shortness of breath during playing about 6 weeks later. Identify the conditions with the radiological image given below?
explanation:
Explanation:

Croup is usually of slower onset than acute epiglottitis and occurs most commonly in children under 2 years of age. It is usually viral in origin and the cases often occur in clusters. The children have biphasic stridor and are often hoarse with a typical barking cough. Airway intervention is required less often, but admission to hospital with oxygenation and humidification, coupled with antibiotics, may be necessary if there are signs of secondary infection

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Bronchitis

  • Bronchitis is an inflammation of the bronchi, typically caused by viruses or bacteria.
  • It does not usually cause stridor or barking cough, which are characteristic of croup.
  • Radiology may show increased bronchovascular markings, but does not show the steeple sign.

Choice B: Laryngomalacia

  • Laryngomalacia is a condition where the laryngeal cartilage is soft, causing intermittent stridor during the first few months of life.
  • It is often self-resolving by age 18-24 months.
  • The condition does not have the barking cough or steeple sign seen in croup.
  • Radiology typically does not show significant findings for laryngomalacia.

Choice C: Epiglottitis

  • Epiglottitis is a bacterial infection of the epiglottis and surrounding tissues, often caused by Haemophilus influenzae.
  • It presents more suddenly with severe respiratory distress, drooling, fever, and stridor.
  • Radiology typically shows a swollen epiglottis (thumbprint sign).
  • Epiglottitis usually requires emergency airway management, which contrasts with the gradual onset of symptoms seen in croup.

Key Takeaway

  • In a child presenting with shortness of breath and a barking cough after a recent history of intubation, the most likely diagnosis is laryngotracheobronchitis (croup).

question_text: For which of the following conditions is the Whitaker test recommended?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Whitaker test measures the pressure gradient between the renal pelvis and bladder to differentiate true obstruction from non-obstructive hydronephrosis. It is mainly used in equivocal upper urinary tract obstruction.

Whitaker Test

  • Definition

A urodynamic study that measures the pressure gradient between the renal pelvis and the bladder to determine the presence of upper urinary tract obstruction.

  • Indications
    • Equivocal cases of upper urinary tract obstruction.
    • Suspected pelvi-ureteric junction (PUJ) obstruction.
    • Post-pyeloplasty follow-up.
    • Differentiating true obstruction from non-obstructive hydronephrosis.
  • Procedure
    • Percutaneous nephrostomy tube placed into the renal pelvis.
    • Bladder catheter inserted for pressure measurement.
    • Fluid infused into the renal pelvis at a rate of 10 ml/min.
    • Pressure gradient between renal pelvis and bladder is measured and recorded.
  • Interpretation
    • <15 cm H2O → No obstruction.
    • 15-22 cm H2O → Indeterminate (needs further evaluation).
    • >22 cm H2O → Significant obstruction present.
  • Advantages
    • Differentiates true obstruction from non-obstructive dilatation.
    • Particularly helpful in post-surgical cases.
  • Limitations
    • Invasive procedure.
    • Rarely used in current practice.
    • Superseded by modern imaging such as:
      • Diuretic renal scan (DTPA / EC scan).
      • Magnetic Resonance Urography (MRU).

Explanation of other options:

Posterior urethral valve (Option B): A lower urinary tract obstruction best diagnosed by voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG).

Urethral atresia (Option C): Congenital absence of urethral patency, usually detected prenatally; Whitaker test is not applicable.

Urethral stricture (Option D): Best investigated with retrograde urethrogram (RUG) or uroflowmetry, not Whitaker test.

Reference: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25015627/

question_text: Which of the following conditions is associated with the holman-miller sign shown in the CT image below?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Juvenile angiofibroma is an uncommon condition that affects adolescent boys and may lead to massive life-threatening episodes of bleeding.
  • Diagnosis is made with contrast CT or MRI. Anterior bowing or indentation of the posterior antral wall (Holman-Miller or antral sign) is the classical finding but may be seen in other expansive lesions in this area.
  • It is a very vascular tumour, which should not be biopsied because of the risk of uncontrollable haemorrhage. Excision is best carried out by an experienced surgeon and is usually performed endoscopically, often using image guidance.
  • Preoperative embolisation of the feeding blood vessels may help to reduce blood loss during surgery.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: Maxillary sinusitis

  • Maxillary sinusitis can cause sinus wall thickening or opacification, but it is not typically associated with the Holman-Miller sign.
  • The condition usually presents with pain, congestion, and facial tenderness, but it does not cause the anterior bowing of the posterior antral wall seen in JNA.

Choice C: Nasal polyp

  • Nasal polyps are benign, non-vascular growths often associated with chronic sinusitis or allergic rhinitis.
  • While they can cause nasal obstruction and sinus issues, they are not typically associated with the distinctive anterior bowing of the maxillary sinus wall seen in JNA.

Choice D: Schwannoma

  • Schwannomas are nerve sheath tumors, and while they can cause mass effects and symptoms based on their location, they do not typically cause the Holman-Miller sign.
  • Schwannomas in the head and neck usually involve cranial nerves, but they do not lead to the characteristic bone deformation seen with JNA.

Key Takeaway

  • The Holman-Miller sign (anterior bowing of the posterior antral wall) is associated with juvenile angiofibroma (JNA), a highly vascular tumor commonly found in adolescent boys.

question_text: Mount Fuji signs on CT is seen in which of the following conditions?
explanation:
Explanation:

The "Mount Fuji sign" is a classic CT finding in tension pneumocephalus, which refers to the accumulation of air under pressure within the cranial cavity.

This air separates and compresses the frontal lobes, creating a characteristic bilobed appearance resembling the peaks of Mount Fuji - hence the name.

It is a neurosurgical emergency, as the trapped intracranial air can increase intracranial pressure and compress brain tissue.

Pneumocephalus/Tension pneumocephalus:

  • Pneumocephalus refers to the presence of air within the cranial cavity.
  • It most frequently occurs as a result of traumatic head injuries.
  • Tension pneumocephalus can be identified on imaging by:
    • Compression of the frontal lobes.
    • Increased spacing between the frontal lobes in the interhemispheric area.
  • This condition is commonly referred to as the "Mount Fuji sign" because its appearance resembles the famous mountain peak in Japan.

Explanation of Other Options:

Pneumoperitoneum (Option B):

  • On erect chest X-ray: free air seen under diaphragm.
  • No "Mount Fuji" sign.
  • Presents with acute abdomen rather than neurological signs.

Pneumomediastinum (Option C):

  • Radiological finding: continuous diaphragm sign or lucent streaks outlining mediastinal structures.
  • Symptoms: chest pain, subcutaneous emphysema - not intracranial symptoms.

Pneumothorax (Option D):

  • Seen as hyperlucent area without lung markings on CXR.
  • No intracranial findings
  • Unrelated to "Mount Fuji" sign.

question_text: Which of the following conditions corresponds to the barium enema image provided below?
explanation:
Explanation:

Diverticulosis refers to the protrusion of the mucosa and submucosa through weak areas in the colonic wall. In a barium enema, this appears as multiple outpouchings filled with contrast, producing the characteristic "saw-tooth" appearance. It is most commonly observed in the sigmoid colon. Patients are often asymptomatic but may occasionally present with abdominal discomfort or altered bowel habits.

Explanation of other options:

Multiple colonic polyps (Option A): Polyps appear as individual rounded lesions projecting into the lumen, not as multiple saw-tooth outpouchings.

Ulcerative colitis (Option B): Radiology typically shows a smooth, featureless colon with loss of haustra, referred to as a "lead pipe colon."

Irritable bowel syndrome (Option D): A functional bowel disorder without structural abnormalities; radiographs do not demonstrate saw-tooth or diverticular changes.

question_text: A 35-year-old patient with a history of dysentery for 6 weeks complains of pain in the right upper abdomen. On ultrasound, a hypoechoic hyperdense lesion is seen in the liver. Based on the USG findings, what is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation

The ultrasound image shows a hypoechoic hyperdense lesion in the liver. Given the patient's clinical history of dysentery, the most likely diagnosis is an amoebic liver abscess.

  • An amoebic liver abscess is caused by the protozoan parasite Entamoeba histolytica, typically contracted through the ingestion of contaminated food or water.
  • On ultrasound, the abscess appears as a well-defined, hypoechoic lesion with variable internal echoes. Mild to moderate oedema in the surrounding liver parenchyma may also be seen.

Explanation of other options:

Pyogenic liver abscess (Option B): A pyogenic liver abscess, caused by bacterial infections like Escherichia coli or Klebsiella pneumoniae, usually presents as multiple hypoechoic lesions on ultrasound, rather than the single lesion shown here. Inflammation in the surrounding liver parenchyma may also be evident.

Hydatid cyst (Option C): Caused by the larval stage of Echinococcus granulosus, hydatid cysts typically appear as well-defined, anechoic, or hypoechoic lesions, often with multiple daughter cysts inside. The provided image shows a single hypoechoic hyperdense lesion, which is inconsistent with a hydatid cyst.

Hemangioma (Option D): Hemangiomas are benign vascular tumours that commonly occur in the liver. They usually appear as hyperechoic lesions with posterior acoustic enhancement on ultrasound. The lesion in the provided image, being hypoechoic and hyperdense, does not fit the typical characteristics of a hemangioma.

question_text: Which among the following is not a feature of carcinoid syndrome?
explanation:
Explanation:

Carcinoid syndrome is caused by the systemic release of vasoactive substances (especially serotonin, bradykinins, and prostaglandins) from neuroendocrine tumors.

Carcinoid syndrome is characterized by the systemic effects of vasoactive substances like serotonin. This typically causes Bronchospasm (constriction), not bronchodilatation.

question_text: All of the following are causes of malignant pleural effusion except?
option_b: Pleural involvement with primary or secondary malignancy
explanation:
Explanation:

Malignant pleural effusion

  • Pleural effusion is a common complication of cancer.
  • This may be due to:
  • Lung cancer: There may be direct involvement of the parietal and/or visceral pleura, collapse of the lung parenchyma and spread to the mediastinal lymphatics, or a combination of these, causing pleural fluid accumulation.
  • Pleural involvement with primary or secondary malignancy: The only primary malignancy of the pleura seen with any regularity is malignant mesothelioma.
    • This is a consequence of asbestos exposure.
    • Mesothelioma commonly presents with breathlessness because of pleural effusions, pain and systemic features of malignancy.
  • Mediastinal lymphatic involvement: In many instances, particularly in breast cancer, there is no evident disease in the pleura. The disease is in the mediastinal lymphatics, which are obstructed, and this upsets the balance of physiological forces that control pleural fluid.

question_text: What is the investigation of choice for focal nodular hyperplasia of liver?
explanation:
• With advances in hepatobiliary imaging, most cases of FNH can be diagnosed radiologically with reasonable certainty.
  • Contrast- enhanced CT and MRI have become accurate methods of diagnosing FNH.
  • FNH typically shows strong hypervascularity in the arterial phase of CT or MRI with central nonenhancing scar.
  • The enhancement fades over time, and the lesion becomes isointense to the liver parenchyma in the portal and delayed phases.
  • When no central scar is seen, however, radiologic diagnosis is difficult, and differentiation from LCA or a malignant mass, especially fibrolamellar HCC, can sometimes be impossible.
  • On occasion, histologic confirmation is necessary, and resection is recommended for definitive diagnosis. Fine-needle aspiration for the diagnosis of FNH has been recommended but is often unrevealing.
