question_text: Most common primary malignant tumor in children
explanation:
m\c primary malignant tumor in children is pilocytic astrocytoma

  • Pilocytic astrocytomas (WHO grade I) are distinguished from infiltrative astrocytomas by their more discrete borders, unique histopathologic and molecular characteristics, and relatively benign behavior.
  • They typically occur in children and young adults and are usually located in the cerebellum, but they may also appear in the region around the third ventricle, optic nerves, spinal cord, and occasionally in the cerebral hemispheres.
  • The histologic separation of these tumors from other astrocytomas is supported by their relative circumscription, unique histopathologic features, and distinct genetic alterations of the MAP kinase pathway, the most common being a KIAA1549-BRAF gene fusion/duplication.
  • Pilocytic astrocytomas grow very slowly and can often be treated by resection alone. Symptomatic recurrence and incompletely resected lesions may be treated with repeat surgery, chemotherapy, or targeted therapies.

question_text: Which among the following statements is false for clinical presentation of hepatocellular carcinoma?
option_a: Commonly occurs usually in the age group of 40-50 years
option_c: Presents with right upper quadrant pain and weight loss
option_d: Physical findings usually present with palpable mass
explanation:
Clinical presentation.

  • Most commonly, patients presenting with HCC are men 50 to 60 years of age who complain of right upper quadrant abdominal pain and weight loss and have a palpable mass.
  • In countries endemic for HBV, presentation at a younger age is common and probably related to childhood infection.
  • Unfortunately, in unscreened populations, HCC tends to be manifested at a later stage because of the lack of symptoms in early stages.
  • Presentation at an advanced stage is often with vague right upper quadrant abdominal pain that sometimes radiates to the right shoulder
  • Nonspecific symptoms of advanced malignant disease, such as anorexia, nausea, lethargy, and weight loss, are also common.
  • Another common presentation of HCC is hepatic decompensation in a patient with known mild cirrhosis or even in patients with unrecognized cirrhosis
  • HCC can rarely be manifested as a rupture, with the sudden onset of abdominal pain followed by hypovolemic shock secondary to intraperitoneal bleeding
  • Other rare presentations include hepatic vein occlusion (Budd-Chiari syndrome), obstructive jaundice, hemobilia, and fever of unknown origin.
  • Less than 1% of cases of HCC are manifested with a paraneoplastic syndrome, usually hypercalcemia, hypoglycemia, and erythrocytosis
  • Small, incidentally noted tumors have become a more common presentation because of the knowledge of specific risk factors, screening programs for diagnosed HBV or HCV infection, and increasing use of high-quality abdominal imaging

Histology of hepatocellular carcinoma

Reference: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1466

question_text: What is the recommended immediate medical treatment for a patient with a severe history of a road traffic accident who exhibits signs of elevated intracranial pressure upon examination?
option_b: Initiate anticoagulant therapy to prevent blood clot formation
explanation:
Explanation:

In a trauma patient with signs of elevated intracranial pressure (ICP), the immediate goal is to reduce brain edema and prevent herniation. Mannitol is a first-line hyperosmolar agent used for this purpose.

Mechanism of Action

  • Osmotic Effect: Mannitol creates an osmotic gradient that draws water out of the brain parenchyma (across an intact blood-brain barrier) into the vasculature, reducing cerebral edema and intracranial volume.
  • Rheologic Effect: It temporarily expands plasma volume, reduces blood viscosity, and improves cerebral blood flow and oxygen delivery.

Explanation of other options:

Administer antibiotics (Option A): Antibiotics are crucial for preventing infection in open skull fractures or base of skull fractures with CSF leak, but they do not directly address acute raised ICP.

Initiate anticoagulant therapy (Option B): Anticoagulants are contraindicated in the acute phase of traumatic brain injury due to the high risk of promoting or worsening intracranial hemorrhage.

Perform immediate surgical intervention (Option C): Surgery (e.g., evacuation of a hematoma, decompressive craniectomy) may be the definitive treatment, but it requires prior imaging (CT scan) to identify the surgical lesion. Medical management with agents like mannitol is often initiated before or while preparing for surgery to stabilize the patient.

Key Takeaways:

  • Mannitol (or hypertonic saline) is a key medical therapy for rapidly lowering raised ICP in traumatic brain injury.

Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10329884/

question_text: Which of the following immunosuppressive agent is useful in induction and maintenance therapy in Crohn's disease?
explanation:
• The immunosuppressive agents AZT, 6-MP, and MTX are effective in maintenance therapy and for the treatment of moderate to severe Crohn disease.
  • AZT and 6-MP are effective for maintaining steroid-induced remission, and weekly IV MTX is effective for both induction and maintenance therapy.
  • Because of the slow onset of action of immunosuppressive agents and to prevent flares, steroids are needed for induction and continued until the transition to immunosuppressive agents is complete.
  • Despite their potential toxicity, these drugs have proved to be relatively safe in patients with Crohn disease; the most common side effects are pancreatitis, hepatitis, fever, and rash.
  • The more disconcerting complications of immunosuppressants include chronic liver disease, bone marrow suppression, and the potential for malignant transformation.
  • Genetic polymorphisms for thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT), which is the primary enzyme that metabolizes AZT and 6-MP, have been identified and suggested for use to regulate therapy according to the measurement of their metabolites (6- thioguanine nucleotides).
  • MTX also has side effects of hepatotoxicity and can cause myelosuppression and should not be used in pregnant women.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1266

question_text: Which one of the following agent used as adjuvant therapy in management of malignant melanoma?
explanation:
• When mutation locks B-RAF protein signalling to 'on', it affects the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) cellular pathway, promoting initiation, malignant transformation, tumour progression and metastasis in the 50% of MM with B-RAF V600 mutations.
  • Targeted therapy in stage IV melanoma using dabrafenib or vemurafenib, which block B-RAF action has shown promising results with metastatic melanoma.
  • Trametinib has a different action on the MAPK pathway: stopping cell growth and promoting apoptosis. Combined use with dabrafenib to counter acquired tumour resistance via MAPK pathway reactivation, shows promising results in stage 4 disease.
  • Also, selective immune checkpoint inhibitors ipilimumab or nivolimumab demonstrate benefit in metastatic or unresectable melanoma.

Malignant melanoma

  • Rising incidence
  • Genetic and acquired risk factors
  • Superfcial spreading form the most common
  • Breslow thickness is the most important prognostic indicator

Sentinel node biopsy (SNB) is useful for staging

question_text: A 44-year-old lady presents to the hospital with a ballotable flank mass. The mass measures 4 cm on CT imaging. Urine examination shows malignant cells. What is the most appropriate management for her condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

A 4 cm ballotable flank mass identified on examination, combined with a CT scan showing a hyper-enhancing solid lesion in the kidney, is highly suggestive of Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC). For tumors measuring less than 4 cm, partial nephrectomy is generally considered the treatment of choice to preserve renal function while ensuring complete tumor removal.

Management of Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC):

General Note:

  • RCC is typically resistant to both radiotherapy and traditional chemotherapy.

Surgical Options:

  • Partial Nephrectomy (Option A):
    • Removes only the tumor while preserving the rest of the kidney.
    • Indications:
      • T1 tumors (<7 cm).
      • Tumors limited to the kidney poles.
      • RCC is a solitary functioning kidney.
  • Radical Nephrectomy (Option C ruled out):
    • Removes the entire kidney along with Gerota's fascia, para-aortic lymph nodes, and the ureter up to the pelvic brim.
    • Indications:
      • Larger tumors.
      • When partial nephrectomy is not technically feasible.

Ablative Techniques:

  • Radiofrequency Ablation (RFA) and Cryoablation:
    • Destroy the tumor using extreme heat or cold.
    • Indications:
      • Patients unfit for surgery.
      • Small T1a lesions (<4 cm).

Systemic Therapy for Advanced/Metastatic RCC:

  • Targeted Therapy:
    • Tyrosine kinase inhibitors (e.g., sunitinib, pazopanib).
    • mTOR inhibitors (e.g., everolimus).
  • Immunotherapy:
    • Immune checkpoint inhibitors (e.g., nivolumab).

Partial nephrectomy combined with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (Option B): Neoadjuvant chemotherapy is generally reserved for muscle-invasive or high-risk renal cell carcinoma, which is not the case with a small, localized 4 cm tumor. Since RCC typically does not respond well to chemotherapy, partial nephrectomy alone is usually adequate in such situations.

Radical nephrectomy with postoperative radiotherapy (Option D): Radiotherapy after surgery is not commonly applied in RCC due to the tumor’s inherent resistance to radiation. Radical nephrectomy is primarily performed for larger or more invasive lesions, whereas partial nephrectomy is preferred for smaller 4 cm tumors to conserve kidney function.

Key Takeaways:

Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC):

  • Solid Enhancing Mass: Appears as a solid lesion with increased enhancement on imaging.
  • Common Histology: Clear cell carcinoma accounts for around 85% of malignant renal tumours.
  • Imaging Characteristics: Typically shows hyper-enhancement after contrast administration. On non-contrast CT (NCCT), heterogeneous enhancement is suggestive of RCC.
  • Genetic Association: Often linked to Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) syndrome, which may present with multiple small tumours within cysts.
  • Extension: RCC has the potential to invade the inferior vena cava (IVC).
  • MRI Utility: Contrast-enhanced MRI is preferred to assess IVC involvement or thrombus formation. It can also help distinguish between benign and malignant thrombi through contrast uptake.
  • Preferred Diagnostic Test: Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) is the investigation of choice for diagnosing and staging RCC. MRI is used when contrast is contraindicated or for further evaluation of complex findings.

question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with a facial lesion associated with itching and occasional bleeding. Based on the image provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a slow-growing malignant tumor arising from the basal layer of the epidermis, commonly affecting sun-exposed areas such as the face. It typically presents as a pearly pink papule with telangiectatic vessels, rolled edges, and a central ulcer with crusting. Although invasive, it rarely metastasizes. BCC accounts for nearly 90% of skin cancers and is categorized into nodular, nodulocystic, superficial, and cystic variants.

Basal Cell Carcinoma (BCC):

  • Also known as Rodent Ulcer.
  • Locally invasive, meaning it destroys surrounding tissues.
  • Referred to as Tear Cancer, as it occurs typically above a line drawn from the ear lobule to the corner of the mouth.
  • Originates from the basal layer of the epidermis.
  • The most common site is the nose, with the inner canthus being another frequent location.

Types of BCC (based on pathology):

  • Nodular:
    • The most common type.
    • Appears as small, slow-growing pearly nodules.
    • Characterized by telangiectatic vessels on the surface.
    • Notable for a central depression called umbilication
    • it can also be pigmented.
  • Cystic
  • Superficial

Management:

  • For non-aggressive tumors on the trunk or extremities, wide local excision with a 2 cm margin is usually sufficient.
  • For large, aggressive tumors affecting vital or cosmetic areas, or recurrent tumors, Mohs micrographic surgery is recommended.

Explanation of other options:

Dermatofibrosarcoma (Option A): A soft tissue sarcoma presenting as reddish-brown plaques; does not show pearly rolled borders with central ulceration.

Marjolin's ulcer (Option B): Refers to malignant transformation (commonly squamous cell carcinoma) in chronic scars or ulcers; image findings are not consistent with Marjolin's ulcer.

Naevus (Option D): A benign melanocytic lesion; image lacks features of a pigmented nevus.

question_text: Which among the following is not the cause of pyelophebitis?
explanation:
• The portal venous system drains the gastrointestinal tract; therefore, any infectious disorder of the gastrointestinal tract can result in an ascending portal vein infection (pyelophlebitis), with exposure of the liver to large amounts of bacteria.
  • Historically, untreated appendicitis was considered the most common cause of hepatic abscess, but with the advent of antibiotics and the development of prompt and effective treatment of acute intraabdominal infections, portal venous infections of the liver have become less frequent.
  • The most common causes of pyelophlebitis are diverticulitis, appendicitis, pancreatitis, inflammatory bowel disease, pelvic inflammatory disease, perforated viscus, and omphalitis in the newborn.
  • Hepatic abscess has also been associated with colorectal malignant disease.
  • In a case-control study from Taiwan, the incidence of gastrointestinal cancers was increased fourfold among patients with pyogenic liver abscess compared with controls.

Pylephlebitis

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding the complications of bladder outlet obstruction?
option_a: Acute retention of urine is sometimes the first symptom of bladder outlet obstruction
option_b: Haematuria may be a complication of BPH
option_c: >750 ml is considered as chronic retention
option_d: Urinary infection and calculi are prone to develop
explanation:
Complications of bladder outlet obstruction (BOO)-

  • Acute retention of urine is sometimes the first symptom of BOO.
  • Chronic retention- In patients whom the residual volume is ≥250mL, the tension in the bladder wall increases owing to the combination of a large volume of residual urine and increased resting and filling bladder pressures (a condition known as high-pressure chronic retention).
  • The increased intramural tension results in functional obstruction of the upper urinary tract with the development of bilateral hydronephrosis.
  • As a result, upper tract infection and renal impairment may develop.
  • Impaired bladder emptying leads to the development of a large volume of residual urine causing urinary infection and calculi to develop.
  • Haematuria- may be a complication of BPH.

BLADDER OUTLET OBSTRUCTION

question_text: Which among the following anatomical part of the gall bladder refers to as Hartmann's pouch?
explanation:
• The gallbladder is a pear-shaped sac that measures around 7 to 10 cm long, with an average capacity of 30 to 50 mL.
  • When obstructed, the gallbladder can distend markedly and contain up to 300 mL of fluid.
  • The gallbladder is located in an anatomic fossa on the inferior surface of the liver.
  • Cantle's line, a vertical plane running from the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the inferior vena cava (IVC) posteriorly divides the liver into right and left lobes.
  • The gallbladder itself is divided into four anatomic areas: the fundus, the body, the infundibulum, and the neck.
  • The fundus is the rounded, blind end that normally extends 1 to 2 cm beyond the liver’s margin and contains most of the smooth muscle of the organ.
  • The body functions as the main storage area and contains most of the elastic tissue allowing for distention.
  • As the body tapers towards the neck of the gallbladder, a mucosal outpouching is present at the junction of the neck and the cystic duct, known as the infundibulum or Hartmann's pouch.
  • Beyond this, the neck of the gallbladder lies in the deepest part of the gallbladder fossa and can extend slightly into the free portion of the hepatoduodenal ligament, where it connects with the cystic duct.

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter 32 Gallbladder and the Extrahepatic Biliary System, pg no: 1393

question_text: Which among the following is not a component of Reynold's pentad?
explanation:
Clinical Manifestations

  • Cholangitis may present as anything from a mild, self-limited episode to a fulminant, potentially life-threatening septicaemia.
  • Patients with gallstone-induced cholangitis are most commonly older and female.
  • The most common presentation is fever, epigastric or right upper quadrant pain,and jaundice.
  • These classic symptoms, known as Charcot's triad, are present in about two-thirds of patients.
  • The illness can progress rapidly with the development of shock and altered mental status, known as Reynolds' pentad (e.g., fever, jaundice, right upper quadrantpain, septic shock, and mental status changes).
  • However, the presentation may be atypical, with little if any fever, jaundice, or pain.

question_text: Which of the following is the most common side effect of cholecystectomy?
explanation:
Explanation:

Steatorrhea (fatty stools) is the most common long-term effect of cholecystectomy, due to continuous bile secretion causing fat malabsorption.

Complications of Cholecystectomy

Early Complications (Intraoperative & Immediate Postoperative):

  • Bile Duct Injury: Accidental injury to the common bile duct (CBD) → bile leakage, fistula, or strictures. More frequent in laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
  • Hemorrhage: From the cystic artery or liver bed; may require hemostasis or transfusion if severe.
  • Bowel Injury: Rare but serious; duodenum or colon may be injured during dissection.
  • Anesthesia-related complications: Aspiration, respiratory depression, hypotension, arrhythmias.

Early Postoperative Complications (0-7 Days):

  • Wound/Port-Site Infection: Presents with fever, erythema, and tenderness. Common in diabetics/immunocompromised.
  • Bile Leak (Biloma): Leakage from cystic duct stump or accessory ducts → abdominal pain, fever, localized fluid collection on imaging.
  • Subhepatic Abscess: RUQ pain, fever, tachycardia; often requires percutaneous drainage.
  • Retained Gallstones: Stones left in CBD → biliary colic or cholangitis.
  • DVT/PE: Due to immobilization; presents with leg swelling or sudden dyspnea. Prevent with early ambulation and anticoagulation.

Late Complications (>7 Days to Months/Years):

  • Steatorrhea (Fatty stools): Most common long-term effect due to continuous bile flow, leading to fat malabsorption.
  • Post-Cholecystectomy Syndrome (PCS): Persistent dyspepsia, bloating, RUQ pain, or diarrhea due to bile reflux or residual stones.
  • Biliary Strictures: Chronic CBD narrowing → jaundice, recurrent cholangitis.
  • Chronic Diarrhea: From altered bile acid metabolism; may respond to bile acid sequestrants (e.g., cholestyramine).
  • Increased Colorectal Cancer Risk (Debatable): Some evidence suggests a small increase due to altered bile acids, though not strongly proven.

Explanation of other options:

Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) (Option A): Rarely occurs as a direct complication of cholecystectomy. It may develop secondary to severe sepsis or intraoperative hypotension, but it is uncommon.

Osteoporosis (Option B): No established association. In rare cases of chronic bile acid diarrhoea with fat malabsorption, vitamin D deficiency may contribute to bone demineralisation, but this is not typically seen after routine cholecystectomy.

Colorectal Cancer (Option D): Some evidence suggests a slight increase in colon cancer risk due to altered bile acid metabolism; however, this remains debatable and is not considered a common or direct outcome of cholecystectomy.

question_text: A 55-year-old man presents with abdominal pain. A CECT (Contrast Enhanced CT) abdomen was done. What is the likely source of pain?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The CT findings of an irregular enhancing lesion in the renal parenchyma are highly suggestive of Renal Cell Carcinoma (RCC).
  • RCC often presents late, as early stages are usually asymptomatic.
  • Classic triad (only in ~10% patients):
    • Hematuria
    • Flank pain
    • Abdominal mass
  • Other clinical clues:
    • Non-reducing left varicocele (due to renal vein thrombosis/obstruction)
    • Systemic symptoms like fever, anemia, weight loss
    • Metastases (lungs, bones, brain) in advanced disease

Treatment:

  • Surgical: Partial nephrectomy (T1 disease <7 cm, solitary kidney, polar tumor) or Radical nephrectomy (larger tumors, locally advanced disease).
  • Non-surgical (selected cases): Ablation (RFA, cryotherapy) in high-risk surgical patients with small tumors (<4 cm).
  • Metastatic/Advanced disease: Targeted therapy (TKIs, mTOR inhibitors) and immunotherapy.

Explanation of other options:

Gall bladder (Option A):

  • Typical Presentation:
    • Right upper quadrant (RUQ) colicky pain, often radiating to the right shoulder or back.
    • Pain may be episodic, especially after fatty meals (biliary colic).
    • Associated features: Nausea, vomiting, fever (if cholecystitis), Murphy's sign positivity.
  • Imaging Features (on Ultrasound/CECT):
    • Gallstones (echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing).
    • Gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm).
    • Pericholecystic fluid collection (acute cholecystitis).
    • Empyema or perforation may be seen in advanced cases.

Spleen (Option B):

  • Typical Presentation:
    • Left upper quadrant (LUQ) abdominal pain, often radiating to the left shoulder (Kehr's sign).
    • Splenic enlargement may cause early satiety or dragging pain.
    • May present acutely in trauma (splenic rupture) with shock and peritonitis.
    • Chronic causes: Splenomegaly in portal hypertension, hematological disorders, or infections.
  • Imaging Features (on USG/CECT):
    • Splenomegaly with homogeneous or heterogeneous enhancement.
    • Hypodense areas if infarction or abscess.
    • Traumatic rupture: Subcapsular hematoma or free peritoneal fluid.

  • Imaging Features (on USG/CECT):
    • Splenomegaly with homogeneous or heterogeneous enhancement.
    • Hypodense areas if infarction or abscess.
    • Traumatic rupture: Subcapsular hematoma or free peritoneal fluid.

question_text: A lady was incidentally diagnosed with a 0.5cm solid mass in her gall bladder on USG which was non mobile, diagnosed as GB polyp. She is asymptomatic. Next step in management?
explanation:
Pt was asymptomatic so observation

Gallbladder polyps

  • Polyps of the gallbladder are incidental findings during radiological imaging of the abdomen. Thepolyps are more often benign(cholesterol polyps, adenomyosis, inflammatory, adenomas or miscellaneous) but may be malignant (adenocarcinoma [80%] or squamous cell carcinoma, or cystadenomas).
  • A majority of polyps remain stable. Cholecystectomy should be considered in symptomatic patients or as prophylaxis to prevent malignant transformation in those who also have gallstones, primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC), biliary colic or pancreatitis.
  • Polyps in patients older than 60 years, sessile polyps with wall thickening greater than 4 mm and polyps larger than 10 mm merit cholecystectomy.
  • Smaller polyps should be kept under observation and need surgery if the size is increasing.

KEYTAKEAWAYS:

Indications for laparoscopic cholecystectomy in case of GB polyp includes:

  • Polyp >1cm
  • Increasing size of polyp on regular screening
  • Poly with stone
  • Age >60yrs

question_text: Which among the following is not a consistent predictor of malignancy in gall bladder polyp?
explanation:
Gallbladder polyp.

  • The only polypoid lesions that have malignant potential and are associated with a significant rate of harbouring malignancy are adenomatous polyps.
  • The most consistent predictors of malignancy in gallbladder polyps are single polyp,size greater than 1 cm, and age older than 50 years.
  • Cholecystectomy is generally recommended for polyps larger than 1 cm and can safely be performed laparoscopically. Polyps smaller than 1 cm can undergo surveillance to demonstrate stability, with the exception in the setting of PSC, where the threshold for cholecystectomy should be lower in the population.

Reference: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, 55. Biliary System, Pg no: 1518

question_text: A 39-year-old patient presented with RTA and was brought to the ER with a pulse rate of 120/min and SBP of <80mmHg. Despite intravenous fluid resuscitation and BT, the patient's condition deteriorates with ongoing profuse bleeding from the liver. Identify the procedure shown in the image done to control massive liver bleed.
explanation:
Explanation:

Pringle's Maneuver

  • Definition: Temporary clamping of the hepatoduodenal ligament to control severe liver bleeding.
  • Structures occluded:
    • Hepatic artery
    • Portal vein
  • Technique:
    • Apply a non-crushing vascular clamp across the porta hepatis.
    • This blocks inflow through the hepatic artery and portal vein.
  • Interpretation of results:
    • Bleeding decreases: Source is from hepatic inflow vessels (hepatic artery or portal vein).
    • Bleeding continues: Suggests injury to hepatic veins or retrohepatic inferior vena cava (IVC).

Explanation of Other Options:

Kocher Maneuver (Option A):

  • Commonly employed during cholecystectomy to mobilize the duodenum.
  • Provides improved access to the gallbladder.
  • It is not intended for controlling liver bleeding.
  • Therefore, it is unsuitable for the management of severe hepatic hemorrhage.

Cattell-Braasch Maneuver (Option C):

  • Performed to mobilize the colon and gain access to retroperitoneal structures such as the kidneys.
  • It does not serve a role in controlling liver hemorrhage.
  • Therefore, it is unrelated to hepatic bleeding management.

Mattox Maneuver (Option D):

  • Involves mobilization of the left colon to expose retroperitoneal structures, including the aorta and inferior vena cava.
  • This technique is not designed for controlling liver bleeding.
  • Unlike Pringle's maneuver, it is not useful in the context of massive hepatic hemorrhage.

question_text: What is the preferred timing of early cholecystectomy after the attack of acute cholecystitis?
explanation:
• Patients who present with acute cholecystitis should receive IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and analgesia.
  • The antibiotics should cover gram-negative enteric organisms as well as anaerobes.
  • Although the inflammation in acute cholecystitis may be sterile in some patients, it is difficult to know who is secondarily infected.
  • Therefore, antibiotics have become a standard part of the initial management of acutecholecystitis in most centers.
  • Cholecystectomy is the definitive treatment for acute cholecystitis.
  • In the past, the timing of cholecystectomy has been a matter of debate. Earlycholecystectomy performed within 72 hours of the onset of the illness is preferred over delayed cholecystectomy that is performed 6 to 10 weeks after initialmedical treatment and recuperation.
  • Several studies have shown that unless the patient is unfit for surgery, early cholecystectomy should be recommended as soon as possible, as it offers the patient a definitive solution in one hospital admission, quicker recovery times, similar complication rates, and an earlier return to work.

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter 32, Gallbladder and the Extrahepatic Biliary System, pg no: 1406.

question_text: A patient presents with pain in the right hypochondrium. Blood investigations showed AST-22IU/L and ALT- 27 IU/L. Serum Bilirubin levels - 5 mg/dl and also ALP-200 mg%. What should be the initial investigation in this patient?
explanation:
Ultrasonography

  • Transabdominal ultrasonography (USG) isthe initial imaging modality of choice asit isaccurate, readilyavailable, inexpensive and quick to perform.
  • However, it is operator dependent and may be compromised by excessive body fat and intraluminal bowel gas. Thesize of the gallbladder and presence of stones or polyps can be determined. Acute calculous cholecystitisis diagnosed radiologically (sensitivity 90-95%) by thickening of the gallbladder wall (>3 mm), presence of pericholecystic fluid or direct tenderness when the probe is pushed against the gallbladder (ultrasonographic Murphy's sign).
  • Additionally, the presence of inflammation around the gallbladder, the size of the CBD and, occasionally, the presence of stones within the extrahepatic biliary tree can be determined.

question_text: Patient underwent cholecystectomy. The histopathology reveals carcinoma of gall bladder with invasion into the muscularis propria. What is the next best step?
explanation:
• Invasion of muscularis propria comes under T1b.

After laparoscopic cholecystectomy is done, the specimen is sent to pathologist for staging, treatment based on staging:

T1a involving mucosa only: no need further intervention

T1b involving muscularis layers → next step: check whether

  • Lymphovascular invasion present
  • Cystic duct margin is positive
  • Poorly differentiated tumour

If any one of these is present - extended cholecystectomy done (extra 2cm of liver resection)

  • T2 and above - radical cholecystectomy is done(4b and 5th segments of liver is removed)

question_text: Which among the following is the primary most common risk factor for the development of gallbladder cancer?
explanation:
Cause

  • Although not proven scientifically, the prevailing theory of gallbladder cancer focuses on chronic inflammation with subsequent development of neoplasia.
  • Therefore, the presence of gallstones is considered to be the primary risk factor, and larger stones (>3 cm) carry an increased risk of cancer development.
  • More than 80% of patients with gallbladder cancer have cholelithiasis, and gallbladder cancer is approximately seven times more common in patients with gallstones than in those without stones.
  • The type of stone does not correlate with incidence of gallbladder cancer. Other risk factors include entities that may also cause inflammation in the gallbladder wall, such as APBJ, choledochal cysts, and PSC.
  • Extensive calcification of the wall of the gallbladder, termed porcelain gallbladder, carries a risk of cancer development.
  • The calcification is probably the result of long-standing inflammation. Whereas the risk of gallbladder cancer is higher in patients with gallbladder wall calcification, malignant disease in this setting is unusual, occurring in less than 10% of patients with porcelain gallbladder.
  • There is some suggestion of an adenoma-carcinoma progression in the development of gallbladder cancer as severe dysplasia and carcinoma in situ are often adjacent to gallbladder carcinomas.
  • However, there is no evidence that patients with gallbladder polyposis carry an increased risk of gallbladder malignancy.
  • Conversely, several studies have demonstrated that the presence of a single gallbladder polyp larger than 10 mm carries an increased malignancy risk and cholecystectomy is generally recommended.

Reference: Sabinston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, 55. Biliary System, Pg no: 1516

question_text: A patient underwent a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for cholelithiasis. A picture of the resected gall bladder is shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Gallbladder specimen shows an exophytic, polypoidal growth with a thickened wall, suggestive of gallbladder carcinoma.

Gall bladder carcinoma

Risk factors

  • Pre-existing gall stone disease
  • Porcelain gallbladder
  • Gallbladder polyps
  • Primary sclerosing cholangitis
  • Chronic infection, such as in typhoid carriers, increases the risk of gallbladder cancer compared to the general population.

Clinical features

  • Patients with gallbladder cancer may be asymptomatic or present with nonspecific symptoms similar to benign gallbladder disease, such as biliary colic or cholecystitis.
  • Late signs: Jaundice, anorexia, and a palpable mass are late signs
    • Indicates poor resectability and lower chances of negative surgical margins.

Laboratory Findings:

  • Nonspecific finding: Anaemia, leukocytosis, mild transaminase elevation
  • Tumor markers: CA19-9 and CEA may be elevated in ~80% of patients.

Diagnosis and Staging:

  • Preoperative diagnosis: Usually suspected on ultrasound and confirmed with CT (thorax, abdomen, pelvis) or MRI/MRCP.
  • Staging aims: Assess local extent and exclude distant metastases.
  • Biopsy: Percutaneous radiology-guided biopsy considered only for unresectable disease before palliative treatment.
  • Laparoscopy: Useful for staging; can detect peritoneal or liver metastases that preclude surgery.
  • PET scan: Useful for detecting metastatic disease.

Management

  • Most patients present with advanced disease; many are unresectable at diagnosis.
  • Staging laparoscopy prevents unnecessary laparotomy in advanced disease.
  • Radical en bloc resection with lymphadenectomy is standard for resectable advanced disease.
  • Early incidental cancers confined to mucosa may not need further surgery.
  • Adjuvant chemotherapy is indicated in high-risk or resected advanced cases.

Explanation of other options:

Mixed stone in gall bladder (Option B): Mixed gallstones, made of cholesterol, bilirubin, and calcium salts, appear as echogenic foci with posterior acoustic shadowing on ultrasound, are visible within the gallbladder, show no associated growths, and may be partially calcified on CT.

Cholecystitis (Option C): Cholecystitis is the inflammation of the gall bladder, often due to gallstones or infection. It can present with acute symptoms like pain, fever, and nausea. Imaging shows gallbladder wall thickening (>3 mm), pericholecystic fluid, and ultrasonographic Murphy's sign.

Choledocholithiasis (Option D): Choledocholithiasis refers to the presence of stones in the common bile duct, and its diagnosis typically requires imaging to show stones in the bile duct.

question_text: The following are the risk factors of carcinoma gallbladder except
option_b: Size of stone >3cm in gall bladder
explanation:
• Several studies have demonstrated that the presence of a single gallbladder polyp larger than 10 mm carries an increased malignancy risk and cholecystectomy is generally recommended.
  • Gallbladder cancer is extremely variable by geographical region and racial-ethnic groups; the highest incidence is among Chileans, Native Americans and residents in parts of northern India, where it accounts for as much as 9% of all biliary tract disease.
  • Women appear to have a higher incidence across all geographical areas.
  • In western practice, gallbladder cancer accounts for less than 1% of new cancer diagnosis.
  • The disease usually presents in the 7th or 8th decade.
  • The aetiology is unclear but there is a suggested association with pre-existing gallstone disease, implying that chronic inflammation may play a role.
  • Calcification of the gallbladder wall, presumably due to chronic inflammation (porcelain gallbladder), is also associated with a small increased risk of cancer.
  • Chronic infection may promote the development of cancer and the risk in typhoid carriers is significantly increased over that of the general population.
  • Patients with PSC, especially with concomitant IBD, and those with an abnormal pancreatic-biliary junction are at greater risk of gallbladder cancer.
  • In patients with gallbladder polyps the risk of malignant transformation increases with increasing size of the polyp.

question_text: What is the amount of mucus secreted by the gall bladder daily?
explanation:
• The gallbladder is a reservoir for bile. During fasting, resistance to flow through the sphincter of Oddi is high, and bile excreted by the liver is diverted to the gallbladder.
  • After feeding, the resistance to flow through the sphincter is reduced, the gallbladder contracts and the bile enters the duodenum. These motor responses of the biliary tract are in part affected by the hormone cholecystokinin.
  • The second function of the gallbladder is concentration of bile by active absorption of water, sodium chloride and bicarbonate via the mucous membrane of the gallbladder.
  • The hepatic bile which enters the gallbladder becomes concentrated 5-10 times, with a corresponding increase in the proportion of bile salts, bile pigments, cholesterol and calcium.
  • The third function of the gallbladder is the secretion of mucus - approximately 20mL is produced per day.
  • With complete obstruction of the cystic duct in an otherwise healthy gallbladder, a mucocoele may develop as a result of ongoing mucus secretion by the gallbladder mucosa.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27th edition , Chapter 67, The gallbladder and bile ducts, Pg no: 1190

question_text: Which lymph node is not visible at the insertion of the cystic artery into the gall bladder?
explanation:
• The cystic artery that supplies the gallbladder is usually a branch of the right hepatic artery (>90% of the time).
  • The course of the cystic artery may vary, but it nearly always is found within the hepatocystic triangle (triangle of Calot), the area bound by the cystic duct, common hepatic duct, and the inferior edge of the liver.
  • When the cystic artery reaches the neck of the gallbladder, it divides into anterior and posterior divisions.
  • Venous return is carried either through small veins that enter directly into the liver or,rarely, to a large cystic vein that carries blood back to the portal vein.
  • Gallbladder lymphatics drain into nodes at the neck of the gallbladder. Frequently, a visible lymph node (Lund's or Mascagni's node, often referred to as Calot's node) overlies the insertion of the cystic artery into the gallbladder wall.
  • The gallbladder receives parasympathetic, sympathetic and sensory innervation through nerve fibers running largely through the gastro hepatic ligament.
  • Parasympathetic (cholinergic) fibers arise from the hepatic branches of the vagus nerve to stimulate activity in the gallbladder, bile ducts, and liver.
  • These vagal branches also have peptide-containing nerves containing agents such as substance P, somatostatin, enkephalins, and vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (VIP).2
  • The sympathetic and sensory branches of the gallbladder, liver, and bile ducts pass through the celiac plexus and control gallbladder relaxation and mediate the pain of biliary colic.

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter 32, Gallbladder and the Extrahepatic Biliary System, Pg no: 1394

Incidence

  • Gallbladder cancer generally occurs in the sixth and seventh decades of life and istwo to three times more common in women than in men.
  • Ethnicity plays an important role in the development of gallbladder cancer, with the highest incidence in women from India and Pakistan.
  • Among North American populations, Native Americans and immigrants from Latin America have the highest rates.
  • In the United States overall, gallbladder cancer is the most common cancer of the biliary tract and the fifth most common gastrointestinal cancer.

question_text: A patient with jaundice, anorexia, and weight loss for 2 months. The gall bladder is palpable, soft and non-tender. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical features of a soft, palpable, non-tender gallbladder associated with jaundice and weight loss is pancreatic head cancer.

  • Pancreatic cancer risk is influenced by both environmental and hereditary factors. Smoking is the strongest environmental risk, with incidence directly proportional to the number of cigarettes smoked, while obesity and diabetes (especially new-onset diabetes) are also associated.
  • Chronic pancreatitis, occupational exposures, and long-term diabetes may further increase risk.
  • Hereditary syndromes associated with pancreatic cancer include:
    • Familial pancreatic cancer
    • Hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1, SPINK1)
    • Peutz-Jeghers syndrome
    • Cystic fibrosis (CFTR mutation)
    • Familial atypical multiple mole melanoma syndrome (CDKN2A mutation)
    • BRCA2 mutations
    • Lynch syndrome
    • Familial adenomatous polyposis
  • Pathogenesis involves progression from pancreatic intraepithelial neoplasia (PanIN) to invasive pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC), with mutations in KRAS, CDKN2A/p16, TP53, and SMAD4 driving tumour development.
  • Pancreatic cancer commonly presents late, with symptoms such as jaundice, weight loss, nausea, pruritus, and, rarely, gastrointestinal bleeding.
  • Courvoisier's law states that a shrunken fibrotic non-palpable gallbladder, along with jaundice, is suggestive of choledocholithiasis, while a palpable gallbladder points to a periampullary mass such as cancer of the head of the pancreas.
  • Diagnosis involves laboratory evaluation, tumour markers like CA 19-9 (sensitive but not specific), and imaging.
  • EUS (Endoscopic ultrasound) with FNA offers high diagnostic accuracy, MRCP provides detailed biliary anatomy, and FDG-PET combined with CT aids in differentiating benign from malignant lesions and detecting occult disease.
  • Treatment depends on the tumour location.
    • For head tumours, pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) is the standard, involving removal of the pancreatic head, duodenum, gallbladder, and bile duct, followed by reconstruction.
    • For body and tail tumours, distal pancreatectomy with splenectomy is performed, with medial-to-lateral or antegrade dissection approaches.

Explanation of other options:

Hepatocellular carcinoma (Option A): Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) often presents with features resembling cirrhosis, including jaundice, spider angiomas, ascites, and splenomegaly. About one-fourth of patients develop metastases to sites such as lymph nodes, lungs, bone marrow, and brain, while splenomegaly may lead to anaemia, thrombocytopenia, or pancytopenia. A palpable gallbladder rules against this diagnosis.

Gall bladder cancer (Option B): Gallbladder cancer usually remains asymptomatic until advanced stages, with many patients presenting with systemic spread, including nodal involvement and distant metastases. Early signs may mimic acute or chronic cholecystitis, with recent change in the quality and frequency of pain, while late-stage disease often manifests as weight loss, jaundice, abdominal mass, and chronic epigastric pain.

Choledocholithiasis (Option D): Choledocholithiasis can present with biliary colic or obstructive jaundice, characterised by dark urine, scleral icterus, and pale stools. Jaundice is often painful due to acute obstruction, causing bile duct distention. Complications include cholangitis, presenting with Charcot's triad of right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice, which may progress to septic shock with altered mental status and hypotension known as Reynolds pentad.

question_text: If radiotherapy is administered along with chemotherapy for bladder cancer, which drug's dosage should be decreased?
explanation:
Explanation:

Gemcitabine is a potent radiosensitizer. When used concurrently with radiotherapy for bladder cancer, its standard systemic dose significantly increases the risk of severe local toxicity, particularly radiation cystitis (severe bladder inflammation), myelosuppression, and gastrointestinal damage. Therefore, in bladder-preserving chemoradiation protocols, a reduced dose of gemcitabine is used to harness its radiosensitizing effects while minimizing unacceptable toxicity to normal tissues.

Explanation of other options:

Cisplatin (Option A): Cisplatin is also a radiosensitizer but is typically used at or near full systemic doses in concurrent chemoradiation regimens for various cancers, including bladder cancer, without the same mandate for significant dose reduction.

Paclitaxel (Option C): Paclitaxel is not a standard component of first-line chemoradiation regimens for bladder cancer.

Ifosfamide (Option D): Ifosfamide is used in regimens for sarcomas and germ cell tumors, not typically for bladder cancer chemoradiation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Gemcitabine requires dose reduction when combined with radiotherapy due to its strong radiosensitizing properties.
  • The goal is to balance efficacy with reduced toxicity to normal organs.

question_text: Which among the following is not included in the Rigler's triad?
explanation:
Gallstones

  • This type of obstruction tends to occur in the elderly secondary to erosion of a large gallstone directly through the gall bladder into the duodenum.
  • Classically, there is impaction about 60 cm proximal to the ileocaecal valve.
  • The patient may have recurrent attacks as the obstruction is frequently incomplete or relapsing as a result of a ball-valve effect.
  • The characteristic radiological sign of gallstone ileus is Rigler’s triad, comprising: small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia and an atypical mineral shadow on radiographs of the abdomen.
  • The presence of two of these radiological signs has been considered pathognomic of gallstone ileus and is encountered in 40-50% of the cases (note than pneumobilia is common following endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy).
  • At laparotomy, the stone is milked proximally away from the site of impaction.
  • It may be possible to crush the stone within the bowel lumen; if not, the intestine is opened at this point and the gallstone removed. If the gallstone is faceted, a careful check for other enteric stones should be made. The region of the gall bladder should not be explored.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1377

question_text: Young male present with history of fever and jaundice. He also has h/o passage of recurrent white thread like structure in stool. USG was s/o 9 cm long CBD structure with 9 mm CBD diameter and proximal dilation of biliary tree. All of the following are correct regarding it except:
option_a: Organism which leads to this reside in snail which act as intermediate host.
option_b: Intra-hepatic bile duct stones also occur due to this parasite.
option_c: Confirmation of condition can be done by USG or urine sample showing parasite.
option_d: Surgical exploration with removal of gall bladder + exploration of CBD and Repeated washout + choledochoduodenostomy.
explanation:
Option A: This is a case of Clonorchis sinensis causing cholangiohepatitis. Snail and Fish act as intermediate hosts for this organism.

Option B: Intra-hepatic bile duct stones are also caused by the parasite producing Mucin rich bile. Intrahepatic bile ducts are dilated with epithelial hyperplasia and peri-ductal fibrosis. These changes may lead to dysplasia causing cholangiocarcinoma.

Option C: Confirmation of the condition requires examination of stool or duodenal aspirate which may show the eggs or adult worms. USG may have characteristic finding of uniform dilation of small peripheral intrahepatic bile ducts with only minimal dilation of the common hepatic and common bile duct. But it is not confirmatory.

Option D: Cholecystectomy with exploration of the common bile duct is performed when indicated. Repeated washouts are necessary during the exploration, as the common bile duct is dilated and contains stones, biliary debris, sludge and mud. This should be followed by choledochoduodenostomy.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 6, Edition: 28th, Pg: 72

question_text: A 55-year-old woman who works as a food handler is found to be excreting Salmonella Typhi in her stool, despite being asymptomatic for several years after an episode of typhoid fever. An ultrasound of her abdomen reveals the presence of cholelithiasis. What is the most common site for chronic carriage of S. Typhi in such individuals?
explanation:
Explanation:

Gallbladder is the most common site of long-term, chronic carriage for Salmonella Typhi.

Following an acute infection, the bacteria can persist within the gallbladder, often forming biofilms on the surface of gallstones. From this reservoir, the bacteria are intermittently shed into the bile and then into the intestines, leading to excretion in the stool and making the individual an asymptomatic carrier capable of transmitting the disease. The historical case of "Typhoid Mary" is the most famous example of such a chronic carrier.

Explanation of Other Options:

Urinary Bladder (Option A): While urinary carriage can occur, especially with S. typhi and in patients with schistosomiasis, it is much less common than gallbladder carriage.

Rectum (Option B): The rectum is part of the excretory path, but it is not the primary site where the bacteria persist.

Peyer's patches (Option D): Peyer's patches in the terminal ileum are the primary site of invasion and multiplication during the acute phase of typhoid fever, but they are not the site of long-term chronic carriage.

question_text: A patient underwent a cholecystectomy, during which black pigmented gallstones were identified. The patient's past medical history includes multiple episodes of shortness of breath and chest pain requiring hospitalization. Which of the following is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

Clinical Association: Black Pigmented Gallstones and Sickle Cell Anemia

  • Black pigmented gallstones are commonly associated with conditions involving increased red blood cell (RBC) turnover.
  • Sickle cell anemia is a genetic disorder characterized by the production of abnormal hemoglobin (hemoglobin S).
  • Hemoglobin S causes sickle-shaped red blood cells, which are:
    • Prone to destruction
    • Lead to chronic hemolytic anemia

Pathophysiology and Clinical Features of Sickle Cell Anemia

  • Hemolysis and Gallstone Formation:
    • Repeated hemolysis results in high levels of bilirubin.
    • Excess bilirubin leads to the formation of black pigmented gallstones.
  • Clinical History:
    • Patients often present with:
      • Recurrent shortness of breath
      • Chest pain
    • These symptoms are likely due to:
      • Vaso-occlusive crises
      • Acute chest syndrome
        → Both are hallmark complications of sickle cell disease.
  • Vaso-occlusion and Systemic Effects:
    • Sickled cells obstruct blood flow, causing vaso-occlusion.
    • Vaso-occlusive crises lead to acute painful episodes that:
      • Can affect any organ system
      • Result in complications such as:
        • Acute chest syndrome
        • Stroke
        • Chronic organ damage

Summary:

  • The combination of:
    • Chronic hemolytic anemia
    • Elevated bilirubin
    • Black pigmented gallstones
    • Recurrent vaso-occlusive symptoms
  • Strongly suggests a diagnosis of sickle cell anemia.

Explanation of other options:

Beta Thalassemia (Option B): Beta thalassemia is another hemoglobinopathy characterized by reduced or absent synthesis of the beta chains of hemoglobin. It can also lead to chronic hemolysis but is less likely to cause the same type of gallstones as seen in sickle cell anemia.

Hb Punjab (Option C): Hb Punjab is a variant of hemoglobin resulting from a mutation. It is generally benign but can be part of compound heterozygous states with other hemoglobinopathies. It is less likely to be associated with the clinical scenario described.

Sideroblastic Anemia (Option D): Sideroblastic anemia involves the presence of ringed sideroblasts in the bone marrow and is primarily a disorder of ineffective iron incorporation into hemoglobin. It does not typically present with the hemolytic features or complications like those seen in sickle cell anemia.

Key Takeaways:

Black pigmented gallstones in a patient with recurrent episodes of shortness of breath and chest pain strongly suggest sickle cell anemia, which is associated with chronic hemolysis and bilirubin stone formation.

question_text: A patient underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy and was discharged after drain removal on day 1. On day 2, he returned with abdominal pain, tachycardia, fever, and ultrasound showing a 5 × 5 cm subhepatic collection. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

Early post-cholecystectomy subhepatic collections are most often due to a bile leak, commonly from the cystic duct stump or an accessory bile duct.

Explanation of other options:

Infection (Option A): Takes 5-7 days to develop; not an early cause of subhepatic collection.

Surgical site pain (Option B): Does not explain fever, tachycardia, or localized fluid collection.

Retained gallstones (Option D): Can cause colic or cholangitis, but not an early subhepatic collection.

question_text: A patient who underwent laparoscopic cholecystectomy 4 days ago now complains of right upper quadrant (RUQ) pain. An ultrasound shows a 300 ml fluid collection in the abdomen. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

A postoperative fluid collection following laparoscopic cholecystectomy is most often a biloma or abscess, especially if the patient presents with RUQ pain and systemic signs.

  • The first-line management is image-guided percutaneous drainage (USG or CT-guided aspiration/drainage).
  • This not only relieves symptoms but also allows fluid analysis to confirm bile leak or infection.
  • Most small biliary leaks resolve once the collection is drained, provided there is no distal obstruction.

Explanation of Other Options:

Exploratory laparotomy (Option A): Reserved for cases where percutaneous/radiological drainage fails, or if there is uncontrolled sepsis or major bile duct injury. Too invasive as the first step.

Start broad-spectrum antibiotics (Option C): May be given adjunctively, but antibiotics alone are inadequate for a 300 ml collection; source control (drainage) is essential.

Prescribe analgesics and discharge (Option D): Unsafe; patient risks sepsis, abscess expansion, or bile peritonitis if the collection is untreated.

Calot's triangle, also known as the cystohepatic triangle, is an important anatomical area during gallbladder surgery. The boundaries of Calot's triangle are defined by:

  • Cystic duct (lateral boundary)
  • Common hepatic duct (medial boundary)
  • The inferior surface of the liver (superior boundary)

The contents of Calot's triangle typically include the cystic artery, which supplies blood to the gallbladder, and the cystic lymph node (Lund’s node). Identification of these structures is crucial during a cholecystectomy to avoid accidental injury to the biliary or vascular systems.

Note: The term "hepatocystic triangle" is often used interchangeably with Calot's triangle. It emphasizes the inclusion of the liver's inferior surface as part of the boundaries, along with the cystic duct and the common hepatic duct.

Explanation of Other Options:

Cystic artery (Option A): Runs within Calot's triangle, but it is an arterial structure, not a duct. It usually arises from the right hepatic artery.

Right hepatic artery (Option C): Supplies right lobe of the liver, located more medially and superiorly, outside Calot's triangle.

Hepatic duct (Option D): Common hepatic duct forms the medial boundary of Calot's triangle, but it does not run from the gallbladder.

question_text: A 50 years old male presented to the hospital with colicky abdominal pain and bilious vomiting. On evaluation, air was present in the CBD. What is the most probable diagnosis?

question_text: A female presents with epigastric pain and right hypochondrial pain radiating to the back with guarding and rigidity in the right hypochondrium. She has had similar episodes for the past 1 year on and off. Most likely diagnosis is
explanation:
• Patients typically complainof right upper quadrant or epigastric pain, which mayradiate to the back. This may be described as colicky but the typical biliary 'colic' more often is dull, continuous and severe, lasting for several minutes or even hours, with associated nausea and vomiting .
  • Frequently, pain starts during the night and wakes the patient; minor episodes may occur intermittently during the day. In the majority of cases the process is limited by the stone slipping back into the body of the gallbladder.
  • The development of acute cholecystitis is marked by fever. Associated symptoms that have a questionable relation to gallstonesinclude dyspepsia, flatulence, food intolerance, particularly to fats, and some alteration in bowel frequency.
  • As pain resolves (spontaneously or with medications) the patient improves and is able to eat and drink again, often only to suffer further episodes. A patient may have several such episodes over a few weeks and then no symptoms for some months. This may culminate in a contracted non-functioning gallbladder with the development of chronic cholecystitis.
  • In acute cholecystitis theright upper quadrant tendernessis exacerbated during inspiration by palpation inthe right subcostal region (Murphy's sign).
  • A mass may become palpable as the omentum walls of an inflamed gallbladder. If resolution does not occur, empyema of the gallbladder may result.
  • The wall may become necrotic and perforate, with the development of localized peritonitis . Occasionally, complete obstruction of the cystic duct leads to reabsorption of bile salts by the gallbladder epithelium and secretion of uninfected mucus, resulting in a mucocele of the gallbladder.

question_text: A patient presents with jaundice. Imaging shows dilation of the common hepatic duct due to an impacted stone in the cystic duct compressing the common bile duct. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The condition described is referred to as Mirizzi's syndrome, in which a stone impacted in the cystic duct or gallbladder neck compresses the common hepatic duct, leading to obstructive jaundice.

Mirizzi's syndrome

  • Seen in 1% of all cholecystectomies, where a gallstone impacts the gallbladder wall, leading to compression and pressure necrosis.
  • The gallstone usually impacts from the Hartmann's pouch, leading to compression of the hepatic duct or common bile duct.
  • Can also occur from the fundus of the gallbladder into the CBD.
  • This often results in adherence to the common hepatic duct (CHD) or common bile duct (CBD) wall and can occasionally lead to a cholecystocholedochal fistula.
  • Clinical features
    • Fever
    • Abdominal pain
    • Obstructive jaundice
    • Upper abdominal tenderness on the right side
    • Possible palpable soft, enlarged liver

Csendes Classification


Investigations

  • Ultrasonography (USG): Initial imaging to assess gallbladder and ducts.
  • CT Scan: Provides detailed imaging of the biliary system.
  • ERCP/ MRCP: Essential for delineating duct anatomy and identifying the site of obstruction.
  • HIDA Scan: Useful for functional assessment of the biliary system.
  • Findings: Dilatation of the intrahepatic biliary system with a block at the common hepatic duct (CHD).

Explanation of other options:

Acute cholecystitis (Option A): Acute cholecystitis is an inflammation of the gallbladder, usually caused by a gallstone obstructing the cystic duct. It presents with right upper quadrant pain and tenderness, but does not typically cause common hepatic duct dilatation or jaundice, unless complicated by a secondary obstruction of the common bile duct.

Porcelain gallbladder (Option B): Refers to calcification of the gallbladder wall, typically from chronic cholecystitis. While it increases the risk of gallbladder cancer, it does not cause biliary obstruction or jaundice, as there is no cystic duct stone compressing the bile ducts.

Cholesterolosis (Option C): Also known as strawberry gallbladder, by lipid deposits in the gallbladder mucosa, giving a strawberry-like appearance on imaging. It is usually asymptomatic and does not cause biliary obstruction or jaundice. or jaundice.

question_text: Which among the following statements is false for epidemiology of liver cell adenoma?
option_b: Associated with use of oral steroids
option_d: Male anabolic steroids predispose to development of liver cell adenoma
explanation:
Liver Cell Adenoma

  • Liver cell adenoma (LCA) is a relatively rare benign proliferation of hepatocytes in the context of a normal liver.
  • It is predominantly found in young women (aged 20–40 years) and is often associated with steroid hormone use, such as long-term oral contraceptive pill (OCP) use.
  • Male anabolic hormone use can also predispose to development of LCA.
  • The female-to-male ratio is approximately 11:1.
  • Other risk factors for LCA include vascular liver diseases, glycogenosis type 1A, and familial adenomatous polyposis
  • LCAs are usually singular, but multiple lesions have been reported in 12% to 30% of cases.
  • Liver adenomatosis is defined by the presence of more than 10 LCAs in the liver. Interestingly, cases with multiple adenomas are not associated with OCP use and do not have as dramatic a female preponderance
  • On histologic evaluation, LCAs are composed of cords of benign hepatocytes containing increased glycogen and fat. Bile ductules are not observed histologically, and the normal architecture of the liver is absent in these lesions. Haemorrhage and necrosis are commonly seen.
  • On the basis of detailed molecular pathology correlation studies, a French collaborative group has recently proposed a molecular-pathologic classification whereby the adenomas are classified as β-catenin mutated adenoma, HNF1A mutated adenoma, inflammatory adenoma, and not otherwise specified adenoma
  • Molecular studies have also identified genetic signatures associated with a higher risk of malignant transformation. Specifically, highest risk of malignant transformation is observed in LCA with β-catenin activation

Liver cell adenoma

Reference: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1463

question_text: Which among the following structure is not included in the portal triad?
explanation:
• The functional anatomy of the liver is composed of eight segments, each supplied by a single portal triad (also called a pedicle) composed of a portal vein, hepatic artery, and bile duct.
  • These segments are further organized into four sectors, separated by scissurae containing the three main hepatic veins
  • The four sectors are even further organized into the right and left liver
  • The terms right liver and left liver are preferable to the terms right lobe and left lobe because there is no external mark that allows the identification of the right and left liver
  • This system was originally described in 1957 by Goldsmith and Woodburne and by It defines hepatic anatomy because it is most relevant to surgery of the liver.

question_text: Which structure forms the superior border of the hepatobiliary triangle?
explanation:
• The cystic artery, a branch of the right hepatic artery, usually arises behind the common hepatic duct. Occasionally, an accessory cystic artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery.
  • Calot's triangle, or the hepatobiliary triangle, was initially described by Calot as the space bordered by the cystic duct inferiorly, the common hepatic duct medially and the superior border of the cystic artery.
  • This has been modified in contemporary literature to be the area bound superiorly bythe inferior surface of the liver, laterally by the cystic duct and the medial borderof the gallbladder and medially by the common hepatic duct.
  • It is an important surgical landmark as the cystic artery usually can be found within its boundaries and should be identified by surgeons performing a cholecystectomy to avoid damage to the extrahepatic biliary system.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 71 Gallbladder and bile ducts, Pg no: 1232.

question_text: A newborn presents with jaundice. Biliary atresia is suspected when jaundice is persistent and exceeds?
explanation:
Explanation:

Biliary atresia is a progressive neonatal condition characterized by partial or complete absence/obstruction of bile ducts, resulting in cholestasis, conjugated hyperbilirubinemia, and progressive liver injury.

A key clinical clue is jaundice persisting beyond 2 weeks of age. Unlike physiological jaundice, which typically resolves within 1-2 weeks, persistent jaundice in neonates warrants evaluation for biliary atresia.

Extra-Hepatic Biliary Atresia (EHBA)

  • Also termed Non-Cystic Obliterative Cholangiopathy.
  • Defined by complete obliteration of extrahepatic bile ducts with extension into intrahepatic ducts at the hilum.
  • Clinical onset: usually 2-6 weeks after birth.

Clinical features:

  • Progressive jaundice (yellowing of skin and sclera).
  • Acholic stools (pale stools).
  • Dark urine due to conjugated bilirubin excretion.
  • May be associated with splenic anomalies (polysplenia or asplenia).

Investigations

  1. Liver Function Tests (LFTs):
    • Elevated conjugated bilirubin.
    • Markers of cholestasis:
      • Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) ↑
      • 5' nucleotidase ↑
      • Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT):
        • Normal: ≤40 U/L
        • 4× elevation: intrahepatic obstruction
        • 10× elevation: extrahepatic obstruction
        • Exception: PFIC types I & II show low GGT
  2. Ultrasound (USG):
    • High-resolution neonatal USG → first-line imaging.
    • Fasting USG: gold standard screening when BA suspected.
    • Findings:
      • Triangular cord sign: hyperechoic area above portal vein (fibrotic bile duct).
      • Non-visualized/micro gallbladder ("gallbladder ghost").
  3. Radionuclide Imaging (HIDA Scan):
    • Uses Tc-labelled iminodiacetic acid derivative.
    • Shows absent/decreased tracer excretion into bowel.
    • Phenobarbitone priming (5 days) improves diagnostic accuracy.
    • Used as screening, not definitive.
  4. Liver Biopsy (Gold Standard):
  5. Investigation of choice.
  6. Shows bile duct proliferation, bile plugs, and fibrosis.

Management

Surgical options:

  • Kasai procedure (Hepaticojejunostomy):
    • Palliative / temporary.
    • Establishes drainage by connecting intrahepatic bile ducts to jejunum.
    • Best results if performed within 8 weeks of life.
  • Definitive therapy: Liver transplantation, required in most cases due to progressive fibrosis and cirrhosis.

Reference: https://www.pathologyoutlines.com/topic/liverextrahepaticbiliaryatresia.html

question_text: A 35 years old male presented with recurrent episodes of abdominal pain, abdominal tenderness, fever and jaundice. The MRCP image of the patient is given below. Most likely diagnosis is:
explanation:
PRIMARY SCLEROSING CHOLANGITIS

  • PSC is a rare idiopathic and progressive biliary tract disease characterized by inflammation and destruction of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts that can lead to liver fibrosis and cirrhosis.
  • Association with hypergammaglobulinemia and markers such as anti-smooth muscle antibodies and anti-nuclear factor suggest an immunological basis; cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene mutations have been associated with the development of PSC.
  • The majority of patients are between 30 and 60 years of age. There appears to be a male predominance and a strong association with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), especially ulcerative colitis (IBD in PSC, 80%; PSC in IBD, 5%).
  • Patients may be asymptomatic, but common symptoms include pruritus, fever, fatigue, right upper quadrant discomfort, jaundice and weight loss.
  • Liver function tests reveal a cholestatic pattern, elevated serum ALP and gamma-glutamyl transpeptidase (GGTP) and smaller rises in the aminotransferases; bilirubin values can be variable. MRCP (or ERCP) may demonstrate stricturing and beading of the bile ducts.
  • Liver biopsy is helpful to confirm the diagnosis (concentric periductal 'onion skinning') and may help guide therapy by excluding cirrhosis. Important differential diagnoses are secondary sclerosing cholangitis, immunoglobulin G4 (IgG4) cholangitis, autoimmune hepatitis, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) cholangiopathy and cholangiocarcinoma. The last may arise in patients with PSC and is difficult to diagnose; a high index of suspicion is required, especially in the setting of unexplained clinical deterioration.
  • Patients with PSC are at increased risk for cholangiocarcinoma and gallbladder cancer, as well as colon cancer in those with concurrent IBD.

question_text: A 70 year old male patient was diagnosed with small, asymptomatic densely calcified hydatid cyst. What would be the appropriate management?
explanation:
• Although the treatment of hepatic hydatid cysts is primarily surgical, alternative options are in evolution.
  • In general, most cysts should be treated; but in older patients with small, asymptomatic, densely calcified cysts, conservative management is appropriate.
  • In preparation for an operation, preoperative steroids have been recommended but are not universally used.
  • The anaesthesiologist should have epinephrine and steroids available in case of an anaphylactic reaction. A number of operations have been used, but in general, the abdomen is completely explored, the liver mobilized, and the cyst exposed.
  • Packing off the abdomen is important because rupture can result in anaphylaxis and diffuse seeding.
  • The cyst is usually then aspirated through a closed suction system and flushed with a scolicidal agent, such as hypertonic The cyst is then unroofed, which can then be followed by a number of possibilities, including excision (or pericystectomy), marsupialization procedures, leaving the cyst open, drainage of the cyst, omentoplasty, and partial hepatectomy to encompass the cyst.
  • Total pericystectomy or formal partial hepatectomy can also be performed without entering the cyst.
  • Both radical (resection) and conservative (drainage and evacuation) surgical approaches appear to be equally effective at controlling disease, although a prospective comparison has never been performed. When bile duct communication is diagnosed preoperatively or at operation, it must be meticulously sought after. Simple suture repair is often sufficient, but major biliary repairs, approaches through the common bile duct, or postoperative ERCP may be necessary.
  • Laparoscopic techniques for drainage and unroofing of cysts have been reported in a number of series, with encouraging results. Recurrence rates after surgical treatment range from 1% to 20% but are generally 5% or less in experienced centers. In the past, percutaneous aspiration of hydatid cysts was contraindicated because of the risk of rupture and uncontrolled spillage. However, percutaneous aspiration with injection of scolicidal agents has been reported with high success rates in highly selected patients.
  • This technique is known as puncture, aspiration, injection, and reaspiration PAIR) and has become more accepted in some centers.
  • Treatment of echinococcosis with albendazole or mebendazole is effective at shrinking cysts in many patients with granulosus infection, but cyst disappearance occurs in well below 50% of patients. Preoperative treatment may decrease the risk of spillage and is a reasonable and safe practice.
  • Medical therapy without definitive resection or drainage should be considered only for widely disseminated disease or poor surgical candidates.

Reference: Sabiston Textbook of Surgery 21st Edition, SECTION X ABDOMEN, Chapter 54, The Liver Pg: 1461

question_text: Which sphincter surrounds the wall of the cystic duct?
explanation:
• The cystic duct is about 3 cm in length but the length is variable.
  • The lumen is usually 1-3 mm in diameter.
  • The mucosa of the cystic duct is arranged in spiral folds known as the valves of Heister and the wall is surrounded by a sphincteric structure called the sphincter of Lutkens.
  • The cystic duct joins the supraduodenal segment of the common hepatic duct in 80% of cases, however the anatomy may vary and the junction may be much lower in the retroduodenal or even retropancreatic part of the bile duct.
  • Occasionally, the cystic duct may join the right hepatic duct or even a right hepatic sectorial duct.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 27th edition, Chapter 67, The gallbladder and bile ducts, Pg no: 1188

question_text:
An 80 years old female presented with colicky pain and jaundice. Serum bilirubin and GGT was raised.MRCP image shows gallstones and CBD stones with dilated biliary radicles. Next step in the
management:
explanation:
Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography

  • This technique is now used only as a therapeutic modality in patients with obstructive jaundice; USG and MRCP have taken over the diagnostic aspect.
  • Using a side-viewing endoscope the ampulla of Vater is identified and cannulated. Injection of water-soluble contrast into the bile duct provides excellent images of the ductal anatomy and can identify causes of obstruction such as calculi and malignant strictures .
  • Bile aspirates can be obtained and sent for cytological and microbiological examination and brushings can be taken from strictures for cytology.
  • Therapeutic interventions such as stone removal or stent placement to relieve obstruction can be performed simultaneously.
  • Cholangioscopy is a relatively new technique in which a thin scope is inserted through the channel of an ERCP scope to visually inspect the bile duct.
  • The main indications include indeterminate or unexplained biliary strictures, nodules or masses and crushing difficult-to-remove bile duct stones with lithotripsy.

question_text: Patient has undergone cholecystectomy few days back and now the patient has presented with upper abdominal pain. MRCP was done which showed leaking of bile from the cystic duct stump. Patient is hemodynamically stable. Which of the following should be next line of management?
explanation:
• Patients who develop jaundice in the postoperative periodneed urgent investigation. This is especially true if the jaundice is attributed to infection and cholangitis.
  • Thefirst step following resuscitationandadministration of appropriate antibiotics is to undertake urgent USG. This will demonstrate whether there is intra- or extrahepatic ductal dilatation.
  • The anatomy may need tobe defined by MRCP or ERCP. The latter is undertaken whentherapeutic maneuvers are planned, such as the removal of an obstructing stone or theinsertion of a stent across a biliary leak.
  • If a fluid collection is present in the subhepatic space, drainage catheters may be required. These can be inserted under radiological control or, if this expertise is not available, at open operation.
  • Small biliary leaks will usually resolve spontaneously, especially if there is no distal obstruction. If the CBD is damaged, the patient should be referred to an appropriate expert for reconstruction.

question_text: What is the ideal time of removal of drains kept for serous collection drainage?
explanation:
• Drains put in to cover perioperative bleeding may usually be removed after 24 hours, e.g. thyroidectomy.
  • Drains put in to drain serous collections usually can be removed after 5 days, e.g. mastectomy.
  • Drains put in because of infection should be left until the infection is subsiding or the drainage is minimal.
  • Drains put in to cover colorectal anastomoses should be removed at about 5-7 days. However, it should be stressed that in no way does a drain prevent any intestinal leakage, but merely may assist any such leakage to drain externally rather than to produce life-threatening peritonitis.
  • Common bile duct T-tubes should remain in for 10 days. However, once the T-tube cholangiogram has shown that there is free flow of bile into the duodenum and that there are no retained stones, some surgeons like to clamp the T-tube prior to removal. The 10-day period is required to minimise the risk of biliary peritonitis after removal. T-tubes are traditionally and intentionally made of latex to stimulate fibrosis, which results in the formation of a tract to allow the drainage of bile if required. It is important to use an alternative to latex if the patient is allergic, bearing in mind the decreased potential for fibrosis of silicone- based T-tubes. The increase in less invasive means of intervention for bile duct pathology has resulted in fewer T-tubes being used.
  • Any suction drain should have the suction taken off prior to removal of the drain. Even in the absence of suction, a blocked drain may be difficult to remove owing to the creation of a relative vacuum as it is pulled out. This can be released by twisting the drain on removal or flushing with a small volume of sterile saline under aseptic conditions.
  • During removal of a chest drain, the patient should be asked to breathe in and hold their breath, thus doing a Valsalva manoeuvre. In this way, no air is sucked into the pleural cavity as the tube is removed. Once the drain is out, a previously inserted purse-string suture should be tied.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 101

explanation:
Patients who develop jaundice in the postoperative period need urgent investigation as it can be attributed to bile duct injury

Treatment:

Initially resuscitation and administration of appropriate antibiotics should be done

Following which USG will demonstrate whether there is intra- or extrahepatic ductal dilatation or biliary leak etc.

Usg guided T-tube/pigtail catheter is inserted and the duct closed around it, the long limb is brought out on the right side and bile is allowed to drain externally.

After 2 weeks, leak usually stops, if leak not stopped, next step is ERCP, it is both diagnostic and therapeutic, so if ERCP shows bile duct injury, stenting and sphincterotomy can be done in the same sitting.

Other investigations in bile duct injury:

Investigation which is of no use is CECT abdomen

(a) Bile leak from the cystic duct stump or minor biliary radical in the gallbladder fossa.

(b) An occluded right posterior sectoral duct.

(c) A bile leak from the divided right posterior sectoral duct.

(d) A bile leak from the main bile duct without any major tissue loss.

  • E2, transected main bile duct with a stricture less than 2 cm from the hilus.
