question_text: 3 days after cholecystectomy, patient developed severe abdominal pain with fever. Her LFT was normal, serum amylase was also normal. What is the most likely cause of her condition?
explanation:
Complications of cholecystectomy

Recovery after laparoscopic cholecystectomy is associated with less pain and faster return to normal activity than open cholecystectomy. The majority of elective patients can have this performed as a day case; however, any patient looking unwell in the postoperative period, with untoward symptoms such as fever, chills or abdominal pain, should be kept under observation.

Complications can occur in 10-15% of cases. Serious complications fall intotwo major areas: access complications and bile duct injuries. The latter are rare, occurring in approximately 0.5% following laparoscopic cholecystectomy.In the main, biliary injury results from poor dissection and a failure to define the surgical anatomy adequately. STRASSBERG ERCP CLASSIFICATION is used for bile duct injuries

  • Patients who develop jaundicein the postoperative period need urgent investigation. If jaundice is attributed to infection and cholangitis. The first step following resuscitation and administration of appropriate antibiotics is toundertake urgent USG.
  • This will demonstrate whether there is intra- or extrahepatic ductal dilatation. The anatomy may need to be defined by MRCP or ERCP. The latter is undertaken when therapeutic maneuvers are planned, such as the removal of an obstructing stone or the insertion of a stent across a biliary leak.
  • If a fluid collection is present in the subhepatic space, drainage catheters may be required. These can be inserted under radiological control or, if this expertise is not available, at open operation. Small biliary leaks will usually resolve spontaneously, especially if there is no distal obstruction.
  • If the CBD is damaged, the patient should be referred to an appropriate expert for reconstruction.

question_text: What are the type of stones in primary choledocholithiasis?
explanation:
Choledocholithiasis.

  • Common bile duct (CBD) stones may be small or large, single or multiple, and are found in 6% to 12% of patients with stones in the gallbladder. The incidence increases with age.
  • About 20% to 25% of patients above the age of 60 with symptomatic gallstones have stones in the common bile duct as well as in the gallbladder.
  • The vast majority of ductal stones in Western countries are formed within the gallbladder and migrate down the cystic duct into the common bile duct. These are classified as secondary CBD stones, in contrast to the primary CBD stones that form in the bile duct itself.
  • Secondary stones are usually cholesterol stones, whereas primary stones areusually of the brown pigment type.
  • The primary stones are associated with biliary stasis and infection, and they are more commonly seen in Asian populations. Biliary stasis leading to the development of primary CBD stones can be caused by biliary strictures, papillary stenosis, tumours, or other (secondary) stones.

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter 32, Gallbladder and the Extrahepatic Biliary System, pg no: 1406- 1407.

question_text: Which is the most common cause of obstruction in a case of cholangitis?
explanation:
Cholangitis.

  • Cholangitis is one of the main complications of choledochal stones.
  • Acute cholangitis is an ascending bacterial infection associated with partial or complete obstruction of the bile ducts.
  • Hepatic bile is sterile, and bile in the bile ducts is kept sterile by continuous antegrade bile flow and by the presence of antibacterial substances in bile, such as immunoglobulin.
  • Mechanical hindrance to bile flow facilitates ascending bacterial contamination from the bowel.
  • Positive bile cultures are common in the presence of bile duct stones as well as with other causes of obstruction.
  • Biliary bacterial contamination alone does not lead to clinical cholangitis; the combination of both significant bacterial contamination and biliary obstruction is required for its development.
  • Gallstones are the most common cause of obstruction in cholangitis. Other causes include primary sclerosing cholangitis, benign and malignant strictures, parasites,instrumentation of the ducts, and indwelling stents, as well as partially obstructed biliary-enteric anastomoses.
  • The most common organisms cultured from bile in patients with cholangitis include E coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Streptococcus faecalis, Enterobacter, and Bacteroidesfragilis.

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter 32, Gallbladder and the Extrahepatic Biliary System, pg no: 1408.

question_text: How much is the dilatation of the common bile duct on ultrasound examination in a patient of gallstones, jaundice and biliary pain which is suggestive of choledocholithiasis?
explanation:
Diagnosis

  • Ultrasonography is useful for documenting stones in the gallbladder (if still present),as well as determining the size of the common bile duct.
  • As stones in the bile ducts tend to move down to the distal part of the common duct behind the duodenum, bowel gas can preclude their detection on ultrasonography.
  • A dilated common bile duct (>8 mm in diameter) on ultrasonography in a patientwith gallstones, jaundice, and biliary pain is highly suggestive of common bileduct stones. If the presence of bile duct stones is in question, magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) provides excellent anatomic detail and has a sensitivity and specificity of 95% and 89%, respectively, for detectingcholedocholithiasis.
  • Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is highly effective at diagnosing choledocholithiasis and in experienced hands, cannulation of the ampulla of Vater and diagnostic cholangiography are achieved in >90% of cases.
  • However, due to the risks associated with the procedure, it is rarely used as a purely diagnostic modality, rather being reserved for cases in which a therapeutic intervention such as stone extraction or sphincterotomy is planned.
  • Endoscopic ultrasound has been demonstrated to be as good as ERCP for detecting common bile duct stones (sensitivity of 95% and specificity of 97%).
  • However, EUS has fewer therapeutic capabilities and requires endoscopic expertise,making it less desirable except in specific clinical scenarios.
  • Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography (PTC) is rarely needed in patients with common bile duct stones but can be performed for both diagnostic and therapeutic reasons in patients with contraindications to endoscopic or surgical approaches.

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter 32, Gallbladder and the Extrahepatic Biliary System, pg no: 1407- 1408.

question_text: Which among the following is not the boundary of the gastrinoma triangle?
option_a: Junction of cystic duct and common bile duct superiorly
option_b: Junction of first and second part of duodenum inferiorly
option_c: Junction of neck and body of pancreas medially
option_d: Junction of second and third part of duodenum inferiorly
explanation:
Explanation:

The gastrinoma triangle is bounded by the junction of the cystic duct and common bile duct (superiorly), junction of the neck and body of pancreas (medially), and junction of the second and third part of the duodenum (inferiorly).

Gastrinomas

  • Gastrinomas may be either sporadic or associated with the autosomal dominantly inherited multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) type I (in which a parathyroid adenoma is almost invariable).
  • The tumours are most commonly found in the 'gastrinoma triangle' (Passaro) defined by the junction of the cystic duct and common bile duct superiorly, the junction of the second and third parts of the duodenum inferiorly, and the junction of the neck and body of the pancreas medially (essentially the superior mesenteric artery).
  • Many are found in the duodenal loop, presumably arising in the G cells found in Brunner's glands.
  • It is extremely important that the duodenal wall is very carefully inspected endoscopically and also at operation. Very often all that can be detected is a small nodule that projects into the medial wall of the duodenum.

Explanation for the other options:

  • A.The junction of the cystic duct and common bile duct is the superior boundary.
  • C.The junction of the neck and body of the pancreas is the medial boundary.
  • D.The junction of the second and third part of the duodenum is the inferior boundary.

Key Takeaways:

The Gastrinoma Triangle (Passaro's Triangle) is defined by the Cystic Duct/CBD junction (superiorly), the Pancreatic Neck/Body junction (medially), and the second/third part of the duodenum junction (inferiorly).

Level:

Must know

question_text: According to Bismuth Corelette classification, which of the following is type III bile duct cancer?
A 45 years old female patient presented to hospital with obstructive jaundice and CBD stone. Patient has a history of cholecystectomy, done 2 years back'. What is the type of stone seen in the CBD?
explanation:
• CBD stones, or choledocholithiasis, are generally silent, and are seen in up to 10% of patients undergoing biliary imaging.
  • Primary common duct stones arise de novo in the bile duct, and secondary common duct stones pass from the gallbladder into the bile duct.
  • Primary common duct stones are generally brown pigment stones, a combination of precipitated bile pigments and cholesterol. Brown pigment stones are associated with bacterial infections where free bilirubin is formed by hydrolyzing enzymes released by bacteria and then precipitates. Brown pigment stones are more common in Asian populations. Secondary stones are more common in the United States.
  • Retained stones are secondary stones found in bile duct within 2 years of cholecystectomy and occur in 1% to 2% of patients
  • Recurrent stones: formed after 2 yrs of cholecystectomy. They are usually brown pigment stones, they are also called as primary bile duct stone.
  • When symptomatic, common duct stones clinical manifestations range from biliary colic to obstructive jaundice, including darkening of the urine, scleral icterus, and lightening of the stools.
  • Jaundice with choledocholithiasis is more likely to be painful because the onset of obstruction is acute, causing rapid distention of the bile duct and activation of pain fibers.
  • Cholangitis presents with right upper quadrant pain, fever, and jaundice, known as Charcot triad, and may progress to septic shock with mental status changes, and hypotension, known as Reynolds pentad, which is an ominous sign, and mortality approaches 100% without prompt treatment.

KEYTAKEAWAYS:

Missed stone\ retained stone: formed within 2yrs of cholecystectomy

Recurrent stones: formed after 2 yrs of cholecystectomy. They are usually brown pigment stones, they are also called as primary bile duct stone.

question_text: 40 year old female patient underwent cholecystectomy, post OP she is complaining pain abdomen. What test is performed to identify the bile leak
explanation:
• The first step following resuscitation and administration of appropriate antibiotics is to undertake urgent USG.
  • This will demonstrate whether there is intra- or extrahepatic ductal dilatation. The anatomy may need to be defined by MRCP or ERCP. The latter is undertaken when therapeutic manoeuvres are planned, such as the removal of an obstructing stone or the insertion of a stent across a biliary leak.
  • If bile duct injury is suspected - CT scan should be performed which shows Ascites or right upper quadrant collection consistent with bilioma.
  • Immediate PCD (percutaneous drain) placement done to control infection.
  • If a fluid collection is present in the subhepatic space, drainage catheters may be required. These can be inserted under radiological control or, if this expertise is not available, at open operation.
  • Electively ERCP is done to know the site and pattern of injury - for which we have a classification known as Strassberg classification.
  • Small biliary leaks will usually resolve spontaneously, especially if there is no distal obstruction. If the CBD is damaged, the patient should be referred to an appropriate expert for reconstruction.

question_text: What is the normal diameter of the main pancreatic duct?
explanation:
• The main pancreatic duct is usually only 2 to 3 mm in diameter and runs midway between the superior and inferior borders of the pancreas, usually closer to the posterior than to the anterior surface.
  • Pressure inside the pancreatic duct is about twice that in the common bile duct, which is thought to prevent reflux of bile into the pancreatic duct.
  • The main pancreatic duct joins with the common bile duct and empties at the ampulla of Vater or major papilla, which is located on the medial aspect of the second portion of the duodenum.
  • The muscle fibres around the ampulla form the sphincter of Oddi, which controls the flow of pancreatic and biliary secretions into the duodenum.
  • Contraction and relaxation of the sphincter is regulated by complex neural and hormonal factors. When the accessory pancreatic duct or lesser duct drains into the duodenum, a lesser papilla can be identified approximately 2 cm proximal to the ampulla of Vater.

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter, Chapter 33, Pancreas. Pg: 1432.

question_text: Label the given diagram correctly for the complexity of sphincter of Oddi
option_a: 1 - inferior choledochal sphincter, 2 - superior choledochal sphincter, 3 - ampullary sphincter, 4 - pancreatic sphincter
option_b: 1 - superior choledochal sphincter, 2 - inferior choledochal sphincter, 3 - pancreatic sphincter, 4 - ampullary sphincter
option_c: 1 - superior choledochal sphincter, 2 - inferior choledochal sphincter, 3 - ampullary sphincter, 4 - pancreatic sphincter
option_d: 1 - superior choledochal sphincter, 2 - ampullary sphincter, 3 - inferior choledochal sphincter, 4 - pancreatic sphincter
explanation:
Explanation:

The complex muscular arrangement of the Sphincter of Oddi regulates the flow of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum. It consists of multiple sphincters surrounding the terminal Common Bile Duct (CBD), Pancreatic Duct, and the Ampulla of Vater.

The correct labeling sequence for the anatomical components is:

  1. Superior choledochal sphincter (around the upper CBD)
  2. Inferior choledochal sphincter (around the lower CBD)
  3. Ampullary sphincter (around the Ampulla of Vater)
  4. Pancreatic sphincter (around the terminal Pancreatic Duct)

Key Takeaways:

The Sphincter of Oddi is a complex of four distinct smooth muscle segments controlling the outflow of biliary and pancreatic secretions.

Level:

Must know

question_text: Which is the most frequent presenting symptom of periampullary carcinoma of pancreas?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most common presenting feature of periampullary carcinoma of pancreas is jaundice.

This is typically obstructive (painless) jaundice because the tumor (even small) is located near the outlet of the common bile duct, causing early obstruction.

Explanation for the other options:

  • Weight loss is a common symptom but usually develops later than jaundice.
  • Abdominal pain is also common but usually occurs later than jaundice.
  • Gastrointestinal bleeding is uncommon unless the tumor ulcerates into the duodenum.

Key Takeaways:

Painless obstructive Jaundice is the most frequent and earliest presenting symptom of carcinomas arising in the head of the pancreas or periampullary region, due to the immediate obstruction of the distal Common Bile Duct.

Level:

Must know

question_text: What is the sign of the gallbladder seen in this USG?
explanation:
Explanation:

The image on the ultrasound (USG) shows the Phrygian cap sign, which is a common anatomical variation of the gallbladder.

Phyrgian cap

  • A Phrygian cap is a congenital variant of the gallbladder characterised by a fold at the fundus that resembles a cap.
  • It is a benign condition and is typically asymptomatic, with its appearance being consistent with a cap-like structure on ultrasound.
  • It has no pathological significance and does not affect gallbladder function.

Explanation of other options:

Murphy sign (Option B): A clinical finding seen in acute cholecystitis, where pain and inspiratory arrest occur upon palpation of the gallbladder. It is not related to the anatomical variation seen in the USG image.

Claw sign (Option C): Claw sign is a radiological feature seen in intussusception, not related to the gallbladder.

Omega sign (Option D): A radiological finding observed in choledochal cysts, where the dilated common bile duct forms an "omega" or "figure-of-8" shape. It does not relate to the anomaly shown in the USG image.

question_text: What is the most common site of gastrinoma in MEN 1 syndrome?
explanation:
Gastrinoma

Definition

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (ZES) is a condition that includes: (i) fulminating ulcer diathesis in the stomach, duodenum or atypical sites; (ii) recurrent ulceration despite 'adequate' therapy; and (iii) non-β islet cell tumors of the pancreas (gastrinoma).

Incidence

This is a rare disease affecting between 0.5 and 4 in a million. Approximately 0.1% of patients with duodenal ulcers have evidence of ZES. Up to 20-25% of ZES is associated with MEN.

Pathology

In sporadic disease the tumors are mostly located in the duodenum (60-80%) and are small (<5 mm) and multiple. In MEN 1, all tumors are in the duodenum. The vast majority (approximately 90%) occur within the 'gastrinoma triangle', an area bounded by the junction of the neck and body of the pancreas medially, the junction of the second and third parts of the duodenum inferiorly and the junction of the cystic and common bile ducts superiorly .

question_text: Which among the following is not a symptom of acute cholecystitis?
explanation:
Clinical Manifestations

    • About 80% of patients with acute cholecystitis give a history compatible with chronic cholecystitis.
    • Acute cholecystitis often begins as an attack of biliary colic with relapsing and remitting pain in the right upper quadrant or epigastrium that may radiate to the right back or interscapular area.
    • In contrast to biliary colic, the pain of acute cholecystitis does not subside. It is unremitting, may persist for several days, and is usually more severe than the pain associated with uncomplicated gallstone disease.
    • The patient is often febrile, complains of anorexia, nausea, and vomiting, and may be reluctant to move as the inflammatory process creates focal peritonitis.
    • On physical examination, tenderness and guarding are usually present in the right upper quadrant.
    • A mass, the gallbladder and adherent omentum, is occasionally palpable; however, guarding may prevent identification of this.
    • Murphy's sign, an inspiratory arrest with deep palpation in the right subcostal area, is characteristic of acute cholecystitis.
    • Laboratory evaluation commonly reveals a mild to moderate leukocytosis (12,000-15,000 cells/mm3). However, a normal WBC does not rule out the diagnosis. An unusually high WBC count (>20,000 cells/mm3) suggests a complicated form of cholecystitis such as gangrenous cholecystitis, perforation, or associated cholangitis.
    • In uncomplicated acute cholecystitis, serum liver chemistries are usually normal, but a mild elevation of serum bilirubin (<4 mg/mL) may be present along with mild elevation of alkaline phosphatase, transaminases, and amylase.
    • Severe jaundice is suggestive of obstruction of the bile ducts. This can be a result of common bile duct stones or severe pericholecystic inflammation secondary to impaction of a stone in the infundibulum of the gallbladder that mechanically obstructs the bile duct, known as Mirizzi's syndrome.
    • In elderly patients and in those with diabetes mellitus, acute cholecystitis may have a subtle presentation resulting in a delay in diagnosis.
    • The differential diagnosis for acute cholecystitis includes but is not limited to pepticulcer disease, pancreatitis, appendicitis, hepatitis, perihepatitis (Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome), myocardial ischemia, pneumonia, pleuritis, and herpes zoster involving the intercostal nerve.

Reference: Schwartz's Principles of Surgery 11th edition, Chapter 32, Gallbladder and the Extrahepatic Biliary System, pg no: 1405-1406.

question_text: Which artery branches and forms the cystic artery?
explanation:
• The cystic artery, a branch of the right hepatic artery, usually arises behind the common hepatic duct.
  • Occasionally, an accessory cystic artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery. In 15% of cases the right hepatic artery and/ or the cystic artery crosses in front of the common hepatic duct and the cystic duct.
  • Calot's triangle, or the hepatobiliary triangle, was initially described by Calot as the space bordered by the cystic duct inferiorly, the common hepatic duct medially and the superior border of the cystic artery.
  • This has been modified in contemporary literature to be the area bound superiorly by the inferior surface of the liver, laterally by the cystic duct and the medial border of the gallbladder and medially by the common hepatic duct.
  • It is an important surgical landmark as the cystic artery usually can be found within its boundaries and should be identified by surgeons performing a cholecystectomy to avoid damage to the extrahepatic biliary system.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 71, Gallbladder and bile ducts Pg no: 1233.

question_text: A 70-year-old woman comes for a routine follow-up, and her liver ultrasound findings are shown below. She is currently asymptomatic but reports a past history of mild right hypochondriac pain that was relieved with analgesics. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The USG shows a thickened gallbladder wall with acoustic shadowing, which, along with the patient's history of mild right hypochondriac pain relieved by analgesics, is indicative of gallbladder stones.

Gallstones

  • Most common biliary pathology.
  • Gallstones can be of three types: Cholesterol, pigment and mixed stones.
    • Cholesterol stones are formed by precipiation of cholestrol and calcium.
    • Pigment stones result from hemolytic conditions or secondary to infections like Clonorchis sinensis and Ascaris lumbricoides.
  • Four major contributors to gall stone formation
    • Supersaturation of secreted bile
    • Concentration of bile in the gallbladder
    • Crystal nucleation
    • Gallbladder dysmotility.

Clinical features

Courvoisier's law

  • A palpable, non-tender gallbladder in association with jaundice is unlikely to be caused by gallstones; more commonly indicates distal common bile duct obstruction, typically due to a periampullary malignancy.

Diagnosis

  • LFT may be abnormal, in cases of biledcut obstruction; MRCP should be then done to rule out choledocholithiasis.
  • USG is the first choice of investigations; findings include
    • Echogenic foci within gallbladder lumen with posterior acoustic shadowing
    • Mobile with patient position change
    • Thickened gallbladder wall if inflammation is present

Treatment:

Asymptomatic gallstones

  • Donot ned intervention
  • Prophylactic cholecystectomy is indicated in asymptomatic cases in follwoing conditions:
    • Large gallstone > 3cm
    • Choledocholithiasis
    • Chronic hemolytic disease
    • Gallbladder polyps > 1cm in diameter
    • Suspicion or risk of malgnancy
    • Porcelain gallbladder

Symptomatic gallstones

  • Cholecystectomy is the treatement of choice.

Explanation of other options:

Amoebic liver abscess (Option B): Amoebic liver abscess presents with fever, right upper quadrant pain, and liver enlargement. It is often seen in patients with a history of amoebic dysentery. The USG would show a hypoechoic mass in the liver, which is not consistent with the findings in this case.

Hydatid cyst (Option C): Hydatid cyst caused by Echinococcus tapeworm infection and is usually found in the liver. The USG appearance of a hydatid cyst typically shows water-lily signs, multilocular cysts, or honeycomb patterns, which is not seen here. Symptoms include abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and jaundice.

Acute cholecystitis (Option D): Acute cholecystitis presents with severe right upper quadrant pain, fever, and Murphy's sign (pain on palpation of the right upper quadrant). It generally presents more acutely and is associated with inflammation and infection, leading to more severe symptoms.

question_text: Which condition is most likely based on image findings?
explanation:
Explanation :

The MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) image shown reveals the dilation of the common bile duct (CBD) along with filling defects, representing gallstones within the duct, referred to as choledocholithiasis.

  • Filling defectson MRCP indicate an obstruction in the bile ducts, commonly caused by gallstones (choledocholithiasis) or other blockages. These defects appear as areas where the bile duct does not fill properly or has reduced signal intensity.
  • Symptoms of choledocholithiasistypically include jaundice, abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.
  • Treatmentoften involves endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) with sphincterotomy and stone extraction.

Explanation of other options:

Stricture (Option A): A bile duct stricture appears as a narrowing or constriction of the bile duct caused by inflammation, scarring, or tumours obstructing the duct. While it can mimic choledocholithiasis on imaging, it does not show the characteristic filling defects seen in choledocholithiasis.

Cholecystitis (Option C): Cholecystitis is the inflammation of the gallbladder, usually due to gallstones blocking the cystic duct. MRCP typically shows gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and gallstones in the gallbladder, but not changes in the bile ducts, so it wouldn't cause CBD dilation or filling defects.

Cholangiocarcinoma (Option D): Cholangiocarcinoma is a malignant tumour of the bile duct epithelium. On MRCP, it can cause bile duct dilation and strictures and may also show intraductal masses or nodules. However, the pattern of obstruction caused by a tumour differs from the filling defects seen with choledocholithiasis, as gallstones, not a mass, cause these defects.

question_text: Identify the type of bile duct injury shown in the image based on the Strasberg classification.
explanation:
Explanation:

The bile duct injury shown in the image is consistent with type A bile duct injury according to the Strasberg classification.

  • The majority of bile duct injuries occur during cholecystectomy, with factors such as anatomical variations, porta hepatis inflammation, poor exposure, limited surgical skill, and aggressive hemostasis contributing to the risk.
  • Misidentification of anatomy, for example, cystic duct being mistaken for the common hepatic duct, is a common cause.
  • Inadequate traction and failure to achieve the critical view of safety increase the risk
  • Clinically, injuries manifest as bile leakage or stricture, with leakage often leading to peritonitis and presenting earlier than stricture.
  • Patients may also develop fever, abdominal pain, and jaundice.
  • The original analysis of biliary reconstruction was based on the Bismuth classification and has been modified by Strasberg. Classification of bile duct injuries is determined by location and helps guide later surgical reconstruction, and is given below.

question_text: What is the most common complication of ERCP?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Pancreatitis is the most frequent complication of Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), occurring in approximately 4-5% of cases.
  • In most patients, it is mild and self-limiting, but in some it may progress to severe necrotizing pancreatitis with significant morbidity and mortality.
  • Pathogenesis involves mechanical, chemical, hydrostatic, enzymatic, and microbiological injury to the pancreas during ERCP.
  • Risk is higher in younger patients, those with sphincter of Oddi dysfunction, and in difficult cannulation.
  • Preventive strategies include rectal indomethacin or diclofenac administered around the time of the procedure, which has been shown to reduce the incidence of post-ERCP pancreatitis.

Explanation of Other Options:

Duodenal perforation (Option A): A serious but less common complication. Occurs due to instrumentation or sphincterotomy. Requires immediate recognition.

Cholangitis (Option B): Important but less frequent complication than pancreatitis. Occurs especially if bile duct drainage is incomplete.

Hemorrhage (Option C): Usually seen post-sphincterotomy. Less common than pancreatitis.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: Identify the arrow-marked structure shown in the image:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The right hepatic artery, as a major branch of the common hepatic artery, is the structure shown in the image and plays a key role in the vascular anatomy within Calot's triangle.
  • Calot's triangle, or the hepatobiliary triangle, was initially described by Calot as the space bordered by the cystic duct inferiorly, the common hepatic duct medially and the superior border of the cystic artery.
  • This has been modified in contemporary literature as the area bound superiorly by the inferior surface of the liver, laterally by the cystic duct and the medial border of the gallbladder and medially by the common hepatic duct ('hepatocystic triangle').
  • It is an important surgical landmark as the cystic artery usually can be found within its boundaries. The cystic lymph node often lies superficial to the cystic artery and acts as a landmark to locate this artery in difficult cases. The cystic artery, a branch of the right hepatic artery, usually arises behind the common hepatic duct

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice B: Left hepatic artery

  • The left hepatic artery supplies the left lobe of the liver but does not pass through Calot's triangle. It does not match the structure in the image.

Choice C: Cystic artery

  • The cystic artery, although located in Calot's triangle, is a branch of the right hepatic artery. The right hepatic artery is the larger structure passing through the triangle, making it the structure marked in the image.

Choice D: Cystic duct

  • The cystic duct connects the gallbladder to the common bile duct but is not a blood vessel. It is located medially in Calot's triangle and is not likely to be the structure indicated by the arrow.

Key Takeaway

  • The right hepatic artery, as a major branch of the common hepatic artery, is the structure shown in the image and plays a key role in the vascular anatomy within Calot's triangle.

question_text: A 30-year-old patient with known peptic ulcer disease presents with persistent abdominal pain despite prolonged medical therapy. Endoscopy reveals ulcers in the jejunum and ileum. His gastric pH is <2, and after stopping PPIs, his serum gastrin level is 10× above normal. What is the most likely lesion, and what are the boundaries of the triangle where it is commonly found?
option_a: Insulinoma; triangle formed formed by only common bile duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
option_b: Insulinoma; triangle formed by cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
option_c: Gastrinoma; triangle formed by cystic duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
option_d: Gastrinoma; triangle formed by only common bile duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas
explanation:
Explanation:

This patient's features are

  • Multiple, recurrent peptic ulcers,
  • Ulcers distal to the duodenal bulb (jejunum/ileum),
  • Gastric pH < 2, and
  • Markedly elevated fasting gastrin levels (>1000 pg/mL)
    which are classic findings of a gastrinoma causing Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (ZES).

Gastrinomas are tumours that secrete excess gastrin, commonly leading to Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, which causes multiple peptic ulcers due to high gastric acid production.

The gastrinoma triangle refers to a specific anatomical region in the pancreas where gastrinomas are most commonly located. (Pissaros triangle) this triangle is bordered by:

  • Junction between cystic duct and CBD (Option D ruled out)
  • Junction of the 2nd and 3rd parts of the duodenum (D2-D3 junction)
  • Junction between the head and neck of the pancreas

Explanation of Other Options:

Insulinoma; triangle formed formed by only common bile duct, junction of D2-D3, neck and body of pancreas (Option A):

  • Insulinoma arises from β-cells of pancreas → causes hypoglycemia, not ulcers.
  • Clinical triad (Whipple's triad): hypoglycemia, neuroglycopenic symptoms, relief after glucose. (Option B ruled out)
  • Located anywhere in pancreas, not confined to Passaro's triangle.

question_text:
A patient presented to emergency department with abdominal pain, fever, and jaundice associated with chills and rigours. Cholangitis was suspected in the patient. Which of the following are components of reynauld's pentad?
1. Jaundice
2. Melena
3. hypotension
4. Altered mentation
5. hematemesis
6. Fever
explanation:
CHARCOT's TRIAD; has 10% mortality if not treated

  1. Fever
  2. Jaundice
  3. Right upper quadrant pain

REYNAULD's PENTAD: has 50% mortality if not treated

  1. Fever
  2. Jaundice
  3. Right upper quadrant pain
  4. Septic shock → hypotension
  5. Altered mentation
  • The diagnosis is confirmed by the finding of dilated bile ducts on ultrasonography, an obstructive picture of liver function tests and organisms identified from blood cultures.
  • Delay in appropriate treatment may result in multi-organ failure secondary to sepsis and broad-spectrum antibiotics, rehydration, and endoscopic or percutaneous transhepatic drainage are urgently required.
  • Biliary stone disease is a common predisposing factor although strictures, pancreatitis, pancreatic tumours and parasites may also be responsible.
  • If an obstructive cause is identifed it must be urgently treated by ERCP, sphincterotomy (± stent) or percutaneous drainage.

question_text: A 55-year-old chronic alcoholic presents with unintentional weight loss. Laboratory findings reveal serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) of 240 IU/L, alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) of 600 ng/ml, and normal AST and ALT levels. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Markedly elevated AFP with raised ALP and normal transaminases in a chronic alcoholic suggests hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

  • HCC is a primary liver malignancy, especially common in patients with chronic liver disease such as alcoholism.
  • A markedly elevated alpha-fetoprotein (AFP >400-500 ng/ml) is highly suggestive of HCC.
  • The patient's normal AST/ALT with elevated ALP indicates a hepatobiliary malignancy rather than inflammatory liver disease.
  • Tumor markers in HCC:
    • AFP >20 ng/ml is seen in ~70% of cases.
    • PIVKA-II (Protein Induced by Vitamin K Absence or Antagonism-II) may also be elevated.
  • Diagnosis:
    • Screening: Ultrasound (USG) for high-risk individuals.
    • Definitive imaging: Triple-phase CT scan is preferred.
      • Arterial phase: HCC shows arterial hyperenhancement.
      • Portal venous phase: Washout begins.
      • Delayed phase: Lesion appears hypodense due to venous washout - a classic feature of HCC.
  • Risk factors for HCC:
    • Cirrhosis, chronic alcohol use, HBV/HCV infections, NAFLD, aflatoxin exposure, anabolic steroids, and several genetic/metabolic disorders (e.g., Wilson's disease, α1-antitrypsin deficiency, porphyria cutanea tarda).

Explanation of other options:

Hepatic adenoma (Option A): Typically occurs in young women using oral contraceptives and does not elevate AFP.

Cholangiocarcinoma (Option B): May raise ALP but not AFP; associated with bile duct origin.

Alcoholic hepatitis (Option D): Usually shows elevated AST > ALT, not normal transaminases or elevated AFP.

question_text: What is the optimal management approach for a patient presenting with fever and abdominal pain five days after experiencing a common bile duct injury resulting in a leak?
explanation:
Explanation:

A patient presenting with fever and pain days after surgery suggests a biloma (bile collection) and bile peritonitis due to a bile leak. The optimal, least invasive, first-line management is ERCP with stenting.

This procedure:

  1. Confirms the site and size of the leak.
  2. Decompresses the biliary tree by sphincterotomy.
  3. Places a stent across the leak, diverting bile flow into the duodenum and allowing the defect to heal spontaneously.

Management of Post-Op Diagnosed Bile Duct Injury

Steps for management:

  • Step 1: Initiate IV antibiotics to control infection.
  • Step 2: Drain biloma using:
    • USG or CT guided percutaneous aspiration
    • Insertion of drain or pigtail
  • Step 3: Perform MRCP (Magnetic Resonance Cholangiopancreatography) for complete cholangiography.
  • Step 4: Consider definitive interventions such as:
    • ERCP (Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography) with stenting
    • Hepatico-jejunostomy

Explanation of other options:

Ultrasound-guided aspiration (Option A): This is an adjunctive procedure to drain an established biloma but does not treat the underlying leak in the bile duct.

Re-exploration and hepaticojejunostomy, and Re-exploration and primary repair (Options C and D): Major reconstructive surgery is reserved for cases where endoscopic management has failed, for complete transections, or for injuries involving significant tissue loss. It is not the first step in a stable patient with a leak.

Key Takeaways:

  • ERCP with stenting is the first-line intervention for a postoperative bile leak.
  • Surgery is reserved for failures of endoscopic management or major injuries.

question_text: A baby was brought with complaints of discharge from the umbilicus of fecal matter. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Discharge of fecal matter from the umbilicus in a neonate indicates a patent vitellointestinal (omphalomesenteric) duct.

  • The vitellointestinal duct (also called the omphalomesenteric duct) is an embryological connection between the yolk sac and the midgut.
  • Normally, it is obliterated by the 7th week of gestation.
  • If it remains patent, it may form a complete fistulous tract from the ileum to the umbilicus, resulting in fecal or meconium discharge from the umbilicus, especially in neonates.
  • Key features:
    • Presentation: Meconium or fecal discharge from umbilicus shortly after birth.
    • Diagnosis: Clinical + confirmation with contrast fistulography or USG.
    • Complication: Risk of volvulus due to fixation of bowel to umbilicus.
    • Management: Surgical excision of the tract and closure of bowel wall.

Explanation of other options:

Umbilical cyst (Option B): A fluid-filled swelling near the umbilicus, often asymptomatic or presenting with clear or mucoid discharge, not fecal material.

Urachal sinus (Option C): A remnant of the urachus (fetal connection between bladder and umbilicus), causing urine-like or serous discharge, not fecal matter.

Urachus (Option D): General term for the embryonic canal between bladder and umbilicus. Persistence may result in urachal anomalies, such as fistula or cyst, but does not involve fecal discharge.

question_text: Identify the surgical procedure shown in the given image.
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts a Whipple's procedure, also known as pancreaticoduodenectomy. It is the standard surgical treatment for resectable pancreatic head carcinoma. The operation involves removal of the pancreatic head, duodenum, a portion of the bile duct, gallbladder, and sometimes part of the stomach. Reconstruction includes three anastomoses: pancreaticojejunostomy, hepaticojejunostomy, and gastrojejunostomy. It is performed only in cases where the tumor is localized without metastasis.

Explanation of other options:

Beger's procedure (Option A): Involves resection of the pancreatic head but preserves the duodenum, bile duct, and stomach.

Frey's procedure (Option C): Includes coring out part of the pancreatic head with longitudinal pancreaticojejunostomy; duodenum is preserved.

Pancreatic division (Option D): Merely divides the pancreas and is not equivalent to the complex resection shown in the image.

Key Takeaways:

  • Whipple's procedure is the definitive surgery for carcinoma of the head of the pancreas.
  • Involves removal of multiple structures and requires three reconstructive anastomoses.
  • Order of anastomoses: pancreaticojejunostomy → hepaticojejunostomy → gastrojejunostomy.

question_text: Which artery is divided in mobilizing the fundus in fundoplication surgery?
explanation:
LAPAROSCOPIC FUNDOPLICATION

  • Five cannulas are inserted in the upper abdomen.
  • The cardia and lower oesophagus are separated from the diaphragmatic hiatus. An appropriate length of oesophagus is mobilised in the mediastinum.

question_text: A young patient in the first decade of life presents with grade II splenic injury with no active bleeding. What is the management?
explanation:
Explanation:

For grade II splenic injury in a hemodynamically stable patient with no active bleeding, non-operative (conservative) management is the treatment of choice. This approach allows preservation of splenic function, thereby avoiding long-term risks like OPSI (Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection).

  • Conservative management includes:
  • ICU admission and close hemodynamic monitoring.
  • Serial clinical and radiological assessment.
  • Restriction of activity until healing.
  • Blood transfusion if required.

AAST Spleen Injury Scale (simplified):

  • Grade I: Subcapsular hematoma <10% or laceration <1 cm.
  • Grade II: Hematoma 10-50%, laceration 1-3 cm (no major vessels).
  • Grade III: Hematoma >50% or >5 cm, laceration >3 cm.
  • Grade IV: Involvement of segmental/hilar vessels with >25% devascularisation.
  • Grade V: Shattered spleen or hilar vascular injury with complete devascularisation.

Explanation of Other Options:

Splenectomy (Option A): Reserved for hemodynamically unstable patients or those with Grade IV-V injuries where bleeding cannot be controlled. Not indicated in a stable child with Grade II injury.

Splenorrhaphy (Option B): Suture repair or partial resection can be done in selected higher-grade injuries when spleen preservation is attempted surgically. Not required for low-grade injuries managed conservatively.

Embolization (Option C): Indicated in active bleeding or contrast blush on CT angiography in hemodynamically stable patients to avoid splenectomy. Not needed in this case as no bleeding is present.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Hemodynamically stable, low-grade splenic injuries (Grade I-II) → Conservative management.
  • High-grade or actively bleeding injuries → Angioembolization or Surgery.
  • Unstable patients → Splenectomy (life > organ).
  • Spleen preservation is crucial in children due to the risk of OPSI.

Management: Management of blunt trauma focuses on vigorous resuscitation.

  • For hemodynamically stable patients with minor splenic injuries, non-operative management (NOM) (conservative) is the preferred approach.
  • Splenectomy is recommended for severe injuries where bleeding control is prioritized over spleen preservation.
  • In cases with active bleeding, splenic angiography and embolization can be used to avoid splenectomy, but this should not delay laparotomy in hemodynamically unstable patients.

question_text: A 32-year-old female with a history of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is scheduled for splenectomy. The surgeon intends to remove all splenic tissue, including any accessory spleen that maybe present. Which of the following is the most common location to search for an accessory spleen during the procedure?
explanation:
Explanation:

Splenunculi are single or multiple accessory spleens that are found in approximately 10-30% of the population. They are located near the hilum of the spleen in 50% of cases and are related to the splenic vessels, or behind the tail of the pancreas in 30%. The remainder are located in the mesocolon, greater omentum or the splenic ligaments. Their significance lies in the fact that failure to identify and remove these at the time of splenectomy may give rise to persistent disease.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Under the left diaphragm

  • Although splenic tissue can rarely be found in ectopic locations, the area under the left diaphragm is not a common site for accessory spleens.

Choice C: Gastrosplenic ligament

  • The gastrosplenic ligament may occasionally contain an accessory spleen, but it is not the most frequent site-it accounts for significantly fewer cases compared to the splenic hilum.

Choice D: Omentum

  • Accessory spleens can be found in the greater omentum, but this location is relatively rare. It is considered only if no accessory spleen is found in the more common areas.

Key Takeaway

  • The splenic hilum is the most common location for an accessory spleen, and it must be carefully examined during splenectomy to prevent persistent or recurrent disease, especially in conditions like ITP.

question_text: Which among the following is not the function of spleen?
explanation:
Splenic function can be summarized into hematopoietic, reservoir, filtration, and immunity.

Hematopoietic

  • During fetal development between 3 to 5 weeks of fetal life, the spleen has important hematopoietic functions, which include white and red blood cell (RBC) production.
  • This production is assumed by the bone marrow during the fifth month of gestation, and under normal conditions, the spleen has no significant hematopoietic function beyond this point.
  • However, in certain pathologic conditions such as myelodysplastic syndrome, the spleen is one of the main organs involved in extramedullary erythropoiesis.

Reservoir

  • The spleen functions as a reservoir, where it pools in platelets. Normally one third of the platelets are pooled within the spleen.
  • Thus, patients with splenomegaly are able to sequestrate large volume of platelets (up to 80%) with resultant thrombocytopenia.
  • Due to that, after splenectomy, patients usually present with thrombocytosis which could be one of the factors that play a role in increasing thrombotic complications after splenectomy.

Filtration

  • The splenic filtration process consists of two methods of blood flow, the closed and open systems.
  • In the closed system, blood flows directly from arteries to veins. In the open system, the blood flows through the arterioles and then trickles through a sieve-like parenchyma made up of reticuloendothelial cells into the splenic sinuses before draining into the venous system.
  • The cellular elements are directed toward these reticuloendothelial cells, in which cellular cleansing processes take place. These include removal of senescent cells, cellular inclusions (e.g., RBC nucleoli), and parasites and the sequestration of RBCs (for maturation) and platelets (reservoir).
  • The plasma is directed to the lymphoid tissue, where soluble antigens stimulate the production of antibodies. RBC morphology, and thus RBC function, is maintained by splenic filtration. Normal RBCs are biconcave and deform easily. This plasticity allows passage through the microvasculature and optimizes the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
  • Imperfect RBCs with inclusions such as nucleoli, Howell-Jolly bodies (nuclear remnant), Heinz bodies (denatured hemoglobin), Pappenheimer bodies (iron granules), acanthocytes (spur cells), codocytes (target cells), and stippling cause these RBCs to undergo cleansing in the spleen.
  • The presence of Howell-Jolly bodies on a peripheral blood smear is one of the most characteristic finding for asplenia; surgical or medical (hemoglobinopathies). Howell-Jolly bodies are strongly basophilic inclusion bodies found in the cytoplasm of RBCs and represent nuclei remnants that were unable to be cleared by a functioning spleen.
  • Aged RBCs with decreased plasticity (>120 days) become trapped and destroyed in the spleen.
  • Abnormal erythrocytes that result from hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell anemia, hereditary spherocytosis, thalassemia, or pyruvate kinase deficiency (PKD) are also trapped and destroyed by the spleen.
  • The overall effect is worsening anemia, splenomegaly, and sometimes autoinfarction of the spleen. Similarly, the spleen is involved in platelet destruction in immune thrombocytopenia (ITP), formerly known as idiopathic thrombocytopenia purpura.

Immunity

  • It functions by antibody synthesis and phagocytosis.
  • Asplenic patients have been found to express subnormal immunoglobulin M levels, and their peripheral blood mononuclear cells exhibit a suppressed immunoglobulin response.
  • Other factors involved in the immune response are opsonins, such as properdin and tuftsin. Opsonins, produced in the spleen, exhibit reduced serum levels after splenectomy.
  • Properdin, a globulin protein also known as factor P, initiates the alternate pathway of complement activation; this increases the destruction of bacteria and abnormal cells.
  • Tuftsin, a tetrapeptide, enhances the phagocytic activity of mononuclear phagocytes and polymorphonuclear leukocytes.
  • Absence of a circulating mediator appears to result in suppressed neutrophil function. The spleen also plays a key role in cleaving tuftsin from the heavy chain of immunoglobulin G; thus, circulating levels of tuftsin are subnormal in asplenic patients.
  • Additionally, splenic filtration may be particularly important for removal of microorganisms for which the host does not have a specific antibody.
  • The immune functions of the spleen become evident after splenectomy, when patients are noted to be at risk for specific infections related to encapsulated bacteria Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenza, and Neisseria meningitidis.
  • Asplenia and hyposplenism could be a result of surgical absence of spleen or lack of functioning of an anatomically present spleen. The most serious sequela is overwhelming postsplenectomy infection (OPSI).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 70, The Spleen, Pg: 1221.

question_text: Which artery gives the arterial blood supply to the spleen?
explanation:
• The splenic artery, a branch of the celiac trunk together with its branches of the short gastric arteries provide the arterial blood supply of the spleen.
  • The splenic artery is a tortuous vessel that gives off multiple branches (16-18 branches) to the pancreas as it travels along its posterior aspect. Understanding the variant anatomy of the splenic artery helps surgical planning to avoid potential intraoperative bleeding.
  • There are two common variations of the splenic artery with regards to the relation between the splenic artery branches and the hilum.
  • The magistral type, which branches into terminal and polar arteries near the hilum of the spleen; and the distributed type, which, as the name implies, gives off its branches early and distant from the hilum.
  • The magistral type of splenic arterial anatomy occurs in 30% of individuals compared with the distributed type (70%).
  • The splenic artery branches to approximately five to six polar arteries and six short gastric arteries.
  • The superior polar artery which sometimes communicates with the short gastric arteries, the superior, middle, and inferior terminal arteries, and an inferior polar artery.
  • Knowing these variable distributions are necessary in performing resections, especially a spleen-preserving distal pancreatectomy, in an effort to preserve splenic function.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 70, The Spleen, Pg: 1220.

question_text: Which among the following ligaments is attached on the diaphragmatic surface of the spleen?
explanation:
• Spleen is an intraperitoneal organ and is suspended in the peritoneal cavity by multiple peritoneal reflections misreferred to as 'ligaments'; at the diaphragmatic surface is the splenophrenic ligament, the visceral surface, and the gastrosplenic, splenorenal, and splenocolic ligaments.
  • In patients without portal hypertension, the splenophrenic and splenocolic ligaments are relatively avascular.
  • The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric vessels in its superior aspect and the left gastroepiploic in its inferior aspect.
  • The splenorenal ligament houses the splenic artery and vein as well as the tail of the pancreas. The tail of the pancreas abuts the splenic hilum in 30% of individuals and is within 1 cm of the hilum in 70% of cases, thus it is important to ligate the splenic vessels within 1 cm from the splenic hilum to avoid injury to the tail of the pancreas.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 70, The Spleen, Pg: 1220.

question_text: A 40-year-old man with a known case of hypertension presented with multiple episodes of hematuria and loin pain. His elder brother passed away due to a stroke at the age of 40. The CT abdomen is shown below. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The combination of loin pain, hematuria, hypertension, and family history of early stroke strongly indicates autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD).
  • The CT findings of multiple bilateral renal cysts confirm the diagnosis.
  • Stroke in the brother suggests possible intracranial berry aneurysm, a known extrarenal complication of ADPKD.

Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (ADPKD):

  • Inheritance: Autosomal dominant; mutations in PKD1 (chromosome 16) or PKD2 (chromosome 4).
  • Pathogenesis: Abnormal polycystin protein → cyst formation → renal enlargement and progressive loss of function.
  • Intrarenal features:
    • Hypertension (most common presenting feature).
    • Hematuria, polyuria, nocturia.
    • Loin pain due to hemorrhage, infection, or stones.
    • Progressive renal failure (usually by 5th-6th decade).
  • Extrarenal features:
    • Polycystic liver disease (most common extrarenal).
    • Cysts in pancreas, spleen, ovaries.
    • Berry aneurysms → subarachnoid hemorrhage, stroke.
    • Mitral valve prolapse, aortic regurgitation.
  • Investigations:
    • CECT: investigation of choice.
    • Ultrasound: screening and diagnosis.
    • IVP: shows spider leg deformity, bell-shaped pelvis, "Swiss cheese" appearance.
    • Renal function tests: elevated urea and creatinine.
  • Management:
    • Control hypertension (ACE inhibitors/ARBs).
    • Supportive: treat infections, nephrolithiasis.
    • Drainage or deroofing of symptomatic cysts.
    • Definitive: renal transplantation once end-stage renal disease develops.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Renal cell carcinoma (Option A): Can cause hematuria and loin pain, but typically appears as a solid renal mass rather than multiple bilateral cysts.

Tuberculosis of the kidney (Option C): Causes hematuria, dysuria, and flank pain with sterile pyuria. CT may show calcifications or contracted kidneys ("putty kidney"), not diffuse cysts.

Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (Option D): Presents in infancy/childhood with hepatic fibrosis and severe renal failure, not in adulthood with preserved renal function until later decades.

Key Takeaway:

ADPKD presents with hypertension, hematuria, loin pain, and a positive family history. CT imaging reveals multiple bilateral cysts, and extrarenal complications (like berry aneurysm leading to stroke) are common. Definitive treatment is renal transplantation.

question_text: A 38-year-old man was brought to the emergency department after sustaining an RTA and injury to the lower chest. On presentation, the patient is stable, and vitals are normal. Chest radiography showed clear lung fields. What is the next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

In cases of Road Traffic Accidents (RTA) where the patient is hemodynamically stable, vital signs are within normal limits, and chest X-ray shows clear lung fields, the most appropriate next step is to perform an extended Focused Assessment with Sonography in Trauma (eFAST).

eFAST (Extended Focused Assessment with Sonography for Trauma)

  • Rapid bedside ultrasound for trauma assessment.
  • Detects life-threatening conditions such as hemoperitoneum, hemothorax, pneumothorax, and pericardial effusion.
  • Used to guide immediate management alongside resuscitation. 

FAST vs. eFAST

Advantages of eFAST:

  • Quick and repeatable.
  • Performed simultaneously with resuscitation.
  • High specificity for detecting significant intraperitoneal bleeding.

Limitations:

  • Operator dependent.
  • Reduced accuracy in obese patients or with bowel gas interference.
  • Low sensitivity (≈29-35%) for hollow viscus or solid organ injuries without hemoperitoneum.
  • Cannot reliably exclude penetrating trauma.
  • Limited in evaluating retroperitoneal injuries.
  • Often needs repeat scans or confirmatory imaging (CT/MRI).

Flow of eFAST Assessment:

  1. Pericardial View → Check for pericardial effusion/tamponade.
  2. Pleural Views → Identify hemothorax or pneumothorax.
  3. Right Upper Quadrant (RUQ) → Detects free fluid near liver/kidney.
  4. Left Upper Quadrant (LUQ) → Detects free fluid near spleen/kidney.
  5. Pelvic View → Detects fluid in pouch of Douglas/rectovesical pouch.

Explanation of Other Options:

Tube thoracostomy (Option B) is primarily used in the management of pneumothorax or hemothorax. In this case, as chest X-ray findings reveal clear lung fields, this intervention is not necessary.

Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) of the chest (Option C) and abdomen (Option D):

  • They are more advanced diagnostic options, but they are relatively invasive.
  • Since the patient remains stable and chest radiography is unremarkable, the most suitable initial test is eFAST.
  • This bedside, non-invasive ultrasound technique rapidly identifies intraperitoneal or retroperitoneal bleeding as well as fluid in the pericardial or pleural spaces.
  • It should be employed before progressing to more detailed imaging studies, if required.

question_text: What is the margin of resection in a case of gastric cancer?
explanation:
• Total gastrectomy is best performed through a long upper midline incision.
  • The stomach is removed en bloc, including the tissues of the entire greater omentum and lesser omentum.
  • In commencing the operation, the transverse colon is completely separated from the greater omentum. The dissection may then be commenced proximally or, more usually, distally.
  • The subpyloric nodes are dissected and the first part of the duodenum is divided, usually with a surgical stapler.
  • The hepatic nodes are dissected down to clear the hepatic artery; this dissection also includes the suprapyloric nodes. The right gastric artery is taken on the hepatic artery. The lymph node dissection is continued to the origin of the left gastric artery, which is divided flush with its origin. The dissection is continued along the splenic artery, taking all of the nodes at the superior aspect of the pancreas and accessible nodes in the splenic hilum. Separation of the stomach from the spleen, if this organ is not going to be removed, is carried out and this then allows access to the nodal tissues around the upper stomach and oesophagogastric junction. The oesophagus can then be divided at an appropriate point using a combination of stay sutures and a soft non-crushing clamp, usually of the right-angled variety.
  • It is important that the resection margins are well clear of the tumour (>5 cm). Involvement of either proximal or distal resection margin carries an appalling prognosis and, if in doubt, frozen section should be performed.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 67, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1175

Prostate Cancer:

Explanation of Other Options:

question_text: All of the following statements are incorrect regarding CXR in thoracic injury except

question_text: During a splenectomy, while the surgeon is separating the spleen from the stomach, significant bleeding occurs. Which artery is the most common source of such bleeding?
explanation:
Explanation:

The short gastric arteries are small but vital branches of the splenic artery that traverse the gastrosplenic ligament to supply the fundus and upper part of the greater curvature of the stomach.

During splenectomy, when the gastrosplenic ligament is divided to free the spleen from the stomach, these short gastric vessels are at risk of tearing, leading to profuse bleeding.

Right gastroepiploic (Option B):

  • Arises from the gastroduodenal artery.
  • Supplies the right part of the greater curvature, near the pylorus - far from the spleen.

Splenic artery (Option D):

  • Runs along the superior border of the pancreas.
  • Usually ligated early in splenectomy to control splenic inflow before gastric mobilization.
  • Direct bleeding from it at this step is unlikely unless dissection is deep or careless.

question_text: Which is the best modality of investigation in a case of a small ampullary tumour of pancreas?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The preferred test to identify a tumour in the head of the pancreas is a contrast-enhanced CT scan.

  • The prothrombin time should be checked, and clotting abnormalities should be corrected with vitamin K or fresh-frozen plasma prior to ERCP.

Explanation for the other options:

  • Ultrasonography is good for screening but lacks sensitivity for small lesions.
  • Contrast-enhanced CT scan is the best for pancreatic head masses in general, but may miss small ampullary lesions due to limited visualization in that area.
  • PET scan is used for assessing metastatic disease, not for primary small tumor identification.

Key Takeaways:

While CECT is excellent for the pancreatic head, Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is the best modality for visualizing small ampullary lesions and obtaining biopsies from them.

question_text: Most common pituitary tumour in clinical practice is:
explanation:
Explanation:

Among pituitary adenomas that present clinically, prolactin-secreting (prolactinomas) are the most common functioning tumours. Functioning adenomas (especially prolactinomas) produce hormonal syndromes that bring patients to clinical attention earlier.

Non-functioning adenomas are also common (often present as macroadenomas with mass effect), but prolactinomas are the most common single subtype encountered in clinical practice.

question_text: Which of the following is the best preferred investigation for Neuroendocrine Tumors (NETs)?
explanation:
Explanation:

PET, specifically 68Ga-DOTA-peptide PET/CT (e.g., 68Ga-DOTATATE / DOTATOC / DOTANOC) is the preferred functional imaging test for localization and whole-body staging of somatostatin-receptor-expressing neuroendocrine tumors because it has higher sensitivity and specificity than conventional SRS (111In-octreotide SPECT).

Pancreatic Neuroendocrine Tumors (PNETs)

Origin:

  • Arise from pluripotent stem cells of the pancreas.

Classification:

  • Functional PNETs: Secrete active hormones → present early with clinical symptoms.
  • Non-functional PNETs: Do not secrete biologically active hormones → diagnosed late, usually due to mass effects.

Subtypes of Functional PNETs:

  • Insulinoma:
    • Most common functional PNET.
    • Usually benign.
    • Presents early with hypoglycaemic symptoms.
  • Gastrinoma:
    • Most common functional malignant PNET.
    • Causes Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
  • VIPoma:
    • Secretes vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP).
    • Associated with watery diarrhoea, hypokalaemia, achlorhydria.
  • Glucagonoma:
    • Linked with diabetes, necrolytic migratory erythema (rash), anaemia.
  • Somatostatinoma:
    • Very rare.
    • Causes diabetes, gallstones, steatorrhoea.
  • Carcinoid Tumor:
    • May secrete serotonin.
  • ACTHoma:
    • Produces ACTH → Cushing's syndrome.
  • GRFoma:
    • Produces growth hormone-releasing factor.

Non-functional PNETs:

  • Do not produce hormones.
  • Usually discovered late due to mass effect (pain, obstruction).

Clinical Features:

  • Functional tumors: Symptomatic early due to hormone hypersecretion.
  • Non-functional tumors: Often asymptomatic until advanced.

Diagnosis:

  • Laboratory Tests: Specific hormone assays or metabolite measurement.
  • Imaging:
    • PET/CT with 68Ga-labeled somatostatin analogs: Current preferred modality for detecting neuroendocrine tumors. (Option D)
    • Somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (SRS): Historical investigation of choice (IOC) for localization of NETs.
      • Exception: Insulinomas → often lack somatostatin receptors, hence not detected by SRS.
      • Rarely used today; largely replaced by PET/CT. (Option B ruled out)

Explanation of Other Options:

Ultrasound (USG) (Option A):

  • Has a limited role as the pancreas is located deep within the abdomen.
  • Small lesions are often missed due to low sensitivity.
  • Primarily useful for detecting larger masses.

MRI (Option C):

  • Provides excellent soft tissue resolution.
  • Valuable for assessing pancreatic tumors and detecting liver metastases.
  • However, it does not provide functional receptor-based information, which is crucial for neuroendocrine tumor localization.

Key Takeaways:

  • Somatostatin Receptor Scintigraphy (SRS):
    • Historically, it was considered the investigation of choice (IOC) for the localization of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors.
    • Detects tumors expressing somatostatin receptors.
    • Limitation: Insulinomas usually do not express somatostatin receptors, making them difficult to detect with SRS.
    • Largely replaced by newer imaging techniques but still referenced as IOC in guidelines.
  • PET/CT with 68Ga-labeled somatostatin analogs:
    • Currently the preferred imaging modality due to higher sensitivity and specificity compared to SRS.
    • Provides both functional and anatomical information for accurate staging and localization.

Reference:

PET/CT imaging of neuroendocrine tumors with 68Gallium-labeled somatostatin analogues: An overview and single institutional experience from India

question_text: MEN 1 false is/are

• Parathyroid adenomas occur in 95% of MEN1 patients, and PHPT is the first clinical manifestation of MEN1 in 90% of patients.

  • In addition, patients are more likely to develop adrenal adenomas and nonendocrine tumors such as angiofibromas, collagenomas, and meningiomas.

question_text: The commonest oncogene involved in cancer pancreas
explanation:
• Pancreatic carcinogenesis probably involves multiple mutations that are inherited and acquired throughout aging.
  • The K-ras oncogene is currently thought to be the most commonly mutated gene in pancreatic cancer, with approximately 90% of tumors having a mutation.
  • This prevalent mutation is present in precursor lesions and is therefore thought to occur early and be essential to pancreatic cancer development. K-ras mutations can be detected in DNA from serum, stool, pancreatic juice, and tissue aspirates of patients with pancreatic cancer, suggesting that the presence of this mutation or others may provide the basis for diagnostic testing in select individuals.
  • The HER2/neu oncogene, homologous to the epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFr), is overexpressed in pancreatic cancers. This receptor is involved in signal transduction pathways that lead to cellular proliferation.
  • Multiple tumor-suppressor genes are deleted and/or mutated in pancreatic cancer, including p53, p16, and DPC4 (Smad 4), and in a minority of cases, BRCA2. Most pancreatic cancers have three or more of the aforementioned mutations.

question_text: Which among the following arteries supply the uncinated process of the pancreas?
explanation:
Explanation:

The uncinate process of the pancreas is primarily supplied by the pancreaticoduodenal arteries, which form an anastomotic network between the celiac trunk and superior mesenteric artery.

Arterial Blood Supply

  • The pancreas is supplied by a complex arterial network arising from the celiac trunk and SMA.
  • The head and uncinate process are supplied by the pancreaticoduodenal arteries (superior and inferior).
  • The superior pancreaticoduodenal artery arises from the gastroduodenal artery and divides into anterior and posterior branches as it runs inferiorly within the pancreaticoduodenal groove.
  • The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery arises from SMA and also divides into anterior and posterior branches as it runs superiorly within pancreaticoduodenal groove.
  • Terminal branches of superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries join each other to form the arcade, which supplies the head and uncinate process of the pancreas and the duodenum.
  • The neck, body, and tail receive arterial supply from the splenic arterial system.
  • Several small branches originate from the length of the splenic artery, including the dorsal pancreatic artery and greater pancreatic artery.
  • The dorsal pancreatic courses posterior to the body of the gland to become the inferior pancreatic artery (also known as the transverse pancreatic artery). The inferior pancreatic artery then runs along the inferior border of the pancreas, terminating at its tail.

Key Takeaways:

The head and uncinate process of the pancreas are primarily supplied by the Pancreaticoduodenal Arteries (forming anterior and posterior arcades), which originate from both the Celiac axis (via GDA) and the SMA.

Level:

Must know

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding management of pancreatic injury except
option_a: Classically the pancreas should be treated with conservative surgery and closed suction drainage
option_b: Injuries to the pancreatic body to the left of the superior mesenteric vessels and to the tail are treated by closed suction drainage alone, with distal pancreatectomy if the duct is involved.
option_c: Whipple's procedure is commonly perform in emergency procedure
option_d: The pylorus can be temporarily closed (pyloric exclusion) in association with a gastric drainage procedure, to minimise pancreatic enzyme stimulation by gastric juice or distension.
explanation:
• Classically the pancreas should be treated with conservative surgery and closed suction drainage. Injuries are treated according to the OIS system of the AAST.
  • Injuries to the pancreatic body to the left of the superior mesenteric vessels and to the tail are treated by closed suction drainage alone, with distal pancreatectomy if the duct is involved.
  • Proximal injuries (to the right of the superior mesenteric artery) are treated as conservatively as possible, although partial pancreatectomy may be necessary.
  • The pylorus can be temporarily closed (pyloric exclusion) in association with a gastric drainage procedure, to minimise pancreatic enzyme stimulation by gastric juice or distension.
  • A Whipple’s procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) is rarely needed and should not be performed in the emergency situation because of the very high associated mortality rate.

A damage control procedure with packing and drainage should be performed and the patient referred for definitive surgery once stabilised.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 29, Edition: 28th, Pg: 381-382

question_text: A 27-year-old male presents with headache, palpitations, and excessive sweating. He has a family history of renal disease. Abdominal ultrasound shows multiple renal and pancreatic cysts, and his 24-hour urinary metanephrine levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The most likely diagnosis is Von Hippel-Lindau (VHL) disease, an autosomal dominant disorder caused by mutation of the VHL gene on chromosome 3.
  • It is characterized by the presence of multiple cysts in the kidneys, pancreas, and other organs, along with an increased risk of developing tumors.
  • In this case, the elevated urinary metanephrines indicate the presence of pheochromocytoma, explaining the patient's symptoms of headache, palpitations, and sweating.
  • VHL is associated with:
    • Hemangioblastomas of the CNS (commonly cerebellum and retina)
    • Cysts of the pancreas, liver, and kidneys
    • Renal cell carcinoma (especially clear cell type)
    • Pheochromocytomas

Explanation of other options:

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type I (Option A): MEN 1 is a genetic condition characterised by tumours of the parathyroid, pancreatic islet cells, and pituitary.

Birt-Hogg-Dube syndrome (Option C): Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome is a rare autosomal dominant condition caused by mutations in the FLCN gene. It is clinically characterised by fibrofolliculomas, multiple lung cysts with risk of spontaneous pneumothorax, and an increased predisposition to renal cell carcinoma.

Tuberous sclerosis (Option D): Tuberous sclerosis complex is an autosomal dominant disorder characterized by the formation of benign tumors in multiple organs, most commonly affecting the brain, kidneys, heart, and skin. Cutaneous findings include ash-leaf macules, shagreen patches, and facial angiofibromas.

question_text: What type of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor is responsible for recurrent episodes of secretory diarrhea?
explanation:
Explanation:

A VIPoma is a rare, functional neuroendocrine tumor originating in the pancreas. Its defining characteristic is the uncontrolled secretion of Vasoactive Intestinal Peptide (VIP).

The excessive VIP hormone overstimulates the cells lining the intestines, causing a massive efflux of water and electrolytes (like potassium) into the bowel lumen. This pathophysiological process results in the hallmark symptom: severe, large-volume watery diarrhea that persists during fasting. This distinct clinical presentation is formally termed Verner-Morrison syndrome, but is also commonly referred to as pancreatic cholera.

Explanation of other options:

Glucagonoma (Option B): These tumors secrete glucagon and cause a syndrome featuring diabetes mellitus, necrolytic migratory erythema, and weight loss, but not secretory diarrhea.

Insulinoma (Option C): These tumors secrete insulin, leading to recurrent hypoglycemia, not diarrhea.

Zollinger Ellison disease (Option D): Caused by gastrinomas, this condition leads to peptic ulcer disease and diarrhea, but the diarrhea is due to acid inactivation of digestive enzymes and malabsorption, not a primary secretory process.

Key Takeaways:

  • VIPoma is characterized by VIP-induced secretory diarrhea.
  • The diarrhea is watery, voluminous, and leads to hypokalemia.

question_text: The most classical symptom of VIPOMA is:
explanation: Answer is B (Secretory Diarrhoea) The principle feature of VIPOMA is large volume secretory Diarrhoea. Diarrhoea is secretory in nature, persists during fasting and is almost always greater than > I Litre per day (>3 Litres per day in 70 percent). A stool volume less than 700 ml per day is proposed to exclude the diagnosis. Most patients do not have accompanying Steatorrhea.  VIPOMAS (Verner-Morrison Syndrome/ Pancreatic Cholera/WDHA  Syndrome)  VIPomas are tumours that secrete large amounts of Vasoactive  Intestinal Peptide (VIP) VIP is an important neurotransmitter ubiquitously present in the CNS  and GIT The most common location of VlPomas is the Pancreas Most common site within the pancreas is the pancreatic tail Usually Solitary Usually Malignant (37-68 % have hepatic metastasis at diagnosis VIP Stimulates Small Intestinal chloride secretion Stimulates smooth muscle contractility Inhibits acid secretion Has vasodilatory effects  Typical Features  (WDHA) Watery Diarrhoea (Large Volume Secretory Diarrhoea leading to dehydration) Hypokalemia (Diarrhoea severe enough to cause hypokalemia) Achlorhydria (Hypochlorhydria from increased small intestinal chloride secretion) The principle Symptoms are large volume diarrhoea (100 %) severe enough to cause hypokalemia (80- 100%), dehydration (83%), hypochlorhydria (54-76%) and flushing (20%) Most patients do not have accompanying Steatorrhea Other Features Increased stool Volume due to increased secretion of sodium and potassium which with the anion account for osmolality of the stool Hyperglycemia (25-50% Hypercalcemia (25-50%) The diagnosis requires demonstration of an elevated plasma VIP level and the presence of large volume secretory diarrhea.

question_text: Most common pancreatic endocrine neoplasm:
explanation:
INSULINOMA

This is an insulin-producing tumour of the pancreas. Insulinomas have been diagnosed in all age groups, with the highest incidence found in the fourth to the sixth decades. Women seem to be slightly more frequently affected

The cornerstone of diagnosis remains Whipple's triad:

  • symptoms induced by fasting;
  • hypoglycaemia at the time of symptoms;
  • symptoms relieved by administration of glucose.

The key test is a 72-hour fast looking for documented endogenous hyperinsulinism in association with symptoms and signs of low plasma glucose (<3.0 mmol/L), elevated insulin and high C-peptide. If the test is negative and the suspicion of insulinoma is high, a prolonged oral glucose tolerance test is done.

question_text: Which organism is not responsible for post splenectomy septicaemia?
explanation:
Explanation:

Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI)

Postoperative complications

  • Immediate complications specific to splenectomy include haemorrhage resulting from a slipped ligature. Haematemesis from gastric mucosal damage and gastric dilatation is uncommon. Left basal atelectasis is common, and a pleural effusion may be present. Adjacent structures at risk during the procedure include the stomach and pancreas. A fistula may result from damage to the greater curvature of the stomach during ligation of the short gastric vessels. Damage to the tail of the pancreas may result in pancreatitis, a localised abscess or a pancreatic fistula.
  • Postoperative thrombocytosis may arise and, if the blood platelet count exceeds 1×106/mL, prophylactic aspirin is recommended. Long-term surveillance programmes have emphasised an increased risk of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. The relative risk and benefit of thromboprophylaxis in this setting has not been assessed adequately.
  • Postsplenectomy septicaemia may result from Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitides, Haemophilus influenzae and Escherichia coli.
  • Long-term surveillance programmes have suggested that the risk of pneumonia, meningitis and major sepsis following splenectomy is increased three-fold. However, the risk is greater in the young patient, in splenectomised patients treated with chemoradiotherapy and in patients who have undergone splenectomy for thalassaemia, sickle cell disease and autoimmune anaemia or thrombocytopenia.

Key Takeaways:

Overwhelming Post-Splenectomy Infection (OPSI) is most commonly caused by encapsulated bacteria like Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and Neisseria meningides. E. coli is also implicated. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is not typically listed among the core organisms causing OPSI.

Level:

Must know
