question_text: most common type of kidney stone?
explanation:
Types of stones

Calcium oxalate stones

This is themost common type of stone, constituting 60-85% of all stones. Hypercalciuria, hypercalcaemia, hyperoxaluria, hyperuricosuria and hypocitraturia are known metabolic abnormalities that can predispose to its formation. Hypercalciuria is the most common metabolic abnormality and occurs as a result of dysregulation of transport at various sites, including the intestine, bone or kidney.

Primary hyperparathyroidism is the most common disease associated with hypercalcaemia and stone disease. Increased parathyroid hormone causes increased bone resorption and increased synthesis of 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3. This causes increased intestinal absorption of calcium, leading to hypercalcaemia and hypercalciuria.

Hyperuricosuria causes uric acid crystal formation, especially in association with acidic urine, over which calcium oxalate crystals aggregate.

question_text: The following image is:
explanation:
The above given image is a T2 weighted MRI showing polycystic kidney disease


  • Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common autosomal dominant genetic cystic renal disease causing chronic renal failure requiring dialysis and renal transplantation.
  • It occurs as a result of mutation in one of two genes (PKD1on chromosome 16 andPKD2on chromosome 4).
  • ADPKD gene loci can be identified in individuals with a family history before the development of cysts begins; this is helpful in screening a potential sibling for kidney donation.
  • ADPKD has variable penetration and approximately 50% of affected individuals eventually develop end-stage renal disease (ESRD).

question_text: Which statement is not true regarding ESWL?
option_b: Generates shockwaves outside the body which are focused on the stones
option_d: Uric acid stones are relatively resistant to ESWL due to their hardness
explanation:
Cystine stones are relatively resistant to ESWL due to their hardness.

ESWL - extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy-

  • Non-invasive method of treating urinary tract stones by generating shockwaves outside the body which are focused on the stones.
  • Renal calculi and stones up to 1.5 cm in size are suitable for this form of treatment.

Complications of ESWL -

  • Infections by bacteria colonising the stones - prophylactic antibiotics given.
  • Hematuria, parenchymal haemorrhage, perirenal haematoma
  • Steinstrasse ('street of stones') - a collection of stone fragments in a ureter after ESWL.

Contraindications to ESWL-

  • Obese patients
  • Pregnant patients
  • Patients taking oral anticoagulants

Cystine stones Cystine stones constitute approximately 1% of stones. Cystinuria is an autosomal recessive inherited disease that causes decreased reabsorption of cystine from the intestine and the proximal tubule of the kidney. Cystine is insoluble even at physiological pH and worsens with increasing acidity. Cystine stones are very hard stones as a result of disulphide bonds and do not fragment with SWL.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1475.

question_text: A male patient presented with complaints of hematuria and recurrent urinary tract infection. You notice the following finding in his CT. What is the likely condition indicated by the arrow in the image?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient, presenting with blood in the urine and recurrent urinary tract infections, was diagnosed with Horseshoe Kidney. CT imaging of the abdomen demonstrated fusion of the kidneys at their lower poles, creating a U-shaped configuration.

Horseshoe Kidney

Definition:

  • A congenital renal anomaly where the lower poles of both kidneys fuse, creating a U-shaped configuration.

Cause & Pathogenesis:

  • Fusion occurs during fetal development at the lower poles.
  • The inferior mesenteric artery obstructs the normal ascent of the fused isthmus, leaving the kidney positioned lower in the abdomen.

Clinical Features:

  • Often asymptomatic.
  • Possible symptoms:
    • Flank or abdominal pain (due to obstruction or renal calculi).
    • Recurrent urinary tract infections (UTIs).
    • Hydronephrosis.
    • Hematuria.
    • Rovsing's Syndrome: hyperextension of the spine leading to nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

Investigations:

  • CT Angiography (Investigation of Choice): Provides detailed assessment of renal anatomy, abnormal vasculature, and complications.
  • CECT (Contrast-Enhanced CT): Alternative when CT angio unavailable.
  • Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP): Characteristic findings include:
    • Medial orientation of calyces ("Hand Joining Sign").
    • High ureteral insertion with anterior displacement ("Flower Vase Sign").

Management:

  • Asymptomatic Cases: Observation with periodic monitoring.
  • Symptomatic Cases:
    • Ureteropelvic Junction (UPJ) Obstruction: Surgical correction (e.g., pyeloplasty).
    • Renal Calculi: Hydration, medical therapy, or surgical stone removal.
    • Recurrent UTIs: Antibiotic therapy and preventive strategies.
  • Isthmus Consideration: Avoid surgical division since it contains functioning renal tissue.
  • Pregnancy: May cause dystocia due to altered renal position.

Explanation of Other Options:

Polycystic kidney disease (Option A) is an inherited disorder characterised by the presence of multiple fluid-filled cysts that progressively enlarge the kidneys. On CT imaging, the condition typically appears as numerous round or oval cysts without evidence of renal fusion. In contrast, the presented CT findings demonstrate fused kidneys, which rules out PKD as the diagnosis.

Hydronephrosis (Option C) results from obstruction in the urinary tract, leading to dilation of the renal pelvis and calyces with swelling of the kidney. On CT imaging, it is identified by fluid-filled dilated collecting systems, but the kidneys remain separate and are not fused. In contrast, the CT scan in this case shows fused kidneys at the lower poles, consistent with a horseshoe kidney rather than hydronephrosis.

Pancake kidney (Option D) is an uncommon congenital malformation in which both kidneys are completely fused, forming a compact, flattened disc-shaped structure. On CT imaging, it presents as a low-lying, flat renal mass in the pelvis or lower abdomen. In contrast, the current case demonstrates a U-shaped fusion at the lower poles, consistent with a horseshoe kidney rather than a pancake kidney.

question_text: A delayed intravenous urogram of a patient is given below. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The delayed contrast excretion from the affected kidney on intravenous urogram indicates an obstruction at the pelviureteric junction (PUJ).
  • PUJ obstruction occurs at the site where the renal pelvis joins the ureter, preventing normal urine flow.
  • It is a well-recognized cause of hydronephrosis, recurrent UTIs, and intermittent flank pain, especially after high fluid intake.

Pelviureteric Junction Obstruction

Causes

  • Congenital:
    • Intrinsic narrowing due to developmental anomaly (atresia/stenosis).
    • Aberrant crossing vessel compressing the PUJ externally.
  • Acquired:
    • Scarring from infections.
    • Kidney stones leading to obstruction (most common acquired cause).
    • Postsurgical strictures.

Clinical Features

  • Intermittent flank pain, often worse after diuresis or heavy fluid intake.
  • Hematuria, particularly if stones are present.
  • Recurrent UTIs.
  • Hydronephrosis, sometimes asymptomatic in early stages.

Investigations

  • Ultrasound: Detects hydronephrosis.
  • Diuretic renal scan (DTPA scan): Investigation of choice for PUJ obstruction.
  • Whitaker's test: Differentiates true obstruction from non-obstructive hydronephrosis by measuring pressure gradients across PUJ.
  • Magnetic resonance urography (MRU): Provides detailed anatomical localization.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Putty kidney (Option B): Represents end-stage renal tuberculosis with a shrunken, calcified, non-functioning kidney - not delayed excretion on IVU.

Staghorn calculus (Option C): A large branching stone occupying renal pelvis and calyces, typically associated with recurrent UTI and urea-splitting organisms (triple phosphate stone).

Cystic kidney (Option D): Multiple fluid-filled sacs within the kidney leading to enlargement; does not present with obstructive delay on IVU

Key Takeaway

Delayed contrast clearance on IVU with hydronephrosis is typical of pelviureteric junction obstruction, most often due to congenital narrowing or an aberrant vessel, and is best evaluated by a diuretic renal scan.

question_text: Suppose the above mentioned patient has clinically N1 nodes on right groin, which side would you operate on?
option_c: Right side, surveillance for left side
explanation:
Inguinal lymph node dissection should always be bilateral even if the patient has unilateral adenopathy on presentation.

Reference: Campbell-Walsh-Wein Urology 12th Edition, Pg: 1764.

question_text: A young girl presents with continuous urinary dribbling since birth, despite normal voiding. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

In females, an ectopic ureter that opens below the sphincter (into the urethra or vagina) presents as continuous dribbling of urine despite normal voiding. This history is pathognomonic.

Explanation of other options:

Ureterocele (Option B): Causes recurrent UTIs and bladder outlet obstruction, not continuous dribbling.

Congenital megaureter (Option C): Presents with hydronephrosis and infections, not continuous leakage.

Vesicoureteric reflux (Option D): Causes recurrent UTIs and hydronephrosis, not continuous wetting.

question_text: A mother brought her 3-month-old male child to the hospital due to an inability to pass urine, with a similar episode occurring 15 days ago. Catheterization was performed without difficulty. A radiograph is provided. What is the appropriate management?
option_c: Endoscopic dilation of the bladder neck
explanation:
Explanation:

Posterior urethral valves (PUV) are managed by endoscopic ablation (destruction) of the obstructing valves to relieve urinary outflow obstruction.

  • This 3-month-old male presents with urinary retention and prior similar episodes, and the radiograph likely shows a "keyhole sign", which is classic for posterior urethral valves (PUV).
  • This condition is the most common cause of lower urinary tract obstruction in male infants, seen in approximately 1 in 4,000 live-born boys.
  • PUV consists of membranous obstructive folds in the posterior urethra, leading to:
    • Bladder distension
    • Urinary tract infections
    • Hydronephrosis
    • Vesicoureteral reflux
    • Long-term complications like bladder dysfunction and renal insufficiency
  • Diagnosis:
    • Ultrasound: Enlarged bladder, bilateral hydronephrosis
    • MCU/VCUG (Micturating Cystourethrogram): Dilated posterior urethra and bladder wall thickening (keyhole sign)
  • Definitive management is endoscopic destruction (ablation) of the valves using a cystoscope.
  • Early intervention is crucial to preserve renal function.

Explanation of other options:

Partial resection of verumontanum (Option A): Typically considered in adult prostatic obstruction scenarios. It does not address posterior urethral valves, which are congenital membrane-like obstructions.

Endoscopic dilation of the bladder neck (Option C): Used in cases of bladder neck obstruction, not PUV. In PUV, the obstruction is distal to the bladder neck, so this procedure would not relieve the obstruction.

Indwelling catheter (Option D): May provide temporary bladder decompression but does not address the underlying cause (PUV). It's supportive, not definitive treatment.

question_text: All of the following are related to acute pyelonephritis, except?
option_a: If untreated, can lead to renal scarring
option_c: Classically, costovertebral angle tenderness is absent
option_d: CECT kidney is the investigation of choice
explanation:
Acute pyelonephritis-

  • More common in females, especially during childhood, at puberty, after intercourse and during pregnancy.
  • Suggested by fever (temperature >38°C), rigors, flank pain, nausea and vomiting, and costovertebral angle tenderness.
  • Cystitis symptoms may or may not be present.
  • Symptoms may vary from a mild illness to a severe illness with septic shock, renal failure and a threat to life.
  • Pyuria is almost always present.
  • Both urine and blood are sent for culture.
  • Imaging of the kidney is necessary in the hospitalised patient to rule out pyonephrosis, perirenal abscess and obstruction of the collecting system by renal calculi.
  • CECT scan - Investigation of choice - Decreased opacification of the affected parenchyma, typically in patchy, wedge-shaped or linear distribution.
  • If untreated, it leads to renal scarring.

Acute pyelonephritis This commonly occurs as a result of ascending infection from organisms in the lower tract, usually caused by Gram-negative bacteria. Haematogenous spread may be seen in patients with diabetes and in immunocompromised hosts, people who inject drugs and patients with bacterial endocarditis. It is more common in females, especially during childhood, at puberty, after intercourse and during pregnancy. Acute pyelonephritis usually presents with fever, chills, flank pain, nausea and vomiting. Loin tenderness may be present. Symptoms may vary from mild to severe illness with septic shock and renal failure. Pyuria is almost always present and its absence in a patient with pyelonephritis may point towards an obstructed urinary tract. Urine and blood should be collected for culture. Escherichia coli and other Gram-negative organisms are commonly responsible. Imaging is necessary when the patient is not responding to antibiotics to rule out pyonephrosis, renal abscess and obstruction. Renal US is often the first imaging modality used. Contrast-enhanced CT (CECT) typically shows decreased patchy opacification of the affected parenchyma.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1471.

question_text: Identify the image.
explanation:
Explanation:

The image depicts Bladder Exstrophy (also known as Ectopia Vesicae), showing the bladder exposed outside the abdomen.

  • It is a rare congenital defect where the urinary bladder is exposed outside the abdomen due to a failure to develop the lower abdominal wall.
  • M/c in males.

Surgical Management of Ectopia Vesicae:

  • Staged Reconstruction with B/L pelvic osteotomies to facilitate abdominal wall closure and reduce tension in the neonatal period.
  • Epispadias repair and reconstruction of the urethra and external genitalia at 6-12 months of age.
  • Bladder Neck Reconstruction (BNR) to treat VUR at 5-7 yrs.

Omphalocele (Option B) is a condition where abdominal organs, such as the intestines or liver, protrude through the abdominal wall at birth, but they are covered by a thin membrane. Unlike bladder exstrophy, the organs are not exposed outside the body without a covering, and the defect is usually located near the umbilical cord area.

Gastroschisis (Option C), the intestines or other abdominal organs protrude through a hole in the abdominal wall, but unlike omphalocele, there is no membrane covering the organs. It usually happens to the right of the umbilical cord. While both involve abdominal wall defects, bladder exstrophy affects the bladder, and the organs in gastroschisis are usually the intestines.

Spina bifida (Option D) is a neural tube defect in which the spinal column doesn't fully close during early fetal development. This condition results in spinal cord and nerve damage. It doesn't involve the exposed bladder, making it quite different from bladder exstrophy, which is primarily a defect in the urinary system.

question_text: All of the following are true regarding emphysematous pyelonephritis, except?
option_d: Gas detected on a CT scan
explanation:
Emphysematous pyelonephritis -

  • Fulminant, necrotising, life-threatening variant of acute pyelonephritis
  • Caused by gas-forming organisms - E Coli (most common), Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Proteus mirabilis.
  • Up to 90% of cases occur in diabetic patients and urinary tract obstruction may be present.
  • Symptoms are suggestive of pyelonephritis and there may be a loin mass.
  • Gas is detected on imaging (plain film, ultrasound, or a CT scan).

Treatment -

  • Intra-venous broad-spectrum antibiotics
  • Percutaneous catheter drainage with relief of obstruction
  • Nephrectomy - in severe cases

Emphysematous pyelonephritis This is an acute-onset, rapidly progressive, possibly lethal form of pyelonephritis characterised by parenchymal necrosis and gas formation, caused by organisms including E. coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Proteus mirabilis. Most patients have diabetes (up to 90%) and they may have obstruction secondary to calculi or papillary necrosis. Increased glucose levels in those with diabetes may provide a substrate for carbon dioxide production from fermentation. Symptoms are suggestive of pyelonephritis and an abdominal mass may be palpable. CECT of the abdomen is diagnostic and shows gas in the renal parenchyma, collecting system or both, along with other features of infection such as abscess, obstruction and perinephric stranding. Early diagnosis, intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics and percutaneous drainage of the abscess and obstructed kidneys have improved outcomes in these patients. Emergency nephrectomy is rarely required and is reserved for patients who do not respond to the described measures.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1471.

question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Wilms' tumour(nephroblastoma) is incorrect?
option_b: Most commonly seen < 5 years of age
option_c: Majority of patients recover due to chemotherapy and radiotherapy
option_d: Lung involvement is uncommon and occurs late
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Lung metastasis is actually common in Wilms tumours and can occur early in the disease, especially if the tumour is not detected and treated promptly.
  • Wilms' Tumor (Nephroblastoma) is a common malignant renal tumour in children (commonly < 5 years of age), usually unilateral but can be bilateral. It is caused by mutations in the WT1 and WT2 genes on chromosome 11. (Option B ruled out)

Key Takeaway Points:

Associated congenital syndromes:

  • WAGR syndrome (Wilms tumour, Aniridia, Genitourinary malformations, mental Retardation).
  • Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome (macroglossia, organomegaly, hemihypertrophy).
  • Denys-Drash syndrome (pseudohermaphroditism, nephropathy).

question_text: A patient presents with recurrent renal calculi, abdominal pain, and altered mentation. Investigations reveal low serum calcium (Ca<sup>2+</sup>) and elevated parathyroid hormone (PTH) levels. Which of the following best explains the underlying disorder?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of hypocalcemia, elevated PTH, and renal stones indicates secondary hyperparathyroidism secondary to chronic kidney disease (CKD), leading to renal osteodystrophy which is a metabolic bone disorder.

This condition represents skeletal changes resulting from disturbances in calcium, phosphate, and PTH metabolism due to CKD.

Explanation of Other Options:

Parathyroid - Hyperparathyroidism (Option B):

  • Refers to primary hyperparathyroidism, caused by parathyroid adenoma, hyperplasia, or carcinoma.
  • Characterized by:
    • ↑ Serum Ca2+
    • ↓ Serum phosphate
    • ↑ PTH.
  • Classic triad: "Bones, stones, abdominal groans, and psychic moans."
  • In contrast, this patient has low calcium, ruling out primary hyperparathyroidism.

Thyroid - Hypothyroidism (Option C):

  • Presents with fatigue, weight gain, bradycardia, cold intolerance, and constipation.
  • Does not alter calcium or PTH significantly.
  • May cause hyponatremia, but not hypocalcemia or hyperparathyroidism.
  • No association with renal calculi or bone resorption.

Adrenal gland - Pheochromocytoma (Option D):

  • Catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla.
  • Characterized by episodic hypertension, palpitations, sweating, and headache.
  • Diagnosed by elevated urinary metanephrines or plasma catecholamines.
  • No impact on calcium metabolism or PTH secretion.

question_text: A 30 year old female presented to the hospital with abdominal pain, weight loss & sterile pyuria. Radiograph is shown below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Tuberculosis of the urinary tract : features like weight loss with sterile Pyuria is suggestive of TB of urinary tract

Features of chronic TB of kidney

  • Putty kidney
  • Kehr's kink
  • Corkscrew golf hole ureter
  • Thimble bladder
  • Putty kidney: extensive dystrophic calcification involving all or most of the kidney, seen as calcified non-functioning renal tissue
  • The disease gradually involves the bladder musculature, which is replaced by fibrous tissue, causing a decrease in the size and capacity of the bladder('thimble' bladder).
  • Urinary bladder involvement is responsible for urinary frequency, which is the most common symptom of GUTB.
  • For microbiological confirmation, at least three consecutive early-morning specimens of urine are examined for acid-fast bacilli. The gold standard for microbiological diagnosis is urine culture. .
  • IVU can pick up the earliest signs of disease activity, such as calyceal distortion.
  • Treatment involves short-course antituberculous therapy (ATT). Rifampicin, isoniazid and pyrazinamide are used sometimes with ethambutol as first-line drugs.

question_text: A patient presents with dysuria and increased frequency of urination. He has a known history of recurrent urinary tract infections caused by Proteus species. A radiographic image reveals a renal calculus.
explanation:
Explanation:

Calcium phosphate stones are radiopaque and often associated with infections by urease-producing organisms like Proteus, which alkalinize the urine.

  • Infections with Proteus species (urease-producing bacteria) increase the urinary pH by converting urea to ammonia.
  • This creates an alkaline environment favorable for the precipitation of calcium phosphate stones, especially apatite-type, or even struvite stones in some cases.
  • These stones are radiopaque and appear clearly on plain radiographs.
  • Though struvite stones are more classic for staghorn formations, calcium phosphate stones are also associated with chronic infection and appear radiopaque.
  • Hence, given the infection with Proteus and radiographic findings, calcium phosphate stones are the most likely diagnosis in this clinical context.

Explanation of other options:

Cysteine (Option B): Cystine stones result from cystinuria and are usually faintly radiopaque. They are not linked to infections with Proteus.

Uric acid (Option C): Uric acid stones are radiolucent, not visible on plain X-rays, and occur in acidic urine. They are not typically associated with infections like Proteus.

Xanthine (Option D): Xanthine stones are rare, occur in hereditary xanthinuria, and are typically radiolucent. They have no relation to infections or Proteus.

question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with recurrent right flank pain, hematuria, and a history of frequent urinary tract infections. Her urine analysis shows a pH of 8.0 (alkaline), and microscopy reveals characteristic crystal structures. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient's combination of alkaline urine, recurrent UTIs, and coffin-lid-shaped crystals on microscopy is diagnostic of triple phosphate (struvite) stones.

These stones are composed of magnesium ammonium phosphate (MgNH₄PO₄·6H₂ O) and form in alkaline urine, typically secondary to urease-producing bacterial infections.

Mechanism:

  • Urease-producing bacteria (e.g., Proteus, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus saprophyticus) hydrolyze urea → ammonia + CO₂.
  • Ammonia alkalinizes the urine → precipitation of magnesium, ammonium, and phosphate ions → struvite stone formation.
  • These stones can grow rapidly, sometimes filling the entire renal pelvis and calyces, forming a staghorn calculus.

Explanation of Other Options:

Ca Oxalate Stones (Option B):

  • Most common type of renal stone overall.
  • Form in acidic urine (pH <6).
  • Characteristic dumbbell or envelope-shaped
  • Associated with hypercalciuria, hyperoxaluria, dehydration, and low citrate levels.
  • Not linked to infections or alkaline urine.
  • Radiopaque on X-ray.

Uric Acid Stones (Option C):

  • Form in acidic urine and are radiolucent (not visible on X-ray).
  • Seen in hyperuricemia, gout, myeloproliferative disorders, or dehydration.
  • Crystals appear rhomboid or rosette-shaped.
  • Not infection-related and do not form in alkaline urine.

Cystine Stones (Option D):

  • Occur in patients with cystinuria, an autosomal recessive defect in renal tubular reabsorption of cystine.
  • Typically form in acidic urine and are hexagonal on microscopy.
  • Common in young individuals; not associated with infection.
  • Radiopaque and may lead to recurrent stones.

Key Takeaway Points:

Common Urease positive bacteria:

  • Proteus
  • Ureaplasma
  • Nocardia
  • Cryptococcus
  • Helicobacter
  • Klebsiella
  • Staphylococcus saprophyticus
  • Staphylococcus aureus

question_text: Which of the following is the most common type of radiolucent renal stone?
explanation:
Explanation:

Uric acid stones are the most common radiolucent stones, associated with acidic urine, gout, and myeloproliferative disorders. They are not seen on plain X-rays but can be detected on ultrasound or CT.

Radiological Appearance of Urinary Stones

Radiopaque Stones (visible on X-ray):

  • Calcium Oxalate stones - Most common (60-85%); radiopaque.
  • Calcium Phosphate stones - Rare; radiopaque.
  • Struvite stones (Triple phosphate / Staghorn calculi) Radiopaque; associated with infection.
  • Cystine stones - Faintly radiopaque (less dense).

Radiolucent Stones (not visible on plain X-ray, but seen on CT/USG):

  • Uric Acid stones - Most common radiolucent stones.
  • Xanthine stones - Rare; seen in xanthinuria.

Stone Types and Features

1. Calcium Oxalate Stones:

  • Most common (60-85% of all stones).
  • Radiology:

question_text: A 35-year-old female undergoes a retrograde pyelogram as part of a workup for recurrent urinary tract infections. The imaging reveals the finding shown for the left kidney. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation of Answer:

The image clearly demonstrates a left double ureter, also known as a duplicated ureter. This is the most common congenital anomaly of the urinary tract. The retrograde pyelogram shows two separate ureters descending from a single renal unit, which can be either partially or completely duplicated.

  • Incomplete Duplication: The two ureters fuse at some point before entering the bladder (a "Y-shaped" ureter).
  • Complete Duplication: Two separate ureters drain their respective moieties (upper and lower poles) of the kidney and enter the bladder via separate orifices. This is often associated with vesicoureteric reflux, particularly into the lower pole moiety.

Explanation of Other Options:

Left pelvi-ureteric junction obstruction (Option B): This would appear as a dilated, "clubbed" renal pelvis with a narrowing at the junction with the ureter, but there would only be a single ureter.

Left staghorn calculus (Option C): A staghorn calculus is a large stone that fills the renal pelvis and extends into multiple calyces, creating a cast of the collecting system. This would appear as a large, radio-opaque shadow, which is not seen.

Left double pelvis (Option D): While a duplicated ureter arises from a duplex collecting system which may have two separate pelves, the term "double ureter" is the most accurate and specific description for the anomaly shown extending down from the kidney.

Key Takeaways: Duplex Collecting System

question_text: A 25-year-old morbidly obese male presents with severe abdominal pain and urinary disturbances. Urine microscopy shows crystals as shown, and renal ultrasound reveals a 2.5 cm kidney stone. What is the treatment of choice for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Urine microscopy showing hexagonal crystals is characteristic of cystine stones seen in cystinuria.
  • Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is the treatment of choice for a 2.5 cm cystine stone, particularly in a morbidly obese patient, as Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL) and ureteroscopy are often less effective. (Option A, D ruled out)

Management of renal stones

Non-surgical

  • Watchful waiting
    • Small (<5 mm), non-obstructive, asymptomatic lower pole renal stones with preserved renal function can be managed with observation and follow-up.
    • Approximately 90% of 4 mm stones and 50% of 6-10 mm stones pass spontaneously.
  • Medical expulsive therapy
    • Tamsulosin is an α1-adrenergic receptor blocker that relaxes distal ureteric smooth muscle.
    • It can be used to facilitate the passage of distal ureteric stones >5 mm and to aid clearance of fragments after SWL.
  • Extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy (ESWL)
    • Indicated if the size of the calculi <2 cm
    • Contraindicated in pregnancy and bleeding diathesis.

question_text: A patient with ureteric calculi is being investigated. What is the investigation of choice for diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Non-contrast CT KUB (CT without contrast of kidney-ureter-bladder region) is the investigation of choice for suspected ureteric calculi because it has very high sensitivity and specificity for stone detection (detects radio-opaque and radiolucent stones), localizes stones accurately, and shows ancillary findings (hydronephrosis).

Ultrasound is useful in children/pregnancy or to screen but has lower sensitivity for mid/ distal ureteric stones. Contrast CT is not required for stone detection and can obscure calculi. Diagnostic ureteroscopy is an invasive test/intervention.

Explanation of other options:

USG KUB (Option A): operator-dependent and less sensitive (useful in pregnancy /paediatrics).

CECT (Option C): unnecessary; contrast can mask stones; used for other indications.

Ureteroscopy (Option D): therapeutic and invasive; not the diagnostic test of choice.

Key takeaways:

NCCT KUB = gold-standard initial imaging for adult suspected ureteric stone (except special populations).

question_text: What is the most frequently occurring location for an intraperitoneal abscess to develop?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The subhepatic region (beneath the liver) is the most common site for intraperitoneal abscess formation.
  • This site is prone because of its anatomical position close to the biliary system and gastrointestinal tract, which allows infections to spread easily into this dependent space.
  • Position-based variations:
    • In a recumbent or lying down patient, the Morrison's pouch (right subhepatic space) is the typical site of collection.
    • In an upright patient, the pelvis (Pouch of Douglas) is the most common site overall.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Suprahepatic (Option A): This area is located above the liver, often associated with subphrenic abscesses. Although abscesses can develop here, it is not the most common site.

Left lobe of the liver (Option C): Abscesses may occur within the liver, but this is not the typical site of intraperitoneal abscess formation.

Left side below diaphragm (Option D): This area may occasionally harbor subphrenic abscesses, but it is far less common compared to the subhepatic space.

Key Takeaway:

The subhepatic space (Morrison's pouch) is the most common site for intraperitoneal abscess formation, particularly in recumbent patients, while the pelvis is the most common site overall in upright patients.

question_text: Nosocomial infections are diagnosed after how many hours of hospitalization/admission?
explanation:
Nosocomial infections, also referred to as healthcare-associated infections (HAI), are infection(s) acquired during the process of receiving health care that was not present during the time of admission.

Nosocomial infections, otherwise known as hospital-acquired infections, are those infections acquired in hospital or healthcare service unit that first appear 48 h or more after hospital admission1or within 30 days after discharge following in patient care.

Various grading and scoring systems exist for specific conditions such as pressure ulcers and diabetic ulcers. The National Nosocomial Infections Surveillance (NNIS) score is commonly used to predict surgical site infections (SSIs). It was established in recognition of the effectiveness of infection surveillance in reducing SSIs. The NNIS score stratified surgical wound infection rates by risk factors. This risk index score ranges from 0 (lowest SSI risk) to 3 (highest SSI risk) with a point allocated for the presence of each of the following risk factors:

  • contaminated or dirty wound;
  • American Society of Anesthesiologists score ≥3;
  • operative time longer than the expected duration for similar procedures (>75th percentile).

question_text: What is the best method to localize an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most effective method to localize extra-adrenal pheochromocytomas is a nuclear medicine scan, such as MIBG scintigraphy or PET scan.

Extra-adrenal pheochromocytomas

  • Extra-adrenal pheochromocytomas (paragangliomas) are catecholamine-producing tumors that originate from the sympathetic or parasympathetic nervous system.
  • They can occur sporadically or as part of hereditary syndromes such as MEN 2, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and other pheochromocytoma-associated syndromes.
  • Elevated plasma and/or urinary metanephrines confirms a catecholamine-secreting tumor (pheochromocytoma/paraganglioma).
    • Metanephrine levels ≥4× the upper limit are diagnostic.
    • Doesnot help in localising the lesion.
  • After biochemical confirmation, CT or MRI is done to locate the tumor.
  • If imaging is negative or shows extra-adrenal disease, functional imaging such as ¹²³I-MIBG,¹¹¹In-octreotide,¹⁴F-fluorodopamine PET is done.

Explanation of other options:

X-ray (Option A): Xray is not suitable for visualising soft tissue tumours like pheochromocytomas or detecting abnormal growths. It is better suited for visualising bones or detecting larger, more obvious structural abnormalities.

VMA excretion (Option C): VMA excretion is a metabolite of catecholamines and can be measured in urine to help diagnose pheochromocytoma. However, while increased VMA (Vanillyl mandelic acid) excretion is suggestive of pheochromocytoma, it does not help localize the tumor.

Clinical examination (Option D): Clinical examination can reveal signs and symptoms of pheochromocytoma, but it is not reliable for localising an extra-adrenal pheochromocytoma. Symptoms like hypertension, sweating, and tachycardia suggest the presence of pheochromocytoma, but further imaging studies (like the nucleotide scan) are required for accurate localisation.

question_text: What is the best investigation to assess renal perfusion?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A DTPA (diethylenetriaminepentaacetate) scan is considered the most effective test for evaluating renal perfusion.
  • This nuclear medicine study involves intravenous injection of a radioactive tracer (DTPA).
  • The tracer is absorbed by the kidneys, and its distribution and clearance are tracked using a gamma camera.
  • This allows assessment of renal function and drainage.

Radioisotope Renal Imaging:

  • Principle: Uses the metastable radioisotope Technetium-99m (99mTc), which emits gamma rays during its decay to 99Tc. It has a 6-hour physical half-life and a 1-day biological half-life, ensuring minimal radiation exposure.
  • Static Imaging: 99mTc is conjugated with Dimercaptosuccinic acid (DMSA) and injected intravenously. Images are obtained 2-3 hours post-injection to evaluate renal anatomy, structure, and functional integrity.
  • Dynamic Imaging: 99mTc is linked to Diethylenetriaminepentaacetate (DTPA) or Mercaptoacetyltriglycine (MAG-3) and administered intravenously. Sequential images capture renal perfusion and excretory dynamics.
  • Interpretation:
    • Absent imaging: Indicates compromised renal blood flow.
    • Delayed transit: Suggests partial obstruction despite adequate perfusion.

Explanation of Other Options:

DMSA (Dimercaptosuccinic acid) Scan (Option B): Evaluates renal parenchymal function and is primarily used for diagnosing or monitoring kidney infections and scarring. It does not provide information about renal blood flow or perfusion.

Retrograde Urethrogram (RGU) (Option C): Focuses on the urethra, assessing injuries or strictures. It does not give insights into renal perfusion or kidney blood flow.

CT Urogram (Option D): A contrast-enhanced imaging study of the kidneys, ureters, and bladder to identify structural abnormalities, tumors, or stones. It does not evaluate renal perfusion or blood flow.

question_text: Identify the disease.
explanation:
Explanation:

A unilocular, well-defined cystic lesion in the kidney on imaging is most consistent with a simple renal cyst.

  • Renal cysts are fluid-filled sacs that develop within the kidneys.
  • Most commonly, they are simple cysts, discovered incidentally on imaging and are usually benign and asymptomatic.
  • Causes:
    • Sporadic (simple cysts, most common)
    • Acquired (e.g., in patients on long-term dialysis)
    • Genetic (e.g., ADPKD)
  • Imaging Appearance:
    • Well-defined, thin-walled, anechoic (on USG)
    • No septations, calcifications, or solid components
    • No post-contrast enhancement (on CT/MRI)
  • Bosniak Classification (CT-based):
    • Category I & II: Benign, no follow-up needed
    • Category IIF: Requires follow-up imaging
    • Category III & IV: High malignancy risk — surgical management advised
  • Key point: Simple renal cysts (Bosniak I) are non-enhancing, thin-walled, and require no further management.

Explanation of other options:

RCC - Renal Cell Carcinoma (Option B): Usually appears as a solid enhancing mass on imaging; may have necrotic or cystic areas, but not a simple unilocular cyst.

ADPKD - Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease (Option C): Presents with multiple bilateral renal cysts, often accompanied by hypertension, hematuria, and family history. Not a solitary cyst.

Hydatid cyst (Option D): Caused by Echinococcus granulosus, typically affects liver or lungs; renal involvement is rare. Imaging may show daughter cysts or water lily sign, not a simple unilocular cyst.

question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding the anatomy of urinary bladder?
option_b: The distal urethral sphincter is made up of striated muscle
option_c: The distal urethral sphincter is supplied by L1-L5 fibres via the pudendal nerve
option_d: The epithelium is closely adherent to the smooth muscle in the region of the trigone.
explanation:
The distal urethral sphincter is supplied by S2-S4 fibres via the pudendal nerve.

Urinary bladder -

  • Lined by transitional epithelium (urothelium).
  • The trigone has the ureteric orifices at its posterolateral angles and internal urethral orifice at its apex.
  • Over the trigone is a thin layer of smooth muscle to which the epithelium is closely adherent (The epithelium is only loosely adherent in the remaining part of the bladder).
  • The muscularis propria of the bladder is formed by detrusor muscle. Its contraction causes bladder emptying.

Proximal/Internal urethral sphincter -

  • Lined by smooth muscle.
  • Innervated by sympathetic fibres in men which prevents retrograde ejaculation.

Distal/External urethral sphincter -

  • Horseshoe-shaped mass of striated muscle.
  • Lies anterior and distal to the prostate in males, or in the proximal two-thirds of the female urethra.
  • Supplied by S2-S4 fibres via the pudendal nerve and by somatic fibres passing through the inferior hypogastric plexus.

Urinary bladder is a hollow muscular layer and consists of three layers: lamina propria, smooth muscle and urothelium. The lamina propria contains a rich plexus of vessels, nerves and lymphatics. The detrusor is made up of a complex haphazard arrangement of smooth muscle, which acts as functional syncytium, and elastic connective tissue, which gives the bladder its viscoelastic properties. The urothelium is an active layer that not only acts as a barrier to protect underlying stroma from irritant urinary toxins and bacteria but also has a role in afferent signalling within the bladder; defects in the urothelial lining are thought to lead to several chronic benign bladder conditions.

Reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 83, The Urinary Bladder, Pg: 1486-1487

question_text: All of the following are lower urinary tract symptoms except?
explanation:
The International Continence Society provides the internationally accepted definitions for symptoms relating to lower urinary tract function.

VOIDING SYMPTOMS:

  1. HESITANCY: when an individual has difficulty initiating micturition, resulting in a delay in the onset of voiding.
  2. POOR FLOW (unimproved by straining): the muscular effort used in order to initiate, maintain or improve the urinary stream.
  3. INTERMITTENT STREAM: when urine flow stops and starts, on one or more occasions.
  4. DRIBBLING: when involuntary loss of urine occurs immediately after the individual has finished passing urine.
  5. INCOMPLETE EMPTYING: the sensation that, at the end of micturition, bladder fullness persists.
  6. STRANGURY: a sensation of constantly needing to be void. Typically, the patient describes having to stand/sit for long periods with the sensation that micturition is imminent.

STORAGE SYMPTOMS:

  1. FREQUENCY - the patient considers that they are void too often during the day.
  2. NOCTURIA - the individual wakes at night at least once to void.
  3. URGENCY - a sudden compelling desire to pass urine that is difficult to defer.
  4. URGE INCONTINENCE - involuntary urinary leakage, often a large volume, immediately preceded by the sensation of urgency.
  5. NOCTURNAL ENURESIS - involuntary loss of urine during sleep.

INVESTIGATION OF CHOICE FOR LUTS; UROFLOWMETRY

Normal uroflowmetry:

Urine flow rate:

  • For a voiding volume of >200ml a peak flow rate of >15ml/s is normal
  • Flow rate <10ml is low

Voiding pressure:

  • Voiding pressure at <60cnm H2O is normal
  • Voiding pressure >80 cm H2O is high

question_text: Identify the investigation modality?
explanation:
Explanation:

Ureteral Injuries - Evaluation and Diagnosis

  • Blunt ureteral injury is rare due to the ureter's retroperitoneal location, but may occur with rapid deceleration trauma.
  • Penetrating trauma to the retroperitoneum warrants high clinical suspicion for ureteral injury.

Evaluation:

  • All suspected cases (especially penetrating injuries) should be evaluated using:
    • Intraoperative inspection
    • IVP (Intravenous Pyelogram)
    • CT Urogram with delayed images (preferred)
    • Retrograde pyelogram (most sensitive for injury detection)

Imaging Recommendations:

  • Use contrast-enhanced CT with delayed imaging to assess urinary excretion and ureteral integrity.

Key Imaging Findings Suggestive of Ureteral Injury:

  • Contrast extravasation
  • Absence of contrast beyond the site of injury
  • Ipsilateral hydronephrosis

Management:

  • If partial transection is identified, ureteral stent placement is often sufficient.

Limitations:

  • IVU and retrograde pyelography are less practical in acute settings and often yield lower quality images.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Intravenous pyelography (IVP)

  • IVP involves injecting contrast intravenously to visualize the renal collecting system and ureters via X-ray.
  • While it provides good images of the kidneys, it is less sensitive than retrograde pyelography for evaluating ureteral injuries and can be challenging in the acute trauma setting.
  • It often requires good renal function, and contrast may not adequately highlight ureteral tears or obstructions.

Choice C: Combined retrograde pyelogram and ureteroscopy

  • While ureteroscopy allows direct visualization of the ureters and can assist in treating injuries (e.g., stenting or biopsy), it is typically a more invasive procedure than retrograde pyelography
  • Retrograde pyelogram provides detailed imaging, whereas ureteroscopy is usually reserved for therapeutic interventions after diagnostic imaging.

Choice D: Antegrade pyelography

  • Antegrade pyelography involves the injection of contrast into the kidney through a percutaneous nephrostomy.
  • This technique is usually performed when a retrograde approach is not feasible, but it is less commonly used for ureteral trauma than the retrograde pyelogram due to its more invasive nature.

Key Takeaway

  • The most sensitive and appropriate imaging modality for diagnosing ureteral injury in trauma cases is retrograde pyelography.

question_text: Whitaker test is done in:
option_b: Hydronephrosis to compare abdominal and urinary bladderpressures
explanation:
Whitaker test: differentiation of obstructive from non obstructive uropathy

  • The Whitaker test,a urodynamic study, combined with antegrade pyelographyhas been used recently to evaluate persistent upper urinary tract dilatation after operative correction of obstruction.
  • This test will differentiate patients with residual or recurrent obstruction from those with dilatation secondary to permanent changes in the musculature.
  • It is useful in evaluating patients with questionable ureteropelvic or ureterovesical junction obstruction, or primary defects in the ureteral musculature, such as prune-belly syndrome.
  • It also well establish when urinary diversion safely can be discontinued in postoperative patients. Percutaneous puncture of the renal pelvis is performed or an indwelling nephrostomy tube is used.
  • The upper urinary tract is then perfused at a constant rate of 5--10 ml/min with saline or diluted contrast media, and a serial pressure recording is made in the renal pelvis and bladder.
  • The high flow rate used will be tolerated easily in a nonobstructed system without a progressive rise in renal pelvic pressure. In obstructed systems abnormally high pressure above 12 cm water or a constant rise in pressure will be recorded. Videotaping of ureteral peristalsis and spot films of the upper urinary tract complete the evaluation.

question_text: Which catheter is used for irrigation of blood clots after TURP?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In the patient with a significant amount of blood clot in the bladder, it will be necessary to place a large-bore irrigation catheter (in the adult, often 20 Fr to 26 Fr) and adequately irrigate the clots from the bladder using normal saline irrigation.
  • Special hematuria catheters are designed to allow large-volume irrigation and clot removal, but if this is unsuccessful, the patient may require urgent operative cystoscopy to evacuate the clot and to identify and fulgurate any bleeding source.

Explanation of other options:

21 French 2 lumen catheter (Option A):

  • While a 2-lumen catheter can be used for some applications, it lacks the extra lumen necessary for efficient irrigation and removal of clots as required in the scenario after TURP.
  • This would be less effective for irrigating blood clots compared to a 3-lumen catheter.

21 French 4 lumen catheter (Option C):

  • A 4-lumen catheter is not typically necessary for the standard postoperative irrigation required after TURP.
  • The additional lumen may not offer a significant benefit and could complicate the procedure.

22 Fr Macloey (Option D):

  • A Macloey catheter is designed for other purposes, such as urinary drainage, and is not tailored for efficient clot irrigation after TURP.
  • The 22 French size may be adequate for drainage, but it doesn't meet the specialized requirements for clot removal.

Key Takeaways:

A 21 French 3 lumen catheter is the appropriate choice for irrigating blood clots after TURP, as it facilitates effective removal and drainage of clots using the three-lumen design.

question_text: What is the likely cause of the following appearance in IVP?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows a cobra head appearance on intravenous pyelogram (IVP), which is characteristic of a ureterocele.

Ureterocele

  • Ureterocele is the congenital dilation of the distal ureter within the bladder wall, due to an obstruction in the development of the distal ureter during fetal growth,
  • can be either be a simple or ectopic type.
    • Simple Ureterocele (Intravesical - 20%):
      • Found entirely within the bladder and associated with a single ureter.
      • Less complex and easier to manage.
    • Ectopic Ureterocele (80%)
      • Extends beyond the bladder and often involves a duplicated ureter.
      • This is more complicated due to its location, which may involve the bladder, neck, or urethra.

Clinical Features

  • Recurrent Urinary Tract Infections (UTIs)/ Urosepsis.
  • Unilateral Hydroureteronephrosis.
  • Palpable Abdominal Mass: Particularly in children, where a distended bladder or large ureterocele might be felt as a mass.

Investigations

  • Ultrasound (USG):The first-line imaging modality revealing hydroureteronephrosis and a cystic structure in the bladder.
  • Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU): Demonstrates a filling defect in the bladder caused by the ureterocele.
  • Cystoscopy: Allows direct visualisation of the ureterocele as a cystic structure that enlarges and collapses with urine flow in the bladder.
  • Intravenous Pyelogram (IVP): The investigation of choice for diagnosing ureterocele, showing the characteristic "adder head" or "cobra head" appearance due to the dilated ureter within the bladder.

Treatment

  • Intravesical Ureterocele: ypically managed with an incision over the cyst wall to allow free flow of urine into the bladder, relieving the obstruction.
  • Ectopic Ureterocele: More complex, often requiring surgical excision of the ureterocele and reimplantation of the ureter into the bladder to correct the abnormal anatomy.

Explanation of other options:

Horseshoe kidney (Option A): congenital anomaly in which the lower poles of the kidneys are fused, forming a U-shape. On IVP, characteristic features include medially oriented calyces (Hand-Joining Sign) and high ureteral insertion with anterior transposition, producing the so-called Flower Vase appearance of the ureters.

Fig: IVP findings in horse-shoe kidney: A) Flower vase appearance; B) Hand-joining sign

Bladder tumour (Option C): ladder tumours may cause various structural changes in the bladder, but it normally does not result in the distinct cobra head appearance seen in the ureterocoele. Bladder tumours are more likely to show mass-like lesions or irregularities in the bladder contour.

Posterior urethral valve (Option D): osterior urethral valves are a congenital abnormality in males where there is a flap-like obstruction in the posterior urethra. This condition is typically diagnosed in infancy or childhood. While an IVP may show associated findings, such as bladder distention or bilateral hydronephrosis, it does not typically cause the cobra head appearance seen in the ureterocoele.

question_text: A 5 years old girl was brought to the hospital with a history of continuous dribbling of urine with a normal voiding pattern. What is the most likely cause?
option_b: Ureteric opening distal to external urinary sphincter
explanation:
Ectopic ureters

  • An ectopic ureter is one that drains to regions other than the bladder. Ectopic ureters are almost always associated with ureteric duplication and are bilateral in 10%. The femaleto-male ratio is 7:1. In females, the ectopic ureter opens either into the urethra below the sphincter or into the vagina .Such a child would complain of incontinence of urine despite normal voiding. In contrast, the male child is always continent as the ureter opens above the external urethral sphincter. Computed tomo-urography (CTU) or magnetic resonance urography (MRU) is diagnostic

question_text: Which statement is not correct regarding arterial and venous supply of urinary bladder?
option_a: The superior and inferior vesical arteries are derived from the anterior trunk of the internal iliac artery
option_b: Branches from the obturator and inferior gluteal arteries (and from the uterine and vaginal arteries in females) also help to supply the bladder
option_c: The veins form a plexus on the lateral and inferior surfaces of the bladder
option_d: In males the prostatic plexus is continuous with the vesical plexus, which drains into the external iliac vein
explanation:
Arterial supply of urinary bladder -

  • The main arterial supply of the bladder is the superior and inferior vesical arteries (derived from the anterior trunk of the internal iliac artery).
  • Branches from the obturator and inferior gluteal arteries (and from the uterine and vaginal arteries in females) also help to supply the bladder.

Venous drainage -

  • The veins form a plexus on the lateral and inferior surfaces of the bladder. Finally drain into the internal iliac veins.
  • In males, the prostatic plexus is continuous with the vesical plexus.
  • In females, similar large veins are continuous with the vaginal plexus.

Arterial supply

  • Superior vesical artery (from the umbilical artery, which arises from the internal iliac artery).
  • Inferior vesical artery (directly from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery, or in females from the vaginal artery, which arises from the internal iliac artery).
  • Division of the contralateral superior vesical pedicle can aid cephalad mobilisation of the bladder for psoas hitch procedures.

Venous drainage Vesical plexuses on the lateral and inferior surfaces of the bladder drain into the internal iliac vein (the prostatic plexus in males and the vaginal plexus in females are continuous with the vesical plexus).

Reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 83, The Urinary Bladder, Pg: 1486.

question_text:
Which of the following are storage symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia?
1. Urgency
2. Enuresis
3. Hesitancy
4. Frequency
5. Dribbling
explanation:
Explanation:

The symptoms of BPH are categorized into voiding (obstructive) and storage (irritative) symptoms. Storage symptoms are related to bladder overactivity and include:

  • Urgency (1): A sudden, compelling desire to urinate.
  • Frequency (4): Increased daytime voiding.
  • Nocturia: Nighttime frequency (not listed, but part of the group).
  • Enuresis (2): Involuntary urination, often at night.

Clinical features:

  • Obstructive symptoms (Voiding):
    • Poor flow/stream
    • Hesitancy (statement 3) (Option A ruled out)
    • Intermittency
    • Incomplete voiding-High post-void residual urine
    • Dribbling of urine (statement 5) (Option B and C ruled out)
  • Irritative symptoms (Storage):
    • Frequency
    • Urgency
    • Nocturia
  • Complications:
    • Retention
    • Haematuria
    • Urinary infection
    • Stone formation

Key Takeaways:

  • Storage (Irritative) symptoms: Urgency, Frequency, Nocturia, Enuresis.
  • Voiding (Obstructive) symptoms: Hesitancy, Poor stream, Intermittency, Incomplete emptying, Dribbling.

question_text: A 56 year old man was working in a benzene factory for a long time. He retired 5 years ago. What would be the possible complication in this patient?
What is the diagnosis based on the X-ray given below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The X-ray image shows radio-opaque shadows within the pelvis, which are consistent with bladder calculi.

Bladder calculi

  • Bladder stones can be classified into primary and secondary types based on their underlying causes.

Explanation of other options:

Renal calculi (Option A): Renal stones are usually located in the kidney or renal pelvis. While they may produce symptoms similar to bladder stones, their position is in the upper urinary tract, meaning they would appear above the bladder rather than inside it.

Schistosomiasis (Option C): Schistosomiasis, caused by Schistosoma species, can involve the bladder, leading to hematuria, fibrosis, and calcification. The resulting bladder wall calcifications produce a characteristic radiographic appearance resembling a fetal head in the pelvis. However, these calcifications differ from radio-opaque bladder stones and would not appear as such.

Ureteric calculi (Option D): Ureteric calculi are stones found in the ureters, the tubes that transport urine from the kidneys to the bladder. They often present with severe flank pain, hematuria, and signs of urinary obstruction. However, they are not typically located within the bladder, and in this case, the X-ray demonstrates radio-opaque shadows confined to the bladder rather than along the ureter.

question_text: A 68-year-old man presents to the outpatient clinic with progressively worsening difficulty in urination over the past 4 months. He reports increased urinary frequency, occasional nocturia, and a sensation of incomplete bladder emptying. He denies hematuria. On further questioning, he mentions an unintentional weight loss of 4 kg over the last 3 months. His father died of prostate cancer at the age of 72. On physical examination, digital rectal examination (DRE) reveals a firm, nodular area over the prostate. His PSA level is elevated for his age group. A prostate MRI shows a suspicious lesion arising from the prostate gland. Based on typical patterns of origin, from which zone of the prostate do carcinomas most commonly arise?
explanation:
Explanation:

The classification of the prostate into different zones by McNeal:

Peripheral zone: Lies mainly posteriorly and from which most carcinomas arise.

Central zone: Lies posterior to the urethral lumen and surrounds the ejaculatory ducts as they pass through the prostate.

Transitional zone: Periurethral in location. Most cases of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) arise from this zone.

question_text: A patient presented to hospital with increased frequency of micturition. On cystoscopy, pale ureteric orifice was seen. Bladder image is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
MRI of the above give image shows short contracted bladder called as thimble bladder, which is a characteristic feature of TB of genitourinary tract

The following image shows the various presentation of renal TB


  • Genitourinary tuberculosis (GUTB) accounts for 15-20% of extrapulmonary cases of TB. It is secondary and caused by haematogenous spread of tubercle bacilli from the thoracic lymph nodes or the lungs.
  • GUTB occurs as a result of either reinfection or reactivation of old TB granulomas. Blood-borne organisms are deposited close to the glomeruli, causing an inflammatory reaction.
  • Macrophages react and granulomas are formed. If bacterial multiplication goes unchecked, caseous necrosis results in the formation of tubercles. Multiple tubercles coalesce and rupture into the collecting system, causing intermittent tuberculous bacilluria and pyuria.
  • The disease spreads through the collecting system with ulceration initially. When bacterial multiplication is halted by the immune system, sequelae due to fibrosis appear .
  • Tubercular obstructing or destructive lesions in the kidneys and ureters are responsible for renal function loss.
  • Involvement of the bladder is secondary to renal disease. The disease gradually involves the bladder musculature, which is replaced by fibrous tissue, causing a decrease in the size and capacity of the bladder('thimble' bladder).Urinary bladder involvement isresponsible for urinary frequency, which isthe most common symptom of GUTB

    KEY TAKEAWAYS:

    Chronic TB features:

    • Cement or putty kidney
    • Golf hole ureter
    • Thimble bladder

    Early TB features:

    • Pale ureteric orifice
    • Blunting of calyx

question_text: Identify the given drain:

The image depicts a Romovac drain, a commonly used closed suction drain that applies negative pressure to collect postoperative fluid.

question_text: What instrument is used to insert this tube?
explanation:
Explanation:

A cystourethroscope is used to insert a double J (DJ) stent through the urethra into the urinary tract.

  • The image referred to is likely that of a double J (DJ) stent, a tube placed within the ureter to ensure patency and drainage from the kidney to the bladder.
  • The insertion of a DJ stent is commonly done through cystoscopy, where a cystourethroscope is introduced via the urethra into the bladder to visualize and access the ureteric orifice.
  • Once visualized, a guidewire is passed into the ureter, followed by the stent.
  • Cystourethroscope is a specialized endoscope used specifically for visualizing and operating on the urethra and bladder.
  • It's the standard instrument for diagnostic and therapeutic urologic interventions such as stent insertion, bladder tumor biopsy, and ureteric stone retrieval.

Explanation of other options:

Nephroscope (Option A): Used for percutaneous access to the renal pelvis during procedures like PCNL; not used for DJ stent insertion.

Ureteroscope (Option C): Used to access and treat ureteric or upper tract stones or tumors but is not used routinely for DJ stent placement, which is usually done under cystoscopic guidance.

Endoscope (Option D): A generic term for any internal visualization tool. It is not specific; cystourethroscope is the accurate, specific term for urinary stent placement.

question_text: What should be the initial course of action for a patient who has presented with a pelvic fracture and a rupture in the membranous urethra?
option_a: A suprapubic catheter should be inserted as soon as possible.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In a patient with a pelvic fracture and ruptured membranous urethra, the initial management is insertion of a suprapubic catheter for urinary diversion.
  • This ensures proper bladder drainage, prevents urinary retention, minimises the risk of extravasation, and avoids further urethral damage.
  • Suprapubic catheterisation serves as a temporary measure until definitive management, such as urethral repair, is performed.
  • Membranous urethral rupture represents a type of posterior urethral injury.
  • The posterior urethra comprises the prostatic and membranous segments, and such injuries are typically associated with pelvic fractures resulting from high-energy trauma (e.g., road traffic accidents).

Explanation of other options:

IVP (Option B): IVP can be useful for evaluating the urinary tract, but it is not the initial step in the management of a ruptured urethra. The patient should be stabilised first, with urinary diversion (via suprapubic catheter), before any imaging studies are done.

MCU should be done (Option D): Micturating Cystourethrogram (MCU) is an imaging study that evaluates the urethra and bladder during voiding. While it may be helpful in assessing the extent of a urethral injury, it is not the first step in management. The priority is to manage the patient's urinary diversion and stabilise them before any imaging studies are performed.

Chronic retention. In patients in whom the residual volume is >250 mL or so, the tension in the bladder wall increases owing to the combination of a large volume of residual urine and increased resting and filling bladder pressures (a condition known as high-pressure chronic retention). The increased intramural tension results in functional obstruction of the upper urinary. As a result, upper tract infection and renal impairment may develop. question_text: A 77 years old man with biopsy proven prostate cancer and serum PSA of 67 presents with following bone scan. What is the likely stage?

Bone scan shows multiple hot-spots suggestive of metastatic disease in a man with prostate cancer.

Once the diagnosis has been established, if metastatic spread is suspected (on the basis of a high PSA [>10 ng/mL], locally advanced disease or presence of Gleason 7 or higher) a bone scan should be carried out. If, however, the PSA is <10 ng/mL, then a bone scan would be performed only on clinical indications. question_text: All of the following are true regarding prostatic calculi, except?
option_a: Endogenous calculi are usually composed of calcium phosphate

Prostatic calculi usually require no treatment.

  • Are of two varieties -
    • Endogenous - Most common
    • Exogenous - Comparatively rare.

  • On radiographs or ultrasound scans, these stones are often seen to form a horseshoe or a circle.

PROSTATIC CALCULI Prostatic calculi are of two varieties: endogenous, which are common, and exogenous, which are comparatively rare. An exogenous prostatic calculus is a urinary (commonly ureteric) calculus that becomes arrested in the prostatic urethra. Endogenous prostatic calculi are usually composed of calcium phosphate combined with about 20% organic material.

question_text: A 77-year-old man presented with worsening hip and back pain. He also reports weight loss and loss of appetite. His PSA levels are elevated. What is the most likely diagnosis here?
explanation:
Explanation:

In an elderly male, new bone pain (especially in the axial skeleton like spine and hips), constitutional symptoms (weight loss, anorexia), and an elevated PSA are a classic presentation of metastatic prostate cancer. Carcinoma prostate, predominantly an adenocarcinoma, is more common in individuals of higher socio-economic status, particularly Afro-Americans, and typically occurs in the 7th-8th decade of life.

It is often asymptomatic in early stages, with symptoms appearing later due to local spread or metastasis, commonly presenting as backache from lumbar vertebral involvement or pelvic and obturator lymph node metastasis.

Diagnosis is based on digital rectal examination (hard, nodular prostate with loss of median sulcus) and confirmed by TRUS-guided biopsy; endorectal MRI is preferred for staging, while TRUS may also be used. Prostascint using radiolabeled monoclonal antibodies detects soft tissue and nodal metastasis. PSA is the primary tumor marker; although nonspecific and elevated in benign conditions, levels >20 ng/mL are strongly suggestive of carcinoma prostate.

Explanation of other options:

Ankylosing spondylitis (Option A): This is an inflammatory arthritis of young men, causing back stiffness and pain but not weight loss or elevated PSA.

Osteosarcoma (Option B): This is a primary bone cancer of children and young adults, not the elderly. It causes a painful bone mass, not diffuse pain.

Osteoclastoma (Giant Cell Tumor of Bone) (Option D): This is a benign but locally aggressive bone tumor typically found around the knees of young adults. It does not cause elevated PSA.

Key Takeaways:

  • Bone pain in an elderly man with an elevated PSA is metastatic prostate cancer until proven otherwise.
  • PSA is a crucial tumor marker for prostate cancer.

question_text: Prostate needle biopsy by single core shows acinar adenocarcinoma, predominant poorly formed glands in cribriform pattern followed by crowded but separated glands and a minor component (5%) of single cell infiltration. What is the grade of tumor?
explanation:
Prostatic biopsy

Histological appearances

The prostate is a glandular structure consisting of ducts and acini; thus, the histological pattern is one of an adenocarcinoma. The prostatic glands are surrounded by a layer of myoepithelial cells. The first change associated with carcinoma is the loss of the basement membrane, with glands appearing to be in confluence. As the cell type becomes less differentiated, more solid sheets of carcinoma cells are seen.

A classification of the histological pattern based on the degree of glandular differentiation and its relation to stroma has been devised by Gleason. Prostate cancers exhibit heterogeneity within tissue, and so two histological areas of the prostate are each scored between 3 and 5. Grades 1 and 2 are now not reported as their outcome is similar to grade 3. Grade 3 cancers almost never metastasise. The scores are added to give an overall Gleason score of between 6 and 10; this (and the volume of the cancer) appears to correlate well with the likelihood of spread and the prognosis. The International Society of Urological Pathology (ISUP) and WHO have recommended a simplified grading system composed of five prognostic grade groups. Each group has prognostic significance and a higher grade group has a poorer prognosis.

Grade groups are as follows:

  • 1 = Gleason score 3 + 3 = 6
  • 2 = Gleason score 3 + 4 = 7
  • 3 = Gleason score 4 + 3 = 7
  • 4 = Gleason score 8 (4 + 4 = 8, 3 + 5 = 8, 5 + 3 = 8)
  • 5 = Gleason score ≥9 (4 + 5 = 9, 5 + 4 = 9, 5 + 5 = 10)

question_text: What is the preferred treatment option for a 85 years old patient, known case of prostate cancer with Gleason score 6, having 2 * 3 cm nodule in prostate and level of PSA is 8 ng/ml?
explanation:
• Age is more than 70 so surgical options are ruled out.
  • Subcapsular orchidectomy can be done in old patients with prostatic ca
  • And all findings are not matched with suspicion of Ca prostate so regular follow up is the ideal.
  • Low-risk disease: For men in their seventies, c vative treatment would usually be the correct approach. Radical surgical treatment might be considered in younger (<70 years) men with this form of the disease and/or with a family history, although, even in this group, some men will elect to pursue a conservative course (active surveillance) when counselled about risks versus benefts (impotence/ incontinence).
  • Intermediate-risk: disease. In younger (<70 years), ftter men, this may be treated by radical prostatectomy or radical radiotherapy. Active monitoring remains an option, particularly for more elderly patients towards the lower end of the risk spectrum. In elderly patients with outfow obstruction, transurethral resection with or without hormone therapy is indicated. The beneft of radical treatment over a conservative approach is likely to be about 25%, given that progression to metastatic disease is of this order of magnitude after 10 years.
  • High-risk disease: These patients are at signifcant risk of disease progression. They need multimodal therapy. Early androgen ablation is favoured if close follow-up is not possible. For the sexually active, a careful conservative approach with the adoption of androgen ablation when symptoms arise is reasonable. Androgen ablation coupled with radiotherapy, perhaps with surgery (radical prostatectomy plus salvage radiotherapy) as part of a multimodal approach, is standard treatment for younger men with T3 disease.
  • Metastatic disease: Once metastases have developed, the outlook is poor. For patients with symptoms, there is no dilemma; androgen ablation will provide symptomatic relief in over two-thirds of patients. For patients with asymptomatic metastases, the timing of treatment is less clear. Systemic chemotherapy with docetaxel should be considered in younger, ftter men.

question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with low back pain and weight loss. He reports progressive urinary difficulty and had an episode of acute urinary retention two days ago, which was relieved by catheterization. Investigations reveal a PSA of 5.2 ng/mL and osteoblastic lesions on lumbosacral spine X-ray. What is the most likely clinical diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of urinary obstructive symptoms, a mildly elevated PSA, and osteoblastic lesions on spinal X-ray strongly suggests prostate cancer with possible bony metastases.

Carcinoma Prostate

  • Prostate carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor in men over 65 years.
  • Typically originates in the peripheral zone of the prostate.
  • Clinical features
    • Early disease is usually asymptomatic and may be detected:
      • Incidentally after TURP for benign disease (T1a/b)
      • By PSA screening (T1c)
      • As a palpable nodule on digital rectal exam (T2)
    • Advanced disease may produce symptoms such as:
      • Bladder outlet obstruction
      • Pelvic pain and hematuria
      • Bone pain, malaise, arthritis-like symptoms, anemia or pancytopenia

Management of Prostate Cancer:

  • Localised cancers can be managed with radical prostatectomy, radiation therapy, or active surveillance.
  • Advanced disease is usually palliative: hormonal ablation is first-line, and chemotherapy is used when hormonal therapy fails, offering short-term benefits.

Explanation of other options:

Benign prostatic hypertrophy (Option A): Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) can lead to urinary symptoms such as difficulty in urination and urinary retention, but it is not associated with weight loss or osteoblastic bone lesions on X-ray. Moreover, while PSA may be mildly elevated in BPH, it typically does not reach the levels often observed in prostate cancer.

Carcinoma bladder (Option B): Bladder cancer can produce urinary symptoms such as hematuria, dysuria, or obstructive voiding, but it rarely causes osteoblastic bone lesions, and PSA elevation is not a typical feature of this condition.

Renal cell cancer (Option D): Renal cell carcinoma typically presents with hematuria, flank pain, and a palpable abdominal mass. However, the patient's urinary symptoms, elevated PSA, and osteoblastic spinal lesions are not characteristic of renal cell carcinoma.

question_text: Which of the following is the most specific clinical use of PSA in management of prostate cancer?
option_d: Prognosis, survival of prostate cancer patient
explanation:
Explanation:

PSA is a glycoprotein produced by prostatic epithelial cells. Altered architecture of the prostate in conditions such as BPH, prostatitis and prostate cancer allows PSA to enter the bloodstream and be detected by a blood test. The commonly used PSA assays measure the total amount of PSA (tPSA). PSA levels can be influenced by certain drugs, most notably 5α-reductase inhibitors used to treat men with LUTS, but also by aspirin, statins and thiazide diuretics. The PSA test can be significantly influenced by a recent UTI and the true PSA level only returns to baseline 6 weeks after eradication of an infection. The finding of a PSA >10 ng/mL is suggestive of cancer and >35 ng/mL is almost diagnostic of advanced prostate cancer, in the absence of active urinary tract infection. A decrease in PSA to the normal range following hormonal ablation is a good prognostic sign. Following radical prostatectomy the serum PSA should fall to undetectable levels (the limit for detection for modern supersensitive assays is <0.03 ng/mL). Men in whom a diagnosis of early prostate cancer might influence treatment option (such as those under 70 years or those with a positive family history who might be offered radical treatment) should be offered a PSA measurement. If the PSA range is 4-10 ng/L, a free-to-total PSA ratio of less than 15% should be suspicious of malignancy.

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Monitoring the response to treatment

  • PSA can be used for treatment monitoring, especially post-radical prostatectomy or androgen deprivation therapy, but this is a secondary use-not the most specific

Choice C: Diagnosing BPH

  • PSA may be elevated in BPH, but it is not used to diagnose BPH specifically, as the elevation is nonspecific and can occur in multiple prostate conditions.

Choice D: Prognosis, survival of prostate cancer patient

  • PSA levels may correlate with tumor burden and prognosis, but this is an indirect association. PSA is not a standalone tool for survival prediction.

Key Takeaway

  • PSA testing is most specifically used for screening prostate cancer, especially in men with risk factors or where early detection may change management.

question_text: A 60-year-old patient undergoes TURP and, three days later, develops drowsiness and altered sensorium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient is experiencing altered sensitivity and drowsiness 3 days after undergoing TURP (Transurethral Resection of the Prostate), raising suspicion for hyponatremia as the most likely diagnosis.

TURP syndrome

  • TURP Syndrome is a complication that can occur after a TURP procedure, which results from excessive absorption of irrigating fluids during the surgery.
  • High volumes of hypotonic irrigation fluid used during the resection, causing dilutional hyponatremia and various neurologic symptoms like confusions and other cerebral events mimicking a stroke.
  • Risk factors
    • Size of prostate > 75g
    • Duration of surgery > 90 minutes
    • Pre-existing hyponatremia
    • Renal failure
  • Treatment
    • Drug of choice: IV furosemide.
    • Mild to moderate cases: IV furosemide and normal saline
    • Severe or symptomatic patients: IV 3% Saline
    • Fluid restriction: Useful after initial stabilisation and correction of severe hyponatremia to prevent further fluid overload.

Explanation of other options:

Hypernatremia (Option A): Symptoms of hypernatremia include thirst, muscle twitching, muscle weakness, seizures and confusion. It is less likely in this case since the patient is experiencing drowsiness, which is more characteristic of hyponatremia.

Stroke (Option C): Stroke can present with altered consciousness or neurological deficits such as hemiparesis or aphasia. However, stroke symptoms typically present suddenly and are not typically related to a postoperative time frame of 3 days. Hyponatremia is a more common cause of these symptoms after TURP.

Meningitis due to spinal anaesthesia (Option D): This is a rare complication, with symptoms including fever, headache, neck stiffness, nausea, vomiting and photophobia.

Reference:

https://litfl.com/turp-syndrome/
