question_text: Which of the following is not true regarding radical prostatectomy for prostate cancer?
option_b: Should be carried out only in men with a life expectancy of < 10 yrs
option_c: Exclusion of metastases would be required before surgery
option_d: Results in a high incidence of impotence
explanation:
Radical prostatectomy is suitable for-

  • Localised disease
  • Carried out only in men with a life expectancy of >10 years.
  • Exclusion of metastases would require a negative bone scan and MRI of the pelvis.

Procedure -

Removal of the prostate down to the distal urethral sphincter, in addition to the seminal vesicles. The bladder neck is reconstituted and anastomosed to the urethra.

It results in a high incidence of impotence, but a low incidence of severe stress incontinence (<2%), which may require the fitting of an artificial urinary sphincter or urethral sling.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 84, The prostate and seminal vesicles, Pg: 1536.

question_text: A patient presents to the OPD with a 6-month history of painful erections and a deviation of the penis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient with a six-month history of painful erections and penile deviation is most likely diagnosed with Peyronie's disease, a condition characterized by fibrous plaque formation in the tunica albuginea.

Peyronie's Disease

  • Condition is characterised by penile deformity, palpable plaques inside the penis, erectile dysfunction and painful erections.
  • Most probable cause involved is minor injury to erect penis with secondary microhemorrhages beneath the tunia albuginea and fibrosis.
  • The fibrous plaques in the tunica albuginea of the penis, causing abnormal curvature during erections.
  • Plaques are typically on the dorsolateral aspect of the penis.
  • Deformity is usually dorsal (towards the abdomen).
  • This is usually and clinical diagnosis, but an MRI may be helpful.

Management

Medical management

  • Most cases improve spontaneously without intervention.
  • Intralesional therapy: Clostridium histolyticum collagenase injections are effective in selected patients.
  • Oral drugs (variable efficacy): Pentoxifylline, Colchicine, Vitamin E.

Surgical management (reserved for severe, persistent cases with significant deformity)

  • Tunica albuginea plication (on the side opposite the curvature)
    • Suitable only if penile length is adequate.
    • Techniques: Nesbit procedure and 16-dot technique.
  • Plaque incision/excision with grafting (e.g., bovine pericardial patch)
    • Used in severe curvature or when penile shortening is a concern.

Explanation of other options:

Priapism (Option B): In priapism, there is a prolonged, painful erection unrelated to sexual activity or curvature, caused by abnormal penile blood flow. It is a urological emergency requiring immediate treatment..

Marion's disease (Option C): A condition causing urinary obstruction due to functional or structural changes at the bladder neck, mimicking prostatic enlargement but without prostate abnormality.

Erectile dysfunction (Option D): Erectile dysfunction is the inability to achieve or maintain an erection sufficient for sexual intercourse. It is not associated with pain or penile curvature. In some cases, pain or discomfort may accompany an erection, but it is not the primary symptom of ED.

question_text: Genetic testing for BRCA 1/BRCA 2 is indicated for all of the following except:
option_a: Breast cancer diagnosed in a postmenopausal female >50 years of age
explanation:
Explanation:

Genetic testing for BRCA1 and BRCA2 mutations is usually not recommended for women diagnosed with breast cancer after the age of 50, as the likelihood of detecting a clinically relevant mutation in this age group is low.

Indications for Testing:

  • Any individual with a known pathogenic or likely pathogenic variant in a cancer susceptibility gene in the family.
  • Breast cancer diagnosed at age ≤50 years.
  • Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) diagnosed at age ≤60 years. (Option D ruled out)
  • Two primary breast cancers in the same individual. (Option C ruled out)
  • Breast cancer at any age with one or more relatives diagnosed with:
    • Breast cancer ≤50 years
    • Invasive ovarian cancer
    • Male breast cancer (Option B ruled out)
    • Pancreatic cancer
    • High-grade or metastatic prostate cancer
  • Breast cancer at any age with two or more affected relatives.
  • Male breast cancer.
  • Personal or family history of three or more of the following conditions:
    • Breast cancer, sarcoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, brain tumour, leukemia
    • Colon cancer, endometrial cancer, thyroid cancer, kidney cancer, dermatological manifestations, macrocephaly, hamartomatous gastrointestinal polyps
    • Lobular breast cancer, diffuse gastric cancer
    • Breast cancer, gastrointestinal cancer, ovarian sex cord tumours, pancreatic cancer, testicular Sertoli cell tumours, or childhood skin pigmentation.

question_text: Which statement is not correct regarding muscle invasive bladder carcinoma?
option_a: Bimanual examination should be performed before and after resection of the tumour
option_b: Complete urinary tract assessment should be performed, including CT, MR and IV urography
option_c: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy does not improve survival rates
option_d: Locally advanced disease may be downstaged by radiotherapy or chemotherapy to enable salvage cystectomy
explanation:
Neoadjuvant chemotherapy improves survival rates.

Muscle invasive bladder carcinoma -

  • Includes T2, T3 and T4
  • Has the worst prognosis as the incidence of metastasis is much more common.
  • Complete urinary tract assessment should be performed, including CT, MR and IV urography
  • A bimanual examination performed both before and after surgery helps in staging these tumours. The bladder should be empty. A mass palpable bimanually at the end of the procedure is stage pT3. When invasion has spread into the prostate in a man or the vagina in a woman it is classified as pT4a. If the tumour is fixed to the lateral pelvic side wall it is staged as pT4b.

Treatment -

  • Radical cystectomy, urinary diversion and thorough lymph node dissection f/b chemotherapy is done depending on the stage of the tumor.
  • Neoadjuvant chemotherapy improves survival rates.
  • Locally advanced disease may be downstaged by radiotherapy or chemotherapy to enable salvage cystectomy.

The management depends upon the stage, grade and risk stratification. Low-risk localised tumours may be managed with endoscopic ablation or segmental excision. Kidney-sparing surgery is important in patients with solitary kidney, renal insufficiency and synchronous bilateral tumours. High-risk tumours warrant radical nephroureterectomy with bladder cuff resection with or without lymphadenectomy. Locally advanced disease is usually treated with cisplatinum-based neoadjuvant chemotherapy to downstage the disease prior to surgical ablation. Adjuvant chemotherapy has been shown to improve survival.

Reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1481.

question_text: All are true regarding non-specific urethritis, except?
option_a: NSU can affect both men and women
option_b: NSU is a STI that is the commonest cause of urethritis
option_c: In around 40% of cases it is due to Gonorrhea
option_d: The standard treatment regimes are azithromycin as a single dose or doxycycline orally for 7 days
explanation:
Explanation:

NSU is an STI that is the most common cause of urethritis in the Western world (Option B).

In around 40% of cases, it is due to Chlamydia trachomatis; in the remaining cases, it is caused by Ureaplasma urealyticum, Trichomonas vaginalis, or Mycoplasma genitalium.

The causative agent in up to 50% of cases is unknown. It can affect both men and women, and asymptomatic infection is common in both (Option A).

In men, dysuria and a white mucopurulent urethral discharge appear up to 6 weeks after sexual intercourse. The urine seems clear but may contain 'threads' or pus cells. Epididymitis is common, and urethral stricture is a potential late complication.

In women, the condition is usually asymptomatic, although it can present as vaginal discharge or as a form of urethrotrigonitis. It may result in cervicitis or pelvic inflammatory disease.

The standard treatment regimens are azithromycin as a single dose or doxycycline orally for 7 days (Option D). Treatment is usually effective, although relapse is common, especially in men, in whom the prostate may act as a reservoir of infection.

question_text: Not true regarding prostatic abscess?
option_b: Severe, unremitting perineal and rectal pain
option_c: Transrectal ultrasound may aid in diagnosis
option_d: Nonsurgical management with antibiotics is the treatment of choice
explanation:
Prostatic abscess -

  • Presents with temperature rising steeply with rigors, severe, unremitting perineal and rectal pain with occasional tenesmus. Can be confused with an anorectal abscess.
  • Antibiotic usage disguises these features.
  • Rectal examination - Enlarged, hot, extremely tender and fluctuant prostate.
  • Transrectal ultrasound or MRI may aid diagnosis.

Treatment -

  • The abscess should be drained without delay by perurethral resection (unroofing the whole cavity) or using a needle via the transrectal or perineal route.
  • Antibiotic therapy.
  • Suprapubic catheterisation if retention of urine present.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 84, The prostate and seminal vesicles, Pg: 1537.

question_text: Which is not a preferable treatment option for chronic prostatitis?
option_a: Trimethoprim or ciprofloxacin penetrate well into the prostate
option_b: Metronidazole is used if the causative organism is Trichomonas
option_c: If Chlamydia is suspected, doxycycline is the antibiotic treatment of choice
option_d: Radical prostatectomy is the treatment of choice
explanation:
Chronic prostatitis -

  • Antibiotic therapy is the mainstay of treatment. Should be administered in accordance with sensitivity tests.
  • Trimethoprim or ciprofloxacin penetrate well into the prostate.
  • If Trichomonas or anaerobes are the responsible agent, a rapid response is obtained from administration of metronidazole (200 mg TDS for 7 days to both partners).
  • If Chlamydia is suspected, doxycycline is the antibiotic treatment of choice.
  • There is little evidence that prostatic massage helps in eradicating the infection.

Chronic prostatitis Many urologists find the diagnosis of chronic prostatitis and 'proctodynia' very difficult as many men present with peri genital pain, testicular pain, prostatic pain exacerbated by sexual intercourse or pain that apparently renders sexual intercourse out of the question. Psychosexual dysfunction in such patients may be the underlying problem.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 84, The prostate and seminal vesicles, Pg: 1537.

option_b: Severe, unremitting perineal and rectal pain
option_c: Transrectal ultrasound may aid in diagnosis
option_d: Nonsurgical management with antibiotics is the treatment of choice
explanation:
Explanation:

Prostatic abscess presents with a temperature rising steeply with rigours, severe, unremitting perineal and rectal pain with occasional tenesmus (Options A and B).

It can be confused with an anorectal abscess.

On rectal examination, the prostate is enlarged, hot, extremely tender and fluctuant.

Transrectal ultrasound or MRI may aid diagnosis (Option C).

The abscess should be drained without delay by perurethral resection (unroofing the whole cavity) or using a needle via the transrectal or perineal route, followed by IV antibiotics.

Suprapubic catheterisation if retention of urine is present.

explanation:
The drugs which can be used to treat prostate cancer include -

A] Androgen deprivation therapy-

  • Flutamide, Cyproterone acetate, Nilutamide, Bicalutamide

B] GnRH (Gonadotrophin Releasing Hormone) analogues-

C] Recently agents such as enzalutamide (a second generation androgen receptor blocker), degarelix (an LHRH antagonist), abiraterone (a drug that blocks the production of testosterone from its precursors) have shown to promote survival in metastatic prostate cancer.

Goserelin

Analogues of gonadotropin-releasing hormone, continued use produces downregulation of the anterior pituitary with consequent fall in testosterone levels.

question_text:
For which type(s) of cancer is prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) typically given?
1. Lung cancer
2. Liver cancer
3. Prostate cancer
4. Breast cancer
explanation:
Explanation:

Prophylactic cranial irradiation (PCI) is primarily used to reduce the risk of brain metastases in cancers that have a high likelihood of spreading to the central nervous system.

Lung Cancer:

  • PCI is most commonly administered in small cell lung cancer (SCLC) due to its aggressive nature and high tendency to metastasize to the brain.
  • It has been shown to improve overall survival and decrease the incidence of brain metastases in patients who respond to initial treatment.

Breast Cancer:

  • PCI may be considered in select cases of breast cancer, particularly in patients at high risk for brain metastases.
  • This includes aggressive subtypes such as HER2-positive and triple-negative breast cancer. 

Options A, B, and D are incorrect.

Reference:

question_text: A patient presents with prostate carcinoma, which has now spread to the vertebra. What is the route of spread to the lumbar vertebra?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The spread of prostate carcinoma to the vertebra most commonly occurs through Batson's plexus, also known as the vertebral venous plexus.
  • This venous network is valveless, which allows retrograde flow of blood from the pelvic venous system to the spinal venous system.
  • This retrograde pathway facilitates the direct hematogenous spread of malignant cells from the prostate to the lumbar vertebrae, explaining the frequent skeletal metastases in advanced prostate cancer.

Routes of Spread in Prostate Carcinoma:

  • Haematogenous spread (most common): Via Batson's plexus → skeletal metastases (pelvic bones, lumbar vertebrae).
  • Local spread: To bladder, seminal vesicles, and rectum.
  • Lymphatic spread: To pelvic and para-aortic nodes.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Transcoelomic spread (Option B): Refers to tumor dissemination across peritoneal surfaces (e.g., ovarian carcinoma), not typical of prostate carcinoma metastasis.

Inferior vesical vein (Option C): Drains the prostate into the internal iliac vein but does not provide a direct channel to the vertebral venous system.

Internal iliac vein (Option D): Drains pelvic organs, including the prostate, but is not the route responsible for vertebral metastasis.

Key Takeaway:

The characteristic spread of prostate carcinoma to the lumbar vertebrae occurs through Batson's plexus, a valveless venous network that allows retrograde flow and facilitates skeletal metastases.

Which of the following is true about colon cancer
1. Colon cancer incidence is decreased by metformin
2. Right and left colon cancers have different presentations
3. Colon cancers can be hereditary
4. Colon cancers frequently metastasize to the liver
explanation:
• Metformin is biguanide commonly used for the treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus but it also helps in reducing the risk of developing colon cancer, it deregulates cellular energy supply by inhibiting aerobic glycolysis.
  • Metformin has shown results to reduce the risk of pancreatic, breast and prostate cancer also
  • NSAID's, aspirin and metformin are drugs having protective effect for colon cancer
  • Colonic cancer can spread locally, via the lymphatics, bloodstream (haematogenous) or across the peritoneal cavity (transcoelomic spread).
  • Direct spread may be longitudinal or radial.
  • Involvement of the lymph nodes by tumour progresses from those closest to the bowel along the course of lymphatics to central nodes
  • Haematogenous spread is most commonly to the liver via the portal vein.
  • Hereditary colon cancer: HNPCC, FAP
  • Colon cancer is associated with consumption of red meat and particularly processed red meat products

  • Cholecystectomy may marginally increase the risk of right colon cancer
  • IBD is a risk factor for colon cancer
  • Left side of the colon is usually present with a change in bowel habit or rectal bleeding, obstruction
  • Right side (proximal lesions) typically present with iron deficiency anaemia, melena or a mass.

question_text: A 68-year-old man presents to the outpatient department with low backache. His prostate-specific antigen (PSA) level is 100 ng/mL. Which of the following drugs is indicated for his treatment?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient's low back pain and markedly elevated PSA (100 ng/mL) suggest prostate cancer.
  • Goserelin, a GnRH agonist, is the drug of choice.
  • It reduces testosterone levels, slowing the growth of testosterone-dependent prostate cancer cells, and is particularly useful in advanced or metastatic disease.

Carcinoma Prostate

  • Prostate carcinoma is the most common malignant tumor in men over 65 years.
  • Typically originates in the peripheral zone of the prostate.
  • Clinical features
    • Early disease is usually asymptomatic and may be detected:
      • Incidentally after TURP for benign disease (T1a/b)
      • By PSA screening (T1c)
      • As a palpable nodule on digital rectal exam (T2)
    • Advanced disease may produce symptoms such as:
      • Bladder outlet obstruction
      • Pelvic pain and hematuria
      • Bone pain, malaise, arthritis-like symptoms, anemia or pancytopenia

Management of Prostate Cancer:

  • Localized cancers can be managed with radical prostatectomy, radiation therapy, or active surveillance.
  • Advanced disease is usually palliative: hormonal ablation is first-line, and chemotherapy is used when hormonal therapy fails, offering short-term benefit.

Hormonal therapy in prostate cancer

  • Hormonal therapy for prostate cancer reduces testosterone, shrinking the tumour. This can be achieved by
    • Orchiectomy
    • GnRH agonists: Goserelin, Leuprolide
    • GnRH antagonists: Degarelix
    • Anti-androgens: Bicalutamide

Explanation of other options:

Somatostatin (Option A): Somatostatin analogues such as octreotide and lanreotide are used in treating conditions like acromegaly, carcinoid tumours, and neuroendocrine tumours.

Terlipressin (Option B): Terlipressin is a synthetic analogue of vasopressin and is primarily used for the management of variceal bleeding in cirrhosis with portal hypertension.

Testosterone (Option D): Testosterone (Option D) is not used to treat prostate cancer because it promotes tumor growth; administering it would worsen the disease rather than provide any benefit.

Reference:

https://www.cancer.org/cancer/types/prostate-cancer/treating/hormone-therapy.html

question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of increasing urinary frequency and nocturia four times per night. Lifestyle modifications, including reducing evening fluid and caffeine intake, have not helped. On examination, the prostate is palpably enlarged with a smooth surface and a firm, rubbery, non-tender consistency. The physician suspects benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH). Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of BPH?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Increased trabeculations in the bladder are not characteristic features of BPH.
  • Trabeculations refer to irregular muscular bands or folds in the bladder wall, commonly seen in conditions of chronic bladder outlet obstruction, where the bladder muscle hypertrophies due to long-term pressure, but increased trabeculations in the bladder is not commonly seen.

Benign Prostate Hyperplasia (BPH)

  • Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) commonly affects men over 50 years.
  • It is the most frequent cause of lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS) and bladder outlet obstruction (BOO) in men, especially those over 70 years of age.
  • Most common site of origin is submucosal glands of the periurethral transitional zone
  • Clinical features include lower urinary tract infections and symtpoms due to bladder outlet obstruction with
    • Decreased urinary flow rate
    • Increased voiding pressure

Evaluation in BPH

Management of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)

  • Conservative measures: Watchful waiting, fluid management (avoid fluid binging and late-night intake), and reduction of caffeine and alcohol.
  • Medical therapy:
    • α-blockers to relax smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck.
    • 5α-reductase inhibitors for men with larger prostates, or combination therapy for glands >35 g, which improves outcomes.
  • Interventional measures:
    • Transurethral resection of the prostate (TURP) - gold standard.
    • HOLEP (holmium laser enucleation), open or robotic simple prostatectomy for very large glands.
    • Minimally invasive options: Prostate artery embolization (PAE), water vapor therapy (Rezum), and other emerging techniques.

Explanation of other options:

J-shaped/ fish hook proximal ureter (Option B), J-shaped/ fish hook distal ureters (Option C): J-shaped or "fish-hook" ureters are commonly seen in bladder outlet obstruction, such as BPH. Increased bladder pressure can alter the course of the ureters, producing tortuosity or a hook-like appearance, particularly in the distal ureters.

Bilateral hydronephrosis (Option D): Hydronephrosis refers to the dilatation or swelling of the kidneys caused by the blockage of urine flow from the bladder. BPH can result in bladder outlet obstruction, which leads to urine backing up into the kidneys, ultimately causing hydronephrosis.

explanation:
Explanation:

  • The MCU image demonstrates a short, narrowed segment involving the bulbar urethra, which is diagnostic of a bulbar urethral stricture.
  • This condition is commonly caused by trauma, especially straddle injuries, or iatrogenic factors like catheterization.
  • Patients typically present with poor urinary stream, straining during micturition, or recurrent urinary tract infections.
  • The retrograde urethrogram (RGU)is considered the gold standard investigation, but MCU is often used in conjunction to assess the proximal urethra and bladder outlet.

Male Urethra: Fibromuscular tube extending from the bladder neck to the meatus and functions to transport urine and semen.

  1. Posterior urethra: Prostatic urethra and membranous urethra.
  2. Anterior urethra: Bulbar urethra, Penile urethra, and Urethral meatus.
  • Urethral Meatus: Vertical slit-like opening at the tip of the glans penis.
  • Glandular Urethra,also known as the fossa navicularis.
  • Penile Urethra: Extends from the meatus to the penoscrotal junction. The longest part of the urethra
  • Bulbar Urethra: Extends from the penoscrotal junction to the bulbomembranous junction.
  • Membranous Urethra: Extends from the bulbomembranous junction to the verumontanum. The shortest, narrowest, and least dilated partis innervated by the pudendal nerve from spinal segments S2-4.
  • Prostatic Urethra: Extends from the bladder neck to the verumontanum and is surrounded by the prostate. The widest and most dilatable part of the urethra.

Explanation of other options:

Membranous urethral injury (Option B): Seen in posterior urethra, usually due to pelvic fractures. Imaging shows extravasation or abrupt cutoff, not a smooth narrowing.

Urethral tear (Option C): Appears as leakage of contrast outside the urethral lumen, unlike the structured narrowing of a stricture.

Prostate hyperplasia (Option D): Produces bladder outlet obstruction but does not cause focal urethral narrowing on MCU.

question_text: A patient with a history of trauma has sustained a rupture of the bulbar urethra. In which anatomical space does urine typically accumulate?
explanation:
Explanation:

The superficial pouch (superficial perineal space) lies between the perineal membrane and superficial fascia. It contains structures such as the root of the penis and the bulb of the penis (which includes the bulbar urethra). In the case of bulbar urethral rupture, urine extravasates into this pouch and collects there.

Anterior vs. Posterior Urethral Injuries

Explanation of other options:

Deep pouch (Option B): Also called the deep perineal space, it lies above the perineal membrane. It does not communicate directly with the bulbar urethra; hence urine does not accumulate here after bulbar rupture.

Rectouterine pouch (Option C): Also known as the pouch of Douglas, it is a peritoneal recess between uterus and rectum (in females). It is unrelated to urethral injury.

Uterovesical pouch (Option D): A peritoneal space between bladder and uterus (in females). It is not involved in bulbar urethral rupture.

Key Takeaways:

  • Bulbar urethral rupture → urine extravasates into superficial perineal pouch.
  • Posterior urethral rupture → associated with pelvic fractures and high-riding prostate.
  • RGU is gold standard for diagnosis of urethral injury.

question_text: A 60-year-old man presents with lower back pain. Imaging reveals sclerotic lesions in the vertebrae. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Carcinoma of the prostate commonly metastasizes to bones, especially the spine, pelvis, ribs, and femur, producing osteoblastic (sclerotic) lesions due to increased osteoblast activity. In elderly males, vertebral sclerotic lesions with back pain are highly suggestive of prostate carcinoma.

Explanation of other options:

Tuberculosis (Option B): Spinal tuberculosis (Pott's disease) leads to vertebral collapse and destruction, producing lytic lesions, not sclerotic ones.

Renal cell carcinoma (Option C): While RCC can metastasize to bone, the lesions are usually lytic rather than sclerotic.

Carcinoma colon (Option D): Colorectal cancer can metastasize to bones but does not typically present with sclerotic lesions; lytic changes are more common.

Carcinoma Prostate with Bone Metastases

Key Takeaways:

  • Sclerotic bone lesions = Prostate cancer metastases.
  • RCC and colon cancers → lytic lesions.
  • Tuberculosis → vertebral destruction and collapse.

question_text: What is the initial management approach for urinary symptoms in a patient with benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)?
explanation:
Explanation:

The first-line therapy for a patient with Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH) is typically Tamsulosin, which is an α-1 adrenergic receptor blocker.

Management of Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia (BPH)

Medical Management

  • First-line Therapy: α-1 Blockers such as Prazosin, Terazosin, Silodosin. The most widely prescribed agent is Tamsulosin (an α-1A selective blocker) (Option B).
  • Second-line Therapy: 5-α Reductase Inhibitors including Finasteride (Option C ruled out), Dutasteride, and Triptorelin pamoate.
  • Combination Therapy: A mix of an α-1 blocker with a 5-α reductase inhibitor is recommended for patients with a significantly enlarged prostate.

Surgical Management

  • Indications:
    • Lack of response to medical treatment
    • Acute urinary retention
      • Initial step: Urethral catheterization
      • If unsuccessful: Suprapubic cystostomy (SPC)
    • Chronic urinary retention with residual urine exceeding 200 ml.
    • Complications such as hydroureter, hydronephrosis, stone formation, recurrent infections, or gross haematuria.
  • Surgical Procedures:
    • Gold Standard: TURP (Transurethral Resection of the Prostate) (Option A ruled out)
    • TUIP (Transurethral Incision of the Prostate)
    • Open Prostatectomy Procedures

Observation (Option D):

  • Suitable for mild, asymptomatic BPH without significant impact on quality of life
  • Requires regular monitoring and lifestyle modifications
  • If symptoms progress, α-1 blockers such as Tamsulosin are initiated, as observation alone is not the standard initial approach

question_text: A young male patient with a history of a motor vehicle accident cannot pass urine. Blood is seen at the meatus. What is the most likely site of urethral injury?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Pelvic fractures from road traffic accidents are the classic cause of membranous urethral injury.
  • The presence of blood at the meatus and inability to void strongly point to this site of injury.
  • Retrograde urethrography typically shows extravasation proximal to the bulbar urethra, confirming a membranous urethral injury.

Membranous Urethra Injury

Location

  • Most often occurs at the bulbomembranous junction.

Common Causes

  • Pelvic fractures following motor vehicle accidents.
  • Severe blunt trauma to the pelvis.

Clinical Features

  • Blood at the urethral meatus.
  • Urinary retention due to urethral disruption.
  • High-riding prostate on digital rectal exam.
  • Pelvic hematoma or suprapubic pain.
  • May be associated with concomitant bladder injury.

Investigations

  • Retrograde urethrography (gold standard) - shows extravasation of contrast.
  • CT urethrography - used in complex cases.
  • Pelvic CT - to assess associated fractures.
  • Cystoscopy - for direct visualization when needed.
  • Classic finding: "Pie in the sky" appearance on IVP with prostatomembranous injury.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Bulbar urethra (Option A): More flexible and commonly injured in straddle injuries or direct perineal trauma, not pelvic fractures.

Spongy urethra (Option B): Another name for penile urethra, injured with direct penile trauma or fracture, not typically with high-impact pelvic injury.

Penile urethra (Option D): Same as spongy urethra; affected by penile fractures or blows to the shaft, not motor vehicle-related pelvic fractures.

Key Takeaway

Membranous urethral injury is strongly associated with pelvic fractures in motor vehicle accidents, presenting with blood at the meatus, urinary retention, and a high-riding prostate, and is best evaluated by retrograde urethrography.

question_text: Management of acute phase of Peyronie's disease?
explanation:
• While the aetiology is uncertain, there is an association with Dupuytren's contracture.
  • The natural history of the condition is that it typically progresses for 18-24 months before stabilising.
  • During this acute (or active) phase of the disease, surgery is not indicated, and a variety of medical treatments have been tried, although none with any good evidence of benefit.
  • When the disease has stabilised (the chronic or stable phase), the crucial issue is whether the patient is still able to have sexual intercourse.
  • If he can, then no treatment is indicated, while if the deformity prevents penetration, or makes it difficult, then corrective treatment is indicated.
  • Using this criterion, only around a quarter of men require treatment.
  • While injections of collagenase have been recently licensed for this condition, the commonest treatment is surgery with the Nesbitt procedure being the most common procedure.
  • This operation corrects the deformity by plicating the convex side of the deformity, thereby straightening the penis, albeit with some accompanying loss of length,

question_text: A young male underwent lumbar sympathectomy, and bilateral L1 ganglia were excised. What is the most common side effect of this procedure?
explanation:
Explanation:

Lumbar sympathectomy interrupts sympathetic innervation responsible for closure of the bladder neck during ejaculation. Disruption of this mechanism results in retrograde ejaculation, where semen enters the bladder instead of being expelled through the urethra. This is the most frequently observed complication following lumbar sympathectomy.

Explanation of other options:

Impotence (Option A): Erectile function is primarily parasympathetic (S2-S4, pelvic splanchnic nerves). Sympathectomy does not usually impair erections.

Bladder dysfunction (Option C): Bladder contraction and emptying are controlled mainly by parasympathetic nerves (S2-S4). Sympathectomy at L1 has minimal effect on detrusor function.

Incontinence (Option D): Continence is maintained by the external urethral sphincter (somatic, pudendal nerve - S2-S4). Since this pathway is intact, incontinence is not a common consequence.

Key Takeaways:

  • Retrograde ejaculation is the most common complication of lumbar sympathectomy.
  • Erection (parasympathetic) and continence (somatic pudendal control) are usually preserved.
  • Lumbar sympathectomy primarily interferes with ejaculatory mechanism.

question_text: Based on the findings from this IVP image, what is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Based on the given findings, the likely diagnosis is bilateral ureterocele.

  • A ureterocele is a cystic dilatation of the terminal ureter as it enters the bladder.
  • On IVP, the classic sign is the "cobra head appearance", caused by contrast outlining the thin wall of the ureterocele while the dilated end protrudes into the bladder lumen.
  • It is more common in females (F:M = 4:1), bilateral in about 10%, and often associated with duplex systems.
  • Large ureteroceles can obstruct the bladder neck or contralateral ureter.
  • In children, infection is a common presentation.
  • Treatment is surgical: endoscopic incision in infants/small children, or excision with ureteric reimplantation.

Explanation of Other Options:

Bladder diverticulum (Option B): An outpouching from the bladder wall seen as a contrast-filled sac outside the bladder contour, usually with a narrow neck communicating with the bladder.

Ectopic ureter (Option C): Opens outside the normal trigonal area (e.g., urethra, vagina). IVP may show a dilated ureter with delayed drainage, often associated with duplex systems.

Vesicoureteric reflux (Option D): Best diagnosed by MCU, not IVP. On IVP, may appear as contrast refluxing from the bladder into the ureter and renal pelvis during filling/micturition.

question_text: Which is not true regarding ischaemic priapism?
option_a: The commoner and is due to venous congestion
option_b: The penis remains erect and remains painless
option_c: Blood taken from the penis shows hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis
explanation:
lschaemic priapism lschaemic or veno-occlusive priapism is the more common. It is due to venous congestion, with consequent thrombosis and ischaemia. The penis remains erect and becomes painful. This is a pathological erection and the glans penis and corpus spongiosum are not involved. The condition is most commonly seen as a side effect of medication, most notably antipsychotic medication and intracavernosal injections. It can also arise as a complication of hypercoagulable blood disorders such as sickle cell disease or leukaemia. A small proportion of cases are caused by malignant disease in the corpora cavernosa or the pelvis.

question_text: An elderly patient with Ca Penis underwent partial penile amputation. Biopsy report came as a T2 lesion. What will be the appropriate timing for lymph node management (clinically N0 nodes)?

question_text: A 3-year-old boy is brought to the pediatric clinic for a routine check-up. During the examination, the physician notes that the boy has unilateral cryptorchidism (right side). The mother reports that the testis has not descended since birth. What is the most likely physiological consequence of untreated cryptorchidism in this patient?
option_a: Normal spermatogenesis in the affected testis
option_b: Increased risk of testicular cancer in adulthood
explanation:
• Increased risk of testicular cancer in adulthood:
    • Mechanism: Untreated cryptorchidism is associated with a significantly higher risk of developing testicular cancer, particularly if the testis remains undescended in adulthood.
    • Statistics: The risk of testicular cancer can be as high as 3-10 times greater in men with a history of cryptorchidism compared to the general population.

Why not the other options?

  • A) Normal spermatogenesis in the affected testis:
    • Explanation: Cryptorchidism impairs spermatogenesis due to increased temperature in the undescended testis, leading to potential infertility and testicular atrophy over time.
  • C) Decreased levels of testosterone:
    • Explanation: Although testosterone production may decline if the testis is severely impaired or atrophic, unilateral cryptorchidism typically does not lead to significant testosterone level reductions if the other testis is functional.
  • D) Increased risk of varicocele formation:
    • Explanation: Varicocele formation is linked to venous drainage issues, primarily occurring on the left side due to anatomical differences, and is not a direct physiological consequence of cryptorchidism.

Key Takeaways:

  • Untreated cryptorchidism poses a significant risk for testicular cancer later in life.
  • Early intervention, typically surgical, is crucial to minimize long-term complications associated with undescended testes.

question_text: A 25-year-old male presents to the urology clinic with complaints of a dull ache in his left scrotum, which worsens after prolonged standing. option_a: Normal spermatogenesis in the affected testis
option_b: Decreased fertility due to impaired spermatogenesis
explanation:
• Decreased fertility due to impaired spermatogenesis:
    • Mechanism: Untreated varicocele leads to increased scrotal temperature due to venous stasis, which negatively impacts sperm production and motility.
    • Consequences: The heat stress and hormonal changes associated with varicocele can impair spermatogenesis, leading to lower sperm counts and potential infertility.

Why not the other options?

  • A) Normal spermatogenesis in the affected testis:
    • Explanation: Varicocele is known to disrupt normal spermatogenesis due to increased temperature and compromised venous drainage, resulting in impaired sperm production.
  • C) Increased testosterone production:
    • Explanation: Varicocele does not enhance testosterone production; it can actually lead to lower testosterone levels due to impaired function of the Leydig cells caused by heat and vascular congestion.
  • D) Elevated levels of inhibin B:
    • Explanation: Inhibin B levels are typically decreased in varicocele, reflecting impaired Sertoli cell function and the detrimental effects of elevated testicular temperature on spermatogenesis.

Common causes of infertility involving testicular disorders

  • Trauma to testis
  • Cryptorchidism
  • Varicocele
  • Orchitis

Key Takeaways:

  • Untreated varicocele is associated with decreased fertility due to compromised spermatogenesis.
  • Management of varicocele, especially in symptomatic patients, is crucial to improve reproductive outcomes.

question_text: Which of the following statements is false about the following image?
option_a: Staphylococcus aureus is the causative organism
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The given image shows Fournier's Gangrene, a severe necrotising infection of the perineum and genital region.
  • It is caused by a polymicrobial infection involving both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.
  • It is not limited to Staphylococcus aureus infection.
  • Rapid progression and systemic toxicity are common, making early recognition and prompt surgical debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics essential.

Fournier's Gangrene

  • Definition:
    • A swiftly advancing necrotizing infection involving the perineum, external genitalia, and perianal area, regarded as a specialised form of necrotizing fasciitis.
  • Causative Organisms:
    • Typically polymicrobial, involving a mix of aerobic and anaerobic bacteria.
    • These organisms trigger aggressive inflammation and destruction of subcutaneous tissues. (Option A)

Clinical Presentation:

  • Key Symptom: Severe genital pain, evolving through distinct phases:
    • Prodromal phase: Fever, malaise, general weakness.
    • Early pain phase: Intense pain, local oedema, and itching.
    • Progressive phase: Increasing pain with erythema.
    • Crepitation phase: Dusky skin discolouration, palpable crepitus.
    • Gangrene phase: Tissue necrosis, foul purulent discharge, with reduced pain due to nerve damage.
  • Severity can range from mild tenderness to fulminant sepsis and shock.

Risk Factors:

  • Diabetes mellitus (Option B ruled out)
  • Peripheral vascular disease
  • Alcoholism
  • Malnutrition
  • Immunocompromised states (e.g., HIV, chemotherapy)

Diagnosis:

  • Based on typical clinical signs.
  • Supported by imaging (CT or MRI to delineate extent) and laboratory tests (raised inflammatory markers).

Management:

  • Initial Measures:
    • Aggressive IV fluid resuscitation
    • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics covering Gram-positive, Gram-negative, and anaerobes
    • Early and extensive surgical debridement of necrotic tissue
  • Additional Interventions:
    • Repeated wound assessment and possible re-debridement (Option C ruled out)
    • Urinary or faecal diversion to limit wound contamination
    • Intensive care monitoring for sepsis and multi-organ dysfunction
    • Negative pressure wound therapy (VAC dressings)
    • Reconstructive procedures such as skin grafting once infection is controlled

The testes remain unaffected (Option D): In Fournier's Gangrene:

  • The testes are typically spared because of their independent dual blood supply.
  • The primary supply comes from the testicular arteries branching directly from the abdominal aorta, while additional collateral circulation is provided by the cremasteric and deferential arteries.
  • This vascular arrangement protects the testes even when surrounding perineal and scrotal tissues undergo extensive necrosis.

question_text: What is the probable diagnosis for an elderly male patient who experienced scrotal pain and discharge, as indicated in the provided image?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient presents with scrotal pain, swelling, and discharge, along with the image showing extensive necrosis, which is highly suggestive of Fournier's gangrene.
  • This is a rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of the perineum, genitalia, and surrounding soft tissues, similar to necrotizing fasciitis.
  • It commonly occurs in immunocompromised states such as diabetes mellitus, alcoholism, malnutrition, and vascular disease.
  • Clinical progression usually follows distinct phases:
    • Prodromal: Fever and lethargy
    • Early: Severe genital pain, edema, erythema
    • Progressive: Skin darkening, crepitus from gas-forming organisms
    • Gangrene: Purulent discharge, necrotic tissue, systemic toxicity
  • Management is aggressive and involves:
    • Immediate resuscitation with fluids
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics (to cover both aerobic and anaerobic bacteria)
    • Urgent surgical debridement of necrotic tissue
    • Urinary/fecal diversion if required to prevent contamination
    • Repeated wound evaluation, VAC dressings, and later skin grafting for reconstruction

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Torsion of the testis (Option A): This presents as sudden, severe scrotal pain with rapid swelling and absent cremasteric reflex. It leads to ischemia and gangrene of the testis if untreated but does not present with soft tissue necrosis and foul-smelling discharge.

Acute epididymo-orchitis (Option B): Typically caused by bacterial infections (eg, E. coli, Chlamydia, Gonorrhea), leading to painful, tender scrotal swelling with fever and dysuria. It is not associated with necrosis or crepitus.

Scrotal carcinoma (Option C): Usually presents as a painless, indurated mass or ulcer with everted edges and an indurated base. It is a chronic, slow-growing lesion and not an acute necrotizing infection like Fournier's gangrene.

Key Takeaway:

Fournier's gangrene is a rapidly progressive necrotizing infection of the perineum and genitalia caused by mixed aerobic and anaerobic bacteria. It requires urgent surgical debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics, as delay in management significantly increases mortality.

question_text: A 35-year-old male presents with a painless testicular mass. After orchidectomy, histopathological examination reveals the presence of Reinke's crystals within the tumor cells. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of Reinke's crystals is pathognomonic for Leydig cell tumor, a sex cord-stromal tumor of the testis.

  • Definition: Rare sex cord-stromal tumor derived from Leydig cells.
  • Epidemiology: Can occur at any age, peak in middle age (20-60 years).
  • Hormonal activity:
    • May secrete androgens → testicular enlargement, precocious puberty in children.
    • May secrete estrogens → gynecomastia, feminization in adults.
  • Gross pathology:
    • Well-circumscribed nodules, usually < 5 cm.
    • Characteristic golden-brown, homogeneous cut surface.
  • Histology:
    • Large polygonal cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.
    • Round central nucleus.
    • Reinke's crystalloids (rod-shaped intracytoplasmic inclusions) present in ~25% of cases.
  • Malignant potential: ~10% in adults, rare in children.
  • Associations: Cryptorchidism, Klinefelter syndrome, Carney complex.

Explanation of Other Options:

Sertoli cell tumor (Option A):

  • Another sex cord-stromal tumor.
  • Typically hormonally silent.
  • Gross: Firm, small nodules, grey-white to yellow cut surface.
  • Histology: Tumor cells arranged in trabeculae, forming cords and tubules.
  • No Reinke's crystalloids.

Seminoma (Option C):

  • Most common testicular germ cell tumor, typically in the 3rd-4th decade.
  • Gross: Homogeneous, grey-white mass without hemorrhage or necrosis.
  • Histology: Large cells with clear cytoplasm, central nuclei.
  • Tumor markers: β-hCG (sometimes elevated), LDH, PLAP, GGT.
  • No Reinke's crystals.

Yolk sac tumor (Option D):

  • Most common testicular tumor in children (1-3 years).
  • Tumor marker: Alpha-fetoprotein (AFP).
  • Histology: Schiller-Duval bodies (glomeruloid structures).
  • Best prognosis among germ cell tumors.

question_text: Reperfusion injury occurs when blood flow is restored after a period of ischemia. During this phase, accumulated metabolites and ions re-enter circulation, creating systemic disturbances. According to surgical principles described in Bailey and Love, which substance is chiefly responsible for the clinically significant component of reperfusion injury?
explanation:
Explanation:

During prolonged ischemia, cells lose membrane integrity and release potassium and acid into surrounding tissues. Once reperfusion occurs, this accumulated potassium rapidly enters the systemic circulation. This sudden potassium surge can cause myocardial depression, dangerous cardiac arrhythmias, vasodilation, worsening hypotension and can contribute significantly to multi organ injury.

During ischemia:

  • Cells lose ATP and membrane pumps begin to fail
  • Potassium leaks out of cells into the interstitial space
  • Acidity increases due to anaerobic metabolism
  • Inflammatory pathways are activated locally

During reperfusion:

  • The accumulated potassium and acids enter systemic circulation
  • Inflammatory mediators and cell fragments activate leukocytes
  • These changes may contribute to acute lung injury, acute kidney injury and multi organ failure

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) reflects the level of consciousness.
Scores range from 3 to 15 and assess:

  • Eye opening
  • Verbal response

The motor score alone, not the verbal response, is most reflective of outcomes after traumatic brain injury (TBI).

Head Injury Severity & GCS

  • Alcohol and drugs may complicate assessment.

  • Minor head injury: GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness (LOC).
  • Mild head injury: GCS 14 or 15 with LOC.
  • Moderate head injury: GCS 9-13.
  • Severe head injury: GCS 3-8.

Key Takeaways:

Motor component of GCS is the best predictor of TBI outcomes.

question_text: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. He has sustained a severe head injury and is found to have a poor GCS score on arrival. CT scan of the head shows no significant abnormality. Despite supportive care, he dies within a few hours. What is the most likely underlying cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely underlying cause in the given scenario is diffuse axonal injury.

  • Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is a primary brain injury caused by shearing forces in high-velocity trauma, leading to widespread disruption of axons.
  • It typically renders the patient immediately comatose and is associated with a poor prognosis.
  • While CT may appear normal or show only small haemorrhagic foci (especially in the corpus callosum and dorsolateral rostral brainstem), MRI is more sensitive and often demonstrates the lesions.
  • Definitive diagnosis is pathological at postmortem.
  • The rapid deterioration and absence of mass lesion on CT make DAI the most likely cause in this patient.

Explanation of Other Options:

SDH (Option A): Usually appears on CT as a crescentic bleed and causes mass effect; absent in this case.

EDH (Option B): Classically presents with a lucid interval and biconvex bleed on CT; not consistent with the history or findings.

Brainstem contusion (Option D): Can cause sudden deterioration but typically visible on imaging.

question_text: What is the probable diagnosis for a 30-year-old woman who experienced nausea and vomiting after being involved in a road traffic accident, and was brought to the emergency room unconscious, based on the findings of the NCCT brain?
explanation:
Explanation:

A woman presenting with nausea and vomiting following a road traffic accident, with NCCT head imaging revealing a lens-shaped (biconvex) collection of blood between the skull's inner surface and the dura mater, is most consistent with a diagnosis of Extradural (Epidural) Hemorrhage.

Epidural Hematoma (EDH) v/s Subdural Hematoma (SDH)

Summary:

  • EDH: Often follows a predictable course with a lucid interval and has a lens-shaped CT appearance.
  • SDH: More variable presentation, typically crescentic on CT, and associated with venous bleeding or cortical vessel injury.

Explanation of Other Options:

Intraparenchymal haemorrhage (Option C) refers to bleeding directly into the brain tissue. On NCCT, it usually appears as a dense, irregularly shaped hyperintense area. The most common causes include chronic hypertension and cerebrovascular accidents rather than trauma. Although loss of consciousness may occur in severe cases, the imaging features do not demonstrate the characteristic lentiform or biconvex pattern typical of extradural haemorrhage.

Subarachnoid haemorrhage (Option D) is bleeding between the brain and arachnoid mater, usually from a ruptured aneurysm. On NCCT, it appears as diffuse hyperdensity in the sulci and basal cisterns. Though trauma and unconsciousness may suggest it, unlike extradural haemorrhage, it does not show the typical biconvex (lens-shaped) collection.

question_text: Which of the following statements is true regarding Taenia solium?
option_a: Eggs are not infective to man
option_c: The eggs do not float in saturated salt solution
explanation:
Explanation:

Taenia solium eggs are heavy and therefore do not float in saturated salt solution during stool examination. Instead, they settle at the bottom, requiring sedimentation techniques for diagnosis. This is a distinguishing diagnostic feature.

Explanation of other options:

Eggs are not infective to man (Option A): Incorrect. Taenia solium eggs are infective to humans, causing cysticercosis when ingested. Humans may act as both definitive and intermediate hosts.

Hooks are absent (Option B): Incorrect. Taenia solium has a scolex (head) with suckers and hooks for intestinal attachment. In contrast, Taenia saginata lacks hooks.

Intermediate host is cow (Option D): Incorrect. The intermediate host of T. solium is the pig, hence it is also called the pork tapeworm. T. saginata (beef tapeworm) uses the cow as its intermediate host.

Key Takeaways:

  • solium eggs do not float in saturated salt solution.
  • Human can be both definitive (intestinal tapeworm) and intermediate host (cysticercosis).
  • Scolex has hooks and suckers (contrast: T. saginata has no hooks).
  • Intermediate host: pig.

While one hand applies downward pressure to the patient's forehead, the tips of the index and middle fingers of the second hand lift the mandible at the chin, which lifts the tongue from the posterior pharynx. The head-tilt/chin-lift maneuver may be used in any patient in whom cervical spine injury is NOT a concern.

question_text:
A 25-year-old man is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. On arrival:
1. GCS: 8/15
2. SpO₂: 85%
3. BP: 100/60 mmHg
4. HR: 60 bpm
On chest examination, breath sounds are absent on the right side.
What is the next best step in management?
option_a: Start IV fluids, give atropine and secure airway
option_b: Secure airway, give oxygen, insert ICD, secure IV line
option_c: Evaluate for head injury and do CT-head
option_d: Administer IV dextrose followed by NCCT head
explanation:
Explanation:

This is a polytrauma patient with airway compromise, hypoxia, and absent breath sounds on one side - indicating a life-threatening chest injury (likely tension pneumothorax or massive pneumothorax).

  • The patient has GCS 8/15, indicating a severe head injury and possible impaired consciousness. Therefore, securing the airway is the priority to prevent further deterioration.
  • Oxygen should be administered to address the low oxygen saturation (85%).
  • The absence of breath sounds on the right side raises concern for tension pneumothorax or large pneumothorax, which can lead to respiratory failure.
  • In this case, the next step is to insert an intercostal chest drain (ICD) to relieve any pneumothorax and re-expand the lung.
  • IV access should be secured for fluid resuscitation or medication administration, but airway and breathing take precedence.

We will follow a primary survey of A, B, C, D, and E to manage this patient, where A is securing the airway, B is giving oxygen and inserting ICD, and C includes IV line.

Explanation of Other Options:

Start IV fluids, give atropine and secure airway (Option A):

  • IV fluids are important but airway and breathing take precedence.
  • Atropine is not required unless HR < 50 bpm with hemodynamic instability.
  • Administering atropine here would delay airway management and is unnecessary.

Evaluate for head injury and do CT-head (Option C):

  • Head CT is indicated only after stabilization.
  • Absent breath sounds + hypoxia = life-threatening chest pathology → must be treated before imaging.

Administer IV dextrose followed by NCCT head (Option D):

  • No evidence of hypoglycemia.
  • Dextrose is not indicated.
  • Imaging again comes after airway, breathing, and circulation are secured.

question_text: A young male with head injury was brought to the emergency in unconscious state. The patient was not able to breath properly, put on ventilatory support. On examination, GCS was 8 with findings of raised ICT. NCCT brain and spinal imaging were normal. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
• This is a form of primary brain injury seen in high-energy accidents that usually renders the patient comatose;
  • it is associated with poor outcomes. It is strictly a pathological diagnosis made at postmortem, but haemorrhagic foci in the corpus callosum and dorsolateral rostral brainstem on CT may be suggestive, although CT often appears normal
  • Magnetic resonance imaging is more sensitive and is employed to evaluate for difuse axonal injury in patients who fail to improve neurologically.
  • IOC for diffuse atonal injury is SWI-MRI

question_text: All of the following are correct regarding meningitis except
option_a: Raised ICP should be excluded before LP
option_b: CSF should be sent for microscopy and culture
option_c: Treatment is broad spectrum antibiotics including anaerobic coverage
explanation:
• Meningitis is a feared complication of neurosurgery and head injury.
  • CT scan allows exclusion of raised intracranial pressure and should be done prior to lumbar puncture.
  • CSF should be sent for microscopy and culture, along with protein and glucose level assay.
  • Treatment is with broad spectrum antibiotics including anaerobic coverage.
  • Empirical therapy is started with 3rd generation cephalosporin + Vancomycin ± Ampicillin.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 706

question_text: A patient sustained a crush injury on their right arm. On examination, the arm is pulseless, swollen, and dark red. What is the best management?
explanation:
Explanation:

This presentation is classic for acute compartment syndrome. The crush injury causes massive swelling within the rigid osteofascial compartments of the arm, leading to:

  • Increased intra-compartmental pressure: Compromising blood flow.
  • Pulselessness: A late sign indicating arterial compromise.
  • Swelling and dark red discoloration: Indicating venous obstruction and tissue ischemia.
    A fasciotomy is an emergency surgical procedure to cut the fascia and release the pressure, restoring circulation and preventing irreversible muscle and nerve damage (necrosis).

Explanation of other options:

Intraosseous administration of fluids (Option A): While fluid resuscitation is important in crush injury to prevent rhabdomyolysis and acute kidney injury, it does not treat the underlying compartment syndrome. The pressure must be released first.

Acidification of urine (Option B): This is sometimes used in specific poisonings (e.g., amphetamines) to enhance excretion. In crush injury, the goal is to alkalinize the urine to prevent myoglobin precipitation in the kidneys and avoid tubular damage.

Hemodialysis (Option D): This is a treatment for established renal failure, which can be a complication of crush injury (rhabdomyolysis) but is not the treatment for the compartment syndrome itself.

Key Takeaways:

  • Compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency. The diagnosis is clinical (pain out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, paresthesia, pulselessness).
  • Fasciotomy is the only definitive treatment.

question_text: A patient with a history of chest trauma and breathlessness is found to have systolic BP 90 mmHg, SpO2 85%, GCS 8/15 and absent breath sounds. What is the next step?
option_a: Secure airway, needle thoracotomy, and IV fluids
option_b: Blood transfusion and send for CT
option_c: Take history, give IV Dextrose and send for eFAST
option_d: CT scan of head and airway securing
explanation:
Explanation:

This is an unstable trauma patient (hypotension, hypoxia, depressed GCS) with absent breath sounds → highly suspicious for tension pneumothorax/large hemothorax. The primary survey (A-B-C) requires immediate airway management (GCS 8 → intubate) plus immediate decompression of the chest (needle thoracostomy or tube thoracostomy) before CT or further diagnostics. IV access and resuscitation follow. Waiting for CT or history in this unstable patient is inappropriate.

Explanation of other options:

Options B/C/D delay immediate life-saving interventions (decompression/airway) - unacceptable in unstable chest trauma.

question_text: A patient is brought to the emergency department after a road traffic accident. On examination, he opens his eyes only to painful stimuli, speaks inappropriate words, and withdraws his limbs in response to pain. What is the most likely Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score?
explanation:
Explanation:

The GCS score is calculated based on the patient's responses: Eye opening to pain (E2), inappropriate verbal response (V3), and withdrawal to pain (M4).

  • The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is used to assess the level of consciousness in trauma patients.
  • It has three components:
    • Eye opening (E): To pain = 2
    • Verbal response (V): Inappropriate words = 3
    • Motor response (M): Withdraws to pain = 4
    • Thus, the total GCS = E2 + V3 + M4 = 9
  • GCS Interpretation:
    • Minor injury: GCS 15 with no loss of consciousness
    • Mild head injury: GCS 14-15 with loss of consciousness
    • Moderate head injury: GCS 9-13
    • Severe head injury: GCS 3-8
  • GCS-P is calculated by subtracting the Pupil Reactivity Score (PRS) from GCS:
    • PRS: 0 = both pupils reactive, 1 = one pupil unreactive, 2 = both unreactive
    • GCS-P range: 1-15
    • A GCS-P ≤8 indicates severe brain injury.

Reference:

https://www.glasgowcomascale.org/what-is-gcs-p/

https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513298/

question_text: A 76-year-old man presents with confusion. He is taking antihypertensive medication and aspirin following a recent myocardial infarction. He recalls a minor fall from a chair three weeks ago. His neurological exam is otherwise normal. Based on the radiograph provided, what is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Subdural hematoma presents with delayed confusion after minor trauma in elderly patients, especially those on antiplatelets or anticoagulants.

  • A subdural hematoma (SDH) results from rupture of the bridging veins between the brain and dura, commonly following minor head trauma.
  • Elderly patients and those on blood thinners (like aspirin) are particularly susceptible.
  • The bleeding accumulates slowly and may become symptomatic days to weeks after the initial injury, as seen in this patient presenting with confusion weeks after a fall.
  • CT scan typically shows a crescent-shaped lesion that can vary in density depending on the age of the bleed:
    • Acute: hyperdense
    • Subacute: isodense
    • Chronic: hypodense
  • This delayed onset of confusion and classic imaging features are consistent with chronic subdural hematoma.

Explanation of other options:

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (Option C): Presents with sudden severe headache ("worst headache of life"), not confusion. CT shows hyperdensity in the basal cisterns and sulci, not a crescentic lesion.

Cerebellar Contusion (Option D): Would show focal hemorrhage in the cerebellum with neurological signs like ataxia or dysmetria, not diffuse confusion.

Mandatory exploration is generally required for injuries in Zone 1of the retroperitoneum.

question_text: Which of the following CT findings is NOT an indication to perform angiography in a splenic trauma patient under conservative management?
explanation:
Explanation

Non-operative management (NOM) is the standard for hemodynamically stable patients with splenic trauma. Angioembolization is a vital adjunct to NOM. Indications for angiography include signs of ongoing bleeding, such as:

Contrast extravasation ("blush") (Option D ruled out)

Pseudoaneurysm formation (Option C ruled out)

Significant hemoperitoneum (Option B ruled out)

A subcapsular hematoma covering 40% surface area (A) is classified as an AAST Grade II injury. This is a stable finding managed conservatively with observation and does not, by itself, mandate angiography.

Key Takeaways:

  • Contrast blush, pseudoaneurysm, and significant hemoperitoneum are indications for angioembolization in splenic trauma.
  • A stable subcapsular hematoma (AAST Grade I-II) is not an indication for angiography.

question_text: What is the classification of the head injury for a patient involved in a road traffic accident who has a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is the standard tool for assessing the level of consciousness after a traumatic brain injury (TBI).


The severity is classified as follows:

  • Mild TBI: GCS 14-15 (Option C and D ruled out)
  • Moderate TBI: GCS 9-13
  • Severe TBI: GCS 3-8 (Option B ruled out)
  • A GCS score of 10 falls within the 9-13 range, which defines a moderate traumatic brain injury.

Key Takeaways:

  • Moderate TBI is classified by a GCS score of 9-13.
  • The GCS assesses eye, verbal, and motor responses.

question_text: A patient with head injury was brought to casualty with GCS-12 CT scan was taken shown in the image.
explanation:
Extradural haematoma

  • Extradural haematoma is a neurosurgical emergency. It results from rupture of an artery, vein or venous sinus, in association with a skull fracture.
  • The classical injury is a fracture to the thin squamous temporal bone, with associated damage to the middle meningeal artery. Transient loss of consciousness is typical, and the patient may then present in the subsequent lucid interval with headache but without any neurological deficit.
  • As the haematoma expands, compensation is exhausted with rapid deterioration. There is contralateral hemiparesis, a reduced conscious level and ipsilateral pupillary dilatation, the cardinal signs of brain compression and herniation.
  • Although this 'talk and die' pattern of deterioration occurs in only one-third of cases, it is critically important to recognise the potential for rapid avoidable secondary brain injury in patients who present neurologically intact.

On CT, extradural haematomas appear as a lentiform (lens-shaped or biconvex) hyperdense lesion between the skull and the brain, constrained by the adherence of the dura to the skull.

Significant extradural haematoma mandates urgent transfer to the most accessible neurosurgical facility for immediate evacuation in deteriorating or comatose patients or those with large bleeds and for close observation with serial imaging in other cases.

The prognosis for promptly evacuated extradural haematoma, without associated primary brain injury, is excellent.

question_text:
A 25-year-old male is brought to the emergency department after a high-speed road traffic accident. He has a GCS of 6, pulse 48/min, and BP 180/100 mmHg. Pupils are sluggishly reactive, and breathing is shallow with irregular patterns. These features suggest Cushing's triad due to raised intracranial pressure.
What should be the immediate management step?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • GCS < 8 → absolute indication for intubation.
  • Bradycardia + hypertension → signs of raised ICP (Cushing's response).
  • Immediate priority = airway + ventilation before any imaging or fluids.
  • IPPV helps maintain oxygenation, control CO2, and reduce intracranial hypertension.

Primary Survey - Structured (cABCDE Framework)

Secondary & Tertiary Survey (Flow of Trauma Care)

Primary Survey (cABCDE) → Immediate Stabilization →Secondary Survey (head-to-toe exam, history, adjunct imaging) → Tertiary Survey (after extubation → find missed subtle injuries, e.g., scaphoid fracture, rotator cuff tear).

Explanation of Other Options:

Urgent CT head (Option A): Incorrect. Imaging is vital but only after stabilization. Performing CT without securing the airway in a GCS < 8 patient risks hypoxia, aspiration, and death.

Thrombolysis (Option C): Incorrect. Thrombolytic therapy has no role in acute trauma. Priority here is airway, not clot dissolution.

Normal saline infusion (Option D): Incorrect. This patient is hypertensive, not hypotensive. Aggressive fluids may worsen raised ICP; the airway must be addressed first.

question_text: Which part of the cranial fossa is injured in Raccoon's eyes?
explanation:
Explanation:

Raccoon Eyes (Periorbital Ecchymosis):

  • Affected Area: Anterior cranial fossa
  • Cause: Typically arises from fractures or traumatic injury to the anterior cranial fossa.
  • Pathophysiology: Hemorrhage from the damaged anterior cranial fossa spreads into the tissues around the eyes.
  • Clinical Feature: Bilateral periorbital bruising, producing the classic dark discoloration known as raccoon eyes.

Cranial Fossa Fractures:

Management:

  • Conservative Management: Recommended for fractures without significant intracranial damage or when located near dural venous sinuses. Focuses on close monitoring, supportive care, and symptom management.
  • Surgical Management: Involves craniotomy and elevation to lift depressed bone fragments, repair associated injuries, and restore normal cranial structure and function.

Explanation of Other Options:

Bone aponeurotic layer (Option D) refers to the connective tissue over the skull, commonly affected in scalp injuries. However, it is not directly associated with raccoon eyes. Raccoon eyes arise from blood collecting in the periorbital area due to trauma to the anterior cranial fossa, rather than from damage to the aponeurotic layer.

question_text: A patient with type 2 diabetes experiences hypoglycemia and falls, resulting in incoherent speech. A CT scan reveals a large subdural hematoma >30 cc. What is the most appropriate immediate management?
option_d: Stabilize the patient and urgently seek a neurosurgical consultation
explanation:
Explanation:

  • This case represents an acute subdural hematoma (SDH) with significant volume (>30 cc) requiring urgent surgical management.
  • On CT, acute SDH appears hyperdense (white), and large hematomas pose a high risk of brain compression and herniation.
  • Emergency craniotomy is the definitive treatment, allowing prompt evacuation of the hematoma to prevent further neurological deterioration and potentially fatal complications.

Fig: CT brain showing subdural hematoma, seen as hyperdense clot that has an irregular border with the brain with mass effect

Acute SDH vs Chronic SDH:

Explanation of other options:

Administer Mannitol (Option A): Mannitol is used to manage elevated intracranial pressure, but it is not the definitive treatment for a large subdural hematoma. While mannitol can temporarily reduce intracranial pressure, it does not address the underlying compression from the hematoma, which requires surgical evacuation.

Administer Aspirin and Clopidogrel (Option B): Antiplatelets and anticoagulants like aspirin and clopidogrel are contraindicated in acute SDH, as these antiplatelet agents could worsen the bleeding.

Stabilize the patient and urgently seek a neurosurgical consultation (Option D): While important, delays the definitive treatment needed in this case. Given the large volume of the hematoma and altered mental status, immediate surgical intervention through craniotomy is required rather than waiting for further consultation.

question_text: An unconscious patient is brought to the emergency department following a road traffic accident. Based on the CT scan image provided, what is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The CT imaging shows a crescent-shaped or concave collection of blood on a CT scan is characteristic of a subdural hematoma, which often results from trauma, such as a road accident.

Subdural hematoma

  • Acute subdural hematoma ypically occurs following high-energy trauma or in elderly patients who sustain a fall while on anticoagulant therapy.
  • Chronic subdural haematoma is a common cause of acute neurological deterioration in older adults.
  • A subdural hematoma develops in the between the dura mater and the brain, usually due to tearing of the dural bridging veins.
  • Symptoms include rapid deterioration, loss of consciousness anf focal deficits.

Management

question_text: In a patient admitted to the Emergency Department following a road traffic accident (RTA), who presents with an altered level of consciousness and a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 10, what is the most likely potential diagnosis suggested by the accompanying CT scan image?
explanation:
Explanation:

Extradural hematoma typically presents on CT as a biconvex or lens-shaped hyperdense lesion, usually in the temporal region. The provided CT image shows these characteristic findings, confirming the diagnosis.

Explanation of other options:

Subdural hematoma (Option A): Caused by rupture of cortical bridging veins; CT shows a concave-convex (crescent-shaped) lesion in the subdural space.

Intracerebral hemorrhage (Option B): Often due to aneurysmal rupture; CT reveals a well-defined hyperdense area with surrounding hypodense edema.

Hemorrhagic contusion (Option D): Typically seen as small punctate hyperdense lesions within the brain parenchyma.

Key Takeaways:

Extradural hematoma appears as a lens-shaped hyperdensity on CT, usually caused by trauma leading to middle meningeal artery rupture.

References: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK518982/

question_text: A 35-year-old male sustains a head injury following a motorcycle accident. He briefly loses consciousness at the scene, regains it, then later develops a severe headache and progressive drowsiness. A CT scan of the head is performed. Which of the following should be the management for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The classic CT appearance of a biconvex (lentiform), hyperdense lesion is characteristic of an epidural (extradural) hematoma.
This condition is a neurosurgical emergency that requires immediate surgical evacuation to prevent brain herniation and death.

Mechanism:

  • Typically results from rupture of the middle meningeal artery due to a temporal bone fracture.
  • Blood collects between the skull and dura mater, causing rapid increase in intracranial pressure (ICP).
  • A "lucid interval" - transient recovery of consciousness after initial loss - is a classic but not universal sign(seen in 15-20% of cases).

Definitive Management:

  • Emergency burr hole decompression (lifesaving measure), followed by
  • Craniotomy for evacuation of the clot and control of bleeding source.

Explanation of Other Options:

Anticoagulants (Option A):

  • Anticoagulants would exacerbate intracranial bleeding.
  • This treatment worsens mass effect and could precipitate fatal herniation.
  • Used only in ischemic conditions, never in hemorrhagic

Observation in ICU (Option C):

  • Appropriate for minor head injuries or small, asymptomatic subdural hematomas.
  • However, this patient shows neurological deterioration (drowsiness) and a large, biconvex lesion, implying significant mass effect -thus, urgent surgery is mandatory.

Mannitol administration (Option D):

  • Mannitol (an osmotic diuretic) may transiently reduce ICP and buy time while preparing for surgery.
  • However, it is not definitive management and must never delay surgical decompression.
  • Prolonged use can lead to hypovolemia and hypotension, worsening cerebral perfusion.

Key Takeaway Points:

Clinical Features of Epidural Hematoma (EDH):

  1. Initial Loss of Consciousness: a brief lucid interval, which occurs in 14% to 21% of EDH cases. Not all patients experience a lucid interval.
  2. Neurological Deterioration: The lucid interval may end with rapid neurological deterioration as the hematoma expands and raises intracranial pressure (ICP).
  3. Variable Consciousness Levels: Some patients may not experience a lucid interval, with presentations ranging from initial unconsciousness to coma.
  4. Posterior Fossa EDH: Rare but severe, accounting for about 5% of EDH cases. Delayed loss of consciousness can occur as the hematoma grows, and patients may become apneic and die if untreated.
  5. Signs of Elevated ICP: As the hematoma enlarges, ipsilateral pupil dilation (due to uncal herniation and oculomotor nerve compression) can occur, along with elevated blood pressure, bradycardia, and irregular breathing (known as the Cushing reflex)

question_text: According to GCS, a verbal score of 1 indicates:
explanation:
Explanation:

A verbal score of 1 on the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) means no verbal response from the patient, indicating the most severe level of impairment in verbal communication.

Glasgow Coma Scale

  • The Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is a tool used to assess a patient's level of consciousness based on three parameters:
    • Eye-opening
    • Verbal response
    • Motor response.
  • Each parameter is scored, and the total GCS score ranges from 3 (deep coma) to 15 (fully awake).

question_text: A 30-year-old male patient known case of pleomorphic adenoma of parotid gland. He was undertaken for a superficial parotidectomy. The main trunk of the facial nerve lies how deep to the tragal pointer?
explanation:
Explanation:

The lower end of the tragal cartilage is one of the landmark to identify facial nerve during superficial parotidectomy.

The facial nerve main trunk lies 1 cm medial and inferior to the tip of the pointer.

Steps of superficial parotidectomy includes:

  • Preparation: many surgeons Use intraoperative facial nerve monitor. Mainly in large tumors and recurrent surgery.
  • Incision: The standard incision is Modified Blair's incision. The incision begins from pretragal skin crease, extends around the ear lobule, gently curving down two fingers breadth below the mandible.
  • Flap elevation: skin flap should be raised superficial to parotid fascia and in neck sub platysmally.
  • Identification of facial nerve: The various landmark are:
    • Tragal pointer- The nerve lies 1 cm medial and below the pointer
    • Tympanomastoid suture line,
    • Superior portion of posterior belly of digastric nerve
    • Posterior auricular artery, styloid process.

Key takeaway:

The facial nerve main trunk lies 1 cm medial and inferior to the tip of the pointer.

Image reference: Operative technique in otolaryngology website.

question_text: Which of the following is the most commonly injured nerve after parotid surgery?
explanation:
Explanation :

  • The facial nerve is the most commonly injured in parotid surgery as it traverses perpendicularly through the parotid gland. land.
  • The cervical branch of the facial nerve is usually involved leading to Bell's palsy.
  • Following parotid surgery auriculotemporal nerve and the greater auricular nerve can also be injured, but less frequently than the facial nerve. (Option B, D ruled out)

Iatrogenic injury to facial nerve

  • The most common cause of facial nerve injury is parotid surgery, followed by mastoid surgery.
  • During mastoid surgery, the site most frequently injured is the second genu of the facial nerve, followed by the vertical segment.
  • Management options include surgical exploration with end-to-end anastomosis and facial nerve grafting
  • Commonly used graft sources include:
    • Greater auricular nerve
    • Sural nerve (preferred for long grafts).

Explanation of other options:

Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option C): Glossopharyngeal nerve lies deep in the neck and is not related anatomically to the parotid gland. Injury to the nerve causes loss of taste in the posterior one-third of the tongue and loss of the gag reflex.

question_text: A 55-year-old male patient known case of carcinoma buccal mucosa was undertaken for neck dissection. During surgery, lymph nodes from level 1, 2, 3 and 4 regions are removed. What is the type of selective neck dissection done in this case?
