question_text: A 25-year-old female patient presented with a bluish, soft, cystic, fluctuant and translucent swelling located in the floor of the mouth. The clinical picture is given below. Which of the following statements about this condition is not true?
option_b: Treatment is surgical excision and marsupialization
option_c: It arises from sub mandibular gland
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Ranula are extravasation cyst (Option A) which originates from the sublingual glands in the floor of the mouth. (Option C)
  • Ranulas are connective tissue lined swelling of extravasated saliva.
  • They usually manifest as a soft, blue-tinged swelling of the floor of mouth (ersembles a Frog's belly), are detected in the second decade of life and may have a female predisposition.
  • They are of Two types: oral and cervical/plunging. (Option D)

question_text: A 45-year-old male patient known case of carcinoma buccal mucosa underwent wide local excision. The reconstruction of the defect created after surgery was done using a local flap. Picture Is given below. This flap receives blood supply from which of the following vessels?
option_a: Submental branch of the facial artery
option_b: Angular branch of the facial artery
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The flap shown in the picture above is the nasolabial flap.It is a type of local flap which is based on angular branch of the facial artery.
  • Local flaps: They may be rotational, advancements transposition.
    • Since the vascularity of the head and neck region is excellent, longer flaps with a narrow pedicle can be safely raised.
  • Nasolabial flap: it is raised from nasolabial crease and is based upon Angular branch of facial artery. It can be superiorly or inferiorly based. It is commonly used for nasal and intraoral defects. (OptionB)

Nasolabial flap: it is raised from nasolabial crease and is based upon Angular branch of facial artery. It can be superiorly or inferiorly based. It is commonly used for nasal and intraoral defects.

question_text: A 45-year-old male patient, known case of carcinoma tongue, underwent hemiglossectomy with modified radical neck dissection. His primary tumour and excised lymph nodes were sent for histopathology examination. In which of the following conditions will adjuvant radiotherapy not be required by the patient?

question_text: A 50-year-old male patient known case of carcinoma lower lip. Picture given below. He was undertaken for wide local excision with neck dissection. The defect arising in the lower lip after surgery is more than 2/3rd of the length of the lip. What should be the appropriate intervention for reconstruction in this case?
explanation:
Explanation:

With larger defects of the lower lip, reconstruction requires either large cheek flaps to be advanced to repair the defect or the use of free tissue transfer.

  • The common forms of cheek flap include the bilateral Gillies fan flaps or the Bernard-Webster cheek flap reconstruction.
  • Abbe flap is based on the main artery of the orbicularis Oris, the Labial artery. A portion of uninvolved lip is rotated across the mouth and placed into the surgical defect of the involved lip.

question_text: A 55-year-old male smoker presented with a mass on the left side of the neck at the level 2 region. An FNAC was done, which was suggestive of metastatic squamous cell carcinoma. A careful endoscopic and radiological examination was done, which revealed the absence of any primary tumour. Which of the following is not a theory for this condition?
option_a: Squamous element of brachial remnants in lymph nodes turning malignant.
option_b: Subclinical primary with nodal metastasis, either due to faster growth rate of the nodal metastasis or sloughing of necrotic carcinoma.
option_c: Primary regressing due to immune hyperactivity.
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The incidence of a neck node with unknown primary originin head and neck region is about 3%.
  • Carcinoma of unknown primary is defined as histologicalconfirmation for at least one of the cervical lymph nodes to be metastatic, in the absence of a primary tumour, which is confirmed by thorough physical, endoscopic and radiological examination.
  • Theories of occurrence include the following:
    1. The squamous element of brachial remnants in lymph nodes turning malignant. (Option A)
    2. The subclinical primary with nodal metastasis, either due to the faster growth rate of the nodal metastasis or the sloughing of necrotic carcinoma. (Option B)

question_text: Fibular flap is commonly used for reconstruction of defects of Hemi mandibulectomy. This flap is based on which of the following artery. What is type of this flap?
option_b: Anterior tibial vessels and regional flap
option_c: Dorsalis pedis vessels and free flap
explanation:
Explanation:

The fibular flap is an example of a free flap, which means that in this type of flaps the donor site and recipient sites are distant from each other and the flap carries it's blood vessels along with it.

Fibular flap is based on peroneal vessels. The fibular flap provides good bone stock and it's robust peroneal supply ensures that multiple osteotomies can be performed.

The flexor hallucis longus muscle and skin can be harvested along with the flap to provide soft tissue reconstruction along with the bone. Up to 25 cm of bone can be harvested.

Key takeaway:

The fibular flap is an example of free flap which means that in this type of flaps the donor site and recipient sites are distant from each other and the flap carries it's blood vessels along with it. Fibular flap is based on peroneal vessels.

question_text: Warthin's tumour is also called?
explanation:
Explanation:

Warthin's tumour is a benign salivary gland tumour, most frequently seen in the parotid gland. It is also referred to as adenolymphoma or papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum, owing to its characteristic histology.

Histological features:

  • Composed of oncocytic epithelial cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm.
  • Shows a bilayered epithelial lining.
  • Contains a prominent lymphoid stroma.

Clinical features:

  • Appears as a painless, cystic swelling.
  • More common in older men.
  • Strongly linked with cigarette smoking.

Pleomorphic adenoma (Option B): This is the most common benign salivary gland tumour, but it differs from Warthin's tumour in its microscopic appearance. It is termed a mixed tumour because it shows both epithelial structures (ductal/glandular elements) and mesenchymal-like areas, which may resemble myxoid tissue, cartilage, or even bone.

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (Option C): This is a malignant salivary gland tumour, unlike the benign Warthin's tumour. It is made up of three main cell types - mucous-producing cells, squamous cells, and intermediate cells - and is known for its variable grade and clinical course.

Acinic cell carcinoma (Option D): This is also a malignant salivary gland tumour, originating from the acinar cells that normally produce serous secretions. It usually presents as a slow-growing mass but carries malignant potential, which sets it apart from benign entities like Warthin's tumour.

explanation:
Pleomorphic adenoma is the most common benign salivary gland tumor, also known as a mixed tumor. It can occur in both major and minor salivary glands. Pleomorphic adenoma is composed of a mixture of different cell types, including epithelial and myoepithelial cells, and it is encapsulated.

A. Adenocarcinoma: Adenocarcinoma is a malignant tumor derived from glandular epithelial tissue. It is less common than pleomorphic adenoma and represents a cancerous (malignant) tumor.

C. Mucoepidermoid tumor: Mucoepidermoid tumor is a common malignant salivary gland tumor that includes both mucus-secreting and squamous cells. It is less common than pleomorphic adenoma.

D. Basal cell carcinoma: Basal cell carcinoma is a type of skin cancer that arises from basal cells in the epidermis.

question_text: A 45-year-old male patient known case of carcinoma buccal mucosa with involvement of mandible underwent wide local excision, Hemi mandibulectomy and Type 1 Modified radical neck dissection. Which of of the following structures are preserved in type 1 Modified radical neck dissection?
option_a: Preserves spinal accessory nerve, internal jugular vein and sternocleidomastoid muscle
option_c: Preserves spinal accessory nerve and internal jugular vein
option_d: Preserves spinal accessory and sternocleidomastoid muscle
explanation:
Explanation:

Radical neck dissection (RND): 

  • it involves removal of level 1 to 5 cervical lymph nodes.
  • It also includes removal of all the three structures spinal accessory nerve, internal jugular vein and sternocleidomastoid muscle.

Modified radical neck dissection (MRND):

  • It includes removal of level 1 to 5 cervical lymph nodes but one, two or all three nonlymphatic structures are preserved.
  • It was introduced to reduce the morbidity created in radical neck dissection.
  • They are of 3 types:

Selective neck dissection (SND):

  • It involves preservation of all three: spinal accessory nerve and internal jugular vein and sternocleidomastoid muscle.
  • Over and above that, it also preserves one or more group of lymph nodes.

Extended Radical Neck dissection (ERND):

  • Removal of one or more additional lymphatic and/or non-lymphatic structures relative to a radical neck dissection.
  • Example: level VII, retropharyngeal lymph nodes, hypoglossal nerve.

Key Takeaway:

MRND Types: Preserve NVM

  1. Preserve XI Nerve
  2. Preserve XI Nerve & IJV
  3. Preserve XI Nerve, IJV & SCM

question_text: A patient presents with swelling in the floor of the mouth. Upon examination, the swelling appears as shown in the image. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is a ranula, a type of mucus retention cyst that develops on the floor of the mouth, typically caused by blockage or rupture of the ducts of the sublingual or submandibular glands. This leads to mucus accumulation and the formation of a cystic swelling.

Ranula

  • A type of extravasation mucocelecaused by the rupture of the main duct or obstructed acini of the sublingual gland.
  • They appear as bluish swellingson the floor of the mouth and resemble the belly of a frog.
  • Typically soft, fluctuant, and painless unless infected.

Location

  • Commonly found in the anterior floor of the mouth.
  • When it extends through the mylohyoid muscle, it presents as a submental swelling known as aplunging ranula.

Diagnosis

  • Confirmed through Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
  • Ultrasound
  • Aspiration of thick, sticky saliva differentiates it from a lymphangioma

Treatment

  • Removal of the sublingual gland is preferred.
  • Incision, drainage, and marsupialisation have low success rates. Although marsupialisation is often adequate, it has a higher recurrence rate compared to sublingual gland excision.
  • OK-432 injection
  • Botulinum toxin injections

Explanation of other options

Cystic hygroma (Option A): A congenital abnormality of the lymphatic system, usually presenting as a soft, cystic swelling in the neck area. It is not typically found on the floor of the mouth.

Dermoid (Option C): Dermoid cysts are developmental cysts that contain various tissues, such as skin, hair follicles, and sebaceous glands. While they can occur on the floor of the mouth, they are not exclusive to this region.

Branchial cyst (Option D):These are congenital cysts that form from remnants of the branchial apparatus. They are primarily found in the neck area and are not commonly seen on the floor of the mouth.

question_text: A 50-year-old male chronic smoker came to OPD with cough, dyspnea, and difficulty swallowing. A palpable lump was present in the neck. Which of the following are smokers most likely to develop?
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient is a chronic smoker presenting with symptoms (cough, dyspnea, dysphagia) and a neck mass. This is a classic presentation for Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma (HNSCC).

Tobacco smoke is the single most significant risk factor for HNSCC, which arises from the mucosal lining of the aerodigestive tract (e.g., larynx, pharynx, oral cavity). The neck mass is highly suggestive of metastatic lymphadenopathy.

Explanation of other options:

Adenocarcinoma (Option A): While smoking is a risk factor for some adenocarcinomas (e.g., lung, esophagus), it is not the most common type in the head and neck region, where SCC predominates.

Large cell carcinoma (Option C): This is a type of lung cancer, not a typical primary head and neck cancer.

Adenoid cystic carcinoma (Option D): This is a salivary gland tumor. Its etiology is not strongly linked to smoking; it is more associated with genetic factors.

Key Takeaways:

  • Squamous cell carcinoma is the most common head and neck cancer.
  • Tobacco use is the primary risk factor for HNSCC.

References: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10179259/#:~:text

question_text: What is the condition depicted in the given image, and what is the next investigation required for management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The condition here is erythroplakia. Erythroplakia is a red, velvety lesion that is often highly suspicious for malignancy, and biopsy is indicated to rule out cancer.

Erythroplakia is a bright red velvety plaque that cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease.

  • Has a higher malignant potential than leukoplakia.

Types:

  • Homogenous
  • Speckled
  • Granular
  • Erythroplakia interspersed with leukoplakia

Management:

  • Biopsy for diagnosis
  • Surgical excision
  • Strict follow-up

Leukoplakia is defined as a white patch or plaque that cannot be rubbed off, and cannot be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other disease.

It is a premalignant lesion and is painless/non-tender.

Types:

  • Homogenous
  • Nodular
  • Speckled
  • Hairy: Associated with EBV. It is not actually hairy but appears so due to the corrugation caused by severe hyperkeratosis and acanthosis. Common in AIDS patients.

Management:

  • Biopsy to rule out carcinoma and confirm diagnosis.
  • Stop smoking/ alcohol/ betel quid.
  • Excision, skin grafting if needed.
  • Regular follow-up.
  • Isotretinoin, tocopherol, and beta-carotene.
  • CO2 laser.

Explanation of Other Options:

Erythroplakia and observation (Option B): Incorrect. Observation is unsafe because erythroplakia has a very high malignant potential, making biopsy mandatory.

Leukoplakia and biopsy (Option C): Leukoplakia is a white patch or plaque that cannot be scraped off. While biopsy is required for leukoplakia too, the lesion in the question is red, not white, hence not leukoplakia.

Leukoplakia and observation (Option D): Observation alone is not appropriate because both leukoplakia and erythroplakia are premalignant lesions requiring histological confirmation.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: Xerostomia, or dry mouth, commonly results from systemic conditions, psychological factors, medications, and destructive processes affecting salivary glands. Which of the following is not a common cause of xerostomia?
explanation:
Explanation:

Cholinergic drugs increase salivary secretion because they stimulate muscarinic receptors. Therefore, they do not cause xerostomia. In fact, they are sometimes used therapeutically to treat dry mouth. Common causes of xerostomia include:

  • Dehydration- reduces total body water and salivary volume (Option A)
  • Chronic anxiety and depression - decrease parasympathetic tone (Option D)
  • Anticholinergic medications - antidepressants, antihistamines, antispasmodics
  • Salivary gland diseases - Sjögren's syndrome, obstruction
  • Radiotherapy to head and neck - damages acinar cells, often permanently (Option C)
  • Aging - physiologic decline in salivary function

question_text: A child under 5 years presents with a painless, soft, fluctuant swelling located on the lateral aspect of the neck. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Cystic hygroma is a congenital lymphatic malformation, commonly seen in infants and young children.
  • Presents as a painless, soft, fluctuant, compressible, and often translucent swelling.
  • Most commonly located in the posterior triangle of the neck but may occur in the submandibular region, face, axilla, or mediastinum.
  • The swelling may increase in size with crying or coughing due to raised venous pressure.
  • Complications include:
    • Sudden enlargement causing airway obstruction.
    • Risk of infection.
  • Management: Complete surgical excision is preferred; sclerosing agents (OK-432, bleomycin) may also be used.

Explanation of Other Options:

Thyroglossal cyst (Option A):

  • Midline neck swelling, not lateral.
  • Moves upward on swallowing or protrusion of the tongue due to its attachment to the foramen cecum via the thyroglossal tract.

Cervical lymphadenopathy (Option C):

  • Represents enlarged lymph nodes.
  • Typically firm, discrete, and may be tender if infective.
  • Associated with systemic or local infection, not a congenital soft fluctuant swelling.

Ranula (Option D):

  • A mucous retention cyst arising from the sublingual gland.
  • Found in the floor of the mouth, not the lateral neck.
  • Appears as a bluish, cystic, fluctuant swelling inside the oral cavity.

Key Takeaway Points:

  • Lateral neck swelling in a child → think cystic hygroma.
  • Midline swelling moving with swallowing → thyroglossal cyst.
  • Floor of mouth swelling → ranula.
  • Firm/tender lymph node → cervical lymphadenopathy.

question_text: What would be the appropriate management for a 28-year-old woman who presents with a painless, gradually enlarging swelling under her tongue (as shown in the image), which becomes more prominent while eating but is not tender or red, and has no significant medical history or history of trauma or infection?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most definitive treatment for a ranula is removal of the sublingual gland, which addresses the source of mucus extravasation and minimizes recurrence.

  • A ranula is a mucous extravasation cyst arising from the sublingual salivary gland due to duct rupture or blockage.
  • It typically presents as:
    • A painless, bluish, dome-shaped swelling on the floor of the mouth.
    • Becomes prominent during meals due to increased salivation.
    • Often fluctuant, non-tender, and transilluminant.
  • Types:
    • Simple ranula: Confined to the floor of the mouth.
    • Plunging ranula: Extends through or around the mylohyoid muscle into the neck.
  • Management:
    • Sublingual gland excision is the gold standard, as it removes the source of mucus production and prevents recurrence.
  • Adjunct: Sometimes accompanied by removal of the ranula itself or marsupialization if needed.

Explanation of other options:

Incision and drainage (Option A): Offers only temporary relief. High recurrence rate and not definitive as it doesn't address the source (gland).

Marsupialization (Option C): Involves suturing the cyst wall to oral mucosa to form a continuous epithelialized tract. It's less invasive and often used in children, but recurrence is more common compared to gland excision.

Excision (Option D): Refers to removing the cyst only, without removing the source gland, leading to a high chance of recurrence.

question_text: Identify the level of lymph node of the neck indicated in the diagram?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The neck's regional lymphatics are divided into seven levels.
  • The most important group is the jugular chain, located adjacent to the internal jugular vein.
  • Other key nodal groups include:
    • Submental
    • Submandibular
    • Preauricular
    • Postauricular
    • Occipital
    • Posterior triangle nodes

Jugular Nodal Levels:

  • Level II: Upper third of carotid sheath
    • Contains jugulodigastric node
    • Drains: nasopharynx, oropharynx (including tonsils), posterolateral oral cavity, superior larynx, and piriform fossae
    • Commonest site of lymph node enlargement
    • Palpable along anterior border of sternocleidomastoid
  • Level III: Middle third of carotid sheath
  • Level IV: Lower third of carotid sheath

The levels are defined as the following:

Level I-the submental and submandibular nodes

Level Ia-the submental nodes; medial to the anterior belly of the digastric muscle bilaterally, symphysis of mandible superiorly, and hyoid inferiorly (Option B Ruled Out)

Level Ib-the submandibular nodes and gland; posterior to the anterior belly of digastric, anterior to the posterior belly of digastric, and inferior to the body of the mandible (Option C Ruled Out)

Level II-upper jugular chain nodes

Level IIa-jugulodigastric nodes; deep to sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle, anterior to the posterior border of the muscle, posterior to the posterior aspect of the posterior belly of digastric, superior to the level of the hyoid, inferior to spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)

Level IIb-submuscular recess; superior to spinal accessory nerve to the level of the skull base

Level III-middle jugular chain nodes; inferior to the hyoid, superior to the level of the cricoid, deep to SCM muscle from posterior border of the muscle to the strap muscles medially

Level IV-lower jugular chain nodes; inferior to the level of the cricoid, superior to the clavicle, deep to SCM muscle from posterior border of the muscle to the strap muscles medially (Option D Ruled Out)

Level V-posterior triangle nodes

Level Va-lateral to the posterior aspect of the SCM muscle, inferior and medial to splenius capitis and trapezius, superior to the spinal accessory nerve

Level Vb-lateral to the posterior aspect of SCM muscle, medial to trapezius, inferior to the spinal accessory nerve, superior to the clavicle

Level VI-anterior compartment nodes; inferior to the hyoid, superior to suprasternal notch, medial to the lateral extent of the strap muscles bilaterally

Level VII-paratracheal nodes; inferior to the suprasternal notch in the upper mediastinum


Key Takeaways:

Level II is the correct node level, located in the upper jugular chain, and drains areas including the naso- and oropharynx, tonsils, and superior larynx.

question_text: Cervical lymph nodes are divided into different anatomical levels based on predictable drainage patterns of the head and neck. Level III nodes refer to a specific group along the mid-jugular chain. Which of the following correctly describes Level III lymph nodes?
explanation:
Explanation:

Level III lymph nodes are the mid-jugular group, located between:

  • The inferior border of the hyoid bone (above)
  • The inferior border of the cricoid cartilage (below)

They lie along the middle third of the internal jugular vein, making them mid cervical nodes.

Cervical lymph node levels:

Level I: Submental and submandibular

Level II: Upper jugular (skull base to hyoid)

Level III: Mid jugular (hyoid to cricoid)

Level IV: Lower jugular (cricoid to clavicle)

Level V: Posterior triangle nodes

Level VI: Pretracheal, paratracheal (central compartment)

  • In Europe and North America this is mainly through cigarette smoking combined with alcohol abuse.
  • Synergism between alcohol abuse and tobacco use in the development of squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) of the head and neck is well established.

question_text: A 55-year-old male patient presented with right sided parotid swelling. CT scan showed involvement of only superficial lobe of parotid gland. Patient underwent superficial parotidectomy. On histopathological examination the tumour showed presence of glandular and cystic structure lined by bilateral epithelium, the stroma contains lymphoid tissue with germinal centres. Picture Is given below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Warthin's tumour is the second most common benign tumour of the salivary glands after pleomorphic adenoma.
  • Histopathological examination of Warthin's tumour shows prominent germinal centres.
    • Warthin’s tumour is composed of ciliated, bi-layered oncocytic epithelium supported by reactive lymphoid
    • The stroma contains lymphoid tissue.
    • The tumour is often glandular and cystic in nature lined by characteristic bilateral epithelium comprising inner columnar surrounded by smaller basal cells.
  • It commonly affects men in their sixth or seventh decades of life.
  • Multicystic appearance with bilateral involvement is common.
  • The treatment of Warthin’s tumour is generally through surgical excision.
  • FNAC will often be diagnostic or at least suggestive of the diagnosis and most tumours are managed through a partial superficial partotidectomy.

Pleomorphic adenoma (Option A):

  • Most common tumour affecting the salivary glands.
  • Pleomorphic adenoma tends to be well demarcated, round or ovoid with broad-based surface bosselations.
  • There may be areas of cystic change and also calcification.
  • Protuberant peri-capsular nodules may be seen, sometimes attached to the main body of the tumour by a slender pedicle.
  • The basic components are ductal elements and myoepithelial cells embedded in a chondromyxoid matrix.

Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma (Option C):

  • ACC is a basaloid tumor containing epithelial and myothelial components with 3 growth patterns:
    • Tubular pattern
    • Solid pattern
    • Cylindrical patterns.
  • Perineural and intraneural invasion is a common feature.
  • It is a slow growing but a highly malignant
  • Pain is a common feature due to Perineural invasion.
  • Microscopically it contains ductal and Modified myoepithelial cells.
  • They have hyperchromatic and angular nuclei and frequently clear cytoplasm.
  • Marked nuclear pleomorphism is seen. Ki -67 immunostaining is helpful immuno marker.

Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (Option D):

  • Mucoepidermoid carcinoma is the most common malignant salivary gland neoplasm
  • It is found more frequently in female patients and can present at any time between the first and ninth decade, but peaks in the fifth decade.
  • Risk factor- Previous radiation exposure.
  • Tumours are predominantly solid, tan-white to pink masses, often cystic filled with a viscous brown fluid.
  • Microscopicaly: The tumour consists of varying proportions of admixed mucinous, epidermoid and intermediate cells

Key Takeaway:

Warthins tumour:

  • Elderly male
  • Biphasic - Lymphoid tissue & Bilayer epithelium.
  • Mx - Superficial parotidectomy

Image reference: Pathology outlines website.

question_text: A male patient operated for parotid is complaining of redness and erythema in the cheek area after 3 months. He is also having sweating after eating. The nerve probably injured is
explanation:
• The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) carries preganglionic parasympathetic fbres from the inferior salivatory nucleus. The Jacobson nerve, a branch of cranial nerve IX, enters via the inferior tympanic canaliculus to form the tympanic plexus in the middle ear. The lesser petrosal nerve carrying the preganglionic fbres from here exits via the foramen ovale, where it synapses with the postganglionic secretomotor parasympathetic fbres in the otic ganglion.
  • These fbres exit the otic ganglion and join the auriculotemporal nerve in the infratemporal fossa, which innervates the parotid gland for the secretion of saliva.
  • Within the gland, acetylcholine (ACh) stimulates both acinar activity and ductal transport, leading to vasodilatation of the glands and contraction of the myoepithelial cells.
  • Atropine decreases salivation by competing with ACh for the salivary receptor site and is useful in reducing salivary secretion.
  • Regeneration of parasympathetic fbres to the sweat glands leads to abnormal autonomic reinnervation.
  • ACh can act as a neurotransmitter for both postganglionic sympathetic and parasympathetic fbres; this might contribute to 'gustatory sweating' (Frey syndrome), which involves sweating and fushing of the skin overlying the parotid region while eating in some patients following parotidectomy
  • Diagnosis: starch iodine test
  • Treatment: botulism injection

question_text: What is the most probable diagnosis for a 40-year-old male patient who has swelling that has been gradually increasing in size over the last two years, with variable consistency and complete mobility upon examination?
explanation:
Explanation:

A parotid tumor typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, mobile swelling with variable consistency, matching the clinical description.

  • The clinical scenario of a 40-year-old male with a gradually increasing swelling over two years, variable consistency, and complete mobility is characteristic of a parotid tumor, the most common salivary gland tumor.
  • These tumors often present in the preauricular region and may go unnoticed for years due to their painless nature and slow growth.
  • They are typically benign, with pleomorphic adenoma being the most common type.
  • The parotid gland is highly mobile in the preauricular region, explaining the free mobility of the tumor.
  • The variable consistency may suggest mixed cellular components seen in pleomorphic adenomas, which often have both epithelial and stromal elements.

Explanation of other options:

Dermoid cyst (Option A): Dermoid cysts are usually congenital, present at birth, and grow very slowly. They typically have a uniform consistency, unlike the variable consistency seen in this case.

  • Common sites: External angular dermoid is the most common type.
  • Symptoms: Painless, soft, smooth, and non-tender swelling.
  • Diagnosis: CT scan to rule out intracranial extension.
  • Treatment: Surgical excision.

Sebaceous cyst (Option C): These are epidermoid cysts, not true sebaceous origin lesions. They usually present as a superficial skin swelling with uniform consistency and may have a central punctum (except on scalp/scrotum).

  • Content: White, cheesy, keratinous material (not sebum).
  • Characteristic: Typically non-mobile relative to deeper tissues and don't grow as slowly over years like parotid tumors.

Cervical lymph node (Option D): Cervical lymphadenopathy usually presents as firm, discrete swellings, which may be tender (especially in infections) and less mobile when compared to freely mobile tumors.

  • Etiology: Infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease.
  • On palpation: Often firmer, less fluctuant, and more nodular than described in the stem.

A 45-year-old patient complained of pain in one side of the neck. She is afraid of eating food as it worsens the pain. Ultrasound imaging of the salivary glands is done and shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
option_c: Osteoma of the floor of the mouth
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The patient describes pain aggravated by meals, which is characteristic of salivary duct obstruction.
  • Ultrasound demonstrates a hyperechoic focus within the submandibular gland/duct, consistent with a salivary stone.
  • This presentation is typical of sialolithiasis, most commonly involving the submandibular gland due to its long, tortuous duct and thick mucin-rich saliva.

Sialolithiasis

Definition

  • Formation of calcified stones (sialoliths) in the ducts or parenchyma of salivary glands.

Epidemiology

  • Most frequent between 30-60 years.
  • Submandibular gland affected in ~85% of cases.

Risk Factors

  • Ductal anomalies causing stasis.
  • Dehydration or reduced salivary flow.
  • Inflammation of ducts.
  • High calcium content in saliva.
  • Certain medications reducing salivary secretion.

Clinical Features

  • Postprandial pain and swelling (classic cyclical presentation).
  • Asymmetrical gland enlargement.
  • Palpable stone in Wharton's duct in some cases.
  • May complicate with infection or abscess.

Investigations

  • Ultrasound: Detects hyperechoic stones with acoustic shadow.
  • Plain radiographs: Can miss radiolucent stones.
  • CT and MR sialography: Highly sensitive for small or deep stones.
  • Sialography: Traditional gold standard; can diagnose and sometimes dislodge stones.
  • Sialendoscopy: Allows direct visualization and retrieval.

Treatment

  • Small distal stones (<5 mm): Endoscopic removal.
  • Larger distal stones (>5 mm): Duct slitting or endoscopic extraction.
  • Intraparenchymal stones: Endoscopy ± shock wave lithotripsy.
  • Refractory/large hilar stones: Surgical excision.
  • Gland excision: Reserved for irreparable or recurrent disease.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Foreign body (Option B): May cause obstruction if introduced into duct but usually follows trauma or ingestion history; ultrasound shows a linear/sharp object, not a calcified stone.

Osteoma of the floor of the mouth (Option C): A benign bone tumor; unrelated to duct obstruction or mealtime pain, and not visualized on salivary gland ultrasound.

Cervical lymphadenopathy (Option D): Enlarged nodes present as neck swellings due to infection or malignancy; does not cause meal-related salivary pain or intraductal hyperechoic foci.

Key Takeaway

Sialolithiasis most often affects the submandibular gland, presenting with postprandial pain and swelling, and is best diagnosed with ultrasound or sialography, with management tailored to stone size and location.

question_text: Identify the statement that is incorrect regarding the condition shown in the image.
option_a: Retention cyst of major salivary glands
option_b: Most common site is lower lip
option_c: Retention cyst of minor salivary glands
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image depicts a retention cyst of a minor salivary gland.
  • Retention cysts of the major salivary glands most commonly occur in the parotid and submandibular glands, whereas the lower lip is a typical site for cysts of the minor salivary glands.

Retention Cyst of Salivary Glands

  • Retention cysts result from the blockage or injury of the salivary gland ducts.
  • Major salivary gland cysts occur in the parotid, submandibular, or sublingual glands.
  • Minor salivary gland cysts are commonly found on the lower lip, buccal mucosa, or palate. (Option B,C ruled out)
  • Diagnosis is confirmed through clinical examination and imaging such as ultrasound or sialography.
  • Treatment: Surgical excision is performed to remove the cyst and prevent recurrence. (Option D ruled out)

question_text: Identify the lesion shown in the image
explanation:
Premalignant lesions

  • The majority of oral cancers do not originate from a preexisting lesion.
  • However, there are a group of oral premalignant lesions, or more accurately described potentially malignant lesions, that are mucosal abnormalities from which oral cancer can arise.
  • These lesions include leukoplakia, erythroplakia, erythroleukoplakia, proliferative verrucous leukoplakia (PVL), oral submucous fibrosis, oral lichen planus and lupus erythematosus, as well as inherited conditions such as epidermolysis bullosa and dyskeratosis congenita.
  • A leukoplakia (2%-4% risk of malignancy) is a white patch or plaque that cannot be rubbed off, while an erythroplakia (20% risk of malignancy) is a bright red velvety plaque, neither of which can be characterized clinically or pathologically as any other recognisable condition.
  • A speckled leukoplakia or erythroleukoplakia is essentially a combination of both; it carries the greatest risk for malignant change.

The management of premalignant lesions is challenging, not least because of an inconsistency with nomenclature internationally but also because the natural history of these lesions remains unclear.

question_text: A 28-year-old female presents with a bluish translucent extravasation cystic sublingual swelling. The swelling is accompanied by visible veins over the swelling and is transilluminant. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical presentation involves a bluish, translucent, cystic swelling in the sublingual region, notable for visible veins and positive transillumination, which are hallmark features of a Ranula.

Explanation of Other Options:

Thyroglossal Duct Cyst (Option A):

  • Typically presents as a firm midline neck swelling near the hyoid bone
  • Rarely occurs in the sublingual region
  • Does not show cystic or bluish appearance
  • Transillumination is usually absent

Dermoid Cyst (Option B):

  • Usually located near the midline, often on the face or neck
  • Texture is firm or doughy rather than cystic
  • Translucency and visible veins are uncommon
  • Transillumination is not a characteristic feature

Sublingual Tumor (Option D):

  • Appears as a swelling in the sublingual area
  • Solid in consistency, not cystic or translucent
  • Transillumination is generally absent
  • Visible veins are not typically seen, unlike in a ranula

question_text: In modified radical neck dissection, which of the following structures is NOT preserved?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In a Modified Radical Neck Dissection (MRND), lymph node groups I-V are removed while preserving one or more non-lymphatic structures (depending on the MRND subtype).
  • The submandibular gland is excised when lymph nodes in level I are cleared, as the gland is intimately related to lymphatic tissue in that region.
  • Thus, unlike the sternocleidomastoid (SCM) muscle, internal jugular vein (IJV), and spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) (which are preserved in MRND), the submandibular gland is not preserved.

Explanation of Other Options:

Sternocleidomastoid muscle (Option A): Preserved in MRND type III. Removal occurs in radical neck dissection but not in MRND.

Internal jugular vein (Option B): Preserved in MRND type II and III. In radical neck dissection, it is routinely sacrificed.

Spinal accessory nerve (Option C): Preserved in all subtypes of MRND. Sacrifice of CN XI in classical radical neck dissection is a major cause of postoperative shoulder dysfunction.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: During oral examination of a chronic smoker, the lesion shown in the image is noted. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows a well-defined white patch on the oral mucosa, which in a chronic smoker is highly suggestive of leukoplakia.

Leukoplakia:

White patch on oral mucosa, defined clinically, excluding conditions like lichen planus, candidiasis, etc.

Aetiology:

  • Smoking, tobacco chewing
  • Alcohol abuse (especially with smoking)
  • Chronic trauma (ill-fitting dentures, cheek bites)
  • Associated with submucous fibrosis, hyperplastic candidiasis, Plummer-Vinson syndrome

Common sites:

  • Buccal mucosa (most common in India)
  • Oral commissures, floor of mouth, tongue, gingivobuccal sulcus, lip mucosa

Clinical types

  • Homogenous: Smooth or wrinkled white patch, lower malignancy risk
  • Nodular (speckled): White patches on an erythematous base, higher malignancy risk

Malignant potential

  • 1-17.5% risk, average 5% malignant transformation
  • Higher risk in dysplastic lesions and certain locations

Treatment:

  • Remove causative factors: Spontaneous regression in some cases.
  • Biopsy: For lesions with high malignant potential.
  • Surgical excision or laser/cryotherapy: For suspicious or small lesions

Explanation of other options:

Erythroplakia (Option A): Erythroplakia presents as a red patch on the oral mucosa, often velvety in appearance, and is also a precancerous lesion. However, the lesion in this case is white, not red.

Fordyce's granules (Option C): These are small, yellow or whitish papules representing ectopic sebaceous glands. They are benign and not related to smoking. They do not appear as a white patch like leukoplakia.

Koplik's spots (Option D): Koplik's spots are small white lesions with a red halo, typically seen on the buccal mucosa during the early stages of measles (rubeola). They are not associated with chronic smoking.

Reference:

Lichen planus

question_text: What is the most common site of a ranula?
explanation:
Explanation:

A ranula is a mucus retention cyst that arises in the floor of the mouth. It results from obstruction or rupture of the sublingual gland duct, leading to saliva pooling in the surrounding tissues. Clinically, it presents as a bluish, dome-shaped, fluctuant swelling beneath the tongue. Larger ranulas can cause discomfort and may interfere with speech, mastication, or swallowing.

question_text: A 7-year-old boy is brought with complaints of headache, vomiting, and neck stiffness for a few days. He had undergone a ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt placement for hydrocephalus a year ago. What is the most common cause of shunt malfunction in this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

Shunt obstruction is the most common cause of VP shunt malfunction, occurring most often at the proximal or distal catheter. Obstruction may result from:

  • Blockage by choroid plexus, blood, or inflammatory debris (proximal end).
  • Blockage by omentum, adhesions, or bowel contents (distal end).

This leads to increased intracranial pressure (ICP) with clinical signs of shunt failure: headache, vomiting, papilledema, irritability, altered sensorium, and meningismus.

A Ventriculoperitoneal (VP) shunt is generally considered for long-term management of hydrocephalus. It is implanted surgically to divert excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the ventricles of the brain to the peritoneal cavity, where it can be absorbed by the body.

Management of Hydrocephalus:

  • Medical: Acetazolamide and furosemide can temporarily reduce CSF production but are not effective long-term.
  • Surgical: (CSF Diversion)
    • Ventriculoperitoneal Shunt: Valved tubing from the ventricle to the peritoneal cavity.
    • Endoscopic Third Ventriculostomy: It is a useful treatment for certain cases of hydrocephalus, especially when there is an obstructive pattern that can be bypassed surgically and not always suitable for all patients and is considered an alternative to shunt placement
  • Intrauterine Treatment: Results are generally poor except in cases associated with fetal meningomyelocele.

Complications: Shunt occlusion (headache, papilledema, vomiting, altered mental status) and bacterial infection leading to meningitis/peritonitis (fever, headache, meningismus), typically caused by Staphylococcus epidermidis.

question_text: Which of the following statements about ranula is incorrect?
option_b: Arises from the submandibular salivary gland
option_c: Bluish, translucent cystic swelling on the floor of the mouth
option_d: Marsupialization or excision is the treatment
explanation:
Explanation:

A ranula is a mucus extravasation cyst, which most commonly arises from the sublingual salivary gland, not the submandibular salivary gland.

Ranula

  • Ranulas are a type of extravasation mucocele, caused by the rupture of the main duct or obstructed acini of the sublingual gland. (Option A ruled out)
  • They appear as bluish, translucent, cystic swelling on the floor of the mouth and resemble the belly of a frog. (Option C ruled out)
  • Commonly found in the anterior floor of the mouth.
  • When it extends through the mylohyoid muscle, it presents as a submental swelling known as a plunging ranula.
  • Typically presents as soft, fluctuant, and painless unless infected.
  • Imaging supports the diagnosis and aspiration yields thick, sticky saliva.
  • Treatment:
    • Excision of the sublingual gland is preferred. (Option D ruled out)
    • Incision, drainage, and marsupialisation have low success rates. Although marsupialisation is often adequate, it has a higher recurrence rate compared to sublingual gland excision.
    • OK-432 injection: Produces inflammation and fibrosis.
    • Botulinum toxin injections

question_text: In patients with suspected airway burns, early decisions about securing the airway are critical because oedema progresses rapidly. Which of the following statements regarding the initial management of an airway burn is correct?
option_c: If intubation is delayed, cricothyroidotomy may be required
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Early elective intubation is safest because airway oedema develops quickly and can obstruct the airway. (Option A)
  • Delaying intubation can make the procedure far more difficult or even impossible due to swelling. (Option B)
  • If intubation becomes impossible due to advanced oedema, a surgical airway such as cricothyroidotomy may be required. (Option C)

question_text: Burn patients must be evaluated for possible inhalational or airway injury. Certain clinical features strongly suggest involvement of the respiratory tract. Which of the following is not a warning sign of burns to the respiratory system?
option_d: All are signs of burns to respiratory system
explanation:
Explanation:

All the listed features are recognized warning signs of airway involvement in burn patients.

Key warning signs of inhalational or airway burns include:

  • Facial or neck burns (Option B)
  • Soot in nostrils or mouth
  • Singed nasal hairs
  • Hoarseness or voice change (Option C)
  • Stridor (Option A)
  • Cough or carbonaceous sputum
  • Respiratory distress

Early recognition is vital because airway oedema progresses rapidly, often requiring early intubation.

question_text: Name the topical agent used in treatment for burn wound reduces cell mediated immunosuppression
explanation:
• Silver sulphadiazine cream (1%). This gives broad spectrum prophylaxis against bacterial colonisation and is particularly effective against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and also methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
  • Silver nitrate solution (0.5%). Again, this is highly effective as a prophylaxis against Pseudomonas colonisation, but it is not as active as silver sulphadiazine cream against some of the gram-negative aerobes. The other disadvantage of this solution is that it needs to be changed or the wounds resoaked every 2-4 hours. It also produces black staining of all the furniture surrounding the patient.
  • Mafenide acetate cream. This is popular, especially in the United States, but is painful to apply. It is usually used as a 5% topical solution, but has been associated with metabolic acidosis.
  • Silver sulphadiazine and cerium nitrate. This is also a very useful burn dressing, especially for full-thickness burns. It induces a sterile eschar on the burned skin and has been shown in certain instances, especially in elderly patients, to reduce some of the cell-mediated immunosuppression that occurs in burns. Cerium nitrate forms a sterile eschar and is especially useful in treating burns when a conservative treatment option has been chosen. Cerium nitrate has also been shown to boost cell-mediated immunity in these patients.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 46, Edition: 28th, Pg: 674

question_text: Extensive burns trigger a systemic inflammatory response that increases capillary permeability even in unburned tissues. This leads to fluid loss from the intravascular space to the interstitium. At what percentage of total body surface area (TBSA) does this systemic capillary leak begin to occur?
explanation:
Explanation:

A burn involving 25 percent TBSA or more triggers a strong systemic inflammatory response. This produces generalized capillary leakage even in areas not directly burned. As a result, significant plasma loss occurs from the circulation, contributing to burn shock.

Burns greater than 20 to 25 percent TBSA cause:

  • Systemic release of inflammatory mediators
  • Increased capillary permeability in uninjured tissues
  • Massive fluid shifts leading to hypovolemia
  • Need for formal fluid resuscitation using the Parkland formula

Smaller burns cause local inflammation only, without systemic vascular leak.

Key takeaways:

  • Burns cause fluid, solute and protein to shift out of the bloodstream into surrounding tissues during the first 36 hours, while red blood cells remain intravascular.
  • In smaller burns, this leakage is limited to the injured area, but once burn size reaches about 10 to 15 percent TBSA, intravascular fluid loss can begin to impair circulation.
  • When burn size reaches 25 percent TBSA or more, the inflammatory response becomes systemic, and fluid loss occurs even from uninjured vessels.

question_text: Topical agents used on burn wounds differ in their antimicrobial coverage and effects on the immune response. One specific combination is known to reduce burn-induced cell-mediated immunosuppression. Which topical agent has this additional benefit?
explanation:
Explanation:

The combination of silver sulphadiazine with cerium nitrate is known to reduce cell-mediated immunosuppression in major burn wounds. Cerium nitrate stabilises the eschar, decreases bacterial load and helps modulate the immune dysfunction seen after extensive burns.It is especially useful in large burns where immunosuppression significantly increases infection risk.

Topical agents used in burn care:

  • Silver sulphadiazine: broad spectrum antibacterial agent, soothing and easy to apply
  • Cerium nitrate: enhances immune function, reduces burn-induced immunosuppression and improves eschar stability
  • Combined preparation is preferred in major burns for immunomodulatory benefit

Silver sulphadiazine cream (1%). This gives broad spectrum prophylaxis against bacterial colonisation and is particularly effective against Pseudomonas aeruginosa and also methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. (Option A)

Silver nitrate solution (0.5%). It is highly effective as a prophylaxis against Pseudomonas colonisation, but it is not as active as silver sulphadiazine cream against some of the gram-negative aerobes. The other disadvantage of this solution is that it needs to be changed, or the wounds resoaked every 2-4 hours. It also produces black staining of all the furniture surrounding the patient. (Option B)

Mafenide acetate cream: This is popular, especially in the USA, but is painful to apply and has been associated with metabolic acidosis. (Option C)

question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents with a deep burn involving the entire back, extending from the neck to the lower lumbar region. What is the preferred sequence of management in this patient?
option_b: First debridement, then reconstruction, and then resuscitation
option_c: First resuscitation, then reconstruction, and then debridement
option_d: First resuscitation, then debridement, and then autograft or allograft
explanation:
• In any case of burns, resuscitation is the first and most critical step using the ABCDE approach: Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability (neurological status) and Exposure (assess extent of burns)
  • Once stabilised, proceed with:
    • Debridement: To remove necrotic tissue
    • Then definitive management, depending on burn depth:
      • 1st & Superficial 2nd-degree burns → Managed with biological dressings (e.g., hydrocolloid or collagen-based dressings)
      • Deep 2nd & 3rd-degree burns → Require skin grafting (autograft is preferred; allograft if autograft not feasible)
  • Fluid Resuscitation:
  • Must begin from the time of burn injury without delay.
  • Immediate fluid resuscitation using Hartmann's solution (Ringer's lactate) guided by the Parkland formula (4 mL/kg/% TBSA burned) to restore intravascular volume and stabilise the patient.
  • Hartmann's solution / Ringer's lactate is preferred as it matches plasma osmolality, is affordable, and maintains intravascular volume.
  • Critical for survival in large burns.

Skin Grafting for Deep Burns:

  • Used in deep 2nd-degree and 3rd-degree burns.
  • Grafts promote primary intention healing:
    • At the base of the wound and
    • Along horizontal margins where it meets unburnt skin.

question_text: A patient who had burns some years back now presents with ulceration over the burns area indicative of malignancy. What is it?
explanation:
Marjolin's ulcer: is a squamous cell carcinoma arising from

  • Chronic burns scar
  • Keloid scar
  • Long standing venous ulcer scar

Chronically inflamed wounds are susceptible to neoplastic transformation. Squamous cell carcinoma was originally reported in chronic burn scars by Marjolin.

Chronic osteomyelitis, pressure sores, venous stasis ulcers, and hidradenitis may also develop neoplastic change.

Biopsies should be performed in cases of chronic wounds that appear clinically atypical. Cutaneous wounds may first exhibit pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasiaa premalignant condition.

Such a diagnosis on biopsy should prompt additional biopsies to exclude squamous cell carcinoma, which may already be present in other areas of the wound.

question_text: A 47-year-old man presents with a chronic non-healing painless ulcer over his scalp for 8 years. He has a history of electric burns to the scalp 8 years ago. The examination findings are shown below. Which of the following statements is true?
option_b: It can progress to squamous cell carcinoma
option_d: Long-duration antibiotics will improve the condition.
explanation:
Explanation:

The chronic non-healing ulcer in this case is highly suggestive of a Marjolin's ulcer, a malignant transformation of long-standing scars or chronic ulcers, most commonly into Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC). The patient's history of burn injury and the chronicity of the lesion strongly support this diagnosis.

Explanation of Other Options

Radiotherapy is useful (Option A):

  • Radiotherapy is not useful for Marjolin's ulcer because these tumors are generally radioresistant.
  • Moreover, radiotherapy can worsen local tissue damage by causing obliterative endarteritis, which further compromises healing.

No lymphatic spread (Option C):

  • While early Marjolin's ulcers are thought to have limited lymphatic drainage due to scarring, lymphatic spread is still possible in advanced disease.
  • Regional lymph node involvement and even distant metastases can occur, hence lymph node assessment is critical.

Long-duration antibiotics will improve the condition (Option D):

  • Antibiotics may control secondary infection, but they cannot treat the malignant transformation.
  • The ulcer's persistence and malignant potential mean that surgery is the definitive treatment, not antibiotics.

question_text: A construction worker presents to the OPD with complaints of white fingers. He has been working in the cement and concrete industry and has spent 20 years using heavy machinery drills and polishing wood and furniture. What is the most likely etiology for this condition?
option_a: Candidal infection of the fingers due to continuous exposure to water
option_c: Continuous exposure to cement and concrete
option_d: Continuous exposure to drills and machines
explanation:
Explanation:

Prolonged use of vibrating tools leads to Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome (HAVS), a known occupational cause of secondary Raynaud's phenomenon or "vibration white finger."

  • The patient's description of "white fingers" in the setting of long-term use of vibrating tools-such as drills and wood polishers-is classic for Hand-Arm Vibration Syndrome (HAVS), also known as Vibration-Induced White Finger (VWF).
  • This is a form of secondary Raynaud's phenomenon triggered by repetitive exposure to vibration from handheld tools, commonly seen in construction workers, carpenters, and machinists.
  • Pathophysiology:
    • Repeated vibration causes damage to the digital blood vessels and nerves, resulting in vasospasm and reduced perfusion.
    • During cold exposure or even stress, the affected fingers may turn pale or white due to ischemia, then bluish (cyanosis), and finally red (reperfusion), mimicking classic Raynaud's phases.
  • Raynaud's Syndrome (Secondary):
    • Occurs due to an underlying cause (like collagen vascular disease or occupational hazard)
    • More severe than Raynaud's disease
    • May lead to digital ulcers or gangrene in chronic cases
    • Poor response to sympathectomy
    • Prevention is key: complete avoidance of vibrating tools
  • Treatment options include:
    • Calcium channel blockers (e.g., nifedipine)
    • Vasodilators
    • Steroids (in autoimmune causes)
    • Behavioral modifications

Explanation of other options:

Candidal infection of the fingers due to continuous exposure to water (Option A): Candida infections may affect wet hands but typically cause erythema and fissures, not vasospastic blanching of fingers.

Exposure to thinners and paints (Option B): Thinners can cause skin irritation or dermatitis, but they are not associated with vascular spasms or Raynaud-like symptoms.

Continuous exposure to cement and concrete (Option C): Cement exposure may lead to contact dermatitis or chemical burns, not episodic digital ischemia and color changes seen in vibration white finger.

question_text: A 2-year-old child with 20% total body surface area (TBSA) burns is being resuscitated according to the Parkland formula. Six hours into resuscitation, the child's urine output is <0.3 mL/kg/hr, vitals are unstable, and extremities are cool. What is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?
option_b: Administer a fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg
explanation:
Explanation:

In burn patients, adequate fluid resuscitation is the cornerstone of management.

Children with >10% TBSA burns require IV fluid resuscitation, usually with Ringer's lactate as per the Parkland formula (Fluid requirement (24 hours) = 4 mL × body weight (kg) × %TBSA burned).

  • Urine output is the best marker of adequacy, with the target being 0.5-1.0 mL/kg/hr.
  • In this case, the child has oliguria, unstable vitals, and cool peripheries, indicating hypoperfusion and inadequate fluid resuscitation.
  • The correct step is to give a fluid bolus of 10 mL/kg crystalloid to restore perfusion, rather than waiting or escalating to vasopressors prematurely.

Explanation of Other Options:

Administer colloids (Option A): Colloids such as albumin are not given in the first 12 hours post-burn because increased capillary permeability causes them to leak, worsening oedema. They are considered after 12-24 hours.

Administer a vasopressor (Option C): Vasopressors are contraindicated in early burn shock because hypovolaemia must first be corrected with fluids; using vasopressors at this stage worsens tissue hypoperfusion.

Reassess in 2 hours (Option D): Delaying intervention risks worsening shock and end-organ damage; immediate action is required.

question_text: Identify the fluid shown below on the basis of composition:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The composition provided exactly matches Ringer's lactate (Hartmann's solution), a balanced crystalloid used widely in surgery, trauma, and fluid resuscitation.
  • Composition:
    • Sodium: 131 mmol/L
    • Chloride: 111 mmol/L
    • Potassium: 5 mmol/L
    • Calcium: 2 mmol/L
    • Lactate: 29 mmol/L (converted to bicarbonate in the liver, acting as a buffer)
    • Osmolarity: 279 mmol/L (close to plasma osmolarity)
  • Uses:
    • Maintenance fluid during surgery
    • Resuscitation in hypovolemia and burns
    • Corrects acidosis (lactate → bicarbonate)
  • Advantage: Unlike normal saline, it does not cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis.

Explanation of Incorrect Options:

Haemaccel (Option A): A colloid plasma expander containing degraded gelatin, sodium chloride, potassium chloride, and calcium chloride. It restores blood volume but does not have the same electrolyte profile as Ringer's lactate.

Isolyte (Option C): An isotonic solution with sodium, potassium, magnesium, chloride, acetate, phosphate, and sometimes dextrose. Its composition differs from Ringer's lactate and is mainly used for hydration and electrolyte balance.

Isolyte M (Option D): Contains sodium, potassium, chloride, acetate, and dextrose, with a different composition, and is used in pediatric maintenance therapy. It does not match the given electrolyte distribution.

Key Takeaway:

Ringer's lactate is a balanced crystalloid solution containing sodium, potassium, calcium, chloride, and lactate, making it the fluid described here. It is preferred in surgical and resuscitation settings due to its buffering capacity and similarity to plasma composition.

question_text: What type of skin graft is used?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A split-thickness skin graft (STSG) includes the epidermis and a portion of the dermis. These grafts are most often harvested from the inner thigh, buttock, or upper arm. They are particularly useful for covering large raw areas because they are easy to harvest, take well, and allow spontaneous healing of the donor site.
  • Healing of donor site: Spontaneous, which allows repeated harvesting.
  • Disadvantage: Greater secondary contraction and poorer cosmetic results compared to full-thickness grafts.
  • Common uses: Burns, trauma, chronic ulcers.

Explanation of Other Options:

Full Thickness (Option B): Includes both the epidermis and the entire dermis. Provides better cosmetic outcomes with minimal contraction but donor site requires closure (cannot heal spontaneously). Used for small, cosmetically important areas (face, eyelids, lips).

Wolfe Graft (Option C): Historical term referring to full-thickness skin grafts; hence, not correct in this case.

Local Flap (Option D): Involves moving adjacent tissue with its blood supply to cover a defect. Unlike grafts, flaps retain their vascular supply. Used when there is exposed bone, tendon, or in cosmetic reconstructions.

question_text: A 55yr old man underwent an operation for lipoma. 11months after surgery he felt itching and burning on the operated site where a scar is formed which is limited to the wound boundary. What is the nature of this lesion
explanation:
Hypertrophic scars do not extend beyond the boundary of the original incision or wound and eventually regress. They are more common in areas of increased tension, wounds crossing tension lines, deep dermal burns and wounds left to heal by secondary intention (longer than 3 weeks).

Keloid scars extend beyond the boundaries of the original incision or wound , do not spontaneously regress and are difficult to treat. The etiology is unknown but genetic predisposition is implicated. They often occur as a result of relatively minor trauma or after surgical scar and mainly in those with darker skin pigmentation.

question_text: A 50-year-old woman presents with a 1.5 cm pigmented facial lesion that has been increasing rapidly in size and is associated with itching. The lesion is shown in the image below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of a rapidly enlarging pigmented lesion on the face, along with associated itching, is highly suggestive of malignant melanoma as the most likely diagnosis.

Malignant Melanoma

  • Melanoma is a malignant tumour arising from melanocytes at the epidermal-dermal junction.
  • Though it is a rare skin cancer, it has a high mortality rate.
  • It presents as a pigmented lesion that enlarges, ulcerates, or bleeds.

Risk Factors

  • Positive family history
  • Fair-skinned/red-haired individuals living close to the equator
  • More than 30 sun-acquired naevi
  • History of five or more significant sunburns before age 16
  • Excessive UV exposure
  • Associated genetic mutations: CDKN2A (chromosome 9p21), MC1R, and TYR genes

Macroscopic Features in a Pre-existing Naevus Suggesting Malignant Change

  • Change in size
  • Change in shape
  • Change in colour
  • Increased thickness (elevation, nodularity, or ulceration)
  • Satellite lesions (pigment spreading into surrounding area)
  • Tingling, itching, or serosanguineous discharge (usually late signs)

Management of Malignant Melanoma

  • Excision biopsy with a 2-3 mm margin of skin and a cuff of subdermal fat is the standard approach.
    Excision margins (based on depth):
    • Melanoma in situ: 5 mm
    • <1 mm depth: 1 cm margin
    • >1 mm depth: 2 cm margin
  • Incision biopsy may be used for large or facial lesions where complete excision would be disfiguring.

Advanced / Stage IV Disease

  • Checkpoint inhibitors like Ipilimumab and Nivolumab are beneficial in unresectable or metastatic disease.
  • BRAF mutations (~50% of cases):
    • Dabrafenib / Vemurafenib (BRAF inhibitors)
    • Trametinib (MEK inhibitor)
    • Combination therapy (BRAF + MEK inhibitors) reduces resistance and improves outcomes.

Prognostic Indicator

  • Breslow thickness (tumor depth measured in mm from the granular layer to the base) is the most important prognostic factor in the absence of nodal spread.

Explanation of Other Options:

Dysplastic nevus (Option A): Also called atypical moles, these have irregular borders, varied pigmentation, and larger size. They carry a higher risk of developing into melanoma but typically grow slowly and do not cause rapid enlargement or significant itching.

Congenital melanocytic nevus (Option B): Present at birth, these are usually large pigmented moles that grow slowly over time. They do not typically grow rapidly in adulthood or cause itching but have an increased risk of melanoma.

Acquired melanocytic nevus (Option C): These are benign, small, symmetrical, and well-defined lesions that develop during childhood or adolescence. They grow slowly and do not typically cause rapid changes or itching.

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding malignant melanoma except
option_b: Superficial spreading form is most common type
option_c: Breslow thickness has no role in prognosis
option_d: Sentinel lymphnode biopsy useful for staging
explanation:
A small proportion of malignant melanoma is genetically mediated and develops at an earlier age. People at most risk of developing malignantmelanoma include: those with genetic syndromes; those with a past history of malignant melanoma or with a first-degree relative who has malignant melanoma; those who have more than 30 sun-acquired naevi or a history of five-significant sunburns before the age of 16; fair-skinned/ red-haired people living close to the equator; anyone with excessive UVR exposure (environmental or salon-delivered); or anyone with immunosuppression (which increases malignant melanoma incidence 20- to 30-fold). Male gender and solitary living are both associated with thicker melanomas at diagnosis. In women, higher socioeconomic status is positively correlated with developing melanoma.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, CHAPTER 45 Pathophysiology of the skin and subcutaneous tissues, Pg: 656

question_text: A woman who sustained third and fourth degree burns on her back has been brought to you. What would be the correct sequence of management?
explanation:
Explanation:

The management of major burns follows a strict, prioritized sequence to address immediate life threats and prevent complications.

  1. Resuscitation: The first priority. (Option C and D ruled out) Major burns cause massive fluid shifts and hypovolemic shock. Immediate fluid resuscitation using a protocol like the Parkland formula is essential to maintain circulation and organ perfusion. Airway assessment is also critical.
  2. Debridement: Once the patient is stabilized, the focus shifts to the wound. Necrotic tissue (eschar) must be removed to prevent infection and prepare the wound bed for healing. Early excision is standard for deep burns.
  3. Grafting (Allograft/Autograft): The definitive wound closure. An autograft (patient's own skin) is the gold standard. An allograft (cadaver skin) or synthetic skin substitute may be used as a temporary cover if autografting isn't immediately possible.

Grades of Burns and their characteritics

Explanation of other options:

Resuscitation → Reconstruction → Debridement (Option A): "Reconstruction" is a late-term cosmetic or functional procedure. Debridement of necrotic tissue must occur before any form of grafting or reconstruction can be attempted.

Key Takeaways:

  • The ABCs (Airway, Breathing, Circulation) of trauma management apply to burns first.
  • The sequence is: Stop the burning process → Resuscitate → Debride → Graft.

question_text: A 30-year-old patient with extensive third-degree burns requires skin grafting. What type of graft is used to cover the post-burn wound?
explanation:
Explanation:

A split-thickness skin graft is preferred in extensive third-degree burns due to its ability to cover large areas and allow donor site regeneration.

  • In cases of extensive third-degree burns, where the epidermis and dermis are destroyed, split-thickness skin grafts (STSGs) are the treatment of choice.
  • These grafts include the epidermis and part of the dermis, which are harvested from a donor site using a dermatome.
  • STSGs can be meshed to expand their surface area, allowing maximum coverage from limited donor skin, an essential advantage in patients with large surface area burns.
  • Key advantages of STSGs:
    • Donor sites heal spontaneously, allowing repeated harvesting.
    • Can be meshed to cover larger areas.
    • Easier graft uptake due to thinner dermis.
    • Common donor sites include the thigh, upper arm, and abdomen.
  • In contrast, full-thickness grafts (Wolfe grafts) are not suitable for large surface area burns due to limited donor site availability and more difficult graft survival.

Explanation of other options:

Full-thickness skin graft (Option B): Involves the entire dermis and epidermis. While it provides better cosmetic outcomes, it is unsuitable for large wounds due to limited donor site availability and poorer graft survival in avascular burn beds.

VAC dressing (Option C): Used for promoting healing in chronic or infected wounds through negative pressure therapy. It is not a grafting method and does not provide skin coverage for extensive burns.

Normal sumag dressing (Option D): Not a recognized or standardized method for burn care or grafting. This appears to be a non-specific or incorrect term in burn wound management.

Reference:

Evolution of skin grafting for treatment of burns - ScienceDirect

question_text: What is true about the procedure shown in the image?
option_b: The image shows a skin graft
option_d: Incisions on the upper limb are done to avoid major vessels
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image depicts escharotomy, and the true statement regarding this procedure is that it is done in circumferential burns.

  • Escharotomy is performed when circumferential deep partial-thickness or full-thickness burns restrict circulation or ventilation. (Option C ruled out)
  • In limbs, oedema under the rigid eschar obstructs venous outflow and eventually arterial inflow, leading to pain, numbness, and tingling.
  • Clinical signs, Doppler assessment, or compartment pressures above 30 mm Hg indicate the need for escharotomy.
  • The procedure involves longitudinal incisions through the burn eschar, usually on the medial and lateral aspects of extremities, to relieve constriction and restore perfusion.
  • For upper limbs, incisions may extend onto the thenar, hypothenar, and fingers.
  • In the chest, escharotomy is indicated when a circumferential burn restricts chest expansion and breathing.
  • Two longitudinal and two horizontal incisions are made to improve ventilation and oxygenation.
  • For the limbs, incisions are placed along the midaxial line to avoid major nerves. (Option D ruled out)
  • Complications include blood loss, release of anaerobic metabolites causing transient hypotension, reactive hyperemia with worsening oedema, and increased compartment pressures that may necessitate fasciotomy.
  • Because of bleeding risks, cutting diathermy and proper dressings are recommended during the procedure.

Explanation of other options:

The image shows a skin graft (Option B): The image shows escharotomy. Skin grafts are of two types: split-thickness and full-thickness. The image below shows a split-thickness graft.

Anterior chest involvement: 9%

question_text: A patient presents with following lesion six months after undergoing open-heart surgery. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most probable diagnosis based on the image and the lesion that developed 6 months after heart surgery is a keloid scar.

Keloid

  • It is characterized by abnormal and excessive growth of scar tissue that grows beyond the boundaries of the original wound and does not regress.
  • It typically appears firm, raised, and extends beyond the margins of the initial injury.
  • Keloid formation seems to be an individual predisposition, and it is more common in African Americans.
  • Sternum is the most common site for Keloid formation.
  • Treatment can be done by intralesional injection of steroids like Triamcinolone.

Explanation of other options:

Hypertrophic scars (Option A): Hypertrophic cars are also raised, they typically remain within the boundaries of the original injury. They may regress over time and are less likely to recur after treatment compared to keloids.

Atrophic scars (Option B): Atrophic scars are pale, flat, and depressed scars that appear sunken or as indentations in the skin due to loss of tissue or collagen.

Contracture (Option D): Contractures occurs when scar tissue forms and tightens, leading to restricted movement of nearby joints or tissues. They typically occur in case of burns or deep wounds. Contractures may result in deformity and functional impairment.

question_text: Which fluid is administered most commonly during intraoperative blood loss?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Crystalloids are the most widely used intraoperative fluids for replacement during minor and moderate surgical blood loss.
  • They are inexpensive, readily available, and effective at maintaining intravascular volume.
  • Ringer's lactate (Hartmann's solution) is the most common choice as it closely matches plasma osmolality and electrolyte composition.
  • Although larger volumes are needed compared to colloids (approx. 3:1 rule for blood loss replacement), their safety, cost-effectiveness, and availability make them the first-line option.

Crystalloids vs Other Fluids

Pediatric & Burn Resuscitation Pearls

  • Modified Parkland Formula (burns):
    TBSA% × Weight (kg) × 4 = mL in 24 hrs
    • ½ in first 8 hrs
    • ½ over next 16 hrs
  • Maintenance fluids in children:
    • First 10 kg → 100 mL/kg/24h
    • Next 10 kg → 50 mL/kg/24h
    • 20 kg → 20 mL/kg/24h

Explanation of Other Options:

Isolyte P (Option A): Incorrect. It is a balanced crystalloid and can be used, but Ringer's lactate and normal saline are more commonly used worldwide due to wider availability and lower cost.

Blood (Option C): Incorrect. Reserved for severe blood loss and anemia. It is not the first-line choice for routine intraoperative replacement because of cost, limited supply, and risks of transfusion reactions.

Colloids (Option D): Incorrect. Although they expand plasma volume more effectively, they are used far less commonly due to high cost and risks (renal injury, anaphylaxis, coagulopathy).

question_text: Child brought to EMR, post incidence half chest, half abdomen, half of upper arm and one leg front and back were involved. Calculate area of burn?
explanation:
Explanation:

Wallace Rule of Nines - Burn Percentage Distribution:

  • Head: 9%
  • Each upper limb: 9%
  • Each lower limb: 18%
  • Anterior torso: 18%
    • Chest: 9%
    • Abdomen: 9%
  • Posterior torso and buttocks: 18%
  • Genitalia: 1%

This rule is a useful aide-memoire in prehospital and emergency settings to estimate the total body surface area (TBSA) affected by burns.

Adjustment for Children - Modified Lund and Browder Chart:

Children have different body proportions compared to adults, requiring modification of burn surface area estimations. Infant's head is proportionally larger than an adult's.

On the modified Lund and Browder chart for children:

  • At birth:
    • Head represents 18% of total body surface area (TBSA).
    • Each lower limb represents 5%.
  • For each year of age:
    • 1% is subtracted from the head.
    • 5% is added to each lower limb.
  • This adjustment continues until the age of 10, by which time:
    • Body proportions approximate those of an adult.

Explanation of other options:

50-60% (Option A): Overestimates the area; would imply nearly the entire anterior torso and both limbs. The case mentions only half of chest and abdomen, one upper limb, and one leg.

40-50% (Option C): Also an overestimate based on the described involvement.

10-15% (Option D): Underestimates the area-does not account for full arm and leg involvement.

Key Takeaways:

20-30% TBSA is the best estimate in a pediatric burn involving half the anterior torso, one upper arm, and one leg (both sides).

question_text: While cooking, a sudden cooker blast caused burns of face with singeing of eyebrows, bilateral upper limbs, and front of chest. What is the burn area?
explanation:
Explanation:

(A/c to Wallace Rule of Nines in adult):

  • Head & neck (anterior + posterior) = 9% total. If only face is burned (anterior head), that's roughly 5%; singeing of eyebrows suggests anterior head/face involvement (we will count 4.5%).
  • Bilateral upper limbs = 9% each = 18% total.
  • Anterior chest = 9%. (Anterior chest and abdomen is 9% each; thus anterior torso as whole is 18%)

Sum (face 4.5 + both arms 18 + anterior chest 9) ≈ 31.5% → thus 27-30%.

Key takeaways:

In adults: head & neck = 9%, each arm = 9%, anterior chest = 9%; adjust if only partial head/face is involved.

  • Use Lund-Browder chart for children/precise assessment.
