question_text: Which among the following is not an advantage of harmonic scalpel device over conventional scalpel?
explanation:
Harmonic scalpel devices

  • The harmonic scalpel is an instrument that uses ultrasound technology to cut tissues while simultaneously sealing them.
  • It utilises a hand-held ultrasound transducer and scalpel which is controlled by a hand switch or foot pedal.
  • During use, the scalpel vibrates in the 20000-50000 Hz range and cuts through tissues, effecting haemostasis by sealing vessels and tissues by means of protein denaturation caused by vibration rather than heat (in a similar manner to whisking an egg white).
  • It provides cutting precision, even through thickened scar tissue, and visibility is enhanced because less smoke is created by this system during use when compared with routine electrosurgery.
  • However, the harmonic scalpel does take longer to cut and coagulate tissues than diathermy, and while diathermy can be used to coagulate a bleeding vessel at any time, the harmonic scalpel can only coagulate as it cuts.
  • It is claimed that patients experience less swelling, bleeding and bruising after the use of the harmonic scalpel than when a conventional scalpel is used, and blood vessels are sealed with a much lower temperature than conventional diathermy and so there is less thermal damage to adjacent tissue, with less charring and desiccation.
  • Furthermore, it is suggested that the use of the harmonic scalpel reduces operative time and recovery is thus enhanced.
  • Currently, the harmonic scalpel is in common use during laparoscopic procedures, as well as in open surgery, such as thyroidectomy, and several plastic surgery operations, e.g. cosmetic breast surgery.
  • There are several such devices on the market, which vary in form and function. Surgeons need to be aware of, and trained in the use of such devices to prevent, complications such as thermal injury of vital structures near to where the energy is activated.
  • There are several manufacturers of harmonic scalpels and the latest versions can seal and divide arteries and veins up to 7 mm in diameter.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 104

question_text: A 28-year-old male presents with a recurrent pilonidal sinus. He undergoes surgical excision of the sinus tract, which type of flap is used in this surgery?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The Rhomboid (Limberg) flap is the standard choice for closure after pilonidal sinus excision.
  • It is an off-midline closure technique, reducing wound tension, preventing midline scar problems, and lowering recurrence rates compared to direct closure.
  • The flap design allows for:
    • Tension-free coverage of the excised area.
    • Flattening of the natal cleft (reduces hair accumulation and recurrence).
    • Faster healing and fewer wound complications.

Explanation of Other Options:

Advancement flap (Option B): Useful for linear defects; less effective in the natal cleft where tension is high.

Rotational flap (Option C): Employed for large circular defects, but not standard in pilonidal sinus repair.

Free flap (Option D): Reserved for complex, large soft tissue defects (e.g., after oncologic resections), not routine pilonidal sinus surgery.

Key Takeaway Points:

Pilonidal Sinus

Definition: Acquired condition in the natal cleft with one or more epithelialized tracts containing hair and debris.

  • Etiology: Hair penetration into skin due to friction and shearing forces → chronic infection and sinus formation.
  • Risk Factors: Young adult males, hirsute individuals, prolonged sitting, poor hygiene.
  • Clinical Features: Pain, swelling, midline pits, recurrent discharge/abscess at sacrococcygeal region.

Surgical Management Options:

  • Incision & Drainage - for acute abscess.
  • Excision & Laying Open (marsupialization) - simple, but longer healing time.
  • Primary Closure - higher recurrence risk.
  • Flap Procedures (preferred for recurrent cases):
    • Rhomboid (Limberg) flap - most widely used, off-midline closure.
    • Karydakis procedure - lateralized flap, reduces midline tension.
    • Bascom procedure - excision of pits with lateral drainage incision.

Treatment Options:

Pilonidal sinus excision and repair by rhomboid flap:

Off-midline closures are associated with lower recurrence rates and faster healing than midline closures.

question_text: Which of the following statements is not true regarding the provided medical condition?
option_a: Repeated radical surgery every 24 hours may be required to adequately manage this condition
option_b: This is a case of Meleney's gangrene
option_c: The condition is caused by β-hemolytic streptococcus and may sometimes be polymicrobial
option_d: Hyperbaric oxygen has no role in the treatment of this condition
explanation:
Explanation:

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy is beneficial in managing necrotizing infections like Meleney's gangrene and not contraindicated.

  • Meleney's gangrene is a form of necrotizing fasciitis, a rapidly progressive soft-tissue infection that involves synergistic polymicrobial activity, often with Group A β-hemolytic Streptococcus and anaerobes or facultative anaerobes such as Staphylococcus, E. coli, and Bacteroides. (Option B,C ruled out)
  • It typically affects post-surgical or immunocompromised patients, especially in the perineal or lower limb regions.
  • Common locations: Lower extremities in over 60% of cases.
  • Predisposing conditions include:
    • Diabetes mellitus
    • Smoking
    • Penetrating trauma (e.g., bites, abrasions)
    • Pressure sores
    • Immunosuppression
    • Intravenous drug abuse
    • Perineal infections (e.g., perianal abscess, Bartholin's cyst)
    • Skin infections (e.g., boils)
  • Clinical features:
    • Early signs:
      • Oedema extending beyond visible erythema
      • "Woody" or hard texture in subcutaneous tissues
      • Difficulty distinguishing fascial planes and muscles on palpation
      • Disproportionate pain compared to the affected area
      • Skin vesicles and soft-tissue crepitus
    • Absence of lymphangitis is typical.
    • Progression: Rapid onset of fever, tachycardia, and rapid progression to septic shock.
    • Radiological findings: Air in the tissues may be visible on radiographs, although urgent treatment should not be delayed for imaging.
  • Management requires:
    • Urgent surgical debridement of necrotic tissue—often repeated every 24 hours until only healthy tissue remains. (Option A ruled out)
    • Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.
    • Supportive care, including fluid resuscitation and hemodynamic monitoring.
    • Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBO) is a useful adjunct as it enhances oxygen delivery to hypoxic tissues, inhibits anaerobic bacterial proliferation, boosts neutrophil activity, and aids in wound healing. Therefore, saying it "has no role" is incorrect.

question_text: Calciphylaxis true is/are
option_c: Reduction in the serum levels of a calcification inhibitory protein, α-2-Heremans-Schmid glycoprotein
explanation:
• Calciphylaxis (calcific uraemic arteriolopathy) is a syndrome of disseminated calcification resulting in both vascular calcification and skin necrosis.
  • It accounts for approximately 4% of patients undergoing surgical intervention for secondary hyperparathyroidism.
  • It presents with expanding painful cutaneous purpuritic lesions, predominantly on the extremities, although it can also be seen on the lower abdomen.
  • The underlying tissue calcification within the arteriolar and small vascular walls leads to ischaemic necrosis and the development of gangrene, which in turn leads to overwhelming sepsis and death.
  • The majority of these patients will have an elevated calcium × phosphate product but it is not usually associated with an extremely high PTH level.
  • The underlying aetiology remains unclear but a number of potential factors have been postulated. A reduction in the serum levels of a calcification inhibitory protein, α-2- Heremans-Schmid glycoprotein, and abnormalities in smooth muscle cell biology in uraemic patients may play a role in the development of the syndrome.
  • Prognosis for these patients is extremely poor, with a mortality of up to 87%. An urgent parathyroidectomy has been shown to decrease pain, improve wound healing and reduce the risk of amputation in these patients. It has also been associated with an increase in median survival.

Calciphylaxis

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, CHAPTER 56, The parathyroid glands, Pg:884.

question_text: Which among the following is not the uses of loose setons?
explanation:
USES OF LOOSE SETONS

  • For long-term palliation to avoid septic and painful exacerbations by establishing effective drainage; most often in Crohn’s disease and in those with problematic fistulae not wishing to countenance the possibility of incontinence.
  • Used before ‘advanced’ techniques (fistulectomy, advancement flap, cutting seton); acute sepsis and secondary extensions are eradicated and a loose seton is passed across the sphincteric component of the primary track to simplify the fistula and allow fibrosis.
  • As part of a staged fistulotomy.
  • As part of a therapeutic strategy to preserve the external sphincter in trans-sphincteric fistulae.
  • Secondary tracks in the ischiorectal fossa are laid open. Access to the site where the primary track crosses the external sphincter may sometimes necessitate division of the anococcygeal ligaments to reach the deep postanal space.
  • The internal sphincter is laid open to the level of the internal opening (or higher if there is a cephalad intersphincteric extension) to eradicate the presumed source and the sepsis in the intersphincteric space.
  • A seton is then passed along the residual track around the denuded external sphincter and tied loosely, and the wounds are dressed.
  • Initial postoperative management includes daily wound irrigation and light wound redressing.
  • The seton is left in place for 3 months and, if there is evidence of good healing, simply removed. Such a strategy certainly protects against the consequences of external sphincter division, with an incidence of healing in the short term of 50–60%.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 80, Edition 28th, Pg: 1439-1440

question_text: Signs and symptoms that cannot be explained by the anatomical distribution of a tumor and are due to substances released from the tumor tissue is known as?
explanation:
Explanation:

Paraneoplastic syndromes are remote effects of cancer that are not caused by the local presence of tumor cells or metastases. They are mediated by hormones, cytokines, or antibodies produced by the tumor cells. These syndromes can affect virtually any organ system (e.g., neurological, endocrine, dermatological, hematological) and are significant because they may be the earliest manifestation of an otherwise occult malignancy.

Examples:

  • Small cell lung cancer → Produces ACTH (leading to Cushing's syndrome) or SIADH (causing hyponatremia).
  • Renal cell carcinoma → Produces erythropoietin (causing polycythemia).
  • Thymoma → Associated with myasthenia gravis (neuromuscular disorder).

Explanation of other options:

Pretumor syndrome and Paratumour syndrome are not recognized medical terms in oncology.

Autocrine phenomenon (Option D): This describes a cell signaling mechanism where a cell produces a substance that binds to receptors on its own surface to stimulate its own growth or activity. It is a mechanism of action, not a clinical syndrome.

Key Takeaways:

  • Paraneoplastic syndromes are systemic effects of cancer unrelated to direct tumor invasion or metastasis.
  • They can be the presenting feature of an unknown cancer.

question_text: A 45-year-old male with diffuse severely contaminated peritonitis undergoes laparotomy. Due to the severity of the contamination, the abdomen is left open after the procedure. Which of the following management strategies would be most beneficial in promoting wound healing and preventing complications in this patient?
option_c: Primary closure of the abdomen immediately after the laparotomy
option_d: Antibiotic irrigation of the wound followed by delayed primary closure
explanation:
Explanation:

Laparostomy (Open Abdomen Management):

  • In cases of severe intraperitoneal sepsis, retroperitoneal swelling or bowel oedema may prevent primary abdominal closure.
  • In such situations, it is appropriate to perform a laparostomy:
    • Leave the abdominal incision open.
    • Cover the abdominal contents with mesh or a saline-soaked dressing.
    • Plan for delayed closure at a later stage.
  • Vacuum-assisted dressings help:
    • Manage high wound exudate volumes.
    • Promote fluid control and tissue adherence.
  • The patient may require multiple returns to the operating theatre for:
    • Gradual fascial re-approximation.
    • Eventual definitive wound closure.

Explanation of other options:

Normal saline-soaked gauze for dressing (Option B):

  • While this may be used initially to cover exposed abdominal contents in an open abdomen, it does not actively assist in wound healing or promote tissue regeneration.
  • Saline-soaked gauze alone does not facilitate the reduction of exudate or help in gradual abdominal closure as effectively as VAC therapy.

Primary closure of the abdomen immediately after the laparotomy (Option C):

  • This is generally not recommended in cases of severe contamination or edema as it increases the risk of wound dehiscence and infection.
  • Immediate closure without addressing these factors can result in fascial separation and worsening of the peritonitis.

Antibiotic irrigation of the wound followed by delayed primary closure (Option D):

  • Although antibiotic irrigation is important in the management of contaminated wounds, it does not provide an active strategy for controlling wound exudate or promoting tissue healing.
  • Delayed primary closure could be considered after infection and contamination are controlled, but VAC therapy offers better management in such situations.

Key Takeaways:

Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) therapy is the most effective approach to promote wound healing, manage wound exudate, and facilitate gradual closure of the abdominal wall in cases of severe contamination and open abdomen.

question_text: Arrange the following stages of wound healing in the correct chronological sequence.
explanation:
Explanation:

Wound healing is a dynamic, orderly, and overlapping biological process that occurs in four distinct but continuous stages:

  • Hemostasis
    • Immediate response after injury.
    • Vasoconstriction, platelet aggregation, and clot formation.
    • Platelets release growth factors like TGF-β, PDGF, VEGF, which initiate chemotaxis, angiogenesis, and extracellular matrix deposition.
    • Coagulation cascade generates thrombin, stabilizing the platelet plug.
  • Inflammation
    • Early phase (Days 1-2): Neutrophils clear debris and bacteria, aided by increased vascular permeability due to histamine and other vasoactive mediators.
    • Late phase (Days 2-3): Macrophages phagocytose necrotic tissue and release growth factors, promoting fibroblast activation and angiogenesis.
    • Clinical signs: rubor, tumor, calor, dolor.
  • Proliferation (Days 3-14):
    • Fibroblasts produce collagen and extracellular matrix.
    • Formation of granulation tissue with angiogenesis.
    • Myofibroblasts induce wound contraction.
  • Remodeling (Weeks-months):
    • Type III collagen is replaced by stronger type I collagen.
    • Tensile strength improves-reaching ~80% of normal skin strength by 12 weeks, with further maturation up to a year.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: A 32-year-old female undergoes emergency laparotomy for perforation peritonitis. Which of the following is the surest sign of wound dehiscence?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The most reliable indicator of wound dehiscence after an emergency laparotomy is the appearance of large amounts of serosanguinous fluid, usually around the sixth postoperative day.
  • This finding suggests a burst abdomen and necessitates immediate surgical re-exploration.

Definition:

  • Wound dehiscence refers to the separation of one or more layers of a surgical wound.

Incidence:

  • Seen in up to 3% of abdominal incisions, most often between the 5th and 8th postoperative day.

Types:

  • Partial dehiscence: Limited to skin and subcutaneous tissue.
  • Complete dehiscence: Involves fascial layers and may present with evisceration (bowel protrusion).

Risk Factors:

  • Systemic: Malnutrition, diabetes, obesity, renal failure, jaundice, sepsis, malignancy, steroid use, emergency surgery.
  • Local: Poor surgical closure, closure under tension, impaired wound healing, raised intra-abdominal pressure.

Clinical Features:

  • Pink, serosanguinous ("salmon-coloured") discharge (Option A).
  • Sensation of a "pop" while coughing or straining.
  • Possible evisceration of abdominal contents.

Management:

  • Partial dehiscence (without evisceration): Reclosure of the fascia is usually required.
  • Complete dehiscence with evisceration: Requires urgent re-exploration and repair.
    • Protect exposed bowel with moist sterile packs.
    • Apply tension sutures during repair.
    • Provide intravenous antibiotics and optimise fluids/electrolytes.

Explanation of Other Options:

Rebound tenderness (Option B) describes pain that occurs when abdominal pressure is suddenly released, reflecting peritoneal irritation or inflammation. It is most often associated with peritonitis and other intra-abdominal pathologies. Although it may indicate complications such as infection or inflammation, it is not a characteristic sign of wound dehiscence.

Hemorrhage (Option C) can develop after surgery due to vascular injury, coagulation abnormalities, or inadequate hemostasis. However, significant bleeding is not a typical manifestation of wound dehiscence, as the latter primarily involves fascial or wound layer disruption rather than vascular compromise.

Hypotension (Option D) may arise postoperatively due to factors like hypovolemia, sepsis, or shock. While it signals systemic instability, it is a nonspecific finding and not diagnostic of wound dehiscence. Identifying its cause requires further evaluation of the patient's overall clinical status.

question_text: A patient who underwent surgery for a lipoma 5 weeks ago now presents with a scar at the incision site that is limited to the original wound boundaries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A hypertrophic scar is characterised by excess collagen deposition leading to a raised scar, but confined within the original wound margins. It commonly develops weeks after injury and may regress with time.

Comparison of Hypertrophic Scar, Keloid, Exuberant Granulation, and Granulation Tissue

Explanation of other options:

Keloid (Option A): Excess collagen deposition extending beyond wound boundaries; persists and grows continuously.

Exuberant granulation (Option B): Overgrowth of granulation tissue above skin level ("proud flesh"), requiring cauterisation or excision.

Granulation tissue (Option D): Normal early healing tissue composed of fibroblasts, capillaries, and inflammatory cells, not raised.

question_text: Pressure greater than how many mmHg causes pressure sores?
explanation:
Explanation:

Pressure sores (also known as decubitus ulcers or pressure ulcers) develop when sustained external pressure on the skin exceeds capillary perfusion pressure, resulting in ischemia and eventual tissue necrosis.

The critical threshold is when pressure rises above 33 mmHg, which surpasses normal capillary pressure (≈25-32 mmHg). At this point, tissue perfusion becomes inadequate, leading to ischemic damage.

Explanation of other options:

Options B, C, and D (45 mmHg, 54 mmHg, 67 mmHg):
Although higher pressures can cause more rapid and severe necrosis, ischemia begins once pressure exceeds 33 mmHg. Prolonged lower-level pressure, particularly over bony prominences like the sacrum and heels, can also result in ulcer formation if unrelieved.

question_text: What is the ideal pressure setting for vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) therapy?
explanation:
Explanation:

The standard and most effective negative pressure setting for VAC therapy is -125 mm Hg, which optimizes wound healing by promoting granulation and fluid removal.

  • Vacuum-Assisted Closure (VAC) therapy is a form of negative pressure wound therapy (NPWT) that enhances healing in both acute and chronic wounds.
  • The system uses a foam dressing sealed with an adhesive drape and connected to a vacuum pump to apply controlled negative pressure.
  • The ideal pressure setting is –125 mm Hg, which has been shown to:
    • Promote granulation tissue formation
    • Decrease local edema
    • Reduce exudate and bacterial colonization
    • Improve perfusion to the wound bed
  • VAC therapy can be used:
    • To secure a skin graft onto a recipient bed
    • For temporary coverage in open abdomen wounds
    • To manage chronic wounds, such as pressure ulcers or diabetic foot ulcers
  • The pressure may be applied continuously or intermittently, based on wound type and patient tolerance.

Explanation of other options:

60 to 80 mm Hg (Option B): This lower setting may be used in sensitive areas or in patients who cannot tolerate standard pressure, but it is not the ideal or most commonly recommended setting.

130 mm Hg (Option C): This is above the recommended pressure and may compromise tissue perfusion, potentially damaging fragile granulation tissue.

80 to 100 mm Hg (Option D): Though acceptable in certain clinical scenarios, this range is less effective than -125 mm Hg for most VAC therapy applications.

question_text:
All of the following are part of the ASEPSIS wound
score except:
explanation:
ASEPSIS Score

The ASEPSIS wound scoring method was created by Wilson et al in 1986 and is an acronym for 

Additional treatment,

Serous discharge,

Erythema,

Purulent exudate,

Separation of deep tissues,

Isolation of bacteria, and

Stay as an inpatient prolonged over 14 days.

Its design was based on signs and symptoms of infected sternal surgical wounds post cardiac surgery. The score is calculated based on the percentage of the wound affected by serous exudate, erythema, purulent exudate, and separation of deep tissues. Additional points are awarded for antibiotic treatment, drainage of pus under local anesthesia, debridement of the wound under general anesthesia, isolation of bacteria, and stay as inpatient prolonged over 14 days.

Scores are grouped into 4 categories:

satisfactory healing (0-10),

disturbance of healing (11-20),

minor SSI (21-30),

moderate SSI (31-40), and

severe SSI (>40).

The original ASEPSIS score is meant to evaluate the surgical site for infections from day 5 to 7 postoperatively.

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC6505358/#:~:text=Note%20that%20the%20 ASEPSIS%20 scoring,then%2040%20as%20severe%20 SSI.

explanation:
Autograft: a graft of tissue from one point to another of the same individual's body

Isograft: graft of tissue between two individuals who are genetically identical( monozygotic twins).

Allograft: an organ or tissue transplanted from one individual to another.

question_text: What is the maximum diameter of the vessel to be sealed by harmonic scalpel devices?
explanation:
Harmonic scalpel devices

  • The harmonic scalpel is an instrument that uses ultrasound technology to cut tissues while simultaneously sealing them. It utilises a hand-held ultrasound transducer and scalpel which is controlled by a hand switch or foot pedal.
  • During use, the scalpel vibrates in the 20000-50000 Hz range and cuts through tissues, effecting haemostasis by sealing vessels and tissues by means of protein denaturation caused by vibration rather than heat (in a similar manner to whisking an egg white).
  • It provides cutting precision, even through thickened scar tissue, and visibility is enhanced because less smoke is created by this system during use when compared with routine electrosurgery.
  • However, the harmonic scalpel does take longer to cut and coagulate tissues than diathermy, and while diathermy can be used to coagulate a bleeding vessel at any time, the harmonic scalpel can only coagulate as it cuts.
  • It is claimed that patients experience less swelling, bleeding and bruising after the use of the harmonic scalpel than when a conventional scalpel is used, and blood vessels are sealed with a much lower temperature than conventional diathermy and so there is less thermal damage to adjacent tissue, with less charring and desiccation.
  • Furthermore, it is suggested that the use of the harmonic scalpel reduces operative time and recovery is thus enhanced.
  • Currently, the harmonic scalpel is in common use during laparoscopic procedures, as well as in open surgery, such as thyroidectomy, and several plastic surgery operations, e.g. cosmetic breast surgery.
  • There are several such devices on the market, which vary in form and function. Surgeons need to be aware of, and trained in the use of such devices to prevent, complications such as thermal injury of vital structures near to where the energy is activated.
  • There are several manufacturers of harmonic scalpels and the latest versions can seal and divide arteries and veins up to 7 mm in diameter.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 104

question_text: A 40-year-old man, chronic-smoker, presents with a lesion on his left ear that has been progressively enlarging over the last 3 months. Vitals are stable, and systemic examination is unremarkable. Histopathology of the lesion reveals keratin pearls. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image shows a cutaneous horn, which along with histopathological evidence of keratin pearls, is diagnostic of Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC).
  • Actinic keratoses are the most frequent premalignant cause of cutaneous horns, while squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is the most common malignant cause.

Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)

  • SCC arises from squamous cells- the flat cells found in the epidermis, mucous membranes, and tissues lining internal organs.
  • It is the second most common type of skin cancer after basal cell carcinoma.

Risk Factors

  • High sunlight (UV) exposure
  • Arsenic exposure
  • Immunosuppression (e.g., organ transplant, HIV)
  • Chronic lymphocytic leukemia
  • Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection

Macroscopic Appearance

  • May present as smooth nodular, verrucous, papillomatous, or ulcerating lesions.
  • Ulcers typically have everted edges and are surrounded by inflamed, indurated skin.

Histology of SCC

  • Characteristic irregular nests or masses of squamous epithelium invade the dermis from the basal layer.
  • Keratin pearls: Concentric, eosinophilic whorls of keratin seen within tumour cell nests — a hallmark of well-differentiated SCC.
  • Tumour cells may show intercellular bridges.
  • Immunohistochemistry: Positive for Cytokeratins 1 and 10.

Fig: Histopathology image of SCC showing keratin pearls.

Broders' Grading of SCC

  • Grade I (Well-differentiated): <25% anaplastic (poorly differentiated) cells- prominent keratin pearls.
  • Grade II (Moderately differentiated): 25-50% anaplastic cells.
  • Grade III (Poorly differentiated): 50-75% anaplastic cells.
  • Grade IV (Undifferentiated): >75% anaplastic cells - keratin pearls often absent.

Management

  • Primary treatment involves wide surgical excision with adequate margins.
  • Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) allows intraoperative histopathological margin assessment.
  • Advanced cases may require radiation therapy or chemotherapy.

Explanation of Other Options:

Nodular melanoma (Option A): A malignant tumour arising from melanocytes. It appears as a darkly pigmented, elevated nodule with irregular borders. Histopathology shows atypical melanocytes without keratinisation.

Basal cell carcinoma (Option B): The most common type of skin cancer, presenting as non-healing ulcers, pearly or translucent papules, or nodules with rolled borders and telangiectasias. Histologically, BCC arises from the basal cells of the epidermis.

Malignant melanoma (Option D): Arises from melanocytes at the epidermal-dermal junction. It presents as a pigmented lesion that enlarges, ulcerates, or bleeds. Histologically, it contains atypical melanocytes and lacks keratinisation.

question_text: What is the earliest age at which a unilateral cleft lip in a newborn can be corrected?
explanation:
Explanation of answer:

Unilateral cleft lip repair is ideally performed at 5–6 months of age, ensuring adequate weight gain and tissue maturity.

  • Cleft lip repair is generally timed based on the "Rule of 10s":
    • At least 10 weeks of age
    • 10 pounds in weight
    • 10 g/dL hemoglobin
  • This rule helps minimize anesthesia-related risks and ensures optimal healing.
  • In practice, definitive surgical repair of the unilateral cleft lip is performed around 5 to 6 months of age, after sufficient facial growth and weight gain have occurred.
  • This allows for better cosmetic and functional outcomes with reduced complications.
  • Earlier correction also promotes better feeding, speech development, and social interaction.

question_text: A patient, three days post-amputation for a crush injury following a road traffic accident, develops severe pain, crepitus on palpation, and a reddish-brown discolored wound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Gas gangrene is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening necrotizing infection caused by Clostridium perfringens(and other clostridial species).
  • It occurs in crush injuries, amputations, or wounds with devitalized tissue exposed to anaerobic conditions.
  • Classical features:
    • Severe pain out of proportion to findings
    • Crepitus (due to gas in tissues)
    • Reddish-brown to black wound discoloration
    • Serosanguineous discharge with a foul "sweetish" odor
    • Rapid systemic toxicity with shock, renal failure, and DIC in severe cases
  • Investigations: X-ray/CT (gas in soft tissue), Gram stain (Gram-positive bacilli without neutrophils).
  • Treatment:
    • Immediate and aggressive surgical debridement or amputation
    • High-dose IV penicillin + clindamycin ± cephalosporins
    • Polyvalent antiserum
    • Hyperbaric oxygen therapy
  • Prevention: Early wound debridement, no primary closure of contaminated wounds, prophylactic penicillin.

Explanation of Other Options

Impetigo (Option B):

  • Superficial bacterial infection (Streptococcus or Staphylococcus).
  • Presents as honey-colored crusts, not deep tissue necrosis or crepitus.

Tetanus (Option C):

  • Caused by Clostridium tetani.
  • Features include trismus (lockjaw), risus sardonicus, opisthotonus.
  • Does not produce gas, crepitus, or discolored wounds.

Cellulitis (Option D):

  • Diffuse bacterial infection of dermis and subcutaneous tissue.
  • Presents with redness, swelling, pain, warmth.
  • No gas formation, crepitus, or foul-smelling discharge.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: A 30-year-old female has low-grade fever, anorexia, and weight loss for 1 week. Barium meal follow-through shows narrowing of the terminal ileum with thickened ileocecal valve and conical cecum. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • In the barium study of the ileum in the case of ileocaecal TB, these are the signs that can be seen in the narrowing of the terminal ileum.
  • Thickening of the ileocecal valve and the thickening of the cecal walls, the cecum appears as a conical shape. In later stages, the ileum is fixed and rigid.

Ileocecal tuberculosis is the most common GI TB site due to rich lymphoid tissue and slow transit.

Ileocecal Tuberculosis:

Explanation of other options:

Ulcerative colitis (Option B): Shows pipe-stem colon, diffuse mucosal disease.

Crohn's disease (Option C): Cobblestone mucosa, skip lesions, transmural inflammation.

Carcinoma cecum (Option D): "Apple core" lesion in cecum, not terminal ileum.

Key Takeaways:

  • Ileocecal TB = most common GI TB.
  • Radiology: conical cecum + thickened valve.
  • Differentials: Crohn's, carcinoma.

question_text: What is the diagnosis based on the image below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis is a carbuncle, given the presence of pus-filled masses with necrotic tissue and a central yellow core, as seen in the image.

Carbuncle

  • Carbuncle is an infection of hair follicles extending into the surrounding and subcutaneous tissue.
  • Its a contagious infection of 2 or more furuncles.
  • The most common causative organism is Staphylococcus aureus.
  • Common sites: Nape of neck,
  • Presents as a red, painful nodule with a tender, fluctuant core, often accompanied by multiple draining sinuses, fever, and regional lymphadenopathy.
  • Complications can include septicemia, abscess formation, and tissue necrosis,
  • Management
    • Glycemic control
    • Incision and drainage
    • Antibiotics: Common first-line oral antibiotics include dicloxacillin and cephalosporins.
    • Surgical Excision: For recurrent or refractory lesions.

Explanation of other options:

Botryomycosis (Option A): A chronic bacterial infection that primarily affects the skin and occasionally soft tissues. It is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus or other bacteria. Unlike a typical carbuncle, botryomycosis presents as granulomatous lesions rather than pus-filled nodules.

Erysipelas (Option B): A superficial, sharply demarcated skin infection affecting the upper dermis, typically arising at sites of broken skin. Caused by beta-hemolytic Streptococcus pyogenes, it presents as a red, swollen, shiny rash rather than a deep abscess with pus or necrosis.

Ecthyma (Option C): A deeper form of impetigo, usually caused by Streptococcus species, presenting as ulcerative, crusted lesions. It differs from a carbuncle, as it does not form a deep abscess with necrotic tissue and a central yellow core.

question_text: A 56-year-old female was treated for a burn wound in the lower limb 5 years ago. Now she has developed an ulcer in the burn scar as shown in the image below. What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The clinical scenario, characterized by a chronic ulcer arising in a burn scar from an injury sustained five years ago, along with the provided image, strongly suggests a diagnosis of Marjolin's Ulcer.

Explanation of Other Options:

Venous Ulcers (Option B): Typically arise due to chronic venous insufficiency, commonly around the ankles. They present as shallow, irregular wounds with a red or yellow base and are not associated with burn scars or long-standing injuries.

Arterial Ulcers (Option C): Result from compromised blood flow due to arterial disease. Usually located on the feet or toes, these ulcers have a punched-out appearance and are unrelated to old burn scars or chronic trauma as seen in Marjolin's ulcer.

Cellulitis (Option D): A bacterial skin infection causing redness, swelling, and pain. It does not manifest as a chronic, non-healing ulcer years after a burn injury, distinguishing it from Marjolin's ulcer.

question_text: Which of the following statements about Marjolin's ulcer is not correct?
option_a: It occurs at the site of chronic wounds or scars
option_c: It can develop into squamous cell carcinoma
option_d: It is radioresistant due to poor vascularity
explanation:
Explanation:

Marjolin's ulcer usually develops over long-standing chronic scars or wounds, such as post-burn scars or chronic ulcers. It is characterized by slow growth and a painless, non-healing ulcer with raised margins. Over time, it may undergo malignant transformation, most commonly to squamous cell carcinoma. The key feature is that it does not progress rapidly but instead develops slowly over years. Surgical excision with appropriate margins is the treatment of choice.


Explanation of other options:

Occurs at sites of chronic wounds or scars (Option A): Correct. Post-burn scars and chronic ulcers are typical sites.

Progression to squamous cell carcinoma (Option C): Correct. Malignant change is most commonly into squamous cell carcinoma.

Radioresistant due to poor vascularity (Option D): Correct. Scar tissue is avascular, making radiotherapy ineffective.

question_text: A diabetic patient presents with sudden-onset severe perineal pain. On examination, there is foul-smelling discharge and visible necrotic tissue, as shown in the image. Which of the following is true regarding the likely diagnosis?
option_a: Anti-gas gangrene serum is indicated for all cases
option_b: Urinary diversion is the next step
option_c: A bilateral orchidectomy must be done
explanation:
Explanation:

Fournier's gangrene is caused by a polymicrobial infection involving both aerobic and anaerobic organisms.

  • The clinical features and image are suggestive of Fournier's gangrene, a rapidly progressing necrotizing fasciitis of the perineum and genitalia.
  • It is most often seen in immunocompromised patients such as diabetics.
  • The infection is polymicrobial, commonly involving:
    • Aerobic bacteria: E. coli, Proteus, Klebsiella, Staphylococcus, Streptococcus
    • Anaerobic bacteria: Bacteroides, Clostridium, Peptostreptococcus
  • Fournier's Gangrene Overview:
    • Definition: Necrotizing infection affecting the perineum, genitalia, or perianal area.
    • Symptoms: Sudden perineal pain, foul discharge, crepitus, dusky skin, and eventual gangrene.
    • Progression Phases: From pain and erythema → crepitus → necrosis and sepsis.
    • Risk Factors: Diabetes, alcoholism, malnutrition, PVD, immunosuppression.
    • Management includes:
      • Fluid resuscitation and broad-spectrum antibiotics
      • Urgent surgical debridement
      • Urinary and fecal diversion in selected cases
      • Wound care and later skin grafting

Explanation of other options:

Anti-gas gangrene serum is indicated for all cases (Option A): Incorrect. Antitoxin is used for Clostridial gas gangrene, not all cases of Fournier's gangrene.

Urinary diversion is the next step (Option B): Incorrect. While urinary diversion may be required to prevent contamination, it is not the immediate next step-surgical debridement takes priority.

A bilateral orchidectomy must be done (Option C): Incorrect. Orchidectomy is reserved only if the testes are involved, which is not routine in all cases.

question_text: Identify the suturing technique used in the following image.
explanation:
Explanation:

The simple interrupted suture is the most basic and commonly used suturing technique.

  • Each stitch is placed individually, tied, and cut, providing security even if one stitch fails.
  • The needle is inserted at right angles to the incision, passes through both wound edges, and exits at right angles.
  • The depth of the bite should equal the distance from the wound edge, and sutures are placed approximately twice that distance apart.
  • Advantages include excellent wound edge approximation and safety, but it is time-consuming.

Explanation of Other Options:

Horizontal Mattress (Option B): Used to distribute tension across wound edges; provides eversion but can impair blood supply.

Vertical Mattress (Option C): Provides good eversion and is useful for deep or irregular wound edges, but may leave cross-hatch marks.

Continuous (Option D): Fast technique using one uninterrupted thread; efficient but carries a risk of complete dehiscence if the suture line breaks.

Key Takeaways:

  • Simple interrupted = most secure, reliable, and versatile.
  • Mattress sutures = tension-relieving, eversion-producing.
  • Continuous = rapid but riskier if suture fails.

question_text: From the image of an ulcer. Identify the wrongly marked structure?
explanation:
Explanation:

'Margin' is the junction between normal epithelium and the ulcer, so it is the boundary of the ulcer. 'Edge ' is the area between the margin and the floor of the ulcer

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Margin

  • The margin is the boundary where the normal epithelium meets the ulcer, and it is correctly marked in the image. This is an important part of ulcer assessment as it helps in identifying the extent of the ulceration.

Choice C: Floor

  • The floor of the ulcer refers to the bottom surface of the ulcer, where tissue may be necrotic or granulated. It is correctly marked in the image as well.

Choice D: Base

  • The base of the ulcer is essentially the same as the floor. It is where the tissue at the bottom of the ulcer resides. Both terms refer to the surface at the bottom of the ulcer that is in contact with underlying tissues.

Key Takeaway

  • The edge of the ulcer is not commonly identified in clinical descriptions, unlike the margin, floor, and base, which are important for proper assessment.

question_text: What would be the subsequent course of action for this injury depicted in the image after a three-day period following a Road Traffic Accident (RTA)?
option_a: Debridement of necrotic tissue with primary closure
option_b: Debridement of necrotic tissue and hyperbaric oxygen
option_d: Clean and close with rotation flap
explanation:
Explanation:

The described injury involves established tissue necrosis, a common sequel to severe crush injuries. The primary goals are to remove non-viable tissue, control infection, and promote healing in the compromised wound bed. Surgical debridement is mandatory to excise all necrotic material. Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT) is a critical adjuvant treatment in such cases. It dramatically increases tissue oxygen tension, which enhances neutrophil-mediated bacterial killing, suppresses anaerobic bacteria, reduces edema, and promotes angiogenesis and fibroblast activity in the ischemic, traumatized tissue surrounding the necrotic area.

Explanation of other options:

Debridement of necrotic tissue with primary closure (Option A): Primary closure of a contaminated, necrotic wound would trap bacteria and lead to a severe infection or abscess formation.

Amputation (Option C): Amputation is a last resort for unsalvageable limbs with complete vascular compromise or overwhelming infection. Conservative measures to preserve the limb must be attempted first.

Clean and close with rotation flap (Option D): A rotation flap requires a clean, well-vascularized bed to survive. Attempting this over a recently debrided, contaminated, and ischemic wound would almost certainly result in flap failure.

Key Takeaways:

  • Debridement is the first step to remove all non-viable tissue.
  • HBOT is a valuable adjunct to improve oxygenation and healing in marginal tissue after crush injuries.

question_text: A 28-year-old male presents with the following lesion over the chest that developed after a traumatic injury one year ago. The lesion has progressively enlarged and now extends beyond the original wound boundary. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

Keloids are excessive scar tissue formations that extend beyond the original wound margin and do not regress spontaneously.

  • Keloids result from abnormal wound healing, characterized by uncontrolled collagen deposition that causes the scar to extend beyond the original site of trauma or surgery.
  • These scars are raised, firm, and often itchy or painful.
  • They do not regress over time and are more common in individuals with darker skin types.
  • The patient's history of trauma, followed by progressive scar growth beyond the original injury boundary, strongly supports the diagnosis of a keloid.

Explanation of other options:

Hemangioma (Option A): Benign vascular tumors present from birth or early infancy; unrelated to trauma and do not present as firm scar-like lesions.

Hypertrophic scar (Option B): Raised scar confined within the boundaries of the original wound; unlike keloids, these often regress over time and are less aggressive.

Neurofibroma (Option D): Benign nerve sheath tumor associated with neurofibromatosis; not typically linked to trauma and does not resemble a scar.

question_text: Which is NOT correct about vacuum-assisted closure (VAC)?
explanation:
Explanation:

VAC / NPWT (Negative Pressure Wound Therapy): well documented effects include reduced wound edema, improved perfusion and granulation tissue formation, and mechanical stimulation that promotes wound healing. The claim that VAC reduces bacterial load is controversial - some studies show reduced wound bioburden, others show no change or even increases; the effect on bacterial counts and infection rates is not uniformly proven. Thus the safest exam answer for "NOT correct" is the definitive statement "reduces bacterial load (Option A)". NPWT can be applied in continuous or intermittent modes (both used) and does promote granulation and reduce edema.

Key takeaways:

VAC/NPWT: good for difficult/large wounds, reduces edema and promotes granulation; effect on microbial load is inconsistent - use adjuncts where infection is suspected.

question_text: A 35-year-old man underwent surgery for ileal perforation. Because of gross contamination, the surgeon closed only the sheath, leaving the skin wound open. Daily wound irrigation was performed, and the wound was closed on postoperative day 5 after ensuring it was clean.What type of wound healing is this?
explanation:
Explanation of Correct Answer:

The described scenario is delayed wound closure after contamination control is healing by tertiary intention, also known as delayed primary closure.

In this method:

  • The wound is initially left open to allow drainage and infection control.
  • After several days (3-5 days), when granulation tissue appears and infection risk is low, the wound is sutured closed.
  • This combines the advantages of infection prevention (secondary healing) and cosmetic outcome (primary closure).

Explanation of Other Options:

Quaternary intention (Option D) is not a recognised term in wound healing. The proper classification includes primary, secondary, and tertiary intention.

Key Takeaway Points:

Phases of Wound Healing

  1. Inflammatory phase (0-3 days):
    1. Hemostasis → clot formation
    2. Neutrophils and macrophages clean the wound
  2. Proliferative phase (3-10 days):
    1. Granulation tissue forms
    2. Fibroblast proliferation and collagen deposition
  3. Remodeling (Maturation) phase (weeks-months):
    1. Collagen type III replaced by type I
    2. Scar formation and strengthening

Tertiary intention waits for phase 1 (inflammation) to subside before closure.

question_text: A patient had a chest trauma, emergency open thoracotomy done, comes under which category of wound?
explanation:
• Option a) Clean wounds (class I) include those in which no infection is present; only skin microflora potentially contaminate the wound, and no hollow viscus that contains microbes is entered. Class I D wounds are similar except that a prosthetic device (e.g., mesh or valve) is inserted.
  • Option b) Clean/contaminated wounds (class II) include those in which a hollow viscus such as the respiratory, alimentary, or genitourinary tracts with indigenous bacterial flora is opened under controlled circumstances without significant spillage of contents
  • Option c) Contaminated wounds (class III) include open accidental wounds encountered early after injury, those with extensive introduction of bacteria into a normally sterile area of the body due to major breaks in sterile technique (e.g., open cardiac massage), gross spillage of viscus contents such as from the intestine, or incision through inflamed, albeit nonpurulent tissue.
  • Option d) Dirty wounds (class IV) include traumatic wounds in which a significant delay in treatment has occurred and in which necrotic tissue is present, those created in the presence of overt infection as evidenced by the presence of purulent material, and those created to access a perforated viscus accompanied by a high degree of contamination.

question_text: A patient underwent mastectomy, and a drain was inserted beneath the flap. What type of drain is it?
explanation:
Drains are placed at wounds or surgical sites to accumulate/drain any free gas, pus etc which would render the surgical site an infection free environment and enhance the healing process.

There are different types of surgical drains which are as follows:

  • Open drains: works on the principle of gravity includes rubber tube or plastic sheets which would drain in gauze pad or stoma bag, increased risk of infection e.g. Penrose drain, corrugated rubber drain
  • Closed drains: works on the principle of suction, includes tubes attached to bag or bottle e.g. Jackson-pratt drain, romovac suction drain
  • Semi closed drain: works on the principle of of capillary effect, eg: ICD tubes

Removal of drain: the POD is important

  1. For bleeding (thyroidectomy) - 24hrs later removed
  2. For serous collections (mastectomy) - 5days
  3. Colorectal surgery (anastomotic leakage) - 5-7 days
  4. CBD drain-T tube - minimum 10 days its must be retained

The only place in alimentary tract surgery where it is still routinely advocated is for esophageal surgery

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK557687/

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding random flap except?
option_a: No specific relationship to where the blood supply enters
option_b: Length to breadth ratio should be more than 1.5:1
option_c: Length to breath ratio can be extended by delaying flap
explanation:
• Random flaps. Three sides of a rectangle, bearing no specific relationship to where the blood supply enters; the length to breadth ratio is no more than 1.5:1.
  • This pattern can be lengthened by ‘delaying’ the flap, a process in which the cuts are partially made and the flap is part lifted at a first operation; it is then replaced, thus ‘training’ the blood supply from a single border of the rectangle.

question_text: All of the following statements are incorrect regarding flap except?
option_a: Random flap: Specific relationship from where blood supply enters
option_b: Free flap: can  be swung around stalk
option_c: Pedicled flap: blood supply isolated, disconnected and then reconnected
option_d: Composite flap: various tissues are transferred together
explanation:
Composite flaps: Various tissues are transferred together, often skin with bone or muscle (osseocutaneous or myocutaneous flaps, respectively).

Option A: Random flaps: Three sides of a rectangle, bearing no specific relationship to where the blood supply enters; the length to breadth ratio is no more than 1.5:1. This pattern can be lengthened by ‘delaying’ the flap, a process in which the cuts are partially made and the flap is part lifted at a first operation; it is then replaced, thus ‘training’ the blood supply from a single border of the rectangle. At a second procedure, it is raised further and finally transferred.

Option B: Free flaps: The blood supply has been isolated, disconnected and then reconnected using microsurgery at the new site

Option C: Pedicled/islanded flaps: The axial blood supply of these flaps means that they can be swung round on a stalk or even fully ‘islanded’ so that the business end of the skin being transferred can have the pedicle buried

option_b: Full-thickness skin grafts are also known as wolfe grafts.
option_c: Full thickness skin grafts can use to cover all sizes of wound

They may be used to provide valuable temporary wound closure before better cosmetic secondary correction after rehabilitation.

question_text: Which among the following tumour shows predominance of Askanazey cells histologically?
explanation:
• Follicular carcinoma can normally only be differentiated from follicular adenoma by the architecture on histology.
  • For this reason, follicular lesions on FNA are unable to be diagnosed as malignant in the absence of clinical features such as metastases.
  • Multiple foci of follicular carcinoma are seldom seen and lymph node involvement is much less common than in papillary carcinoma.
  • Blood-borne metastases are more common and the eventual mortality rate, although still low, is twice that of papillary cancer.
  • Hurthle cell tumours are a rare variant of follicular neoplasm in which oxyphil (Hurthle, Askanazy) cells predominate histologically.
  • Hurthle cell cancers are associated with a poorer prognosis.

question_text: In which of the following condition, serum calcitonin is the most sensitive biomarker for detection and surveillance?
explanation:
Calcitonin

  • Calcitonin is a 32-amino acid protein secreted by the parafollicular C cells.
  • Normally, serum calcitonin levels are highest in infancy, decline rapidly in early childhood, then remain relatively stable through adulthood (although absolute levels can fluctuate minute to minute).
  • Calcitonin does not appear to play a significant role in calcium homeostasis despite its known mechanisms of action at the level of the bone, gut, and kidney.
  • Serum calcitonin is the most sensitive biomarker for the detection and surveillance of medullary thyroid cancer (MTC), which is a malignancy of the parafollicular C cells.
  • This test is performed in patients with-or family members at risk for-MTC or multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 (MEN2; see below).
  • There is controversy around the utility of measuring serum calcitonin as a routine screening test in the evaluation of a thyroid nodule.
  • Calcitonin is currently measured using a variety of methods, including radioimmunoassays, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and immunochemiluminometric assay, with differing sensitivities, specificities, and reference ranges.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 882

• Are tumours of the parafollicular (C cells) derived from the neural crest. rather than the cells of the thyroid follicle as are other primary thyroid carcinomas.
  • The cells are not unlike those of a carcinoid tumour and on histological analysis a characteristic amyloid stroma is seen.
  • High levels of serum calcitonin and carcinoembryonic antigen are produced by many medullary tumours, which should be tested for in suspected cases.
  • Calcitonin levels fall after resection and rise again with recurrence, making it a valuable tumour marker in the follow-up of patients with this disease.
  • Diarrhoea is a feature in 30% of cases and this may be due to 5-hydroxytryptamine or prostaglandins produced by the tumour cells.

question_text: Commonest glial tumors is?
explanation:
• Low-grade gliomas (WHO grade II) have a peak incidence in the fourth decade of life, and commonly present with seizures initially.

Active treatment consists of maximal resection, high-dose focused radiation therapy, and chemotherapy administered locally as carmustine wafers at the time of resection and/or systemically with oral temozolomide.

question_text: All are the following statements are correct regarding split thickness skin graft except?
option_a: Split-thickness skin graft can be expand from ratio of 1:1.5 to 1:6
option_b: Most used donor site is thigh
option_c: Vascularisation is not needed for graft take on a bed
option_d: Graft failure commonly caused by pus, exudates or residual dead tissue beneath the skin.
explanation:
Split-thickness skin grafts

  • Split-thickness skin grafts are taken with either hand-held or powered skin knives.

The most used donor site is the thigh, with the buttock preferable in children and cosmetically sensitive individuals. For larger grafts, almost any flat surface can be harvested, including the scalp if shaved (a very good and useful donor site).

  • The thickness of the graft harvested, ease of graft ‘take’ and donor site healing must be weighed against the lack of durability of thin split-thickness skin grafts.
  • Split grafts can be perforated to allow exudates to escape and improve ‘take’; they can be further meshed to allow expansion.
  • This is carried out on a device that cuts a series of slits along the skin, allowing it to expand from a ratio of anything from 1:1.5 to about 1:6.
  • Grafts will only take on a bed on which they can become vascularised. Preparation of the wound bed is therefore an essential part of a successful graft.
  • Graft failure is commonly caused by pus, exudate or residual dead tissue beneath the skin, haematoma or shearing forces. A clean healthy wound bed with a meshed graft tied in place to stop movement will encourage success.

Split-thickness skin grafts consist of epidermis and a variable amount of dermis and are sometimes referred to as Thiersch grafts. They are commonly harvested from the thigh using a dermatome or graft knife to achieve a consistent depth. It is relatively simple to harvest large areas of skin to reconstruct sizeable defects such as those following a significant burn injury

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 47, Plastic and reconstructive surgery, Pg: 686

question_text: What is the behaviour of the suture material which returns to its original length once the tension is released?
explanation:
Tensile behaviour. Suture materials behave differently depending upon their deformability and flexibility.

  • Some may be ‘elastic’, where the material will return to its original length once any tension is released, while others may be ‘plastic’, in which case this phenomenon does not occur.
  • Sutures may be deformable, in that a circular cross-section may be converted to an oval shape, or they may be more rigid and have the somewhat irritating capacity to kink and coil.
  • Many synthetic materials demonstrate ‘memory’, so that they keep curling up in the shape they adopted within the packaging.
  • A sharp but gentle pull on the suture material helps to diminish this memory, but the more memory a suture material has, the lower is the knot security.
  • Therefore, knotting technique also plays a significant role in any suture line’s tensile strength and it is important to recognise that sutures lose 50% of their strength at the knot.

Reference: Love & Bailey short practice of surgery, chapter: 7, Edition: 27th, Pg: 90

question_text: What should be the size of the balloon used for pneumatic dilatation in the treatment of achalasia disease?
explanation:
PNEUMATIC DILATATION

  • This involves stretching the cardia with a balloon to disrupt the muscle and render it less competent. The treatment was first described by Plummer.
  • Many varieties of balloon have been used but, nowadays, plastic balloons with a precisely controlled external diameter are used.
  • If the pressure in the balloon is too high, the balloon is designed to split along its length rather than expanding further.
  • Balloons of 30–40 mm in diameter are available and are inserted over a guidewire.
  • Perforation is the major complication. With a 30-mm balloon, the incidence of perforation should be less than 0.5%. The risk of perforation increases with bigger balloons, and they should be used cautiously for progressive dilatation over a period of weeks.
  • Forceful dilatation is curative in 75-85% of cases. The results are best in patients aged over 45 years.

Serial pneumatic dilatation has similar efficacy to surgical myotomy in selected patients. Features that predict optimal response are: patients older than 45 years, female, those with an undilated oesophagus, those who have responded to first dilatation and those with type Il achalasia. Perforation is uncommon; the reported incidence averaged about 1.9%(0-16%). With a 30-mm balloon, the chance of perforation should be less than 0.5%. The risk of perforation increases with bigger balloons, which should be used cautiously for progressive dilatation over weeks. It is important to have an experienced endoscopist performing the procedure and surgical back-up in case of perforation.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 66, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1123

question_text: Which among the following type of thyroiditis is caused due to fibrosis of the thyroid gland?
explanation:
Riedel Thyroiditis

  • Riedel thyroiditis, also known as Riedel struma or chronic fibrous thyroiditis, is an extremely rare and poorly understood inflammatory process causing diffuse destruction and fibrosis of the thyroid.
  • The primary theories for the etiology of this disease are that it is either an autoimmune process or a specific fibrotic disorder related to multifocal fibrosclerosis.
  • The most relevant finding in Riedel thyroiditis is the presence of an extremely firm and constricting gland that can be very uncomfortable for patients.
  • The fibrotic process often extends into surrounding structures, including the aerodigestive tract and RLN, which may cause clinically significant airway obstruction, dysphagia, and dysphonia.
  • Patients with Riedel thyroiditis have the biochemical markers of hypothyroidism. Imaging is necessary to rule out other causes of the dramatic local symptoms.
  • Ultrasound characteristics often demonstrate a diffusely hypoechoic gland with ill-defined borders.
  • FNA cytology reveals dense fibrotic changes but cannot be reliably distinguished from fibrotic changes often associated with anaplastic thyroid cancer (ATC).
  • Medical treatment to treat the inflammatory component of Riedel thyroiditis traditionally consists of corticosteroids and tamoxifen.
  • Other agents such as mycophenolate and rituximab also have been used.
  • Thyroid hormone supplementation/replacement is used to treat the associated hypothyroidism.
  • Surgical resection is often indicated to rule out malignancy such as ATC or primary thyroid lymphoma or to treat aerodigestive tract obstruction.
  • Surgery is usually extremely challenging due to the firmness of the gland and obliteration or normal planes and landmarks.
  • Partial resection of only the affected components is recommended, with simple wedge resection of the isthmus being the most common surgical therapy for relief of tracheal compression.
  • There is no evidence to suggest that Riedel thyroiditis is associated with an increased risk of thyroid malignancy.

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 37, Edition: 21st, Pg: 885

question_text: Which is not true regarding renal agenesis?
option_d: The ipsilateral testis and vas deferens are usually absent
explanation:
Renal agenesis is the complete absence of one kidney.

  • It results from failure of connection between the metanephric blastema and the ipsilateral ureteric bud.
  • This condition is an autosomal dominant trait with incomplete penetrance.
  • Typically, there is an absent ipsilateral ureter and the ipsilateral hemi-trigone is missing in the bladder.
  • The remaining kidney is usually hypertrophic but may also be dysplastic.
  • In addition, the ipsilateral testis and vas deferens are usually absent and in some patients the adrenal gland on the affected side is missing as well.
  • Females with the condition may have an absent ovary or Fallopian tube.
  • Renal agenesis is different from renal aplasia where there is a small dysplastic kidney.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1466.

question_text: All of the following are causes for vesico-vaginal fistula, except?
explanation:
Anterior colporrhaphy can lead to formation of vesicovaginal fistula.

Causes of vesicovaginal fistula include -

  • Obstetric- Protracted or neglected labour.
  • Gynaecological- Total hysterectomy and anterior colporrhaphy.
  • Radiotherapy.
  • Direct neoplastic infiltration. Exceptionally, carcinoma of the cervix ulcerates through the anterior fornix to implicate the bladder.

Reference: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 83, The Urinary Bladder, Pg: 1505.

question_text: A patient fell from a train onto the railway track and injured both his legs severely. He was urgently taken to the hospital ,and the following procedure was performed (image shown below). What is the rationale for performing this procedure?
explanation:
Explanation:

In cases of severe lower limb trauma, such as crush injuries sustained from railway accidents, amputation is often performed as a life-saving procedure. When there is irreversible ischemia, uncontrollable bleeding, or extensive tissue damage, limb salvage is not possible, and delaying surgery increases the risk of septicemia, shock, and death.

Thus, the rationale here is not cosmetic or functional, but to save the patient's life.

Indications for Amputation:

  • Dead Limb: Gangrene
  • Deadly Limb
    • Wet gangrene
    • Spreading cellulitis
    • Arteriovenous fistula
    • Malignancy (e.g., sarcoma)
  • Dead loss of limb:
    • Severe rest pain due to irreversible critical leg ischemia
    • Paralysis
    • Severe contracture
    • Trauma (irreparable damage)

Local Amputation:

  • For small-vessel disease (e.g., diabetes): Gangrene of toes may require local amputation. If the metatarsophalangeal joint is involved, ray excision may be necessary.

Major Amputation:

  • Below-knee Amputation: Preserves knee joint, offering better prosthetic use.
  • Above-knee Amputation: For poor circulation or non-mobilizing patients.
  • Knee Disarticulation: Preserves femur and patella for better prosthetic function.

Post-operative care:

  • Pain Management: Regular opiate use.
  • Limb Care: Prevent pressure ulcers on the remaining limb.
  • Exercise: Prevent deformities, build strength, and improve mobility.

Complications:

  • Early: Hemorrhage, infection, gas gangrene, and wound dehiscence.
  • Late: Phantom limb pain, stump ulceration, DVT, and pulmonary embolism

Explanation of Other Options

Better fit for prosthesis (Option A):

  • Prosthetic fitting is indeed easier and more functional after a below-knee amputation compared to above-knee, since the knee joint is preserved.
  • However, in this emergency case, the primary goal was not prosthetic rehabilitation but immediate life-saving intervention.

Reduces risk of cancer (Option C):

  • Amputation can be indicated for malignant tumors (e.g., osteogenic sarcoma, soft tissue sarcoma) when limb-sparing procedures are not feasible.
  • In this patient, there was no evidence of malignancy.
  • The rationale was trauma management, not cancer risk reduction.

Good cosmetic outcomes (Option D):

  • Cosmetic considerations are not the main indication for amputations, especially in emergency trauma cases.
  • Post-traumatic amputations often have poor cosmetic outcomes and require reconstructive procedures or prosthesis later.

question_text: Which is not true regarding genitourinary tuberculosis?
option_c: Involves the distal ureters and bladder
explanation:
Genitourinary tuberculosis-

  • Caused by dissemination of the organism through the bloodstream and is thus always secondary TB. There is either reinfection or reactivation of old TB.
  • It is a cause of sterile pyuria.
  • Spreads from the kidney to involve the distal ureters and bladder around ureteric orifices.

Treatment -

  • Short-course of anti-tubercular drugs as fewer organisms are involved compared with pulmonary TB and drugs tend to concentrate in the urine.
  • Surgery is done for excision of dead tissue (partial or total nephrectomy) and reconstructive surgery (for ureteric strictures, augmentation cystoplasty).

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1472.

question_text: What is the Z-plasty technique?
explanation:
Explanation:

Z-plasty is a classic local transposition/advancement technique (three-limb Z formation) used primarily to lengthen a contracted linear scar, change scar direction to fall along skin lines, and break up straight-line scars. The central limb is aligned with the scar and two triangular flaps are transposed; the effect is a lengthening of the central limb and reorientation of the scar. Although it involves local transposition of triangular flaps (Option D ruled out), its primary purpose in exam terms is scar lengthening/releasing contracture (answer A).

Explanation of other options:

Technique of flap creation (Option B): partly true (Z-plasty makes local triangular flaps) but the classical definition emphasizes lengthening/reorientation rather than simply "flap creation."

Zig-zag suture (Option C): not accurate; Z-plasty is a flap design, not merely suture pattern.

Local transposition flap (Option D): technically, Z-plasty is a form of local transposition, but the exam wording expects the specific goal: scar lengthening.
