explanation: Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 47, Plastic and reconstructive surgery, Pg: 691

question_text: Arterial grafts can be use in CABG?
explanation:
• The use of the radial artery as a second or alternative arterial bypass graft has enjoyed a revival in recent times. This has been driven to some extent by the developing concept of total arterial revascularisation and the belief that this will help improve long-term results of coronary surgery. Different randomised controlled studies have demonstrated excellent patency rates at 1 and 5 years.
  • In assessing a patient in whom a radial artery harvest is planned, an Allen's test should be performed. Alternative arterial bypass grafts include the gastroepiploic artery and the inferior epigastric artery.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 59, Cardiac Surgery, Pg: 950.

question_text: All statements are incorrect regarding aneurysmal bleeding investigation except?
option_a: All patient requires LP for diagnosis of SAH
option_b: CSF supernatant should be analysed by spectrophotometry
option_c: Sensitivity of CT increase with time to diagnose SAH
explanation:
• In light of this, patients with a suggestive history and negative CT scan will require LP, especially where presentation is delayed. The CSF supernatant should be analysed by spectrophotometry (visual inspection is not reliable) for the spectra of haemoglobin breakdown products oxyhaemoglobin and bilirubin.
  • These are clearly detectable in samples taken at least 6 and preferably 12 hours after SAH, but not in CSF mixed with fresh blood due to traumatic puncture, and analysed immediately. Failure to exclude SAH with an appropriate delayed LP may necessitate formal cerebral angiography, and the risks this entails.
  • Catheter angiography generally involves access to both vertebral and carotid arteries through the femoral artery under local anaesthetic. This allows visualisation of the vascular anatomy by injection of contrast medium with simultaneous screening.
  • The serious potential risks include ischaemic stroke or arterial dissection (1-2%), and renal failure or allergic reactions attributable to contrast.

Option A: CT scan is the imaging of first choice, and, when performed within 12 hours of ictus, will confirm bleeding in more than 98% of cases. This makes a diagnostic LP unnecessary

Option C: The sensitivity of a CT scan, however, deteriorates to less than 50% at 1 week after a bleed.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 710

question_text: Identify the test provided in the image below.
explanation:
Explanation:

The given image shows Allen's test.

  • Allen's Testis a clinical manoeuvre used to assess the blood flow to the hand, specifically evaluating the patency of the radial and ulnar arteries.
  • It is commonly used before procedures like inserting an arterial line or taking a blood sample from the radial artery.
  • Procedure:
    • The patient is asked to make a fist, compressing the radial and ulnar arteries simultaneously.
    • The patient is then asked to open their hand (which should appear pale).
    • Once the hand is open, the examiner releases one of the arteries (usually the ulnar artery).
  • Interpretation
    • The test is positive if normal colour returns to the hand quickly (within 5-10 seconds), indicating adequate collateral circulation.
    • If there is a delay in the colour return or no return, this may suggest compromised blood flow through the released artery, which could indicate arterial occlusion & the radial artery should not be pricked.

Explanation of other options:

Adson's test (Option B):

  • Used to diagnose thoracic outlet syndrome (TOS), which occurs due to compression of the brachial plexus or subclavian artery in the thoracic outlet.
  • The patient is instructed to extend their neck and turn their head toward the arm being tested while the examiner palpates the radial pulse. The patient then takes a deep breath.
  • A positive test is indicated by a reduction or disappearance of the radial pulse, suggesting compression in the thoracic outlet.

Elevated arm stress test (Option C):

  • Evaluates thoracic outlet syndrome by assessing the compression of neurovascular structures in the thoracic outlet.
  • The patient’s arms are raised above the head and held for 1-2 minutes.
  • A positive test occurs if the patient experiences symptoms of numbness, tingling, or a decrease in the radial pulse, which indicates compression of the neurovascular bundle in the thoracic outlet.

Nicoladoni's test (Option D): Nicoladoni's test is used to assess for increased intracranial pressure (ICP) or brainstem compression. The test is positive if the patient exhibits a sudden drop in pulse or blood pressure when their head is tilted backwards (in a hyperextended position).

question_text: Which among the following diseases is also known as serocystic disease of the Brodie?
explanation:
Phyllodes tumour (Serocystic disease of Brodie or Cystosarcoma phyllodes) -

  • Benign
  • Usually occur in women over the age of 40 years but can appear in younger women.
  • They present as a large, sometimes massive tumour with an unevenly bosselated surface.
  • Occasionally, ulceration of overlying skin occurs because of pressure necrosis.
  • Mobile on the chest wall
  • Only very rarely develop features of a sarcomatous tumour.
  • These may metastasise via the bloodstream.

Treatment

Treatment for the benign type is enucleation in young women or wide local excision. Massive tumours, recurrent tumours and those of the malignant type will require mastectomy.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 58, Edition: 28th, Pg: 922-923

question_text: A 17-year-old woman with no comorbidities presents with numbness and paraesthesia of the fingers along with the characteristic finding as shown in the image below. She has no history of smoking or history of other illnesses. She mentions the episodes occur when she is under excess stress or during cold temperatures. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

A young woman presenting with numbness, tingling sensations (paresthesia), and bluish discoloration of the fingers during exposure to cold or emotional stress, without any history of smoking, comorbid conditions, or other underlying illnesses, most likely has Raynaud's Phenomenon.

Phases of Raynaud's Phenomenon:

  • Pallor: The first stage, where the skin becomes pale or whitish because of reduced blood flow caused by vasospasm.
  • Cyanosis: This stage follows, marked by a bluish or purplish discoloration due to persistent lack of oxygen in the tissues.
  • Rubor: The final stage, in which the skin turns red as circulation is restored and the affected area rewarms.

Explanation of Other Options:

Buerger's Disease (Thromboangiitis Obliterans) (Option A): This is an inflammatory disorder involving small- and medium-sized arteries and veins, leading to thrombus formation and impaired circulation. It primarily affects young male smokers and is associated with ischemic pain, ulcerations, and sometimes gangrene of the extremities. Given the absence of smoking history, vascular risk factors, or ulcerative features, this condition is unlikely in the presented case.

Atherosclerosis (Option B): A condition marked by deposition of lipid-rich plaques within arterial walls, more common in older individuals with risk factors such as smoking, dyslipidemia, hypertension, or diabetes. It typically causes chronic manifestations like claudication and ischemic pain, rather than acute, stress- or cold-induced symptoms. Since the patient is young, without comorbidities or risk factors, this explanation is less probable.

Giant Cell Arteritis (GCA) (Option D): An inflammatory vasculitis that targets large arteries, usually in individuals over 50 years of age. It presents with symptoms such as temporal headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, and vision disturbances. This makes it an unsuitable diagnosis for the current young female patient.

question_text: Which among the following diseases shows claw sign on barium enema study?
explanation:
Imaging in intussusception

  • A plain abdominal field usually reveals evidence of small or large bowel obstruction with an absent caecal gas shadow in ileocolic cases.
  • A soft tissue opacity is often visible in children.
  • A barium enema may be used to diagnose the presence of an ileocolic intussusception (the claw sign) but does not demonstrate small bowel intussusception.
  • An abdominal ultrasound scan has a high diagnostic sensitivity in children, demonstrating the typical doughnut appearance of concentric rings in transverse section.
  • CT scanning is currently considered the most sensitive radiological method to confirm intussusception, with a reported diagnostic accuracy of 58-100%.
  • The characteristic features of CT scan include a 'target'- or 'sausage'- shaped soft-tissue mass with a layering effect; mesenteric vessels within the bowel lumen are also typical.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 78, Edition: 28th, Pg: 1384-1385

question_text: Which among the following diseases shows Kantor string sign on barium enema study?
explanation:
Radiology.

  • CTE or magnetic resonance enterography (MRE) are often used as the initial assessment of Crohn disease to complement direct ileocolonoscopy.
  • Imaging studies can provide information regarding severity of inflammation, length, and focality and identify complications (e.g., obstruction or fistula).
  • In addition, these studies support surgical planning and the evaluation of response to medical therapy.
  • Previously, barium enema was commonly used to identify features of Crohn For example, long lengths of narrowed terminal ileum (Kantor string sign) may be present with long-standing disease.
  • Segmental and irregular patterns of bowel involvement may be Fistulas between adjacent bowel loops and organs may be apparent

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 50, Edition: 21st, Pg: 1263

question_text: Which among the following diseases is referred to as jeep disease?
explanation:
Pilonidal sinus

  • The term pilonidal sinus describes a condition found in the natal cleft overlying the coccyx, consisting of one or more, usually non-infected, midline openings, which communicate with a fibrous track lined by granulation tissue and containing hair lying loosely within the lumen.
  • A common affliction amongst the military, it has been referred to as ‘jeep disease’.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter 80, Edition 28th, Pg: 1423

question_text: Which type of graft rejection is characterised by intravascular thrombosis?
explanation:
Hyperacute rejection is an immediate graft destruction due to ABO or preformed anti-HLA antibodies. It is characterised by intravascular thrombosis and interstitial haemorrhage.


Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 88, Kidney transplantation and the principles of transplantation, Pg: 1600.

question_text: Imminent gangrene in peripheral vascular disease (PVD) is associated with an ankle-brachial pressure index (ABPI) of less than:
explanation:
Explanation:

ABPI - ankle-brachial pressure index is the ratio of the systolic pressure at the ankle to that in the ipsilateral arm. It is interpreted as the highest pressure in the dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial or peroneal artery serving as the numerator, with the highest brachial systolic pressure being the denominator. Patients with an ABPI of <0.50 are twice as likely to deteriorate as patients with an ABPI of >0.50, and a deteriorating ABI is predictive of future limb loss. Interpretation of various measurements of ABPI is as follows:

  • ≥0.9 - normal (Option A ruled out)
  • 7-0.9 - mild arterial disease (claudication may be absent or mild) (Option B ruled out)
  • ~0.5 - suggests critical ischemia / rest pain may occur (Option C ruled out)
  • <0.3 - indicates severe ischemia / impending tissue necrosis (imminent gangrene)

It should be noted that low ABPI reflects very poor distal perfusion. When ABPI drops below about 0.3 the perfusion is insufficient to sustain tissue and necrosis/gangrene is imminent.

Key takeaways:

ABPI <0.5 → rest pain; <0.3 → imminent necrosis/gangrene.

question_text: A 50-year-old diabetic man presents with progressive pain in his calf. He now prefers to sleep in a seated position with his leg hanging down to get relief. The pain is worse in his toes and feet, aggravated by movement and pressure. It increases when lying down and with foot elevation but is reduced by dependency. What is the most likely cause?
explanation:
Explanation:

This presentation is classic for ischemic rest pain, a sign of critical limb ischemia from advanced peripheral arterial disease (PAD).

Ischemic Rest Pain is a severe symptom of advanced arterial insufficiency due to ischemic neuritis, often progressing to gangrene or amputation if untreated.

  • Pain: Burning, confined to the forefoot or ischemic toe/ulcer.
  • Aggravated by: Elevation or horizontal leg position; occurs at night, preventing sleep.
  • Relieved by: Dependent position (leg hanging down).
  • Features: Severe, opioid-resistant pain; may cause leg/foot swelling if constantly dependent.
  • Differentiation: Forefoot pain vs calf nocturnal cramps (common in elderly).
  • Associated signs: Trophic changes - muscle wasting, thin skin, thick nails, hair loss.

Explanation of other options:

Sciatica (Option B): This is neuropathic pain radiating from the back down the leg, typically worsened by sitting or spinal movement, not specifically relieved by dependency.

Neurological claudication (Option C): Seen in spinal stenosis; pain is induced by walking and relieved by sitting or bending forward (spinal flexion), not by leg dependency.

Venous claudication (Option D): Caused by venous outflow obstruction; pain is a bursting sensation that worsens with dependency and is relieved by leg elevation.

Key Takeaways:

  • Ischemic rest pain is a burning pain in the forefoot that occurs at rest and is relieved by dependency.
  • It is a red flag for critical limb ischemia in diabetic patients.

question_text: True statement about intermittent claudication:
option_b: Most common site is the calf
option_c: Claudication distance can vary from day to day
option_d: Relieved after getting out of bed and walking
explanation:
Intermittent claudication occurs as a result of anaerobic muscle metabolism and is classically described as debilitating cramp-like pain felt in the muscles that is:

  • brought on by walking;
  • not present on taking the first step (unlike osteoarthritis);
  • relieved by rest in both the standing and sitting positions, usually within 5 minutes (unlike nerve compression from a lumbar intervertebral disc prolapse or osteoarthritis of the spine or spinal stenosis, which are typically relieved only when resting in the sitting position for longer than 5 minutes).

The distance that a patient is able to walk without stopping varies (claudication distance) only slightly from day to day. It is decreased, first, by increasing the work demands and hence oxygen requirements of the muscles affected, e.g. walking up hill, increasing the speed of walking and/or carrying heavy weights, and, second, by general health conditions that reduce the oxygen delivery capacity of the arterial system, e.g. anemia or cardiorespiratory disease.

The muscle group affected by claudication is classically one anatomical level below the level of arterial disease and is usually felt in the posterior calf as the superficial femoral artery is the most commonly affected artery (70% of cases).

Aortoiliac disease (30% of cases) may cause thigh or buttock claudication; Leriche's syndrome is buttock claudication combined with sexual impotence, which is secondary to arterial insufficiency

question_text: long lasting results in CABG are obtained by?
explanation:
Selection of conduit

Venous grafts

The long saphenous vein is the most commonly used venous conduit as it is straightforward to harvest, provides good length and is easy to handle. Historical studies showed a limited long term patency rate forlong saphenous vein grafts (50-60% at 10 years). However, recent studies suggest that early postoperative use of lipid-lowering agents and antiplatelet agents such as low-dose aspirin can improve vein graft long-term patency.

Arterial grafts

Theleft internal mammary artery (LIMA),or internal thoracic artery, has become the conduit of choice for LAD grafting. Evidence from the mid-1980s to the present day suggests a10-year patency rate of >95%,with a lower reoperation rate.

The use of the radial artery as an alternative arterial bypass graft has undergone a recent revival. This has been driven by the belief that total arterial revascularization (avoiding venous conduits) might improve long-term results of coronary surgery.

question_text: While washing clothes in cold water, a female patient exhibits color changes in her hands from white to red. Which of the following drugs is best suited for this patient?
explanation:
Explanation:

The described symptoms triphasic color changes (white, blue, red) triggered by cold exposure are pathognomonic for Raynaud's phenomenon.

Raynaud Phenomenon is an episodic reduction in blood flow to the fingers, triggered by cold or stress, presenting with pallor (ischemia), cyanosis (deoxygenation), and rubor (reperfusion with swelling/tingling) along with cold sensitivity and pain.

It may be primary (idiopathic, benign) or secondary (due to connective tissue diseases like scleroderma or lupus, often severe).

Diagnosis is clinical, supported by nailfold capillaroscopy and blood tests for underlying autoimmune disease.

Management includes lifestyle changes (avoiding cold, stress, smoking, beta-blockers, caffeine), vasodilators (calcium channel blockers, alpha-blockers), and in refractory cases, surgical sympathectomy.

Explanation of other options:

ACE inhibitors (Option A): While sometimes used off-label, they are not first-line. Their effect is less direct and potent than CCBs for vasospasm.

Thiazides (Option C): Thiazides are diuretics used for hypertension and edema; they do not have vasodilatory properties for peripheral vessels and can sometimes exacerbate Raynaud's.

Alpha-blockers (Option D): Alpha-blockers (e.g., Prazosin) can be used as second or third-line agents but are not the preferred first choice due to side effects like orthostatic hypotension.

Key Takeaways:

  • Calcium channel blockers are the first-line drug class for managing Raynaud's phenomenon.
  • The mechanism is inhibition of vascular smooth muscle contraction, leading to vasodilation.

question_text: What will be the cerebral perfusion pressure for mean arterial pressure of 100 mm Hg and intracranial pressure of 10 mm Hg?
explanation:
• The brain depends on continuous perfusion for oxygen and glucose delivery, and hence survival.
  • Normal cerebral blood flow (CBF) is about 55 mL per minute for every 100 grams of brain tissue. Ischaemia results when this rate drops below 20 mL per minute, and even lower levels will result in infarction unless promptly corrected.
  • Flow depends on cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP), the difference between mean arterial pressure (MAP) and intracranial pressure (ICP).

CPP (75-105 mmHg) = MAP (90-110 mmHg) - ICP (5-15 mmHg)

  • Typical normal values are given in parentheses. In fact, in the normal brain, variations in vascular tone maintain a constant CBF across a range of MAP between 50 and 150 mmHg (or higher in the setting of chronic hypertension), and a corresponding range of CPP, the process of cerebral autoregulation.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 28, Edition: 28th, Pg: 360

question_text: A 38 years old female was brain dead and she signed for organ donation previously, family members also accepted. Which of the following patients is an ideal recipient?
option_a: 70 years old female on dialysis for chronic renal failure
option_b: 50 years chronic alcoholic patient with irreversible liver damage
option_c: 14 years old boy with multiorgan failure
option_d: 35 years old female with renal failure
explanation:
Most transplant organs are from deceased donors, of which there are two types: donation after brainstem death (DBD) and donation after circulatory death (DCD).

Selection of patients for transplantation

  • Potential transplant recipients undergo a rigorous work-up process to identify major comorbidities that would preclude transplant surgery. Age per se is not a contraindication to renal transplantation and it is now common to transplant patients in their seventies as long as they have the necessary cardiovascular fitness.
  • Uncontrolled infection and most malignancies are contraindications to transplantation. Patients with ESRD have a greatly increased risk of cardiovascular disease and require a chest radiograph, electrocardiogram (ECG) and, if indicated, an echocardiogram.
  • Patients with a history of diabetes or ischaemic heart disease should undergo a stress echocardiogram and sometimes coronary angiography.
  • There are a number of technical considerations before a patient is deemed suitable for transplantation. The iliac blood vessels must be suitable for anastomosis and there must be a means of draining the transplant ureter.
  • In patients with a history of vascular disease or deep venous thrombosis, the iliac arterial and venous system should be assessed by Doppler ultrasound scanning and possibly also MRA or CT angiography.

question_text: 20 years old male met with road traffic accident and suffered with upper limb injury with laceration over arm. Radial and ulnar pulse not felt. He had longitudinal tear in brachial artery of 2.5 cm length. Ideal repair is
option_d: Segmental resection of the vessel with replacement by reverse saphenous vein graft
explanation:
Upper limb vascular injuries:

  • The brachial artery is best exposed through a longitudinal incision along the medial aspect of the upper arm over the groove between the triceps and biceps muscles.
  • Proximal brachial artery injuries may require control of the infraclavicular axillary artery.
  • Balloon catheter thrombectomy and flushing with heparinized saline followed by debridement of damaged arterial wall are essential to successful repair. Lacerated veins should be ligated.
  • However, if there is extensive soft tissue injury and collateral venous flow is compromised, the vein should be repaired. In repairing both venous and arterial injuries, the vein should be repaired first.
  • If the duration of arterial occlusion and ischemia is a concern, temporary intraluminal shunts may be placed in the artery.
  • Primary arterial repair of undamaged ends of vessel (end-to-end anastomosis) should be performed only if the repair is tension free.
  • Saphenous vein interposition should be chosen whenever vessel injury is extensive or if primary tension-free repair is not possible. PTFE needs to remain a second choice to autologous vein in the management of injuries of the brachial artery and forearm vessels.

question_text: A 50-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with a sudden, severe headache described as "the worst headache of her life." Her blood pressure is 160/100 mmHg. A non-contrast CT scan of the brain reveals a subarachnoid hemorrhage. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

Angiography is the definitive next step to identify the source of bleeding, typically a ruptured aneurysm, in subarachnoid hemorrhage.

  • In the setting of a confirmed subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) on CT scan, cerebral angiography-most commonly digital subtraction angiography (DSA)-is the next crucial step.
  • This allows identification of the bleeding source, typically a ruptured cerebral aneurysm, and helps plan for definitive treatment via surgical clipping or endovascular coiling.
  • While supportive care is also important, such as blood pressure control and preventing complications like vasospasm, localizing the aneurysm is a priority before proceeding to any definitive intervention.
  • Once the aneurysm is identified, treatment decisions are made depending on the location, size, and accessibility of the aneurysm, along with the patient's neurologic status.

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage:

  • Causes:
    • Most common: Trauma
    • Ruptured Aneurysm: Most commonly located in the Circle of Willis.
    • Arteriovenous Malformation (AVM)
    • Perimesencephalic SAH: Bleeding is confined to the basal cisterns due to venous bleeding and is associated with a better prognosis.
  • Risk factors:
    • Female sex
    • Hypertension
    • Smoking & Cocaine use
    • Genetic disorders (e.g., adult polycystic kidney disease, Marfan syndrome)
  • Symptoms:
    • Thunderclap Headache: Sudden and severe headache.
    • Associated with Seizures (10%), Unresponsiveness (50%) and Vomiting (70%)
  • Diagnosis:
    • CT Scan: First-line imaging, effective within 12 hours of onset, and its sensitivity decreases after one week.
    • Lumbar Puncture: Used if CT is negative but SAH is suspected.
    • Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA): Gold standard for visualising aneurysms.
  • Management:
    • Surgical or endovascular intervention and addressing complications such as vasospasm and electrolyte imbalances.
    • Early and effective treatment is crucial for improving outcomes.

Explanation of other options:

Nimodipine (Option A): A calcium channel blocker used to prevent delayed cerebral ischemia due to vasospasm after SAH, but not the initial or most urgent step after diagnosis.

Surgery (Option C): Although surgical intervention is often necessary, angiography must precede it to precisely locate the aneurysm and decide whether surgery or endovascular coiling is appropriate.

Fibrinolytic therapy (Option D): Contraindicated in SAH; it increases the risk of worsening intracranial bleeding and is used for ischemic strokes, not hemorrhagic ones.

question_text: A patient presents with calf pain while walking a certain distance. The pain is severe enough that he must stop and rest before continuing. According to Boyd's grading, which of the following grades best describes this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

The described presentation is Grade III intermittent claudication according to Boyd's classification.

  • Key Feature:Pain occurs while walking and is severe enough that the patient is forced to stop and rest.
  • Mechanism:Reduced arterial perfusion fails to meet the metabolic demands of exercising muscles.
  • Clinical implication:Signifies significant peripheral arterial disease, requiring urgent vascular evaluation and intervention.

Explanation of Other Options:

Grade 1 (Option A):

  • Pain appears only after walking a certain distance (claudication distance).
  • Subsides as collateral circulation increases.
  • Does not force the patient to stop immediately.

Grade 2 (Option B):

  • Pain persists even while walking, but the patient can continue with effort.
  • Functional capacity still preserved, though impaired.

Grade 4 (Option D):

  • Represents rest pain.
  • Pain persists even without exertion, indicating critical limb ischemia.
  • Most severe stage, often preceding gangrene.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: Which of the following provides long-lasting results in a coronary artery bypass graft (CABG)?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Internal Mammary Artery (IMA), particularly the Left IMA (LIMA) grafted to the Left Anterior Descending (LAD) artery, is the gold standard conduit for CABG. It has exceptional long-term patency rates (>90% at 10 years) because it is a living artery resistant to atherosclerosis and has a diameter and flow characteristics well-suited to coronary circulation.

Vascular Graft:

Explanation:

Long saphenous vein (Option A): While commonly used due to its length and accessibility, vein grafts have a significantly higher rate of attrition due to intimal hyperplasia and atherosclerosis, with lower long-term patency.

PTFE (Option C): Synthetic grafts like PTFE have very poor patency rates in the low-pressure coronary system and are not used for CABG.

Gastroepiploic artery (Option D): This is an arterial conduit sometimes used as a second choice. While better than vein grafts, its long-term patency does not surpass that of the IMA.

Key Takeaways:

  • The LIMA-to-LAD graft is the most important graft in CABG and provides the best long-term survival benefit.
  • "Arterial grafts last longer than venous grafts."

question_text: A patient presents with sudden onset right leg pain. An investigation was done, and the obtained image is shown below. What is the investigation?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The image represents an ultrasound Doppler study, which measures blood flow velocity in vessels.
  • It is the first-line investigation for suspected acute limb ischemia, as it can quickly detect occlusion or stenosis.
  • Doppler can identify obstruction at the femoral, popliteal, or tibial arteries, helping guide further management.

Ultrasound Doppler

  • Principle: Uses sound waves and Doppler effect to visualize flow and detect turbulence/obstruction.
  • Advantages: Non-invasive, bedside, rapid, no contrast needed.
  • Uses: Diagnosis of arterial thrombosis, embolism, venous thrombosis, varicose veins, vascular anomalies.

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Digital subtraction angiography (Option A): Invasive contrast study, reserved for detailed vascular mapping or when an intervention (angioplasty/stent) is planned. Not first-line in acute limb pain.

MR angiography (Option C): Non-invasive and useful for vascular imaging, but less available, time-consuming, and not practical in emergencies.

Plethysmography (Option D): Measures limb blood volume changes to assess circulation; not used for acute arterial occlusion.

Key Takeaway

In sudden limb pain with suspected vascular compromise, the best initial test is ultrasound Doppler, as it is safe, rapid, and effective in detecting arterial blockages

Reference: NIH Link.

question_text: A 55-year-old male patient presents with hematuria and a neovascular mass in the left kidney on a CT scan, as shown below. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The presence of hematuria and a neovascular mass in the left kidney on CT imaging strongly suggests a renal tumor, most likely a benign Renal Angiomyolipoma (AML).

Renal Angiomyolipoma (AML)

Explanation of Other Options:

Renal cell carcinoma (RCC) (Option A) is a malignant kidney tumor that typically presents as a solid, heterogeneous mass with irregular margins and areas of necrosis. Although RCC can exhibit new blood vessel formation, it does not contain the fat components or the characteristic vascular patterns seen in angiomyolipomas (AMLs). The identification of these benign features in imaging suggests the lesion is more consistent with AML rather than RCC.

Renal Oncocytoma (Option B) is a non-cancerous kidney tumor that generally presents as a well-defined, solid mass with uniform enhancement and occasionally a central scar visible on CT or MRI scans. Unlike Angiomyolipomas (AMLs), it does not exhibit a fatty component or a pronounced neovascular pattern. Its lower vascularity makes it an unlikely diagnosis in this scenario

Renal cysts (Option D) are fluid-filled, non-enhancing structures with smooth walls on imaging. They lack vascularity and neovascular features. Additionally, renal cysts typically do not cause hematuria or present as a neovascular mass, making them an unlikely diagnosis in this scenario.

question_text: A 42-year-old man presents with a gradually enlarging, dilated, and tortuous vein in his lower limb. He reports a penetrating injury at the same site 10 years ago. On examination, the swelling is pulsatile. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

An A-V Fistula is an abnormal communication between an artery and a vein. In this patient, the presence of:

  • History of penetrating trauma (a known cause of acquired AVF),
  • Dilated tortuous venous swelling,
  • Pulsatility,
  • Thrill and continuous machinery murmur on auscultation,

all point to the diagnosis of an Arteriovenous Fistula.

Pathophysiology:

  • Direct arterial blood enters the venous system, arterializing the vein.
  • This increases venous return and cardiac output, which may progress to high-output cardiac failure.
  • Long-standing AVFs can cause venous hypertension and limb changes.

Special Sign:

  • Nicoladoni-Branham sign: On compression of the artery proximal to the fistula, the swelling decreases in size, the thrill disappears, and the pulse slows.

Explanation of Other Options:

Varicose vein (Option A):

  • Dilated, tortuous superficial veins due to valve incompetence.
  • Typically non-pulsatile and not associated with trauma or arterial communication.

Angiofibroma (Option B):

  • Benign vascular fibrous tumor, often seen in nasopharynx of adolescent males.
  • Not relevant to extremity veins and not trauma-related.

Hemangioma (Option C):

  • Benign vascular tumor, usually congenital, seen in infants/children.
  • Presents as soft red/blue swelling, not pulsatile, and not associated with trauma.

Key takeaway Points:

Surgically created Arterio-Venous fistula: It is commonly used for patients with end-stage renal disease who require hemodialysis.

Examples of Surgically created fistulas are:

  • Brescia-Cimino fistula: It is created between the Radial artery and the Cephalic vein.
  • Snuff Box fistula: It is created between the Posterior branch of the radial artery and Cephalic vein
  • Feinberg fistula: It is created between the Radial artery and the Basilic vein.

question_text:
A chronic smoker presents with leg pain after walking 100 meters, relieved by rest.
On examination, dorsalis pedis, anterior tibial, and posterior tibial pulses are absent bilaterally, but no gangrene is noted. Which of the following statements correctly describes his condition?
option_a: Pain is more at night and sleep
option_b: Pain aggravated by standing and relieved by bending forward
option_c: Development of pain on the 1st step of walking
option_d: Pain develops after walking some distance and is relieved by rest
explanation:
Explanation:

The patient has classic intermittent claudication, the hallmark symptom of Peripheral Arterial Disease (PAD) due to atherosclerotic occlusion of lower limb arteries.

Definition:

Intermittent claudication is exercise-induced ischemic muscle pain, which occurs after walking a certain distance and is relieved by rest.

Mechanism:

  • During exertion, oxygen demand > supply due to arterial narrowing (atherosclerosis).
  • Ischemic metabolites (e.g., lactate) accumulate → cramping pain (classically in calves).
  • Pain resolves with rest when oxygen demand decreases.

Explanation of Other Options:

Pain is more at night and sleep (Option A):

Suggests ischemic rest pain (Grade IV PAD), not intermittent claudication.

  • Occurs in critical limb ischemia (end-stage PAD).
  • Worsens at night when legs are at heart level
  • Relieved by hanging leg over the bed.

Pain aggravated by standing and relieved by bending forward (Option B):

Describes neurogenic claudication, not vascular.

  • Seen in lumbar canal stenosis.
  • Pain due to nerve compression, not ischemia.
  • Improves with flexion (shopping cart sign).

Development of pain on the 1st step of walking (Option C):

Describes neurogenic claudication, not vascular.

  • Seen in lumbar canal stenosis.
  • Pain due to nerve compression, not ischemia.
  • Improves with flexion (shopping cart sign).

question_text: A 62-year-old patient presents with pain in the calf muscles while walking. The pain subsides with rest. Which of the following is not typically seen in intermittent claudication?
option_a: Cramping in the muscles during exercise
option_b: Pain starts with taking the first step
option_c: The most common cause is atheroma
option_d: The level of occlusion cannot be decided based on symptoms
explanation:
Explanation :

  • Intermittent claudicationtypically involves cramping pain in the calf muscles during exercise (such as walking), which subsides with rest.
  • The pain usually starts after walking for a certain distance and is relieved by rest, not immediately upon taking the first step.

Boyd's classification of intermittent claudication:

Explanation of other options:

Cramping in the muscles during exercise (Option A): Intermittent claudication is characterised by pain or cramping in the muscles during exercise, usually affecting the lower extremities.

The most common cause is atheroma (Option C): Atheroma, which is the accumulation of fatty plaques in the arteries, is the primary cause of intermittent claudication. The narrowing of the arteries due to atheroma restricts blood flow to the muscles during physical activity, resulting in pain.

Level of occlusion cannot be decided based on symptoms (Option D): The exact level of arterial occlusion cannot be determined by symptoms alone in intermittent claudication. Diagnostic tests, such as ankle-brachial index (ABI) or angiography, are needed to assess the location and extent of arterial blockage.

question_text: Identify the edges of the lesion given in the image:
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Rolled-out edges are classically seen in Basal Cell Carcinoma (Rodent ulcer).
  • They appear pearly white, rounded, and rolled outward due to the proliferation of basal cells at the margin of the ulcer.
  • This characteristic appearance helps differentiate BCC from squamous cell carcinoma and vascular ulcers.
  • BCC is slow-growing, locally invasive, and rarely metastasizes, but early recognition of rolled edges is crucial for diagnosis.

Morphologically, an ulcer has 4 parts:

  • Base: Surface on which ulcer rests (usually underlying muscles/bones)
  • Floor: Exposed surface of ulcer (usually seen as purulent discharge/granulation tissue/red and moist)
  • Margin: Junction between normal epithelium & ulcer
  • Edge: Area between margin & floor

Explanation of Other Options:

Everted edge (Option A):

  • Typical of Squamous Cell Carcinoma.
  • Caused by malignant cells spilling over onto adjacent skin.
  • Appears raised, firm, and irregular.

Sloping edge (Option C):

  • Seen in healing ulcers or varicose ulcers.
  • Shows a "red, blue, white" triad:
    • Red (healthy granulation)
    • Blue (epithelial proliferation)
    • White (scar tissue).

Punched-out edge (Option D):

  • Found in arterial/ischemic ulcers, trophic ulcers, and gummatous syphilitic ulcers.
  • Edges are sharply cut, with a "punched-out" appearance due to endarteritis and tissue necrosis.

Key Takeaway Points:

Reference: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC1360405/

question_text: Most common cause of spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage?
explanation:
Spontaneous subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is usually the result of -

  • Bleeding from a ruptured aneurysm (~80% of SAH)
  • Arteriovenous malformation (AVM)

Most ruptured aneurysms are located in the circle of Willis, at branch points in the arterial tree associated with turbulent blood flow.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 48, Cranial neurosurgery, Pg: 708-709.

question_text: Which type of intracranial hemorrhage is most likely depicted in the image given below?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • A Subdural Hematoma (SDH) occurs between the dura mater and arachnoid mater.
  • It typically results from tearing of bridging veins due to acceleration-deceleration injuries.
  • On CT scan, SDH appears as a crescent-shaped collection that follows the contour of the brain.
  • Unlike extradural hemorrhage, SDH can cross suture lines, but does not cross dural reflections (falx, tentorium).
  • It may present as acute (rapid deterioration after trauma) or chronic (weeks after minor injury, especially in elderly or alcoholics).
  • Management depends on severity:
    • Small and stable hematomas → conservative management.
    • Large/symptomatic hematomas → burr hole drainage or craniotomy.

Explanation of Other Options:

Extradural Hemorrhage (Option A):

  • Located between the dura and inner skull.
  • Caused by middle meningeal artery rupture, often with a temporal bone fracture.
  • CT scan shows a biconvex/lens-shaped lesion that does not cross sutures.
  • Classically associated with a lucid interval followed by rapid deterioration.

Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (Option B):

  • Bleeding into the subarachnoid space, usually due to ruptured berry aneurysm or trauma.
  • Presents with sudden severe "thunderclap" headache, neck stiffness, photophobia.
  • On CT, blood is seen in basal cisterns or sulci, not crescent-shaped.

Intraparenchymal Hemorrhage (Option D):

  • Bleeding occurs within brain parenchyma itself.
  • Common causes: uncontrolled hypertension, amyloid angiopathy, trauma, or vascular malformations.
  • Appears as a localized hyperdense area within brain tissue on CT.

Key Takeaway Points:

question_text: A 25-year-old patient had an RTA and was initially conscious but later became unconscious and subsequently died. On postmortem examination, multiple petechial haemorrhages were seen in the corpus callosum, but no significant findings were seen on CT brain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The most likely diagnosis based on the clinical features given of becoming unconscious after initially being conscious, with no changes on CT brain, but postmortem findings of multiple petechial haemorrhages in the corpus callosum, is suggestive of diffuse axonal injury.

  • Diffuse axonal injury refers to damage to axons away from the neuronal cell body caused by rotational acceleration-deceleration trauma affecting the brain’s white matter tracts, leading to structural or functional disruption.
  • It arises due to the disruption of axoplasmic flow. It can also occur due to sudden angular acceleration, such as blast injuries, even without a direct skull impact.
  • Radiological imaging usually underrepresents the extent of this injury as most lesions are microscopic, often showing only punctate haemorrhages and loss of grey-white matter differentiation.
  • DAI severity is graded:
    • Grade I involves peripheral gray-white matter junctions
    • Grade II affects the corpus callosum, especially the splenium and posterior body
    • Grade III extends to the dorsolateral midbrain or brainstem.
  • Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) is the most sensitive technique for identifying acute, nonhemorrhagic DAI, with lesions showing hyperintensity on DWI and hypointensity on ADC.
  • Susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) is highly effective for detecting associated microhemorrhages, as shown below.
  • Clinically, it is often recognised when patients present with significant neurological impairment despite relatively mild imaging findings, and predicting long-term outcomes remains challenging.

It is considered a major cause of loss of consciousness in patients without mass lesions and may occur alone or in combination with other injuries, like epidural or subdural hematomas.

  • Microscopically, it is marked by axonal swelling and focal hemorrhagic lesions.
  • These swellings can be detected using silver impregnation or immunohistochemical stains for axonal proteins like amyloid precursor protein and α-synuclein. These axonal retraction balls appear as shown below.
  • Over time, microglial proliferation occurs in the affected cortical regions, followed by degeneration of the damaged fibre tracts.

Explanation of other options:

Subarachnoid haemorrhage (Option A): Subarachnoid haemorrhage (SAH) is bleeding into the subarachnoid space, most often due to rupture of an arterial aneurysm, less commonly from arteriovenous malformations, or sometimes with no identifiable cause. CT scan shows hyperdense blood in basal cisterns or diffusely in the subarachnoid space, often extending into ventricles.

Subdural hematoma (Option C): Refers to bleeding between the dura mater and arachnoid mater, typically from the tearing of veins that traverse the subdural space. Characterised by a "comma" shape on axial CT, as shown below.

Extradural hematoma (Option D): Extradural hematoma is commonly associated with a fracture of the squamous part of the temporal bone and is marked by a biconvex density on CT, as shown below.

Reference: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5204088/

question_text: Which of the following statements is not true regarding autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)?
option_a: Polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 play a critical role
option_c: Visible haematuria occurs in up to 40% of patients with ADPKD
option_d: Hypertension is the least common manifestation of ADPKD
explanation:
Explanation:

Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) results from mutations in Polycystin-1 (chromosome 16) and polycystin-2 (chromosome 4) (Option A).

Features:

  • Renal size increases with age, leading to flank or abdominal masses in some patients.
  • Cysts contain clear fluid, thick brown material or coagulated blood.
  • Visible haematuriaoccurs in up to 40% of patients with ADPKD (Option C).
  • Cyst haemorrhageis a frequent complication with or without haematuria, depending on whether the cyst communicates with the collecting system or not.
  • Hypertensionis the most common manifestation of ADPKD and a major contributor to renal disease progression and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
  • After the age of 20 years, most patients are hypertensive.
  • Associated with intracranial aneurysmsin 10% of cases (Option B).

question_text: Not true regarding ADPKD?
option_a: Polycystin-1 and polycystin-2 play a critical role
option_c: Visible haematuria occurs in up to 40% of patients with ADPKD
option_d: Hypertension is the least common manifestation of ADPKD
explanation:
Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD)-

  • Due to mutations in Polycystin-1 (chromosome 16) and polycystin-2 (chromosome 4).

Features -

  • Renal size increases with age resulting in a flank or abdominal mass in some patients.
  • Cysts contain clear fluid, thick brown material or coagulated blood.
  • Visible haematuria occurs in up to 40% of patients with ADPKD.
  • Cyst haemorrhage is a frequent complication with or without haematuria, depending on whether the cyst communicates with the collecting system or not.
  • Hypertension is the most common manifestation of ADPKD and a major contributor to renal disease progression and cardiovascular morbidity and mortality.
  • After the age of 20 years, most patients are hypertensive.
  • Associated with intracranial aneurysms in 10% of cases.

VHL disease is a rare autosomal dominant disorder that is characterised by multiple pathologies, including clear-cell RCC (ccRCC), pheochromocytoma, retinal angiomas and haemangioblastomas of the brainstem, cerebellum or spinal cord.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery 28th Edition, Chapter 82, The Kidney and Ureter, Pg: 1482.

question_text: Which artery is the most common site for a peripheral aneurysm?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The popliteal artery is the most common site for a peripheral aneurysm.
  • Accounts for 70% of all peripheral aneurysms.
  • Mostly diagnosed in men in their 7th decade of life.
  • Aneurysms in this location are more frequent due to the anatomical structure of the popliteal artery and its exposure to mechanical stress in the knee area.
  • Popliteal artery aneurysms are often associated with degenerative changes in the arterial wall, such as atherosclerosis.
  • If a popliteal artery aneurysm is detected, the abdominal aorta must be examined, because ~1/3rd of patients also have an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA).

Presentations

  • Swelling behind knee
  • Symptoms due to complications like severe ischemia following thrombosis or distal ischemia due to emboli.
  • These aneurysms are more likely to thrombose/embolize than rupture

Diagnosis

  • Duplex ultrasonography (DUS) for confirmation
  • CT/MRA/DSA used for distal run-off vessel assessment.

Management

  • Asymptomatic: Repair if >20 mm, or smaller if thrombus present.
  • Symptomatic: Should be considered for repair. Two techniques for surgical repair may be used
    • Exclusion bypass: A medial approach with ligation and saphenous vein graft
    • Inlay graft repair: A posterior approach, useful for neurovascular compression.

question_text: Which of the following is most likely to be seen due to the rupture of a saccular aneurysm?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • Saccular (berry) aneurysms commonly arise at arterial branch points in the circle of Willis.
  • When they rupture, blood accumulates in the subarachnoid space, located between the arachnoid and pia mater.
  • This leads to subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH), classically presenting with sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache.

Saccular Aneurysm and SAH

  • Definition: Outpouching of vessel wall due to weakness at arterial bifurcations.
  • Sites: Most frequent at the anterior communicating artery, posterior communicating artery, and MCA bifurcations.
  • Risk factors: Hypertension, smoking, polycystic kidney disease, connective tissue disorders.
  • Clinical presentation: Sudden severe headache, photophobia, neck stiffness, loss of consciousness.
  • Imaging: CT head shows blood in basal cisterns or sulci.
  • Complications: Rebleeding, vasospasm (causing ischemia), and communicating hydrocephalus (secondary).

Explanation of Incorrect Options

Subdural hemorrhage (Option A): Results from rupture of bridging veins, usually following trauma; appears as a crescent-shaped collection on CT.

Intracerebral hemorrhage (Option C): Bleeding into brain parenchyma, often from hypertension or trauma; not the typical result of a berry aneurysm rupture.

Hydrocephalus (Option D): Accumulation of CSF leading to raised intracranial pressure; may occur as a late complication of SAH, but not the primary immediate event.

Key Takeaway

Rupture of a saccular aneurysm most often causes subarachnoid hemorrhage, presenting with a sudden severe headache, and confirmed by CT imaging.

question_text: A old lady, known for Atrial fibrillation developed sudden arterial occlusive disease. Which of the following has the poorest prognosis?
explanation:
Sudden occlusion of an artery is usually caused by an embolus. It may also happen when thrombosis occurs on an atherosclerotic plaque, although the outcome is usually less dramatic because collaterals are likely to have developed in chronic arterial stenosis.

Embolic occlusion

  • An embolus is an object that has become lodged in a vessel and causes obstruction, having been carried in the bloodstream from another site. It is often a thrombus that has become detached from the heart or a more proximal vessel.
  • Sources include the left atrium in atrial fibrillation; a left ventricular mural thrombus following myocardial infarction; vegetations on heart valves in infective endocarditis; and thrombi in aneurysms and on atherosclerotic plaques. Emboli may lodge in any organ and cause ischaemic symptoms.

Arm and leg- pain, pallor, paraesthesia, paralysis and pulselessness (the five Ps of acute limb ischaemia [ALI]) . Acute arterial occlusion due to an embolus differs from occlusion due to thrombosis on pre-existing atheroma; in the latter case a collateral circulation has often built up over time . It is essential to differentiate between the two as they require different management.

question_text: A patient is diagnosed with Stanford type B aortic dissection. What is the most appropriate initial management of this patient?
option_d: Administer beta blocker and intensive blood monitoring
explanation:
Explanation:

Initial management of Stanford type B aortic dissection includes medical therapy with beta blockers and close hemodynamic monitoring to control blood pressure and prevent progression.

  • Aortic dissection occurs when a tear in the intima of the aorta allows blood to track between the layers of the vessel wall, creating a false lumen.
  • The Stanford classification divides dissections based on whether the ascending aorta is involved:
    • Type A: Involves the ascending aorta - requires surgical management.
    • Type B: Involves only the descending aorta - primarily managed medically unless complications arise.
  • Classifications of aortic dissection:

  • Initial treatment for Stanford type B dissection:
    • Beta blockers (e.g., labetalol, esmolol): reduce shear stress by lowering heart rate and blood pressure.
    • Target systolic BP <120 mmHg and HR <60 bpm.
    • Pain management and intensive care monitoring are essential to watch for signs of progression or complications (e.g., organ ischemia).
  • Only complicated type B dissections (e.g., ongoing pain, rupture, organ malperfusion) require intervention such as endovascular stenting.

Explanation of other options:

Bypass graft (Option A): Used in surgical repair of Type A dissections or in complicated cases with organ ischemia in type B; not first-line for uncomplicated Stanford B dissection.

Percutaneous endovascular stent (Option B): Reserved for complicated type B dissections with malperfusion or rupture; not appropriate as initial management in uncomplicated cases.

Balloon dilation (Option C): Used in valvular or vascular stenosis, not indicated in aortic dissection and may worsen the tear by increasing intraluminal pressure.

question_text: Hepatic parenchymal disruption involving 50% of hepatic lobe is which grade of AAST liver injury?
explanation:
AAST LIVER INJURY SCALE:

Grade I

  • Hematoma: subcapsular, <10% surface area
  • Laceration: capsular tear, <1 cm parenchymal depth

Grade II

  • Hematoma: subcapsular, 10-50% surface area
  • Hematoma: intraparenchymal <10 cm diameter
  • Laceration: capsular tear 1-3 cm parenchymal depth, <10 cm length

Grade III

  • Hematoma: subcapsular, >50% surface area; ruptured subcapsular or parenchymal hematoma
  • Hematoma: intraparenchymal >10 cm
  • Laceration: capsular tear >3 cm parenchymal depth
  • Vascular injury with active bleeding contained within liver parenchyma

Grade IV

  • Laceration: parenchymal disruption involving 25-75% of a hepatic lobe or involves 1-3 Couinaud segments
  • Vascular injury with active bleeding breaching the liver parenchyma into the peritoneum

Grade V

  • Laceration: parenchymal disruption involving >75% of hepatic lobe
  • Vascular: juxtahepatic venous injuries (retrohepatic vena cava / central major hepatic veins)

Reference: Sabiston textbook of Surgery, chapter: 17, Edition: 21st, Pg: 417

question_text: A 30 year old man presents with cramping gluteal pain after walking 500 meters. Which is the vessel involved?
option_b: Arterial disease with femoral artery involvement
explanation:
Intermittent claudication occurs as a result of anaerobic muscle metabolism and is classically described as debilitating cramp-like pain felt in the muscles that is:

  • brought on by walking;
  • not present on taking the first step (unlike osteoarthritis);
  • relieved by rest in both the standing and sitting positions, usually within 5 minutes

(unlike nerve compression from a lumbar intervertebral disc prolapse or osteoarthritis of the spine or spinal stenosis, which are typically relieved only when resting in the sitting position for longer than 5 minutes).

The distance that a patient is able to walk without stopping varies (claudication distance) only slightly from day to day. It is decreased, first, by increasing the work demands and hence oxygen requirements of the muscles affected, e.g. walking up hill, increasing the speed of walking and/or carrying heavy weights, and, second, by general health conditions that reduce the oxygen delivery capacity of the arterial system, e.g. anemia or cardiorespiratory disease.

The muscle group affected by claudication is classically one anatomical level below the level of arterial disease and is usually felt in the posterior calf as the superficial femoral artery is the most commonly affected artery (70% of cases).

Aortoiliac disease (30% of cases) may cause thigh or buttock claudication; Leriche's syndrome is buttock claudication combined with sexual impotence, which is secondary to arterial insufficiency

question_text: Which of the following venous structures is most commonly affected in the image below?
explanation:
Explanation:

Varicose veins are dilated, tortuous superficial veins caused by venous valve incompetence.

  • The Great Saphenous Vein (GSV) is the most commonly affected vein, accounting for nearly 60% of cases, especially along the medial aspect of the thigh and leg.
  • Risk factors include age, female gender, family history, pregnancy, obesity, and prolonged standing.
  • Duplex ultrasound is the gold standard investigation to confirm reflux and map venous anatomy.
  • Treatment options include endovenous ablation, sclerotherapy, or surgical ligation and stripping, along with compression therapy.

Explanation of Other Options:

Perforators (Option A): Perforator incompetence can occur, often secondary to GSV/SSV reflux, but isolated perforator varicosities are less common.

Short Saphenous Vein (Option B): Incompetence occurs in ~20% of cases, classically producing posterolateral calf varicosities.

Deep Veins (Option D): Deep vein disease (e.g., DVT sequelae) can lead to chronic venous insufficiency, but isolated superficial varicose veins most commonly involve the GSV.

Key Takeaways:

  • Most common vein affected in varicose veins = Great Saphenous Vein (60%).
  • Short Saphenous Vein (20%) and perforators less frequent.
  • Always confirm anatomy and reflux with duplex ultrasound before intervention.

question_text: A patient presented with varicose veins, as shown in ithe mage. What is the investigation of choice for this condition?
explanation:
Explanation:

Duplex Scan for Venous Insufficiency

Definition: Duplex scanning is the preferred, non-invasive imaging method for evaluating venous insufficiency, including varicose veins. It combines conventional ultrasound and Doppler techniques to visualize blood flow and detect reflux or other venous abnormalities.

Patient Position:

  • Standing or with significant trunk elevation.
  • Supine positioning should be avoided as it may keep valves open and produce inaccurate results.

Objectives:

  • Identify reflux in both superficial and deep veins.
  • Determine the distribution and extent of reflux in superficial veins.
  • Detect any obstruction within the deep venous system.
  • Evaluate the suitability of incompetent superficial veins for treatment options.

Applications:

  • Assessment of venous valve function.
  • Mapping of superficial and deep venous reflux for surgical or interventional planning.
  • Helps guide therapy for varicose veins or other chronic venous insufficiency conditions.

Duplex Ultrasound Evaluation of Venous Insufficiency:

Explanation of Other Options:

Plethysmography (Option B): Measures limb or organ volume changes to assess venous function but is less precise and less specific than duplex ultrasound for evaluating varicose veins.

MRI (Option C): Primarily used for complex soft tissue imaging; duplex ultrasound is preferred for routine venous assessment due to accuracy and cost-effectiveness.

CT Scan (Option D): Involves ionizing radiation and is not recommended for routine evaluation of varicose veins; duplex ultrasound is safer and non-invasive.

Key Takeaway:

question_text: Identify the false statement regarding fluid therapy for shock.
option_a: First line therapy is putting a short wide bore intravenous cannula and start Infusion.
option_b: Albumin should not be the start in immediate period
option_c: Ringer lactate is most physiological fluid and ideal crystalloid.
option_d: It is ideal to give inotropic agents regardless of preload to heart.
explanation:
If inotropic agents given before achieving adequate preload it will deplete myocardium of oxygen stores and decrease coronary perfusion, so this should not be first priority.

  • In early period of shock vascular permeability would be high so albumin Will not stand in vascular system and start to accumulate in interstitial space.
  • Ringer lactate is ideal physiological fluid as it has all contents required For plasma.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 2, Edition: 28th, Pg: 18

question_text: All of the following statements are correct regarding crush syndrome except
option_a: Fasciotomy can be performing after 24 hours of entrapment
option_b: Prolonged crushing of muscle leads to a reperfusion injury when the casualty is rescued
option_c: The myoglobinuria that occurs, leads to renal failure from tubular obstruction
option_d: A mannitol-alkaline diuresis of up to 8 liters per day should be maintained
explanation:
OPTION A- A late fasciotomy, when it is obvious that the muscles of that compartment must be dead, is only likely to cause a massive release of myoglobin, as well as potentially introducing infection into dead tissue.

Therefore, best NOT to perform a fasciotomy in cases where entrapment has been for over 12 hours.

  • Prolonged crushing of muscle leads to a reperfusion injury when the casualty is rescued (Option B)
  • This releases myoglobin and vasoactive mediators into the circulation. It also sequesters many liters of fluid, reducing the intravascular volume and resulting in renal vasoconstriction and ischemia. The myoglobinuria leads to renal failure from tubular obstruction. (Option C)
  • The treatment of crushed casualties should begin as soon as they are discovered. Rescuers must be alert to the presence of associated injuries.
  • Aggressive volume- loading of patients, preferably before extrication, is the best treatment. After provision of first aid and starting intravenous fluids the patient should be catheterized to measure urine output. In adults, a saline infusion of 1000-1500 mL per hour should be initiated. This should be continued until myoglobin is no longer detectable in the urine.
  • Mannitol administration can reduce the reperfusion component of this injury. Once a flow of urine is observed, a mannitol-alkaline diuresis of up to 8 liters per day should be maintained, keeping the urinary pH greater than 6.5.

Reference: Bailey & Love's short practice of surgery, chapter: 33, Edition: 28th, Pg: 458

question_text: What is the most probable cause of this condition?
explanation:
Lymphedema refers to tissue swelling caused by an accumulation of protein-rich fluid that's usually drained through the body's lymphatic system. It most commonly affects the arms or legs, but can also occur in the chest wall, abdomen, neck and genitals.

Lymphedema signs and symptoms include:

  • Swelling of part or all of the arm or leg, including fingers or toes
  • A feeling of heaviness or tightness
  • Restricted range of motion
  • Recurring infections
  • Hardening and thickening of the skin (fibrosis)

Signs and symptoms can range from mild to severe. Lymphedema caused by cancer treatment may not occur until months or years after treatment.

Causes

The lymphatic system is a network of vessels that carry protein-rich lymph fluid throughout the body. It's part of your immune system. Lymph nodes act as filters and contain cells that fight infection and cancer.

The lymph fluid is pushed through the lymph vessels by muscle contractions as you move through the tasks of your day and small pumps in the wall of the lymph vessels. Lymphedema occurs when the lymph vessels are not able to adequately drain lymph fluid, usually from an arm or leg.

The most common causes of lymphedema include:

  • Cancer. If cancer cells block lymph vessels, lymphedema may result. For instance, a tumor growing near a lymph node or lymph vessel could enlarge enough to block the flow of the lymph fluid.
  • Radiation treatment for cancer.Radiation can cause scarring and inflammation of lymph nodes or lymph vessels.
  • Surgery.In cancer surgery, lymph nodes are often removed to see if the disease has spread. However, this doesn't always result in lymphedema.
  • Parasites.In developing countries in the tropics, the most common cause of lymphedema is infection with threadlike worms that clog the lymph nodes.

Less commonly, lymphedema results from inherited conditions in which the lymphatic system doesn't develop properly.

Reference : https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/lymphedema/symptoms-causes/syc-20374682.

question_text: An elderly male with a history of long-term intravenous drug use presents with a progressively enlarging swelling in the right groin. On examination, the swelling is non-fluctuant but pulsatile, and distal pulses in the same limb are diminished. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The clinical findings - pulsatile groin swelling, reduced distal pulses, and history of IV drug abuse - strongly suggest a femoral artery pseudoaneurysm.
  • CT angiography is the gold standard investigation for vascular pathologies, providing detailed information on vessel anatomy, extent of aneurysm, and planning for intervention.
  • Surgical repair or endovascular embolisation is definitive management to prevent rupture, distal ischemia, or limb-threatening complications

Explanation of Other Options:

Oral antibiotics and observation (Option B)

  • Antibiotics are indicated for infection, abscess, or cellulitis.
  • A pulsatile mass is not infectious in origin but vascular, so conservative management is inappropriate.

Compression stockings (Option C) are used to treat venous insufficiency or varicose veins.

Incision and drainage (Option D) are typically used for abscesses or collections of pus, & should be avoided in this case.

question_text: Which type of ulcer is given below?
explanation:
Explanation:

The ulcer shown is a venous ulcer, typically located in the gaiter area of the leg with irregular sloping edges and surrounding hyperpigmentation due to chronic venous insufficiency.

  • Venous ulcers are the most common type of leg ulcer and are usually caused by chronic venous hypertension due to incompetent valves in superficial or deep veins.
  • The classic location is the medial malleolus or the gaiter area (lower third of the leg above the ankle).
  • Characteristic features of venous ulcers include:
    • Irregular margins with a sloping edge
    • Shallow, moist base with granulation tissue
    • Brownish discoloration of surrounding skin (due to hemosiderin deposition)
    • Associated stasis dermatitis or lipodermatosclerosis
    • Pain may be mild or absent, typically relieved by elevation
  • Healing requires:
    • Leg elevation
    • Compression therapy
    • Management of varicose veins or deep vein insufficiency

Explanation of other options:

Arterial ulcer (Option B): Occurs over pressure points like toes or heels; has punched-out edges, pale or necrotic base, very painful, and absent distal pulses—unlike the moist, shallow venous ulcer.

Pressure ulcer (Option C): Occurs over bony prominences (sacrum, trochanter, heels) due to prolonged pressure, commonly in bedridden patients; not typically seen in ambulatory individuals.

Diabetic ulcer (Option D): Also known as neuropathic ulcer, commonly found on plantar surfaces or metatarsal heads in patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathy; they are deep, painless, and often have a punched-out appearance.

question_text: A patient presents with dull, aching pain and tortuous veins in both lower limbs. Which test would be appropriate for evaluating superficial femoral vein competence?
explanation:
Explanation:

The Brodie-Trendelenburg test/ Trendelenburg I test is performed to assess the patency of the saphenofemoral junction (saphenofemoral incompetence).

Brodie-Trendelenburg Test.

  • The patient is asked to lie in the supine position.
  • The leg is elevated, the vein is emptied by milking, and a tourniquet is tied just below the saphenofemoral junction.
  • The patient is asked to stand up quickly.
  • The tourniquet is released.

Interpretation:

  • Rapid filling of blood from above signifies saphenofemoral incompetence.

Explanation of other options:

Fegan's test (Option A):

  • Tests for the perforator.
  • On standing, the line of varicosity is marked, and then the veins are emptied in the supine position.
  • The examiner palpates along the marked line and notices any pits or gaps in the deep fascia that signify perforator incompetence at that site.

Homan's test (Option B): Test for deep vein thrombosis (DVT) rather than venous insufficiency. It involves dorsiflexing the foot and assessing for pain in the calf, which may suggest a clot.

Modified Perthe's test (Option C): Used for testing deep vein thrombosis (DVT), the limb is elevated to empty the veins and a tourniquet is applied at the saphenofemoral junction. The patient is then asked to walk for a few minutes. If the dilated veins become more prominent during walking, it indicates deep venous obstruction.

question_text: What is the likely reason behind the occurrence of surgical emphysema in a patient following an emergency tracheostomy performed outside of the hospital?
explanation:
Explanation:

Surgical emphysema (subcutaneous emphysema) occurs when air leaks into the soft tissues. After a tracheostomy, this is often due to an inadequate seal between the tracheostomy tube and the tracheal wall. If the skin and subcutaneous tissues are sutured too tightly around the tube, air from the trachea can be forced into the surrounding subcutaneous tissue during exhalation or coughing, instead of exiting through the tube or the stoma. This is a common technical error in hastily performed emergency procedures.

Explanation of other options:

Puncture of posterior wall (Option A): While a posterior tracheal wall puncture is a serious complication that can cause mediastinal emphysema, it is a less common cause of widespread subcutaneous emphysema compared to a tight skin closure.

High tracheostomy (Option B): A high tracheostomy (above the 2nd tracheal ring) increases the risk of subglottic stenosis and tube displacement but is not a direct cause of subcutaneous emphysema.

Blockage of the tube (Option C): A blocked tube would cause respiratory distress and difficulty in ventilating the patient, but it would not directly force air into the subcutaneous tissues.

Key Takeaways:

  • Subcutaneous emphysema post-tracheostomy is often a technical complication from creating an overly tight closure around the tube.
  • The stoma should allow a small air leak to prevent this complication.

References: https://rc.rcjournal.com/content/respcare/62/6/799.full.pdf

question_text: What is the attitude of fingers in collar-button abscess?
explanation:
Explanation:

This is a subfascial infection of a web space and is usually caused by skin trauma that becomes infected; it often occurs in laborers. The adherence of the palmar web space skin to the

Palmar fascia prevents lateral spread, so the infection courses dorsally, resulting in both palmar web space tenderness and dorsal web space swelling and tenderness. The adjacent fingers will be held in abduction with pain on adduction. Incision and drainage, often using separate volar and dorsal incisions, is mandatory, and follows the same treatment as for any abscess or deep-space infection

Incorrect Choices Explanation

Choice A: Flexion

  • Flexion is the characteristic posture in flexor tendon sheath infections (suppurative tenosynovitis), not collar-button abscesses.

Choice C: Adduction

  • Adduction would worsen pain in a collar-button abscess due to pressure on the infected web space; it's not the resting position.

Choice D: Extension

  • Extension is not a notable feature in collar-button abscesses. There is no forced extension posture associated with this infection.

Key Takeaway

  • Collar-button abscess causes the affected fingers to assume an abducted position due to swelling and tenderness in the web space.

question_text: Which of the following organisms is responsible for causing erythrasma?
explanation:
Explanation:

Erythrasma is a superficial bacterial skin infection caused by Corynebacterium minutissimum, a Gram-positive, non-spore-forming rod. It typically affects intertriginous areas such as the groin, axillae, and toe webs. On Wood's lamp examination, the lesions show a coral-red fluorescence due to porphyrin production. Treatment includes topical or oral erythromycin and clindamycin.

Explanation of other options:

Corynebacterium diphtheriae (Option A): Causes diphtheria, producing exotoxin that leads to pseudomembranous pharyngitis, not erythrasma.

Corynebacterium tenuis (Option C): Associated with trichomycosis axillaris (bacterial colonization of axillary hair shafts), not erythrasma.

Diphtheroids (Option D): General term for skin commensal Corynebacterium species, but minutissimum specifically causes erythrasma.

Key Takeaways:

  • Erythrasma = Corynebacterium minutissimum.
  • Characteristic feature: coral-red fluorescence under Wood's lamp.
  • Common in diabetics, obese individuals, and tropical climates.

question_text: A 7-year-old boy presents with progressive non-retractable foreskin and tense, white preputial skin. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Explanation:

The given clinical scenario of progressive phimosis, along with the image showing white preputial skin, suggests a diagnosis of balanitis xerotica obliterans.

  • Balanitis xerotica obliterans (BXO), also known as lichen sclerosus (LS), is a chronic inflammatory condition of the foreskin, possibly autoimmune in origin, that may also extend to the distal urethra.
  • It is rare before five years of age and presents in boys with progressive phimosis, depigmentation and scarring of the prepuce, white indurated skin, dysuria, and ballooning during urination. The condition is characterised by fibrosis of the foreskin and sometimes involvement of the glans, producing white patches.
  • Complications include meatal stenosis and penile urethral strictures, which are often long and challenging to treat and hence continuous follow-up is essential.
  • LS can present in two phases: active and burnt out, with patients frequently showing poor urinary flow.
  • Diagnosis is usually clinical, but a biopsy provides confirmation.
  • Investigations such as uroflowmetry, retrograde urethrogram (RGU), and voiding cystourethrogram (VCUG) aid in assessing urethral involvement.
  • Management typically requires circumcision, although topical corticosteroids may help in some cases.

Explanation of other options:

Recurrent balanoposthitis (Option A): Recurrent balanoposthitis is inflammation of the glans penis and foreskin caused by infection, irritation, or trauma. Symptoms include pain, itching, rash, dysuria, and non-urethral penile discharge. While most boys experience only one or two episodes requiring no treatment, repeated recurrences may warrant circumcision.

Urethral meatus stenosis (Option B): It is a complication of balanitis xerotica obliterans but since the image does not show meatal stenosis.

Paraphimosis (Option C): Paraphimosis occurs when the foreskin is pulled back behind the glans and cannot be moved forward again, leading to swelling and pain of the glans. If manual reduction is unsuccessful, urgent intervention with a dorsal slit or circumcision is required.

explanation:
Explanation:

Grade IV pressure sores involve full-thickness tissue loss with exposure of muscle, bone, or supporting structures, which matches the findings in the image.

  • Pressure sores, also called decubitus ulcers or bedsores, are localized injuries to skin and underlying tissue due to prolonged pressure.
  • The National Pressure Injury Advisory Panel (NPIAP) classifies them into four grades based on severity:
    • Grade I: Non-blanchable erythema with intact skin.
    • Grade II: Partial-thickness skin loss involving epidermis and dermis.
