question_text: Please determine the instrument provided.
explanation:
Explanation:

The instrument shown in the image is a Linear Stapler.

Linear Stapler:

Components:

  • Handle
  • Shaft
  • Anvil
  • Stapling cartridge

Applications:

  • Creating side-to-side anastomoses
  • Closing the ends with a transverse staple
  • Used to close the bowel completely or partially

Explanation of Other Options:

Skin stapler (Option B) is primarily used for closure of superficial skin wounds rather than internal tissue repair. Unlike the linear stapler, it does not facilitate straight-line closures or anastomoses within the bowel. Its application is restricted to the external approximation of skin edges.

Circular stapler, also called EEA stapler (End to End Anastomosis) (Option C), is specifically designed for creating anastomoses in tubular organs such as the intestine or blood vessels. It produces a circular line of staples, allowing the ends of the tube-like structures to be joined together securely. Unlike the linear stapler, which is intended for straight-line closures or side-to-side anastomosis, the circular stapler is not suitable for such applications.

Curved stapler (Option D) is designed for use in difficult-to-access regions, most commonly within the gastrointestinal tract. However, similar to the circular stapler, it is not intended for creating a straight-line closure. That specific function is carried out by a linear stapler.

question_text: A 42-year-old male presents to the outpatient department with a swelling in the back of his neck that has been present for almost a year. The swelling has not increased in size. On examination, it is non-pulsatile, and the slip sign is positive, with the swelling measuring 3x3 cm. Which of the following statements is most likely true?
option_d: Excision can be done if the patient requests it
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The presentation (slow-growing, soft, mobile swelling with positive slip sign) is typical of a lipoma, the most common benign soft tissue tumor.
  • Lipomas are usually asymptomatic and do not require treatment unless:
    • Cosmetic concern
    • Symptomatic (pain, pressure)
    • Rapid increase in size (rare)
  • Excision is curative and can be offered if the patient requests removal.

Lipoma:

  • A lipoma is a benign tumour composed of mature adipocytes (fat cells) and is the most common soft tissue tumor.
  • These tumors are generally soft, mobile, and painless masses found beneath the skin.
  • Most frequently found on the trunk, shoulders, neck, and arms.
  • Histologically, lipomas consist of mature fat cells that are identical to normal adipose tissue but are encapsulated by a thin fibrous capsule, distinguishing them from the surrounding tissue.
  • Lipomas are typically slow-growing, soft, and non-tender.
  • They are usually asymptomatic but can cause discomfort if they compress nearby structures or are located in a site prone to friction or pressure.
  • On physical examination, lipomas are well-circumscribed, mobile masses that can vary in size from a few millimetres to several centimetres.
  • Slip sign: Positive
  • Very low risk of malignant transformation into liposarcoma. (Option A ruled out)

Management:

  • Most lipomas do not require treatment unless they become symptomatic, grow rapidly, or cause cosmetic concerns.
  • Surgical excision is the definitive treatment and is usually curative.
  • Liposuction may also be an option for larger lipomas, but complete excision is preferred to prevent recurrence.

Explanation of other options:

FNAC (Option B) can help in diagnosing soft tissue tumors, it is not mandatory when the lesion shows classic features of a lipoma. In most cases, the diagnosis can be confidently made from the history and clinical examination, such as identifying a soft, mobile, and painless swelling.

PET (Option C) scans are primarily utilized for staging established malignancies like lymphoma or other aggressive cancers. Since this swelling shows no evidence of malignancy, a PET scan is not indicated in this scenario.

question_text: Elderly man with a long-standing mole over the face which is increasing in size and showing irregular borders. Diagnosis:
explanation:
Superficial spreading melanoma (SSM).

  • This is the most common presentation (70%); usually arises in a pre-existing nevus after several years of slow change, followed by rapid growth in the months before presentation .Nodularity within SSM heralds the onset of the vertical growth phase.

Nodular melanoma (NM).

  • NM accounts for 15% of all malignant melanoma and tends to be more aggressive than SSM, with a shorter clinical onset. These lesions often arise de novo in skin and are more common in men than in women, often presenting in middle age and usually on the trunk, head or neck .They typically appear as blue/black papules, 1-2cm in diameter, and because they lack the horizontal growth phase they tend to be sharply demarcated. Up to 5% are amelanotic.

Lentigo maligna melanoma.

  • LMM was previously also known as Hutchinson's melanotic freckle. This variant presents as a slow-growing, variegated brown macule on the face, neck or hands of the elderly .They are positively correlated with prolonged, intense sun exposure and affect women more than men. They account for between 5% and 10% of malignant melanomas. LMMs are thought to have less metastatic potential than other variants as they take longer to enter a vertical growth phase. Nonetheless, when they have entered the vertical growth phase their metastatic potential is the same as any other melanoma.

Acral lentiginous melanoma (ALM).

  • ALM affects the soles and palms. It is rare in white-skinned individuals (2-8% of malignant melanoma) but more common in Afro-Caribbean, Hispanic and Asian populations (35-60%). It usually presents as a fat, irregular macule in later life; 25% are amelanotic and may mimic a fungal infection or pyogenic granuloma.

question_text: What type of graft is used when a patient undergoes skin grafting following a road traffic accident in which the graft is harvested from the patient's own body?
explanation:
Explanation:

A graft taken directly from a patient's own tissues is referred to as an autograft.

Types of Grafts

  • Autograft (Option A):
    • Source: Tissue transferred from one site to another within the same individual.
    • Advantages: No risk of immune rejection; high long-term success.
    • Disadvantages: Requires a donor site, leading to added morbidity.
  • Allograft (Option C ruled out):
    • Source: Tissue obtained from another person of the same species.
    • Advantages: Provides access to larger tissue volumes.
    • Disadvantages: Immune rejection risk; requires immunosuppressive therapy.
  • Xenograft (Option B ruled out):
    • Source: Tissue taken from a different species (e.g., pig to human).
    • Advantages: Easily available; often used as temporary grafts.
    • Disadvantages: High chance of immune rejection; usually not permanent.
  • Isograft (Option D ruled out):
    • Source: Tissue transplanted between genetically identical individuals.
    • Advantages: No immune rejection due to genetic identity.
    • Disadvantages: Very limited availability (only in identical twins).

Subtypes of Xenografts:

  • Concordant Xenograft: Between closely related species (e.g., primate to human).
    • Better immune compatibility, lower chance of hyperacute rejection.
  • Discordant Xenograft: Between distantly related species (e.g., pig to human).
    • Poor compatibility, high likelihood of hyperacute rejection.

Reference:

Classic and Current Opinions in Human Organ and Tissue Transplantation - PMC

question_text: What does the inclusion of a split-thickness skin graft in wound closure on the thigh entail?
option_b: Epidermis and variable part of the dermis
explanation:
Explanation:

A split-thickness skin graft (STSG or Thiersch graft) is defined by its composition: it includes the entire epidermis and a variable portion of the dermis. The thickness can be calibrated (e.g., thin, intermediate, thick) based on how much dermis is harvested. This is in contrast to a full-thickness skin graft, which includes the entire dermis.


Explanation of other options:

Epidermis and full dermis (Option A): This describes a full-thickness skin graft (Wolfe graft), not a split-thickness graft.

Epidermis, dermis and fat (Option C): A graft that includes subcutaneous fat is a composite graft, which is used for specialized reconstructions requiring bulk.

Epidermis only (Option D): A graft consisting solely of epidermis is not practically possible, as the epidermis is avascular and too fragile to harvest and transplant on its own.

Key Takeaways:

  • A split-thickness skin graft includes the epidermis and a variable amount of the underlying dermis.
  • It is the workhorse graft for covering large wounds where primary closure is not possible.

question_text: The image below shows a pressure sore. Which stage does this belong to?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The given image corresponds to a Stage 4 pressure sore, the most advanced type of ulcer.
  • Stage 4 ulcers show extensive tissue damage extending through the skin into deeper structures such as muscle, tendon, and bone.
  • They are associated with a high risk of infection, osteomyelitis, and sepsis if not managed promptly.

Pressure Sore Stages

  • Stage I (Option A ruled out): Non-blanchable erythema of intact skin. No break in the epidermis.
  • Stage II (Option B ruled out): Partial-thickness skin loss involving epidermis and dermis. Presents as a shallow open ulcer or blister.
  • Stage III (Option C ruled out): Full-thickness skin loss with damage to subcutaneous tissue but not extending through underlying fascia.
  • Stage IV: Full-thickness skin loss with exposure of bone, muscle, tendon, or joint. Often accompanied by undermining and tunneling.

Key Takeaway:

Stage 4 pressure ulcers are the most severe form, with deep tissue involvement and high risk of complications, requiring aggressive wound care, debridement, and often surgical intervention.

question_text: Which nerve gives rise to the recurrent laryngeal nerve?
explanation:
Explanation:

  • The recurrent laryngeal nerve (RLN) is a branch of the vagus nerve.
  • The nerve recurs around the arch of the aorta on the left and the subclavian artery on the right.
  • The clinical significance of this is that on the left, the nerve has a longer course to reach the tracheoesophageal groove and therefore runs in a medial plane.
  • On the right, the course is shorter, and the nerve runs more obliquely to reach the tracheoesophageal groove.
  • Approximately 2% of nerves on the right are non-recurrent and will enter the larynx from above.

explanation: When the preoperative diagnosis is considered reasonably certain, the incision that is widely used for appendicectomy is the so-called gridiron incision. question_text: Grade of glioblastoma multiforme:
explanation:
Glioma Overview:

  1. Definition:
    • Intrinsic tumors with glial histology.
    • Subtypes include astrocytomas, oligodendrogliomas, ependymomas, and mixed tumors.
  2. Diagnosis:
    • Tissue diagnosis is essential.
    • Imaging often predicts both glial origin and tumor grade.
  3. Subtypes and Grades:
    • Astrocytomas:Subtype of glioma.
    • Oligodendrogliomas:Subtype of glioma.
    • Ependymomas:Subtype of glioma.
    • Mixed Tumors:Gliomas with mixed histology.
  4. Clinical Presentation:
    • Low-Grade Glioma (WHO Grade II):
      • Peak incidence in the fourth decade.
      • Commonly presents with seizures initially.
    • High-Grade Gliomas:
      • Anaplastic Astrocytoma (WHO Grade III):
        • Intermediate grade.
        • Higher malignancy than low-grade gliomas.
      • Glioblastoma (WHO Grade IV):
        • Most common and aggressive glial tumor.
        • Typically presents de novo.
        • Peak incidence in the fifth and sixth decades.
        • Can also arise by transformation of low-grade tumors.

question_text: A 26 years old male was operated for redness over the perineal area. Post op day 5 image is given below. Which of the following statements is correct about this condition?
option_a: Caused by mixed aerobic anaerobic infection
option_b: Urinary diversion is required in this patient
option_d: Anti-gas gangrene serum should always be considered
explanation:
Fournier's gangrene (necrotising fasciitis)

This is progressive infection of the genitalia and perineum. It is usually caused by mixed bacterial flora(Escherichia coli, Bacteroides spp.,Streptococcus pyogenes, Staphylococcus aureus). It may be associated with diabetes, cancer, malnutrition, recent urogenital or colorectal instrumentation or trauma.

The hallmark is rapid progression from symptoms and signs of cellulitis. There is erythema, swelling, pain and blister formation with ultimately foul-smelling necrotic lesions but the testis and urethra remain unaffected.It is a surgical emergency.Progression from genitalia to perineum to abdominal wall occurs extremely rapidly. There is an increased risk of bacterial septicaemia. It will lead to death if untreated.

Treatment involves a combination of broad-spectrum antibiotics and extensive surgical debridement and hyper basic oxygen therapy
